properties.rationale:
🛑 A DISCIPLINE SLIP, RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXED: this ChangeEvent was written AFTER the code, unlike increments 1-3 where it preceded the edit. The impact-check skill says record first, and the reason is not ceremony — the blast radius is meant to be the work list, and computing it afterwards means it described work already done. Nothing was harmed here because the plan node already carried the scope, but the ordering was wrong and saying so is cheaper than pretending otherwise.

⭐⭐ THE FINDING WORTH MORE THAN THE MIGRATION — absorbing a `#[non_exhaustive]` type converts a RUNTIME FALLBACK into a COMPILE-TIME GUARANTEE. Two wildcard match arms became unreachable: `keys.rs` had `_ => None` and `vocabulary.rs` had `other => "<unsupported endpoint>"`. Both existed ONLY because the enums lived in another crate — `#[non_exhaustive]` has no effect inside the defining crate. `vocabulary.rs`'s own comment said *"a variant added UPSTREAM must not silently read as matches-nothing"*, and after today there IS no upstream. Both arms were removed, so a new `Value` or `EdgeEndpoint` variant is now a build error instead of a string a reader has to notice. **Nothing in the plan predicted this, and it is a genuine improvement rather than a cost.**

🛑 THREE MECHANICAL TRAPS, EACH CHEAP AND EACH INVISIBLE TO THE GATE THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT:
① INTEGRATION TESTS ARE SEPARATE CRATES. The blanket rewrite turned `dynograph_core::Value` into `crate::foundation::core::Value` everywhere — right inside the lib, wrong in `tests/*.rs` where `crate::` is the test binary. 12 files needed `reflow2_core::` instead.
② `props!` IS `#[macro_export]`, so it lives at the CRATE ROOT, not in the module it is written in. `crate::props`, never `crate::foundation::core::props`.
③ **`--no-default-features` CLIPPY DOES NOT COMPILE FEATURE-GATED FILES.** The identical `props!` error sat in `fulltext_tests.rs` behind `#[cfg(feature = "fulltext")]` and passed that gate THREE TIMES, surfacing only when the workspace suite enabled the feature. Same shape as increment 2's `#[cfg(test)]` defect: **a gate trusted for coverage it structurally cannot provide.** CI runs both forms and would have caught it; the local habit of reading the narrow gate as the wide one is the actual defect.

**THE DEPENDENCY IS GONE, VERIFIED THREE WAYS:** `cargo tree -p reflow2-core` and `-p reflow2-mcp` both report zero dynograph crates; `Cargo.lock` holds zero; no manifest names one. The only mention left was a stale crate DESCRIPTION ("...over dynograph-foundation"), now corrected.

The seven external crates that came with it are declared in reflow2's own `[workspace.dependencies]` for the first time: `rocksdb`, `tantivy`, `rmp-serde`, `lru`, `serde_yaml`, `uuid`, `thiserror`, plus `tracing` which nothing had declared. `rocksdb` stays at **0.24 verbatim** per `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately`.

⭐ THIS MODULE IS PUBLIC WHERE THE OTHER THREE ABSORPTIONS ARE NOT. `stats`, `fuzzy` and `graphalg` are `pub(crate)` on the ground that `ifc:core-api` records 277 public functions growing by default. That argument does not reach here: `lib.rs` already re-exported `DynoError`, `Schema`, `Value`, `StoredNode` and `StoredEdge`, and `reflow2-mcp` names `DynoError` 35 times and `StoredNode` 21 times. Making them private would be a breaking change dressed as tidiness.

properties.name: Increment 3 of the absorption — the graph algorithms come in-tree, and this is the first increment carrying real intellectual content
properties.rationale:
This is the first increment where the plan's own warning applies. Increments 1 and 2 were self-contained arithmetic with no external crates and one or two call sites; this carries a Leiden community-detection implementation, a DFS lowlink cut walk, and Tarjan SCC — the code you would least want to reimplement, which under ABSORPTION inverts into the argument FOR: difficulty-to-rewrite stops being a cost and becomes the reason the code is worth owning.

⭐ THE CLOSURE WAS COMPUTED, NOT ESTIMATED, and the method matters because the first attempt at it was wrong. An earlier pass grepped `crate::[a-z_]+` and missed `use crate::{a, b}` forms, and separately truncated the crate's file list at 12 — so it reported 7 unneeded files when there are 11, and 3,832 lines split differently. Re-run over every file with both import shapes, the split is 1,844 needed / 1,988 dropped. **A closure measured with a pattern that cannot see one of the two syntaxes is not a closure.**

🛑 THE CONDITION FROM `dec:absorbed-code-is-distributed-by-function` APPLIES HERE FOR THE FIRST TIME: absorbing behaviour that was modelled as a `required` interface deletes the framing that explained why reflow2 had no requirement for it. `ifc:req-dyno-graph-api` says "reflow2 NEEDS graph algorithms from outside"; once they are in-tree, nothing says why reflow2 detects communities with Leiden. Anthony stated the reason himself on 2026-08-17 — *"I wanted graph theory to undergird everything ... graph theory was important to my concept of reflow2"* — and it has never been written as a requirement. It is captured now, at `proposed`, because a requirement is his word and not session residue.

TAKEN, 1,844 lines in 8 files, verified as the transitive closure rather than guessed: `error.rs` (62), `graph.rs` (334), `components.rs` (134), `scc.rs` (169), `cycles.rs` (154), `cuts.rs` (223), `communities.rs` (695), `lib.rs` (73).

NOT TAKEN, 1,988 lines in 11 files — **51% of the crate**: betweenness, centrality, closeness, clustering, eigenvector, link_prediction, maxflow, pagerank, paths, shortest_path, toposort. reflow2 calls none of them.

⭐ `cuts.rs` DOES NOT NEED `maxflow.rs`, which is the one result worth checking rather than assuming: articulation points and bridges are computed by a DFS lowlink walk, not by a min-cut, so `max_flow_min_cut` (248 lines) stays behind. A closure taken on the intuition that "cuts need flow" would have dragged it in.

The absorbed code lands in a NEW component `cmp:graph-algorithms`, under `sys:foundation` — Anthony's name, chosen because reflow2 already has a `cmp:graph` for its own graph module and the two are different things. That collision was found before the code moved, not during.

⭐ THE PROVENANCE RULE HOLDS: repo, tag, commit, file, what was taken and what was deliberately left, in a header on the absorbed code. The recorded objection to absorbing is that vendoring turns a visible dependency into an invisible one, and the pin's written history has no successor once the code is in-tree; the header is that successor.

⚠️ WHAT TO WATCH ON THE NEXT ONE: increments 1 and 2 were both self-contained arithmetic with no external crates and one or two call sites. Increment 3 (graph algorithms, 1,844 lines, a Leiden implementation) is the first that carries real intellectual content, and increments 4 and 5 carry 62 files of churn and a RocksDB engine. **Nothing learned from these two should be read as evidence that the rest are easy.**

The recorded objection to absorbing is that vendoring converts a visible dependency into an invisible one: the pin at `reflow2.toml` carries a written reason for every bump, and once code is in-tree that record has no successor. So every increment names the exact TAG and the exact FILES, in the ChangeEvent and in a header on the absorbed code itself. A later reader must be able to find what this came from.

MEASURED on reflow2's own graph: 125 review records carrying 610 edges; four of the eight most central nodes were acknowledgements and are now none, with real components rising (rel:v0170 +75%, cmp:detect +41%); and surprising_connections went 16 to 32 — the bookkeeping edges were SUPPRESSING half the real surprises by tying communities together, which is the opposite of the predicted pollution.

properties.rationale:
⭐ THE CHANGE IS ONE BULLET AND THE EVIDENCE FOR IT TOOK A DAY. The flatness had already been measured across seven designs and read TWICE as a fact about users — first as "real designs are two rungs deep so nobody needs depth", then as "the sample is contaminated so nothing can be concluded". Both readings were wrong in the same direction: they treated an instruction's absence as evidence about the world. Anthony's framing is what turned it — *"the hierarchy is there"* — and a trial run on reflow2 itself produced the counterfactual in one pass.

🛑 WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: no code changed. `contain_component`, `level` and `hierarchy_issues` all already existed and all already worked; the only thing missing was an instruction to use them. A defect whose fix is a paragraph is worth naming as such, because the temptation on finding a gap this size is to build something.

⚠️ AND THE STEP DOES NOT MAKE DEPTH A TARGET. It says recover what is there and say so when there is nothing. `dec:idea-breadth-and-depth-are-measured-and-the-balance-is-asked-about` records Anthony's own counter-argument — prefer-composition-over-inheritance, deep hierarchies are rigid — and it stands. Today's trial shows depth is RECOVERABLE and that the recovered shape passes span of control; it does not show depth is better, and those are different claims.

📌 THE SYMMETRY IS STILL BROKEN AT THE OTHER END. adopt now recovers the structure an artifact HAS. genesis correctly DEFERS the structure a design NEEDS and nothing derives it — `propose_allocation` exists, is served, and appears in no skill. `dec:idea-does-the-deferred-structuring-step-need-a-skill-of-its-own` holds that question with five options and no answer.

The bullet carries its own evidence: every design adopt had ever produced came out FLAT — dev_storyflow 101 components with zero containing another, mapwright 15 with zero, music_graph 25 with two — because the instructions never once said to nest. Re-run on reflow2 itself with only this step added, the same artifact yielded four rungs, `hierarchy_issues` 0, and no parent over the 3–7 span-of-control bound, while the hand-built functional design of the same system exceeds it in four places.

It also states two limits so the step is not mistaken for the whole job: FLAT IS AN HONEST ANSWER when the artifact is flat, and nesting cannot recover the FUNCTIONAL carving — measured twice on reflow2 (86 core modules loose in one directory; a star-shaped import graph with three hubs at fan-in 49/42/41 and 45% of modules importing only those). properties.summary:
Implements `dec:should-a-realizes-edge-say-that-nobody-checked-the-file-still-obeys-the-rule`, option (b), settled on Anthony's word 2026-08-16.

WHAT CHANGED. `REALIZES` gains `conformance: unchecked | reviewed | verified`, defaulting to `unchecked` (`schema/build.yaml`). `realizes()` and `link_artifact` take it; `ArtifactLink` returns what was stored. `DesignGraph::conformance_tally()` counts every realizing link by bucket and names up to ten unchecked ones, and `evidence_report` carries the tally so the number is reachable from the served surface.

⭐ THE MEASURED ANSWER ON REFLOW2'S OWN DESIGN, taken end-to-end through a restarted server: 223 REALIZING LINKS, 223 UNCHECKED, 0 reviewed, 0 verified, 0 unrecognised. That sentence could not be produced at all before this change, and it is the entire deliverable — not the ceremony of setting a field, but the count that makes the silence visible.

WHY IT EXISTS, and the evidence came from OUTSIDE the project: a Requirement said the calendar day is the person's CIVIL date; the code used UTC; the Capability said `realized`; the artifact's checksum matched so `reconcile_artifacts` was silent. Every signal in the graph was green and A USER FOUND THE BUG IN THE PRODUCT. Nothing distinguished a file CHECKED AGAINST THE RULE from a file MERELY HASHED, and the two produced identical reports. Alex's Grok session, 2026-08-14, item 5.

WHY IT IS NOT A DETECTOR: reflow2 reads a DESIGN, never a running system, and judging whether code implements a civil-date rule is program analysis it deliberately stays out of (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). This RECORDS what a person knows; it computes nothing about code.

⭐ WHY (b) BEAT (a), documenting the hole — and this is the general principle rather than a preference: A DOCUMENTED HOLE IS SOMETHING A READER MUST REMEMBER; A DEFAULT OF `unchecked` IS SOMETHING THE GRAPH SAYS OUT LOUD EVERY TIME, WITH NOBODY REMEMBERING ANYTHING. The same move landed twice already this month and was right both times: #200 stopped INJECTING a default nobody chose, #213 started REPORTING the property nobody declared.

WHERE THE READER LIVES, and both alternatives were rejected for stated reasons. NOT `coverage_report`: it requires a caller-supplied file sweep, and making somebody sweep a tree to learn that nobody has checked anything puts a cost in front of the one number that should be free. NOT `loop_status`: every edge starts `unchecked`, so a large figure that never moves is exactly the signal-trained-to-be-ignored failure `req:the-loop-can-say-what-this-session-owes` was built to end — hours earlier, in this same session. `evidence_report` takes no arguments, is read on demand rather than nagged, and already speaks in this idiom.

DELIBERATE SHAPE:
- `conformance` DOES NOT FOLLOW `completeness` INTO OPTIMISM. `completeness` defaults to `complete`; conformance defaults to `unchecked`, because registering a file says it exists and never that anyone checked it.
- THE SAMPLE IS CAPPED AT TEN AND THE COUNT IS NOT. A truncated list that also truncated the count would under-report the problem, the one direction this must never fail in.
- A MISSING VALUE COUNTS AS `unchecked`, never as a separate unknown bucket — otherwise the number that matters shrinks for a reason that is not progress.
- AN UNRECOGNISED VALUE IS NAMED, not folded into a bucket: silently counting it as checked would be the flattering reading of an unreadable one.

⚠️ WHAT MUTATION TESTING TAUGHT, and it changed what could be tested. Mutating the fallback to report a missing conformance as `verified` killed only ONE case, which was suspicious — and the reason is that the schema `default:` MATERIALISES the property at write time. A probe confirmed it: a freshly written edge stores `conformance: "unchecked"` explicitly. So the in-code fallback covers ONLY edges written before the property existed, and that shape CANNOT be constructed through the API, because a property once written cannot be removed (`fact:defect-a-property-once-written-cannot-be-removed`, found earlier the same day). It is therefore proven against the real graph rather than in a unit test — all 223 links predate the property and all 223 report `unchecked`.

VERIFIED. 11 cases, all passing. Three mutations, each killing the right case: capping the count as well as the sample; defaulting link_artifact to optimism; and the fallback mutation above, whose partial kill was itself the finding. Two counterweights pin the distinction that defines the feature — a COMPLETE artifact is still unchecked, and a MATCHING CHECKSUM is still unchecked, which is precisely the shipped-bug case: complete, hashed, green, wrong.

NO SCHEMA STAMP MOVEMENT: an edge PROPERTY is not counted by the version stamp — 29 node types, 61 edge types, unchanged — so no upgrade document is owed.

NOT DONE, named rather than left to be discovered. Nothing MOVES an edge off `unchecked` except a caller saying so, and nothing forces that; the honest claim is that the silence is now countable, not that it will be broken. Option (d), raising unchecked links as a gap, is deliberately deferred — 223 gaps on day one is noise, and it costs almost nothing later because the data now exists. And the 223 are not triaged here; this change measures them, it does not fix them.

properties.description:
MEASURED, not argued, on music_graph's real committed export (327 nodes / 939 edges, store built under 0.20.0, both fields added later in v0.24.0 and never backfilled).

THE DEFECT: `default:` in the schema YAML is executed by dynograph-core at WRITE time (schema.rs:507 inserts any missing property that declares one), so importing an export MATERIALISED `granularity: atomic` and `volatility: stable` onto every Artifact the document honestly said nothing about. Their restore, walking the run-book's own §0b procedure on a fresh clone with no design work at all: `--diff` of the imported file against the store it had just built reported design_changed 35 of 35 Artifacts, edges_changed 0, content hash d10d80da -> cef7db52, and the pre-commit hook blocked a commit on a machine where nobody had designed anything.

MEASURED HERE, BOTH DIRECTIONS, through import -> re-export on their real file: as shipped, 35 nodes came back different, gaining exactly Artifact.granularity and Artifact.volatility; with the two `default:` tokens removed, 0 nodes changed and nothing was invented. The real gate agrees — `reflow2_check.py` against their export went from 5 findings including ROUND TRIP to 4, the remaining four being their own genuine artifact drift, which they can fix honestly.

⭐ WHY THIS ROUTE AND NOT THE THREE THEY PROPOSED. The reader ALREADY supplies the safe reading: coverage.rs:209 `.unwrap_or("atomic")` and drift.rs:436 `.unwrap_or("stable")`. So the schema default was redundant with the code — it changed no report's verdict and bought nothing, while costing the round trip. Their (a) backfill-on-import writes values nobody chose into every consumer store permanently; their (b) exclude-defaults-from-the-hash is the route cap:defaults-are-not-serialized argues CANNOT work, because absence would come to mean "nobody said OR somebody chose the default", and it would weaken the hash for the 71 properties that legitimately keep defaults; their (c) print-what-was-defaulted leaves the gate red and the restore broken and only explains it. Anthony chose the fourth.

⚠️ THIS REVERSES A DELIBERATE BL-198 KEEP, on his word, and the earlier reasoning was not wrong: `stable` IS the safe reading. What changed is the measurement that the safe reading already lives in the reader. tests/schema_defaults.rs asserted `schema_default("Artifact","granularity") == Some("atomic")`; it now asserts None, and the declared-defaults floor moves 71 -> 69.

FORWARD-ONLY, so nothing already written moves: reflow2's own Artifacts keep the values they hold, its export does not churn, and its own round trip stays clean (verified — no ROUND TRIP finding on docs/design/reflow2.json). music_graph's store has no values to keep, which is exactly why their case comes out clean.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and stated rather than discovered later: how many other consumer designs predate v0.24.0; whether any OTHER node type carries the same unbackfilled shape (the same defect would be invisible until someone restores); and F24, the latent-surface-never-re-probes finding, sits on the same restore path and is NOT addressed here.

BL-159: the two records of the build-gate contract are now cross-checked by the build. AGENTS.md's "A change is done when all of these are clean" block and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` were two hand-kept records of one contract, and following the documented one exactly still produced a red build (PR #27). `skill_lint.py` now fails if a `cargo`/`python3` gate in ci.yml appears in NEITHER the block nor the blockquote that names deliberate omissions, if a listed command is spelled differently from the way CI runs it, or if either list names a gate CI has stopped running. FOUR CHECKS RATHER THAN THE ROW'S ONE, and the extra one is the load-bearing one: the row proposed COVERAGE only, but the defect that filed BL-159 was a FLAGS difference on a gate that WAS listed (`-p reflow2-core` clippy lacking `-D warnings`), which coverage alone cannot see — so identity and fidelity are checked separately. THE SPLIT THAT KEEPS IT HONEST is BL-160's threshold lesson again: the lint OBSERVES (is this ci.yml line a gate at all — mechanical, in code), the document JUDGES (does it belong in the everyday local subset — in AGENTS.md, where a human reads it). FOUND ON DAY ONE, which is the payoff: `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` and `test_check_doc_versions` were in ci.yml and in neither list. The second is the trap the design anticipated — `check_doc_versions` is a substring of `test_check_doc_versions`, so a substring match would have reported the second as already covered; matching is exact on the script stem. THE CHECK CAUGHT A DEFECT IN ITSELF on its own commit: scanning the whole blockquote read the backticked words `cargo` and `python3` out of the new paragraph describing the lint and reported them as gates CI had stopped running. REPORTED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: reverting the first-paragraph scoping ALONE leaves every check green, because the runner-word exclusion covers today's prose — the two are not redundant in general, and the scoping is pinned on synthetic text where the redundancy cannot hide it.

BL-160: a registered checksum's LENGTH is a dialect too, and the compensation lived in the wrong layer. reflow2's own designs register `hexdigest()[:16]` (build_design_graph.py) while an honest caller running `sha256sum` supplies all 64, and `reconcile_artifacts` compared STRINGS — so a full sweep of a provably clean tree reported 51 phantom drifts in the same minute `reflow2_check.py` said "OK — design and build agree". The gate was right for the wrong reason: it carried a Python workaround truncating the observation to the registered length, which no other consumer had. This is BL-125 in a second form and takes the same verdict — a false red on a gate whose whole job is to be believed is worse than no gate. `artifact::checksums_agree` now answers it in the core for every consumer, on BOTH the drift comparison and `set_artifact_checksum`'s would-move-the-baseline guard (the half that would have failed a BL-157 bulk sweep on every short-registered artifact), and the Python workaround is DELETED rather than duplicated by the next consumer. Required is a real PREFIX relationship, never truncate-both-to-N, and it applies to the `sha256:` dialect only. properties.rationale:
⭐ THE PLAN'S OWN SELLING POINT IS WHAT FAILED, AND THAT IS WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY DONE. "Stop after any of" was the argument for the ordering — it is what made the plan safe to approve, and it is repeated in three PR bodies. A reader who takes it at face value at increment 4 will start a step they cannot finish or ship.

🛑 HOW IT WAS MISSED WHEN THE PLAN WAS COSTED. The scoping measured each crate's SIZE and each crate's IMPORT COUNT, and it measured the dependency direction between crates (storage depends on core, which is why core was ordered first). What it never asked is whether the two share TYPES ACROSS THE BOUNDARY — a re-export is invisible to a line count and to a dependency arrow alike. **A dependency graph tells you what needs what to build; it does not tell you what breaks if you take one and not the other.**

⭐ AND IT WAS FOUND BY SCOUTING BEFORE WRITING CODE, which is the only reason it cost nothing. The increment-4 scout ran the multiline-aware import scan — the one whose absence caused the increment-3 error — and it surfaced two sites importing `Value` through `dynograph_storage` rather than `dynograph_core`. Two files out of eighty-six. **The signal was two lines wide and it invalidated a five-step plan.**

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: increments 1-3 shipped and are genuinely independent; three of six crates are gone and no new external crate entered the tree. The stopping point the plan named after increment 3 is real and was reached.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary:
`dec:absorb-the-foundation-subset-and-end-the-dependency` promises "five increments, each independently shippable, stop after any of". **That is true for 1, 2 and 3 and FALSE for 4 and 5.** They are one increment, and the plan is corrected to say so.

MEASURED, not reasoned: `dynograph-storage/src/lib.rs:32` re-exports `pub use dynograph_core::{DynoError, Schema, Value}`, and `StoredNode.properties` is `HashMap<String, Value>` of that same type. So absorbing `dynograph-core` while `dynograph-storage` remains an external dependency gives reflow2 TWO distinct types called `Value` and TWO called `DynoError` — the in-tree ones, and the ones every `StorageEngine` call keeps returning. 48 reflow2 files name `DynoError`, 33 name `Value`. Nothing would compile.

NO ORDERING AVOIDS IT. Storage cannot go first: it DEPENDS ON core. Keeping the absorbed core unused until storage lands is not absorbing anything. The only honest options were to merge the two or to stop after increment 3.

properties.rationale:
⭐ THE MECHANISM PROVED ITSELF BY BEING WRONG, TWICE, AND THAT IS THE RECORD WORTH KEEPING.

FIRST, THE CLASS WAS MISCAST. Charging all 18 writers with "search before creating" produced 11 failures — but `genesis` runs on an EMPTY GRAPH by definition, `impact-check` records a ChangeEvent which is new by nature, and `parallel-work` records a claim. Those were not omissions; the class was too coarse. Splitting MINTS out of WRITES cut the list to 14, every one real. **The refinement came from RUNNING it, not from thinking harder before writing it** — which is the argument for construction over inspection, arriving from inside the thing being built.

SECOND, THE OBLIGATIONS WERE LITERAL PHRASES and 13 of the 29 first-run failures were matching artifacts rather than deficiencies. `OPTIMIZE_CONTRACT`'s own comment had predicted exactly this and the warning was in the file being edited. The trap then bit a THIRD time during the fix: new `impact-check` text wrapped "could not\nestablish" across a newline and failed for the documented reason. The line was reflowed; the check was not weakened. The governing rule is now written beside the classes — ADDING A PHRASING FOR THE SAME OBLIGATION IS LEGITIMATE, REMOVING THE OBLIGATION IS NOT.

⭐ WHAT IT FOUND, which is the payoff Anthony asked for: EIGHT skills that mint concept nodes never said to search first — a mechanic `capture-intent` and `brainstorm` both carry. Nobody had noticed because until now nothing could ask a per-class question. That is "a successful skill does something the others do not", surfaced automatically rather than discovered by accident.

📌 AND THE SECOND REASON IS CREDIBILITY, NOT MAINTENANCE. Anthony: *"having reflow2 reflect all the principles it says it will do for other projects is not necessarily a functional win, but it is a 'marketing' win in terms that reflow2 'looks the part'."* It is stronger than that: `dec:mosa-conformance` asks whether reflow2 should report MOSA conformance for other people's designs, and its own skill surface would have failed the severability criterion — three contracts that cannot be composed, applied selectively, or replaced independently.

BL-198 step 1 landed by REMOVING `default:` from ten properties, not by changing code. The route changed on a measurement: `default:` in the schema YAML is not documentation — dynograph-core applies it at WRITE time (schema.rs:507 inserts any missing property that declares one), which is where 3,207 stored values across 59% of the design came from. So export-side suppression could never have worked — the store cannot tell a chosen value from an injected one — and the real fix is one YAML token per property. FORWARD-ONLY: nodes already written keep what they hold, so the export does not churn and compare_designs sees nothing; the phantom-diff cost this epoch was scoped around does not arise on this route at all. TEN of 81 removed, 71 kept, and the RATIO is the finding: three mechanically-obvious candidates turned out to be meaningful and were kept on evidence.
acknowledge_defect can record whose judgement it was, and a gate keeps the family aligned
properties.rationale:
ROOT-CAUSED 2026-08-29 with the `root-cause` skill, from three CI failures on PR #366 against the ENFORCED `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word`.

THE CAUSE IS NOT THIS TOOL. `cap:an-acknowledgement-says-whose-judgement-it-was` was built 2026-08-23 and reached `acknowledge_gap` and `acknowledge_gaps` only; the sibling was left behind.

    acknowledge_gap(s)   HAS the param    168 acknowledgements,  51 attributed
    acknowledge_defect   NO param          12 acknowledgements,   0 attributed

🛑 THE ZERO IS STRUCTURAL, NOT NEGLIGENCE — there was no field to fill, so the tool could not attribute even when the caller wanted to, while `heal.rs` asserted in a comment that "the user just settled it".

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT THAT KILLED THE COMFORTABLE READING: 51 of 168 looked like a 30% compliance rate and an argument that callers skip the field. Every one of those 51 approver edges is dated 2026-08-23 or 2026-08-24 — the day the parameter shipped and the day after — so the 117 without one are pre-fix history and there is NO evidence the parameter is skipped when it exists. That is what makes its ABSENCE the cause rather than caller behaviour.

Two other candidates were refuted rather than dropped: that something else minted these ids (`heal.rs:164` does), and that the gate's scope is wrong because `ver:acknowledgement-not-structure` excludes `decision:ack:` from the design network (the capability text explicitly says an absent approver "will be reported by check_intent_authority", so the design intends the gate to cover acknowledgements).

⭐⭐ IT PINS THE CLASS, NOT THE INSTANCE. Adding a parameter to one tool fixes twelve nodes and nothing about the next capability that lands on one sibling and not the others. What was maintained by hand with nothing checking it was the FAMILY. The invariant was observed failing against the pre-fix surface: it names `acknowledge_defect` and passes the two siblings that were already correct.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: why `acknowledge_defect` was missed on 2026-08-23 — overlooked or deliberately deferred. Nothing in the code or the graph says, and guessing would put a false cause in the record. Also open: whether the 117 unattributed historical acknowledgements should be backfilled or left as honest history.

The brainstorm skill connects the dots
properties.rationale:
Anthony gave his word 2026-08-21 on the first of the two halves he named: "the brainstorm skill is the perfect place to start linking ideas. it is like when a person starts 'connecting the dots'."

MEASURED BEFORE BUILDING: 145 brainstormed ideas joined by 12 edges; 111 of them reached no other idea within two hops; the most common edge on an idea was its author.

THE MISSING LEG WAS THE INSTRUCTION, NOT THE TOOL. The connective vocabulary had existed the whole time - twelve wildcard relation types in the inference layer (CONTRADICTS, EVOLVES_INTO, DEPENDS_ON, CAUSES, BLOCKS, DUPLICATES, ANTICIPATES, OBSOLETES, RISKS, MITIGATES, TRIGGERS, VIOLATES), used 81 times across the graph and 29 times between two Decisions - and the brainstorm skill named none of them.

THE SKILL IS THE RIGHT HOME FOR ONE REASON THAT OUTWEIGHS THE OTHERS: the near-matches are already in hand at capture. The skill already requires a search before writing, and the dedup guard already returns the nodes it judged close. That list was read to avoid a duplicate and then discarded, every single time. Linking there costs one judgement, not a pass.

THE STEP TAKES THE THIRD SHAPE rather than either extreme. Merely offering candidates depends on the agent choosing well, which is the status quo that produced 12 edges across 145 ideas. Requiring an edge manufactures relations to satisfy an instruction, and a false neighbour is worse than a missing one because anything that searches by neighbourhood repeats it. So the step asks for the honest edges AND for a written line when none is drawn - the same shape distinct_from already uses on the dedup guard, and the only one of the three that leaves a record of the judgement either way.

DOGFOODED on the idea that produced it, which now carries three edges drawn under the new step.

STILL MISSING: the third leg. Nothing yet notices an idea that names no relation and no line. That detector is what would make this hold across sessions rather than depending on each agent reading the skill.
properties.summary: The brainstorm skill now links each new idea to the ones it actually relates to, and records an explicit line when no relation is honest.

properties.name: The open ladder is built; reflow2 declares a `part` rung and the backends nest where they live
properties.rationale:
⭐ THE COMPILER CAUGHT WHAT REVIEW WOULD HAVE MISSED. Adding the `UnknownLevel` variant broke three exhaustive matches in `detect.rs` — source, severity and title. That is the `#[non_exhaustive]` finding from the absorption paying off: the enum is reflow2's own now, so a new variant is a BUILD ERROR rather than a wildcard arm silently swallowing it.

⭐ THE FIRST MODELLING ATTEMPT WAS WRONG AND THE CHECK CAUGHT IT, twice over. Nesting the implementations inside `cmp:byte-store` under the CLOSED ladder gave two `level_mismatch` findings, which is what exposed the floor in the first place; and promoting `byte-store` to `subsystem` would only have pushed the mismatch up into `sys:foundation`. The fix was not a workaround but the feature.

🛑 AND IT SURFACED A REAL DEFECT IN A DIFFERENT COMPONENT, fixed in the same change. `add_component`'s required-field resolver looked its fallback up by STORED PROPERTY NAME and asked for `description` — but a Component stores that text as `purpose`. So the lookup always missed on an existing Component and **EVERY REVISE OF A COMPONENT WAS REFUSED with "no such node exists yet to take it from"**, about a node sitting right there. Found by trying to set `level` on `cmp:rocksdb-backend`; the node came straight back from `get_node` a moment later, which is what made the error's confidence visible as wrong. `Capability` is unaffected because it really does store `description` — which is why the bug survived and why a test covering only Capability would have stayed green. Regression test added that asserts the premise itself: a Component has `purpose` and has no `description`.

⚠️ WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: `Component.level` is now a plain string, so the schema no longer rejects a typo at write time. That validation moves from the schema to `hierarchy_issues`, which REPORTS rather than refuses. This is the report-don't-judge posture and it is a real trade — a bad level now lands in the graph and is surfaced, instead of being blocked. `seam_coverage`'s `altitude` argument already takes a level string and was left alone; it compares names and never ranks, so an open ladder does not change it.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
Implements `dec:the-decomposition-ladder-is-open-not-a-fixed-enum`.

`Component.level` was a closed enum with `component` at rank 0 — a hard FLOOR, so a part of a component could not be expressed at all. It is now a plain string naming a rung on THIS design's ladder, declared as `Project.decomposition_levels` (a `list:string`, ordered bottom-first). Absent means the built-in `DEFAULT_RUNGS` — the same five names in the same order — so nothing that predates this moves and no data migrates.

`hierarchy.rs::Level` (an enum with a `rank()` match arm) becomes `Ladder`, a struct over the declared rungs. **`Ladder::rank()` returns `None` for a name that is not on the ladder — never `Some(0)`.** The old `Level::from_key` mapped anything unrecognised to `Component`, so a typo silently became the finest rung and every containment above it read as a mismatch nobody could explain. That silent fallback is gone, and the ordering now has exactly ONE home instead of being declared in both the YAML and the Rust.

New finding `unknown_level` replaces the validation the enum used to give: an off-ladder level is reported BY NAME, and every level-arithmetic check skips that component rather than ranking it. It surfaces as a gap at severity 0.55.

DEMONSTRATED ON THIS DESIGN, end to end through the MCP surface: `proj:reflow2` now declares `[part, component, subsystem, system, system_of_systems, enterprise]`, and `cmp:rocksdb-backend` / `cmp:memory-backend` moved from `sys:foundation` to `cmp:byte-store` at the new `part` rung — where they actually live, in one file. `move_component` returned `level_note: null` (exactly one rung apart) and `hierarchy_issues` is 0 across the whole design.

Six new hierarchy tests, including a four-deep non-software ladder (organelle ▸ cell ▸ tissue ▸ organ ▸ organism) that nests cleanly and still catches a skipped rung — proving rank comes from POSITION, not from any name reflow2 knows.

Core 1,458 / 0 (was 1,452), workspace 1,766 / 0 (was 1,760).

DEFECT, found and fixed 2026-08-12: tools/export_via_binary.py MATERIALIZED 182 property values nobody chose, and shipped them in a release. It imports the source document into a FRESH temp graph, and import runs every node through schema validation, which INSERTS any declared property the node omits (dynograph schema.rs). So 91 Artifacts that honestly carried no `granularity`/`volatility` came back out asserting `atomic`/`stable`. Measured across the record: 81 of 172 artifacts carried granularity through PR #155 (exported via the live server), then 172 of 172 in v0.28.0 and PR #157, both exported through this tool. THIS IS fact:bl-198's DEFECT REINTRODUCED BY THE TOOL BUILT TO FIX THE STAMP, and its cost arrived exactly as BL-198 predicted: compare_designs against the live graph reported 91 phantom changes, the same instrument that has twice produced a false data-loss claim here. NOTHING WAS LOST — the live store was always correct; the RECORD over-asserted. AND THE TOOL CANNOT REPAIR ITS OWN DAMAGE: after the round trip nothing can tell an injected value from a chosen one, which is BL-198's whole point. So the fix is two-part. (1) The record is re-exported DIRECTLY from the real store with the new binary, which gives the correct stamp AND changes no property — the temp graph was only ever needed because the running server held the lock, so freeing the lock removes the need for the round trip entirely. (2) The tool now DIFFS what it wrote against its source and reports every (node_type, property) it materialized, refusing to be silent about it; it cannot undo the injection, so it names it and tells the caller to export directly instead.

properties.rationale:
THE RESOLUTION TURNED ON A DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING: a detector reporting absence of a RECORD is not the same as absence of a CHECK, and the two want opposite responses. Writing a new test to satisfy a recording gap would be the tail wagging the dog; recording a check that does not exist would be the forgery the gap exists to prevent. Measuring first is what told them apart — 47 passing cases and three verified consumers.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLOSE, and `covers: partial` is the mechanism that says so rather than a caveat in prose nobody reads. The tests are UPSTREAM's, absorbed with the code, and verify the algorithms in isolation. The capability claims something stronger — that reflow2 owns this theory — and three things remain unchecked: that the absorption preserved behaviour (`cap:certify-restructuring` was never run against it), that `paths.rs`/`error.rs` do anything (0 tests, and `paths` has no reflow2 call site at all), and that reflow2's own eight consumed entry points give right answers on design-shaped graphs.

properties.name: The two missing legs — the edge that had never once been drawn now gets asked for
properties.rationale:
🛑 THE MEASUREMENT THAT REFRAMED THE WORK: `INVALIDATES` shipped in #321 WITH its reader, deliberately, so the marker would not become a comment nobody consults — and a day later, tool served the whole time, **zero edges had ever been drawn.** The open question was never "which of six mechanisms": five were ways to make the sixth get used, and the sixth already existed.

⭐⭐ THE GENERAL LESSON, bigger than this feature: a vocabulary reaches real work only with THREE LEGS — a typed TOOL, an INSTRUCTION that names it, and a COMPUTATION THAT NOTICES ITS ABSENCE. #321 built the first and wired the READ side into one skill. Nothing told anyone to WRITE one, and nothing noticed that none existed. **A vocabulary can be reachable, documented, wired to a reader, and still dead — and nothing in the loop reports a zero-use edge.**

⚠️ AND A NUMBER IN THIS WORK WAS WRONG IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT. The "median shortlist is 1, 78% silent" figure that justified the session-scoped design was measured against an EDGE-ONLY reader — 56% of observations. Reading `subject_id` too raised reach to 97% and necessarily lengthened the lists; honest figures are 71% silent, median 1, mean 4.3, p90 13, max 40. **A measurement taken against a narrower implementation than the one that shipped is not evidence about the one that shipped**, and the first draft of the computation would have answered barely half the question while looking exactly like one that answered all of it.

properties.rationale:
FOUND BY A BRAINSTORM, NOT BY A DETECTOR, AND THAT IS THE LESSON. Anthony asked whether markdown handoffs could be replaced by the graph, reaching the conclusion from TRANSPORTABILITY — the note lives on one laptop and he has two machines. Looking for prior art surfaced his own accepted decision saying the same thing from STALENESS, and the hook contradicting both.

Nothing in reflow2 could have caught this: the design has no way to notice that a repository file enforces a practice a Decision forbids. `dec:idea-should-reflow2-carry-its-own-git-discipline` already records the general shape — the enforcement is automated while the TRACKING of enforcement is manual, so a check and the rule it serves are joined by nothing.

WHAT MAKES THE RETIREMENT SAFE RATHER THAN LOSSY: the durable half of every handoff note is already a `TemporalFact` and the design already carries dozens of them. The transient half was always a retelling of what `loop_status` and the forge compute.

⚠️ THE REGRESSION, STATED: this trades an enforced-but-wrong mechanism for a correct-but-unenforced one. Nothing now blocks a session from ending without recording what it learned, and tonight showed enforcement works where reading does not — four DesignRules broken by an agent holding all nineteen, and the only one that held was the one that stopped the build.

properties.name: The handshake writes down who connected and what they agreed to speak
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word 2026-08-28, choosing this over asking the reporter to wrap his MCP command with a tee script.

⭐ THE DESIGN CONSTRAINT IS THE WHOLE POINT: THE ANSWER MUST BE READABLE WHEN THE PROTOCOL IS NOT WORKING. This exists because of `fact:the-signpost-instructs-a-party-that-cannot-act-and-the-absent-client-was-named` — a client that reads only `content` gets a stub from every structured tool, so the question "why can I not read anything?" CANNOT be answered through a tool reply. It has to reach disk. That is why this is a sidecar and not a field on `graph_report.served_by`, which is exactly the reply such a client cannot read.

WHY IT ANSWERS THE RIGHT QUESTION. `structuredContent` arrived in MCP `2025-06-18`, and rmcp still negotiates `2024-11-05` and `2025-03-26`. If a reporting client requested a revision that PREDATES the field, version-gating is the spec-sanctioned fix. If it requested a modern one and still reads only `content`, that is a conformance gap and version-gating would do nothing. Those need different remedies and nothing could tell them apart.

⚠️ IT RECORDS WHAT THE REVISION CONTAINS, NEVER WHAT THE CLIENT READS. The derived field is named `protocol_has_structured_content`, not `supports_structured_content`, and carries a note saying so. The distinction is the entire subject of this investigation: a negotiated version is what a client CLAIMS to speak, not proof of what it implemented. A flattering name here would be the same overreach `fact:a-findings-name-can-claim-more-than-its-data-...` describes, committed while fixing its cousin.

⚠️ THE COUPLING THIS ACCEPTS, NAMED BEFORE IT IS TAKEN. `negotiate_protocol_version` is `pub(crate)` in rmcp, so overriding `initialize` means MIRRORING a four-line rule this crate cannot call: echo the client's version if `supported_protocol_versions()` contains it, else the server's fallback. A test pins the rule, following the precedent set by the test that pins which version `ProtocolVersion::LATEST` resolves to — this project already refuses to let an rmcp move happen silently.

NO TIMESTAMP INSIDE THE FILE. It is overwritten on every handshake, so it always describes the CURRENT connection, and the file's own mtime says when. Inventing a clock for a field a reader can get from the filesystem would add a dependency and a thing to be wrong about.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: reflow2 overrides `ServerHandler::initialize` to record the client's self-reported name and version, the protocol revision it REQUESTED, the revision negotiated, and what this server offers — written to `<graph>.client.json` beside the store, alongside the existing `.meta.json` and `.server.json` sidecars. Answers "which client am I and what did we agree on?" for every future field report, without the reporter instrumenting their own machine.
