properties.name: The import decision's rationale is corrected before the ruling
properties.rationale:
A DECISION IS SETTLED ON ITS RATIONALE, SO CORRECTING THE RATIONALE FIRST IS THE WHOLE POINT. Accepting it as written would embalm a false claim about this project's own history at the moment it becomes binding — and an accepted Decision is what `where-am-i` reads back to the user as "what you decided", which is where a fiction does the most damage.

THE TWO EDITS PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, and both are recorded rather than only the convenient one. Withdrawing the rename leg WEAKENS the case for reporting: that leg argued the write-time guard cannot reach the real cause, and on this graph it reaches all nine. Closing the laundering cost STRENGTHENS it: the one price the decision admitted paying is now paid down by a detector that did not exist when it was drafted.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED: the decision text itself, and the three arguments that carry it — an import ASSERTS NOTHING and reproduces a state the document is evidence of; refusal left this design's own 3388-node export unrestorable with hand-editing the export as the only remedy, which is the one thing the project tells users never to do; and `ImportReport` already answers this same question three times the other way (`skipped_edges`, `integrity_note`, `provenance_note`), so refusing here would have one import refusing what its neighbour two lines up reports. None of those three rested on the rename claim.

STATUS IS NOT MOVED BY THIS EVENT. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is ENFORCED and `check_intent_authority` fails the build on settled intent with no approver, so the ruling is Anthony's and is asked for separately. This only makes the thing he is ruling on true.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary: `dec:a-restore-reports-an-unresolvable-reference-rather-than-refusing-it` is about to be put to Anthony for a ruling, and its rationale contains a claim measured false the same day. Two edits, both to the rationale, none to the decision text: (1) the sentence "four capabilities renamed after the fact was written" is withdrawn and replaced with what was actually measured — those four ids never existed as nodes, so all nine of this graph's dangling values were wrong when written and every one would have been refused at write time; (2) the stated COST — "import is now a path by which a dangling reference can enter a graph that did not have one — an export/import laundering route the write guard closes" — is updated, because that route is no longer silent: the `dangling_reference` rule shipped in #373 reports an unresolvable reference on its own terms whatever the node's degree, so anything an import launders is detected on the next sweep rather than never.

properties.name: The installer stops skipping the one ignore entry most likely to be already tracked, and the remedy it prints works on a directory
Orientation says what is DELIVERED, and a lint keeps every report reachable
properties.rationale:
🛑 THE CHECK WAS WRITTEN FIRST AND OBSERVED FAILING, against the unfixed tree, exit 1: `named in NO skill: ['consumption_report', 'flow_report', 'ility_report', 'maturity_report', 'readiness_report', 'release_report']`. Six of fourteen. That sentence is the only evidence the failing-first step happened, which is why it is here rather than implied.

WHY THE RULE IS `*_report` AND NOT A LIST OF "EVALUATIVE" TOOLS. A hand-kept list of which tools matter is the thing that rots — the same defect this session found in `node_ref` this morning, where a judgement made once for one property was never recorded for any other. A suffix already used consistently in the code needs no maintenance and cannot silently omit a new report.

THE REGISTER CARRIES TWO KINDS OF ENTRY AND SAYS WHICH. "needs no skill" is settled; "GAP:" is a routing hole recorded rather than papered over. A test enforces the prefix, because a gap that reads as settled never gets fixed — and the cheap way to pass this check would have been to name every orphan report in whatever skill was nearest, which would satisfy the lint and defeat its purpose.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX. Naming was measured; INVOCATION was not. A report named in a skill is reachable, not necessarily read — and the 93-session skill-adoption result says what predicts use is an always-injected surface, which a skill is not. So this closes the "unreachable" half and leaves the "unread" half open, and the two must not be confused. The honest test of whether it worked is whether a later session, asked "is my project doing what it is supposed to do", answers with a delivery number instead of a defect count.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
Fixes `fact:the-instruction-surface-routes-to-hygiene-and-not-to-whether-the-thing-works` on both the instance and the class.

THE INSTANCE — `where-am-i` now has a step 3, "How much of it is actually working", leading with the delivery line from `graph_report_markdown` and saying what it means: something satisfies each requirement, the capability is built, its check passes, computed from the thread rather than read off a status field. It says out loud that this is usually the question the user came with, and that a report which only ever lists debt reads as a hygiene tool whatever else it can do. It also BOUNDS the number in the same breath — it measures the design's own chain, not the running system.

THE CLASS — `skill_lint.py` gained the mirror of its oldest check. It already walked skills → tools ("every referenced tool exists"); nothing walked tools → skills, so a report could be built, correct, verified and reachable by nobody with every gate green. Now every served `*_report` must be named in some skill or carry a written reason in `UNROUTED_REPORTS`.

ROUTED, each into the skill whose job it serves rather than wherever it fit: `maturity_report` → where-am-i (the trajectory behind the snapshot), `readiness_report` → plan-increments (a GATED_ON rung decides what can ship when), `ility_report` → check-health (it reads the same sweep and says what the defects MEAN), `consumption_report` → retire-from-design (what nothing consumes is where retirement candidates come from, and its refusal to answer is itself the finding).

EXEMPTED WITH REASONS, and the two are different: `release_report` "needs no skill" — cutting a release is a repo procedure, not a design-loop step. `flow_report` is a "GAP:" — nothing owns inspecting an existing Flow; capture-intent and adopt CREATE flows and no skill reads one back. Naming it in capture-intent would have been inventing a use to satisfy the check, which is the failure the check exists to find one level up.

properties.name: The instructions can be read in parts, and the signpost speaks to the agent
properties.rationale:
Both items are from Alex's 2026-08-27 field report, re-measured against 0.41.0 source before anything was designed.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT CORRECTED THE RECORDED DIAGNOSIS, which is why it was taken first. `fact:defect-the-served-instructions-put-their-standing-rules-where-a-client-cap-deletes-them` (2026-08-15) said the ordering is "worst-first-lost" and that report-friction sits AFTER the cut, making the defect self-sealing — the agent loses the instruction telling it to report the loss. Measured on the current document, that is no longer true: the standing rules sit at 3.5%, 4.5% and 7.6%, and "## If reflow2 gets in your way, say so" sits at 63%, INSIDE his 73% cut. It reached him. What he actually lost was the tail — the gap→question handshake at 73.8% and the entire tool inventory at 78%. That fact proposed three fix shapes; the first was already done, and this builds the other two.

⚠️ THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS THE WRONG ONE, and measuring stopped it. `get_instructions` sends 56,257 bytes for a 26,846-byte document — 2.1×, the exact duplication removed from every other tool in August for being "the difference between an answer a client could read and one it refused". The tempting move is to remove it here too. THAT WOULD HAVE MADE THINGS WORSE FOR THE ONE USER WHO REPORTED IT: the prose tools reach him precisely BECAUSE they duplicate into `content`, and stripping the copy would have left him with nothing at all. Sectioning solves the size without taking away the field he can actually read.

📌 THE SIGNPOST CHANGE IS OPTION (d) OF `dec:idea-how-does-a-content-only-client-get-an-answer`, taken deliberately as COMPLEMENTARY. That node records (d) as strictly improving every other option and foreclosing none, so this does not pre-empt Alex's pending answer on which protocol revision his client negotiated — the question that still decides between (a), (b) and (c). The defect it fixes is that the stub instructed a party not in the room: the AGENT reads it and cannot change its own harness, so for exactly the population it was written for it named no action anybody could take.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
`get_instructions` gains an optional `section`, and every reply now carries a `sections` manifest with `total_bytes` and `returned_bytes` — so a client-side cap is DETECTABLE (one field disagrees with what the reader holds) and RECOVERABLE (the parts can be fetched one at a time). The largest section is 11,260 bytes against the ~19.5 KB cap that truncated a real consumer twice, so every section is individually deliverable on the harness that could not take the whole document. An unknown slug is refused and lists the legal ones. A test pins that the sections rejoin into the document byte for byte, and everything before the first `##` becomes `overview` so no byte is unreachable by slug.

Separately, the `STRUCTURED_ONLY` signpost was rewritten to address the AGENT rather than the client: it now names the prose tools, the fact that refusals arrive in `content` intact, and `export_graph` with a `path` — and states that these do not replace `search_design` before a create or `loop_status` before finishing.

properties.name: The five-module kernel stops being split across sys:store and sys:vocabulary and becomes sys:foundation — the placement fix that removes a subsystem cycle without touching a line of Rust
properties.subject: record

properties.name: The misnamed defect category is renamed and the unscoped sweep returns what it examined — both breaks taken now under rule:fix-it-properly-while-it-is-still-cheap, reversing dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key
The two unallocated capabilities are given owning parts
properties.rationale:
BOTH ANSWERS COME FROM THE SAME RULING, applied deliberately rather than by taste: `chg:allocation-follows-the-code-not-the-neighbour` (2026-08-25) — allocate to the module whose code implements the function, move it, do not dual-allocate.

WHY `cmp:service` AND NOT `cmp:main`. The refusal is not the flag. `--read-only` is parsed in `main.rs`, but the enforcement is `ReflowService::write_lock`, which every mutating handler must obtain and no write can avoid; making it fallible turned all 98 write sites into compile errors until each was handled, and it caught `share()` as a SECOND assembly point that had to inherit the mode or read-only would have held for the process and evaporated for every actual client. Allocating to the entry point would file the function against the switch rather than the guard, and would point somewhere the refusal is not if the mode ever becomes settable another way. `art:service` already REALIZED both `cmp:service` and this capability, so the two layers now agree instead of only one of them holding the answer — the cross-layer check that change event was created by.

WHY A NEW PART RATHER THAN `cmp:temporal`. `manual_work.rs` is a real source module with a linked, checksummed artifact and no part of its own — the same shape as the 31 modules the 2026-08-25 sweep found. Crediting it to `cmp:temporal` because both write TemporalFacts is exactly the neighbour-misfiling that sweep corrected in 19 places, and it would have been a fresh instance of the class the day after the correction. `cmp:tools-temporal`, where the two tools are declared, is excluded by `dec:the-tool-surface-slices-hold-no-function-of-their-own`. Filing it by purpose under `sub:session-posture` was offered and declined for the same reason.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, and it was named when the choice was put: whether reflow2 should keep minting a part per module at all. Every leaf here is a module, so "which part owns this function" and "which file implements it" have collapsed into one question — which makes allocation cheap to get right and makes the allocation layer a second copy of the file tree. `dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition` holds the line at the SYSTEM level (functional, not the file tree) and says nothing about the leaves. That is a decomposition-grain decision nobody has made.

The containment `sys:time-history CONTAINS cmp:manual-work` skips the subsystem rung, which `hierarchy_issues` will read as a missing intermediate level. Done knowingly: all six existing children of `sys:time-history` sit the same way, so this matches its siblings rather than inventing a subsystem for one module. If that rung is ever added it should be added for all seven at once.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary: The design's only two open gaps were both `unallocated_capability`, on the two capabilities that landed in #350 and #351. Both are now owned, on Anthony's word 2026-08-26. "A server can refuse every write" → `cmp:service`, where `ReflowService::write_lock` enforces it. "A session records the work it did by hand" → `cmp:manual-work`, a NEW part created for `crates/reflow2-core/src/manual_work.rs`, contained by `sys:time-history` alongside `cmp:temporal`, with `art:manual-work` REALIZES it so the artifact layer and the allocation layer agree.

properties.description:
music_graph F24, reported 2026-08-16 on the run-book's own §0b restore path — the SIBLING of F23, which v0.32.0 fixed an hour earlier. Both fire on the same walk, so a consumer restoring on 0.32.0 got past F23 cleanly and straight into this.

WHAT HAPPENED: the MCP server started against an empty directory and said so truthfully — 'no design graph has ever been started at .reflow2/graph … exactly one tool is served'. Ninety seconds later `--import` built a full 327-node store underneath it. NOTHING RE-PROBES, so the surface is chosen once at startup and every design tool stayed absent for the rest of the session; the export could not be refreshed from the very session that had just done the restore. ⭐ AND THE SHARP EDGE IS THE COMBINATION: at that moment the graph exists, the pre-commit hook is blocking commits, and THE ONLY TOOL ON OFFER IS THE ONE THAT STARTS A DESIGN — against a directory that now has one. The latent surface's own warning that it is 'easy to accept by accident' is aimed at exactly this and cannot be acted on from inside it.

THEIR ASK (a) IS NOT BUILDABLE AND THAT IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN QUIETLY SUBSTITUTING: 're-probe when a tool is called and promote latent → full surface in place'. The tool router is fixed per service and MCP clients cache the tool list, so a surface cannot grow tools mid-session without a list-changed notification and client support for it. What CAN be done is their (b) and (c), and both are here.

(b) `reflow2_start_design` NOW RE-PROBES BEFORE IT CREATES ANYTHING, via `describe_at` — which reads only the sidecar files, opens no store, takes no lock, and therefore cannot mint an identity by looking. If a design is present it REFUSES: `started: false`, `a_design_is_already_here: true`, the design named, nothing created, and the instruction that actually attaches the surface (a FULL client restart, not merely a /mcp reconnect). It also says in words that a restore has NOT failed and must not be re-run — the wrong recovery was the expensive one available.

(c) The handshake blurb now says its own claim HAS A SHELF LIFE, names `--import` as the way a design appears underneath it, and points at the restart. Previously the blurb was true when printed and false ninety seconds later with nothing to say so.

MUTATION-CHECKED TWICE, each killing exactly one test and no other: removing the re-probe fails ONLY the arrived-design case; widening the guard from `describe_at`'s state to `design_present()` fails ONLY the opted-in counterweight. ⭐ THAT SECOND ONE IS THE POINT OF THE CHANGE'S SHAPE. `design_present` deliberately treats a bare `.reflow2/` directory as opted in — that is how the window between `reflow2 init` and the first write is covered — but OPTED IN IS NOT DESIGNED, and conflating them would make the tool refuse on exactly the projects that most need it: set up, never written to. The guard therefore keys on `Design | Unnamed`, never on directory existence.

THE ORDINARY PATH IS PINNED TOO, because a refusal that fired on an undesigned directory would stop a machine-wide install from ever starting a design at all.

SERVED SURFACE UNCHANGED — 149 toolsnaps match. The tool DESCRIPTION did not move; only its behaviour when a design is already there, and the handshake instructions, which toolsnaps do not pin.

NOT FIXED, and stated rather than left to be discovered: the surface still cannot change mid-session, so after the refusal the design tools remain absent until the client restarts. This makes the dead end SAY what it is; it does not remove it.
properties.name: The one tool a latent server offers stops offering to start a design over one that arrived after startup — music_graph F24
properties.subject: system

properties.description:
Fixes `fact:defect-the-launch-wrapper-cannot-see-a-schema-change`, and the investigation found the defect was WIDER than the fact recorded.

⭐ THE FRAMING THAT MATTERS, and it is sharper than 'the hash was incomplete': THIS HASH IS A GATE IN FRONT OF CARGO'S OWN CHANGE DETECTION. When it decides nothing moved, cargo is never invoked, so cargo's `rerun-if-changed` logic never gets to run. Anything the wrapper misses is therefore not merely untracked — it is actively shielded from the mechanism that would have caught it.

TWO OMISSIONS, and the second was not in the original report:

① `schema/*.yaml`, `include_str!`d by reflow2-core (schema.rs:19-38). A schema-only edit left the hash identical, so the wrapper printed 'binary current, skipping build' and served the previous VOCABULARY. Measured 2026-08-16: `describe_schema` answered with the pre-#199 `change_type` enum while main already declared `defect_fix`, and this session nearly recorded the exact fiction #199 had been merged hours earlier to end.

② `getting-started/skills/**/SKILL.md`, embedded by `crates/reflow2-mcp/build.rs`. THIS ONE IS WORSE AND WAS INVISIBLE UNTIL LOOKED FOR: build.rs ALREADY declares `cargo:rerun-if-changed` on the kit (build.rs:29,50), so cargo would have rebuilt correctly on its own. The wrapper defeated a mechanism that was already right. Editing a SKILL.md served the old text with no warning — and skills change far more often than the schema does.

MEASURED, FOUR CASES, each against both the old and new formula:

    schema edit   new MOVED   old NOT MOVED    <- ①
    SKILL.md edit new MOVED   old NOT MOVED    <- ②
    test edit     new NOT     old NOT          <- counterweight
    src edit      new MOVED   old MOVED        <- counterweight

THE TWO COUNTERWEIGHTS ARE THE POINT. Tests stay OUT deliberately — they are separate cargo targets and cannot change the binary this serves, so including them would rebuild on every test edit and train people to distrust the wrapper. And a `src/*.rs` edit still moves both formulas, so nothing that already worked regressed.

📌 ONE-TIME COST, stated so it does not read as a fault: the first launch after this change rebuilds once regardless, because the stored `.reflow2-mcp.srchash` stamp was computed under the old formula and cannot match the new one. Observed and expected; stable from the second launch.

NOT A REGISTERED ARTIFACT and nothing tests it — which is why the four-case measurement is recorded here rather than as a Verification. CONSUMERS ARE UNAFFECTED throughout: they run an installed release binary, never this wrapper.

NOT FIXED: the wrapper still cannot notice that a RUNNING server has gone stale — it only decides what to build at launch. A session whose server started before a schema change still needs `--stop-shared`, and nothing tells it so.
properties.name: The launch wrapper's hash covers the schema and the skills — the two trees compiled into the binary from outside src/, both of which it was silently blind to
properties.subject: system

properties.name: The lens finally rides the skill response — and the drift it accumulated was a real bug
properties.rationale:
🛑 A MONTH ON A BRANCH COST TWO REAL DEFECTS, AND THAT IS THE DURABLE LESSON.

**1. THE WRITE-LOCK BUG, which would have shipped silently.** `lens_for_response` took `self.write_lock()` to perform a READ. Harmless when written on 2026-08-19; not harmless now. On 2026-08-26 `write_lock` became fallible AND began refusing outright on a `--read-only` server. Landing the branch unchanged would have returned `None` on every read-only deployment — **disabling the lens precisely on the surface a stranger reads the design through, which is where speaking their vocabulary matters most.** Computing a lens is a read; the original said otherwise and no test would have caught it, because no test ran against a read-only service. Now `self.graph.read()`.

**2. THE FIVE HANDLER TESTS NEVER RAN BECAUSE THEY NEVER COMPILED.** The commit message called them "unrun". They were unrunnable: `GetSkillReq` / `ListSkillsReq` had moved from `skills` to `tools::skills_tools` in the tool-surface refactor, and `name` on two request types had become `Option<String>`. **"Unrun tests" and "tests that do not compile" are different states and the commit recorded the softer one.** All five pass now, alongside the six core tests.

⭐ THE CHERRY-PICK CONFLICTED AND THE CONFLICT WAS INFORMATION. `skills.rs` was refactored after the branch: the tool handlers moved to `tools/skills_tools.rs` and the file kept only helpers. Resolving the conflict textually would have re-added structs that already exist elsewhere. The lens was instead applied BY HAND to the two files it actually belongs in — which is how the write-lock bug was noticed at all.

📌 WHY IT MATTERED ENOUGH TO GO BACK FOR. A user reported twice, months apart, that reflow2 "still speaks its own jargon and never asks who I am". Both reports were correct and neither was a missing idea: the only two skills that instruct asking are `where-am-i` and `capture-intent`, which a regular user runs and a new user does not. **A mechanism that only fires on the path its author walks is indistinguishable from a working one, from where the author stands** — and the design recorded the capability, so every reading of the graph said the mechanism existed.

⚠️ AND THE LIMIT THE CAPABILITY ALWAYS NAMED IS UNCHANGED: the tests prove the lens computes and is attached. They do not prove an agent ACTS on it, and nothing proves the translation is any good. This closes delivery. **Whether the words that come out are the reader's words remains unmeasured**, and the trial that would measure it — a real gap list narrated to a reader with a stated non-software background — is still the missing instrument.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: `get_skill` and `list_skills` now carry a `lens` field: who the design knows how to speak to, or a plain statement that it knows nobody. Moves `cap:the-skill-response-carries-the-lens` from `in_progress` to `realized` — it was built 2026-08-19 on branch `lens-hint-rides-the-loop-rail` (commit e01c760), deliberately not marked realized at the v0.36.0 cut, and never merged. Verified live against the real binary: a `get_skill` response now returns keys [body, description, lens, name]. Workspace suite 1835 passed / 0 failed across 163 binaries, reconciling exactly against 1824 + 11 across 161 + 2.

properties.description:
Fifth and last theme of the triage-fixes increment, and the only one whose SHAPE was undecided when it started.

⭐ THE RECONNAISSANCE DECIDED IT, AND IT RULED OUT THE OBVIOUS ANSWER FIRST: only 2 of this design's 2,367 nodes carry `created_at`. So "what did this session write" is NOT computable from timestamps and never was — the design has no clock, by design. Anthony chose the baseline that IS computable: the COMMITTED EXPORT. `loop_status(since_export: true)` reports the nodes the durable record does not hold yet, and the gaps and defects standing on them.

WHY THAT BASELINE IS ARGUABLY BETTER THAN A CLOCK RATHER THAN MERELY AVAILABLE: the export is the only copy that survives losing the gitignored graph directory, so "what is not in the record" is the question with consequences. A session that ends with its work unexported has lost it whatever the timestamps say.

⚠️ AND THE FLAW IS STATED ON EVERY ANSWER, in `note`, rather than left to be discovered: THE BASELINE MOVES whenever anyone exports — including this session mid-flight, and another seat on a shared graph. It is not a session boundary; it is a record boundary that usually coincides with one.

OFF BY DEFAULT, on Anthony's second ruling: it reads and parses the committed export, and the ordinary orientation call has no reason to pay for that. The unscoped reply is byte-identical to before. That mirrors `sync_debt`, which already defers its expensive half until something has moved.

SCOPED HONESTLY, AND ONLY WHERE IT CAN BE: only the two debt classes carrying `affected_ids` — gaps and structural defects — can be attributed to ground, so only they are scoped. EVERY OTHER COUNTER STAYS DESIGN-WIDE and the note says so, because a scoped answer that quietly dropped the rest would be the "nothing is owed" failure this project refuses everywhere else.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT THAT MATTERS MOST is the empty baseline: no readable record and a genuinely new design look IDENTICAL from here, so the answer says which it cannot tell rather than implying a clean session. Mutation-checked — removing that branch fails exactly that one test, and ignoring the baseline entirely fails exactly the fully-recorded case.

MEASURED END TO END through a real server over stdio, on a scratch graph: create, export, create one more, ask — `unexported_nodes: 1`, sample `['req:new']`, and the unscoped call omits the block entirely.

📌 AND F24 ARRIVED ON ME WHILE PROVING IT: the MCP client caches tool schemas for the session, so the newly added `since_export` was unusable from the session that added it — the server accepted the field and the client sent it as a string. That is the same class as the latent-surface dead end fixed this morning, and it is why the verification was done by driving the binary directly.
properties.name: loop_status gains since_export — debt on ground the committed record does not hold yet, which is the closest a clockless design can get to what this session owes
properties.subject: system

properties.description:
TWO defects from the StoryFlow fleet's 2026-08-15/16 log, both verified in source before the fix and both with the reporter's diagnosis CORRECTED. They ship together because they are one shape: a signal that could not express its own limit.

① A QUESTION NOT CREATED BY gap_to_prompt WAS PERMANENTLY UNANSWERABLE. `set_question_status` derived the Question id by string formatting from the gap id (`detect.rs:700-702`) and did a single `get_node`, so a hand-authored Question was unreachable — while `open_questions` published its `question_id` and `answer_question` refused to take one. The loop then reported 'follow it up rather than asking again' about something it structurally could not close, and the next seat re-asks the user what they already ruled on. FIX: `resolve_question_id` tries the DERIVED id first and the argument verbatim second, so every existing caller is byte-identical and the unreachable case becomes reachable; the MCP tool now accepts `gap_id` OR `question_id`; and the refusal names the ids that DO exist rather than only the miss — the round trip the reporter had no way to shortcut. `withdraw_question` shares the resolver and gains the same reach.

② `sync` REPORTED `in_step` WHILE THIS GRAPH HELD UNEXPORTED WORK. ⚠️ THE REPORTER'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG AND THE CORRECTION IS THE FINDING: they called it a measure-itself bug. The mechanism is exactly as they described — the cheap gate compares the file against the hash this graph last wrote it with (`sync_debt.rs:199`) and `bare()` hardcodes `nodes_not_here_total: 0` — but `ver:the-record-moved-is-surfaced` pins 'ordinary unexported work is NEVER reported' as the property the whole design rests on. The code is CORRECT. The defect is that NOTHING covered the other direction, and `in_step` in a field called `sync` was read as covering both. FIX: every sync entry now carries `live_nodes` beside `export_nodes`, and the in-step line says how many nodes have never been exported. It changes no state and no verdict — unexported work is still not `behind`, because that would tell a session to import over its own unsaved work.

MEASURED, AND THE REPRODUCTION IS WHY ② IS RECORDED RATHER THAN FILED: at the start of the session that fixed it, `loop_status.sync` reported `in_step` with `nodes_not_here_total: 0` for reflow2's OWN export while two TemporalFacts sat live and absent from it — an earlier session's entire triage of music_graph F23 and F24. The previous handoff had recorded 'nothing behind' on the strength of that green. They survived only because this session exported for an unrelated reason.

MUTATION-CHECKED THREE WAYS, each killing exactly the test that names it and no other: dropping the verbatim fallback fails the hand-authored and withdraw cases only; swapping the resolver order so the verbatim id wins fails ONLY the collision counterweight, which is the case proving a widened lookup did not become a guessing one; and firing the unexported warning on `live >= export` instead of `>` fails ONLY the fully-exported counterweight, which is what stops a reading aid becoming a false alarm on the path every ordinary session takes.

THE SERVED SURFACE CHANGED, deliberately and only by WIDENING: `answer_question.gap_id` leaves the required list and `question_id` joins the schema, so no existing caller breaks. Toolsnap regenerated (149).

BOUNDS, stated rather than discovered later: the sync counts are NODES ONLY — counting edges means walking every node's adjacency, which costs what the export costs, and paying that on the ordinary path is the one thing this check exists to avoid, so an edge-only divergence stays invisible. They are counts, not ids, so equal counts with different ids still pass: this is a reading aid, never a durability guarantee. And neither fix addresses why an ANSWERED question still does not become design — reflow2's own loop has carried '1 answered question never reached the design' for days, and that gap is real independently of the id scheme.
properties.name: A question is answerable by either id, and an in-step record says how much of this graph it does not hold — two signals that could not previously be wrong out loud
properties.subject: system

properties.name: MemoryBackend moves HashMap → BTreeMap; export build 1,137ms → 236ms
properties.rationale:
⚖️ THE TRADE IS REAL AND WAS PUT IN THE COMMIT RATHER THAN OMITTED. `BTreeMap` insert is O(log n) where `HashMap` was O(1), and import measured 890.6 ms -> 966.8 ms, about 8% SLOWER. It is worth it on the round trip — a session's load+save goes 2,266 ms -> 1,421 ms, 37% better — but a report carrying only the 4.8x would have been selecting the evidence.

🛑 SCOPE, WHICH MATTERS AND IS EASY TO OVERSTATE: THIS DOES NOT MAKE TODAY'S REFLOW2 FASTER. Production runs on RocksDB, whose prefix iterator is already a range scan. What it speeds up is (a) the 1,452-test core suite, which runs entirely on `MemoryBackend`, and (b) the database-free session model under discussion in `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability`, where the memory backend IS the store.

⭐⭐ THIRD DEFECT OF ONE SHAPE IN ONE FILE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING — not three coincidences. A linear scan standing in where an indexed lookup belongs: twice in the write buffer (#330 — the buffered `get`, and the `prefix_scan` pre-flight) and once here in the backing store. All three were invisible at test scale and quadratic at design scale, because the cost is a product of two things that are both small in a unit test and both large in a real design.

⭐ AND ALL THREE WERE FOUND THE SAME WAY: read the code, count the operations, check the arithmetic against the stopwatch BEFORE changing anything. 42M comparisons at ~25 ns predicts ~1.06 s against 1,137 ms measured. The method is transferable and the habit is the transferable part — the first hypothesis in #330 was wrong (adjacency read-modify-write) and reading the code killed it before any code was written.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
Merged as #331. `MemoryBackend` held each column family in a `HashMap`, but `KvBackend` requires ORDERED prefix iteration — so `prefix_scan` iterated the whole column family, filtered by prefix, and sorted the result: O(n log n) per scan, on the backend whose entire purpose is to be the fast path. `export_graph` calls `outgoing()` once per node, so exporting reflow2's own design was 3,149 scans over a 13,414-entry adjacency map, ~42M key comparisons.

Six `BTreeMap`s now, and `prefix_scan` is a range query — seek to the prefix, take while it matches. `BTreeMap` orders keys lexicographically, the same order RocksDB's default byte-wise comparator gives, so the trait's ordered-scan contract is satisfied BY CONSTRUCTION and the sort was deleted rather than optimised.

MEASURED (release, in-memory backend, fulltext on, 3,149 nodes / 13,414 edges):

    build export doc   1,137.3 ms -> 236.5 ms   (4.8x)
    serialize to JSON     31.0 ms ->  28.8 ms
    TOTAL session save 1,168.3 ms -> 265.3 ms   (4.4x)

Workspace 1760 / 0, core 1452 / 0, both clippy gates, fmt, twelve python gates and the design gate green; CI green on both jobs.

properties.name: Nine dangling TemporalFact.subject_id references repointed, and the rename story behind four of them was false
properties.rationale:
🛑 THE RECORDED CAUSE FOR FOUR OF THESE WAS FALSE, AND CORRECTING IT MATTERS BECAUSE A PROPOSED DECISION RESTS ON IT. `dec:a-restore-reports-an-unresolvable-reference-rather-than-refusing-it` says the nine are "five instances of a `prj:`/`proj:` typo, four capabilities renamed after the fact was written", and the INVALIDATES note on `fact:defect-a-property-naming-a-node-is-unguarded-while-edges-are-not` repeats it: "four were VALID WHEN WRITTEN and broke later when the target was renamed".

MEASURED 2026-08-29, and it refutes that. `git log -S '"node_id": "cap:link-artifacts"' -- docs/design/reflow2.json` returns ZERO commits, and the same for `cap:reconcile-artifacts`, `cap:thin-install` and `cap:gap-to-prompt`. The identical probe against a real capability (`cap:adopt`) returns one. **These ids never existed as nodes.** They were wrong when written — the same class as the five typos, not rename-rot.

WHY IT CHANGES SOMETHING RATHER THAN BEING A TIDY-UP: that decision argues the write-time guard cannot reach the real cause, because "the renames that produce most real dangles are unreachable by ANY write-time check". On this graph there were no renames. All nine would have been refused at write time by the guard #366 shipped, which weakens one leg of the argument for reporting rather than refusing on import. THE DECISION'S MAIN ARGUMENT IS UNTOUCHED and still looks right — an import ASSERTS NOTHING, it reproduces a state the document is evidence of, and refusing there substitutes the tool's judgement for a reality it is being handed. Only the supporting claim about renames is withdrawn, and it is withdrawn on evidence rather than on preference.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: that renames never break references — only that none of THIS graph's nine came from one, so the rename case remains hypothetical here rather than demonstrated. The separate detection defect this work surfaced is recorded at `fact:a-dangling-reference-is-only-detected-when-the-node-is-also-edgeless`.

The onboarding skill is written — a newcomer can be told where new work belongs
properties.rationale:
WRITTEN AS A SKILL RATHER THAN A TOOL because the answer is a judgement assembled from six reads, not a computation — which part SHOULD own a new thing is exactly the kind of call `dec:report-dont-judge` says reflow2 reports toward and never makes. A tool would have to pick, and picking is the user's.

THE THREE-WAY DISTINCTION IS STATED AT THE TOP because it is the thing most likely to send someone to the wrong place: where-am-i answers what the system IS, impact-check answers what a change to something EXISTING would break, and this answers where something NEW belongs. The first is often the right thing to run before this one, and the skill says so rather than assuming the reader has.

IT ENDS BY REFUSING TO SURVEY. "Give one recommendation first, then the runner-up and what would make it win" — a newcomer handed five balanced candidates has been given the original problem back with more words attached. That is `req:a-question-arrives-with-a-reading` applied to an answer instead of to a question.

⚠️ THE LINT CAUGHT THREE THINGS AND ALL THREE WERE REAL. Two backticked level values (`component`, `subsystem`) read as unknown tool names and needed the field-term allowlist; a stray directory created by a mis-scoped shell command appeared as two nameless skills; and `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command` requires a command per served skill, so the skill would have shipped reachable only by `get_skill`. None of the three would have been caught by reading the file.

`getting-started/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md`, served, mirrored, and reachable by the `/where-does-it-go` command. Moves `cap:onboarding` from `planned` to `realized` and delivers `req:onboard-newcomer`, accepted since the eight-requirement batch and unbuilt since — BL-101.

NO CORE CHANGE, exactly as the capability said: it assembles machinery that already existed and had never been pointed at this question. `search_design` on the user's own words, `scan_nodes` with `level` for the right rung, `design_regions` and `granularity_report` to narrow, `propagate_from` for what each candidate would reach, `GOVERNED_BY` plus `alternatives_for` and `recall_resolutions` for what already rules there, `AUTHORED_BY` for who to ask, `claim_report` for who is in it now, and `coverage_report` / `detect_gaps` / `seam_report` for what the design cannot see.

THE REQUIREMENT'S HARDEST CLAUSE IS STEP 5 AND IT IS NON-OPTIONAL: "say honestly which parts of the real system the design does not cover". A confident answer drawn from a design that does not model the relevant part is worse than no answer, because the person receiving it cannot tell the silence was ignorance rather than absence.

⭐ AND THE CLAUSE THAT IS NOT IN THE REQUIREMENT BUT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THE SKILL: give the newcomer a NAME. `AUTHORED_BY` means a ruling can be handed over as "this was Anna's call and here is why" rather than as a wall. A decision with a person attached is one a new hire can ask about.

properties.name: The optimize skill ships, with its n=2 stated in its own text
properties.rationale:
Anthony asked for it after the procedure had been run twice by hand - once on the test suite (the schema parse cached, 41.3 ms -> 266 us, suite 191.8 s -> 96.5 s) and once on the product surface (the 26-48 s cold start, measured and deliberately left unfixed for want of a budget). He chose (c) then (a): run it again first, then write the skill.

Both runs are what the skill is made of, and its honest-limits section says so - steps 4, 6 and 7 each caught a real mistake, while steps 1, 2 and 3 are discipline generalised from two cases. skill_lint pins all ten clauses INCLUDING the n=2 admission, because every one of them is a clause a hurrying reader would happily drop: writing the budget first feels like ceremony when you can already see the fix, stopping under budget feels like leaving value on the table, and asserting structure instead of a duration is more work than a threshold.

The skill also contradicts the framing it was asked under, on purpose: it does NOT wait for black boxes to be identified, because both runs succeeded with no contract on the module.

properties.name: loop_status stops re-reading a hundred megabytes
properties.rationale:
⭐⭐ THE RULE THAT SHIPPED IS THE SECOND ONE TRIED, AND THE FIRST ONE'S FAILURE IS THE MORE USEFUL RECORD. The first attempt at ② refused to track anything under the OS temp directory, reasoning that scratch is not a SHARED record — which is what `req:a-seat-learns-the-record-moved-before-it-writes` exists for. FIFTEEN TESTS IN `the_record_moved_and_the_session_is_told` FAILED AND EVERY ONE WAS RIGHT: a hermetic test puts a genuine shared record in a temp dir, and so does a CI workspace and so does a container. One of them is named "the case the whole thing exists for — your brother pushed, you pulled". The rule fit every path on one machine and would have silenced the feature for everyone whose workspace sits under /tmp. The defect was never WHERE records live; it is that the list only grows. So the bound is on COUNT and assumes nothing about anybody's filesystem — and it is SLOWER than the wrong rule (23.6s rather than 14.3s) because it keeps six targets rather than two. That is the correct trade.

⭐⭐ AND CAUSE ① SHIPPED PAST TEN PASSING TESTS, because every one ran on an in-memory graph small enough that 483 scans were instant. Correctness was verified and cost was never measured once. AGENTS.md already says it — "compiling is not the finish line, and neither is a green unit test" — and what caught this was not a gate but a user asking for something else. A rollup that walks the graph needs a measurement at real scale before it merges.

🛑 A THIRD ERROR, RECORDED BECAUSE IT SHAPED THE WORK: the 40s was first attributed to cause ① on nothing but two similar numbers, and a fix was recommended on that basis. Scoping ① left `loop_status` unmoved; the cost was ②. Two numbers agreeing is not causation, and the attribution should have been measured before it was stated.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: `loop_status` measured 40.5s over the shared server on this graph (3,083 nodes / 13,188 edges) — the call `cap:loop-status` promises is ONE CHEAP CALL and every session is told to run. Two independent causes, both fixed. ① `invalidated_findings` asked `incoming()` of every Verification and TemporalFact, and each walks the whole edge set: 483 nodes x a full-graph scan, 39s, to return 1.2 KB saying nothing was claimed. The rollups now ask only about the rows they annotate (`invalidated_verifications`); the exhaustive form stays for the standalone tool. ② The list of synced records was unbounded — 16 targets totalling 102 MB, fourteen of them one-off probe dumps from past sessions, three belonging to another project, all re-read every time. A roll now opens the 6 most recently modified and reports the rest in `not_checked`. MEASURED AFTER: `loop_status` 23.6s, `sync_status` 28.3s -> 11.8s.

properties.name: F-01 fixed at the cause: a stated replay contract was maintained by hand, and is now pinned by a round-trip test
properties.rationale:
FIRST WORKED EXAMPLE OF `rule:an-issue-is-root-caused-then-pinned-by-a-test-then-fixed`, written the same day.

THE FIRST-ORDER READING WAS WRONG AND WOULD HAVE PATCHED THE WRONG THING. "The budgeted reply withheld a field" is true and leads to making the budget keep `suggested_depth` — which fixes today and leaves the class open.

THE ROOT CAUSE: `GapCandidate` states a replay contract in its own doc comment — "a compact row handed straight back to `gap_to_prompt` has to deserialize" — and enforces it FIELD BY FIELD. Two fields carried `#[serde(default)]` and two did not, so the contract held wherever somebody remembered and broke wherever nobody did. The cause is a stated contract maintained by hand with nothing checking it; the budget and the handshake then cancelled on exactly the designs where both matter.

THE PIN IS THE ROUND TRIP, NOT THE FIELD. It serializes every budgeted row and reads it back, and separately deserializes a row whose optional fields are ABSENT rather than empty — which is what `skip_serializing_if` produces and what a caller reconstructing a row by hand sends. Any future field added without a default fails it.

⚠️ HONEST LIMIT: the test was written after the diagnosis and verified passing, not verified FAILING against the unfixed code first. Step ② of the rule it exemplifies was therefore weaker than the rule asks, on the rule's own first outing.

Reported by hxm_program as F-01: a budgeted `detect_gaps` replayed into `gaps_to_prompts` exactly as documented was refused with `invalid GapCandidate: missing field 'suggested_depth'`. 11 tests pass in that file.

properties.name: The content-store retirement now OBSOLETES everything its own text says it removed, not just one capability of five. FOUND WITHIN MINUTES OF SHIPPING THE READER FIX, 2026-08-12, and BY that fix: with `discontinued` finally visible on a read, `cap:content-manifest` came back `realized / discontinued:false` for a tool that no longer exists. `dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued` (accepted 2026-08-09) names its casualties explicitly — "content_put / content_get / content_exists / CONTENT_MANIFEST, content.rs, content_tools.rs, the --content-path flag, and BOTH TEST FILES" — but its OBSOLETES edges reached `cap:content-store` and the five Decisions it supersedes, and nothing else. THE RECORD CONTRADICTED ITSELF: the prose said removed, the structure said live. FOUR NODES WERE STRANDED, AND THE TWO WORST ARE VERIFICATIONS. `ver:content-store` and `ver:content-surface` both read `passing`, last_run_at 2026-07-31, for test files deleted on 2026-08-09 — a PASSING CHECK IS THE STRONGEST CLAIM THIS SYSTEM MAKES, and both were attached to nothing while sitting inside the 138-passing count the graph report shows. `cap:content-manifest` (realized) and `cap:session-artifacts` (VERIFIED, and its whole mechanism was content_put) were the other two. THIS RECORDS AN EXISTING DECISION RATHER THAN MAKING A NEW ONE — Anthony's word 2026-08-12, "go ahead and draw the edges", given after being shown that it moves delivery arithmetic, silences three detectors on those nodes, and changes the confirmed/passing counts. He was asked precisely because this project treats those numbers carefully; the edges make the structure agree with prose he had already accepted. ⭐ THE GENERALISABLE PART, and the reason this is worth reading later: A RETIREMENT IS DRAWN ONE EDGE AT A TIME WHILE THE THING BEING RETIRED IS A CLUSTER — a capability, its siblings, its verifications, its artifacts. Nothing checks that a discontinuation covers everything its own decision text names, and nothing did here. That gap is why four nodes sat wrong for three days with every gate green, and it is a candidate detector: a Decision whose text names removals that carry no OBSOLETES.
The root-cause skill ships, and the design generates the candidates
properties.rationale:
⭐ ANTHONY CORRECTED THE DESIGN TWICE WHILE IT WAS BEING BUILT, and both corrections are in the shipped skill.

FIRST: the costing had been aimed at the wrong thing. Option (c) of `dec:idea-should-reflow2-serve-a-root-cause-analysis-method` — surfacing a known cause automatically at the moment of a symptom — was measured in detail before he said the point was "not so much can the graph help determine root cause... it is more to direct the agent how to properly do the steps." The target is the AGENT'S PROCESS, which was question 1 on that node's own must-check list, and it had been answered by assumption rather than by asking.

SECOND, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MADE THE SKILL WORTH SHIPPING: the first draft over-corrected into pure process guidance, with step ③ reading "write down at least three candidate causes". He pushed back — "you can often start fishbone analysis on inspecting the design... there is value in looking at a design (and if it is a software code base... you can inspect the implementation of the design also)". He was right, and the weakness was concrete: an exhortation to think of three produces two real candidates and a filler that exists to satisfy the instruction. Step ③ now walks NINE BONES, each answered by a CALL rather than by memory, and names the artifact layer as the bridge from a symptom to the source files that could have produced it.

🛑 WHY A SKILL AND NOT AN ENFORCED RULE, since the rule already existed. `rule:an-issue-is-root-caused-then-pinned-by-a-test-then-fixed` is Anthony's own and is `enforced: false` by his own decision, for a reason its text states: nothing in a diff or a CI run can see whether a test was FAILING before the fix, so an enforced version could only check something weaker, and a check that reads as enforcement while measuring something else is worse than no check. What a skill changes is DELIVERY, not force — a rule is read once at handshake and states an intention; a skill is pulled at the moment of the work and states an action. The same distinction `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` already draws for conventions.

⚠️ THE SESSION THAT BUILT IT SUPPLIED ITS OWN EXAMPLES, WHICH IS WHY THEY ARE SPECIFIC. Three wrong diagnoses were made and refuted in the course of costing one option: that `search_design` was slow (refuted — `get_node` was equally slow), that every graph call was slow (refuted — this session's own calls plainly were not), and that the cost was per-TCP-connection (refuted — calls 2 and 3 on one connection were just as slow). The actual cause, found only by a discriminating test with a proper MCP handshake, is a ONE-TIME PER-SESSION HYDRATE: 41.11s for the first graph-touching call, then 0.05s and 0.04s. A defect report claiming reflow2 had a severe read-performance problem was one step from being filed, and every step of it felt like understanding.

properties.summary: The 22nd served skill. `/root-cause` walks nine steps in order: state the symptom as an observation (not a diagnosis); search for precedent; GENERATE candidates from the design along nine bones; name the measurement that would REFUTE each; take it and check the result rather than that the call finished; ask what CLASS this is; pin it with a test observed failing; fix at the cause and record the cause as a CAUSES edge; and say what could not be established. Shipped with a slash command, mirrored to the .claude and .grok trees, compiled into the binary by build.rs, and pinned by `ver:the-root-cause-skill-forces-rather-than-exhorts`.

properties.name: Question.gap_id's declaration states why it is not a node reference
properties.rationale:
THE SWEEP GOT WIDER WHEN IT WAS RUN WITHOUT A FLOOR, and the count of kinds went from the expected three to four. The root-cause pass measured only the three properties `heal.rs` names. Re-swept 2026-08-29 across EVERY `*_id` property with no minimum-instance floor:

    TemporalFact.subject_id        334 values, 334 resolve   a NODE REFERENCE
    Snapshot.target_id             196 values, 192 resolve   a HISTORICAL ANCHOR
    Question.gap_id                 57 values,   0 resolve   a COMPUTED-FINDING REFERENCE
    Resource.dependency_graph_id      1 value,    0 resolve   a CROSS-DESIGN REFERENCE

The fourth was not in any earlier reading and is a kind nobody had named: it holds `dynograph-foundation`, which is a GRAPH id rather than a node id, and it is not a declared property at all — the store is a property bag, so it was written and never validated against anything.

⚠️ AND THREE MORE ARE DECLARED BUT HAVE NEVER BEEN WRITTEN: `ReadinessAssessment.target_id`, `DimensionAssessment.target_id`, `DimensionObservation.target_id`, all at zero instances. They read like node references — an assessment OF a node — but whether a scored node's later deletion makes the assessment wrong (a node reference) or leaves it as the surviving record of what was scored (a historical anchor) is exactly the `subject_id`-versus-`target_id` question again, and with no instances there is no evidence to settle it either way. Recorded as undecided ON PURPOSE rather than guessed, because a wrong `node_ref` on an unpopulated type would be a rule nobody could have tested.

WHY THE SCHEMA IS EDITED AND THE FLAG IS NOT. Every instinct here says "declare them and let the guard sort it out", and that is the move this change refuses. `Snapshot.target_id` MUST NOT be declared: four of its values dangle today and all four are correct — three artifacts deleted at `epoch:content-store-discontinued` and `ctr:anthony` merged into `who:ajs`. A snapshot exists to preserve what a node was, so a snapshot pointing at nothing is the mechanism working. Declaring it would make `dangling_reference` fire on correct history, which is the failure this project judges worse than no detector at all.
properties.subject: record
properties.summary:
Adding the reason to two schema property descriptions — `Snapshot.target_id` (schema/temporal.yaml) and `Question.gap_id` (schema/core.yaml) — so a reader meets the judgement at the point of the declaration rather than inferring it from an absent flag. Closes the defect named by `fact:which-properties-are-node-references-is-a-judgement-made-once-and-never-recorded-for-the-others`: `subject_id` and `target_id` are declared IDENTICALLY apart from `node_ref` and nothing said why, so the next reader either declares it and breaks history, or leaves it and never learns the omission was deliberate.

THE SCHEMA IS THE RIGHT PLACE BECAUSE IT IS SERVED. The YAML is `include_str!`d into reflow2-core and reaches agents through `describe_schema`, so a sentence here is read at the moment somebody is deciding what a property means. That is the same reasoning `dec:skills-served` applies to skills, and the same reasoning the revise-design correction applies to tool descriptions — the text an agent reads at call time is the text that governs.

properties.description:
FOLDED INTO `req:a-report-says-what-it-swept-and-whether-its-checks-ran` on Anthony's word, because it is the same theme arriving from a different direction: `propose_heal` could not say whether its scorer RAN, and the toolsnap gate could not say WHAT IT READ.

THE DEFECT (`fact:defect-the-toolsnap-gate-defaults-to-a-binary-nobody-rebuilt`): `tools/toolsnap.py` defaulted `--bin` to `target/debug/reflow2-mcp` and printed 'ALL 149 TOOLSNAPS MATCH' against whatever build happened to be there. Found by accident — a tool description was changed, RELEASE was rebuilt, and the gate reported the surface unchanged while the committed snapshot still held the old text.

THE FIX IS OUTPUT, NOT POLICY: every verdict — match, drift AND regenerate — now ends with the binary it read and that binary's build time, and adds a loud STALE warning naming the offending file when any `crates/**/src/*.rs` is newer.

⚠️ THE DEFAULT DELIBERATELY STAYS `target/debug`, which is the opposite of the obvious fix and the reason is measured: `ci.yml:93` runs `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp` — a debug build — in the same job before the toolsnap step at `:142`. Pointing the default at release would aim CI at a binary it never builds, converting a local-only defect into a CI one. This also CORRECTS the first version of the fact, which left CI's exposure unestablished: CI was never exposed.

MTIME IS A WEAK SIGNAL AND IS USED ACCORDINGLY. Git operations can leave sources older than a build — which is exactly why the launch wrapper hashes CONTENT instead — so mtime here only ever ADDS a warning and never suppresses one. A false negative therefore costs nothing that was not already lost, and a false positive costs one rebuild.

DEMONSTRATED LIVE, BOTH DIRECTIONS, on the working tree that produced it: against the stale binary the gate printed the STALE warning naming `crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/query.rs`; after `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp` the same command printed the verdict and the binary line with no warning. So the case fires and the counterweight is silent, measured rather than asserted.

NOT DONE: `tools/toolsnap.py` is not a registered Artifact, so this change moved no checksum and the design records it against `cmp:packaging` instead. Several gate scripts are in that position and nobody has decided whether they should be registered.

THE FOUR SHARE NO SUBSYSTEM AND ONE SHAPE: reflow2 HELD the information and the reply withheld it, so a session had to reconstruct by hand what was already computed. That is the same failure as a vacuous zero reading as a pass, one layer over — which is why they shipped together rather than as four patches.

Two of them were caught only because the reporter did work the tool should have done: the degrade cause was found by DIFFING TWO OF ITS OWN CALLS, and `unused_answers` would have named it on the first read. The `deferred` fix is deliberately NOT a silencing. Adding `deferred` to the `dropped`/`met` skip was the obvious repair and the wrong one: those two are FINISHED and this one is POSTPONED, parking is a decision that expires, and dropping the row would make live intent go quiet (`req:no-idea-goes-quiet`). properties.rationale:
Anthony chose option (b) of `dec:idea-what-notices-an-idea-that-connects-to-nothing` on 2026-08-21, and asked for the idea to be brainstormed, linked, accepted and then built — which is what happened, in that order.

THE PREREQUISITE WAS PART OF THE ACCEPTANCE, not a caveat on it. The skill asked for "no real relation" in PROSE, and prose cannot be told apart from silence. So the first thing built was a structural home for the judgement: `Decision.no_relation_note`. Everything else rests on it.

⭐ WHAT THE BRAINSTORM ITSELF PROVED, and it is the reason the linking step exists. Four searches run before writing turned up a COLLISION nobody had noticed — brainstorm/SKILL.md step 2 forbids running detect-and-ask over brainstormed nodes, and a detector on unlinked ideas is exactly that — and then turned up its RESOLUTION, `req:detecting-is-not-asking`, written eleven days earlier. Neither node mentioned the other. BOTH halves of that finding came out of the near-matches the linking step spends, not out of thinking harder.

MEASURED AFTER LINKING: against a population where 115 of 147 ideas reach zero other ideas within two hops, the newly captured idea reached 2 at one hop, 4 at two and 9 at three. That is the "one search instead of four" Anthony described, working.

THE THREE STATES THE BUILD DISTINGUISHES: linked; reviewed and deliberately unlinked; nobody looked. Only the third is a finding. Fourteen tests exist mostly to pin that boundary — a blank note is not an answer, one bad link writes none of them, and a detector with nothing to run on says nothing rather than reporting "0 of 0".

NOT BUILT, AND DELIBERATELY: cluster search, the second half Anthony named. It was measured to be ORDERED AFTER this one — built before linking existed it would have returned nothing for 77% of ideas, which reads as a broken feature rather than an unlinked graph.

properties.name: Three genuine internal contracts are declared, and 56 non-seams are named as such
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word 2026-08-27, choosing to work the real candidates over three alternatives after being shown that 56 of the 64 are not seams.

⚠️ A PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THIS WORK WAS WRONG, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE USEFUL PART. This event first stated that declaring these contracts COULD NOT move the seam metric, citing `fact:coupling-and-contract-are-recorded-in-vocabularies-that-never-meet`: couplings come from DEPENDS_ON, contracts from PROVIDES/CONSUMES, and on this design the two sets were "disjoint by construction". **It moved: 8 of 72 covered became 13 of 72.**

The August measurement was true WHEN TAKEN and its explanation was incomplete. The sets were disjoint because every contract then sat at the SUBSYSTEM boundary while every coupling sat between MODULES — an accident of where contracts had been declared, not a property of the schema. Declaring a contract between two modules that DO carry a DEPENDS_ON edge makes the sets intersect, and five did: detect↔llm, ingest↔llm, ingest↔sanitize, export↔provenance, graph↔provenance.

⭐ SO THE METRIC WAS NEVER STUCK — IT WAS UNREACHABLE FROM WHERE THE CONTRACTS WERE. "Disjoint by construction" reads as a property of the design that no work can change, and it is not; it is a description of a state that this change altered. That distinction matters because the first reading argues for leaving the number alone forever.

🛑 AND ONE OF THE EIGHT STAYED UNCOVERED, CORRECTLY. `cmp:agent`↔`cmp:llm` is still uncovered because BOTH sides PROVIDE `ifc:llm-backend` — agent.rs is an alternative implementation of the trait, not a consumer of llm.rs — so there is no provides/consumes PAIR between them. That is honest modelling producing an uncovered coupling, and it must not be "fixed" by drawing a CONSUMES edge that would assert a relationship the code does not have.

WHY THESE THREE, from the modules' own words rather than from taste:
- `llm.rs` opens *"the one seam between the deterministic core and any LLM"*. It had no Interface node while being the design's most explicitly named boundary. Five modules name `LlmBackend`; `cmp:llm` and `cmp:agent` both PROVIDE it (agent.rs is the ambient-agent ADAPTER, which is why it both provides this and consumes `ifc:ambient-agent`), and detect, ingest and drift consume it.
- `sanitize.rs` opens *"the ingress trust boundary"*, and `req:trust-boundary-at-ingress` is accepted intent. Its error model is the contract: stripping must be SAID OUT LOUD, because a boundary that cleans text silently leaves the reader believing they saw the original.
- `provenance.rs` writes files BESIDE the store that a DIFFERENT VINTAGE of the binary reads. That is a cross-version file-format contract by definition, and six modules read or write it.

WHY NOT THE OTHER TWO. `cmp:graph`↔`cmp:schema` is a compile-time embed of the vocabulary, and `cmp:agent`↔`cmp:nodes` is use of node-type constants. Both are ordinary internal calls, and declaring a contract for them would be the same alarm-on-correct-work that the 56 impl-block pairs represent. Recorded here rather than left silent so the next reader knows they were examined and rejected, not missed.

⚠️ EVERY SPEC WAS FILLED IN, DELIBERATELY. An Interface whose fields are all `unspecified` is a node, not a contract — `seam_report` reports unspecified as UNSTATED rather than as agreement precisely so that cannot pass for one. Medium, paradigm, payload format, operations, payload schema, auth, transport security and error model are set on all three.

Only 8 were candidates. Three real contracts are now declared and fully specified: `ifc:llm-backend`, `ifc:ingress-trust-boundary`, `ifc:provenance-sidecar`, each with both sides wired. properties.rationale:
🛑 FOUND BY WALKING INTO IT, TWENTY MINUTES AFTER THE FIRST CUT SHIPPED — and by the agent, on itself, not by a user this time. Recording a brainstorm exactly as the `brainstorm` skill instructs (step 4: relate the new idea to what is already there) drew ANTICIPATES edges from an ACCEPTED Decision and from a TemporalFact to parked ideas. The sweep reported both, and the defect count went 78 -> 80 for following the instructions. That is the same complaint hxm_program filed, surviving the fix meant to answer it.

WHY EITHER SIDE IS RIGHT HERE WHILE `contradiction` NEEDS BOTH, and the asymmetry falls out of what each finding CLAIMS rather than from taste. `unresolved_setup` says "X anticipates Y but nothing follows through" — the complaint is that Y IS UNRESOLVED. When Y is a parked idea, Y being unresolved is exactly what `proposed` MEANS: the recorded idea IS the follow-through, and demanding more is demanding that a brainstorm be finished. When X is parked, a musing anticipating something real has committed to no setup at all. A contradiction, by contrast, is real as soon as ONE side asserts something, which is why it stops at both (`a_proposed_decision_is_not_treated_as_withdrawn`).

⚠️ AND A RULE KEYED ON BOTH ENDPOINTS COULD NEVER HAVE REACHED THE SECOND CASE AT ALL. A TemporalFact is not a Decision and can never be parked, so no tightening of the both-sides rule would have helped; the shape had to change. Worth keeping because it is the general lesson: a predicate scoped to one node type cannot express a rule about edges whose other end is any type.

📌 THE COST SIDE, STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: 28 findings across the two cuts now disappear with nothing anywhere saying they were suppressed or why. `art:heal` realizes `cap:a-sweep-says-what-it-could-not-have-found`, and the existing `parks` mechanism COUNTS parked nodes in `swept.parked` rather than silencing them. properties.name: The batch write buffer gets an index; hydrate 8.83s → 0.91s
properties.rationale:
THE CAUSE WAS FOUND BY ARITHMETIC BEFORE IT WAS FOUND BY A PROFILER, and the arithmetic is why the diagnosis was trustworthy. Buffer at end of import ~44,000 ops; average during the edge loop ~23,000; two endpoint checks per edge gives 2 x 13,390 x 23,000 = ~616M comparisons. Divided into the measured 8,398 ms that is ~13.6 ns per comparison — exactly what a branch plus a slice compare costs. The model also predicted the 2,000-node point at 0.99 s against 1.14 s measured, so it was checked at two scales before any code changed.

⭐ THE FIRST HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG AND SAYING SO IS THE LESSON. The obvious guess was "adjacency lists are read-modify-write per edge insert". Reading the code killed it: `adj_out_key(graph_id, from_id, edge_type, to_id)` includes the target id, so every edge is its OWN key — three puts, no reads. The real cost was on the READ side, in a helper nobody would look at when thinking about write performance. **A performance guess that names a plausible mechanism is worth exactly nothing until the code is read.**

⚠️ WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: `import_graph` already builds a map of every node id in the document, so it could have skipped the endpoint existence check entirely and got a similar speedup. Rejected — that weakens a store invariant (`create_edge` refuses dangling edges, and the comment above it records the defect that motivated the refusal) to work around a lookup bug, and it would have fixed exactly one caller while leaving every other batch reader slow.

VERIFIED: 1,452 core tests pass, including the two corners this could have broken — `buffer_aware_get_late_put_resurrects_after_prefix_delete` and `batch_prefix_delete_visible_within_batch`. clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` and fmt clean. clippy also caught the now-dead `BufferedOp::affecting`, the linear-scan helper this replaced, which was removed.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
`StorageEngine`'s write buffer was a bare `Vec<BufferedOp>`, and every buffered read did `buffer.iter().rev().find_map(|op| op.affecting(cf, key))` — a linear scan of the entire buffer, per lookup. `DesignGraph::create_edge` checks that both endpoints exist, so importing a design costs two buffered reads per edge while the buffer keeps growing, which is quadratic.

The buffer is now a `WriteBuffer` struct: the ordered `Vec` is kept (the backend applies it in order, and a late Put must resurrect a key an earlier PrefixDelete tombstoned), with a `BTreeMap<(CfId, Vec<u8>), usize>` mapping an exact key to the POSITION of its latest Put/Delete, plus a separate small list of PrefixDelete positions. Lookups resolve by comparing positions, so ordering semantics are unchanged. `BTreeMap` rather than `HashMap` because the same index also serves `prefix_scan`, whose pre-flight (`buffer_touches_scan`, now deleted) was a second linear walk — it is answered by a range query now, and the overlay applies only the ops that actually bear on the range, still in insertion order.

MEASURED on reflow2's own design (3,140 nodes / 13,390 edges), release, in-memory backend, no full-text index:

    TOTAL to queryable   8,828 ms  ->    909 ms   (9.7x)
    of which import      8,398 ms  ->    705 ms  (11.9x)

Every batch reader benefits, not just import: the bulk tools, `apply_heal` and merge application all read through the same buffered path.

The same name collision that forced `cmp:graph-algorithms` in increment 3 applies here, which is why this is not called `cmp:schema-core` or folded into the existing node.

Every other absorption left the majority behind — 82% of vector, 75% of resolution, 42% of graph. reflow2 imports eight of core's names and needs all four of its files. "Only take what we need" happened to mean "take all of it", and that is a measurement rather than a concession.

⭐ IT IS ALSO WHY INCREMENTS 4 AND 5 COULD NOT BE SPLIT. `dynograph-storage` re-exported `DynoError`, `Schema` and `Value` from here, and `StoredNode.properties` is a `HashMap<String, Value>` of this very type — so taking this in-tree while storage stayed external would have given reflow2 two of each. See `chg:increments-4-and-5-are-one-increment`.

In the code the same clash bites harder: every absorbed file said `crate::graph` meaning ITS graph module, which in reflow2 resolves to `DesignGraph`. The imports were rewritten to `crate::graphalg::` for that reason.

WHO USES IT: `cmp:structure` and `cmp:allocate` (both in `sys:coherence-loop`) and `cmp:flow` (in `sys:vocabulary`) — which is why it sits in `sys:foundation` rather than inside any one of them. ⚖️ IT CARRIES `#![allow(dead_code)]`, deliberately. Eight items are unused from reflow2's point of view — two error variants, three policy variants, two accessors, a helper. They stay because the files are kept VERBATIM so they remain diffable against upstream, which is what the provenance requirement actually rests on. Anthony, 2026-08-24: *"don't trim now - if we decide it isn't necessary, then we can trim in the future."*

properties.name: handshake

📌 The near-match offered was `cap:the-handshake-is-written-down-beside-the-graph` — the FUNCTION. This is the PART that holds it.

⭐ IT IS A FILE BECAUSE THE PROTOCOL MAY BE THE BROKEN THING. It exists for a client whose every structured tool reply is an unreadable stub, so the question it answers — *which client am I, and what did we agree on?* — cannot be answered through a tool reply. It reaches disk, where a person opens it and pastes it into a report.

⚠️ IT MIRRORS A RULE IT CANNOT CALL. rmcp's `negotiate_protocol_version` is `pub(crate)`, so this reproduces four lines: echo the client's requested version if `supported_protocol_versions()` contains it, else the server's fallback. A test pins that so an rmcp change is loud rather than a silent divergence in what this server answers `initialize` with.

Placed under `sub:serving` beside `cmp:service` and `cmp:shared`, because what it does is the connection handshake. Given a part of its own under the ruling recorded as `chg:allocation-follows-the-code-not-the-neighbour` (2026-08-25): it is a real, checksummed module, so crediting its function to `cmp:service` next door would be the neighbour-misfiling that ruling corrects.

properties.name: memory-backend
properties.purpose:
The volatile `KvBackend` implementation: six `BTreeMap`s, one per column family. No durability, no cross-key atomicity beyond the single-threaded `commit_batch` loop.

`crates/reflow2-core/src/foundation/store/backend.rs` (`MemoryBackend`). Reached through `DesignGraph::open_in_memory`, and it needs no cargo feature — `reflow2-core`'s `default = []` means this is the backend you get unless somebody asks for the other one.

⭐ IT IS NOT A TEST DOUBLE, WHICH IS THE THING MOST LIKELY TO BE ASSUMED ABOUT IT. Measured 2026-08-25: **1,452 core tests pass on it with no RocksDB and no full-text index** — schema validation, the golden thread, adjacency traversal, every detector, HEAL, propagation, the graph algorithms. It serves the same `KvBackend` trait through the same code path, so what passes here is not a weaker claim than what passes on RocksDB; it is the same claim minus durability.

⭐ `BTreeMap` AND NOT `HashMap`, AND THAT IS A CONTRACT NOT A TASTE (`chg:the-memory-backend-keeps-its-keys-ordered`, #331). The trait requires ORDERED prefix iteration. A hash map meant iterating the whole column family, filtering, and sorting — O(n log n) per scan. Measured: `export_graph` calls `outgoing()` once per node, so exporting reflow2's own design was ~42M key comparisons and 1,137 ms; as a range query it is 236 ms. The trade is real — inserts went O(1) to O(log n), import ~8% slower — and the round trip is 37% better.

⇒ THIS IS THE COMPONENT THE NO-DATABASE QUESTION TURNS ON. If `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability` resolves toward the document as the enduring artifact, this becomes the only backend and `cmp:rocksdb-backend` is what gets retired.

MODELLED 2026-08-25 alongside its sibling; neither had a node before. Kept distinct from `chg:the-memory-backend-keeps-its-keys-ordered`, which is the CHANGE that altered this component, not the component itself.

properties.name: packaging
properties.purpose:
How reflow2 SHIPS — the part of the system that turns a build into something a consumer can install, pin and run.

Owns what already exists and was never modelled: release.yml's per-platform binary matrix (linux-x86_64, macos-arm64, macos-x86_64), the consumer kit and its manifest, and the install/update path. Adds the container image: a Dockerfile, a linux/amd64 (and possibly linux/arm64) build, version tagging from [workspace.package] so consumers pin rather than chase latest, publication to a pullable registry, and a non-root runtime uid that matches the mounted volume's ownership.

RECORDED BECAUSE THE BLIND SPOT WAS PRE-EXISTING, not because the container created it. The design's 54 other components mirror Rust modules, so nothing owned the shipping path even though the release workflow, the kit and the installer are real, load-bearing artifacts and req:frictionless-update is accepted intent. Capturing flo2's container requirement is what walked into it.

Also carries the documentation obligation that comes with a server image: reflow2 has NO authentication, --http-allow-host is DNS-rebinding protection only, and the image must be stated to require a private network behind a gateway that does authorize.

The graph registry: a process-level map from graph_id to an open design, owning the per-graph metadata that today rides on ReflowService as per-process state — graph_path, content_path, identity, and the write_gen counter the loop nudge reads (service.rs:94-99).

New module, does not exist today. What binds the process to one graph is the CLI contract and the startup path in main.rs, not the core: DesignGraph::open_rocksdb (graph.rs:113) is already a plain function call with no process-global state, and ReflowService.graph is already Arc<RwLock<DesignGraph>> (service.rs:74) because several sessions already share one server. So this component is a map of things already shaped to be shared, plus a lifecycle — on-demand bounded opening, single-flight so concurrent first requests for one graph collapse into one open, an idle timeout per graph, and a cap on simultaneously open graphs with a stated error at the cap.

properties.name: rocksdb-backend
properties.purpose:
The durable `KvBackend` implementation: RocksDB over six named column families, one column family per key space, with the engine's exclusive write lock coming from RocksDB's own directory lock.

`crates/reflow2-core/src/foundation/store/backend.rs` (`RocksBackend`). Reached only through `DesignGraph::open_rocksdb`.

🛑 IT IS OPT-IN AND ALWAYS HAS BEEN. `reflow2-core` declares `default = []`; only `reflow2-mcp` enables `features = ["rocksdb", "fulltext"]`. Measured 2026-08-25: 1,452 of the core's tests pass with this component absent entirely. Without the feature `open_rocksdb` fails loud rather than falling back, which is `req:no-silent-fallback` applied to a missing backend.

⚠️ EXTERNAL DEPENDENCY, DELIBERATELY PINNED WHERE IT IS: `rocksdb` 0.24 — the historically-unmaintained wrapper. `rust-rocksdb` 0.52 is the maintained one; the numbers are NOT comparable (different crates, independent numbering). `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately` keeps that 86-file migration to one variable.

⚖️ WHAT IT COSTS, measured: a ~19-minute `librocksdb-sys` C++ compile on a clean build, and the bulk of a target directory that reached 263 GiB. What it buys: durability across a process restart and larger-than-RAM working sets. `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability` is the open question about whether that trade is worth it.

MODELLED 2026-08-25, and it did not exist as a node until then — which is why "can we retire RocksDB?" had no answer: the design had nothing to point at.

Absorbed from `dynograph-text` at v0.12.0 on 2026-08-24 into `crates/reflow2-core/src/foundation/text.rs` — 847 lines, reached only through the `fulltext` feature.

🛑 IT WAS INVISIBLE TO EVERY EARLIER COSTING OF THE ABSORPTION. reflow2 never named `dynograph-text` in any manifest: it arrived transitively through `dynograph-storage`'s optional `fulltext` feature, which reflow2 enables. ⚠️ AND IT IS THE ONE PIECE WITH A KNOWN HISTORY OF LEAKING. In-tree that class of leak stops being possible: there is no boundary left for a type to cross unnoticed.

(Distinct from `dep:dynograph-foundation`, the Resource recording the external dependency this ENDS, and from reflow2's own search module, which is the caller rather than the index.)
