• **Switch to `rust-rocksdb` 0.52 during the absorption** — the maintained crate, but an API change stacked on top of the largest migration in the plan.

📌 STILL PARKED, and deliberately: `dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds` (redb, fjall, LMDB, SQLite). Anthony, same exchange: *"I know we brainstormed switching to redb, but I'm still not convinced that is the right move - so that one stays parked for a time."* **Parked is not rejected**, and the spike he asked for stays owed. Note the ordering that makes it possible at all: the `KvBackend` trait is `pub(crate)` inside dynograph-storage, so no spike can be written from reflow2 until increment 4 lands.
properties.name: DECIDED — absorb the `rocksdb` 0.24 pin exactly as it is, and switch to the maintained `rust-rocksdb` in its own later PR
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the decision is small and the reasoning is the whole of it: absorbing verbatim is not laziness, it is keeping the number of variables at one.

⭐ THE FINDING IS ANTHONY'S AND IT WAS NOT VISIBLE FROM INSIDE THE PLAN. The absorption scoping measured lines, files, closures and type boundaries — and never asked whether the external crate being inherited was the right one. **A migration that faithfully carries a dependency forward will faithfully carry a bad choice of dependency forward too**, and nothing in the costing would have said so.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-24 by Anthony: *"I kind of don't want to be dependent upon dynograph-foundation anymore"* and *"by absorbing, I don't mean all dynograph-foundation crates - I mean only the ones that are needed in reflow2."*

This CHOOSES among the options `dec:idea-cannibalize-dynograph-foundation-into-reflow2` costed and left open. That node stays as the record of the options; this one records the choice and the plan.

═══ 🛑 THE PLAN WAS CORRECTED 2026-08-24 — IT WAS FIVE INCREMENTS AND IT IS FOUR ═══

**As first written this decision promised "five increments, each independently shippable, stop after any of". That was true for 1, 2 and 3 and FALSE for 4 and 5.** The prior text is preserved at `snap:epoch:the-absorption:dec:absorb-the-foundation-subset-and-end-the-dependency`; the correction is `chg:increments-4-and-5-are-one-increment`.

WHY: `dynograph-storage/src/lib.rs:32` re-exports `pub use dynograph_core::{DynoError, Schema, Value}`, and `StoredNode.properties` is `HashMap<String, Value>` of that same type. Absorbing core while storage stays external gives reflow2 TWO distinct types called `Value` and TWO called `DynoError` — the in-tree ones, and the ones every `StorageEngine` call keeps returning. 48 files name `DynoError`, 33 name `Value`. Nothing compiles. No ordering avoids it: storage DEPENDS ON core, so it cannot go first.

⭐ HOW THE COSTING MISSED IT: it measured each crate's SIZE, each crate's IMPORT COUNT, and the dependency DIRECTION between crates. It never asked whether two crates share TYPES ACROSS the boundary. **A dependency graph tells you what needs what to build; it does not tell you what breaks if you take one and not the other.** Found by scouting before writing code — two import sites out of eighty-six, and the signal was two lines wide.

═══ WHY THE EARLIER RECOMMENDATION IS NO LONGER THE RIGHT ONE ═══

The brainstorm states the trap plainly: **"Two problems look like one here and have different answers. (a) DEAD WEIGHT ... (b) THE DEPENDENCY ITSELF ... Option C solves (a) and does nothing for (b)."** Option C was recommended and deferred. Anthony has now said which he is solving: **(b)**. C removes two crates from the manifest and leaves the dependency where it is. This is trimmed option A.

⭐ ITS REOPENING TRIGGERS WERE NOT WHAT REOPENED IT. The node named two — the pin-confirmation cost recurring, or reflow2 needing to CHANGE foundation behaviour. **Neither happened.** What reopened it is a third thing that node had already written as option D's counter: *"the reason for absorbing is not technical, it is about what reflow2 IS."* **A deferral's stated triggers are not the only way back in**, and a reader who treats them as exhaustive will hold a decision closed against its owner.

═══ IT STAYS INSIDE THE OWNERSHIP BOUND ═══

`dec:idea-dynograph-crates-independent-in-code-coupled-in-release` sets a bound this decision must respect: *"reflow2's design has no standing to decide [dynograph's structure] ... the only options reflow2 can weigh honestly on its own are A (accept it) and E (take less)."* **This is E, taken to its end.** Every step happens in reflow2's own repository, needs no upstream change, and decides nothing about dynograph-foundation's release structure, its other four crates, or its other consumers. That question stays open and stays theirs.

═══ THE MEASUREMENT THAT DID NOT EXIST BEFORE ═══

Measured 2026-08-24 at v0.12.0 (`b5a9f74`), file by file, from every `use dynograph_*` in reflow2 and the internal closure of what those names reach:

    crate                 needed    total    dead
    dynograph-core         1,941    1,941      0%   the whole type vocabulary
    dynograph-storage      2,728    2,836      4%   (+2,187 lines of its own tests)
    dynograph-text           847      847      0%   ⇐ NOT IN ANY EARLIER COUNT
    dynograph-graph        2,219    3,832     42%   ⇐ corrected from 1,844/52%
    dynograph-resolution     300    1,211     75%
    dynograph-vector         436    2,377     82%

⇒ **about +15% to reflow2's 53,005-line tree, not the +27% the all-crates figure implied.**

🛑 **SIX CRATES, NOT FIVE.** `dynograph-storage` depends on `dynograph-text` for the `fulltext` feature, and reflow2 USES fulltext. 847 lines, and it brings **tantivy 0.26**. No COSTING of the absorption ever counted it.

OTHER EXTERNAL CRATES INHERITED: `rmp-serde`, `lru`, `rand`, `serde_yaml`, `uuid`, `thiserror`, `tantivy`.

═══ WHAT REFLOW2 WOULD OWN FOREVER — the real cost, and it is not line count ═══

  ~2,700 lines of RocksDB storage engine (backend, keys, cache, engine/*)
    847 lines of tantivy-backed full-text index
    695 lines of Leiden community detection
  1,752 lines of schema engine (core/schema.rs)

═══ ONE RECORDED OBJECTION WEAKENS, ONE STANDS ═══

⭐ WEAKER — *"you lose the upstream's fixes silently."* **Upstream is Anthony's own repository.** No vendor, no third party. And storyflow keeps dynograph-foundation alive through its REST surface, which `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface` measured as disjoint from reflow2's Rust-library surface. The repo does not die and storyflow is untouched; reflow2 stops linking it, that is all.

🛑 STANDS — *"Vendoring converts a visible dependency into an invisible one."* The pin carries a written reason for every bump; the v0.11→v0.12 note recording a `TextHit` type leak is real history with no successor once the code is in-tree. MITIGATION, required rather than optional: each increment records a ChangeEvent naming the exact TAG absorbed and the FILES taken, and each absorbed module carries a header saying the same.

═══ THE PLAN — FOUR increments ═══

  ✅ 1. VECTOR → `stats.rs` (436 lines, 1 importing file). SHIPPED, PR #326.
  ✅ 2. RESOLUTION → `fuzzy.rs` (300 lines, 3 files). SHIPPED, PR #327 — and it took
        dynograph-vector out of the BUILD GRAPH with it, discharging increment 1's caveat.
  ✅ 3. GRAPH → `graphalg/` (2,219 lines, 3 files). SHIPPED, PR #328.
        ⭐ ZERO new external dependencies. Dropped 1,613 lines in nine files.
  ⬜ 4. CORE + STORAGE + TEXT, TOGETHER AND NOT SEPARABLE (~5,516 lines, ~86 files).
        Brings rocksdb and tantivy. **THIS IS THE ONE THAT ENDS THE DEPENDENCY.**

⭐ AFTER 1-3 — reached 2026-08-24: three of six crates gone, ~2,955 lines moved, 7 files of
churn, and NO new external crate in the tree. **This is a genuine stopping point and it is the
LAST one.** Step 4 has no interior stopping point at all, which is precisely what the original
plan got wrong.

🛑 STEPS 1-3 SHRANK THE DEPENDENCY; ONLY STEP 4 ENDS IT. "We absorbed the foundation" said before
step 4 lands would be false.

═══ WHAT THIS DECIDES BY CONSTRUCTION, AND WHAT IT CANCELS ═══

`dec:idea-is-the-foundation-a-subsystem-or-a-supplier` is answered by construction on completion: no supplier left to be. The five `ifc:req-dyno-*` interfaces are then RETIRED on the record — they were true — not deleted.

🛑 CANCELS mirroring dynograph's published surface into reflow2, dropped on Anthony's word the same day it was proposed: absorbing removes the seam a mirror would describe, so the two are ALTERNATIVES. The flo2 → reflow2 mirror is unaffected. Also moot: the v0.13.0 pin parked since 2026-08-19.
properties.name: DECIDED — absorb only what reflow2 needs from dynograph-foundation and end the dependency, in FOUR increments: three you can stop after, and a fourth that cannot be split
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own node rather than by editing the brainstorm, because that node's value is the OPTIONS and their costs and it should keep reading as where the thinking happened.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT LESSON, and it is the second time in one day: the earlier costing measured whole crates and stated honestly what it had not measured. Measuring the missing part changed the headline from +27% to +15% AND found a sixth crate (`dynograph-text`, and tantivy behind it) that no costing of this idea mentions. **A number that answers a narrower question than the one being asked is not evidence about the wider one** — the same shape as the edge-only shortlist measurement corrected earlier today, one level up.

🛑 A STALE PREMISE FOUND WHILE READING THE SIBLINGS, and it is not corrected here because correcting another node's text is a separate act: `dec:idea-dynograph-crates-independent-in-code-coupled-in-release` states that this decision is recorded in reflow2's graph "because dynograph-foundation has no reflow2 design of its own". **It has one.** Verified 2026-08-24 with `describe_designs`, which opens nothing: graph_id `dynograph-foundation`, origin `adopted`, minted by 0.16.0, with a committed 179-node export and a `docs/published-surface.json` carrying 15 published Interfaces. The premise was true when written and is false now.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-24 by Anthony — *"go with (c), distribute by function"* — after asking the question that forced it: **"are these components being taken from dynograph-foundation being added to an existing subsystem or a new subsystem?"**

Each absorbed piece joins the component that USES it. `dynograph-core`'s types land in `sys:foundation` beside `cmp:schema` and `cmp:nodes` because that is what they are; the graph algorithms join the graph component; the storage engine joins `sys:store`. **No `sys:absorbed-foundation` is created.**

═══ WHY NOT A DEDICATED SUBSYSTEM ═══

It was the obvious alternative and it is the wrong one: a subsystem for absorbed code would **rebuild in the model the very boundary the absorption removes**. The point of absorbing is that there is no supplier any more. Keeping a labelled block of "their code" preserves a seam that has stopped existing, and every later reader would have to be told it means "historically foreign" rather than "architecturally separate".

Provenance does not need a subsystem to survive. It lives in the file headers (tag, commit, file, what was taken, what was not) and in each increment's ChangeEvent, so **"what came from outside?" stays answerable without a structural marker**.

═══ ⭐⭐ THIS RESOLVES `dec:idea-is-the-foundation-a-subsystem-or-a-supplier`, AND BY HIS OWN EARLIER ARGUMENT ═══

That node has been open since 2026-08-17 with three options: A leave it a supplier (what the design says today), B add it as a ninth black box, C complete the supplier treatment.

**The answer is none of them, because absorption dissolves the question.** And the way it dissolves is the interesting part:

Option B was rejected on a specific ground — *"a subsystem you do not build, cannot change, and release separately is not a subsystem — modelling it as one asserts ownership reflow2 does not have."* **Absorption removes all three objections at once.** After it, reflow2 DOES build it, CAN change it, and does NOT release it separately. The objection was never to the idea; it was to the ownership, and the ownership is what changed.

And his motivation on that node is the strongest argument for distributing rather than fencing: *"I wanted graph theory to undergird everything ... graph theory was important to my concept of reflow2."* **Something that undergirds everything is not a box beside everything.** Option (c) puts it where he said it belonged a week before this decision was taken.

⚠️ Option C's finding SURVIVES and is not closed by this: the design's picture of its supplier is partial — `dynograph-text` is consumed transitively with no interface node, and "what does the foundation offer that we do not take?" is unanswerable from the graph. For the crates being absorbed that stops mattering. For anything left external it still does.

═══ 🛑 THE CONDITION ON INCREMENTS 3-5, from his other question ═══

He also asked: *"I'd imagine in adding these, we are building capabilities/functions that have no requirements in reflow2?"* **Correct, and it is a real hazard from increment 3 onward.**

Today those behaviours are modelled as `ifc:req-dyno-*` at `designation: required` — which is a legitimate way to have no requirement: reflow2 is not claiming to DO the thing, it is claiming to NEED it. Absorption deletes that framing. Nothing would then say why reflow2 stores in RocksDB or detects communities with Leiden.

⇒ **WRITING THE REQUIREMENT IS PART OF THE INCREMENT, NOT CLEANUP AFTER IT.** reflow2 has a detector for exactly this (`unmotivated_capability`), so the design will say so rather than anyone having to remember — but a gap raised after the code lands is a gap raised late.

⭐ INCREMENT 1 IS CLEAN AND THAT IS WHY IT WENT FIRST: `stats.rs` is implementation beneath `cap:dimensions`, which already SATISFIES `req:coherence`. No new capability, no new requirement owed. It also got NO component of its own — 35 lines of arithmetic do not earn one, and minting `cmp:stats` would be the over-engineering this project watches for.

═══ ⚠️ THE SNAG THIS ORDER WALKS INTO ═══

`cmp:graph` exists in BOTH designs for different things — reflow2's graph module and dynograph's graph crate. It is one of the three id collisions that would have blocked the mirror. **Increment 3 needs a distinct component name for the absorbed algorithms**, decided before the code moves rather than discovered while moving it.
properties.name: DECIDED — absorbed foundation code is distributed BY FUNCTION into the components that use it, and no "absorbed" subsystem is created
properties.rationale:
Recorded separately from the absorption plan because it answers a MODELLING question rather than a scoping one, and because it settles a decision open for a week on grounds that node could not have reached: it weighed where the boundary should sit while the supplier existed, and this changes whether there is a supplier.

⭐ THE PATTERN WORTH KEEPING: an option rejected for a reason can become correct when the reason stops holding, and nothing re-examines it automatically. Option B was rejected because reflow2 did not own the code. Nobody would have re-read that node on the day the ownership changed — it surfaced only because Anthony asked where the absorbed components go. **A rejection carries its ground; when the ground moves the rejection is worth re-reading, and no mechanism does that.**

properties.decision: The distinction req:skill-adherence-is-measured offered is REAL, and it is drawn here: dec:loop-status-state-not-history governs what the LOOP may reason from when it computes debt, and adoption data may never enter that computation. It does not forbid the KIT reporting a fact about itself. Three things make the line enforceable rather than promised: (1) adoption is counted in SESSION state — the hook's per-session tally file — and in transcripts read offline, never in the design graph, so it is not graph state and cannot be reasoned from as if it were; (2) no adoption field is read by loop_status, detect_gaps or detect_defects; (3) a check asserts that the loop's answer is UNCHANGED whether or not adoption data exists, which is what converts the separation from a convention into a property. The test to apply to any future addition: does this measurement ever change what the loop says is owed? If yes, it is forbidden regardless of what it is called.
properties.name: The kit may report its own adoption, because adoption never reaches the debt computation — and a test holds that line rather than a promise
properties.rationale:
WHY THE DISTINCTION IS NOT A RATIONALISATION, which is what the requirement asked to be settled. dec:loop-status-state-not-history exists to protect ONE thing: the answer to "what does this design still need?" must not depend on who did what. If debt read run history, two identical designs would owe different things because their session logs differ, and the design would stop being the single source of truth. That is the harm, and it is specific. Adoption answers a different question, for a different reader, with a different consequence — "is the TOOL being used as intended?", read by the maintainer, changing the TOOL. It never touches the protected answer. So the distinction is not "a different name for the same thing"; it is a different question that happens to be answered from the same kind of evidence, and the decision constrains the QUESTION rather than the evidence.

THE PRECEDENT ALREADY EXISTS AND WAS FOUND RATHER THAN INVENTED. tools/surface_usage.py has done exactly this since 2026-08-01: it reads session transcripts offline, counts get_skill calls among them, and states in its own module docstring that it "writes nothing back into any design — 'looking is not writing' (dec:loop-status-state-not-history). Nothing here becomes graph state." So the shape this decision blesses was already shipping and already reasoned; what was missing was the ruling that makes it deliberate rather than incidental, and a place for the near-real-time half.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY BUILT UNDER IT, and why it is small. The measurement half largely existed. The hole named by chg:undefer-skill-adherence-measurement is different and narrower: cap:skill-triggers recognises SHAPES, every shape it knows is a shape in the graph-write stream, and "no skill has been loaded" is not a graph write — so the one situation the user kept having to correct by hand was the one situation the mechanism structurally could not see. Counting get_skill per session closes that, and it is session state by nature.

THE COST THIS ACCEPTS, stated because the file it lands in resists exactly this. A new arming branch is a NEW interruption, and ver:skill-triggers' own counterweight says a trigger that fires on correct work is the failure BL-23 and BL-42 both name. So the branch is placed LAST, after every other Stop branch has declined, and is conjoined tightly: the session must have TOUCHED reflow2 (a total bypass is already caught upstream), must have edited at least the bypass threshold of files (so a trivial or read-only session is silent), and must have loaded ZERO skills. It therefore fires only on the session that did everything else right and still never opened a skill — which is precisely the case a human had to catch, twice, by asking.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. This measures LOADING, not FOLLOWING. An agent can call get_skill and ignore every word of it, and nothing here would know. Adherence in the strong sense stays unmeasured, and the requirement's name should not be read as claiming otherwise. The honest claim is that not-loading is now visible where it was invisible.

BOUNDARY CARRIED FORWARD from the requirement, unchanged: whatever is reported respects report-friction's redaction discipline — tool names and argument SHAPES, node TYPES not ids, counts not contents — because reflow2 installs into other people's projects and the thing being measured is the user, not their design.

Approved by Anthony 2026-08-07 ("yes, build it") against the recommendation as stated, after he asked for the question in plain terms. The prior "yes, build it" of 2026-08-06 un-deferred the requirement; this settles the precondition it carried.

properties.decision: Take a claim when you need one and start — but publish it by pushing it, every time, not only when contested; a claim nobody can see is not a claim. When two claims cross, the winner is whichever landed first in git history, and both parties can verify that independently. Rejected: a coordination service or lock manager (contradicts dec:multi-writer-architecture, and single-writer exclusion is the observed failure), and asking before every claim (the fleet measured that timidity starves the pool).
properties.name: Seats coordinate by announcement and provable order, never by exclusion
properties.rationale: The StoryFlow fleet runs 15+ concurrent seats on exactly this rule — grab-and-go, announce always, crossings settled "first-on-disk, both provable". reflow2 has better material for the provable half than a markdown timestamp: a content-hash chain and git order. The alternative people reach for by reflex is a lock, and a lock is exactly what took five of six sessions offline on 2026-07-25.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, closing the pointer-granularity question under `cap:content-store` before anything is built.

reflow2 BUILDS NO RETRIEVAL LAYER. No span vocabulary, no chunk-addressing scheme, no offsets in the schema, no search into blobs. Reading a 1000-page document and finding the relevant passage is the AGENT's job, and an agent already does it well.

WHY THIS IS DOCTRINE RATHER THAN A SHORTCUT. It is the division of labour reflow2 already has, applied to a new component. `dec:three-party-checks`: "The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides." Navigating content is squarely the first of those. The precedent is consistent across the system — reflow2 performs NO FILE I/O, and `coverage_report` and `reconcile_artifacts` take what the agent observed rather than scanning; `dec:corpus-ingest-mechanism` makes extraction itself the agent's job through the SP-3b handshake. Adding a blob changes where bytes live, not who reads them.

THE ONE PART THAT IS NOT THE AGENT'S JOB, and it is the whole reason this decision is not simply "do nothing": NAVIGATING is the agent's, RECORDING WHERE IT LANDED is the graph's. If an agent reads a corpus, extracts a requirement, and the graph stores only "this came from that document", then auditing that requirement later means RE-RUNNING A NON-DETERMINISTIC SEARCH — and a different agent may land elsewhere and reach a different conclusion. The design would hold a provenance link that does not reproduce, which is a link that cannot do the one job provenance has.

THE MECHANISM IS A CONVENTION, NOT A FEATURE. `Fragment.content_ref` already exists and is already declared as "pointer to the source content (path/hash)" — an opaque string. The agent writes whatever locator suits the medium alongside the content hash: a line range for markdown, a page for a PDF, a timestamp for a transcript, a cell for a spreadsheet. reflow2 STORES IT, RETURNS IT, AND NEVER INTERPRETS IT — no parsing, no validation of the locator's shape, no computation over it. The next agent knows what to do with it because it is the same kind of agent that wrote it. Zero new vocabulary, zero new code, and the audit trail reproduces.

A CORRECTION ON THE RECORD, because the argument that nearly went the other way was wrong. It was argued that spans go stale when a document is edited, and that content-addressed chunks were therefore safer. That objection assumed MUTABLE FILES, which `dec:where-content-lives` had already ruled out: blobs are content-addressed and immutable, so an edited document is a DIFFERENT HASH rather than the same one with shifted lines. A locator into a content-addressed blob cannot rot. The staleness case was smuggling in an assumption the storage decision had already removed.

PRIOR ART CHECKED, so nobody reviews it again. The official MCP memory server (`modelcontextprotocol/servers/src/memory`) was read on Anthony's prompt. Its model is entities / relations / observations in a JSONL file, eight tools, substring search. IT OFFERS NOTHING ON THIS QUESTION because it never meets it — no chunking, no external pointers, no spans, no large content; everything is short atomic strings held inline. What it DOES corroborate is the deeper answer: its stated rule is "observations should be atomic — one fact per observation", i.e. decompose at WRITE time so there is never a large thing to search at READ time. That is the same conclusion `cap:session-memory` reached independently ("a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation"). EXPLICITLY NOT IMPORTED: `read_graph` returning the entire graph (at 1000+ nodes it would swamp a context window; `cap:bounded-reads` is better and exists for this reason); untyped free-string entity types (the typed schema is what makes detectors computable at all); and delete-without-history, which is what `req:intent-preserved` forbids and `retire-from-design` exists to prevent.
properties.name: The agent navigates content; the graph records where it landed — an opaque locator reflow2 never parses
properties.rationale:
Anthony's framing, and it is sharper than "do not reinvent the wheel": the capability already exists in the system, it just does not live in reflow2. An agent that can be told to review a thousand pages does not need reflow2 to teach it how.

THE METHOD FINDING, which is the second instance today and therefore a pattern rather than a coincidence. Two design forks were recorded, both with genuine options and real trade-offs, and BOTH DISSOLVED WHEN SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE DESIGN WAS CHECKED rather than chosen between. `dec:where-content-lives` collapsed once `object_store` turned the storage backend into runtime configuration; this one collapsed once the agent's own capabilities were counted as part of the system. In both cases the recorded options were honest and the deliberation was not wasted — it is what made the dissolution recognisable. The habit worth keeping: before choosing between branches of a fork, ask what already exists that would make the fork unnecessary. Design inward only after looking outward.

Left as a convention deliberately rather than a validated field, because validating a locator's shape would mean reflow2 deciding what media exist — and the moment someone stores something nobody anticipated, a validator becomes a refusal of correct work. An opaque string costs nothing and forecloses nothing.

properties.decision:
`gap_id` keys a gap on its RULE alone when the gap is an AGGREGATE — one per project, whose `affected_ids` are the whole population the rule ranges over rather than the nodes the finding is about. Every other gap keeps hashing its affected set. Today exactly one source qualifies: `unvalidated_capability`.

The discriminator is an explicit `GapSource::is_aggregate()` written as an exhaustive match, not a wildcard, so a future aggregate detector has to come to this function and decide rather than silently inheriting per-node keying.

NOT KEYED ON `GapScope::Project`, which is the obvious-looking answer and is wrong. `unsatisfied_requirement` and `status_contradiction` are project-SCOPED but carry a single requirement each, and `kpp_breached` is per-KPP. Keying on scope would collapse every unsatisfied requirement in the design into one gap sharing one judgement — accept one and the rest go silent. A test pins this specific trap (`a_project_scoped_but_per_node_gap_still_keys_on_its_subject`) and a mutation confirms it fails when the trap is taken.

Also NOT chosen: (b) expiring only when a member is removed, which keeps the id unstable and merely narrows when it moves; (c) letting each acknowledgement declare its own expiry condition, which is more machinery than the problem needs and puts the judgement about mechanism into every reason string; (d) modelling rollups as a different KIND of gap, which is a schema change for something the id function can express.
properties.name: An aggregate gap is keyed on its rule; every other gap still keys on its subject
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word, 2026-07-30: he was told the finding had a close sibling in the defect-side mechanism and said that was a good approach.

WORTH RECORDING PRECISELY, because the reading that prompted this was half wrong. The sibling was described as "defect acknowledgements expire by shape, and this is the gap side catching up". Reading the code showed `heal.rs`'s `issue_id(category, affected)` hashes its affected set exactly as `gap_id` does — the defect side has no cleverer keying. What it actually has is the `retired` REPORTING that `reviewed_gaps` already implements too. So mirroring the sibling alone would not have fixed anything: the churn comes from the id derivation, and the fix had to be there. The sibling still earns its place, because `retired` reporting is what makes a stable id safe — when the rule stops firing the standing review is shown as retired rather than silently kept.

THE TRADE-OFF IS REAL AND ACCEPTED. A stable id means a capability added later is covered by the earlier judgement without a fresh look. That is what a STANDING disposition means — "validation is tracked in the trials programme" is a claim about the practice, not about any one capability — and it is what the twenty re-acknowledgements were each re-asserting unchanged. The growth stays visible without the churn: a review records the count it was made at in its own reason, and the live gap's title carries the count now, so a reader comparing them sees the set grew.

THE MIGRATION IS DELIBERATE AND VISIBLE. The rollup's id moves once, from the member-hashed `gap:80f8bc457bfe9e16` to the stable `gap:0a77650b58242054`, so the twenty historical acknowledgements no longer match it and one fresh acknowledgement is needed — the last one this gap should ever need. Those twenty are left exactly as they are rather than withdrawn: withdrawal marks a Decision `superseded`, which would claim the judgement was revoked, and it was not. `reviewed_gaps` reports them as `retired` instead, which is the honest description — the judgement was real and the situation it named has moved on.

properties.decision:
EPIGRAPH — "Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." — Robert Frost, 'The Road Not Taken'. Aptly, the poem is itself a hindsight tale: the speaker concedes the two roads were worn 'really about the same' and foresees telling it 'with a sigh' ages hence — the difference is authored in retrospect, not known at the fork. That is this decision's whole bet: credit for a road taken is assigned in hindsight, by the human, never scored in advance. (Unofficially, 'the Robert Frost decision.')

reflow2 holds every Decision's alternatives as UNRANKED, forkable siblings — not a scored trade-study runner-up. The design is modelled as a navigable decision-MDP: the graph is the world-model (propagate/detect/compare evaluate a fork's consequences before anything is built), branches are the replay, and the reward signal is two-channel — the structural detectors (in-model holes: SPOFs, cycles, gaps) plus field trials (out-of-model holes only a real episode reveals, e.g. BL-74's loop-on-virtue collapse). Alternatives are stored cheaply (the unchosen option + its rationale, at the decision's epoch) and their consequence design is COMPUTED on demand by forking that epoch and replaying — never eagerly maintained as N full parallel designs, which would combinatorially explode and rot as the main line moves on (a non-stationary design). Which fork to expand is chosen by where the surprise is — a fresh defect, a failed trial, or a rationale that already flags doubt points back to a decision (high 'TD error') — not by enumerating the whole tree. Crucially the human is the reward function and does the credit assignment and policy update; reflow2 supplies the replay buffer and the world-model but never auto-optimizes a design by replay-and-score.
properties.name: Alternatives are unranked forkable siblings; the human judges in hindsight, not a stored score
properties.rationale: User decided the ranked-vs-unranked scope 2026-07-22 after developing the idea across three framings — choose-your-own-adventure (the decision tree you can turn back to), Analysis of Alternatives (the runner-up kept live), and a reinforcement-learning gridworld (replay an episode until you cross without falling in a hole). Unranked over a scored AoA because reflow2 routes judgment to the human (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks): a stored ranking would be the system asserting a preference it cannot honestly hold, and design episodes are too few, too expensive and too subjective for a stationary reward anyway. Derived-over-stored (store the fork, compute the consequence) is reflow2's recurring lesson (dec:certainty-derived, dec:component-verified-computed) and the only defence against an eagerly-maintained alternative rotting under a moving main line. Model-based-planning-not-model-free-crashing is the whole point of a design brain: propagate_change computes the blast radius before you edit, so you simulate the hole instead of falling in it — but BL-74 proves some holes are out-of-model and only a field episode finds them. This unifies the branch (BL-70), merge (dec:merge-three-way / dec:merge-conflict-semantics — how a forked road comes home) and claims (BL-44) threads under one primitive: alternatives as first-class, forkable, comparable, mergeable. The hindsight pass that motivated it is the mechanism already working by hand — dec:merge-survivor-provenance carries a 'reconsider' note tracing a near-bad merge back to its own fork. Deferred to their own decisions: how an alternative attaches to a Decision in the schema, the fork/branch ref layer (BL-70), the 'when has an episode taught us enough to revise' trigger, and the tool surface.

properties.decision:
`release_without_manifest` is raised at severity 0.85, above `reflow2_check`'s default `--gap-threshold` of 0.8, so a Release that is pinned to an epoch, deployed, and includes nothing FAILS the gate rather than appearing as a note.

It joins the band of findings that say the design asserts something untrue — failing_verification 0.80, kpp_contradicted 0.85, kpp_unbound 0.90, kpp_breached 0.95 — rather than the band below it, which holds questions waiting for a human. Its sibling `release_without_epoch` stays at 0.6 and stays a question: WHICH epoch a release belongs to is a judgement, and nothing false has been asserted by the edge's absence.

A genuinely contentless release — a re-tag, a docs-only republish — remains a real state. It is red until somebody acknowledges it with a reason on the record, never red forever.

DISTINCT FROM the requirement it settles a question about: that says the state shall be REPORTED, and would be satisfied by a detector of any severity. This says how loud the report is, which is a separate choice with its own cost — a red build on a contentless release — and could be reversed without touching the requirement at all.
properties.name: DECIDED — a published release recording that it shipped nothing stops the build
properties.rationale:
ANTHONY'S CALL, 2026-08-21, asked as a direct choice between stopping the build, staying a note at 0.65, and expressing it as a DesignRule carrying enforcement. He chose to stop the build.

THE EVIDENCE PUT TO HIM, AND IT IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT: a note was already demonstrably not enough. The v0.38.0 cut passed `reflow2_check` GREEN with 96 notes scrolling past it, and that is exactly how a tag was pushed, built, published and asset-verified over an empty manifest. A finding nobody is made to read is not a finding.

THE COST WAS STATED BEFORE HE CHOSE: a release that really did ship no new content will red-build until acknowledged, which is one call with his reason attached.

WHY NOT THE DESIGNRULE ROUTE, which was offered and not taken: it is the cleaner separation of "how bad" from "does CI fail", and it would have needed checking that the rule actually reaches `reflow2_check`. Left on the table rather than refuted — if severity ever has to be tuned for a reason unrelated to CI, that is the route back.

THE NUMBER IS NOT TUNED TO THE THRESHOLD. 0.85 sits above 0.80 with room, deliberately, so raising `--gap-threshold` one notch does not silently drop the rule out of the gate — the failure mode this whole line of work exists to prevent.

properties.decision:
A property whose value is an id is NOT automatically a node reference. Four kinds exist in this design, measured 2026-08-29 across every `*_id` property with no minimum-instance floor, and only the first takes `node_ref: true`:

① **NODE REFERENCE** — names a node that must exist for the record to mean anything. Dangling is a real defect. `TemporalFact.subject_id` (334 values, 334 resolve). DECLARED.

② **HISTORICAL ANCHOR** — resolves when written, and is EXPECTED to stop resolving. The record exists to survive its target. `Snapshot.target_id` (196 values, 192 resolve; all 4 dangles correct). NOT DECLARED.

③ **COMPUTED-FINDING REFERENCE** — names something calculated and never stored as a node, so it resolves to nothing by construction. `Question.gap_id` (57 values, 0 resolve — the correct reading, not rot). NOT DECLARED.

④ **CROSS-DESIGN REFERENCE** — names a GRAPH rather than a node. `Resource.dependency_graph_id` (1 value, `dynograph-foundation`). NOT DECLARED, and not a declared property at all.

THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS: `node_ref` is applied only to ① — and where it is withheld, THE DECLARATION ITSELF SAYS WHY, in the schema description, because that is the text a reader meets. Done for `Snapshot.target_id` and `Question.gap_id`.

⚠️ THREE ARE DECLARED AND HAVE NEVER BEEN WRITTEN, so they are recorded as UNDECIDED rather than assigned: `ReadinessAssessment.target_id`, `DimensionAssessment.target_id`, `DimensionObservation.target_id`, all at zero instances. Whether a scored node's later deletion makes the assessment wrong (①) or leaves it as the surviving record of what was scored (②) is the same question, and there is no evidence to settle it. Decide when the first one is written.
properties.name: An id-valued property is one of four kinds, and only one of them is a node reference
properties.rationale:
Recorded on Anthony's word 2026-08-29 — "record the judgement for target_id and gap_id" — after `fact:which-properties-are-node-references-is-a-judgement-made-once-and-never-recorded-for-the-others` found the judgement had been made exactly once, for one property, and never written down for any other.

THREE NEAR-MATCHES WERE OFFERED AND ALL THREE READ IN FULL; THIS IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF RECORD. The two facts are MEASUREMENTS — one of the detection hole, one of the cause — and they keep their own numbers and caveats. `dec:a-restore-reports-an-unresolvable-reference-rather-than-refusing-it` is a decision about what an IMPORT does when it meets an unresolvable value. This is the standing rule about which properties are references AT ALL, which is upstream of both: it decides what the guard and the detector are even looking at.

THE DEFECT WAS THE SILENCE, NOT A MISSING FLAG. `subject_id` and `target_id` are declared identically — `type: string, required: true, indexed: true` — and differ only in `node_ref`. Nothing said why, so the next reader had two moves and both were bad: declare it, and a detector starts firing on correct history; leave it, and never learn the omission was deliberate. An unrecorded judgement is indistinguishable from an oversight, and this design has now spent three sessions rediscovering the same class because of it.

⭐ THE FOURTH KIND WAS FOUND BY DROPPING A THRESHOLD, WHICH IS WORTH KEEPING AS METHOD. The root-cause pass swept only the three properties `heal.rs` names, with a three-instance floor to filter noise. Re-run with no floor, `Resource.dependency_graph_id` appeared — one value, naming a graph rather than a node, undeclared in the schema entirely. A filter set to suppress noise had been suppressing a whole category, which is the same shape as the defect that started this thread: an instrument that looks complete because the cases it misses are the ones it cannot see.

WHY NOT SIMPLY DECLARE EVERYTHING THAT LOOKS LIKE A POINTER, which is the tempting simplification: it would refuse every Question this design has ever written (kind ③ resolves to nothing by construction) and make `dangling_reference` report four correct historical records as defects (kind ②). A rule that fires on correct work is worse than no rule — the standing judgement behind `supporting is not conflict` and behind the `required`-designation skip in `unprovided_interface`.

THE THREE UNDECIDED ONES ARE LEFT UNDECIDED ON PURPOSE. Guessing a `node_ref` for a type with zero instances would assert a rule nobody could have tested, at exactly the moment there is no evidence — and a wrong guess would be discovered by the first person to write one, as a refusal they cannot act on.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-26, accepting a ruling the agent drafted and put to him with its alternative. The last two of the thirty-three leaf parts `unallocated_component` reported as holding no function: `cmp:memory-backend` and `cmp:rocksdb-backend`.

═══ WHAT THEY ARE ═══

They are the two interchangeable implementations behind `ifc:kv-backend`, both PROVIDES, sitting under `cmp:byte-store`. Neither carries an Artifact, because neither is one file. `cap:store` — "schema-validated graph store" — is already allocated to `cmp:schema`, `cmp:byte-store` and `cmp:nodes`.

═══ THE RULING ═══

**An interchangeable implementation is named by the contract it satisfies, not by a function of its own.** Both backends already say what they are for, in the design's own vocabulary: they PROVIDE `ifc:kv-backend`. Neither adds a capability the other lacks — that is what makes them swappable, and the whole point of the interface.

The alternative was to allocate `cap:store` to both. Declined: it would put one capability on five components, at which point the WHAT→WHERE binding stops binding anything and says only "somewhere in the storage subsystem". Schema validation is not what a byte backend does.

═══ WHOSE WORD THIS IS ═══

⚠️ **THE REASONING IS THE AGENT'S; THE ACCEPTANCE IS THE OWNER'S, AND THE TWO ARE RECORDED SEPARATELY ON PURPOSE.** It was drafted on 2026-08-25 from the session's own reading, deliberately left `proposed` overnight rather than accepted on his behalf, and put to him as an open question alongside the finished work. He accepted it on 2026-08-26 without amendment.

That distinction is the same one `dec:idea-a-user-carries-a-persona-that-shapes-every-reply` says is load-bearing between a SELF-DESCRIBED and an ASSIGNED reading, and it is worth keeping here for the same reason: a later reader asking "did he actually decide this, or did an agent decide it and nobody objected?" gets a straight answer. He did decide it. He did not originate it.

📌 `cmp:rocksdb-backend` is additionally governed by `dec:the-rust-rocksdb-switch-is-parked-until-the-store-question-settles`. That parks the SWITCH between backends; this parks the question of what either one is FOR. Different questions, both live on the same node.
properties.name: DECIDED — the two byte-store backends hold no function of their own: what they are for is the contract they provide
properties.rationale:
Kept separate from the tool-surface ruling because the justification is genuinely different, and one decision covering both would let a later reader apply the wrong reason to the wrong parts. The tool slices are empty because a surface must not hold its subject's function; these two are empty because two implementations of one contract cannot differ in what they are for without ceasing to be interchangeable.

Recorded as a Decision rather than left as an acknowledgement so that the judgement carries its author and its reasoning, and so a structural detector can read the ruling rather than a reviewer having to remember it.

properties.decision: ACCEPTED on Anthony's word, 2026-08-08: "when we add in unplanned change to a version, we should just slip the other versions up one to accommodate (what was scheduled for v0.25.0 gets pushed to v0.26.0 and what was scheduled for v0.26.0 gets automatically pushed to v0.27.0 and so on)." The planned increment is NOT re-scoped to make room, and the unplanned work is NOT held back to protect the number: the number moves and the plan travels with it, intact. APPLIED IMMEDIATELY to the v0.25.0 cut, which shipped the storyflow HEAL disclosure fixes rather than the READ half epoch:v0250-planned was scoped for. WHAT THIS SETTLES that was otherwise decided ad hoc each time: an unplanned cut has three possible responses — rename the planned increment's contents into the new number (which silently redefines what was agreed), drop items to fit (which asserts a withdrawal nobody made), or slip. Slipping is the only one that changes no promise, and it means a plan's CONTENT is stable while its DATE is not — which is what req:plans-move-honestly already says about confidence decaying with horizon. WHAT IT COSTS, and it is worth stating: every slip renames four or more planned epochs, and the version number is currently baked into their IDs (epoch:v0250-planned), which cannot be renamed. So the routine act this decision makes routine is the one the current id scheme handles worst — see dec:idea-a-planned-increment-is-named-by-content-not-by-number.
properties.name: When unplanned work takes a version number, every planned increment slips up one rather than being re-scoped or squeezed in
properties.rationale: Recorded because it was decided in conversation and would otherwise be re-derived at every cut, which is the failure this project exists to prevent. The immediate trigger: v0.25.0 shipped unplanned work, and I stopped mid-cut rather than assume what should happen to the planned increment — the answer was a policy, not a one-off. Anthony's phrasing makes it automatic ("and so on"), so it is a rule a session can apply without asking again.

properties.decision:
UNDECIDED, recorded 2026-07-28. schema/structure.yaml:108 declares an Anchor node type with design_intent, key_decisions, checksum and created_at. Nothing in the core creates it, nothing reads it, there is no node::ANCHOR constant, and reflow2's own design contains ZERO instances. It was superseded: temporal.rs:62 describes Snapshot as "a checksummed baseline (generalizes the P2 to P3 Anchor)", and Snapshot has 14 live instances while DriftEvent has 37.

THE PART THAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN TIDYING: the schema still advertises the type, and does so from BOTH SIDES of a relationship that cannot exist.

(1) describe_schema returns Anchor to any agent asking what the vocabulary contains, serving this hint with it — "A checksummed baseline of the design taken when leaving P2 for a build round (P3). Not extracted from prose — created by the workflow at the structure to build transition. DriftEvents reference the Anchor they diverged from."

(2) AMENDED 2026-07-28, reviewing resync_protocol.json and phase_transitions.json: DriftEvent's OWN extraction_hint (schema/verify.yaml:63) makes the matching claim from the other end — "A recorded divergence between the design (graph/Anchor) and reality (filesystem/build). Produced by drift detection, not extracted from prose. References the Anchor it diverged from via DEPENDS_ON." No DriftEvent references an Anchor, because none exists; all 37 reference something else. So the vocabulary describes a DEPENDS_ON relationship between two types in both directions, and that relationship has zero instances and no code path that could create one. An agent reading either hint and following it creates a node nothing will ever read, and believes it has anchored a build round.

Three options. (a) RETIRE the type from the schema, which is the honest reading if Snapshot fully covers it — but removing a node type strands any graph that already carries one, the same objection that kept `review` and `simulation` in Verification.method when the taxonomy grew. (b) IMPLEMENT it, if the P2-to-P3 anchoring semantics are meant to survive as something distinct from a general Snapshot. (c) REDIRECT — keep the name as an alias or documented synonym of Snapshot so old graphs still load, while the discovery surface stops advertising it as a separate thing to create.

Whichever is chosen, TWO hints must move with it, not one — that is what the amendment adds. And the question underneath is the same one dec:one-retire-edge asks about edges: what should CONSULT the retirement, and does a retired vocabulary item stop being offered or get offered with a warning?
properties.name: OPEN — the Anchor node type is superseded by Snapshot but still advertised: retire it or implement it?
properties.rationale: Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow's workflow_master.json, whose architecture_anchor is the mechanism this type was modelled on. Recorded rather than fixed because all three options are defensible and the choice is Anthony's — it is a vocabulary call, and those have been his every time. Note the shape it shares with the other findings from this review: a schema declaring something no computation reaches (req:functional-vocabulary-computes), a default asserting a choice nobody made (req:defaults-do-not-assert, req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert), and now a whole TYPE advertised on the discovery surface after being superseded. This is the same defect at node-type granularity, which is the level the earlier sweeps did not examine — they measured properties, not types.

properties.decision: detect_gaps sorts anchored gaps before project-level phase nudges, severity within each band.
properties.name: A gap that names nodes outranks a phase nudge
properties.rationale: A named gap says something is wrong NOW; a nudge says what comes next. Ranking 'next' above 'broken' made three brownfield trials do the useless thing first. Nudges are demoted, never suppressed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: gap-surfacing disciplines 3 and 8.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, on three calls put to him after the mechanism was measured rather than assumed. His original framing is preserved in the snapshot at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:arrival-delta`.

WHAT ARRIVES, PER SCHEDULED ITEM — his three outcomes, the complement he did not name, and a FIFTH his four assume away:
  - DELIVERED — the plan held. Computed from the golden thread (`req:completion-computed`), never asserted.
  - DEFERRED — still intended, the date moved; the report names where it now points.
  - DISCONTINUED — no longer intended at all. Distinct from deferred the way `retire-from-design` distinguishes them: one is a date change, the other a withdrawal.
  - DELIVERED BUT NEVER PLANNED — reported as `added_after_baseline`, work scheduled here after the commitment was taken. A delta measured only against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it, and that is usually where the estimate went.
  - OUTSTANDING — still pointed at a moment that has arrived, and not delivered. THE FOUR ASSUME EVERY UNDELIVERED ITEM WAS CONSCIOUSLY MOVED OR DROPPED, and the commonest case is that nobody touched it and it did not happen. Calling that `discontinued` would put a withdrawal on the record nobody made; calling it `deferred` would invent a date nobody chose. It is exactly the question `req:plans-move-honestly` says must be ASKED and never defaulted — transferred or discontinued — so it is reported as its own outcome and put to the user.

CALL 1 — THE BASELINE IS THE TARGET'S FIRST SNAPSHOT, with every later one returned as the movement trail. The brainstorm said the LAST snapshot, and that does not compute what he asked for: two replans leave epoch 3 holding {A,B,C} then {A,C}, so reading the last says the plan was always {A,C} and B's slip vanishes from the very report meant to show it. Where no snapshot exists the plan has never been recorded as moving, so the live edges ARE the original plan and are the baseline — stated as `BaselineSource`, not implied. ACCEPTED WRINKLE, named rather than hidden: the baseline is whenever a snapshot first happened to be taken, which may predate the plan being complete; where the baseline captured an empty plan the report says so in `notes` and the trail shows the growth.

CALL 2 — `snapshot_node` EXCLUDES BY EDGE ROLE, NOT ENDPOINT TYPE. See `dec:commitment-edges-survive-snapshots`, minted for it.

CALL 3 — A LOSSY SCHEDULE EDIT WITH NO RECORDED CHANGE IS REFUSED, mirroring `record_change` refusing a planned epoch. Removing a `SCHEDULED_FOR`, re-pointing it, or rewriting its modality all destroy a claim; each is refused while the plan is unrecorded, with the refusal naming the `record_change` that unblocks it. ADDING to a plan is deliberately NOT guarded — it destroys no earlier claim, and taxing it would punish correct work, which is the mistake this project keeps finding in detectors. `delete_node` is guarded from both directions too, because retiring a scheduled requirement is precisely how discontinuation happens and would otherwise walk straight past the refusal.

WHAT IS COMPUTED VERSUS STORED, unchanged and load-bearing: NOTHING about the outcome is written down. The plan lives in the epoch's snapshots, delivery is computed from the thread, and storing the result would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first — the same argument that keeps `achieved` out of the `modality` enum.

WHAT FALLS OUT: `missed_obligations`, the `required` claims that did not land — computed violations rather than slips, and the scheduling face of a KPP. And once several epochs have arrived, the confidence `req:plans-move-honestly` wants a planned claim to carry can be MEASURED from arrival history rather than authored — Anthony's Black-Scholes analogy, answered with observation.

DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: delivery is not dated to an epoch, so "delivered during this window but never scheduled anywhere" is not computable and is not claimed. `added_after_baseline` answers the narrower, answerable question, and `notes` says which one was answered.
properties.name: What happens when an epoch arrives: the delta is computed against the FIRST snapshot, and a lossy schedule edit is refused
properties.rationale:
MEASURED BEFORE DECIDED, and two of the three calls exist because the measuring found something the brainstorm had not.

The mechanism claim held: `snapshot_node` really does chain incoming edges, so snapshotting the epoch captures every schedule edge pointing at it — the whole plan in one call. And `record_change`'s planned-epoch refusal keys on the epoch you FILE INTO, not the node you snapshot, so a replan files into the current arrived epoch with the planned epoch as its subject. That also answers the open question inside `cap:plan-movement-recorded`: filing in the arrived epoch is sufficient, and planned epochs need no revision chain of their own.

But the trap was WORSE than the brainstorm stated, which is call 2. And "the last snapshot" would have under-reported exactly the slip the report exists to show, which is call 1. Both were found by reading the code rather than reasoning about it — the same method that found the wrong-direction edge in `dec:epoch-pins-a-version-combination`.

The fifth outcome came from asking what happens to an item nobody touches, which is the ordinary case and the one the four-outcome framing has no room for. Forcing it into `discontinued` or `deferred` would have made the report assert a decision that was never taken — the failure `dec:report-dont-judge` exists to prevent, arriving through a vocabulary that was simply too small.

Mutation-checked, all three calls: empty the commitment-edge list and the snapshot test fails; take the baseline from the last snapshot instead of the first and the two-replan test fails; make the guard always allow and all three refusal tests fail.

properties.decision: possible_duplicate is a DETECT gap; HEAL merges only on a human-drawn DUPLICATES edge.
properties.name: Suspected duplicates are asked, never merged
properties.rationale: apply_heal deletes a node with no undo, so merge is safe only because the endpoints were asserted; a heuristic must not drive it. A gap can be acknowledged, a HEAL defect cannot be dismissed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: 3dtictactoe trial, BL-27/BL-29.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-10: *"agreed on the 'behavioural rather than lexical' approach."*

SETTLED: if repeated attention to a node is ever used as a priority signal, the unit of evidence is that a search surfaced the node AND the agent then FETCHED IT IN FULL. Not the BM25 score, not the appearance in a ranked list.

WHY THIS AXIS COULD BE SETTLED WHILE THE REST STAYS OPEN. The lexical route was measured and found unusable in the form anybody would reach for: `search_design` returns BM25, which is unbounded and query-dependent — the query "export" scored its top hit at 4.48 and a longer query on the same subject scored 35.75, eight times higher for the same topic. Any accumulation of raw scores weights verbose queries over terse ones and would drift with whoever (or whatever model) writes the query. A behavioural unit needs no score at all, so it sidesteps comparability entirely and cannot be gamed by query length.

⭐ ANTHONY'S FRAMING, AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN DECORATIVE: *"this is a bit like a Q-table in reinforcement learning... the more that a search appears, the more that it is reinforced."* Three consequences follow from taking that seriously, and none of them is obvious from the counter idea alone.

(1) A Q-VALUE DECAYS AND A COUNTER DOES NOT. Reinforcement learning applies a learning rate precisely so that recent evidence outweighs old; a plain tally never forgets. Without decay, whatever was hot in a project's first month dominates its ranking forever, and a node read ten times in July and never since reads as more critical than one read three times this week. ⇒ IF THIS IS BUILT, RECENCY IS PART OF THE UPDATE RULE, NOT A LATER REFINEMENT.

(2) VISIT COUNT IS NOT VALUE. In a Q-table the update is driven by REWARD; the visit count is exploration bookkeeping. "Searched often" is a visit count. What Anthony actually wants is closer to Q — did going there PAY OFF — and that is the deeper argument for the behavioural unit he chose: choosing to read a node in full is a weak revealed preference, where appearing in a list is not even that.
⚠️ THE ANALOGY BREAKS HERE AND THE BREAK MUST BE RECORDED: THERE IS NO REWARD SIGNAL. Nothing observes whether reading a node helped. The agent's choice to read is a proxy for relevance, not a measurement of outcome, and treating it as reward would assert an observation nobody makes. The RL framing supplies STRUCTURE (decay, exploration) and does NOT supply the thing that makes Q-learning converge.

(3) 🛑 THE EXPLORATION TRAP, AND IT IS `dec:bl-155` ARRIVING BY A NEW ROAD. A reinforcement scheme reinforces what has already been visited. A node nothing surfaces is never read, so it never accumulates, so it never rises — permanently. That is exactly bl-155's finding that reflow2 cannot tell "unused" from "unreachable", and `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` already drew the consequence that counts may justify optimising and never, alone, justify cutting. THE RL FRAMING ADDS THE REMEDY SHAPE THAT THE EARLIER FRAMING LACKED: greedy exploitation of an under-explored table converges on a local optimum, and the standard answers are an exploration term or optimistic initialisation. ⇒ ANY ATTENTION RANKING NEEDS A DELIBERATE EXPLORATION COMPONENT — something that surfaces never-touched nodes on purpose — or it will bury exactly the material a discoverability problem is already hiding. Recorded as a REQUIRED PROPERTY of any such design, not as a nice-to-have.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, and `dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important` stays OPEN for all of it: whether attention should be tracked at all; where the record lives (`dec:how-should-reflow2-log-its-own-usage` holds that); how it composes with ranking by CONSEQUENCE (`dec:idea-a-critical-path-through-the-undecided`); and whether a bounded top-5 draws from one merged score or two lists. This decision closes one axis so the others can be argued without re-litigating it.

STILL BINDING FROM THE OPEN NODE: the search history is LOCAL BY CONSTRUCTION and never enters a telemetry payload — `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` governs what LEAVES a design and names search queries as the worst offender. And review records and bookkeeping must be excluded from any accumulation, per the exclusion list `fact:graph-analysis-covers-a-third-of-the-edge-types` had to learn the expensive way.
properties.name: Attention is measured by what was READ, not by what a search scored — behavioural, not lexical
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than by editing the brainstorm node into an answer, per `dec:reopen-supersedes`' principle that the record should show both that a question was asked and how it was settled. It deliberately does NOT obsolete `dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important`: Anthony settled the lexical-versus-behavioural axis, not whether to build any of this, so superseding the whole question would claim more than he said.

The Q-table framing is recorded as design content rather than as a metaphor because it produces three testable properties the counter idea did not have — decay, the visit-count-is-not-value distinction, and an exploration term — and because its BREAK is as informative as its fit: there is no reward signal here, and an implementation that pretended otherwise would be asserting an observation nobody makes.

Consequence (3) is the one worth carrying forward. bl-155's unused-versus-unreachable finding has been restated three times in this design as a warning; the RL framing is the first time it has arrived with a known remedy shape attached.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-05, taking OPTION (c) from the options this node recorded while open. The measurement below is unchanged; what follows it is the choice and what it does not cover.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT THAT FORCED IT, from the first real trial of cap:corpus-ingest over six dev_storyflow architecture documents. `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio` against the auto-merge threshold of 90:

  95  dynograph-vector   vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG
  94  dynograph-storage  vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG
  93  dynograph-extract  vs dynograph-context     <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG
  91  dynograph-server   vs dynograph-query       <- SILENTLY MERGED, WRONG
  84  Auth Service       vs Authentication Service (NOT merged — and this is the case the feature EXISTS for)

ONE DOCUMENT DECLARING NINE CRATES PRODUCED FIVE NODES. 44% of an architecture destroyed silently, and the survivors asserted something FALSE rather than merely being incomplete: `cmp:dynograph-core` carried the name "dynograph-storage".

WHY NO THRESHOLD REPAIRS IT, which is the reason (a) was rejected: 95 was a sibling pair and 84 a true duplicate, so the ORDERING is inverted and no cutoff separates them. `docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md` asserted "90 on a token-sorted ratio is near-identity"; measured, that is false for the names real systems use.

THE CHOICE — A DIFFERENT QUESTION, NOT A BETTER NUMBER. Before auto-merging, both names are tokenised on every non-alphanumeric (deliberately NOT `name_tokens`, which splits on whitespace and so cannot see inside `dynograph-core`). A merge is REFUSED when either side carries a whole word the other does not ABBREVIATE. "core" and "storage" are not spellings of each other; "auth" and "authentication" are, with a three-character minimum because below that almost anything prefixes anything. An unpaired extra word is distinguishing too, so `Auth Service` and `Auth Service v2` stay apart — the case the scope doc warned collapsing would lose. Reordered tokens still converge, so BL-186's ordering fix is untouched.

AND THE REFUSAL SAYS WHICH WORD DID IT. `MergeCandidate.distinguished_by` carries e.g. "`storage` has no counterpart in \"dynograph-core\"". "These two were not merged" is not something a person can rule on; naming the word is. `None` means the score simply fell short, which needs no explanation.

THE SECOND FIX IN THE SAME CHANGE: `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` was a `usize` for one day and is now `Vec<CorpusMerge>`, each entry carrying the DOCUMENT that caused it — which the single-document report structurally cannot know. A merge is the one thing an ingest does WITHOUT ASKING and cannot undo by re-running, and the aggregate had reduced it to a number at exactly the scale where that matters most.

VERIFIED, AND MUTATION-CHECKED: `tests/sibling_merge.rs` pins nine crates staying nine, an abbreviation still merging, a version suffix staying apart, reordered tokens still converging, and the refusal naming its word. Disabling the discriminator returns 5-of-9 and fails exactly the three tests that name those properties while leaving the two that should be insensitive passing. Re-run against the real dev_storyflow document that found it: 9 of 9 crates survive, each with its own name.

⭐ WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT REMAINS: the destructive direction is handled; the MISSING direction is untouched. `Read Cache` ~ `Local Store` is still invisible — not a low score, no score at all — so two documents that RENAMED the same thing still produce two nodes. This decision makes the lexical pass safe, not sufficient. `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` is where that half lives, and this trial is the strongest evidence yet for it: the lexical signal here was not merely weak, it was INVERTED, which is the argument a semantic tiebreaker has been waiting for.

ALSO NOT SETTLED: the ask band is still noisy. The same trial's eleven merge candidates were ELEVEN OUT OF ELEVEN FALSE POSITIVES. The discriminator now labels the sibling ones, which should make them skimmable rather than gruelling, but nobody has measured the band again since.

STILL NOT MEASURED, and it bounds every number above: what this does across the other 1,118 documents. The trial was SIX documents chosen for topical overlap; 44% is one document's crate list, not a corpus-wide rate.
properties.name: DECIDED — a merge needs a discriminator, not a threshold: siblings are held apart by whole-word difference
properties.rationale:
Moved to accepted on Anthony's explicit instruction ("fix the fuzzy_merges regression, then the token discriminator"), which chose option (c) over the four alternatives this node had recorded.

The measurement is kept in full rather than trimmed to the conclusion, because the numbers are what make the fix defensible and what would otherwise be re-derived: "fuzzy matching is too aggressive" decays into folklore within a session, and "95 for a sibling pair, 84 for a true duplicate" does not.

Two things are deliberately recorded as NOT fixed — the missing-convergence direction and the noisy ask band — so this does not read as having closed the resolution question. It closed the destructive half of it. The one that remains is the one that needs embeddings, and saying so here is what stops the next session treating lexical resolution as done.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-07, verbatim: "the backlog needs to be retired once and for all - I approve whatever decisions need to be made to make this action occur." This settles dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph, open since 2026-08-04 with five options and no choice, and it supersedes it.

THE CHOICE IS OPTION (a) — ROUTE EACH ROW TO THE TYPE IT ALREADY IS — and it is only available now because the one category that had no home was given one. dec:defects-are-temporal-facts (accepted 2026-08-06) closed it: a defect found by USING a built capability is a TemporalFact with fact_type "defect". So all four categories the 2026-08-04 taxonomy identified now have a destination:

  (i)   a defect against a shipped capability  -> TemporalFact, fact_type "defect", basis "measured",
        HAS_TEMPORAL_FACT from the node it indicts, VALID_TO set when fixed
  (ii)  unbuilt work                            -> a Capability at `planned` behind a Requirement
  (iii) an open design question                 -> a `proposed` Decision
  (iv)  a discovered limit                      -> a Constraint or a DesignRule

OPTION (d) IS EXPLICITLY NOT TAKEN. Deriving a markdown backlog from the graph was the fallback that kept the file alive as a projection; "retired once and for all" is a stronger instruction than that, and dec:views-are-projections already covers rendering if anyone later wants a view. The file is DELETED, and its history stays in git where deleted files live.

THE MEASURED SCOPE, taken 2026-08-07 rather than carried from the 2026-08-04 note: docs/backlog.md is 3,356 lines / 589,326 bytes / 217 distinct BL ids. 129 open rows under "Next up", 9 under "Bigger threads", plus a "Closed" section that is already only short pointers to the CHANGELOG and a "Deliberate deferrals" section. 22 other files reference it, including AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, COORD.md and README.md, and CLAUDE.md names it as one of the three things to read at session start — so retiring the file is not finished until those pointers are too.

⭐ THE FAILURE MODE THIS DECISION MUST NOT PRODUCE, quoted from the decision it supersedes because it is the whole risk: "A row moved in as one long `description` rebuilds backlog.md inside the graph with worse ergonomics and no gain — and that failure would be invisible, because it would look like progress." So a row is migrated only when it becomes STRUCTURE: the node it bears on named by an EDGE, what was measured in a TYPED property, and whether it is still true carried by a status or a temporal bound. The prose hangs off that as explanation. A migration that produces 138 nodes of narrative and no edges has failed while appearing to succeed, and the honest test is whether the loop can see the result — not whether the file got shorter.

WHAT IS STILL OWED AND IS NOT SOLVED BY THIS. dec:defects-are-temporal-facts says it in its own words: nothing in the LOOP reads defect facts yet. `statement` is fulltext so search_design finds them, but `loop_status` does not count open defects — measured again today, and it does not. So a migrated defect is DISCOVERABLE, not SURFACED. Retiring the file therefore trades a document nobody queries for nodes the loop does not yet count, and that reader is the next increment. Recorded here so the trade is a choice rather than a discovery.

CLOSED ROWS ARE NOT MIGRATED. The "Closed" section is already only stable-id pointers into the CHANGELOG, and a finished item's value is history that git holds. Migrating them would import 100+ nodes that indict nothing and are true of nothing.
properties.name: The backlog is retired: every open row becomes the node type it already was, and docs/backlog.md is deleted rather than derived
properties.rationale: Accepted rather than left `proposed` because Anthony's approval was explicit, unprompted and general ("whatever decisions need to be made"), which is the standard dec:three-party-checks sets — the human decides, and here they did, in advance and in writing. He had already stated the preference on 2026-08-04 ("I wanted to stop using the BL... instead, I wanted everything in the graph") and it sat unchosen for three days while the file grew. The cost of leaving it open is measured on the superseded node: 6 of 8 rows filed in one session referenced by zero graph nodes, and four things re-derived in that same session that were already written down. The falsifiable test from dec:what-lives-where applies to reflow2 itself and it has been failing it: if reflow2 works, reflow2 would not need a 589 KB markdown backlog.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony, 2026-08-06: "the responsibility to backup the reflow2 graph is probably more the responsibility of the flo2 project? reflow2 only needs to provide the documentation on how to update reflow2 properly so that any graph data is persistent."

THE BOUNDARY, and it is cleaner than it first looked: BACKUP IS A PROPERTY OF WHERE THE DATA LIVES — the consumer's volume, their storage account, their retention window, their compliance rules. reflow2 knows none of those and cannot learn them. A design tool that shipped an opinionated backup would be wrong for most projects that installed it, and would be carrying operational burden that dec:multi-writer-architecture already rejected on exactly those grounds.

WHAT REFLOW2 OWES INSTEAD, and this is the whole of it:
(1) A DOCUMENTED UPDATE PATH — getting-started/UPDATING.md, which ships in the consumer kit rather than living in this repo's docs, per rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party. It states where the design actually lives, that the binary and the design are separate in every deployment shape, and the ONE mistake that looks like data loss: mounting the store directory instead of its parent leaves the identity sidecar behind, and a store opened without its identity PRESENTS AS AN EMPTY DESIGN while the data sits untouched on disk beside it.
(2) HONEST PRIMITIVES a consumer can build a backup FROM: export_graph is a complete, deterministic, content-hashed snapshot; --import is a restore that preserves graph_id, so a restored design IS the same design rather than a copy sharing a name; and for the repo-file model the committed export means git is already an off-host backup, versioned and replicated for free.
(3) NOT LYING when something is off. This is where the boundary stops being purely documentary, and it is the part that remains reflow2's problem: the version stamp reports an older store as "additive only — everything in it still reads", and there is NO verdict at all for the reverse. See dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments and the downgrade gap.

WHY THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE TWO DEPLOYMENT SHAPES MATTERS HERE: under the repo-file model (dec:multi-writer-architecture, accepted) the export is committed, so backup is solved by git and nobody has to think about it. A HOSTED SERVER HAS NO REPO — the same asymmetry that makes --content-path's default wrong for a container — so the hosted case is the one that needs real backup work, and it is precisely the case that belongs to whoever runs the server. flo2 owns flo2's volume.

WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND NOT CHOSEN: reflow2 shipping snapshot/restore/off-host-push machinery, in the shape storyflow's scripts/ops already proves out (safe-deploy: snapshot, deploy, fingerprint node counts by type, alarm on any user-data decrease, off-host copy verified rather than assumed, receipts kept). Those concepts are sound and a consumer should borrow them — the doc points at the shape. They are not reflow2's to run, because every one of them is parameterised by facts only the consumer has.

⚠️ ONE THING THIS DECISION DOES NOT SETTLE, recorded so it is not read as settled: reflow2 gives a consumer a stronger fingerprint than node counts, because the export is content-hashed and deterministic. Whether a comparison helper belongs in the shipped kit — as reflow2_check.py's dependency reconciliation now does for pins — is a separate question from whether reflow2 runs backups, and it has not been asked.
properties.name: Backing up a design is the consumer's job; what reflow2 owes is a documented update path and honest primitives
properties.rationale:
Captured on Anthony's word, 2026-08-06, and it NARROWS a requirement rather than growing one: req:hosted-state-outlives-the-image already says designs must survive a container replacement, and this says who is responsible for the case where they do not. Scoping it down was his call and it is the right one — the alternative was reflow2 acquiring a backup subsystem parameterised by facts it cannot know.

Recorded as a Decision rather than a Requirement because it says what reflow2 will NOT do, and the positive half it implies (the doc) is a deliverable that already exists rather than intent awaiting satisfaction.

THE PART WORTH RE-READING LATER: the boundary holds for backup and does NOT hold for honesty. "We do not back your data up" is a fair thing for a tool to say. "We opened a store an older binary wrote and said nothing" is not, and no amount of documentation fixes it — which is why the downgrade gate stayed on the queue as work rather than being absorbed into this decision as prose.

properties.decision:
A test written from the requirement and a test written to match the code are indistinguishable in the graph — and this repo records the difference in PROSE

*Anthony, 2026-08-03, on test-driven design: "Developing tests as you design is extremely important. It shapes system architecture, forces clear thinking about edge cases early, and prevents the tight coupling that makes retrofitting tests painful." His named risk is the one that bites here: "Confirmation bias: Testing code you already wrote proves what it does, not necessarily what it should do."* MEASURED: Verification carries criteria, kind, last_run_at, level, method, name, status — no field for when the check was authored, and none for whether it preceded the code. Yet 7 of reflow2's 105 verifications assert in their NAME that the test came first (ver:constructors-preserve: *"WRITTEN BEFORE THE FIX: all 6 defect cases failed and all 3 counterweights passed"*), two of them written on 2026-08-03. So the repo already practises test-first, already records it, and records it where NO COMPUTATION CAN READ IT — [BL-143]'s shape (an opinion smuggled in as data) and dec:edge-orthogonality's, from a new direction. The consequence is precise: a passing check written from the requirement and a passing check written to match the implementation are the same node, same status, same everything. reflow2 asserts dec:passing-is-verified — *verified means a check that passes* — while being unable to say what the check was evidence of. THE GUARD RAIL IS ANTHONY'S OWN CAVEAT — *"may not apply to or be feasible for all project types."* The adopt skill exists entirely for systems that already ship, where every recovered test is necessarily after the fact; a reading that scored that as failure would repeat exactly [BL-179]'s punish-correct-work trap. So: record the fact, report the signal, never grade it. Fix shape, and it pairs with [BL-143]'s already-decided criterion field on the same node type — one schema touch rather than two, which matters because a schema change pulls in the minor bump, the upgrade doc and the foundation-migration checklist. Candidates: an optional authored_at (order derivable against the Artifact's own dates), or an explicit provenance-of-evidence enum saying whether the check was written from the intent or from the implementation. Deciding which is the row. Size M
