properties.decision:
reflow2's own decomposition is the functional systems a design-graph tool IS — foundation, vocabulary, store, coherence-loop, human-channel, time-history, intake, agent-surface, documentation, packaging — with the Rust modules re-parented under them as implementation. The as-built crate grouping (reflow2-core / -mcp / kit) is retired from the as-designed view.

CORRECTED 2026-08-02: this said "the seven functional systems" and named seven. There were EIGHT — `sys:documentation` joined later under `dec:documentation-has-no-operational-coupling`, which accepts that documentation is part of the product while having no operational coupling, so it forms an island the detectors are told to expect. The choice this decision records was unchanged; only its enumeration had gone stale, which is why that was a correction on the record rather than a superseding decision (`dec:reopen-supersedes` governs reversals, not arithmetic). Found by re-measuring a claim rather than re-reading it: the decision's prose said seven while `scan_nodes` said eight.

AMENDED 2026-08-20, and THIS ONE IS NOT ARITHMETIC. There are now NINE. `sys:foundation` was CREATED under `dec:the-kernel-is-its-own-system` (accepted, Anthony's word) and holds cmp:nodes, cmp:schema, cmp:graph, cmp:provenance and cmp:identity — five modules that had been split across `sys:vocabulary` and `sys:store`, with identity in no system at all. Unlike the 2026-08-02 correction, the carving itself moved: a system exists now that did not exist before. It does not overturn this decision, it follows from it — a design-graph tool fundamentally IS a typed store of identified nodes, and that is one function, not two halves of two. The bisection was measured, not argued: it was the entire cause of a `sys:store` <-> `sys:vocabulary` cycle, while the modules themselves are acyclic (`fact:the-modules-are-acyclic-but-the-declared-subsystems-are-not`).

THE COUNT THAT WAS NOT WRONG, recorded so nobody "fixes" it twice: the 14 distinct cross-system pairs cited in `dec:maturity-restructuring-delta` are DIRECTED pairs; counted undirected the same 51 edges span 12. Both are right, they answer different questions, and the recorded figure means directed.

AMENDED AGAIN 2026-08-20, same day, on Anthony's word: there are now TEN. `cmp:packaging` — how reflow2 SHIPS: the per-platform binary matrix, the consumer kit and its manifest, the install and update path, the container image — is PROMOTED from a leaf component to a subsystem. It had been floating at the root of the spine declaring itself a leaf, which is why "what are the top-level parts?" answered differently by declared level than by position. Promotion rather than placement-under-something because the graph says it is real and finished: four capabilities, three of them realized, with `art:release-workflow` behind them, serving accepted intent in `req:frictionless-update`. Something that shipped is not scaffolding.

ITS ID KEEPS THE `cmp:` PREFIX AND THAT IS COSMETIC, recorded so nobody reads meaning into it. The other nine carry `sys:`. reflow2 has no rename operation, and fabricating a migration to a new id would destroy the node's snapshot history for a prefix. ALSO IN THIS EPOCH, and it is a PLACEMENT rather than a change to the carving: `cmp:registry` was moved inside `sys:agent-surface`. It had no parent at all. properties.decision: Every bulk form attempts every item, collects each failure with its index, and if any item failed discards the whole batch and returns the complete failure list. A rejected batch is returned as an ERROR carrying the failures in its data, never as a payload with applied:false.
properties.name: A bulk write is all-or-nothing AND reports every failure — the refusal-semantics question was a false choice
properties.rationale: BL-153 posed this as a choice — "one refusal semantics to define (all-or-nothing, or per-item findings?)" — and the two were never exclusive. ALL-OR-NOTHING COSTS NOTHING HERE: the store already has an atomic batch (begin_batch/commit_batch/discard_batch) that HEAL's apply step and import_graph both use, and a partial bulk write leaves a design in a state nobody chose. PER-ITEM FINDINGS ARE SEPARATELY NECESSARY: BL-118 files exactly the opposite defect against import_graph — "validation is fail-fast, one error per attempt" — and BL-139 records what it costs, that the adopt loop's corrective re-import is where it breaks. A bulk form surfacing one error per round trip would replace N writes with N retries and save nobody anything. The failure carries its INDEX as well as its id because an id alone cannot tell two identical entries apart, and a list an agent generated is exactly where a duplicate turns up. The error-not-payload choice follows the same rule as everywhere else: a tool result reads as success, so "nothing was written" dressed as a result is the silent-failure shape this project forbids.

properties.decision: Any bulk form over a tool that records a JUDGEMENT carries that judgement per item, never hoisted to a call-level argument: set_artifact_checksums takes a disposition per artifact, acknowledge_gaps a reason per gap, and gaps_to_prompts groups answers per gap. A shared timestamp is allowed because it is a fact about the call; a shared disposition is not, because it would be a shared decision.
properties.name: A bulk form collapses the round trip, never the judgement
properties.rationale: BL-153 stated the trap before the build: "a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent, so a bulk form needs per-item dispositions or it is worse than the loop." This is the line that keeps dec:two-sided-accept ("silent drift-accept does not exist") and dec:ask-not-repair true under a bulk surface — 244 accepts now cost one call and still 244 decisions. It is also the distinction that let dec:manifest-derived-is-not-manifest-accepted go the other way and take no per-item disposition at all: a DERIVATION records no judgement, so there is none to preserve. For gaps_to_prompts the per-item grouping is additionally mechanical, not only doctrinal: grouping answers by gap is what stops two gaps' prompt ids colliding, so no gap is ever replayed against another's answers — and a half-answered batch is refused rather than half-served, because serving half would record some questions and silently drop the rest.

properties.decision: A new CALIBRATED_AGAINST edge runs from a fitted node to the evidence its value was derived from (an Artifact or a Verification). A VERIFIES edge whose Verification IS, or PRODUCES, evidence its own target was calibrated against is reported as CONSUMED — a fit, not a test — and is excluded from the count of independent evidence. A capability whose only passing checks are consumed is reported as not independently verified.
properties.name: Circular validation is made structurally visible by a CALIBRATED_AGAINST edge, never detected analytically
properties.rationale: Anthony's call, 2026-08-01. BL-136's closing evidence decides the shape and rules out the alternatives: the project that hit this built four independent internal diagnostics — a back-solve, a coefficient locus, a space-time frontier and a physical-floor proof — and every one narrowed the question correctly while none could have found the defect. Only the outside source could. So a circular check is not a weak check to be strengthened from inside; NO INTERNAL EVIDENCE CAN DETECT IT, BY CONSTRUCTION. That rules out any analytic detector and leaves exactly one move: record what a value was fitted to, and refuse to let that same evidence count as its validation. An edge rather than a provenance value because the detector is then a graph query rather than a scan, and because the relation carries WHAT was consumed, which a provenance enum cannot. The `calibrated` provenance value (BL-120(d), and what the originating project actually built) stays open and is not foreclosed — it answers HOW the value entered, a different question from WHAT it consumed. Stakes, from the same closing entry: a single-point fit does not merely get a number wrong, it can silently hold a wrong EQUATION in agreement with the data — the fitted coefficient absorbed a structural error in the functional form and agreed with the anchor anyway.

properties.decision: CALIBRATED_AGAINST is entered in the structural direction table (nodes.rs structural_rule) as (forward: Upstream, backward: Downstream), the same shape as REALIZES and VERIFIES. From the fitted node you reach the evidence its authority rests on; from the evidence you reach every value that would be wrong if it were superseded.
properties.name: CALIBRATED_AGAINST is a traceability edge — when the anchor moves, every value fitted to it is in the blast radius
properties.rationale: Asked deliberately because the table's own comment says it is the question nobody asks: 'Twice now a new edge type has reached a Release without anyone asking whether the impact table should know about it, and nothing checks that question is asked' — INCLUDES and then SCHEDULED_FOR, each found only when disconnected_community fired on an island the new edge had failed to join. This is the third such edge and the question was put before the code was written rather than after a detector complained. The answer is yes on the merits: a calibration is a genuine dependency of a value on a piece of evidence, so when the anchor is corrected or superseded, every value fitted to it is exactly the blast radius propagate_change exists to compute — which is the payoff BL-136 asks for, since a wrong functional form absorbed into a fitted coefficient is only findable when the outside source arrives and someone can see what rested on the old one. Direction matches REALIZES because the evidence is the source of truth and the fitted value is downstream of it. Consequence accepted and stated rather than discovered: this puts CALIBRATED_AGAINST into design_network(), so it counts toward centrality, communities and single-point-of-failure — the surface BL-124 has just shown is sensitive to edge-set changes. On reflow2's own graph the effect is nil today because the design carries no fitted values, and that is a measurement, not an assumption.

properties.decision:
UNDECIDED. Raised by Anthony 2026-07-25 from his own situation: he is in Long Island, his brother is in Washington State, they want to work on one design at the same time and to see each other's projects. FOUR ROADS, and the middle ones are not the obvious winners. (a) GIT IS ALREADY THE CENTRAL SERVER — the design is a file in the repo, the repo already spans both coasts, and the claims layer that shipped 2026-07-25 already answers "who has what in hand" the moment either side pulls. Nothing to host, nothing to secure, nothing to pay for, and no new place for the design to live. What it cannot do is tell you about a claim before the other person pushes. (b) A HOSTED MCP over HTTPS — one server process holding the graph, both people's agents connecting to it, so a claim is visible the moment it is made and a design is reachable by someone who never cloned the repo. Costs: ~~reflow2-mcp serves stdio only today (rmcp's streamable-HTTP transport exists, the binary does not use it)~~ **— THAT CLAIM IS STALE, see the 2026-08-26 correction below —** authentication does not exist at all, and it puts the design on a machine — which weakens but does not erase dec:repo-file-embedded's objection, since the machine would be Anthony's own droplet rather than a vendor's. NOTE WHAT MAKES (b) CHEAPER THAN IT LOOKS: one server process with many clients is ALREADY compatible with the single-writer store, because there is still exactly one writer — the server. (c) HYBRID — host a read/publish surface for reaching and browsing designs, keep writes local and merge through git, so the durable record never moves. THE CHEAPEST FIRST CUT, worth naming because it needs almost no core work: one server process PER PROJECT, each with its own graph path and its own token, and project selection becomes which URL the agent points at — no graph_id plumbing, no multi-tenancy, and a per-project blast radius if one goes wrong. A private tailnet instead of public TLS removes the authentication problem for exactly two people, which is the population this actually has. (d) ONE LIVE SHARED WORKING TREE on a droplet — both people editing the same checkout simultaneously, seeing each other's edits, with a push to a "true" git repo every so often for permanent storage (Anthony, 2026-07-25). THE DESIGN HALF OF THIS IS (b) AND IS SOUND; THE CODE HALF INVERTS THE PROPERTY IT IS REACHING FOR. A shared checkout does not remove conflicts, it removes conflict DETECTION: with one copy there is no common ancestor to merge against, so two agents doing read-modify-write on one file interleave into last-write-wins with no marker, no three-way merge and nothing to review — strictly less safe than what they have now. It also shares the things git assumes are private (one index, one HEAD, one branch: `git checkout` on his side changes files under her mid-edit), shares the build directory and the graph's single-writer lock, and makes the droplet a single point of failure for two people who can currently both work on a plane. The batched push is its own cost: history granularity, attribution and bisect all collapse into one commit, the gates that are supposed to gate a commit are replaced by a timer, and "every so often" is precisely the size of the loss window when the droplet dies.

SHARPENED 2026-08-11 — THE PUBLISHING CASE ARRIVES WITH A NAME, AND IT BREAKS AN ASSUMPTION EVERY OPTION ABOVE SHARES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony is thinking out loud; nothing here settles this decision, which stays `proposed`.

⭐ DELIBERATELY SHARPENED RATHER THAN OPENED AS A NEW NODE. This node's own rationale already named the gap it is being filled with — "what it does NOT deliver is the publishing case, and that is the strongest argument on the hosted side" — so a second node would have been the near-duplicate the search-first rule exists to prevent. What follows is new EVIDENCE on the same question, not a new question.

HIS WORDS, 2026-08-11: "I want to use reflow2 within flo2. it is purposefully designed to allow collaboration on projects via a web app. if one user posts some brainstorm idea or identifies gaps, the other user shouldn't have to run some terminal commands in order to see that (especially non technical people using web app where no CLI exists)."

⭐⭐ THE ASSUMPTION THAT JUST BROKE, and it is the reason this is worth re-weighing rather than merely noting. EVERY option above was weighed for TWO TECHNICAL PEOPLE WITH TERMINALS. Option (a) — "git is already the central server" — is only free if both parties can run git. The moment one participant is a non-technical user of a web app, (a) stops being free and starts being impossible: there is no shell to run `git pull` in, no checkout to pull into, and no way to run the import that makes a pulled file readable by the tools.

THE CONCRETE FRICTION HE IS OBJECTING TO, measured today rather than supposed: for a second person to SEE a brainstormed idea in a form the tools can answer questions about, they must today (1) `git pull`, (2) run `reflow2-mcp --graph-path .reflow2/graph --import docs/design/reflow2.json`, and (3) have a merge driver configured per-clone or meet a raw text conflict in a 4 MB JSON file. That is three technical steps between one person recording a thought and another person seeing it. For an agent-driven CLI user it is friction; for a web-app user it is a wall.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE, stated separately so neither is overclaimed:
- It does NOT re-open `dec:multi-writer-architecture` (accepted 2026-07-25, "no hosted service"). That decision answered how two WRITERS avoid clobbering each other, and its rejection of hosting rested on `req:persistence` and `req:invocation` — both of which describe where a design DURABLY LIVES. A read/publish surface does not move the durable record, which is exactly why option (c) exists here.
- It DOES weaken option (a) as a general answer, because (a)'s cheapness was priced for participants who all have a shell.
- ⚠️ It sits against `dec:one-process-many-stores` (ACCEPTED, conditional) and `rule:per-design-state-is-never-a-process-global`, which already contemplate a hosted reflow2 holding N single-writer stores. So the hosted direction is NOT unexplored ground — it is partly built toward, and `req:a-session-cannot-address-another-design` is the guard that must be proven before it ships.
- `fact:the-hosted-case-breaks-the-git-transport-and-the-access-topology-is-now-stated` already recorded the same collision from the other side, on 2026-08-09.

THE NEW QUESTION THIS RAISES, which none of (a)–(d) answers: WHO IS THE WRITER when the participant is a web-app user? reflow2's loop is ask-the-human-and-record-an-ATTRIBUTABLE-answer. Today attribution comes from a Contributor a local agent names. Through a web app, the app is the MCP client and the human is behind it — so either flo2 passes identity through to reflow2 on every write, or every contribution from that surface is attributed to "flo2" and the confirmation ledger stops meaning what it says. ⭐ THAT IS A HARDER PROBLEM THAN THE TRANSPORT, and it is the one most likely to be discovered late.

⚠️ A REPO-BOUNDARY NOTE, so nobody skips it: flo2 is a SEPARATE PROJECT with its own design graph and its own owners. Nothing here may be built into flo2 from this repo without Anthony's word (AGENTS.md rule 6). What reflow2 can decide alone is whether it OFFERS a surface flo2 could consume; whether flo2 consumes it is flo2's decision to record.

NOT DECIDED, and deliberately not ranked. Option (c) — publish/read hosted, writes stay local — is the one this evidence pushes hardest on, but it is also the one whose attribution story is least worked out.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ SHARPENED 2026-08-26 — THE TRANSPORT COST IN OPTION (b) WAS ALREADY PAID, AND THIS NODE HAS BEEN CARRYING A STALE CLAIM FOR A MONTH
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Sharpened rather than forked, following this node's own 2026-08-11 precedent: new evidence on the same question.

Anthony brought research: *"STDIO Transport (One-to-One): the MCP server runs as a local child process spawned directly by a single client... a strict, private 1:1 pipe... It cannot be shared with other clients. HTTP / SSE Transport (Many-to-One): the MCP server operates as an independent, centralized service running on a port. This allows multiple distinct clients over the network to connect, authenticate, and send concurrent requests to the same server process."*

🛑 **THAT RESEARCH IS CORRECT AND IT FALSIFIES A COST LINE IN OPTION (b) ABOVE.** This node says reflow2-mcp *"serves stdio only today (rmcp's streamable-HTTP transport exists, the binary does not use it)"*. **That was true on 2026-07-25 and became false in v0.14.0.** Verified on the binary 2026-08-26:

    --http <ADDR>   "Serve over HTTP on this address instead of stdio, so SEVERAL sessions
                     share one design (req:sessions-share-a-graph). One process holds the
                     graph — the store is single-writer, and with one server there is still
                     exactly one writer — while every client session gets its own seat."

`cap:shared-sessions` is BUILT and `ver:shared-sessions` — *"Two sessions share one design over real HTTP, with seats that differ"* — is PASSING. `cmp:mcp-http`, `cmp:shared` and `cmp:proxy` are the three components that do it. A shared server was running on `http://127.0.0.1:40233/` during this very session.

⭐ **SO OPTION (b)'s REMAINING COST IS AUTHENTICATION AND REACHABILITY, NOT TRANSPORT.** The flag's own help says it: *"Bind to a loopback or tailnet address: there is no authentication yet, so anything that can reach the port can write the design."* The many-to-one server Anthony's research describes is not a thing reflow2 would have to build — it is a thing reflow2 already runs, on loopback, every day.

⭐ **AND IT INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMS OPTION (c)'s CHEAPEST-FIRST-CUT.** That option already proposed *"one server process PER PROJECT, each with its own graph path and its own token"* and *"a private tailnet instead of public TLS"*. The binary's own help text now recommends exactly that binding. The gap between (c)-as-written and (c)-as-shipped is a token and a non-loopback bind.

📌 **A CONSEQUENCE FOR `rule:mcp-and-the-graph-are-the-only-common-ground`, settled the same day.** If reflow2 targets ANY MCP CLIENT, and several DIFFERENT products are to work one design at once — Claude Code and Cursor on the same graph — then stdio cannot serve them, because stdio is 1:1 with the process that spawned it. **Multi-product collaboration is an HTTP-only capability by protocol construction, not by implementation choice.** That is a stronger argument for the hosted direction than any of (a)–(d) made, and none of them made it.

⚠️ WHAT IS STILL UNCHANGED AND MUST NOT BE READ AS SOLVED: the attribution question from 2026-08-11 — who is the writer when the client is a web app — is untouched by any of this. Transport was never the hard half.
properties.name: DECIDED — option (c): a hosted READ/PUBLISH surface, writes stay local, one server per project on a tailnet
properties.rationale:
Settled by Anthony 2026-08-26, after a month open, choosing option (c) from four roads put to him with corrected costs.

WHY THE COSTS WERE RE-PUT RATHER THAN THE OLD ONES REUSED: this node had carried a stale claim since 2026-07-25 — that reflow2-mcp "serves stdio only" — which became false in v0.14.0. Deciding on the old text would have meant deciding against a cost estimate that was wrong in the direction that mattered, since the transport both (b) and (c) need is BUILT and passing. The correction and its verification are written into the decision text above.

WHAT MAKES (c) THE RIGHT SHAPE RATHER THAN MERELY THE CHEAP ONE: the durable record does not move. `dec:multi-writer-architecture` (accepted 2026-07-25, no hosted service) rested on `req:persistence` and `req:invocation`, both of which describe where a design DURABLY LIVES — and a read/publish surface leaves that in the repo. So this is not a reversal of that decision; it is the option that was always compatible with it, which is why (c) existed among the original four.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, KEPT BECAUSE CHOOSING DOES NOT ANSWER IT: (c) is the road whose ATTRIBUTION story is least worked out. Who is the writer when the participant is a web-app user? Today attribution comes from a Contributor a local agent names; through flo2 the app is the MCP client and the human is behind it. Nothing in this choice answers that, and the node has flagged it as harder than the transport since 2026-08-11. **It is now the blocking question rather than a footnote.**

ALSO UNCHANGED: a hosted surface adds a second place a design is reachable from, which is a real change to the threat surface even on a tailnet, and authentication does not exist at all today. The binary's own `--http` help says so — "there is no authentication yet, so anything that can reach the port can write the design."

WHAT IS NOT YET DECIDED AND MUST NOT BE READ INTO THIS: whether flo2 consumes the surface. flo2 is a separate project with its own graph and owners (AGENTS.md rule 6). This settles only that reflow2 OFFERS one.

properties.decision: Requirement certainty is a computed reading, never a stored third axis: status accepted/met → user-confirmed; status deferred/dropped → settled out (also the user's word); status proposed → asserted (provenance authored/planned/imported) or recovered (provenance inferred/reconciled/healed). The load-bearing doctrine: an agent captures requirements at proposed and ONLY the user's answer moves the status — accepted, met, deferred and dropped are all user-only verbs. Reports render the certainty breakdown directly so no session reconstructs it in prose.
properties.name: A Requirement's certainty is derived from status × provenance; every move off proposed is the user's word
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-75 vocabulary session, from their fleet trial: where-am-i had to caveat user-confirmed vs recovered in prose every session). Derived over stored for the BL-73 reason — a third stored property can contradict the two axes that already span the space, and the backlog's own warning was 'decide deliberately, not additively'. Every-move-off-proposed rather than accepted-only because an agent dropping a requirement on its own judgment is exactly the silent decision the loop exists to prevent — and this is BL-12 sketch idea 2's example made real ('a requirement moves to accepted only on the human's say-so'), enforced culturally in the skills and the tool description today; the mechanical half stays with BL-41. 'Recovered' over the trial's 'adopted' because it matches the graph's own vocabulary (cap:adopt: 'Recover a design from an existing system') and names the fact, not the workflow. No schema change: the whole defect was the read side — the second time this week (BL-73) the vocabulary was already sufficient and unread.

properties.decision:
SETTLED ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-15: option (c), split the axis. He was shown four options and chose the one that addresses the pattern rather than the loudest instance.

DISTINCT FROM its two neighbours by design: the FACT measures the problem and counts its occurrences; the IDEA held the four unmade options; THIS records the choice and what was built.

WHAT WAS BUILT, the same day:
· `ChangeSubject { System, Record }` — a new OPTIONAL property on ChangeEvent. Absent means nobody said and is NEVER inferred from `change_type`, because the mapping is not total: a `resync` can be either.
· `ChangeType::DefectFix` — 'the design was right and the code was wrong', distinct from `TestFailureFix`, which is the same repair with different PROVENANCE (a check caught it). That difference is one this project already cares about everywhere else.
· Both reachable from `add_change_event`, and the tool description now says the two questions are two questions.
· The two internal call sites now STATE their axis: a `design_holds` accept is `system` (the file moved; the move carried no design meaning), and a first baseline is `record` — the case the axis was named for. `record_change` passes None on purpose: the generic path cannot know, and a guess would be a claim nobody made.

⭐ THE SPLIT WAS ALREADY NAMED IN THE CODE AND LEFT UNUSABLE, which is the whole argument. `BaselineEstablished`'s own doc comment reads: 'the odd one out, and deliberately so. Every other variant answers why the THING changed; this one says the thing did not change and only the design's KNOWLEDGE of it did.' An axis with exactly one member, reserved so nobody could reach it — and five forced choices followed.

THE EVIDENCE, and the count is the argument: five sessions, four people, three projects, two independent tool surfaces. `chg:duplicate-merge-needs-a-human-20260808` and `chg:accept-acb06c45b63a7b6d` used `test_failure_fix` where no test existed; `chg:arrival-delta-decided` used `scope_change` to mean 'an open question was settled'; Alex tried `bugfix`, was refused, and wrote 'the enum forces a lie'; and the edit recording his report used `resync` to mean 'our knowledge moved and the thing did not'. THE SAME MISSING MEANING WAS ABSENT FROM `set_artifact_checksum`'s DISPOSITION TOO — one absence is a wording gap, two independent absences of one category is a category the vocabulary did not have.

PROVEN: 5 tests, MUTATION-CHECKED TWICE, each killing exactly one counterweight. Defaulting an unstated axis to `system` kills only `an_unstated_axis_stays_unstated`. Deriving the axis from `change_type` kills only `one_change_type_appears_on_both_axes` — the test that pins `Resync` appearing on BOTH axes, which is why the mapping cannot be inferred. The reserved-value counterweight holds throughout: `baseline_established` is still `set_artifact_checksum`'s alone.

📌 THE STAMP DOES NOT MOVE, verified rather than assumed: `GraphStamp` carries type NAMES and COUNTS only — no properties, no enum values — so both halves are invisible to it and NO UPGRADE DOC IS OWED. The flip side is worth knowing and is the stamp's blind spot again: a consumer cannot learn from the stamp that a property appeared.

NOT SETTLED: whether anything should READ `subject` — it is expressible now and nothing computes from it, which is this project's own recurring 'declared and read by nothing' risk, taken knowingly. And 'an open question was settled' still has no `change_type` value; the axis now lets `resync`+`record` say it honestly, which may be enough or may not.
properties.name: `change_type` answers WHY; a new `subject` answers WHICH AXIS — the system changed, or only the design's knowledge of it did
properties.rationale: Recorded as his ruling with what was built attached, so a later reader sees the choice and its consequence in one place. He chose (c) over (a) after the evidence showed at least three missing meanings rather than one — adding a single value would have fixed the loudest case and left the mechanism that produced all five.

properties.decision:
🔄 **WIDENED 2026-08-14 to ALL TWENTY SERVED SKILLS** by `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command` (accepted, option A). The exception below still stands exactly as reasoned — skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED, and only commands are installed — but the SET is no longer eight. **Twenty-two command files now ship** (twenty fronting a skill, plus `debt.md` and `decisions.md` which front tools), and `skill_lint` now fails a skill that no command names, so the number cannot silently fall behind again. The original ruling, and its reasoning, is kept below unedited.

════════ AS RULED 2026-07-28 ════════

The eight slash commands (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) are INSTALLED into a consumer project's `.claude/commands/`. Skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28.
properties.name: Slash commands ship with the kit — the one narrow exception to serving everything
properties.rationale:
QUALIFIES `dec:skills-served` rather than overturning it, and the distinction is what makes the exception safe.

WHY THAT DECISION EXISTS: a copied skill goes stale, and the agent then loads last release's content in preference to what the server would serve. That happened here for four releases running without anything noticing, which is why nothing is copied.

WHY A COMMAND IS DIFFERENT: each is four lines that name a skill and say how to report the answer. There is no version-coupled content in it. When the skill behind it changes, the command is still correct, because the skill is fetched fresh at use time — the command is a pointer, and the thing it points at is the thing that moves.

THE ONE WAY IT CAN ROT, and it is now closed: a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that, so the failure is caught in this repo rather than discovered in a consumer's, where the symptom would be an agent reporting it cannot find a skill the user was told to use. The mirror is byte-checked too, so `.claude/commands` cannot drift from the kit source.

WHAT IT COSTS IF WE ARE WRONG: eight small files in a consumer repo, each independently deletable, none of which changes behaviour when stale. Compare the cost of a stale skill, which silently answers with last release's method.

WHY IT WAS WORTH DOING AT ALL: without them a consumer install is experienced as BROKEN rather than thin — the skills are reachable and nothing tells you they are. That is the same invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, one layer up: the pointer now reaches the agent, and the commands are what make the reachable thing usable.

properties.decision:
`snapshot_node` skips edges whose other endpoint is a bookkeeping node type, and `DesignEpoch` is on that list. Anthony's call 2026-07-31, of three offered: FIX IT by excluding on the edge's own role — a named `COMMITMENT_EDGES` list holding `SCHEDULED_FOR` — rather than leaving the epoch as the only route or deferring it to separate work.

THE PROXY WAS EXACT WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN AND STOPPED BEING SO. Every edge to a `DesignEpoch` used to be audit trail (`AT_EPOCH`, `OCCURS_DURING`), so excluding the endpoint type excluded the role, and the rule read as correct because it WAS correct. `SCHEDULED_FOR` broke it: an edge to an epoch is now a COMMITMENT — when this was due — which is design content by any reading, and `req:intent-preserved` says the past is never overwritten.

WHAT IT COST WHILE IT HELD, and why this is a defect rather than a preference: `record_change` on a scheduled requirement — the obvious, natural way to record "this slipped" — captured a snapshot with the schedule edge silently dropped. The old due date was destroyed by the very call whose entire job is preserving it, and the call REPORTED SUCCESS. Only the epoch-side snapshot preserved it, and nothing said so. The trap `dec:arrival-delta` named was therefore worse than stated: it is not merely that re-pointing an edge loses the slip, it is that the correct-looking remedy lost it too.

The audit trail it travels with is still excluded, and a test pins that: `AT_EPOCH` on the same node stays out. Role, not endpoint.

REJECTED: leaving it, with the epoch-side snapshot documented as the only route — the obvious wrong route would stay silently lossy, and a convention that has to be known is not a property. REJECTED: taking it as separate work — it is the substrate the arrival delta reads, so building the delta on a lossy capture would have shipped a report whose inputs quietly disagreed with each other.
properties.name: A snapshot excludes by edge ROLE, not by endpoint type — a commitment to an epoch is design content
properties.rationale:
FOUND BY READING THE CODE THE DECISION DEPENDED ON, not by a detector — and nothing could have flagged it. A snapshot that drops an edge is indistinguishable from a snapshot of a node that never had one: there is no second, contradicting fact to make the loss computable. That is the same blind spot recorded in `dec:epoch-pins-a-version-combination` ("a single edge pointing the wrong way creates no cycle and trips no detector"), one layer down — here it is an edge's ABSENCE from a record, which is even quieter than a wrong edge's presence.

The general shape is worth keeping, because this project keeps meeting it: a rule that was exactly right for the vocabulary existing when it was written, and became wrong when the vocabulary grew, WITHOUT anything changing at the site of the rule. `BOOKKEEPING_TYPES` was never edited; `SCHEDULED_FOR` was added somewhere else entirely. Proxies decay silently when the thing they proxy for moves.

Mutation-checked: empty `COMMITMENT_EDGES` and `a_schedule_edge_survives_a_snapshot_of_the_item` fails, while the epoch-side test keeps passing — which is also the evidence that the two routes were genuinely asymmetric before this.

properties.decision: A capability's verification state is three-valued: verified (a passing check of its own), component_verified (no check of its own, but a component it is allocated to carries a passing one — computed at read time, never written), and unchecked. The coverage line reports the third state as its own clause; detect_gaps replaces the N per-capability unverified alarms with ONE component_granularity_verification gap per carrying component at 0.35 — listing the riding capabilities, acknowledgeable once; status_contradiction accepts component-granularity proof for a verified status claim; loop_status counts component_verified as proven. A failing component suite carries nothing: passing-is-verified holds at every granularity.
properties.name: Component-granularity verification is a computed third state, one question per component
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-73 vocabulary session, from their own fleet's field trial): a brownfield adopt with real per-service suites plus a 137-file integration suite read as '0/20 capabilities verified' and cost 21 near-identical acknowledge writes. Computed state over a bulk-attest write because the graph should record exactly what was checked — the component — and derive what that means one hop away; manufactured capability-level VERIFIES edges would be indistinguishable from direct checks forever after. The word component_verified because it says where the check lives. One gap per component because the residual question ('is component granularity enough for these?') is genuinely per-component and deserves to be asked once, not N times — the BL-42 lesson again: a loud detector needs a different question, not a tuned number. The write side needed nothing: VERIFIES accepts any target and even carries an unused coverage enum — the whole defect was the read side.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and recorded as BRAINSTORMING rather than as a proposal — Anthony's own framing, 2026-07-25, thinking out loud. His starting doubt is the right one and had not been written down: claiming a cluster of nodes says nothing about the REPOSITORY, and if the design and the code share one repo, two people working different clusters still collide in git even when they never touch the same node. FOUR IDEAS AS HE PUT THEM. (1) reflow2 REPLACES git — the graph defines who may touch what, and git becomes an internal implementation detail. (2) The graph is a set of TEMPORARY LOCAL repos, pushed upstream only once work is done and no conflicts exist. (3) Each session opens a TEMPORARY WORKTREE BRANCH holding an identical copy of the graph; the person works there, then reflow2's own merge reconciles the copy back and the temporary is deleted. (4) A WEBSOCKET pushing every change to every user, giving live simultaneous collaboration. WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, and it matters for ranking them: the collision is in the export FILE, not in the graph, and reflow2 already answers file-level collision semantically — BL-80's three-way merge compares per node and per property against the common ancestor and mints each real conflict as a Question with a deterministic id, and `--merge`/`--merge-apply` run it without a server. So idea 3 is not new machinery; it is mostly a PROCEDURE over machinery that exists, and a git worktree already gives each person their own checkout with its own `.reflow2/graph` (the store lock is per-directory). The missing piece is small and specific: git supports per-path merge drivers — this repo already uses `merge=union` for COORD.md — so registering the design export with a driver that calls reflow2's own merge would make two people working different clusters merge automatically, and make a genuine overlap arrive as a Question instead of as conflict markers in a 500KB JSON file. Idea 2 is idea 3 with extra steps, since git branches are already local until pushed. Idea 1 would make reflow2 a version-control system, contradicts dec:repo-file-embedded and req:persistence, and would have to reinvent what it currently inherits for free. Idea 4 is the simultaneity road already held open by dec:central-host and BL-99, with the counter-argument recorded there: this tool's loop is deliberate and attributable rather than live.
properties.name: OPEN — how are two people's simultaneous edits kept apart: worktrees, temporary repos, or a live channel?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming on purpose. Anthony called it thinking out loud, and the first honest thing to do with four ideas is to write them down as four ideas rather than pick one and start building — which is precisely the practice dec:exploratory-staging is about. Two notes for whoever takes it up. The ranking above is a finding, not a decision: it says which ideas are cheap and which are large, and the cheap one is testable this week by two people on one design without a line of new Rust. And the doubt that started it should survive into whatever gets built — a claim on a cluster of nodes is not a claim on a repository, so any answer here has to say what happens to the CODE two people are writing beside the design, not only what happens to the graph.

properties.decision:
Anthony's call 2026-07-31, on a measurement that inverted the assumption the earlier decisions were written under.

MEASURED FIRST, on reflow2's own material: its entire design prose is 3.5 MB across 64 markdown files; the design export is 1.7 MB; the whole `.git` history is 81 MB. AND 29 SESSION TRANSCRIPTS COME TO 115.8 MB, A MEAN OF 4.0 MB EACH — already 1.4× the entire repository history, accumulated in a couple of weeks.

THE CORRECTION THIS FORCES. `dec:content-manifest` states that "raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first". THAT IS WRONG, and it is recorded here rather than edited into his accepted text. Documents are noise and images are occasional; TRANSCRIPTS ARE THE GROWTH, by an order of magnitude, and they recur every session forever.

WHY A SIZE CAP IS THE WRONG LEVER, which is the whole point. A 4 MB file passes any sane per-file threshold. What ends a repository is not one large object but 4 MB × EVERY SESSION, PERMANENTLY, UNPRUNABLE — git history cannot be trimmed without rewriting it and breaking every clone. Even assuming JSONL compresses to roughly a third, 500 sessions is a repository of several hundred megabytes, and "clone and you have everything" stops being a feature.

SO THE CONTROL IS WHAT GETS STORED. Session transcripts go in BY EXCEPTION, not by default — kept when a specific claim needs its receipt, not routinely. This is not a new position, only a newly-connected one: `cap:session-memory` already says "a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation: leaning on it recreates the markdown problem one level down." It named the size and named the danger; nobody had joined that to repository growth.

A SIZE GUARD STILL, AND HONESTLY SCOPED. `put` refuses above a threshold with an EXPLICIT, RECORDED OVERRIDE — the idiom this project already uses everywhere: `export_graph`'s `accept_divergence`, `set_artifact_checksum`'s required disposition, `record_change` refusing a planned epoch, the schedule-loss guard. Refuse loudly, allow deliberately, record the choice. It catches the catastrophic accident — a video, a dataset — and NOT the real risk, which is stated so nobody mistakes it for the answer. The threshold is anchored to GitHub's 100 MB hard block rather than a number invented to feel safe (`req:defaults-do-not-assert`): past that the problem stops being local and becomes a failed push someone else has to understand.

AND THE MANIFEST REPORTS TOTAL BYTES AND THE LARGEST ENTRIES. Report, never judge (`dec:report-dont-judge`): no threshold, just visibility on every check. This is the piece that would have surfaced the finding without anyone measuring by hand, which is the argument for it.

NOT GIT LFS. It reintroduces the second distribution channel `dec:where-content-lives` chose committed blobs to avoid, and breaks the clone-and-you-have-everything property that decision was made for.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS, stated so it is a condition rather than a hedge: if distillation keeps proving insufficient — if people genuinely reach for raw transcripts often — then storing them routinely is correct, and the answer becomes LFS or an external store. That REOPENS `dec:where-content-lives` rather than patching around it.
properties.name: What bounds the store is WHAT gets stored, not how big it is — transcripts by exception, a cap only for the catastrophic case
properties.rationale:
The recommendation changed shape when it was measured, which is the part worth keeping. The obvious answer to "nothing bounds repo growth" is a size cap, and a size cap would not have caught the thing that is actually growing — it would have shipped, looked prudent, and left the repository on the same trajectory.

Anthony asked for the recommendation rather than taking his own earlier "committed, no cap" as settled, which is what created room for the measurement. Worth noting because the useful move was cheap: four `du` and `ls` calls against real material, rather than reasoning about what a content store might contain.

The correction to `dec:content-manifest` is recorded here rather than edited into it, per `dec:reopen-supersedes` — the earlier claim was reasonable when written and is simply wrong, and overwriting it would erase the fact that the project believed something else on the evidence it had.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, delivering `req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry` and closing the last open question under `cap:content-store`.

A COMMITTED MANIFEST, plain text, mapping CONTENT HASH → ORIGINAL FILENAME → WHAT REFERENCES IT. One artefact, two jobs, which is why it was chosen over either job's narrower answer:

1. COMPLETENESS. Once content exists, the export document holds only pointers, so handing someone `reflow2.json` alone gives them a design whose diagrams silently fail to resolve. The manifest makes "do I have everything?" a set comparison — hashes listed against hashes present — rather than a discovery made when a picture does not open. That is `req:content-reaches-every-seat`'s fail-loud requirement made checkable by a person, not only by the tool.

2. LEGIBILITY IN GIT. A content-addressed blob lands as `blobs/ab/cdef…` and git reports it as an added file with a hex name that tells a reviewer nothing. The manifest is text, so the same change also appears in a diff as a readable line — `architecture-sketch.png` added, referencing `dec:x` — which is what a human actually reads in `git log -p`.

`.gitattributes` MARKS THE BLOB DIRECTORY `binary`. Two concrete effects, and the second is the one that matters: git stops attempting diffs it cannot produce, and — critically — stops applying line-ending conversion, which would CORRUPT a PNG on a checkout configured for CRLF. That is silent data loss on someone else's machine, and one line prevents it.

WHY THE BINARY WORRY WAS SMALLER THAN IT LOOKED, recorded because the reasoning nearly went the other way. Git's weaknesses with binaries are poor diffs, poor delta compression, and unresolvable merge conflicts. IMMUTABLE CONTENT ADDRESSING removes two of the three outright: a blob is never updated, so an "edit" is a NEW FILE with a new name — git sees an addition, which is the clearest possible signal — and two people adding different blobs add different files, so a binary merge conflict cannot arise. The only conflict is on the pointer inside the export, which the `merge.reflow2` driver already handles. WHAT REMAINS IS GROWTH: every version is a new file that stays forever, and that is the size-cap question `dec:where-content-lives` deliberately left open.

DELIBERATELY NOT DECIDED HERE: whether the manifest lives inside the export document or beside it as its own committed file. Both satisfy the requirement; the second keeps the export byte-stable diff properties simpler and is the likelier answer, but it is an implementation choice for build time rather than a design commitment.
properties.name: A committed manifest — hash to filename to referenced-by — plus .gitattributes marking blobs binary
properties.rationale:
Taken because one artefact answered two questions that arrived independently — the export-completeness gap found by an impact-check, and Anthony's worry about git legibility for binaries. When a single small thing satisfies two unrelated needs, that is usually the right shape rather than a coincidence.

The `.gitattributes` line is the part with a real failure behind it rather than an inconvenience: line-ending conversion silently corrupting a binary on a differently-configured checkout is the kind of fault that appears as "the diagram is broken on my machine" weeks later, with nothing in the history to point at.

The binary-churn analysis is recorded because the initial framing — mine — overstated the problem, and correcting it is what made the manifest a legibility feature rather than a workaround. Content addressing had already solved most of what was being worried about; naming which part it did NOT solve (growth) is what keeps the remaining risk visible instead of assumed handled.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, refining `dec:where-content-lives` (accepted) per `dec:reopen-supersedes`. The proposal and its measurement are preserved in the snapshot taken before this edit.

THE STORE IS HAND-ROLLED, SYNCHRONOUS, AND LIVES IN `reflow2-core`. Three operations — `put(bytes) -> hash`, `get(hash) -> bytes`, `exists(hash)` — over `sha2` (already a core dependency) and `std::fs`, with write-to-temp-then-rename for atomicity. Zero new crates.

WHY, MEASURED RATHER THAN REASONED. `object_store` 0.14.1 with `default-features = false, features = ["fs"]` resolves 68 crates, **36 of them new to reflow2**. About 24 arrive through `url`'s internationalised-domain-name machinery — the whole ICU4X stack, `zerovec`/`yoke`/`tinystr`, `idna`, `percent-encoding` — which a local content-addressed store never calls. The accepted decision's note that cloud features off "avoids reqwest and the crypto providers" was true and did not describe the tree.

AND IT UN-DOES A COMPLICATION RATHER THAN ADDING ONE. `dec:where-content-lives` split hash-in-core from store-in-mcp ONLY because `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio. A synchronous `std::fs` store keeps `reflow2-core` free of a runtime — measured, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2 — and keeps the store deterministic and in-memory-testable alongside everything else in the core. THAT PART OF `dec:where-content-lives` IS SUPERSEDED; its other two parts (blobs committed to the repo; content-addressed, immutable, fail-loud pointers) STAND UNCHANGED.

`object_store` IS THE DOCUMENTED UPGRADE PATH, recorded rather than discarded. It is the right crate for multi-cloud object storage and remains the answer if a cloud backend is ever wanted: it presents one trait over local filesystem, in-memory, S3, GCS, Azure and HTTP/WebDAV, so the backend becomes runtime configuration. The three-function interface above is deliberately the shape it slots behind — content addressing is what makes the swap safe, because a blob fetched from anywhere verifies against its own hash. Adopting it later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says. WHEN THAT DAY COMES, the costs already measured apply: 36 new crates, an async runtime reaching the core (or the hash/store split reinstated), and a declaration per `dec:design-dependencies-declared`.

WHAT WE GIVE UP TODAY, stated so nobody rediscovers it: multipart uploads, conditional writes, listing and prefix semantics, and cloud backends. Immutable content-addressed blobs need none of them — there are no paths to list, no partial writes to resume, and no update-in-place to make conditional.
properties.name: Hand-rolled synchronous content store in reflow2-core, zero new dependencies; object_store is the documented upgrade path
properties.rationale:
Anthony's call on a measurement the accepted decision had itself demanded before adoption. That clause — "STILL TO CHECK BEFORE ADOPTING: its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed" — is the only reason this surfaced before code rather than after, and it is worth noting as a habit: a decision that names what it has NOT verified does work a confident decision would not.

The deciding argument was not dependency count for its own sake. It was that `object_store`'s value is uniformity across backends, and the feature set it exists to provide — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — is precisely the set an immutable content-addressed store does not have. Paying 36 crates and an async runtime for capabilities the use case forecloses is the wrong trade at this size, and the trade reverses the moment a cloud backend is real.

Recorded as an upgrade path rather than a rejection, because the alternative to a hand-rolled store is not "no library forever" — it is "no library until there is something a library does better". Writing that down is what stops the next session re-running the same evaluation from scratch.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-04, taking the split this node had already written down while it was open: CLAIMS IN THE GRAPH for who has what, COORD.md RETAINED for the conventions and the merge-conflict doctrine, and the IN-PROGRESS TABLE DELETED rather than maintained in two places — because two places for the same fact is the failure the whole documents-into-the-graph move exists to end.

THE STATED BLOCKER DISSOLVED RATHER THAN BEING OVERRULED, which is worth recording precisely because this node held itself open on it since 2026-07-25. The rationale read: "a claim board is a coordination mechanism between two people, and switching it unilaterally would mean one of them silently changing where the other must look; that is Anthony's brother's call as much as his." Anthony, 2026-08-04: "my brother hasn't actively developed any of this apart from offering feedback." So there is no second writer to strand — the premise was that two people coordinate through this board, and only one of them has ever written to it. The caution was correct when written and the fact it was resting on turned out not to hold. THE CONSEQUENCE IS NARROWER THAN THE DECISION LOOKS: reflow2 still has no live multi-writer case, so the claims layer remains UNPROVEN under contention. This move proves it under a single writer only, and that limit should not be quietly forgotten the first time a second person appears.

⭐ THE PREREQUISITE WAS RUN, AND IT PASSED ON A CAPABILITY THE MARKDOWN STRUCTURALLY CANNOT HAVE. This node named its own gate — "nobody has used claim_region for real yet, so the first move is to run it on one real piece of work and see whether claim_report says something a person would have said." Run 2026-08-04 on the live work: `claim_region` with seed `cap:corpus-ingest`, depth 2, contributor `who:ajs`, carrying BL-186's note. `claim_report` returned the claim, zero overlaps, zero stale — and `liveness: "live"`, COMPUTED from the claiming seat's host and pid rather than stored. Its own advisory states the payoff: "`gone` means that session has exited and the claim is a ghost (excluded from overlaps), `unknown` means it was made on another machine or before seats were recorded — unknown is never read as free, because taking work somebody is actively doing is the expensive mistake."

THAT IS THE DIRECT FIX FOR THE FAILURE THAT PROMPTED THIS, and it is not the reason first given. This node argued the gain was that a computed region FOLLOWS THE DESIGN instead of going stale as a hand-typed file list. True, but secondary. The measured failure is different: on 2026-08-04 COORD.md was carrying BL-186 as in-progress after #73 had landed it, and the file itself contains a note recording that this was the THIRD STALE CLAIM FOUND IN ONE SWEEP. A markdown line cannot know its author walked away — a claim is only ever retired by someone remembering to retire it, which is exactly the class of thing people forget. Liveness computed from the session means an abandoned claim reads `gone` on its own, with nobody remembering anything. The markdown board was not merely going stale; IT HAD NO MECHANISM BY WHICH IT COULD EVER NOT.

WHAT IS KNOWINGLY GIVEN UP, restated at the point of deciding rather than left in the open-question text where it would read as unresolved: COORD.md's in-progress table was readable by a human with no reflow2 and no binary, and it appeared as a diff in every pull request. A graph claim does neither — it travels in the committed export, so it is visible, but reading it needs the tool. That is accepted deliberately. The conventions, the handles table and the merge-conflict doctrine STAY in COORD.md for exactly that reason: they are addressed to someone who may not have reflow2 running, and they are prose about practice rather than facts about state.

THE STANDING RULE THIS SETS, and it is the general form: A DOCUMENT SHOULD HOLD WHAT IS ADDRESSED TO SOMEONE WITHOUT THE TOOL, AND THE GRAPH SHOULD HOLD WHAT THE TOOL CAN COMPUTE. COORD.md splits cleanly along that line — practice stays, state goes. It is the same test as `dec:the-transition-is-two-halves-and-reads-are-the-unscheduled-one` ("can you delete this document and regenerate it from the graph?"), and the in-progress table is the first thing in this repo to pass it by being deleted rather than by already having been derived.
properties.name: DECIDED — the claim board moves into the graph; COORD.md keeps the conventions and the conflict doctrine
properties.rationale:
Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it was a genuinely good test of the claims layer.

MOVED TO ACCEPTED 2026-08-04 on Anthony's explicit word, after its own stated prerequisite was run for the first time. Two things are recorded here that a later reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. FIRST, the decision did not overrule its objection — the objection's premise (two people coordinating) turned out to be false, and saying so is different from deciding against it, because if a second writer ever appears the caution becomes live again rather than having been settled. SECOND, the reason for the move is not the reason originally given: computed-region-follows-the-design was the argument, and computed LIVENESS turned out to be what actually fixes the observed failure. The original argument was not wrong, it was aimed at the wrong half — worth keeping, because it is the second time in this project a fork resolved on something outside the recorded options (see the method finding on dec:agent-navigates-content).

The unproven-under-contention limit is stated on the node rather than left implicit: a single-writer proof is what was obtained, and the claims layer's real case is still ahead of it.

properties.decision:
ifc:core-api — the DesignGraph API that `cmp:graph` provides and `cmp:service` consumes — is the sole operational path between the design store and the agent surface. Accepted as a SPOF, like dec:graph-spof-accepted and dec:service-spof-accepted.

📌 CORRECTED 2026-08-21, and the prior wording is in `snap:epoch:v0380:dec:core-api-spof-accepted`. This said the path ran "between the Design Store and the Agent Surface subsystems", which stopped being true and was not noticed. `cmp:graph` sits in `sys:foundation`, not `sys:store` — `sys:store` contains only `cmp:export` and `cmp:search`. The rationale below already recorded that BL-83a moved the provider to `cmp:graph`; what nobody updated was the sentence naming which subsystems the bridge joins, so the decision described a topology that had moved under it.

THE JUDGEMENT WAS AND REMAINS CORRECT — one store, one surface over it, and the bridge between them is inherently single. Only the description was stale, which is the more insidious of the two: a wrong decision gets argued with, while a right decision describing the wrong parts is read straight past.
properties.name: The DesignGraph API is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: One store, one surface over it (req:agent-native, single-writer storage): the bridge between them is inherently single. Surfaced when BL-83a retired cmp:core and moved the API's provider to cmp:graph; the topology is honest, not a defect to engineer away.

properties.decision:
`ifc:core-api` moves from `published` to `internal`. The published surface is now three boundaries — `ifc:mcp-tools`, `ifc:mcp-tools-http`, `ifc:graph-export` — and every one of them passes the test: agents call the tool surfaces, and other tools and designs read the export document.

THE SAME TEST THAT SETTLED `ifc:graph-read`, applied here and failing: is anybody outside this project's control writing code against it? No. `reflow2-core` is not on crates.io, its only dependant is `reflow2-mcp` by local path in the same workspace, and users receive binaries and speak MCP rather than linking the library.

WHAT IT WAS DOING WHILE PUBLISHED, which is the concrete harm rather than a tidiness argument: `export_surface` is the document handed to another team or a vendor, and this was in it. Asked "what may I build against?", reflow2 answered with the entire Rust API of an undistributed crate — 277 public functions, described in two of nine fields.

THE UNDERLYING PROBLEM IS THAT ITS NAME IS ITS SCOPE. "DesignGraph API" means whatever that struct exposes today, and it grows whenever anyone adds a method. A contract whose scope grows by default cannot be relied on or satisfied by a second implementation. That is not fixable by writing more prose about it; the route to real contracts here is more narrow interfaces like `ifc:graph-read`, whose five operations are named and where adding a sixth is a deliberate act.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN IT — the same two triggers as `ifc:graph-read`, either sufficient: `reflow2-core` is published as a crate for others to build on, or an implementation is wanted from somebody other than this project. Neither holds today.

WHAT WAS FIXED ALONGSIDE, all of it recorded rather than silently tidied:
  — `spec` held a 2026-07-28 changelog note in place of a specification; the note is history and now lives in the change record and the snapshot, and the field describes the contract.
  — `payload_schema` read `unspecified` while eleven `schema/*.yaml` artifacts carried `SPECIFIES` edges with `format: json_schema`. The design contradicted itself about whether its own contract was written down; the field now names them.
  — `error_model`, `endpoint`, `payload_format`, `auth` and `transport_security` were unstated. All are now stated, and the last three are `none` — a fact about a library boundary with no wire, no principal and no channel, not a gap.
  — `operations` is now an explicit statement that this boundary CANNOT enumerate its operations, rather than a blank that reads as unfinished paperwork.
  — `dec:core-api-spof-accepted` named a topology that had moved; corrected, with the prior wording in `snap:epoch:v0380:dec:core-api-spof-accepted`.

🛑 ONE FINDING COULD NOT BE FIXED, AND THE REASON IS THE MORE INTERESTING RESULT. Nothing verifies this contract, and nothing verifies ANY contract in this design, because **`VERIFIES` cannot target an Interface at all**: the schema enumerates its targets as Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule and Constraint. An attempt to attach `ver:store` — which does validate the eleven schema files that specify this boundary — was refused by the edge validator.

So reflow2 can check a rule, a budget, a part and a file, and cannot check a CONTRACT. Interfaces are the nodes a modular open-systems approach turns on, and they are the one kind of node the design cannot attach evidence to. That edge's own schema comments record it under-enumerating its targets TWICE before — Requirement and Constraint were each true in a real design before the list admitted it — so Interface may be the third instance of the same pattern rather than a deliberate exclusion. Left as an open question rather than fixed on the way past: widening a `to` list is a schema change and belongs to its own decision.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED: both `sys:foundation` and `cmp:graph` provide it, and both `sys:agent-surface` and `cmp:service` consume it, which is why this one interface generated 16 of the design's declared contract pairs from what the SPOF decision calls a single path. Whether a subsystem should re-declare what its own module declares is a modelling question about levels, not a defect to repair on the way past.
properties.name: DECIDED — the DesignGraph API is withdrawn from the published surface
properties.rationale:
ANTHONY'S CALL, 2026-08-21: "go with your recommendation to fix all the findings and put internal", after a review that laid out seven findings and named which of them were judgement rather than fact.

WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN JUST DONE. Withdrawing a published designation is a statement about what this project commits to — the opposite direction from publishing, and equally his to make. And `internal` is the DEFAULT, so a boundary sitting at it carries no evidence of whether anyone considered the question. Without this node, a later reader finds the same ambiguity that made the review necessary in the first place.

THE REVIEW ITSELF IS THE THING WORTH KEEPING, more than the answer: the test is "who outside your control writes code against this?", and it is re-applicable to every boundary rather than being a verdict about this one.

properties.decision: DECIDED (b) THE SP-3b HANDSHAKE, on Anthony's word 2026-07-27. `ingest` goes on the MCP surface with the AGENT as the backend: reflow2 returns the extraction prompts and the agent returns the JSON. No LLM provider dependency is added, so the agent-native deferral stands. (a) an agent-driven skill walking the folder was rejected, not unconsidered: it is cheaper and consistent with every other reflow2 skill, but it moves the disciplines ingest.rs enforces IN CODE — never cascade-fail, no phantom edges, provenance on everything, time-aware resolution, and now the resolution bands and the structural subset pass — into prose an agent is asked to follow. An instruction is weaker than a type system, and docs/sharpening.md names that exact failure: shaping the model until the tool goes quiet. THE DECIDING CONSEQUENCE is what it does to the missing extraction passes: a pass written in Rust behind the handshake is reusable by every future ingest and testable without a model, while the same pass written into a skill is prose that cannot be regression-tested at all. Since Decision and Verification passes are the two-thirds of the requester's ask that reflow2 cannot currently see, the option that makes those passes worth writing is the option that delivers the feature.
properties.name: A folder of documents goes through the ingest handshake, not a skill
properties.rationale: Scoped 2026-07-26 by reading ingest.rs, graph.rs and the schema after Anthony asked whether reflow2 could take a colleague's years of markdown. The reading moved the work in BOTH directions. (1) BL-97 called cross-document identity the hard part; it is largely BUILT — fuzzy_match resolves each extracted node against every existing node of that type in the whole graph, so ingesting forty specs already converges, with the merges reported and prior states snapshotted rather than clobbered. What is missing there is COST, not capability: scan_nodes is a full type scan run once per extracted node, so a corpus is quadratic. (2) The gap nobody had named is COVERAGE OF THE ASK: ingest creates exactly eight node types, and Verification and Decision are not among them. The request was 'requirements, test results, designer intent' — reflow2 extracts the first and neither of the others, so a corpus run today would return a design with no test evidence and no rationale, from documents containing both, and nothing would say so. Full write-up in docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md, including the auto-merge-at-90 tension with dec:ask-not-repair at corpus scale, and the fifth instance of this project's recurring shape: the schema's per-type resolution thresholds are declared and read by nothing.

properties.decision: DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) WHAT IS IN THE REPOSITORY, in his own decomposition — this is the load-bearing part, because getting it wrong is what produced the objection this decision had to overturn. A NON-CODE PROJECT puts TWO things under version control: the reflow2 design graph, and the design artifacts. A CODE PROJECT puts THREE: the reflow2 design graph, the design artifacts, and the actual implemented code. THE FIRST TWO ARE THE CONSTANT. The implemented system is the only term that varies, and it is present in exactly one of the two cases. THE OBJECTION THIS OVERTURNS, which was mine and not his: the weakness recorded against this option said deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. It conflated the SUBJECT SYSTEM with the DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS, and a sweep only ever covers what is in the repository. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So a derived scope is not a code-only convenience. It is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for a non-code project than for software, because there the tracked artifacts are the whole of what a coverage question could ever have been asking about. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, AND SPECIAL BY BEING MORE THAN THE NORM, NOT LESS — 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. It is the one case where the third term exists, so one sweep sees the implemented system alongside the graph and the artifacts. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is exactly why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on: a default inferred from the common case would quietly assume an implemented system that most subjects do not have. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SWEEP ITSELF. Of the three tracked things, the design GRAPH is the one that must be excluded — a design cannot be its own subject, and `docs/design` is a named exclusion in reflow2's own sweep for exactly that reason. The other two are swept: the artifacts always, the implemented code when there is any. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).
properties.name: Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system
properties.rationale: Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.

properties.decision:
Answers option (b) of dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph WITHOUT adding a node type, which was that option's strongest objection.

THE MECHANISM. A defect found by use is recorded as a `TemporalFact`: `subject_id` = the node it indicts, `fact_type` = "defect", `statement` = the claim (FULLTEXT-INDEXED, so search_design finds it), `value` = JSON carrying the measurement, `basis` = "measured" (never "forecast" — a defect is observed), `confidence` = how sure the observer is. Edges: HAS_TEMPORAL_FACT from the indicted node, ABOUT_ENTITY back to it, VALID_FROM the epoch it was observed. VALID_TO is set WHEN IT IS FIXED — absent means still true.

WHY THIS TYPE AND NOT A NEW ONE. Four reasons, each checked rather than assumed. (1) TemporalFact's own extraction_hint already says "a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs", and a defect is exactly that: true of the build from the epoch it was found until the epoch it was fixed. (2) `fact_type` is `{ type: string, indexed: true }` — free-form and INDEXED, not an enum, so "defect" needs no schema change. (3) THERE IS A SHIPPING PRECEDENT for using fact_type as a discriminator a reader queries: crates/reflow2-core/src/readiness.rs:57 marks readiness assertions this way and reads them back. This is not a new convention, it is an existing one applied to a second case. (4) The prior against new vocabulary is heavy and documented — this project proposed and WITHDREW two node types in one week (Attestation to TemporalFact, Hazard to DesignRule + CONSTRAINS) — and dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph itself flagged TemporalFact as probably already the shape.

WHAT THIS FIXES, precisely. The graph had no way to say "this capability is BUILT, VERIFIED, and does not do what it claims". Verification answers whether a check PASSES, and every defect of this kind sat under a passing check. DriftEvent answers whether code moved away from the design, and in these cases code and design AGREED and both were wrong. HEAL's issues are computed from graph shape and vanish between runs. So the largest category of backlog row had nowhere to go, which is why it went to markdown.

THE LIFECYCLE IS THE PART MARKDOWN DID BY HAND. A row today is annotated "DONE 2026-08-05" in prose. Here, fixing a defect means setting VALID_TO to the epoch that fixed it, so "is this still broken?" is a graph question rather than a reading-comprehension one — and the history survives instead of being overwritten.

MEASURED STARTING POINT: reflow2's own graph contained ZERO TemporalFacts before this decision, despite BL-68 building the measured/forecast distinction for them. The type was built, correct, and unused.

WHAT IS STILL OWED, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS. Nothing in the LOOP reads these yet. `statement` is fulltext so search_design finds them today — genuinely better than grepping a 592 KB file, and the reason this is worth doing before the reader exists — but loop_status does not count open defects, and until it does, a defect recorded here is discoverable rather than SURFACED. That reader is the next increment and it is a Rust change. Recorded so the gap is on the record rather than discovered later: writing facts nothing reads is this project's own recurring declared-and-read-by-nothing failure, and doing it knowingly with the reader scheduled is different from doing it by accident.

NOT CLAIMED: that this retires docs/backlog.md. Three of the four backlog categories already had homes (unbuilt work is a planned Capability, an open question is a proposed Decision, a discovered limit is a Constraint or DesignRule) and were not being used either. This decision closes the one category that had NO home. Deriving the markdown from the graph is option (d) and remains open.
properties.name: A defect found by USING a built capability is a TemporalFact with fact_type "defect" — no new vocabulary, and the lifecycle comes free
properties.rationale: Chosen rather than left open because dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph has held five options and no choice since 2026-08-04, and the cost of that is measured: 218 backlog rows, 592 KB, and an accepted decision (dec:export-once-per-pr) violated and re-derived for the third time in the very session that asked for the fix. Anthony called it embarrassing and asked for it as first priority; the conservative option — reuse an existing type with an existing reader precedent — is the one that can ship now. Left `proposed` with him as approver rather than accepted: dec:three-party-checks says the human decides, and this changes how the project records its own learning.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-05: "I like and approve: a tool that describes the design at a given path — id, label, node counts, mint stamp — without binding to it. Your agent walks the tree (which it can, as you said); reflow2 says what's in each .reflow2 it finds. That splits cleanly along the no-file-I/O rule."

THE SHAPE. Two responsibilities, split along the line this project already draws. THE AGENT FINDS THE DIRECTORIES — walking a tree for `.reflow2` is file IO, which reflow2 does not do and does not need to, because the ambient agent does it well (`dec:agent-navigates-content`, and its parent `dec:three-party-checks`: "the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides"). REFLOW2 SAYS WHAT IS IN ONE — given a path, it reports the design's identity: graph id, label, how many nodes of what kind, the stamp it was minted under. Neither half can do the other's job, and the split is the same one that already governs content navigation and coverage sweeps.

⭐ WHAT IT REPLACES, AND WHY THE OBVIOUS ASK WAS THE WRONG ONE. Anthony first asked for "a reflow2 tool to simply return all graph_ids". Measured before answering: that returns ONE PER STORE. Storage keys are `{graph_id}\x00{type}\x00{id}` and `dynograph_storage::keys::graph_prefix` exists, so the FOUNDATION supports many graphs per store — but reflow2 opens one graph per store by convention (`DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID`, one `.reflow2` per project), and the three graphs in the hxm_program field report are three separate STORES. Enumerating within a store is therefore a true answer to a question nobody has. Describing a store found on disk is the question that was actually being asked.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE. It settles the DISCOVERY half of `req:a-session-chooses-its-design` — how an agent learns what designs exist before anything is created, which is what would have prevented the accidental third graph (`dec:no-design-here-never-looked`).
