So: you capture, reflow2 notices and KEEPS noticing, it can suggest, you decide.

A NEW FILE IS SEEN BY NOTHING. The CI gate builds its observation list by iterating THE ARTIFACTS THE DESIGN ALREADY KNOWS and never walks the disk; reconcile_artifacts does no file I/O at all, so the caller supplies what is looked at. `undocumented_addition` therefore exists as a drift kind THE GATE STRUCTURALLY CANNOT PRODUCE. Add a file, commit, push: every check stays green. The Stop hook does not fire either, because it triggers on GRAPH WRITES and adding a file is not one.

⇒ REFLOW2 IS PROACTIVE ABOUT INTENT IT HOLDS AND BLIND TO REALITY IT DOES NOT. Every automatic mechanism reasons over the graph. The moment the question is "what exists that I was never told about?", nothing looks.

⚠️ AND THE SAME BLIND SPOT WAS JUST FOUND IN THE INSTRUMENT: wall_check walked design-outward-to-files and could not report a file nobody registered, until it was taught to derive its walk roots from the claimed paths. The gate has the identical shape and has not been taught. That the same structural error appeared independently in the tool and the gate is the finding, not the coincidence.

=== OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN ===

  (a) THE GATE SWEEPS THE ROOTS THE DESIGN ALREADY POINTS AT and reports files no Artifact claims. Smallest, needs no configuration, and is exactly what wall_check now does — the code exists. Turns 'I forgot' from invisible into a note. ⚠️ Whether it should turn the build RED is a governance question with an owner and must be asked, not assumed.
  (b) MAKE ALLOCATION TIMING RECORDABLE — a date or basis on ALLOCATED_TO. This is the stated TRIGGER of dec:idea-is-allocation-running-ahead-of-the-seams, parked precisely because 156 ALLOCATED_TO edges carry only weight_basis and nothing dates an allocation. Taking it would unpark that question rather than only answering this one.
  (c) A DE FACTO ALLOCATION DETECTOR: when an unclaimed file's neighbours all sit in one component, propose that component. Uses propose_allocation, which already exists and already refuses to apply itself. Strongest reach, and the most likely to propose something confidently wrong — imports are coupling, not intent.
  (d) DO NOTHING; keep it human discipline. The honest option, and the status quo. It is what produced fifteen unmodelled modules and a missed skills_tools over a single day of development.

=== COUNTER-ARGUMENT, BESIDE THE IDEA RATHER THAN AGAINST IT ===

Watching artifacts appear risks re-introducing exactly what the last-responsible-moment ruling was FOR. If every new file prompts 'which black box does this belong to?', the design is pushed back toward allocating early — at the moment of writing a file, which is often earlier than the moment of knowing. The distinction that keeps both: NOTICING a file is unmodelled is not the same as DEMANDING it be allocated. The first is a fact about coverage; the second is a decision about structure. An option that conflates them would undo the ruling while appearing to implement it.

RELATED AND ALREADY SETTLED: dec:idea-allocation-waits-for-the-last-responsible-moment (accepted). PARKED, AND THIS MAY BE ITS TRIGGER: dec:idea-is-allocation-running-ahead-of-the-seams.
properties.name: OPEN — the last responsible moment is agreed, but what WATCHES for it to arrive? Today's measurement says nothing does, and a seven-day-old counter-argument predicted exactly that

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-21: "does each of the 10 subsystems have a defined interface contract? this is probably related to the tests for each subsystem. I had mentioned at some point that it would be nice to able to swap out a module for another (related to MOSA), but that is only possible if you defined contracts for each module/subsystem. I also feel like if you have defined contracts, you could mock its behavior for testing purposes."

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THE ANSWER TO THE DIRECT QUESTION: NO — ZERO OF TEN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

FOUR of the ten subsystems declare a provided interface at all. Of those four:
  sys:foundation    -> ifc:core-api       spec = a 2026-07-28 note saying the old `medium: REST` was a schema default and wrong
  sys:store         -> ifc:graph-export   spec = the same kind of correction note
  sys:human-channel -> ifc:reasoning-channel   NO SPEC
  sys:time-history  -> ifc:temporal-api        NO SPEC

Both "specs" are PROVENANCE CORRECTIONS. They are true and useful and they name no operation, no input and no output. **Not one subsystem publishes something you could substitute against or mock from.** The other six provide nothing.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN LAZY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    designation   count   with a substantive spec
    required        9            9  of 9
    published       4            2  of 4   (the other two are correction notes)
    internal        4            0  of 4

REFLOW2 HAS WRITTEN CAREFUL CONTRACTS FOR EVERYTHING IT DEPENDS ON AND ALMOST NONE FOR WHAT IT OFFERS. That is not an oversight anyone made; it is what happens by default. You specify what you CONSUME because you must know what to expect from someone else. You leave what you PROVIDE unspecified because you are on both sides of it and nothing ever forces the question. `internal` — module to module, exactly where a swap would happen — is 0 of 4.

⭐ AND THIS IS PRECISELY WHAT BLOCKS BOTH THINGS HE NAMED. Substitution matches what a module OFFERS. A mock stands in for what a module offers its callers. Both need the PROVIDED side specified, and the provided side is the side nobody wrote.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ ONE MISSING THING, NOW TRACEABLY THREE RETURNS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  1. SUBSTITUTABILITY / MOSA        — swap a module that meets the contract (2026-08-20)
  2. DERIVABLE FAILURE-MODE TESTING — edge cases from input boundaries, failure modes from output promises (2026-08-20)
  3. MOCKABLE TEST DOUBLES          — NEW TODAY, and the cheapest of the three to demonstrate

All three are blocked by the same gap, and the gap already has a number: 192 capabilities, 3 declaring inputs, 3 declaring outputs, 0 declaring a signature. `set_capability_signature` EXISTS and is verified — it was built precisely because the fields were unwritable at 0 of 170. It is now used on 3 of 192. **The TOOL leg is built. The INSTRUCTION and the DETECTOR are not.**

📌 MOCKING IS THE SHARPEST ARGUMENT OF THE THREE and it is worth saying why. Substitutability is a someday benefit — nobody is swapping the store this quarter. Derivable tests are a maybe: it is still unmeasured whether declared inputs produce cases nobody had thought of. **A mock pays immediately and locally**: a test that stands `sys:store` up against a fake instead of a real RocksDB is faster, and it is the only way to test the failure modes of a dependency you cannot make fail on demand. It is also the return with the shortest path to proving the contract is REAL — a contract you can mock is one you have actually specified, and a mock that diverges from the real module is a contract violation you can detect.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑 A REAL TENSION, RECORDED RATHER THAN RESOLVED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Earlier reasoning held that six subsystems present nothing BECAUSE NOTHING CONSUMES THEM, and that declaring interfaces for symmetry would FABRICATE CONTRACTS — asserting an agreement no two parties ever made. That argument is good and it is still good.

His MOSA argument cuts the other way: a contract is what makes substitution possible, so it is needed whether or not anything consumes it TODAY. An interface nobody consumes is not a fiction if the point of writing it is that someone else could implement it.

**BOTH ARE RIGHT ABOUT DIFFERENT THINGS.** The fabrication risk is real for a CONSUMES edge — that asserts a relationship. It is much weaker for a PROVIDES spec, which asserts only "this is what I offer", a statement the module can make alone and be held to. That distinction is not currently drawn anywhere, and drawing it may dissolve the tension entirely.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THE OPTIONS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

(a) SPECIFY ONE SUBSYSTEM'S PROVIDED CONTRACT AND MOCK IT. `sys:store` is the candidate: 2 components, it already provides `ifc:graph-export`, and it is the dependency most worth faking in a test (real RocksDB is the slowest thing in the suite). Write the spec, build a mock against it, and see whether the mock catches anything. SMALLEST THING THAT PROVES ALL THREE RETURNS AT ONCE, because a contract you can mock is one you have really written.

(b) THE THREE LEGS FOR CAPABILITY SIGNATURES. Instruction plus detector for `inputs`/`outputs`, since the tool exists. Cheap, and it moves 3-of-192 rather than answering a question. It is the ENABLER for (a) at scale but proves nothing on its own — and building the legs before knowing the vocabulary earns its keep is how 189 empty fields happen twice.

(c) DECLARE THE MISSING PROVIDED INTERFACES for the six silent subsystems. Directly answers his question. RISKS exactly the fabrication the earlier reasoning warns of, unless the provides-versus-consumes distinction above is settled first.

(d) MEASURE WHETHER A CONTRACT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT ANYTHING. Take the last N real defects and ask how many a specified provided interface would have prevented or caught. Answers "is this worth it" before any of the above, and it is the option that could kill the whole line of work honestly.

NOT KNOWN: whether reflow2's own architecture even permits module substitution. Nearly every function is an `impl DesignGraph` method on one shared struct — which is also why attributing a test to a module mechanically was so hard today. A design where everything hangs off one god-struct may be UNSWAPPABLE regardless of what contracts get written, and that is measurable before committing to any option here.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ EXTENDED 2026-08-21 — OPTIMISATION IS THE FOURTH RETURN, AND HE RATES IT ABOVE SUBSTITUTABILITY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

HIS WORDS: "the other thing I'd like to do is optimize. I feel that this is much easier if you do this internal to a module and one by one. if you have a contract with other modules, then you can really focus only on the internals of your black box (I think technically this is a white box since you can see what's inside). you can optimize one module at a time. this is probably more important than being able to swap out a module for another, but still the same principle."

📐 HIS TERMINOLOGY POINT IS CORRECT AND WORTH KEEPING. Black box and white box are the same element seen from the two sides of one contract. SUBSTITUTION is the black-box activity — you replace the inside and only the contract matters. OPTIMISATION is the white-box activity — you keep the contract and rework the inside. **They are duals across the same boundary, which is why one contract buys both.** The design carries `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (accepted) and has no complementary word for the other view; nothing breaks without one, but the pairing is worth naming because it explains why these two returns arrive together.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑🛑 BUT A CONTRACT IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SO PLAINLY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Optimising one module needs THREE things. The contract is only the first:

  (i)   A WALL — so a change to the inside cannot leak out.
        STATUS: 0 of 10 subsystems publish a contract (measured above).
  (ii)  A TARGET — what "better" means, and when to stop.
        STATUS: 1 Constraint in the entire design, and it is a SEMANTIC limit
        ("what complementary-pairing can ever catch"), not a budget.
        0 DimensionAssessments. **There is no stated performance target anywhere.**
  (iii) A MEASUREMENT — so you can tell whether you improved anything.
        STATUS: no benches directory, no criterion dependency, and not one
        `Instant::now()` or `elapsed()` in any test or tool. **Nothing in this
        repository measures how long anything takes.**

⭐⭐ AND THE ORDERING IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE INTUITION IN HIS MESSAGE. You CAN optimise a module with no contract, given a target and a measurement — people do it every day; they just risk breaking a caller and finding out later. You CANNOT optimise with a contract and no measurement: you can only change things and believe you improved them. **So for OPTIMISATION the contract is the LEAST urgent of the three, even though for SUBSTITUTION it is the most urgent.** The two returns want the same contract but not in the same order, and doing contracts first because they serve both would put the cheapest missing piece last.

📌 THIS IS ALSO WHERE HIS OWN OVER-ENGINEERING CONCERN BITES HARDEST. Optimising without a stated target is the definition of gold-plating: there is no condition under which you are finished, so the work ends when attention runs out. A budget is what makes optimisation STOP. `Constraint` + `budget_report` is exactly that machinery, built, and used once — on something that is not a budget.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
📐 AND ISOLATION IS PARTIAL HERE FOR A REASON THAT IS NOT ABOUT CONTRACTS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    54 core modules
    43 of them add methods to the SHARED `DesignGraph` struct (58 impl blocks)
    42 of them DO define types of their own

So modules own their OUTPUT types and not their STATE. Every one reads the same store through the same accessors. That means the internals a module can freely rework are its ALGORITHMS, and the internals it cannot are its DATA REPRESENTATION — changing how detection stores or indexes anything touches everybody. **Which caps what "optimise one module at a time" can reach**: constant factors and query shape, yes; a different index or layout, no. A contract at the seam does not change that, because the coupling is through shared state rather than through the interface.

⇒ A FIFTH OPTION FOR THE LIST ABOVE:

(e) GIVE ONE MODULE A TARGET AND A MEASUREMENT, AND OPTIMISE IT. Pick the slowest thing in the suite, state a budget as a `Constraint`, measure it, improve it, and see whether the budget was what made the work stop. CHEAPEST OF ALL THE OPTIONS — it needs no contract, no schema change and no new vocabulary, and it exercises `Constraint` + `budget_report`, which stand at 1 use. It also produces the first performance number this project has ever had, which every other option here would eventually need.
properties.name: OPEN — zero of ten subsystems publish a contract. Would writing one buy substitution, derivable tests, a mock, or optimisation?

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Source: Alex Sligar's 2026-08-05 research, specifically Zep/Graphiti, described there as "temporal knowledge graphs that encode what happened, when, and how entities relate over time" for agents that "must reason about evolving facts". Graphiti's distinguishing feature in that family is BI-TEMPORALITY: every fact carries both when it was true in the world and when the system came to know it. STILL OPEN.

WHAT REFLOW2 HAS, CHECKED IN schema/temporal.yaml RATHER THAN RECALLED: TemporalFact carries VALID_FROM and VALID_TO, both pointing at a DesignEpoch, plus `basis: measured|forecast` and an author-stated `confidence`. So the design already models world-time properly, and BL-68 already separated observation from projection — which is the harder half of what Graphiti does and reflow2 got there independently. What TemporalFact does NOT carry is any epoch for when the assertion ENTERED the record. ChangeEvent has `detected_at`, DriftEvent has `detected_at`, DimensionObservation has `observed_at` — the arrival time exists on the EVENTS but not on the FACT.

THE CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this may be worth more than schema tidiness: a retroactively discovered fact is written with VALID_FROM at the epoch it became true, and the record then reads as though the design always knew. "The beamline analysis code has assumed a single detector since 2016" and "we discovered in August 2026 that the beamline analysis code has assumed a single detector since 2016" become the same node. The second is the more useful sentence, because it tells a reader that everything designed between 2016 and 2026 was designed in ignorance of it — and that is exactly the reasoning a brownfield adoption needs. This is Anthony's own operating context (a ten-year-old bluesky/tiled stack being evolved on the fly), not a hypothetical.

WHERE IT ALREADY BITES, POSSIBLY: cap:as-of-epoch answers "what did the design say at epoch n" from snapshots. If retroactive facts are written with early VALID_FROM, an as-of-epoch answer can attribute knowledge to a past epoch that nobody had then — a subtler version of the same fiction dec:readiness-forecast-is-a-temporal-fact was created to stop. NOT VERIFIED: whether as-of-epoch actually reads TemporalFact validity or only Snapshots was not checked, and that determines whether this is a live defect or only a modelling gap. Check before treating it as either.

WHAT IS CHEAP: adding a RECORDED_AT epoch edge (or reusing AT_EPOCH, which already means "belongs to" for Snapshot and ChangeEvent) is additive, and req:defaults-do-not-assert has a clean answer for the backfill — absent means unstated, which reads as unstated.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT: nothing currently READS TemporalFact validity for anything a user sees, and reflow2's record already has a long list of declared-and-read-by-nothing fields (embedding_field, Project.domain) that this would join. A second time axis is also a real conceptual cost on a vocabulary that is already large, and the honest test is whether any computation would use it — which is the same bar dec:exploratory-staging is being held to. If the answer is "only a human reading the node would notice", the cheaper fix is prose in the fact's statement, not schema.
properties.name: OPEN — should a TemporalFact record WHEN IT WAS LEARNED as well as when it was true, since VALID_FROM/VALID_TO carry only world-time and a retroactive discovery loses its own arrival?
properties.rationale: Recorded as an idea because the missing half was verified in the schema and the brownfield consequence is Anthony's actual working context, but the deciding test — does any computation read it — is unanswered, and that test is what dec:exploratory-staging established as the bar for new vocabulary. Also recorded because BL-68 already made the harder measured/forecast distinction, which makes this the same argument one step along rather than a new idea.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-21: "it sounds like the changes to make it work for 10000 logged in users would be changes to dynograph-foundation, not necessarily to reflow2? ... rocksdb was developed by meta ... it'd be surprising to me if rocksdb can't support maybe 10000000 logged in users ... I'd rather build reflow2 now to be used by thousands of users rather than building it for like 10 people now and having to completely redesign it later to scale."

⭐ HIS INSTINCT IS RIGHT ABOUT THE BYTE LAYER, AND THE CODE IS BETTER PREPARED THAN EXPECTED. READ 2026-08-21 in dynograph-foundation: `KvBackend` IS A TRAIT (`crates/dynograph-storage/src/backend.rs:210`, `Send + Sync`) with two implementations already — `MemoryBackend` and `RocksBackend`. `StorageEngine` holds `backend: Box<dyn KvBackend>`, and its own comment says why: "keeps `StorageEngine` a single concrete type regardless of which backend is in use, so both constructors return the same type and THE REGISTRY HOLDS THEM UNIFORMLY". Somebody already designed for the registry case. ⇒ A DIFFERENT BYTE STORE FOR HOSTING — object storage, a networked KV, something sharded — IS A NEW `impl KvBackend` INSIDE dynograph-foundation AND NEEDS NO REFLOW2 CHANGE AT ALL, because reflow2 holds `StorageEngine`, which does not change type. That is his hypothesis, confirmed by reading rather than assumed.

⭐ AND HIS POINT ABOUT ROCKSDB IS RIGHT FOR THE REASON HE SUSPECTED. RocksDB at Meta's scale runs FEW instances with enormous keyspaces, not ten thousand instances side by side. The engine is not the ceiling. What would be expensive at 10k is not RocksDB's throughput but the number of OPEN INSTANCES: reflow2's unit is one design = one directory = one `StorageEngine`, and each carries a schema Arc, an LRU read cache behind a Mutex, a write buffer and a tantivy full-text index. Disk is not the problem — measured, reflow2's own 2862-node design is an 8 MB store, so 10k of those is ~80 GB, which is ordinary. Live instances in one process is the problem.

🛑 SO THE SPLIT IS NOT THE ONE HIS QUESTION ASSUMES, AND THIS IS THE USEFUL PART. dynograph-foundation owns WHAT THE BYTES LIVE ON, and is already shaped to take a new answer. reflow2 owns HOW MANY DESIGNS A PROCESS HOLDS OPEN AND WHETHER A DESIGN IS A DIRECTORY — `DesignGraph { engine: StorageEngine }`, one per design, welded. **That second thing is where 10k bites, and it is reflow2's, not dynograph's.**

⭐ THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE MAY DESERVE RE-READING FOR THE HOSTED CASE SPECIFICALLY. `dec:one-process-many-stores` considered "many designs inside a single store, relying on graph_id namespacing" and rejected it. Two things are worth noticing. First, the mechanism already exists: every key is namespaced by graph_id today (`keys::edge_key(graph_id, ..)`, `adj_out_key(graph_id, ..)`), so co-habiting is not new machinery. Second, EVERY REASON GIVEN FOR THE REJECTION IS A LOCAL-CASE REASON — the per-project directory, per-project export, backups and `--import` restore, the sidecar identity files, the git merge driver, and "a project's design lives under its own .reflow2/". A hosted tenant at flo2.io has no repo, no git merge driver and no `.reflow2/` on anybody's laptop. ⇒ The rejection may be entirely correct for local and not binding for hosted, which would give TWO SHAPES OVER ONE CODEBASE rather than a fork. Nobody has tested that reading; it is offered as a question, not a conclusion.

⭐ WHAT ACTUALLY BUYS THE OPTIONALITY HE WANTS. He is asking not to have to redesign later. The thing that secures that is NOT choosing the backend now — that choice is already deferred, cleanly, behind `KvBackend`. It is keeping THE UNIT OF A DESIGN a decision reflow2 can still change. Today "a design is a directory with its own engine" is welded into `DesignGraph`, so moving to "a design is a namespace inside a shared engine" is a change to reflow2's core type rather than a configuration. Whether that weld should be loosened — and what it would cost — is the open question, and it is the same shape as the `ifc:graph-read` work done today one level up: a concrete type where a contract would let the thing behind it change.

🛑 THE NUMBER NOBODY HAS: how many `StorageEngine` instances actually fit in one process before it degrades. Everything above is structure, not measurement. That number decides whether the registry-with-a-cap in `dec:one-process-many-stores` is sufficient at flo2's scale or whether partitioning is required, and it is cheaply measurable — open N stores, watch memory and file handles. It should be measured before the registry is designed, not after.

⚠️ ONE LIMIT ON THE GOOD NEWS: `KvBackend` is `pub(crate)`. The byte layer is swappable from INSIDE dynograph-foundation and not from outside it, so a new backend is a change to that repo rather than something reflow2 or flo2 could supply. That is fine while the same person owns both, and worth knowing before anyone plans otherwise.
properties.name: OPEN — at 10k tenants, which layer changes? The byte store is already swappable; what is welded is "one design = one directory = one engine", and that is reflow2's
properties.rationale:
Captured under the brainstorm skill. Recorded as ideas, nothing promoted, nothing settled.

Kept separate from `dec:idea-does-serving-flo2-cost-the-local-case` because that one asks what hosting COSTS the existing use case and what would prove it safe; this asks WHICH LAYER the scaling work lands in. They are answered by different people looking at different repos, and one can be settled without the other.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-26, thinking out loud: *"what are some things we can do to increase the probability that an agent will use reflow2 skills and tools in a project? what would make the agent say, I have the perfect skill or tool needed for problem X? hopefully, by adding depth and layers, we can start seeing much more clearly why and when some skills/tools are used."*

**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.** Nothing here is decided; the options are put down so a later session meets the reasoning rather than re-deriving it.

═══ THE FRAME BEING PROPOSED: FOUR LAYERS, AND A SKIP HAPPENS AT THE WEAKEST ONE ═══

For an agent to use a skill, four things must all hold. They fail independently, they want different fixes, and reflow2 has not worked them equally:

① **KNOWN** — the agent is aware the thing exists. *(Worked: `list_skills`, `get_skill`, served-not-installed, the handshake catalogue, 24 slash commands.)*

② **RECOGNISED** — the agent notices THIS MOMENT is that skill's moment. *(Worked hard: `cap:skill-triggers`, the three-event loop nudge, `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue`.)*

③ **WORTH IT** — the agent believes the skill beats what it would do unaided. *(BARELY WORKED AT ALL. There is no node arguing that a skill produces a better answer than competent improvisation; the whole surface argues that skipping is non-compliant, which is a different claim and a weaker motivator for something that is not trying to comply.)*

④ **VISIBLE** — something can see whether it happened. *(PARTLY BUILT — see the correction below.)*

⚠️ **CORRECTION MADE IN THE SAME SESSION, AND THE MISTAKE IS WORTH KEEPING.** This node first asserted that layer ④ was DEFERRED, reasoning from `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session`, which says so in its own text. That was true when that requirement was written and is now FALSE: `req:skill-adherence-is-measured` is **`accepted`**, and `cap:skill-loads-are-counted` is **built and `verified`**.

**The error is the one this project keeps recording: reading a claim out of one node's prose instead of the node it is about.**

**What layer ④ actually holds now:** skill LOADS are counted, and their absence is announced at session end. **What it still does not hold:** any notion of which skill SHOULD have been loaded for the work that was done.

═══ THE EVIDENCE THAT ③ IS THE BOTTLENECK ═══

`req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` records the same failure twice, six days apart, and the second is the damning one: **`cap:skill-triggers` was `verified` and firing correctly, and the user still had to be the reminder.** Layer ② was WORKING and it was not enough.

It also names the structural ceiling on ②: every shape that capability recognises is a shape in the GRAPH-WRITE stream, so it requires the agent to have already touched the graph. *A skill load is not a graph write.* No amount of work on ② reaches an agent that never started.

⭐ AND THE MEASUREMENT MOST WORTH REPEATING: both observations were made on sessions with **more** context about reflow2 than any consumer's agent will ever have. That is a BEST case, not a typical one.

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) Attack layer ③ directly: make the skill's ADVANTAGE legible at the moment of choice.** ⚠️ Counter: self-promotion inside a tool result, and it cannot be honest without evidence.

**(b) Keep hardening ② and accept the ceiling.** ⚠️ Counter: measured twice as insufficient, and the ceiling is structural.

**(c) Finish layer ④ — the half that is missing.** ⚠️ Counter: `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` may forbid the obvious implementation, and that must be settled BEFORE anything is built.

**(d) Reject the frame.** Perhaps the real variable is CONTEXT BUDGET: a skill costs tokens to load mid-task, and an agent under pressure economises. **Nothing has tested this, and it would explain the measured facts as well as ③ does.**

═══ WHY THE FRAME MIGHT EARN ITS KEEP ═══

It gives every future idea a place to attach: a proposal that improves ① when the bottleneck is ③ can be recognised as such before it is built. **It is a diagnostic, not a design.**

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
═══ 📌 SHARPENED 2026-08-26 BY A USER REPORT — AND THE FRAME HAS A HOLE ═══

*A user reported, relayed, that they were "probably not understanding all the skills in reflow2". Recorded here rather than as a new node because this node's own rationale says splitting would "lose the comparison, which is the only part that does any work". Written without the user's domain or employer; the design record is public.*

⭐ **EVERY ONE OF THE FOUR LAYERS IS ABOUT THE AGENT. NONE IS ABOUT THE PERSON.** The frame reads "for an AGENT to use a skill, four things must hold" — and a human who does not know what reflow2 is FOR fails before layer ① is reached. That is a candidate **layer ⓪ — ORIENTED: the person knows what this tool does and what it will ask of them.**

Whether ⓪ belongs in the frame is the open part. Two readings, and they lead to different work:

- **⓪ IS REAL.** reflow2 asks the human questions — gaps, decisions, who they are. A user who cannot answer *"what is this for?"* cannot answer those either, and no amount of agent-side triggering helps.
- **⓪ IS A MIRAGE, and the report is really ① or ③ seen from the user's chair.** reflow2 is AGENT-DRIVEN. The user never picks a skill; they see the consequence of the agent picking one. *"I do not understand the skills"* may be *"the agent never reached for one, and I noticed."* **Then a tutorial teaches the wrong party.**

🛑 **NOTHING WE HAVE DISTINGUISHES THESE**, and that is the same hole layer ④ already names: loads are counted, but not whether the RIGHT skill was owed. `dec:bl-155`'s warning applies exactly — it could not tell *unused* from *unreachable*, and this cannot tell *uninformed user* from *unreaching agent*.

📌 **WHAT IS ACTUALLY MEASURED TODAY, so ① is not overstated:** 22 served skills, 163 tools, `list_skills` / `get_skill` / `find_tools`, `docs/skills-and-tools.md`, 24 slash commands. All answer *"what is there?"*. **None answers *"where do I start?"*** — `genesis` covers a new PROJECT, `adopt` covers existing CODE, and nothing covers a new PERSON.

⭐ **AND A WORKED EXAMPLE OF THE FRAME FAILING BELOW ALL FOUR LAYERS**, measured the same day: `fact:the-lens-that-carries-the-persona-was-built-on-a-branch-and-never-shipped`. The mechanism that would carry a reader's background to the agent was built, core-tested, and left on an unmerged branch. That is not ①, ②, ③ or ④ — the thing was never in the surface at all, while the design recorded the capability as existing. **A fifth failure mode: the mechanism is in the DESIGN and not in the BUILD.** Whether the frame should carry that too, or whether it belongs to release hygiene rather than adoption, is unsettled.

⚠️ **THE COUNTERWEIGHT ON ALL OF IT:** n=1, relayed, from a user who cannot share specifics. This project's own history says the tempting fix is the wrong one. Before building a guide, the honest step is the one `report_manual_work` now exists to catch — get the case in the user's own words, and find out whether they wanted a skill they could not find or never knew a skill was owed.
properties.name: OPEN — an agent skips a skill at one of four layers, and a fifth may sit under them: which is reflow2's real bottleneck?
properties.rationale:
Recorded as one Decision because it is one question — WHERE does the failure live — and the layers are its options rather than separate questions. Splitting it would lose the comparison, which is the only part that does any work.

The counter-argument to the frame itself is written in as option (d) rather than left out, because a frame that cannot be wrong is not a diagnostic.

SHARPENED 2026-08-26. A user report about not understanding the skills was recorded HERE rather than as a parallel node, on that same reasoning. It contributes two things the frame did not have: a candidate layer ⓪ (the PERSON, where all four existing layers are about the AGENT), and a worked example of a failure that sits below all of them — a mechanism present in the design and absent from the build. Both are offered as questions about the frame rather than as extensions of it, because a diagnostic that grows a layer every time a report arrives has stopped diagnosing.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-17, supplying a taxonomy of AI-coding-agent pitfalls: "here are some other pitfalls I've seen that we should really weave into the fabric of reflow2 to prevent."

⭐ THE TRIAGE IS THE CONTRIBUTION, NOT THE LIST. reflow2 is a design graph and a coherence engine. It is not a linter, a package resolver, a type checker or a test runner. Recording "reflow2 prevents hallucinated packages" would be reflow2 claiming a capability it cannot have — which is `epoch:instruments-stop-overstating` committed by the very act of writing down the cure for it. So the list splits three ways and the split is what has to be decided before anything is built.

═══ CLASS A — REFLOW2 ALREADY DOES THIS. The move is to SAY SO, not to build again.
• "Tunnel vision: fixing a bug in one file silently breaks a dependency in another" — this is `propagate_change` and the impact-check skill, and it is reflow2's single most central competence. The blast radius exists for exactly this.
• "Context drift: as the conversation grows longer the agent forgets earlier architectural constraints" — the graph IS the memory outside the context window; `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` is the same finding already accepted.
• "Design bloat: dozens of unnecessary patterns, interfaces and abstractions" — an abstraction nothing asked for is `unmotivated_capability`, an existing gap; `granularity_report` reports the design/build mismatch in both directions.
• "Blind compliance: the agent implements your flawed logic instead of questioning it" — PARTLY. `detect_gaps` putting questions to the human, `CONTRADICTS` with its `contradiction` detector, and `dec:three-party-checks` ("the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides") are the answer to the fraction of this that is a NEW requirement conflicting with a SETTLED one. The rest of it — a flaw with nothing in the graph to contradict — is Class C.

═══ CLASS B — REFLOW2 COULD REACH THIS AND CURRENTLY DOES NOT. The real candidate work.
• OSCILLATION — "agents get stuck repeatedly adding and removing the exact same line". Computable from checksum history: a value returning to a previous one is a loop. MEASURED AND BOUNDED — see `dec:idea-an-artifact-whose-checksum-returns-is-an-agent-going-in-circles`; the history is far too thin today to support it.
• MUTATION-PROOF ON A CHECK — "hollow test suites", "tautological testing", and his own best practice "mutate code to test tests". reflow2 CANNOT read an assertion and judge it tautological. It CAN record whether anybody PROVED the check can fail. Its own practice already does this informally and in prose: `ver:search-first-forces-a-choice` records "MUTATION-CHECKED THREE WAYS, each verified applied before running rather than assumed" and then, remarkably, "A FOURTH MUTATION EXPOSED A VACUOUS TEST OF MY OWN" — reflow2 caught its own hollow test by mutation, and had nowhere structured to put that fact. ⇒ This is a candidate SHARPENING of `req:a-finding-has-somewhere-to-put-its-evidence` (accepted, epoch:instruments-stop-overstating) rather than a new requirement: the evidence field that requirement asks for is exactly where "this check was proven able to fail" belongs.
• A DEPENDENCY THE DESIGN NEVER DECLARED — the reachable half of "ghost packages". reflow2 cannot know whether `numpy.frobnicate()` exists, but `declare_dependency` / `reconcile_dependencies` can say that the build imports something the design never named. That catches the invented-dependency case at the design boundary while claiming nothing about the registry.

═══ CLASS C — REFLOW2 CAN NEVER DO THIS, AND MUST SAY SO RATHER THAN IMPLY IT.
• Whether a library method or package EXISTS (a resolver/language-server job).
• Whether an API is DEPRECATED (a registry/changelog job).
• Whether an assertion is TAUTOLOGICAL, or a mock has hollowed the path out (reading code semantically).
• Whether YOUR LOGIC IS FLAWED when nothing in the design contradicts it.
• Strict typing — a build-tool choice. It could be a DesignRule a project adopts; it is not something reflow2 can enforce or check.
⇒ These belong in reflow2's design ONLY as stated non-goals. A tool that lets a user believe it is watching for hallucinated packages has done more harm than one that says plainly it is not.

📌 AND THE ONE THAT CUTS ACROSS ALL THREE: "review diffs, not files; never accept a full-file rewrite blindly." reflow2 has the design-graph analogue ALREADY and learned it the hard way TODAY — `create_node`'s `revision` block names the properties a write replaced and their prior values, which is what caught this session overwriting a Decision's history. The open question is whether that is enough, or whether the same discipline should reach the artifact layer.
properties.name: OPEN — of the known AI-agent failure modes, which can reflow2 actually reach? Three classes, and writing the third into its design would be the overstating failure itself
properties.rationale: Recorded as brainstorming. The triage is the contribution: reflow2 already answers four of these, could reach three more, and can never reach five. Writing the last five into its design as things it prevents would be the exact overstating failure this whole increment exists to end — a tool that lets a user believe it is watching for hallucinated packages has done more harm than one that says plainly it is not.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — the boundary question underneath dec:idea-outward-docs-are-rendered-from-the-graph, 2026-08-11. Separate node because it has an answer whichever way that one goes. Nothing here is intent.

THE OBSERVATION: reflow2's outward-facing docs are not one kind of thing, and rendering the wrong ones would hollow them out.

  PROJECTABLE — the content IS graph state, and every staleness found today lives here
    three-axes.md      what the schema holds on each axis; the status column is a COUNT
    overview.md        the type counts, the reading order, what is built vs planned
    genesis.md         what the genesis tool does and what it returns
    artifact-linking.md    what link_artifact / reconcile_artifacts return
    impact-propagation.md  what propagate_from returns — a worked blast radius IS an example
    gap-surfacing.md   what detect_gaps returns, and the live gap list
    heal-process.md    what propose_heal returns
    viewpoints.md      the catalogue itself is a table of what renders

  IRREDUCIBLE ARGUMENT — no graph query produces this, and a rendered version would be worse
    vision.md          the four lifecycle transitions and WHY they break. An argument, not data.
    partnership.md     the LLM failure-mode taxonomy. Most of it is not in the graph and should
                       not be — "sycophancy" is not a node type. Its value is the reasoning.
    operating-environment.md   the Kennewick-vs-Mars argument for why environments matter, about
                       a layer with ZERO instances — so a projection would render an empty page
                       for the doc that explains why the layer should exist at all.

⭐ THE THIRD CASE IS THE INTERESTING ONE AND IT BREAKS THE SIMPLE SPLIT. `operating-environment.md` argues for a capability that has never been used. A pure projection of it renders nothing, because there is nothing to project — the doc's whole job is to explain something the graph does NOT yet hold. Any rendering scheme has to allow a doc to be ABOUT AN ABSENCE without confessing itself into uselessness. The same is true of every doc describing planned work.

⭐ AND THE SPLIT IS NOT PER-DOC, IT IS PER-PARAGRAPH. `overview.md` is mostly reading order and argument, with one sentence carrying "29 node types, 60 edge types" — which is the sentence that went wrong. `three-axes.md` is mostly explanation with one STATUS COLUMN that is wrong. So the natural unit is a SECTION, not a file, which is the argument for option (c) in the parent node — embed rendered blocks in prose — rather than rendering whole documents.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) Per-section markers: prose files with fenced regions regenerated from a named tool call, and a CI check that re-renders and diffs. Facts under the gate, argument left alone, absence expressible because the prose around the block says what the empty block means.
(b) Two doc classes with different rules — `docs/rendered/` regenerated wholesale and gate-checked, `docs/` hand-written and exempt. Cleaner to enforce, and it splits a reader's attention across two directories.
(c) Render everything and accept that argument-shaped docs become thin. Rejected on sight here, recorded so nobody re-proposes it: it would delete the reasoning that is the most valuable content reflow2 has.
(d) Render nothing; instead add a CHECK that every factual claim in a doc matches the graph. Keeps all prose, needs the claims to be machine-identifiable — which is `check_doc_versions.py` generalised beyond version strings, and that tool already proves the pattern works (it FAILS when a pattern matches nothing, so rewording a doc breaks the build loudly instead of silently disabling the check).

📌 (d) IS CHEAPER THAN IT LOOKS AND IS NOT MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE WITH (a). `tools/check_doc_versions.py` is already a CI gate that asserts doc claims against the build, anchored on literal phrases, deliberately failing when a pattern matches nothing. Extending its anchors from version strings to type counts would have caught `overview.md`'s "60 edge types" this morning for the cost of one line.
properties.name: OPEN — which outward-facing docs can NEVER be a projection, and how do rendered facts and irreducible argument sit together on one page?
properties.rationale: Rendering the docs is not one decision — some docs ARE graph state, some are argument no query produces, and one (operating-environment) argues for a layer with zero instances, so a projection of it renders an empty page. The natural unit turns out to be a section rather than a file, which changes what the parent question is actually choosing between.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — 2026-08-11, from Anthony bringing the Defense Acquisition University criteria for a good requirement into the discussion. Nothing here is intent.

THE CRITERIA HE CITED, in his framing. Individual requirement: NECESSARY (addresses a true operational gap), UNAMBIGUOUS (everyone reads it the same way), VERIFIABLE/TESTABLE (has criteria that can be practically proven), FEASIBLE (achievable within technology and budget), IMPLEMENTATION-FREE (what the system must deliver, not how to build it), MEASURABLE (quantifiable data, not vague adjectives). Full set: COMPLETE, CONSISTENT, TRACEABLE.

WHAT REFLOW2 ACTUALLY CHECKS, sorted against that list:
  SET-LEVEL — partially covered, structurally
    Traceable   forward only, via the golden thread. Backward is unchecked — see
                dec:idea-should-a-requirement-trace-back-to-its-demand-signal
    Consistent  partially, via CONTRADICTS and dimension drift
    Complete    approximated by the gap detectors, never claimed
  INDIVIDUAL — ZERO OF SIX. Necessary, Unambiguous, Verifiable, Feasible, Implementation-Free and
    Measurable are all properties of the TEXT, and no reflow2 computation reads requirement text
    for quality at all. `unverified_capability` is the nearest thing and it asks whether a check
    EXISTS, never whether the requirement is phrased so that a check is POSSIBLE — a different
    question with the same words in it.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) Nothing changes; state the boundary explicitly somewhere a user will read it, so "reflow2 does
    not grade your prose" is a known limit rather than a surprise.
(b) A three-party check: the LLM judges the six against the text, the graph records the judgement
    and who made it, the human decides. Fits dec:three-party-checks exactly and needs no new
    detector.
(c) A deterministic subset only — e.g. MEASURABLE is partly mechanical (does the statement contain
    a number and a unit?), and IMPLEMENTATION-FREE has weak mechanical tells. Cheap, and cheap in
    the bad way: a keyword heuristic that grades prose will be wrong confidently.

⭐ THE ARGUMENT FOR (a)/(b) OVER ANY DETECTOR: `req:deterministic-core` is accepted — the core is
deterministic and LLM-free. Judging "is this unambiguous" is irreducibly a language judgement. So
the six do not belong in detect.rs at all; if they belong anywhere it is the skill layer, where an
LLM already reads and the human already decides.

⚠️ THE HONEST COUNTER-EXAMPLE, recorded because it cuts against the whole frame. Of the storyflow
feedback's three ranked asks, #1 was NOT implementation-free — it named the mechanism outright
("model VERIFIES onto DesignRule") — and it is the one that got built. #2 and #3 were stated as
node-type wishes and did not. So on this evidence MEASURABLE and VERIFIABLE predicted delivery and
IMPLEMENTATION-FREE anti-predicted it. When the system under design IS the modelling vocabulary,
"what not how" gets genuinely slippery, and applying DAU to reflow2's own requirements needs that
caveat or it will reject the requirements that work.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 have any opinion on whether a Requirement is WELL WRITTEN, and if so whose job is it?
properties.rationale: Anthony brought a mature external standard to bear and it partitions cleanly: reflow2 covers the set-level characteristics structurally and none of the six individual ones, because those are text judgements and the core is deliberately LLM-free. Whether that boundary is a deliberate design position or an unnoticed hole has never been stated either way.

properties.decision: A design's identity is a UUID minted at genesis and stored in the graph; the friendly name is a label on top of it. A seat's identity is the harness session id it was already given. Rejected: deriving from the project name or path (two designs can share both, and the id must survive being copied), and a registry that hands out ids (that is the coordination this avoids, and there is no service to host it).
properties.name: Names are assigned with zero coordination, never derived from shared state
properties.rationale: Neither identifier is negotiated with anybody, so neither can race — unique by construction at one seat or fifteen. The fleet reached this by DELETING a whole mint-race guard: the race was an artifact of deriving the handle by reading a shared roster, so removing the derivation removed the race rather than patching it. reflow2 has the derived-identity bug twice today — every in-memory graph answered DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID until mirroring needed open_in_memory_as, and claims record a label rather than an owner.

properties.decision: BL-139's open half, and it is ANTHONY'S because it changes published behaviour rather than fixing a defect. `create_node` merges — its own description says "a partial props object edits" — and `import_graph` does not: re-importing an existing Requirement carrying only `{lineage: "derived"}` fails with `Requirement.statement: required property is missing`. The adopt workflow is import → detect → correct → re-import, so the mismatch lands precisely on the corrective step the skill prescribes. TWO OPTIONS, and the row already judged them: "(2) is honest and cheap; (1) is what the workflow actually wants." (1) MERGE AT PROPERTY LEVEL, like `create_node`. (2) SAY PLAINLY that documents must carry complete nodes — DONE 2026-08-02, in `import_graph`'s own description, so the cheap half is delivered whichever way this goes. THE COST OF (1), which is why it is not a one-word swap and why nobody should make it casually. FIRST, it crosses THREE PUBLISHED BOUNDARIES — `ifc:core-api`, `ifc:graph-export` and `ifc:mcp-tools` — measured, not guessed: `propagate_from("art:export")` reported 705 impacted nodes and `propagate_change` on this session's own edit reported 723, both crossing exactly those three. SECOND, and this is the part no boundary count shows: MERGING MAKES IMPORT NON-IDEMPOTENT FOR DELETION. Today a document is a complete statement of the nodes it names, so re-importing without a property REMOVES it and an export→import round trip reproduces the design exactly. Under (1) a property can only ever be added or changed, never dropped, and restoring a backup would silently retain whatever the live graph had accumulated since. That is a change to what an import MEANS, and it makes the migration and backup jobs this module exists for weaker in exchange for making the adopt loop smoother. THIRD, a middle path exists and should be considered rather than skipped: keep whole-node semantics as the default and let the DOCUMENT ask for merge explicitly (a per-node or per-document flag), so the adopt loop gets what it wants without redefining backup restore for everyone.
properties.name: OPEN — does import_graph merge a partial node like create_node, or keep demanding whole ones?
properties.rationale: Recorded proposed rather than decided, because AGENTS.md puts a Decision reaching `accepted` on the per-session side — that write is the user's signature. Raised now with the measurement attached because the row's framing ("make import_graph merge like create_node") reads as a small fix and the design says otherwise: this is the third time on this project that grep suggested a one-word swap and the graph reported a published-boundary change, and every previous time measuring first was what corrected it.

properties.decision: The install registers reflow2 with the agent at USER scope — the MCP server, the ten slash commands, the coherence-loop hooks and a `reflow2` command on PATH — so every project on the machine has it with no per-project setup. `reflow2_init.py` survives, but its job narrows: it writes the pointer file and project-scope config for a repo OTHER PEOPLE work on, so their agent is told reflow2 governs this code. Solo work needs none of it. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28, choosing "machine-wide, repo init optional" over "machine-wide only" and over "keep per-project, just make it one word".
properties.name: reflow2 installs once per machine; the in-repo half is optional and only for repos you share
properties.rationale:
WHY NOT "MACHINE-WIDE ONLY", which is simpler: a teammate cloning the repo would get no signal that reflow2 governs it unless they had already installed reflow2 themselves and thought to look. That is the invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, and retiring the per-project installer would rebuild it deliberately.

WHY NOT "JUST MAKE IT ONE WORD" (`reflow2 init .` instead of a python path): it fixes the typing and none of the arithmetic. Still one step per project, still a re-run after every upgrade, and still the case that a user who forgets it experiences reflow2 as absent.

WHAT MADE MACHINE-WIDE SAFE TO CHOOSE AT ALL, and without it the answer would have been different: the server is registered with `--only-if-present`, so a directory that never opted into a design gets the LATENT surface and nothing is created in it. Without that flag, a user-scope registration would drop a RocksDB store into every folder a session is ever opened in — and litter in someone's repo is a worse first impression than the setup step it removed. The loop-nudge hook is gated the same way and for the same reason: registered globally, silent wherever `.reflow2/` does not exist.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE: `dec:skills-served` and `req:thin-install` stand exactly as they were. The skills and working instructions are still served, still never copied, and upgrading reflow2 still produces no diff in a consumer repo. This decision is about WHERE the pointers are installed, not about what is served — and it makes the thin install thinner, since the common case now installs nothing into a project at all.

properties.decision:
RE-OPENED 2026-08-09 on Anthony's word, after storyflow gap D arrived and the same defect reproduced in this design within the hour.

WHAT WAS DECIDED BEFORE, AND WHY IT IS NOT ENOUGH NOW. dec:documentation-has-no-operational-coupling (ACCEPTED, 2026-07-24) met a legitimate island, tried three bridges, refused all of them as lies, accepted the island, and concluded: "flagging it is a false positive of the BL-84 family, and THE FIX BELONGS IN THE DETECTOR RATHER THAN IN THE DESIGN." That fix was never built. The decision records why — the specific island DISSOLVED on its own when cap:session-memory turned out to belong to both cmp:docs and cmp:temporal, giving documentation a real tie rather than a manufactured one. So the disposition became moot and the general principle it stated was left unimplemented. The old decision is NOT wrong and is NOT being un-accepted (dec:reopen-supersedes); what is re-opened is the clause it deferred.

WHAT CHANGED, and it is two independent measurements on the same day. (1) storyflow's governance model is a 121-node cluster tripping `disconnected_community` with `generate_bridge` proposed — a remedy that would fabricate traceability between fleet-operations governance and product design, which are two genuinely separate concerns sharing a repo. (2) THIS DESIGN reproduced it at 5 nodes: capturing governance requirements under dec:governance-integrates-not-splits produced heal:33d1548dae64e97a with the same suggested fix, and no honest bridge existed.

⭐ THE PART THAT MAKES THIS URGENT RATHER THAN TIDY: both clusters are GOVERNANCE, and both GROW as governance is captured properly. dec:governance-integrates-not-splits has just committed this project to exactly that growth. So the detector currently penalises the work the project decided to do, and gets louder the better the work goes.

⚠️ AND THE CONSTRAINT BOTH PROJECTS ARRIVED AT INDEPENDENTLY, SIXTEEN DAYS APART — this is the strongest evidence available that the shape is right, and it is also the trap. The 2026-07-24 decision: "the exemption must not be written in a way that hides a genuine disconnection." storyflow, 2026-08-09: "a real disconnection would arrive inside a 121-node warning everybody has already learned to ignore." Same sentence, two authors, neither aware of the other.

THE OPTIONS.
(A) A DECLARED PARTITION — a marker on a Project or Component saying this subtree is deliberately separate, so the detector reports "N declared partitions, 0 undeclared". Same shape as `granularity`'s opaque-vs-pending_expansion and as `enforced`'s tri-state, which is the argument for it: reflow2 has twice decided that a CHOICE and an UNFINISHED STATE must not look identical, and this is the third instance. COUNTER: a marker is exactly the kind of thing that gets set once and never revisited, and dec:idea-detect-vocabulary-that-nothing-reaches warns in its own text that "another marker nothing reads" would be a fourth instance of the very disease.
(B) TEACH THE DETECTOR THE CATEGORY, as the 2026-07-24 decision assumed — infer that a cluster of purely-governance or purely-documentation nodes has no operational coupling by nature, the way dec:operational-spof already excludes non-operating things from SPOF findings. CHEAPER for the user, no new vocabulary. COUNTER: an inference cannot be argued with, and a genuine governance island would be hidden by the same rule that exempts the legitimate one.
(C) FIX ONLY THE SUGGESTED REMEDY — leave the finding, drop `generate_bridge` where no honest edge exists, and say so. THE SMALLEST HONEST STEP, and it removes the part storyflow called corrupting. COUNTER: it leaves the permanent un-clearable warning, which is the half that makes people stop reading.
(D) ACCEPT ISLAND BY ISLAND, as today. COUNTER: an acknowledgement is a one-time answer to a finding whose size keeps changing — acknowledged at 88 it now reads 121, and nothing says when it became a different finding.

NOTHING IS PROMOTED. The requirement req:a-cluster-can-be-declared-deliberately-separate states the need; this node holds the unmade choice about its shape, and (A) is written first only because it is what both reporters proposed, not because it is recommended.
properties.name: DECIDED — stop proposing fabrication now; declare partitions next, and only if something reads the declaration back
properties.rationale: SETTLED 2026-08-09 by Anthony: "agree with: C now, A next with the read-back, not B, not D." The four options and their counter-arguments are preserved above rather than pruned, so a later reader can see what was weighed and not merely what won. The read-back condition is not decoration: it is what stops option A becoming the fourth instance of the disease `dec:idea-detect-vocabulary-that-nothing-reaches` documents, and it is written into `req:a-cluster-can-be-declared-deliberately-separate` as an acceptance test rather than left as an intention.

properties.decision:
PROPOSED as a proof of concept, Anthony 2026-07-27. ⭐ EXECUTED 2026-08-06 at his instruction ("let's trial this out"), after being parked for ten days — and with flo2 SUBSTITUTED FOR STORYFLOW, because storyflow's adopt was never finished while flo2 is actively developed, has a live one-directional dependency on reflow2, has its own graph on the same machine, is built by a second person, and had just generated a real cross-design event.

THE ORIGINAL PROPOSAL: build a reflow2 design graph inside storyflow and another inside dynograph-foundation, then have an agent LINK them through their published surfaces and identify where the interfaces are incompatible. WHAT IT WAS MEANT TO PROVE: whether dec:nested-graphs (a graph per ownership boundary) and cap:mirror-surface hold up on designs nobody built to be composed.

=== WHAT WAS ACTUALLY RUN ===
Three real designs, their committed exports, composed against reflow2's live design in a throwaway in-memory graph (nothing written to any of them): reflow2 (1497 nodes, graph_id `reflow2`), dynograph-foundation (179 nodes, graph_id `dynograph-foundation`, export written by reflow2 0.16.0), flo2 (77 nodes, graph_id `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2`, written by 0.24.0). compose_and_analyse then pair_designs, each pair in turn.

=== RESULT 1: THE MECHANISM WORKS ===
Both compositions imported cleanly with ZERO SKIPPED EDGES — 179 nodes / 270 edges from dynograph-foundation, 77 / 181 from flo2. Ids namespaced as designed; neither source design touched.

⭐ CROSS-VERSION COMPOSITION SURVIVED, AND THAT IS A REAL DATA POINT: dynograph-foundation's export was written by reflow2 0.16.0 and imported into a 0.24.0 graph with nothing dropped. [BL-216] filed the three-graphs-three-versions worry on 2026-08-05 as something that "becomes load-bearing the moment cross-graph linking lands". It landed, and it did not bite. That is evidence, not proof — one export, eight minor versions apart, no schema change between them that this design happened to use.

⭐ RESULT 2: A TRUE POSITIVE, AND IT IS THE SEAM THIS WHOLE SESSION WAS ABOUT.
The flo2 pairing reported exactly one CONFLICT: `ifc:core-api` (ours, medium `library`) against `ifc:model-provider-api` (flo2, medium `REST`), names matching at 80/100 — "very likely the same contract, but they cannot be connected as either is currently built." That is precisely the flo2↔reflow2 problem: flo2 is a web app that needs an HTTP surface, reflow2 exposes a library/stdio one, and closing it is what dec:one-process-many-stores and req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image exist to do. THE TOOL COMPUTED IT FROM TWO DESIGNS NOBODY BUILT TO BE COMPOSED, AND NOBODY TOLD IT THE ANSWER. That is the single strongest piece of evidence this project has that the composition idea is sound.

⚠️ RESULT 3: ZERO PAIRED BOUNDARIES ON BOTH PAIRS, AND THE REASON IS ONE MISSING LABEL.
paired = 0 against dynograph-foundation AND against flo2. seam_findings = 0 on both — which does NOT mean the designs agree; it means NOTHING IS CONNECTED ACROSS THE SEAM. All 15 of dynograph-foundation's published interfaces landed in DEAD SURFACE ("they publish this and nothing here requires it"), and 5 of flo2's did.

THE CAUSE IS SINGULAR: REFLOW2 DECLARES NO `required` INTERFACE ANYWHERE. Pairing matches complements — published/both against required/both, never like with like — so with nothing required, nothing can ever pair. reflow2 compiles against dynograph-core; that dependency is real, load-bearing, already declared in the version manifest (req:design-dependencies-declared, accepted, verified) — AND INVISIBLE TO THE SEAM MACHINERY.

⚠️ THE MOST DANGEROUS NUMBER IN THE RUN IS `unmet_needs: 0`. It reads as "nothing is missing" and it means "we never said we needed anything". A design that has declared no needs cannot have an unmet one. Anyone reading that field without reading `dead_surface: 15` beside it would conclude the seam was healthy.

RELATED, AND THE SAME ROOT: reflow2 holds FIVE Interfaces for 1497 nodes, two of which were created the previous night, and both of those came back as `unclassified_ours` — the tool naming rather than counting them precisely because `internal` is the DEFAULT and cannot distinguish "deliberately internal" from "never classified". This is maturity_report's SEAMS 0 OF 73 appearing as data instead of as a score. A near-miss makes it concrete: dynograph-foundation ALSO publishes an `ifc:core-api`, and reflow2 has one too, and they cannot pair because both are `published` — like-with-like, correctly refused.

⚠️ RESULT 4: TWO FINDINGS THAT BEAR ON THE FEDERATION IDEA RAISED THE SAME DAY.
(1) flo2's graph_id is `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2` while the other two are `reflow2` and `dynograph-foundation` — an opaque mint beside two readable labels. dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs proposes listing graph_ids in a config file; nobody hand-writes `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2` and knows what they typed, so either identity gains a human-facing name or that mechanism needs a different key.
(2) THE ACCESS MODEL ANTHONY DESCRIBED CANNOT BE EXPRESSED IN THE GRAPH AT ALL. He specified: userAJ read/write on all three; userAlex read-only on reflow2, read/write on flo2. `who:ajs` and `who:alex` exist as Contributors and AUTHORED_BY records who DID write something, but there is no node type, edge type or property for who MAY write something. That is not a limitation the trial hit — it is a vocabulary that does not exist, and it is the concrete form of the permission-versus-convenience question left open on dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments.

=== WHAT THIS ANSWERS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT ===
ANSWERED: dec:nested-graphs and the composition capabilities hold up on three real designs built at different times by different hands against a moving foundation. Nothing crashed, nothing was silently dropped, the ids namespaced, and the one genuine incompatibility was found and explained in a sentence a person can act on.
NOT ANSWERED, because the run could not reach it: whether seam_report's contract comparison is any good. It needs PAIRS, and there were none. The dependency this decision named — req:interface-spec-complete first, or run against today's thin spec — turns out to have been the wrong dependency: the blocker was not that the spec is thin, it is that nothing is LABELLED as required.

=== THE CHEAPEST NEXT STEP, NOT TAKEN HERE ===
Declare reflow2's `required` interfaces — what it consumes from dynograph-foundation, and what flo2 must be able to reach. A handful of nodes. It would convert 15 dead surfaces into real pairs or real unmet needs, and it is the prerequisite for seam_report ever having anything to compare. Recorded rather than done, because it is design about reflow2's own boundaries and belongs to Anthony's word rather than an agent's tidying.
properties.name: RUN 2026-08-06 — composition proved on reflow2 + flo2 + dynograph-foundation: the linking works, the labelling does not exist
properties.rationale:
Anthony's own framing, and it lands on intent reflow2 already holds: req:design-composes (accepted), dec:nested-graphs (DECIDED — a design is its own graph when separately owned, released or shared, which is exactly three sibling repos), cap:mirror-surface and cap:publish-surface (both built). So the LINKING half exists and the COMPARING half does not. Recorded originally as a decision point rather than a plan because the sequencing was a real choice: structure the interface spec first, or run the PoC against today's thin spec to find out what it cannot say.

⭐ THE SEQUENCING QUESTION IS NOW ANSWERED, AND BOTH BRANCHES WERE WRONG. Running it first was right, and what it found was not "the spec is too thin to compare" — it was that there is nothing to compare, because no boundary on this side is labelled as a need. req:interface-spec-complete was recorded as this PoC's prerequisite; it is not. The prerequisite is a `required` designation on the interfaces reflow2 actually consumes, which is smaller and more specific than making the spec structurally complete.

The second payoff predicted when this was proposed did land: it was the first time reflow2 was pointed at designs it did not author, twice, which is the adopt path Anthony says his real work almost always starts from. The result — clean import, correct namespacing, one true positive, and an honest zero everywhere the design had not been labelled — is the behaviour that path needs.

Kept as `proposed` rather than moved to accepted: the PoC RAN, but what it proposed to prove is only half proven. seam_report was never exercised because pairing produced nothing to feed it, and that half stays open until reflow2 declares what it requires. Recorded via chg:linked-repos-trial-run.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, from work he has done: State Funerals for US Presidents (he worked President Bush's) — hundreds to thousands of people planning simultaneously, an echeloned plan (NORTHCOM OPLAN → JTF-NCR → each service → each unit), and events arriving during the run that the plan must react to in minutes. His words: "using a common github repo may no longer work". THE DECOMPOSITION THAT MAKES IT TRACTABLE IS ALREADY DECIDED: dec:nested-graphs (c) says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary, so a thousand planners are not a thousand writers on one store — they are ~100-200 graphs of 5-20 writers each, linked by mirrored published surfaces. Echelons own their plans; that is both the software answer and how the organisation actually works. FOUR ROADS for the tier itself. (a) NOTHING NEW — federation plus git, accepting minutes of latency; cheapest, and it fails only the react-in-near-real-time half. (b) ONE PROCESS PER GRAPH over streamable HTTP (rmcp has the transport, reflow2 serves stdio only), writes going to the store and the export DERIVED as the archival record; at federation scale the process-per-project cut already named in dec:central-host is also the natural sharding — one process per ownership boundary is one staff. (c) ONE SHARED MULTI-WRITER STORE, which means replacing single-writer RocksDB and owning consensus; most work, least alignment with a design that already shards by authority. (d) EVENT-SOURCED LOG plus materialised views — attractive because a plan IS a change history, expensive because every detector currently reads a materialised graph. WHAT BREAKS TODAY, in order: single-writer per graph (the six-seat outage of 2026-07-25 was this at tiny scale), the whole-document write path (769 KB for 606 nodes; a funeral federation is 10^5-10^6 nodes changing continuously), git-round-trip latency, nothing that pushes, no identity or authorization, and req:stale-seat-knows going from one bad afternoon to a systemic property.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 grow a live tier for hundreds of simultaneous planners, alongside the repo file?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming because it is explicitly distant-future ("probably distant future") and because it challenges the PREMISE of two decisions rather than their reasoning — which is the honest thing to record, not to act on. dec:multi-writer-architecture chose repo-file-plus-merge on a rationale resting on concurrency being hypothetical; dec:central-host's rationale says outright that this tool "does not need" simultaneity "and may be harmed by it". A thousand people replanning a state funeral under events is the named counter-case both were missing, and per dec:reopen-supersedes the move is a new decision point, never flipping those back. NOTE THE PART THAT NEEDS NO DECISION: the ownership boundary federation already draws is the natural AUTHORIZATION boundary — you write your echelon's graph and read your superior's published surface — so authz needs enforcement, not a new concept, and Interface.designation internal|published is already the read primitive. Also settled by inspection: ordering without a shared git history needs no global clock, because the same federation shape gives a total order WITHIN each boundary (the store, proved by the content-hash chain) and dated coordinates ACROSS boundaries (a mirror already carries whose design, which version, when) — exactly how echelons coordinate. Full reasoning in docs/planning-at-scale.md.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS A MEASURED FIELD DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Reported 2026-08-05 from the hxm_program session, item 4 of six.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED, in the reporter's words: "After the capture batch, `loop_status` reported `unsurfaced_gaps: 0` — but `detect_gaps` had never been run, and when it did run it found 3 REAL PHASE-LEVEL GAPS." Their conclusion is the sentence worth keeping: "AN AGENT THAT TRUSTS `clean: true` HAS NO REASON TO RUN THE DETECTOR."

⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT SIMPLY A MISSING TIMESTAMP. `loop_status` is the call the SessionStart hook and the server instructions both push every session to run FIRST, described as "the one cheap call that says what the coherence loop is owed". It is the orientation surface. A false clean there does not mislead one report — it tells the agent the loop is settled at the exact moment the loop has not started.

AND IT COLLIDES WITH AN ACCEPTED DECISION RATHER THAN JUST BEING AN OVERSIGHT. `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` is ACCEPTED: "Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history" — with the stated reason that LOOKING IS NOT WRITING, so counting runs would reward bookkeeping. That ruling is right and it is exactly what produces this: a gap that has never been detected is not IN the state, so state-derived debt cannot see it. The defect is downstream of a correct decision, which is why it needs a decision rather than a patch.

THIS IS THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE SHAPE IN A WEEK, AND THE PATTERN NOW HAS A NAME IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECORD: [BL-206], the coherence gate reporting OK over 20 artifacts it never swept; [BL-208], the export-lineage guard reporting nothing because a shallow checkout meant it could not see `HEAD~1`; and `dec:no-design-here-never-looked`, filed from the same report, where "this directory has no design yet" was asserted without looking. The carried sentence from BL-208 was "a guard whose no-op path is silent will eventually run nowhere and say so to nobody". THIS IS THE READING-SURFACE VERSION: A COUNT THAT CANNOT DISTINGUISH ZERO FROM UNMEASURED READS AS ZERO.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) THE REPORTER'S SUGGESTION — a `last_gap_scan` timestamp, or a `scanned: false` field. Cheap and directly answers it. Counter: a timestamp IS run history, which is what `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` deliberately excluded, so taking it means amending that decision rather than quietly contradicting it — and the amendment has to explain why THIS history is legitimate when run-counting was not. The distinguishing argument, if it is taken: recording that a detector RAN is not the same as crediting the agent for running it; one is a property of the reading, the other is a score. (b) MAKE THE ABSENCE STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN TEMPORAL — report `unsurfaced_gaps` as unknown until a scan has ever produced a gap-or-none result for the current graph revision, keyed on state rather than on time. Fits the accepted decision without amending it. Counter: needs a notion of "the graph revision a scan covered", which does not exist. (c) NEVER REPORT A ZERO — say "run detect_gaps" whenever the count is zero, whatever the cause. Crude, honest, costs nothing, and would have prevented the observed failure. Counter: it makes a genuinely clean design nag forever, which is how a signal gets trained to be ignored — the exact failure [BL-191] fixed for volatile artifacts. (d) LEAVE IT AND RELY ON THE STOP HOOK, which the reporter notes DID catch this ("the stop-hook nudge caught this — 'bookkeeping is not the loop' — which worked"). Counter: the hook fires at the END of a session, and the false clean is read at the START.

NOT CHECKED, and it widens or narrows this considerably: whether the other zero-valued counters in `loop_status` have the same property — `unexamined_claims`, `unproven_capabilities`, `undispositioned_drift`, `unwritten_answers`. If they are all state-derived in the same way, this is one defect with five faces rather than one field.
properties.name: OPEN — loop_status reports unsurfaced_gaps 0 before detect_gaps has ever run, so "clean" and "never scanned" are the same answer
properties.rationale:
Filed as its own node rather than a backlog row because the fix is not obvious and the obvious fix contradicts an accepted decision. `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` says debt is computed from state and never from run history, for a good stated reason; a `last_gap_scan` timestamp is run history. Whoever takes this has to either amend that decision with an argument for why recording a reading differs from scoring an agent, or find a state-shaped answer. A backlog row would have carried the symptom and lost the collision.

The three-instance pattern is written out because this is the point at which it stops being a coincidence: two gates and now the orientation call, all reporting a confident absence they never measured. Naming it once, with the instances, is cheaper than finding it a fourth time.

The unchecked item — whether the other four counters share the property — is stated because it decides whether this is one row or five, and nobody has looked.

properties.decision: loop_status reports what the coherence loop is owed — anchored gaps never surfaced, questions waiting or answered-but-unwritten, structural defects, capabilities claiming realized/verified with no passing check, drift awaiting disposition, claims never examined — computed entirely from current graph state. reflow2 does not track when tools were run: phase nudges are excluded (guidance, not debt), and the write tools carry static loop_hint pointers at the next loop step in their own results.
properties.name: Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history
properties.rationale: From the StoryFlow fleet trial (BL-74): under operational load the agent kept bookkeeping via raw tools while the loop skills silently stopped — 'a design-discipline tool that depends on being remembered will lose to operational urgency every time; fire on a trigger, not on virtue.' Run-history ('no detect_gaps since Tuesday') is not honestly computable here: the core takes no clock, and looking-is-not-writing is doctrine — recording reads so observation could be tracked would make looking mutate the record. Outstanding debt is the state-based equivalent and the actionable truth regardless of who ran what when. The hint rides the tool result the agent already reads (zero extra round-trip to see it), and loop_status is the cheap computation a client hook can fire on its own events — rung a of the BL-74 ladder builds on exactly this call. Decided 2026-07-21.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT SETTLED. Surfaced by running impact-check on chg:content-path-no-default AFTER the edit rather than before — the blast radius named ifc:mcp-tools as a boundary crossing, which is exactly the "changed one side of a contract" case that skill exists to catch. STILL OPEN.

WHAT THE FIX DID. Removing `default_value` from `--content-path` makes the refusal in `ReflowService::content_store` reachable, which is correct for the WRITE path and is what ver:content-surface already claims. But all four content tools route through that same method (content_tools.rs:97, :129, :155, :185), so `content_manifest` and `content_exists` now refuse too. Before the fix, `content_manifest` on an unconfigured server ANSWERED — `entries: []`, `total_bytes: 0`, `store_root: "./reflow2-content"` — and that answer was worse than useless, because the root it named did not exist. So the fix is not a regression; the question is whether refusing is the RIGHT answer or merely a less-wrong one.

THE CASE FOR REFUSING (what ships now): a manifest says "whether the bytes are here", and with no store there is no "here". `req:no-silent-fallback` argues the same way for reads as for writes, and the refusal names the remedy.

THE CASE FOR ANSWERING, and it is not weak: cap:content-manifest exists for the person "handed the design ON ITS OWN", and its whole point is that `missing` names content the graph references and this checkout does not have — "so a diagram that will not open is a named finding rather than a silent absence". That reader has NO store by definition. Refusing tells them to configure one before they can be told what they are missing, which inverts the capability. The honest answer for them is every referenced hash listed under `missing`, `orphaned: []`, and the store named as absent. `content_exists` has the same shape: it is documented as the cheap "do I have everything?" call.

WHY IT IS MOOT TODAY AND WILL NOT STAY MOOT: reflow2's own graph references ZERO content (136 Fragments, 0 with a `content_ref`), so both behaviours return the same information here. The distinction only bites once a design actually points at bytes — which is exactly when the person who needs it is the one who cannot answer it. Deciding it now costs nothing; discovering it then costs a user.

BEARS ON req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session, which sits in the direct ring of this change. Whether "reachable" means "the tools are present and say what is wrong" or "the store exists without anyone choosing where" is the requirement's own ambiguity, and it should be read before this is settled rather than after.
