properties.name: ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 — content_manifest and content_exists ANSWER when no store is configured; only content_put and content_get refuse
properties.rationale:
Resolved by Anthony 2026-08-06, taking the ANSWER branch: the reader cap:content-manifest exists for is "someone handed the design ON ITS OWN", and that reader has no store by definition, so refusing them inverts the capability. Surfaced only because impact-check was run on chg:content-path-no-default and named ifc:mcp-tools as a boundary crossing — without it the refusal would have shipped on all four tools unnoticed, which is the value of that skill stated concretely rather than in principle.

WHAT SHIPPED: DesignGraph::content_manifest now takes Option<&ContentStore>. With None, every referenced hash reports missing, orphaned is empty (no bytes exist to be unreferenced), total_bytes is 0, and store_root says "(no content store configured)" in words instead of naming a directory nobody chose. ReflowService::content_store_for_reading returns Option and is used by the two read tools; content_store (the refusing form) still backs content_put and content_get unchanged.

WHY THE SPLIT IS PRINCIPLED RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE: req:no-silent-fallback forbids INVENTING a location, and neither path does that any more — the write refuses and names the remedy, the read reports absence as absence. The old behaviour violated it in the worst way, answering with a store_root of "./reflow2-content" for a directory that existed nowhere. Both halves now say something true.

PROVEN, not asserted: crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/tools.rs the_manifest_answers_without_a_store_while_writes_still_refuse holds all three behaviours in one case, deliberately beside a_server_with_no_content_store_says_so_instead_of_choosing_one so the pair reads as the contract. 70/70 tools tests and 15/15 core content tests pass; clippy -D warnings clean across both crates.

properties.decision: release_includes_all derives a release's whole manifest from the design and writes it in one call, with `apply` defaulting to false so the derivation is reported before anything is written. Entries already in the manifest are reported as already_present and their frozen as_checksum is never recomputed.
properties.name: A bulk derivation is not a bulk accept, and it writes nothing until asked
properties.rationale: BL-153 flagged the counterweight to state before building: dec:two-sided-accept and dec:ask-not-repair mean a bulk form must not become a silent one, and "a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent". Those decisions bound bulk DISPOSITIONS — a judgement taken about each item. No disposition is taken here: the graph is asked what the project contains and answers, and the one judgement a human still owns (which release ships it) is the argument the caller supplies. So the family does not apply, and a per-item disposition would be ceremony over a derivation. What DOES apply is the no-silent-write bar: hence apply defaults to false, matching reconcile_artifacts' record_events, because a call that packages a release is the one you most want to read before you run it. The frozen-checksum guard is the harder half — a derivation that recomputed every entry would rewrite the manifest of a shipped release each time the live drift baseline moved, silently and in bulk, which is the axis-Z sin the frozen copy exists to prevent.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-02, thinking out loud after asking what a functional decomposition of reflow2 would be. Nothing here is intent; nothing has been promoted. THE DISTINCTION HE IS DRAWING, in his words: 'this is a different kind of delta from capability increments to more of breadboard design to production grade production design. it may involve keeping the same functions, but restructuring the design/packaging and/or which functions are allocated to which systems/services.' And the general form: 'knowing what I know now, would I have designed this the same way?' — which he says 'should almost be a reflow2 skill', and which applies to ANY design, not only reflow2's. EXPLICITLY NOT A REWRITE: 'I wasn't really saying to develop a reflow3. in fact, as the graph can support epochs and capability increments, we can evolve from the engineering mockup to full production grade morphing in the reflow2 graph for any design project.' TWO ORTHOGONAL AXES OF CHANGE, which is the load-bearing idea. (1) A CAPABILITY INCREMENT grows the function set — new requirements, new capabilities, delivered against a schedule. reflow2 models this well already: `DesignEpoch`, `SCHEDULED_FOR` with modality, `Release`/`INCLUDES`, and readiness gating on the increment. (2) A MATURITY RESTRUCTURING holds the function set INVARIANT and moves everything else — allocation, packaging, which functions live in which system or service, which seams are declared. reflow2 models this barely at all as a first-class thing, although the parts exist. THE PARTS THAT ALREADY EXIST, so this is assembly rather than invention: `ALLOCATED_TO` and `CONTAINS` already carry the allocation map that a restructuring moves; `evaluate_allocation` and `propose_allocation` already score and propose it; `dec:parallel-alternatives` plus `analyze_alternatives` already fork a design in SPACE (rather than time) and lay N variants side by side on the same measures; `compare_designs` already bands a difference into design content versus supporting layer; and `record_change` already snapshots a node's EDGES as well as its properties (BL-63), so a re-parenting is recoverable rather than lossy — which is what makes in-place evolution safe and is the technical reason a reflow3 is not needed. WHAT WOULD GIVE IT TEETH, and the part worth arguing about: a restructuring is SAFE EXACTLY WHEN FUNCTION IS PROVABLY PRESERVED, and that is computable rather than promised. The invariant is: no Capability added or removed, no SATISFIES edge changed — only `ALLOCATED_TO` / `CONTAINS` / Interface edges moved. `compare_designs` already reports at that granularity, so a skill could CERTIFY a restructuring rather than assert it. That is the difference between a refactor someone hopes is safe and one the graph checked, and it is the same move `dec:passing-is-verified` makes for tests. WHAT IS MISSING, three things, none of them large. (a) NO SKILL asks the question: of fifteen served skills, `revise-design` handles one node the user changed their mind about, `retire-from-design` handles removal, `check-health` finds structural DEFECTS (cycles, single points of failure, islands) — none asks whether the structure is the one you would CHOOSE now, which is a different question from whether it is broken. (b) NO VOCABULARY MARKS THE EPOCH AS A MATURITY STEP: `DesignEpoch.epoch_type` offers `baseline | revision | milestone | incident_response | release_cut`, and a restructuring is none of those; `ChangeEvent.change_type` offers `refactor`, which does not distinguish a code refactor from a design re-allocation. (c) NO MATURITY LADDER FOR THE DESIGN ITSELF: `ReadinessAssessment` (TRL/MRL 1-9) was built for the enabling TECHNOLOGIES an increment leans on, not for the design's own structural maturity — whether it should also apply to the design is an open question, and the hardware ladder Anthony named (breadboard, engineering mockup, EVT, DVT, PVT, pilot run, mass production) is the vocabulary he is reaching for. THE OBSERVATION THAT PROMPTED IT, measured rather than asserted: reflow2's own design carries EIGHT functional systems (`dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition`, accepted 2026-07-23) and exactly THREE Interfaces, none of which sits between two of those systems — while 51 `DEPENDS_ON` edges cross system boundaries against 22 that stay inside one, over 14 distinct system pairs, the two largest being coherence-loop to store and coherence-loop to vocabulary at 16 each. So the functional blocks are declared on the containment axis and their seams are not declared at all, which is what a MOSA reading would want first (`dec:mosa-conformance`, also proposed).
properties.name: OPEN — is "the same functions, structured as I would structure them NOW" a second kind of delta the graph should model?
properties.rationale: Recorded through the brainstorm skill because Anthony was working the idea through rather than deciding it, and explicitly withdrew the stronger reading (no reflow3). ANTHONY'S CLOSING GENERALISATION, 2026-08-02, and it is the most important sentence in the discussion because it changes what the whole thing IS: 'this is really a realization that probably all designs start immature (breadboard or engineering mockup) and then morph to a more refined structure. this allows reflow2 to build in how designs typically go where initially getting function right is the first objective, then you go towards getting the structure/packaging right. this is often iterative and organic.' THE CONSEQUENCE, which reframes every measurement taken today: reflow2's 51 undeclared cross-system dependencies are NOT technical debt and NOT a criticism of any decision — they are the expected state of a design that has been correctly prioritising function. A design at that point is ON the normal trajectory, not off it. Which means the thing reflow2 should learn is not 'detect bad structure' but 'know that this trajectory EXISTS and where a design is along it' — the same move `dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement` makes for technology maturity, applied to the design's own structure. A tool that reported undeclared seams as defects would be punishing correct early-phase work, which is exactly the failure `cap:coverage` avoids by refusing to be a score, and exactly what `sharpening.md` §2 calls accommodation if the design were then bent to silence it. WHAT THAT IMPLIES FOR THE VOCABULARY QUESTION, sharpening option (c) rather than answering it: if function-first-then-structure is the norm, a maturity ladder for the DESIGN is not a nice-to-have bolted onto readiness — it is the axis along which every design moves, and 'where am I on it' becomes a first-class question a design brain should answer. The counter-argument stays on the record beside it: a distinction earns its keep only when a computation reads it (`dec:edge-orthogonality`), so the ladder is worth vocabulary only if something computes position along it rather than merely labelling it. Kept as ONE question because the skill Anthony wants ('would I design it this way now?') is the human-facing form and the second delta type is what the graph needs to hold its answer. Options are prose rather than registered alternatives, deliberately, so it raises no `undecided_decision_point` while it is still a musing.

properties.decision: The three-way merge (cap:merge-designs, dec:merge-three-way) resolves per node, per property, and per edge against the base by this case table. NODES/PROPERTIES: only one side changed a property -> take it; both changed it differently -> conflict. add/add (same id, no base) -> treated as modify/modify against an empty base: matching properties merge, each differing property is a conflict. delete/delete -> node gone, no conflict. delete/modify (one side removes the node, the other changes it) -> RETAIN-AND-ASK: the proposal keeps the modified node and raises a conflict asking the human to confirm the deletion or keep it, leaning toward keeping — deletion is the destructive side and must be re-justified, never the silent default (req:intent-preserved, retire-vs-delete). Symmetric in both directions. EDGES: first-class design content and get the identical three-way rule — one-sided add or remove -> take it; the same edge changed differently on both sides, or one side removes while the other changes it -> conflict; never silently drop an edge one side deliberately cut (req:no-silent-fallback). CONFLICT REPRESENTATION: a both-sides conflict is a Question node with source 'merge_conflict', a deterministic id (FNV over base + node/edge id + property, the existing gap-id normalization), carrying the base/ours/theirs values; it reuses the existing answer_question / open_questions machinery and writes nothing until dispositioned, and its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung (BL-80 #5) replays a recorded resolution against. No new node type — the schema stays 28.
properties.name: The merge conflict case table: retain-and-ask on delete, edges symmetric with nodes, conflicts are Questions
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option, closing the sub-decisions dec:merge-three-way explicitly deferred. Retain-and-ask over a neutral conflict because losing a node is not symmetric with keeping it: req:intent-preserved and the retire-vs-delete distinction make a delete the move that must be justified, so the proposal keeps the node and asks rather than treating erasure as an equal default. Edges symmetric with nodes because they carry the golden thread — a lighter union-and-keep-wins rule would override a deliberate one-sided edge removal without asking, which is exactly the silent drop req:no-silent-fallback forbids; compare_designs already bands edge divergence, so the input is there. Reuse Question over a dedicated MergeConflict type for the recurring schema-minimalism reason (the vocabulary was already sufficient — same lesson as dec:certainty-derived and dec:component-verified-computed): the answer/open-questions machinery, the deterministic FNV gap-id normalization, and the human-decides routing all already exist, and reusing them makes the conflict rerere-ready for free (BL-80 #5) while keeping the schema at 28 node types. With this, the merge is fully specified — nothing left but the build and its verification.

properties.decision: reflow2 records how a human resolved a merge conflict and offers it back when the same conflict recurs (git's rerere), on three axes the user decided. (1) STORAGE — in the graph, as an answered Question (source=merge_resolution) whose id IS the conflict's content fingerprint: reuses the answer_question/open_questions machinery, travels with the design in the export, no schema change (stays 28 node types) — exactly what dec:merge-conflict-semantics anticipated ('reuse Question; its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung replays against'). (2) BEHAVIOR — advisory: a recorded resolution is surfaced as a suggestion on the matching conflict, and the human still confirms (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks). apply_merge applies only what it is given; an opt-in use_recorded lets the human bulk-accept every recorded suggestion in one move (the confirmation is passing the flag), and apply refuses if any conflict still has neither an explicit nor a recorded decision. (3) KEY — content only: the fingerprint is over (property, base value, ours value, theirs value), independent of which node, so ONE resolution replays across ALL nodes with the identical conflict — this is git's model and what delivers the motivating BL-73 win (20 near-identical conflicts, 21 near-identical hand-resolutions → resolve the shape once). apply_merge records every applied property/edge-property resolution keyed by content, so the memory grows as you work.
properties.name: rerere: record a conflict resolution content-keyed in the graph, replay it advisory-only
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option. Content-only keying because it is the whole point: the BL-73 field pain was N near-identical conflicts across different nodes, and a per-node key would give near-zero reuse and miss exactly that case; content-only is git's proven model, and pairing it with advisory behavior keeps over-reach visible (the human sees each application). Advisory over auto-apply because the three-party doctrine puts the decision with the human — but the recorded suggestion plus a bulk-accept toggle kills the repetitive grind without silently resolving on the human's behalf. Reuse-Question over a new node type or a side cache is the recurring no-schema-change lesson AND keeps the memory inside the design that travels in the export (a side rr-cache would be a second source of truth that a teammate importing the design would not receive). Scoped in v1 to property and edge-property conflicts (a clear base/ours/theirs value triple, and the N-near-identical shape); node-type and delete/modify keys are deferred (no clean value triple), as is aging/pruning the memory. Extends cap:merge-designs; the conflict ids the merge already mints were built for exactly this (dec:merge-conflict-semantics).

properties.decision: When HEAL merges DUPLICATES-asserted nodes, the survivor is picked by provenance rank (authored > planned > imported > reconciled > inferred > healed); node id breaks ties. Pre-provenance graphs are unchanged.
properties.name: Merge survivor is chosen by provenance, id breaks ties
properties.rationale: User decided option 2 for BL-29 (2026-07-20): provenance is the closest thing the graph has to 'who asserted this and how deliberately'. Refinement from the 2026-07-20 self-adopt live session: a node with UNSET provenance defaults to authored, which made two genesis stubs tie against authored+verified survivors and nearly win on alphabetical id — set provenance explicitly on both sides before proposing a merge, and consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision.

properties.decision: The design merge is a three-way typed merge exposed as a core op (MCP tool + CLI flag), the write-side sibling of compare_designs. (1) Inputs are three explicit export documents — a common ancestor (base), ours, theirs; git supplies the base (git merge-base + the committed reflow2.json at that commit), so reflow2 does not build its own commit DAG for this rung. The multi-parent/ref layer that would let reflow2 find its own merge-base is deferred to BL-70/#3. (2) The algorithm is git's trivial-merge case table run per node and per property against the base over typed values, not lines: only one side changed a property -> take it; both sides changed it differently -> a structured conflict. (3) It produces a merge proposal — auto-resolved one-sided changes plus a list of both-sides conflicts rendered as Questions ('node X.prop Y: base=A, ours=B, theirs=C — which?') — and writes NOTHING to the graph. The human dispositions the conflict Questions, then an explicit apply commits the merge. Compare reports and never writes; merge does the same until the human has looked.
properties.name: The three-way merge takes explicit inputs over git's DAG, and reports a proposal it never auto-applies
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, both the recommended option. Explicit-inputs-over-git because the exports are already git-committed (dec:repo-file-embedded) and git already tracks the merge-base — building a second DAG inside reflow2 would reimplement what git provides and contradicts 'export/import is the right-sized git bundle analogue' (BL-80's explicit do-NOT-import list). It keeps rung #1 shippable now and defers the ref/branch layer to where it belongs (BL-70). compare_designs already computes the typed per-property diff this consumes, so the input side is built. Report-a-proposal-never-auto-apply because a both-sides conflict IS a Question and the graph must not silently pick a side (dec:report-dont-judge, req:human-decides, req:no-silent-fallback); mirroring compare's read-only contract keeps the sibling honest, and the explicit apply is the disposition gate (dec:two-sided-accept's spirit — no silent write) without a staging area (BL-80 explicitly rejects the index). Typed per-node/per-property conflicts are strictly better than git's line markers — the key 'graph is not files' caveat. This specifies BL-12's merge problem: rung #1 (this algorithm over three documents) + #2 (the retained ancestor, here git's) = the L core of BL-12. Deferred to their own decisions: delete/modify and add/add conflict semantics (retire-vs-delete makes a delete meaningful, so delete/modify must go to the human, never auto-resolve), edge-merge banding, and the exact shape of the conflict Question.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, 2026-07-25, supplied the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (OUSD(R&E) Systems Engineering and Architecture, February 2025, Distribution A) and was explicit about the frame: "just taking principles, concepts and ideas from this. not looking to implement mosa exactly over this document." So this records what the guidebook's concepts illuminate about reflow2, not a plan to become a MOSA tool. THE DEFINITION IT GIVES: "an acquisition and design approach consisting of a technical and business architecture that supports using system interfaces compliant with widely supported and consensus-based standards... A MOSA system structure allows for severable components to be incrementally added, removed, or replaced throughout the life cycle" (10 U.S.C. 4401, mandated for all DoD acquisition programs to the maximum extent practicable). ITS FIVE-STEP FRAMEWORK is a process, not a document: Plan, Modularize, Identify Interfaces, Define Interfaces, Standardize Interfaces — and reflow2 can already model a process rather than only a product (cap:model-process, Flow nodes), so the framework is expressible as a Flow whose steps the graph can be checked against. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS, from Table D-1 "MOSA Conformance Criteria and Verification Methods": most of what MOSA asks a program to demonstrate, reflow2 already computes for other reasons. Their MODULARITY criterion — "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled, and organized into functional categories" — is the Leiden modularity score, community detection and the god-component detector that graph_report already prints. Their MOSA OBJECTIVES criterion — "demonstrate severable modular components" — is propagate_change: if the blast radius of a change inside a module stops at that module's interfaces the module is severable, and if it leaks past them the module is not modular whatever the architecture diagram says. That is severability as a COMPUTED property rather than an assertion, which is the same move dec:certainty-derived made for requirement status and cap:derived-completion made for delivery. Their MOSA MODULES criterion — "implement minimal functions, are functionally independent, encapsulated, and traceable to requirements" — is the god-component detector plus the golden thread. Their LIFE CYCLE CHARACTERISTICS criterion — severable, replaceable, interoperable, allowing competition — is the severability computation plus the alternatives layer, where interchangeable suppliers behind one interface are exactly an analysis of alternatives. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it is one vocabulary item and one check. (1) NOTHING MARKS AN INTERFACE AS KEY. MOSA's whole discipline turns on designating major/modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open; reflow2 has Interface nodes, provides/consumes and SPECIFIES, but no way to say "this one is the published boundary and that one is internal plumbing". BL-45 found the identical hole from the opposite direction — external dependencies between reflow2 projects — and recorded it as "nothing marks an Interface external-facing". Two independent routes to one missing property is the strongest evidence this design has for a vocabulary addition. (2) NOTHING CHECKS STANDARDS COMPLIANCE, and the vocabulary for it is present and unused: DesignRule is defined as a chosen standard or convention with an `enforced` flag, and there are zero DesignRules in any graph — the same schema-present-practice-absent shape as the temporal axis and the KPP vocabulary before them. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea rather than used to bury it: MOSA is domain vocabulary for defence acquisition, and req:design-anything says the vocabulary stays neutral. A MOSA conformance report is therefore a VIEW — a projection over computations that already exist, in the acquisition community's words — and not a set of new node types. Building it as a view keeps the core neutral (dec:views-are-projections) and any renderer fill-in remains a defect. If it were ever built as schema, reflow2 would have taken on one domain's language as its own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 report MOSA conformance, given it already computes most of the criteria?
properties.rationale: Recorded 2026-07-25 as brainstorming from the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook Anthony supplied, on his framing: principles and concepts, not an implementation of MOSA. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ("let's promote both") into the two things the guidebook actually exposed as missing, both now accepted: req:key-interfaces (the design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read the distinction) and req:modularity-computed (severability and cohesion are computed from the graph, not asserted by the diagram). Both are GOVERNED_BY this decision. WHAT STAYS OPEN is the question this decision was opened on, and it is narrower now: whether reflow2 ships a MOSA-BRANDED report. The requirements are domain-neutral by construction — published boundary, severable part — so they can be built without answering it, and the acquisition community's words for the same criteria belong in a view over the computation rather than in the schema (dec:views-are-projections, req:design-anything). Deciding otherwise would adopt one domain's language as reflow2's own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning. SEQUENCING, and it is not arbitrary: req:key-interfaces comes first because req:modularity-computed depends on it — severability is only checkable once the design knows where a boundary is. req:design-composes also links through published boundaries, so the same property serves the federation thread; that is the second independent route to it, after BL-45 found the identical hole from the system-of-systems side on 2026-07-20.

properties.alternatives: [{"option":"repo file, merge on pull","outcome":"chosen","note":"contradicts nothing; reuses the built merge machinery; needs BL-44 claims"},{"option":"hosted service","outcome":"rejected","note":"contradicts req:persistence and req:invocation (both accepted); supersedes dec:repo-file-embedded; design leaves the user's machine; permanent operational burden"},{"option":"hybrid: hosted coordination, local designs","outcome":"rejected","note":"keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface; the claims layer approximates the benefit without a server"}]
properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25: the design STAYS a graph-in-a-repo-file, and many writers are handled by merging on pull. No hosted service, no shared writable store. Each person's design lives at ./.reflow2/graph in their own checkout, git moves it, and genuinely overlapping work is resolved by the three-way merge that already exists — typed per-node and per-property against the common ancestor, with each conflict minted as a Question carrying a deterministic id, and recorded resolutions replayable across near-identical conflicts (rerere). THIS CONFIRMS dec:repo-file-embedded RATHER THAN SUPERSEDING IT. That is the outcome worth noting: this was the first field-sourced re-opening of a settled decision, triggered because dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale said the concurrency argument was 'hypothetical while there is one writer' and fifteen developers made it concrete. The precondition genuinely changed, the decision was genuinely re-opened, and the original answer survived contact with the new evidence. A re-opening that ends where it started is not wasted — it converts an assumption into a tested position. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY. A HOSTED SERVICE: rejected on cost against confirmed intent, not on taste. It contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project'), both accepted, so choosing it would have required retiring or revising confirmed intent rather than merely adding machinery. It also puts the design on a machine the user does not control, carries permanent operational burden, and breaks the session-transcript identity for everyone but the local user (a local path resolves for one person and silently misses for the rest). A HYBRID — hosted claims and presence over local designs: rejected as the weaker version of the same trade. It keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface to run, and buys live visibility that the claims layer can approximate without a server. WHAT THIS COMMITS TO BUILDING: the scoping primitive (BL-44 cluster claims) so two people do not collide in the first place, and merge-on-pull ergonomics. The honest weakness accepted with this choice: no live view of what others hold, so overlap surfaces at merge time rather than before it — which is exactly the trade git itself makes, and the one this project's users already understand.
properties.name: Many writers keep the repo file and merge on pull — no hosted service
properties.rationale: Raised by the user and his brother, 2026-07-24, from a concrete scenario rather than speculation. This is the first field-sourced trigger to re-open a settled decision, and it is worth recording WHY it counts as one: dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale reads "the service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer." Fifteen developers is that hypothesis arriving, so the decision is not being second-guessed — its stated precondition has changed. That is exactly the signal cap:revise-trigger is being built to surface automatically; here it arrived by conversation instead, which is itself evidence the trigger is worth building. Held proposed deliberately: the architecture question is upstream of every feature beneath it (req:concurrent-planning among them), and starting to build under an unmade decision is how a design acquires an architecture nobody chose. The counter-argument that belongs in the weighing, so it is not lost: reflow2's loop is built around asking a human and recording an attributable answer — deliberate, sequential, credited — and simultaneous editing may be the wrong shape for that product even where it is technically reachable. What the raised scenario actually asks for is non-colliding parallel work plus good merges, which may be reachable without a service at all.

properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25 by Anthony: option (c), A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY WITH LEVELS INSIDE EACH. A design is its own graph when something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED — and a subtree of one graph otherwise. The hierarchy does not decide; authority does. That is the shape federated systems engineering actually uses, and it makes the split rule non-arbitrary: you can always answer "why is this its own design?" with a name, a release train, or a recipient. WHAT FOLLOWS, and each is an obligation rather than a detail. (1) THE COORDINATE. Edges cannot cross stores because the schema validates both endpoints, so a link between designs is not an edge: the other side's published surface is MIRRORED into your graph as local nodes, and the mirror carries the coordinate — which design it came from, at what content hash, when. Your own components then PROVIDE and CONSUME the mirrored Interface with ordinary local edges, so the golden thread works unchanged and foreignness is a property of the NODE rather than of the link. Same reasoning as dec:fork-point-address: a coordinate resolved against a document, never a live ref layer. (2) ROLL-UP. A parent's view of a composed child must derive from the child's own evidence or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires unsatisfied in the parent forever — cap:derived-completion's computation one level up. (3) FRESHNESS. A mirror is a dated claim about a VERSION, so a newer surface with a different hash makes it stale and that must be detectable, never assumed current (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). (4) THE SEAM. Two teams changing the boundary itself still collide, in the one place the merge machinery does not reach; the published-surface document is what they are actually negotiating over. THE ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because req:roads-not-taken says they are part of the record. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL was not rejected — it was BUILT FIRST and remains correct for everything inside one ownership boundary; cap:scoped-analysis delivers it, and (c) is a superset rather than a replacement. What (a) alone could not do is give two owners separate write locks, separate release trains, or a way to share one part without sharing everything. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM was rejected as a RULE, not as a possibility: a system that is separately owned still gets its own graph under (c), but depth alone stops being sufficient reason, because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check, and a three-level tower of graphs inside one team buys none of what those cost. THE TENSION THIS RESOLVES, and it should be resolved out loud: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the destination as "one graph the whole company plans in". Under (c) that is no longer the destination — an enterprise is many designs federated at ownership boundaries, and the CEO's objectives are one design that others mirror rather than one graph everyone writes into. That document now describes a road not taken and should say so.
properties.name: DECIDED — a graph per ownership boundary, levels inside each
properties.rationale: Raised 2026-07-25 as brainstorming, because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. Promoted to intent the same day, and COLLAPSED the same day on his word ("let's do (c) option"). THE SEQUENCE IS THE ARGUMENT for why this was worth holding open for a few hours rather than deciding immediately: option (a)'s scope filter was built FIRST precisely because it forecloses nothing, so by the time the decision was made there was working evidence about what per-level analysis actually feels like — and (a) turned out to be a subset of (c) rather than a rival to it. Deciding on day one would have been a guess; deciding after building the cheap half was a choice with evidence behind it. WHY (c) OVER (b), stated as the discriminator that survived from the brainstorm: every seam between designs costs a coordinate, an evidence roll-up and a freshness check, so a level earns its own graph only when it is separately owned, released or shared. A three-level tower of graphs inside one team pays all of that and buys none of it. (b) is not forbidden by this — a separately-owned system still gets its own design — it is that DEPTH stops being sufficient reason. WHAT THIS COSTS, recorded so nobody is surprised: docs/org-scale-vision.md's "one graph the whole company plans in" is now a road not taken, and req:concurrent-planning's answer changes shape — ownership boundaries become the primary isolation mechanism, with the claims layer and the merge driver serving work INSIDE one boundary rather than across all of them. The first rung built on this decision is the coordinate (cap:mirror-surface): the other side's published surface mirrored as local nodes carrying which design, which hash, and when.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS A MEASURED FIELD DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Reported 2026-08-05 from a real session on `hxm_program`, Anthony's own working repo at NSLS-II. Nothing here is settled.

⭐ WHAT HAPPENED, AND IT IS AN ACCIDENT THE TOOL CAUSED RATHER THAN FAILED TO PREVENT. A session rooted at the repo root was told "this directory has no design yet" and offered only `reflow2_start_design`. TWO POPULATED GRAPHS EXISTED ONE AND TWO DIRECTORIES DOWN:

    ~/git_projects/hxm_program/.reflow2                      37bbd9a6e0e75369  "hxm_program"          minted 0.23.0 TODAY
    ~/git_projects/hxm_program/simulated_beamlines/.reflow2  8a9ce30fedd213e5  "simulated_beamlines"  minted 0.17.0
    ~/git_projects/hxm_program/simulated_beamlines/HEX/.reflow2  6771abb9b0683423  "HEX"              minted 0.22.1

The user believed the design lived at `simulated_beamlines`. By the time that surfaced, the agent HAD ALREADY MINTED A NEW ROOT GRAPH. The reporter's own summary: "One directory listing would have prevented the accidental third graph."

WHY THIS IS THE SEVERE ONE OF THE SIX FILED. Every other item in the report is friction — this one produced a WRONG ARTEFACT in the user's repository, silently, and the user did not learn of it until later. It is also the exact failure shape this project has been finding all week and naming in its own words: A GREEN OR CONFIDENT ANSWER FROM SOMETHING THAT NEVER LOOKED. `reflow2_check` reported OK over 20 artifacts it never swept ([BL-206]); the export-lineage guard reported nothing because it could not see `HEAD~1` ([BL-208]); `loop_status` reports `unsurfaced_gaps: 0` before `detect_gaps` has ever run (item 4 of this same report). "No design here" is that sentence again, addressed to a person deciding whether to create one.

AND IT IS WORSE THAN THE OTHERS IN ONE RESPECT: the other three report a state, and this one INVITES AN IRREVERSIBLE ACT on the strength of it. A design minted in the wrong place is not a bad reading; it is a fourth thing to reconcile.

THE SECOND HALF, WHICH THE REPORT COUPLES TO IT: SESSION BINDING. "The MCP server binds to the session's working directory. From a root-rooted session there is no way to write into the nested HEX graph — the user would have to open a session in that directory." Verified against this repo's own `.mcp.json`: the launcher is passed `--graph-path ./.reflow2/graph`, a RELATIVE path with NO ANCESTOR WALK. So which design you are editing is decided by where your shell happened to be. Also reported: choosing the new root graph "required a manual `/mcp` reconnect after `start_design`, because the running server predated the design and kept serving only `start_design`."

⚠️ THIS FALSIFIES ADVICE GIVEN THE SAME DAY, and the correction belongs on the record next to it. Asked how to structure exactly these repos, this agent answered that a single graph needs no restructuring because `Artifact.location` is an opaque string and reflow2 performs no file IO — so one graph could register artifacts across sibling repos. TRUE OF ARTIFACT LOCATIONS AND FALSE OF THE THING THAT MATTERS: with cwd-binding and no ancestor walk, "one graph" silently means "every session must start at the repo root", and a session opened one directory down does not find it — it offers to mint another. The advice was given from the schema and the doctrine (`dec:install-once-per-machine`) without checking the launcher. THE SAME METHOD ERROR AS THE `export_surface` CORRECTION AN HOUR EARLIER: an absence asserted from a description rather than read from the code.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) SCAN BEFORE OFFERING TO MINT — the reporter's own suggestion: "no design here, but 2 exist below: [paths, labels]. Use one of those, or really start fresh?" Cheapest, and it directly prevents the accident that occurred. Counter: reflow2 performs NO FILE IO by doctrine (`dec:agent-navigates-content`), so the scan cannot be reflow2's — it has to be the agent's, which makes this an instruction in the served surface rather than a tool, and instructions are weaker than a type system. That may be the honest answer rather than a weakness, but it should be chosen rather than defaulted to. (b) WALK ANCESTORS WHEN RESOLVING THE GRAPH PATH, the way git finds `.git`. Familiar and predictable; counter: it silently changes which design a session writes to based on cwd depth, which is the same class of surprise, and `--graph-path` is explicit today. (c) A GRAPH SELECTOR — "design tools take an optional graph ref, defaulting to the nearest `.reflow2`" (reporter's 2a). The largest, and it is the one that would also answer the nested-write problem. Counter: it makes every tool call carry an ambient target, and this project has been careful that a claim without a seat is refused rather than guessed (`dec:stateless-seat-handle`). (d) HOT-LOAD THE FULL SURFACE AFTER `start_design` (reporter's 2b) — narrower, fixes only the reconnect papercut, and is independent of the rest.

WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED: `dec:install-once-per-machine` (the in-repo half is optional), `.mcp.json` passing a RELATIVE `--graph-path`, and the fact that three graphs of three different mint versions (0.17.0 / 0.22.1 / 0.23.0) now coexist in one repo with no stated compatibility policy — the report's item 6.

NOT CHECKED: whether `reflow2_start_design` could refuse, rather than warn, when a `.reflow2` exists below it. Refusing is stronger than reporting and may be right for an act this hard to undo.
properties.name: OPEN — "this directory has no design yet" is asserted without looking, and it minted a THIRD graph on a repo that already had two
properties.rationale:
Filed from a first-hand field report on Anthony's real work rather than from self-host, which is the second time in one day that pointing reflow2 at something it did not author produced a finding self-host could not. That pattern is now three-for-three ([BL-199], [BL-213], this) and is the strongest standing argument for keeping external use in rotation.

Recorded as its own node rather than as one of six backlog rows because it is categorically different from the other five: those are friction, this one CAUSED a wrong artefact in a user's repository and invited an irreversible act on the strength of an unchecked claim. Filing it beside "version skew is a papercut" would flatten that.

The falsified advice is written into the node deliberately. It was given today, confidently, from doctrine rather than from the launcher — and an agent reading this later needs to see that the one-graph recommendation rested on a fact nobody had checked, not just that it was incomplete.

properties.decision:
reflow2 will not tell you a test is hollow. It cannot read an assertion and see that it says `true === true`, cannot see that mocking has hollowed the execution path out, and cannot see an exception swallowed inside a test that then exits zero. A Verification marked `passing` is a CLAIM SOMEBODY MADE, and reflow2 records it, counts it toward coverage, and reports it as passing.

WHOSE JOB IT IS: a mutation-testing tool, a coverage tool that measures real paths, and a reviewer who runs the check with the code deliberately broken.

⚠️ WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN, and this one is the most load-bearing of the four. Verification coverage is one of reflow2's headline numbers — "123 of 162 capabilities verified" appears in its own report. THAT NUMBER COUNTS CHECKS, NOT CONFIDENCE. A design can reach 100% verified on tests that could not fail, and reflow2 would report full coverage and be correct about what it measured. Anthony named tautological testing, excessive mocking and swallowed exceptions as a pitfall class on 2026-08-17; none of the three is visible from here.

⭐ AND REFLOW2 HAS ALREADY BEEN BITTEN BY IT, which is why this is evidenced rather than theoretical. `ver:search-first-forces-a-choice` records: "A FOURTH MUTATION EXPOSED A VACUOUS TEST OF MY OWN ... the first revision test passed whether or not the guard was there, because a revision with no near neighbour has nothing to report either way." A hollow test inside reflow2's own suite, found by mutating the code — not by anything reflow2 computed. Its status said `passing` throughout, truthfully.

⇒ WHAT REFLOW2 DOES DO NEARBY: it distinguishes a check that PASSES from one that merely EXISTS (a `planned` check does not silence `unverified_capability`), it reports when a check last ran and flags a stale-but-passing one, and it refuses to treat component-granularity coverage as capability coverage. So it polices the BOOKKEEPING around checks rigorously and the CONTENT of them not at all.

📌 THE ADJACENT WORK, and it is the reachable half rather than a contradiction of this non-goal: reflow2 could record whether a check was PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL — mutation-checked — because that is a fact an author can state and a reader can rely on. It cannot judge the check; it can carry the claim. That is a candidate use of the evidence field `req:a-finding-has-somewhere-to-put-its-evidence` asks for. This non-goal covers the judging, not the recording.

RECORDED AS A NON-GOAL, 2026-08-17. Retiring it is part of shipping anything that voids it.
properties.name: NON-GOAL — reflow2 does not judge whether a check is MEANINGFUL; a passing Verification is a claim it records, never one it validates
properties.rationale: Verification coverage is a headline reflow2 number and it counts checks, not confidence — a design can reach 100% verified on tests that could not fail. Evidenced rather than theoretical: reflow2's own suite carried a hollow test that reported passing truthfully throughout, found by mutating code rather than by anything reflow2 computed. It polices the bookkeeping around checks rigorously and their content not at all.

properties.decision:
reflow2 has no notion of the outside world's calendar. It will not tell you that an endpoint was deprecated two years ago, that a framework version is unsupported, or that a pattern has fallen out of use. Everything it knows about currency is INTERNAL: whether the design and the build agree with each other, and when a claim was last checked.

WHOSE JOB IT IS: the upstream project's changelog, a dependency auditor, a deprecation linter, or a person who follows the ecosystem.

⚠️ WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN. Anthony named it on 2026-08-17: agents "frequently mix legacy version code with modern framework configurations", and "the code looks structurally perfect but relies on an API endpoint deprecated years ago". STRUCTURALLY PERFECT IS EXACTLY WHAT REFLOW2 CHECKS. A design whose thread is complete, whose artifacts match their checksums and whose verifications pass can be built entirely on dead APIs, and every reflow2 report will be green — correctly. The greenness is about internal coherence and says nothing about the world.

⇒ WHAT REFLOW2 DOES DO NEARBY: it dates its own claims. `search_design` returns `as_of` and `age_days` on a fact that carries one, an expired `valid_to` reads as expired, and the confirmation ledger reports when a claim was last checked against reality. So reflow2 can tell you THAT NOBODY HAS LOOKED IN SIX WEEKS — which is the honest signal available to it — but never that what they would find has changed.

RECORDED AS A NON-GOAL, 2026-08-17. Retiring it is part of shipping anything that voids it.
properties.name: NON-GOAL — reflow2 does not know whether an API, version or practice is current or deprecated
properties.rationale: reflow2's greenness is about internal coherence between design and build, and a design built entirely on dead APIs is internally coherent. It can report that nobody has checked in six weeks; it can never report that the world moved. Written down because "structurally perfect" is precisely what reflow2 measures, which makes this the easiest wrong inference on the list.

properties.decision:
reflow2 will not check that a dependency named in your design or your code is real. It does not resolve package registries, read a language server, or import anything. A capability can name `numpy.frobnicate()` and reflow2 will record it, thread it, and report on it exactly as it would a real one.

WHOSE JOB IT IS: a package manager (`pip check`, `npm ls`, `cargo tree`), a language server, or a type checker. Those resolve names against reality; reflow2 resolves names against the DESIGN.

⚠️ WHY THIS IS WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN LEFT SILENT. Anthony named hallucinated dependencies as a top AI-agent pitfall on 2026-08-17, and reflow2's own description — a design brain that keeps a project coherent — invites the assumption that it is watching. It is not. A clean health report and a hallucinated import are entirely compatible, and the clean report would be TRUE while the inference drawn from it was false. That is the vacuous-zero failure `epoch:instruments-stop-overstating` exists to end, arriving through absence rather than through a bad number.

⇒ WHAT REFLOW2 DOES DO NEARBY, so this is a boundary and not a shrug: `declare_dependency` records what the design says it depends on, and `reconcile_dependencies` compares that against what was OBSERVED in the build. So reflow2 can tell you the build imports something the design never declared — the design-boundary half of the problem — while claiming nothing about whether the thing exists in the world.

RECORDED AS A NON-GOAL, 2026-08-17. A non-goal is a statement about the CURRENT build, not a promise about the future: if this is ever built, retiring this decision is part of shipping it. A stale non-goal is a false statement in the opposite direction, which is the failure AGENTS.md committed by telling a reader that a `/mcp` reconnect picks up a rebuild.
properties.name: NON-GOAL — reflow2 does not verify that a named package, library or method EXISTS
properties.rationale: reflow2 resolves names against the design, never against the world. Silence on that boundary reads as coverage, and a clean health report beside a hallucinated import would be true while the inference from it was false — absence producing the same harm as a vacuous zero. Written down so the assumption cannot be made quietly.

properties.decision:
reflow2 will not evaluate whether what you asked for is a good idea, whether your logic holds, or whether your requirement will produce the outcome you want. It records intent faithfully and threads it rigorously. A design can be perfectly coherent and completely wrong, and reflow2 will report it as coherent — correctly.

WHOSE JOB IT IS: a person who understands the domain. Reflow2's own doctrine already says so — `dec:three-party-checks`: "the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides."

⚠️ WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN. Anthony named it as the deepest of the AI-agent pitfalls on 2026-08-17: "if your initial prompt contains a logical flaw, the agent will perfectly implement your flawed logic instead of questioning it." A DESIGN GRAPH DOES NOT FIX THAT — it makes the flawed logic durable, traceable and consistently applied, which is arguably worse than leaving it in a chat log, because now it has authority. Recording intent well and recording intent CORRECTLY are different acts, and reflow2 only does the first.

⇒ WHAT REFLOW2 DOES DO NEARBY, and it is a real fraction of the problem rather than a consolation: it catches DISAGREEMENT WITH YOURSELF. A `CONTRADICTS` edge and the `contradiction` detector surface a new claim that conflicts with a settled one; `kpp_contradicted` does it for inviolable intent; `detect_gaps` puts the questions it cannot answer back to you rather than guessing. So when a flawed instruction contradicts something you already decided, reflow2 will say so. When the flaw is consistent with everything else you have said, nothing in the graph can see it.

📌 THE HONEST FRAMING FOR A USER: reflow2 raises the cost of being INCONSISTENT and does nothing to the cost of being WRONG. That asymmetry is worth knowing before relying on it.

RECORDED AS A NON-GOAL, 2026-08-17. Retiring it is part of shipping anything that voids it — though of the four, this is the one least likely ever to be voided.
properties.name: NON-GOAL — reflow2 does not tell you your requirement is WRONG; it can only tell you it disagrees with something you already settled
properties.rationale: A design graph does not fix a flawed premise; it makes the flaw durable, traceable and consistently applied, which is arguably worse than a chat log because it now carries authority. What reflow2 can genuinely catch is disagreement with something already settled, via CONTRADICTS and the contradiction detector. It raises the cost of being inconsistent and does nothing to the cost of being wrong — an asymmetry worth stating before anyone relies on it.

properties.decision:
PROPOSED, NOT SETTLED. Submitted by @ajs from flo2 (docs/proposals/multi-graph-hosting.md, written against reflow2 0.24.0) as the concrete architectural answer to the hosting question that req:many-designs-one-service deliberately left open — that requirement's own statement says "this is deliberately silent on where the designs live: one process per design and one holding many are both answers to it, and that is the hosting question, not this requirement." This is that question being answered.

THE ANSWER: one process opens, serves and closes SEVERAL design graphs at once, with each client session attached to exactly one — instead of the process binding one graph directory at startup and holding it for its whole life.

TWO MISREADINGS KILLED EXPLICITLY, because both make the change sound far more dangerous than it is. (1) IT DOES NOT RELAX SINGLE-WRITER. RocksDB's exclusive lock is held PER DIRECTORY; nothing prevents one process holding many directories and many locks. Each design keeps exactly the single-writer guarantee it has today. The proposal is to hold N single-writer stores, not to make one store multi-writer. (2) IT IS NOT MANY DESIGNS INSIDE ONE STORE. graph_id already namespaces every stored key, so co-habiting is technically possible — and it is the wrong answer.

THE ALTERNATIVE CONSIDERED AND REJECTED — many designs inside a single RocksDB store, relying on graph_id namespacing. Rejected because it would collapse the per-project directory the rest of reflow2 is built on: per-project export and the committed design document, backups and --import restore, the sidecar identity/version/sync files, the git merge driver, and the plain fact that a project's design lives under its own .reflow2/. It also makes identity.rs's silent failure mode — a design opened under the wrong id presents as EMPTY — considerably easier to hit. The gain is a smaller number of open RocksDB instances, which is a resource optimisation, not an architectural benefit. NOTE: this is the same shape as dec:idea-many-graphs-one-store, which Anthony raised as a brainstorm on 2026-08-05; this proposal answers it in the negative for the HOSTING case.

WHY THIS IS SMALLER THAN IT SOUNDS — the groundwork is already in place, and this is the part worth reading before estimating. ReflowService.graph is already Arc<RwLock<DesignGraph>> (crates/reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs:74), chosen precisely because several client sessions share one server (req:sessions-share-a-graph) — a registry of graphs is a map of things already shaped to be shared. Seats are already per-session not per-process (service.rs:88-93, req:seat-per-client). Per-session service instances already exist and already carry graph, graph_path and content_path (service.rs:2484-2492), so attaching a session to a CHOSEN graph is a change to where those fields come from, not to their existence. Identity is already out-of-band and per-store (crates/reflow2-core/src/identity.rs), designed to be read BEFORE the design is opened — exactly what a registry must do. HTTP already exists (--http and --serve-shared since v0.14.0). Opening is already a plain function call with no process-global state (DesignGraph::open_rocksdb, crates/reflow2-core/src/graph.rs:113). What binds the process to one graph is the CLI contract and the startup path in main.rs, not the core.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAS TO CHANGE. (1) A graph registry with a lifecycle: a process-level map from graph key to open graph, carrying the metadata that currently rides on the service — graph_path, content_path, identity, and the write_gen counter the loop nudge reads (service.rs:94-99), all becoming per-graph. Opening must be on demand and BOUNDED: a cold open builds the full-text index and takes seconds on a large design (shared.rs allows 30 seconds), so the first request cannot be treated as cheap and concurrent first requests for the same graph must collapse into one open rather than racing. Eviction needs a policy — each open graph costs a RocksDB instance with its own block cache, file handles and tantivy index — so an idle timeout per graph (the existing --idle-timeout is per PROCESS) plus a cap on simultaneously open graphs, with a clear error at the cap rather than silent thrashing. (2) How a session says which graph it wants: today --graph-path, fixed for the process lifetime. SELECTION SHOULD BE BY graph_id, NOT BY PATH — a path is a property of the server's filesystem and leaks it to clients, while graph_id is the durable name the design already answers to; the registry maps id to path. Candidates in order of preference: an HTTP path prefix (/g/<graph_id>/, visible in logs and routable by ordinary proxies), an MCP initialize parameter, or a tool call that attaches the session — the last is the worst, because it makes every session stateful in a way a reconnect silently loses and leaves a window in which a session is connected to nothing. (3) The rendezvous convention: shared.rs publishes a sidecar beside each store saying a server holds this graph and where it is, and the election is arbitrated by whichever spawned process wins the RocksDB lock — a convention that assumes one server per graph. A multi-graph server holds several stores and therefore several rendezvous claims, and should publish into EACH held graph's sidecar so an unrelated local session that opens that directory attaches rather than failing its open. (4) Not breaking the single-graph path: the overwhelmingly common case is one project, one directory, --graph-path, and it must keep working exactly as it does, including --only-if-present and the latent surface (main.rs:772) which is what makes reflow2 installable machine-wide without minting a store in every directory. THE CLEANEST FRAMING: single-graph mode is multi-graph mode with a registry of one, pre-populated at startup and with selection defaulted — NOT a second code path. (5) Commands that open the store directly: --import, --export and --stop-shared open it outside the server and currently instruct the user to stop the server first; with one server holding many graphs, "stop the server" becomes a much more expensive instruction because it evicts every other project, so these should either route through the running server or grow a per-graph release.

RISKS ACCEPTED WITH THIS SHAPE. Isolation regressions are silent and severe — a handler that reaches the wrong graph corrupts a design rather than erroring, which is why it is carried as its own requirement rather than as a note here. Resource exhaustion: N open graphs is N block caches and N tantivy indices, and without a cap a busy server degrades in a way that looks like reflow2 being slow. Failure blast radius grows: today a panic loses one project's session; serving fifty, it loses fifty. And flo2 becomes schedule-coupled to this work — under the per-project-process alternative flo2 could have been built entirely around an unchanged reflow2, and that coupling is being accepted deliberately.
properties.name: ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 (conditional) — a hosted reflow2 holds N single-writer stores in one process, one lock each; the directory stays the unit of a design
properties.rationale:
Raised by @ajs from flo2's side of the seam, 2026-08-05, and it is the first time the hosting question has arrived with a concrete consumer behind it rather than as an architecture preference. WHY IT IS RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN AS A RE-OPENING OF dec:multi-writer-architecture: Anthony authorized re-opening that decision on 2026-08-05 ("yes, re-open it"), and per dec:reopen-supersedes a re-opening mints a NEW decision rather than flipping the accepted node — but that new decision ALREADY EXISTS as dec:central-host, whose own rationale says exactly this and cites the same rule. Minting a third node for the same seam would have been the duplicate HEAL later flags and somebody has to merge. So this records the concrete ANSWER and hangs it under dec:central-host, which holds the question.

WHAT IS GENUINELY NEW HERE, and the reason this is not a rerun of the 2026-07-25 argument: dec:multi-writer-architecture rejected a hosted service on cost against confirmed intent — it contradicts req:persistence ("the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo") and req:invocation ("the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio"). Neither objection is answered by this proposal and both still stand for the LOCAL case. What changed is that flo2 is a hosted web app whose whole premise is that somebody who cannot clone a repository or run a CLI can still take part in designing something — and that premise is already accepted intent here, as req:design-reachable-without-the-repo. The proposal does not ask the local case to move; it asks for a second deployment shape alongside it, which is precisely what rule:no-foreclosure was written to keep reachable ("build nothing today that forecloses growing into a hosted, multi-user, multi-project service"). This is that rule being cashed in.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody rediscovers it: dec:multi-writer-architecture's rejection of a hosted service turned partly on permanent operational burden and on putting the design on a machine the user does not control. A container image and a graph registry do not make either objection false — they make it somebody's job. The proposal is explicit that reflow2 has NO AUTHENTICATION OF ANY KIND today and that authorization is flo2's job at the layer in front; reflow2's obligation is only that a session bound to graph X cannot address graph Y. If that split is not stated and held, this decision quietly converts an accepted "no hosted service" into a hosted service with no security story, which is the drift dec:reopen-supersedes exists to prevent.

WHAT WAS CHECKED AND FOUND SOUND, recorded because it is the natural place to look and it is the wrong place: the export is NOT incomplete. Every node type created during a session appears in export_graph's output, including Question, ChangeEvent and Fragment, and adopt_on_import correctly preserves graph_id so a clone adopts the design's identity rather than minting a new one.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and it is Anthony's call. The schema declares BOTH `SUPERSEDES` and `OBSOLETES` for the same relationship — one node retiring another on the record — and NEITHER is read by any computation. The choice is which one is the real vocabulary, and then making it mean something. Option A: keep `OBSOLETES` (the one the code and the retire-from-design skill already use) and delete `SUPERSEDES` from the schema and from docs/three-axes.md. Option B: keep `SUPERSEDES` (the one the schema's own doc comment describes as "target retired on the record") and migrate the code. Option C: both survive with a stated distinction — but nobody has yet said what that distinction would be, and two words for one relationship is how a vocabulary rots.
properties.name: OPEN — retirement is two edge types and neither is consulted: which one survives?
properties.rationale:
FOUND BY THE SCHEMA SWEEP, 2026-07-28, and it is the `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` shape at edge level rather than property level.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. `SUPERSEDES` has ZERO references in the entire Rust source: nothing creates it, nothing reads it. It is nonetheless documented in `nodes.rs` ("source supersedes target — target retired on the record") and named in `docs/three-axes.md` as part of what covers the time axis. `OBSOLETES` is the one actually in use — `collapse_decision` draws it when a chosen alternative retires the losers, and the retire-from-design skill instructs users to draw it for a capability or component with a successor. But `OBSOLETES` has NO READER either: grep across the whole core crate finds the constant, the one create site, and a doc comment. No rollup, detector or report consults it.

WHAT THAT MEANS TODAY, stated exactly rather than dramatised: retiring something marks it and changes nothing downstream. A retired capability still counts in every rollup, still raises its gaps, still appears in delivery arithmetic. It is currently LATENT — reflow2's own design contains zero instances of either edge, so the retire path has never been exercised on this project — but the skill is actively telling users to draw an edge that has no effect, which is worse than an edge nobody knows about.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST HOUSEKEEPING. `req:intent-preserved` ("the past is never overwritten") is the requirement retirement serves, and the retire-from-design skill exists precisely to force the question "was this ever true?" — history retired on the record versus a mistake deleted. That whole discipline currently terminates in an edge nothing reads. Whichever edge survives, the deciding question is the same: what SHOULD consult it — delivery roll-up, the gap detectors, `graph_report`'s counts — and does a retired node stop counting, or count separately?

DELIBERATELY LEFT `proposed`: this is a vocabulary choice with migration consequences for anyone who already drew either edge, and `dec:certainty-derived` forbids recording it as settled on the user's behalf.

properties.decision: single_point_of_failure candidates are Components, Interfaces, Resources, Environments.
properties.name: Only things that operate can be single points of failure
properties.rationale: The suggested fix is add_redundancy, and redundancy is only coherent for running parts; a golden thread converges on intent by design, so intent hubs are the thread working. 22 of 22 false positives cleared, 4 true survivors. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); BL-5.

properties.decision:
Anthony asked 2026-07-31 whether a "start here" file or node should tell a newly-cloned agent what it needs to pick up where the last person left off — offered explicitly as an idea to explore, with the observation that reflow2 often already has something. It does, and the answer is: BUILD THE VIEW, NOT THE DOCUMENT.

NO START-HERE FILE. Two recorded positions already forbid it, and neither is a stretch. `req:session-memory-in-graph`: "a summary written at the end is the one a busy session never gets to, and an end-of-session digest is a retelling rather than a record." And `dec:what-lives-where`'s whole storyflow lesson is prose-you-navigate losing to graph-you-query. A START-HERE.md is `dev_storyflow` in miniature — it would go stale, and STALENESS IN AN ORIENTATION DOCUMENT IS THE WORST PLACE FOR IT, because it is the first thing read and the reader has nothing yet to check it against.

THE NEED IS REAL AND MOSTLY ALREADY DESIGNED. Three planned capabilities cover it between them: `cap:what-next` (which of the agreed things to do now, ranked so an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it), `cap:onboarding` (where does a new piece of work belong, for someone who did not build the system), and `cap:session-memory` (what the last session learned, queryable rather than narrated). None needs a document; all three are projections, which is what `dec:views-are-projections` already says every view is.

WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it belongs in `cap:what-next` rather than in a new thing: WHICH FEW DECISIONS SHAPE EVERYTHING ELSE. Neither what-next nor where-am-i answers it today, and it is what a newcomer actually needs — not the task list, but the handful of choices that explain why the rest looks as it does.

EVIDENCE AGAINST URGENCY, recorded because it is the kind of thing that otherwise gets built on a feeling. `where-am-i` DID orient a fresh agent on this design earlier the same day: 627 nodes, roughly six calls, using `scan_nodes` with `brief: true` and reading six Decisions in full. It scales today because reads are bounded (`cap:bounded-reads`). The concern that it stops working is a FORECAST, not yet an observation — worth watching rather than pre-solving, and worth re-measuring when the answer changes rather than assuming it has.

SO THE ORDER IS: build `cap:what-next`, whose blocker has already cleared, and add the shaping-decisions section to it. Do not add a fourth thing beside three planned ones that already answer the question.
properties.name: No START-HERE document — orientation is a projection, and writing it down would be dev_storyflow in miniature
properties.rationale:
Taken on the recommendation rather than the request, which is the point worth noting: the question was "should we write a start-here document", and the honest answer was that the artefact would work against the reason the project exists. Anthony's own framing left room for that — "maybe this isn't needed because an agent using reflow2 can already quickly know what a project is about" — and the measurement supports it.

The more useful outcome was not the answer but what looking produced: `cap:what-next` states a prerequisite that has since been met, and nothing surfaced it. A capability that records its own blocking condition in prose has written a trigger that nothing fires. That is the same shape as every other declared-but-unread property this project keeps finding, and it is the argument for the shaping-decisions section being a COMPUTATION rather than another paragraph.

The in-degree caveat is kept deliberately. The first version of the idea looked convincing because the top three results were genuinely load-bearing; the top result was not, and reporting the idea without that would have been reporting a demo rather than a measurement.

properties.decision:
PROPOSED, APPROVER `who:ajs`. His shape, 2026-08-10: *"maybe we do a top 4 and bottom 1 that always appears in the where-am-i?"*

TWO CONSTRAINTS HE STATED IN THE SAME BREATH, AND BOTH LOWER THE BAR ON PURPOSE.

(1) APPROXIMATION IS EXPLICITLY ACCEPTABLE: *"this doesn't have to be an exact 'what is the most pressing decision'. getting something in the general ballpark of what decisions I need to make or a rough 'top 5' is better than an equal set of 60+ decisions."* THIS IS AN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION AND IT SHOULD BE READ AS ONE. It means the ranking need not be defensible item by item — only roughly right at the head — which disposes of the standing objection that every candidate signal is too noisy. A flat list of 83 is the baseline being beaten, and it is a low bar. RECORDED BECAUSE THE OPPOSITE INSTINCT IS THE DEFAULT ONE: this project's habit is to refuse to compute what it cannot compute honestly, and here the user has said in advance that rough is what he wants.

(2) UNRANKED IS NOT DISCARDED: *"it is not like we are throwing the unmade decisions aside and saying 'these are not ranked well, therefore not important and we'll never make a decision on them'."* Nothing leaves the pile by ranking low, and the display must not read as a shortlist of what matters.

⭐⭐ AND HE NAMED THE FLAW HIMSELF, WHICH IS WHY THE SHAPE HAS FIVE SLOTS AND NOT FOUR: *"which has a side effect of saying things not searched for are not important, which is not true."*

⇒ THE BOTTOM SLOT IS THE EXPLORATION TERM, ARRIVED AT INDEPENDENTLY AND FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION. `dec:attention-is-measured-behaviourally-not-lexically` records, from the reinforcement-learning framing, that any attention ranking reinforces what has already been visited — so a node nothing surfaces is never read, never accumulates, and never rises, permanently; and that the standard remedies are an exploration term or optimistic initialisation. Anthony reached the same requirement from the user-experience side, before seeing that consequence applied. **THE TOP FOUR ARE EXPLOITATION AND THE BOTTOM ONE IS EXPLORATION.** A convergence from two independent directions is the strongest evidence this design gets that a property is real rather than clever.

THE SUBTLETY THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE BOTTOM SLOT WORKS AT ALL: "bottom 1" IS NOT A RANK, IT IS A HUGE TIE. Under any attention signal, everything never surfaced scores identically — measured 2026-08-10, 61 of 83 open decisions govern nothing and would sit in that tie under a consequence ranking too. So the slot needs a TIEBREAK, and the choice of tiebreak is the whole design:
  - DETERMINISTIC (always the same one) STARVES THE REST and is the failure mode dressed as a feature.
  - RANDOM among the never-touched is ε-greedy proper, and samples the set over time.
  - OLDEST-UNSEEN is random's better-behaved cousin: it guarantees coverage instead of merely expecting it, and it makes the slot's promise checkable.

COVERAGE IS COMPUTABLE AND SHOULD BE STATED RATHER THAN FELT: one slot per orientation against 61 unranked items is 61 orientations to see them all once. That is months at any normal cadence. If that is too slow the answer is more slots or an oldest-first draw, and the number is the argument — not a preference.

WHAT THIS SHAPE DOES NOT DEPEND ON, and why it can ship first: the slot structure is independent of HOW the top four are ranked. Any signal fills it — consequence (`dec:idea-a-critical-path-through-the-undecided`), attention (`dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important`), or the already-accepted rule in `req:what-next` that an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. IT IS THEREFORE BUILDABLE BEFORE EITHER OPEN QUESTION IS SETTLED, using whatever ranking exists, which makes it the smallest useful increment in this whole thread.

TWO THINGS THE DISPLAY MUST SAY, given constraint (2): that the bottom slot is a DELIBERATE sample of the unranked and not the least important thing, and how many open decisions are not shown. A five-item list that silently stands for 83 is the false completeness `where-am-i` already forbids ("never report from a page as if it were the whole set").

OPEN, NOT SETTLED HERE: the tiebreak (random vs oldest-unseen); whether four is the right exploitation width; whether the ranking behind the top four is one merged score or two lists; and whether the same shape belongs in `loop_status` as well as `where-am-i`.
properties.name: PROPOSED — where-am-i shows four ranked open decisions and one deliberately UNRANKED, and a rough ranking is explicitly good enough
properties.rationale:
Anthony's shape, recorded as its own Decision rather than folded into either open ranking question because it is separable from both and shippable before either — the slot structure works with any ranking, including the one `req:what-next` already accepts. Folding it into a brainstorm node would bury the one piece of this thread that can be built now.

The convergence is the part worth preserving. The exploration requirement was derived an hour earlier from the Q-table framing as a consequence nobody had asked for; Anthony proposed the bottom slot from the user-experience side without reference to it. Two independent derivations of the same property is stronger evidence than either, and a later session that finds only one of them would be free to drop it as over-engineering.

The acceptance criterion is recorded as prominently as the shape because it cuts against this project's own reflex. reflow2 repeatedly refuses to compute what it cannot compute honestly — `dec:readiness-is-an-observation-the-threshold-is-the-judgement` is the canonical case. Here the user has pre-authorised a rough answer, and without that on the record the natural instinct is to refuse to rank at all and ship nothing.

properties.decision: PROPOSED, AWAITING ANTHONY'S WORD — the code is built and tested this way, but the rule shape is a judgement he should ratify. BL-176's fix could have taken either form. THE FORM NOT TAKEN: extend the inclusion list — count REALIZES plus DOCUMENTS plus SPECIFIES (plus PRODUCES incoming, plus SATISFIES) as attaching an Artifact. This is what the field report asked for and it would have closed the reported case. THE FORM TAKEN: invert it. An Artifact is an orphan when EVERY edge it carries, in either direction, is bookkeeping — INCLUDES from a Release, CHANGED from a ChangeEvent, YIELDED from a Fragment, AT_EPOCH. Anything else attaches. REASONING, and it is a generalisation of the bug rather than a preference: an inclusion list has to be extended every time the vocabulary grows, and until someone remembers, correctly-modelled work reads as a defect. That IS this bug — the list said REALIZES and the schema had since grown DOCUMENTS and SPECIFIES. BL-170 was the same shape from another direction, a hidden inclusion list making a region invisible, and BL-114 witnessed this same detector doing it twice in an unrelated repo. An exclusion list fails the other way: a new DESIGN edge counts as attachment the day it is added and needs no edit here, while only a new BOOKKEEPING edge needs a line. THE COUNTERWEIGHT THAT DEFINES THE RULE'S LIMIT: this is deliberately NOT the degree-zero rule the Decision arm of the same detector uses. Degree-zero was settled for Decisions by measurement and is right there — but almost every Artifact in a mature graph carries a Release INCLUDES edge, so degree-zero would silence orphan_node everywhere. The distinction is that bookkeeping edges are drawn by the machinery, not by anyone saying what the file is FOR. WHAT STILL FIRES, pinned by tests: an Artifact attached by nothing, and a document artifact with no DOCUMENTS edge — because BL-176 was explicit that this doc describes nothing either IS worth saying, so artifact_type must never be a free pass. THE HONEST LIMIT, and it is BL-199: reflow2's own graph goes 0 to 0 across this change and cannot demonstrate the fix, because all 139 of its artifacts carry REALIZES — including 32 of its 35 documents and specs, against the link-artifacts skill's own instruction. The evidence is the six new tests and the field measurement, never this graph. THE RISK OF THE CHOSEN FORM, stated so it is not discovered later: if a future bookkeeping edge type is added and nobody adds it here, it will silently count as attachment and quiet the detector for those nodes. That is the mirror of the failure being fixed, and it is accepted as the smaller one because bookkeeping edge types are added rarely and deliberately while design edge types are added often.
properties.name: What ATTACHES an Artifact is defined by excluding bookkeeping, not by listing the edges that count
properties.rationale: Recorded because the choice is invisible in the diff — both forms produce the same result on every case anyone has reported, and they differ only in how they FAIL as the vocabulary grows. A future maintainer reading `ARTIFACT_BOOKKEEPING` should find the reason it is an exclusion list rather than rediscovering the argument, and Anthony should get to overrule it while it is still cheap.

properties.decision:
DECIDED AND BUILT 2026-08-09, Anthony's word, closing the condition dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge set on 2026-08-08.

THAT DECISION SAID: build the first cut from CLAIMS, and \"decide on OWNED_BY only after that is built and SHOWN TO BE INSUFFICIENT\". Its rationale named the disqualifying evidence in advance — \"if claims turn out to model the wrong thing (they are TRANSIENT WORK-IN-HAND, while ownership is DURABLE and survives the session), that is a real distinction and the edge becomes justified on evidence rather than on anticipation.\"
