A Verification is how this design records that something was CHECKED. Refusing to connect them said a limit may be stated and computed but never independently verified. AND THE ASYMMETRY WAS ODD ON ITS FACE: `DesignRule` was already in the list, and `unverified_enforced_rule` exists precisely so a gate-blocking rule owes a passing check. A Constraint is the DesignRule's sibling — the imposed limit beside the chosen one — and nothing in the schema explained why they were split.

HOW IT AROSE: `ver:side_e_slo_gate_unwired_2026_08_09` VERIFIES `con:side_e_perf_slos_are_enforced_nowhere` in dev_storyflow — a check measuring whether a performance constraint is actually enforced. The 2026-08-08 narrowing of `VERIFIES` from `*` to an enumeration derived its list from a census that found five types at 95/27/13/2/1 edges and MISSED TWO CARRYING ONE EDGE EACH. See `fact:defect-a-schema-narrowing-orphaned-live-edges-and-no-export-is-ever-imported`.

NOT SETTLED BY THIS, and left open on purpose: whether `Project` belongs; whether the list should be re-derived across all three known designs; and whether any detector should READ the new edge — admitting it makes the claim expressible, and nothing yet computes anything from it.
properties.name: A Verification MAY verify a Constraint — a check that measures whether a limit holds is a real modelling need, and Project stays out
properties.rationale: Recorded as his ruling rather than as an agent's fix because it is a schema change with real data on both sides: the wrong answer either destroys a legitimate edge or admits everything. He chose the option that repairs the design without touching anyone's data. The Project half was deliberately NOT bundled with it — the reporter who found both asked for them to be judged separately, and folding them together would have settled a second question nobody put.

properties.decision:
RECORDED SO THE CHOICE IS MADE DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN BY DEFAULT. Anthony approved bundling `record_was_incorrect` into the schema increment (2026-08-09); this node exists so that adding the enum value does not silently foreclose the better fix, which may make it unnecessary.

THE OBSERVATION THAT STARTED IT, dragon Boss (`cca98fbf`, dev_storyflow, 2026-08-09), correcting an edge that asserted a runtime dependency the code never had: *"the ChangeEvent hint itself says DriftEvent is the design-vs-reality construct, BUT `propagate_change` takes a ChangeEvent, so recording it as drift would have cost me the impact check."* And the conclusion, which is the part worth keeping: **"the honest modelling and the useful tooling point at different node types, and I chose the tooling."**

THAT IS A TOOL SHAPING THE RECORD. A caller who wants a blast radius must record their finding as a ChangeEvent whether or not it is one, because that is the only node type `propagate_change` accepts. So the ledger fills with design-evolution entries that are actually drift observations — and no detector can tell them apart afterwards, because by then they are the same type.

--- OPTION A — ADD `record_was_incorrect` TO ChangeEvent (the approved path) ---
FOR: cheap, certain, and read — `changelog_view` buckets on `change_type`, so the value does work immediately. Bundled into a schema-clustered increment, its stamp cost is shared. AGAINST: it grows ChangeEvent to cover a case the schema already says belongs elsewhere. `ChangeEvent`'s own hint calls itself "the design-evolution log; DISTINCT from DriftEvent, which records design-vs-reality divergence rather than intended change" — and a record that was wrong from the start is divergence, not intended change. So A makes the ledger MORE expressive and the type boundary LESS true.

--- OPTION B — TEACH `propagate_change` TO SEED FROM A DriftEvent ---
FOR: fixes the cause rather than the symptom. `DriftEvent` already exists and already means exactly this; nothing new is declared, so `dec:edge-orthogonality`'s test is satisfied without growing vocabulary. It would also remove the incentive that currently mis-types every drift finding somebody wanted a blast radius for. AGAINST: a real piece of design work, not a one-line enum addition — the propagation walk starts from what a ChangeEvent CHANGED, and a DriftEvent's equivalent anchor has to be defined rather than assumed. Unknown whether it moves the stamp.

--- OPTION C — BOTH ---
They are not exclusive: A gives the ledger a truthful value for corrections that ARE design evolution; B gives drift findings their impact check without lying about their type. FOR: the two solve different halves. AGAINST: doing A first removes most of the pain, which is exactly how B never gets built.

⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: A ships, the pain goes away, and B is never revisited — leaving the tool still shaping the record for every future drift finding. This node is the guard against that, and it should be read before `req:the-ledger-can-say-the-record-was-wrong` is built.

NOTHING IS PROMOTED. Anthony has approved the bundling of A, not a choice between A and B.
properties.name: OPEN — should `propagate_change` seed from a DriftEvent, so the honest modelling and the useful tooling stop pointing at different node types?
properties.rationale: Minted alongside Anthony's approval to bundle the enum value, precisely because approving A is not the same as rejecting B, and an unrecorded alternative is one nobody argues with later. The evidence is a consumer's account of choosing the wrong node type on purpose because the right one lost them a tool — which is a stronger signal than a feature request, since it shows the surface changing what people record rather than merely what they can express.

properties.decision:
OPEN. `SPECIFIES` is currently NOT traversed by propagation. `nodes.rs` says so explicitly: "Structural edges not listed (e.g. SPECIFIES, DOCUMENTS, temporal bookkeeping) are intentionally not traversed."

THE ARGUMENT FOR TRAVERSING IT. It is grouped with DOCUMENTS, and the two are not alike. DOCUMENTS is human explanation — prose changing does not implicate the code. SPECIFIES is a MACHINE-READABLE CONTRACT: an OpenAPI file, a JSON schema, an IDL. When that changes, the implementation behind the interface may now be wrong, which is the definition of blast radius. Had SPECIFIES propagated and the edges been drawn, adding `Verification.description` to `schema/verify.yaml` would have lit up `ifc:mcp-tools` at the moment of the edit, which is exactly the miss that `req:declared-vocabulary-is-reachable-from-the-surface` exists for.

Direction would follow REALIZES, which has the same Artifact->target shape: forward Upstream, backward Downstream.

WHY IT IS NOT DECIDED NOW, and this is the substantive part rather than caution. It changes every blast radius in the graph, and it lands in the same window as two other changes that push the same dial the OTHER way:
  - `dec:the-default-scope-depth-should-be-two` SHRINKS regions (accepted, not yet built).
  - the future SE work adds subsystem interfaces, whose PROVIDES/CONSUMES edges ARE traversed and therefore GROW regions.
Turning all three at once means nobody can attribute the result. The sequence that stays measurable: land depth 2 and re-measure the 56-component sweep; then draw the SPECIFIES edges (which changes nothing while the edge is untraversed); then decide THIS with a before-and-after in hand.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: rerun the same instrument that produced `fact:defect-a-scoped-detector-at-its-default-depth-returns-two-thirds-of-the-design` with SPECIFIES traversable, and read what happens to the 50..60 spread. If regions stay discriminating, traverse it. If they do not, the contract relationship stays recorded-but-not-propagated, which is still strictly better than today's nothing.
properties.name: Whether a change to a contract artifact should reach the interface it specifies — measure after the depth change, do not decide ahead of it
properties.rationale:
RAISED BY ANTHONY'S QUESTION, 2026-08-17, which is what surfaced the whole thread: "in a system that builds a graph to represent relationships between two things, why is there no edge between these? it also sounds like some type of API contract."

The answer was that the edge exists, is defined for exactly this ("an OpenAPI / protobuf / JSON-schema / IDL file SPECIFIES an Interface (its authoritative contract)"), carries a `format` property listing `json_schema`, and has ZERO instances in the entire graph. It was written for INGEST — its `extraction_hint` is a prompt for pulling structure out of a user's documents — so it was built for other people's projects and never turned on this one. `rule:the-self-host-always-trails-what-it-teaches` is the right frame: the accurate reading is not "reflow2 failed to model itself" but "this is now catchable, for everyone".

An agent proposed and recommended nothing on this one at first pass and explicitly put it to the owner; the recommendation above (measure, do not decide) replaces that after the coupling was found.

properties.decision: On a durable open, refuse when the identity sidecar is absent AND the store directory already held data AND the legacy probe finds no design under the old shared id. "Already held data" is answered BEFORE the store is opened, from the filesystem alone: a `.sst` file, or a non-empty write-ahead log. Opening creates the directory, so the evidence exists for exactly one line. All three prior behaviours are unchanged — a sidecar that is present is read (and still refused if unreadable), a genuinely fresh store still mints, and a pre-identity graph under the shared id is still adopted.
properties.name: A lost identity sidecar is caught by what the filesystem can see, because the store cannot be asked what designs it holds
properties.rationale:
THE CHECK THIS REPLACES IS ONE WE CANNOT WRITE. The honest question is "does this store hold a design under ANY id", and it cannot be asked: graph_id namespaces every stored key and dynograph-storage exposes no enumeration of ids — count_nodes(graph_id, type) requires the very id you are trying to discover. dynograph-storage is pinned by git tag v0.12.0 in the workspace Cargo.toml, so acquiring that scan means a change to another repository, a new tag, and a bump here. That is a real option and it is the BETTER fix; it is not this fix.

"The store already held data, and it is not the legacy design" answers the same question from outside, with nothing but read_dir. It is a PROXY, and the ways it is wrong are worth stating rather than discovering: a store created and opened but never written, whose sidecar is then lost, is refused though nothing is at stake — the refusal names how to proceed, and the alternative (minting over a live design) is unbounded, so the tie breaks toward refusing. A store whose data files were deleted while the directory survived would not be caught, which is not a case a mis-scoped mount produces.

WHY A PROXY NOW BEATS THE REAL CHECK LATER. cap:hosted-state-on-a-volume is BUILT, not planned — art:dockerfile realizes it — and it already ships knowing this exact failure. Dockerfile:78-82 says so in capitals: a store opened without its identity sidecar "finds nothing and PRESENTS AS AN EMPTY DESIGN, reporting nothing wrong", and mounting `.../graph` rather than its parent "is a plausible-looking mistake that silently loses a project. MOUNT THE PARENT." The mitigation for a known silent-data-loss path was a comment addressed to the one person who cannot read it: the operator gets no error, because there is no error. The capability's own statement already says the required behaviour is to refuse.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, so nobody reads more into a green check: it does not RECOVER the design. The store still holds it, under an id nothing can now name. Recovery needs the sidecar restored from backup, or the scan above — at which point the id could be read back off the store and the refusal could become self-healing. That is the follow-on this defers, and the reason to prefer the foundation change eventually rather than instead.

The asymmetry it removes was already visible in the code: an UNREADABLE sidecar was refused with "reflow2 will not guess", while an ABSENT one minted silently — and absent is the likelier of the two on a mounted volume.

properties.decision: THE HARD CONSTRAINT FIRST, because it rules out the literal proposal: no harness discovers skills from an MCP server. Claude Code, OpenCode and Copilot read `.claude/skills/`, Grok CLI reads `.grok/skills/` (docs/skills/README.md), and a skill that is not in one of those directories is not a skill — it is a file nobody loads. So "reference something in the MCP to discover all those skills" cannot be honoured as harness-native skills today. What CAN be honoured is the substance: nothing in the project changes after setup, and updates ride the package. FOUR PIECES, separable, in increasing cost. (1) SERVER INSTRUCTIONS — already how reflow2 delivers its loop doctrine (the paragraph in every session's context comes from the server, versioned with the binary, zero repo files). The catalogue of skills, one line each, belongs here: that is exactly what a skill's frontmatter description does, and it is what makes progressive disclosure work. (2) A `reflow2_skill(name)` TOOL returning the body on demand, with `list_skills` alongside. Works in EVERY MCP client including Grok, needs no filesystem copy, and always matches the binary. (3) MCP PROMPTS — reflow2 declares only `enable_tools()`; adding `enable_prompts()` would serve the command-shaped skills as `/mcp__reflow2__<name>` slash commands with zero files in the repo. Claude-Code-shaped, so it complements (2) rather than replacing it. (4) LOCAL OVERRIDE — a skill present in the project's own `.claude/skills/` wins over the served one, so customisation survives and the served set is a default rather than a cage. WHAT THE PROJECT WOULD STILL HOLD after all four: the pointer paragraph, `.mcp.json` (and the other harnesses' formats), `.reflow2/` and its gitignore line. That is his brother's proposal exactly.
properties.name: OPEN — do the skills come from the server instead of being copied into the project?
properties.rationale: Feedback from Anthony's brother, 2026-07-25, and it names the same failure shape reflow2 keeps finding in itself: a COPY drifts, and the fix is to remove the copying rather than to refresh it better — the same reasoning that retired the fleet's mint-race guard in dec:identity-out-of-band, and the same one behind computed-not-remembered everywhere else in this project. The evidence is already on the record: the installer's docstring concedes that the kit freezes while reflow2 moves, and reflow2's OWN kit manifest went four releases stale with nothing noticing. THE HONEST COST, recorded beside the idea: a harness-native skill is auto-matched by the harness from its description without the agent being asked, and a served skill is not — the agent has to know to call for it. Moving skills to the server therefore trades the harness's own progressive disclosure for freshness, and the mitigation (the catalogue in the server instructions) is a hand-built version of what the harness does for free. That trade is the decision, and it is worth putting to both brothers rather than assuming: one of them is the consumer whose repo churns, the other is the one who would maintain two delivery paths.

properties.decision:
Option (a) from req:snapshot-per-revision-not-per-epoch, in a form that keeps existing ids stable. The FIRST capture of a node in an epoch keeps the id `snap:{epoch}:{node}` exactly as before. A genuine SECOND revision in the same epoch appends `:r2`, `:r3`, so HAS_SNAPSHOT becomes one-to-many precisely when history requires it and not before. An IDENTICAL re-capture returns the existing snapshot instead of minting a duplicate — compared against the TAIL of the chain and nothing earlier. A ceiling of 64 distinct snapshots per (epoch, node) errors rather than growing history quietly, and is checked only when a new capture is actually needed, so an idempotent retry against a full chain still succeeds.

NOT chosen: (b) refusing a second record_change in one epoch, and (c) keeping one snapshot per epoch and making the second call a no-op.
properties.name: Snapshot identity is per revision, but only when a revision actually happened
properties.rationale:
Truest to req:intent-preserved, which is the requirement this bug violated — (c) preserves the original but still discards the intermediate, which is losing history on purpose rather than by accident, and (b) pushes epoch hygiene onto the caller when an epoch is meant to bound a round of WORK, not a single edit.

The first-capture id is left unsuffixed because existing graphs and committed exports carry those ids and a test pins one; suffixing everything would have rewritten history to fix a bug about not rewriting history.

Idempotence on an unchanged re-capture is the mirror of the bug being fixed: snapshotting a node that has not moved is a no-op, not a new version, and minting one would make the history claim edits that never happened. It also keeps record_change safe to retry.

TAIL-ONLY COMPARISON, and it is the load-bearing detail. A node edited A -> B -> A inside one epoch has three genuine revisions. Comparing against ANY earlier snapshot would match the first A-capture and hand it back for the third, recording two — hiding an edit that DID happen. That is the same class of loss as the overwrite this fixes, just quieter, and it would have shipped as a half-fix. Matching only the tail also keeps the `:rN` order readable as the order the revisions occurred in, which is the only ordering a reader has: every snapshot in an epoch is pinned to that one epoch and carries no sequence of its own.

The 64 ceiling is a signal, not a storage limit: a node revised that many times inside one epoch means the epoch has stopped bounding anything, and the error says so.

RECORDED AT `proposed`: the requirement itself said the shape of the fix was a choice and none of the options was obviously right. Anthony directed the work be finished, not this particular shape — so the shape is on the record awaiting his word, and reopening it supersedes rather than un-accepts (dec:reopen-supersedes).

properties.decision:
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: option (a), mint-and-carry, with the refusal from (d) as its backstop. Decided but NOT YET BUILT.

The shape. A tool mints a seat and returns it; the client passes it on the calls that care (`claim_region`, `release_claim`, the stale-seat check). `ClaimReq.seat` already accepts one, documented today as "pass your own only if you have a durable handle for the session (a fleet worker name); it is a name, never a lock" — so the argument exists and what is missing is the minting and the discipline around it. This is transport-independent by construction: it works identically on stdio, on legacy Streamable HTTP and on the sessionless transport, where today identity is inherited from whatever the transport happened to do and quietly differs between them.

THE BACKSTOP IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF. Option (a) alone has a quiet failure mode: an agent that forgets the handle silently gets fresh-seat-per-request behaviour again, which is the exact bug being fixed, reintroduced by omission. So when a claim-family call arrives on a sessionless transport WITHOUT a seat argument, it is REFUSED by name, saying what would have worked — never served by minting a per-request seat and reporting success. That is `req:no-silent-fallback` applied to identity, and it is what makes the option safe rather than merely correct when used correctly.

NOT CHOSEN, on the record. (b) Derive the seat from what a stateless request already carries — rmcp reconstructs a `ClientInfo` per request via `peer_info_for_stateless_request` — rejected because nothing in those headers is guaranteed stable or unique per client, so it trades a loud missing parameter for a quiet wrong answer. (c) One seat per server PROCESS on the sessionless transport — rejected because it is precisely the regression `req:seat-per-client` was written against, `claim_report` telling six sessions they are each other. (d) Refusing the claim family on sessionless HTTP outright — kept as (a)'s backstop rather than as the whole answer, because as the whole answer it makes `cap:remote-sessions` conditional on a protocol version and narrows what reflow2 offers.
properties.name: A seat is minted on request and carried as a tool argument, and a claim without one is refused rather than guessed
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word, given 2026-07-30 when the four options and their costs were put to him. The requirement itself (`req:seat-identity-survives-stateless-mcp`) named this as the open part — "deciding how a client obtains and carries the handle without making every tool call carry a parameter no human should have to think about" — so this closes the fork the requirement opened rather than inventing a new one.

Why the backstop decided it. The three rejected options each fail quietly: (b) returns a wrong seat, (c) returns a shared one, and bare (a) returns a fresh one — and in all three cases the call SUCCEEDS. This design's standing objection to that shape is recorded in `req:no-silent-fallback` and was the reason `ver:stateless-seat` exists at all: the original bug was not that seats were wrong but that nothing said so. A refusal is the only branch that cannot rot silently.

Composes with `dec:identity-out-of-band`, which already holds that names are assigned with zero coordination rather than derived from shared state — a server-minted handle is that principle one layer up. It also matches where the MCP 2026-07-28 revision itself points: "servers that need cross-call state use explicit, server-minted handles passed as ordinary tool arguments."

Not urgent, and the measurement says why: `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` reports one seat per client on stdio and on HTTP at 2025-06-18, `proxy.rs` pins 2025-06-18 on both handshakes so shared and remote mode are unaffected, and rmcp's `ProtocolVersion::LATEST` is still `V_2025_11_25`. It becomes urgent the moment an external client negotiates 2026-07-28 against a shared `--http` server.

WHEN IT LANDS: `ver:stateless-seat` flips to passing on its own evidence, `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` exits zero and is worth promoting from a baseline to a CI gate, and `decision:ack:350d55cf9c8c3247` — the acknowledgement holding the failing check acceptable — should be WITHDRAWN rather than left standing.

properties.decision: Every epoch on the retrospective chain corresponds to a real shipped release with a real git tag and date (v0.4.0 through v0.10.1), plus the pre-existing genesis and post-v0.5.0-hardening epochs. Each Decision is anchored to the epoch of the earliest release whose committed export actually contains it — evidence from the repo, not reconstruction from memory. Each Release is pinned to its own epoch. Epochs before v0.9.0 carry no checksum, because their exports predate the hash chain; they say so in their description rather than claiming one. Going forward, an epoch is cut as work happens so nothing needs backfilling again.
properties.name: The epoch chain is backfilled from shipped releases only — real tags, or nothing
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24 among three options. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVES: (a) forward-only — anchor from today and leave the past alone. Rejected because all 34 existing decisions are the ones actually worth re-opening; a fork layer that can only fork decisions made after it was built is a fork layer with nothing to fork. (b) full reconstruction — invent an epoch per work session across the whole history and synthesize the missing snapshots. Rejected because most of those boundaries are guesses, and a fabricated epoch is worse than an absent one: it looks like evidence. Release tags are the natural resolution because they are the only points in this project's history that are independently attested (a tag, a date, a published binary, a committed export), and because "the design as of the release that shipped it" is the question a fork actually asks. The cost is deliberately accepted: the 9 founding decisions anchor to v0.4.0, the earliest tag carrying an export, which is their earliest EVIDENCE rather than their origin — recorded as such in that epoch's description instead of being silently presented as the date they were made. FOUND WHILE DOING THIS: reflow2's own temporal axis was nearly unused — zero Snapshots, 8 of 42 ChangeEvents pinned, no Decision anchored at all, the chain stopped four days back — because add_change_event (cheap, epoch-free) had been used throughout where record_change (pins and snapshots) was meant. The fork layer's foundation was missing, not merely its ref layer.

properties.cutoff_note: Boundary materialised 2026-08-21, when the check was built — the moment this decision said to record it. 356 settled nodes are exempt (217 Decisions, 126 Requirements, 13 DesignRules); 63 already carry an approver. Anthony was quoted 121 of 214 on 2026-08-09 and the design has grown by roughly two hundred settled nodes since, so this set is the state on the day the detector landed, not that day's. THE ROLLING READING IS DELIBERATE AND OVERRULEABLE: fixing the boundary at 2026-08-09 instead would hand him 222 items settled since to review one at a time, which is the backfill he refused, arriving late rather than early. Narrowing it to that export is a mechanical change if he wants those questions. ADDING AN ID HERE IS NOT A WAY TO GO GREEN: this is a dated boundary, and the honest routes are to record his approval or to move the status back to proposed.
properties.decision:
GRANDFATHER IT. The check owed by rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word applies only to nodes that reach a settled state AFTER a recorded cutoff. Everything settled before the cutoff is out of its scope permanently, and is NOT backfilled.

Anthony, 2026-08-11, answering the question put to him as gap:9d265ef455a2e245 / question:9d265ef455a2e245.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT MADE THIS A QUESTION AT ALL, taken before it was asked rather than after:

  accepted Decisions (excluding `decision:ack:` review records)   105, of which  50 carry any AUTHORED_BY,  47 to who:ajs
  Requirements moved off `proposed`                               109, of which  43 carry any AUTHORED_BY,  36 to who:ajs
  TOTAL SETTLED                                                   214, of which  93 carry any AUTHORED_BY,  83 to who:ajs

So 121 of 214 settled nodes carry nobody's name. Every one of them moved on the owner's word — the word simply was never recorded as an edge. A check written to the letter of the spec would therefore have gone red against 57% of the settled design on the day it landed, and NONE of those would have been violations.

⭐ THIS IS THE SIBLING CLAUSE'S TRAP, ONE RULE OVER, AND IT WAS NOT NAMED IN THE SPEC. rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path is advisory for exactly this reason, in its own words: "an honest detector would fail against the entire existing tool surface on the day it was written, and the only ways to make it green would be to block every build or to attach a check that proves nothing." The authority rule's detector spec listed ONE precondition (resolve the forked owner identity) and missed this one. The fork is now resolved — 6 Contributors, `ctr:anthony` gone, `who:ajs` sole owner identity — so the FIRST precondition is met and this is what was underneath it.

WHY FORWARD-ONLY IS THE ANSWER AND NOT A CONCESSION. The threat the rule was made enforced against is an AGENT WRITING IN THE OWNER'S VOICE (rule text, 2026-08-09: "what one person needs protection from is not another person; it is an agent writing in his voice"). That threat is entirely prospective. The 121 are not that threat; they are bookkeeping that predates the rule. A check scoped to them would be measuring conformance to a convention that did not exist when they were written — the same error as dec:reopen-supersedes' "7 of 14 obsoleted-but-accepted", which turned out to be measuring conformance and not deviation.

WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY, recorded so neither is re-litigated:

(1) BACKFILL THE 121, then enforce across everything. Rejected. It would record the owner's approval 121 times on nodes no agent can individually evidence, and it makes the check green BY CONSTRUCTION — which is precisely the green-washing cap:governance-proposal's own description forbids ("never attach a verification to close the finding, because a graph node green-washes exactly like a document"). The attribution would be defensible in aggregate and unevidenced one by one, which is the worst combination: queryable and unfounded. dev_storyflow's finding ⑮ is the same shape — edges that are queryable and wrong are strictly worse than prose that is honestly informal.

(2) FLIP THE RULE BACK TO ADVISORY. Rejected. It reverses the owner's explicit 2026-08-09 answer ("stop the build") to buy nothing but a closed gap, and it would leave this project with zero enforced rules that actually enforce.

⚠️ THE MECHANISM IS A REAL DESIGN CHOICE INSIDE THIS DECISION, NOT A FREE ONE. A Decision carries NO TIMESTAMP (the same limit that stops what_next scoring staleness), so "after the cutoff" cannot key on a date. It must key on the design's own time axis — a DesignEpoch, or the ChangeEvent boundary at which the detector lands — which is what req:graph-indexes-snapshots exists to make answerable without a git lookup. The cutoff epoch is to be recorded WHEN THE DETECTOR IS BUILT, not now: minting it in advance would date the rule to a moment nothing enforced.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO. It does not close gap:9d265ef455a2e245. That gap is unverified_enforced_rule and needs a PASSING Verification, and no check exists yet — the gap stays open as honest debt, and acknowledging it here would be recording a judgement the owner did not make. It also says nothing about rule:bl-41, the OTHER enforced rule with no detector (gap:b5ca966a38d7f372), which is a different problem: a rule about LLM behaviour that graph state may not be able to detect at all, and the first real customer for req:a-rule-says-whether-it-can-be-checked-at-all.

📌 THIS DECISION IS THE FIRST NODE BORN COMPLIANT WITH THE RULE IT SHAPES — settled only on the owner's word, and carrying an AUTHORED_BY approver edge to who:ajs recording that word at the moment it was given.
properties.name: The authority detector binds on what is settled from here, not on the 121 settled nodes that predate it
properties.rationale: The rule was made enforced to stop an agent settling intent in the owner's voice — a prospective threat. The 121 unattributed settled nodes are not that threat; they are bookkeeping predating the rule, and 121 of 214 means an unscoped check would go red on history rather than on violations. Backfilling would make the check green by construction on evidence no agent holds; reverting to advisory would discard the owner's explicit answer. Forward-only is the only option that leaves the check meaning something on the day it lands.

properties.decision:
DECIDED AND DONE 2026-08-09, Anthony's word: \"let's discontinue the content store.\" Supersedes dec:where-content-lives, dec:what-lives-where, dec:content-store-implementation, dec:content-manifest and dec:content-growth-is-bounded-by-what-not-by-size.

⭐ THE EVIDENCE WAS USAGE, MEASURED IN EVERY PROJECT THAT HAS IT — reflow2's own design: no --content-path configured, no .reflow2/content directory, and 0 of 148 Fragments carrying a content_ref. flo2: no content path. dev_storyflow: no content directory. THREE PROJECTS, ZERO USE, on a feature that is built, tested and documented.

HIS ARGUMENT, in his words: the bytes cannot fully live in a repo because it would become a huge object rapidly; dev_storyflow's 700+ documents have been ingested and \"those documents are no longer really needed\"; better to put important design artifacts directly in the git repo in something like a design_artifacts folder; it is another feature that must be maintained; and in flo2 the blob could reach terabytes needing backup, security and per-project separation.

AND AN ARGUMENT NOBODY HAD MADE: dec:where-content-lives settled on a content-addressed store whose blobs are COMMITTED TO GIT. Git is already a content-addressed store. The design was a content-addressed layer inside a content-addressed system, and the dedup and integrity hash it provided were both things git already gives anything committed.

AND A FOUNDING MOTIVATION THAT DID NOT SURVIVE: the store was partly built to make sessions \"stateful\" by holding transcripts. cap:session-memory already rejected that mechanism in its own text — \"a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation: leaning on it recreates the markdown problem one level down.\" Its actual design needs no store: takeaways as first-class graph content, the transcript a Fragment carrying a session UUID. See dec:idea-is-session-context-already-in-the-graph.

WHAT WAS REMOVED: content_put / content_get / content_exists / content_manifest, crates/reflow2-core/src/content.rs, crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/content_tools.rs, the --content-path flag, both test files, and the loop nudge's session-artifacts advisory (which told sessions to content_put a rendering).

⚠️ TWO ACCEPTED REQUIREMENTS ARE NOW UNSATISFIED ON PURPOSE, AND THAT IS THE HONEST STATE RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. Both are Anthony's own words from 2026-07-31 and the store was their answer:
  · req:agent-artifacts-are-captured — \"in many sessions, the agent will create artifacts... having all these artifacts automatically stored in the reflow2 blob storage would be great.\"
  · req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed — ingest keeps the original corpus documents, so the corpus becomes part of the design rather than an input consumed and discarded.
He was shown both in the impact check and chose to KEEP THEM OPEN AND UNANSWERED rather than drop them or claim a replacement. The design_artifacts folder is the intended answer and is UNBUILT, so recording it as satisfied would be fiction. detect_gaps will now ask about them, and that question is the retirement working rather than a bug.

THREE OTHER REQUIREMENTS EXISTED ONLY BECAUSE THE STORE DID and go quiet with it: req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session (a surface for it), req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry (a warning about pointers the export cannot carry), and req:content-reaches-every-seat. Their statuses are Anthony's to move; nothing was changed on his behalf.

⚠️ AND THE REPLACEMENT RESTS ON THE SCHEMA'S WEAKEST JOIN, stated so it is not discovered later: a design_artifacts folder puts the weight on Artifact.location and Fragment.title, which is the field dev_storyflow filed FOUR defects about on this same day — unvalidated paths, a literal ellipsis matching nothing, title-vs-source ambiguity, and no way to ask \"is this path already in the graph?\". That is an argument for fixing `location` before leaning on it, not against the plan.

RETIRED ON THE RECORD, NOT DELETED (retire-from-design, Path A). The capability, its verifications and its artifacts keep their nodes and their history; the ChangeEvent carrying change_type `deprecation` is the marker, because Capability.status has no terminal value — which is exactly dec:idea-does-a-capability-need-a-cancelled-state, still open and still Anthony's, and this is now its first real instance.
properties.name: The content store is discontinued — built, shipped, correct, and used zero times
properties.rationale:
Recorded as a new Decision rather than by editing the five it supersedes, per dec:reopen-supersedes: an accepted decision is never un-accepted, a later one obsoletes it.

The two unsatisfied requirements are named in the decision itself rather than left to be inferred from a gap report, because \"we removed the thing that answered your stated need\" is the part a later reader most needs and the part a tidy graph would hide.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-25 by Anthony, in one line: *"make the ladder open."* Asked as a straight fork — add `assembly` as a sixth enum value, or make the ladder user-defined — and he took the second.

═══ WHAT IS BEING REPLACED ═══

`schema/structure.yaml:18` declares `Component.level` as a CLOSED enum: `[component, subsystem, system, system_of_systems, enterprise]`, default `component`. `crates/reflow2-core/src/hierarchy.rs` mirrors it as `enum Level` with `as_str`, `from_key` and `rank()` (component = 0 … enterprise = 4). `hierarchy_issues` compares the ranks either side of a `CONTAINS` and reports `level_mismatch` when a parent is not exactly one rung above its child.

⇒ **`component` IS A HARD FLOOR.** There is no value to give a part of a component, so that containment cannot be expressed at all. Measured 2026-08-25 by hitting it — `fact:the-level-ladder-has-a-hard-floor-at-component-and-no-assembly-rung`, which is the EVIDENCE; this node is the DECISION taken because of it.

═══ WHY OPEN AND NOT ONE MORE RUNG ═══

Anthony's research gives the canonical four-tier hierarchy — System / Subsystem / **Assembly** / Component — and reflow2 is missing the third. Adding `assembly` would have fixed the case that exposed this and cost almost nothing.

⭐⭐ IT WAS DECLINED BECAUSE OF THE STRONGER POINT IN HIS OWN RESEARCH: **"atomic" SHIFTS BY DOMAIN.** In his table the atomic unit is a microprocessor chip for aerospace and a single code module for software. A ladder with fixed named rungs asserts that every domain bottoms out at the same conceptual depth, and his examples show they do not. One more enum value would move the floor down one and leave the assertion in place.

It also matches ORIGINAL intent rather than adding to it. `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (accepted, his words, 2026-08-07) already says *"this continues down further and further as the design needs... from code projects to biology projects."* The closed enum is what makes the downward half of that unsatisfiable.

═══ WHAT THIS MUST NOT INHERIT ═══

🛑 THE LADDER IS DECLARED TWICE AND NOTHING CHECKS THEY AGREE — `schema/structure.yaml` and `hierarchy.rs::Level`. `from_key` maps any unrecognised string to `Component`, so a rung added to the YAML and forgotten in Rust silently ranks 0 and every containment involving it reads as a mismatch. **A silent fallback, in a project holding `req:no-silent-fallback` at critical priority**, and the same two-places-one-truth shape the absorption found in `#[non_exhaustive]` match arms. An open ladder makes this worse if carried forward, because the rungs stop being a compile-time set at all: the ordering has to become DATA with exactly one home.

═══ WHAT IS NOT SETTLED, AND MUST NOT BE ASSUMED ═══

The decision is that the ladder is open. HOW is not decided, and these are the real questions:
- **Where do the rungs live?** Per-design nodes, a property on the Project, or a document — and what happens to a design that never declares any.
- **Do the five current names survive as a default ladder?** 93 components carry them today; whatever ships must not invalidate them or force a migration on anyone.
- **Does `hierarchy_issues` still demand exactly-one-rung steps?** With user-defined rungs, "one level at a time" is a claim about the user's ladder, not about a universal one.
- **What replaces `rank()`** now that ordering is data rather than a match arm.
- **What else keys on the enum** — `scan_nodes(level=…)`, `move_component`, the level-spine-disagreement detector, the granularity guidance.

📌 THE STOPPING RULES ARE REFERENCE, NOT MECHANISM. Anthony's four rules for how deep to go — procurement black box, LRU/maintenance, single discipline or owner, verification cost — are recorded on the evidence fact. Nothing in reflow2 says how deep is deep enough, and an open ladder makes that question sharper rather than answering it. Rule 1 lands on a known gap: nothing distinguishes a component that was BOUGHT from one that was BUILT.

⚠️ NOTHING WAS IMPLEMENTED. Decided at the end of a long session, immediately before Anthony went to bed. No code, no schema change, no branch.

KEPT DISTINCT from `fact:the-level-ladder-has-a-hard-floor-at-component-and-no-assembly-rung` after reading it: that is a dated MEASUREMENT of the floor and carries the research and the stopping rules. This is the CHOICE made in response, with the road not taken and its reasoning. Folding a decision into an observation would lose which one is evidence and which one is a commitment.
properties.name: DECIDED — the decomposition ladder becomes OPEN: a design defines its own rungs, as many as it needs, instead of choosing from five fixed names
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than as a note on the requirement, because it is a CHOICE between two named options that was actually made, and the road not taken has reasoning worth keeping: adding `assembly` was cheaper, sufficient for the case that exposed the problem, and rejected on the domain-shifting-atomicity argument rather than on cost.

ACCEPTED rather than proposed because Anthony gave it as an instruction in his own words, not as a musing.

properties.decision:
ACCEPTED by Anthony, 2026-08-17. All three parts, with part (3) settled narrowly.

(1) `DEFAULT_SCOPE_DEPTH` becomes 2. At 3 the scoped detectors do not narrow: measured over all 56 Components of reflow2's own design, each returns 50-60 of the 83 gaps (median 55) and a region of 595-903 nodes. At 2 the same sweep returns 2-27 (median 4) over regions of 267-601. See `fact:defect-a-scoped-detector-at-its-default-depth-returns-two-thirds-of-the-design`.

WHY 2 AND NOT 1, which is the part the measurement alone does not settle. The golden thread runs Requirement -> Capability -> Component -> Artifact -> Verification. From a Component its capabilities are one hop; the requirements they satisfy and the checks that verify them are two. So depth 2 is exactly one component's own thread. Depth 1 stops short of the requirements, so a team would stop being told when its own capability satisfies nothing. Depth 3 reaches the neighbours' threads, which is the program again.

(2) The docstring that justifies 3 is corrected. It argues the third hop is needed to reach 'a contained child component's capabilities' — but `scope_region` puts the whole containment closure into the seed set BEFORE taking the radius, so those capabilities are one hop from an owned node, not three. The reason given for the default is not a reason the code needs. This part needed nobody's permission and was always going to be done.

(3) `detect_gaps`' description stops claiming its region is 'the same computation claim_region uses ... so "my area" means one thing everywhere'. SETTLED AS: DELETE THE SENTENCE. The alternative — actually reconciling `scope_region` and `claimed_region` — is NOT taken here and is NOT to be bundled in: it changes what a claim covers, which is what two people believe they have each taken responsibility for. That deserves its own decision, and `scope.rs` already records it as possibly a defect in the claims layer.
properties.name: The default scope depth drops from 3 to 2, and the two definitions of "a region" stop being described as one
properties.rationale:
ACCEPTED ON ANTHONY'S WORD after a plain-English walkthrough of all three parts with a recommendation on each.

WHAT WAS REJECTED. Leaving the default at 3 and telling callers to pass a depth: the measurement says the default is what almost everyone gets, and a tool whose out-of-the-box answer is 'two thirds of the design, called your part' fails the epoch this sits in. Also rejected: making `design_regions` quietly use a different depth from the scoped detectors, which would have hidden the defect behind a second opinion instead of naming it. Also rejected, and this is part (3): reconciling the two region computations as a rider on a default change.

HIS STANDING GROUND, restated the same day and applying directly here: 'I'm more interested in doing things right. If that requires redoing work, so be it - I prefer quality. So if adding SPECIFIES is right, then we have our answer regardless of the amount of work that it includes.' The cost of a correct change is not an argument against it before 1.0. See `rule:fix-it-properly-while-it-is-still-cheap`.

COST OF HAVING DECIDED LATER, kept on the record because the standing rule asks for it: every session that scoped between the measurement and this ruling was told its part held two thirds of the design's gaps, and any judgement made on that number — 'my area is the messy one' — was made on a figure that was the same for every area.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-25, choosing to STAGE the store inversion after every blocker was measured.

**STAGE 1, DECIDED NOW:** `reflow2.json` becomes the DURABLE copy. The design is auto-exported without anybody remembering to — on session end, plus a debounce — to a path git does not track.

**STAGE 2, NOT DECIDED:** whether RocksDB is removed and `MemoryBackend` becomes the only backend. That stays open and gets decided on evidence from stage 1 running in daily use, not on prediction.

═══ WHY STAGED RATHER THAN BOTH AT ONCE ═══

⭐ **STAGE 1 IS ADDITIVE AND REVERSIBLE.** RocksDB stays while the export proves itself. If auto-export turns out to be wrong, nothing has been removed and the store is still authoritative. If it is right, stage 2 becomes a deletion of something already redundant rather than a bet.

**IT IS THE PROJECT'S OWN DISCIPLINE, ONE LEVEL UP.** `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately` exists because mixing a dependency swap into a migration gives a failure two candidate causes; `dec:the-rust-rocksdb-switch-is-parked-until-the-store-question-settles` applied the same rule to WHETHER a component exists. This applies it to the order of two decisions.

═══ THE EVIDENCE THAT MADE STAGE 1 DECIDABLE ═══

    core tests with no DB and no index          1,452 pass
    load to fully searchable, no database       1,156 ms
    save (build export doc + serialize)           265 ms
    hydrate fidelity (confirmation ledger)      208 / 208, ZERO differing fields
    resident memory, largest design in existence  ~21 MB (58 MB peak)
    session-end detection                       ALREADY BUILT
    exposure today, on a DISCIPLINED session    299 MINUTES

⭐⭐ **THE OBSERVING HALF OF THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS AND DOES NOTHING.** `impl Drop for SeatLease { fn drop(&mut self) { release_seat(&self.seat); } }` — RAII, so a client that disconnects, crashes or is killed is observed without an orderly shutdown and without any harness. That is precisely the objection that killed the Stop-hook answer: *"the guarantee cannot live in the harness, because the harness is the thing that might not come back."* `release_seat` then writes nothing. **The gap is one action on an event that already fires.**

🛑 **AND THE PATH MATTERS, MEASURED THE SAME DAY.** Auto-exporting to the COMMITTED path severs the lineage chain and turns the design gate red on every branch — reproduced, not argued (`fact:auto-export-really-does-sever-the-lineage-and-a-separate-path-dissolves-it`). The durability write and the archival write are different acts for different audiences and MUST NOT share a file. A separate gitignored path dissolves the collision entirely and leaves `dec:export-once-per-pr` exactly as written.

═══ THE TRADE BEING ACCEPTED, STATED PLAINLY ═══

RocksDB's WAL gives PER-WRITE durability. Write-temp-and-rename gives ALL-OR-NOTHING at the write cadence. At 265 ms per save and a few-seconds debounce the exposure is SECONDS — against a measured 299-minute window on the committed copy today. **This is a judgement about acceptable loss, not a measurement gap, and it is being made deliberately.**

═══ WHAT STAGE 2 STILL OWES ═══

1. **Daily-use evidence** that auto-export actually fires and the durable copy is never behind by more than the debounce.
2. **`last_synced`** — the one thing a hydrate loses. Three lines of JSON; it must endure before the store can stop being authoritative, or `req:stale-seat-knows` has no baseline after a hydrate.
3. **`CF_EMBEDDINGS`** has no field in `GraphExport`. Theoretical today (nothing outside tests writes vectors), real the moment `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` lands.
4. ⚠️ **THE MULTI-DESIGN QUESTION, WHICH IS NOT A LAPTOP QUESTION.** A server holding many designs in `MemoryBackend` holds them ALL in RAM. Irrelevant for one person; it is the whole design for a hosted tier, and eviction is not built. `dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants` is where that lives.

📌 `dec:the-rust-rocksdb-switch-is-parked-until-the-store-question-settles` STAYS PARKED and its unparking condition is unchanged: this question settling either way. Stage 1 does not settle it — stage 2 does.
properties.name: DECIDED — the export becomes the durable copy, written automatically; removing RocksDB is a SEPARATE, later decision made on evidence
properties.rationale:
Settled by the user against three recorded alternatives (decide both at once; decide only the mechanism; decline the inversion), so the roads not taken keep their reasoning.

Recorded as ONE decision with two stages rather than as two nodes, because the staging IS the decision — splitting it would lose the reason the second is deferred, which is the only interesting part. Stage 2 gets its own node when it is actually taken.

The residual risk is written into the decision rather than beside it: per-write durability is being traded for cadence-bounded durability on purpose, and a later reader must meet that trade rather than discover it.

properties.decision:
`cargo test` ABORTS EVERY REMAINING TEST BINARY the moment one fails. This workspace has ~155 of them behind a ~13-minute run, so a change carrying N independent failures cost N FULL CYCLES — fix one, wait, discover the next, wait again. `--no-fail-fast` appeared nowhere: not in AGENTS.md's gate block, not in `ci.yml`. Both now carry it, on both the workspace and core-only gates.

═══ MEASURED, ON THE CHANGE THAT FOUND IT ═══

Adding ONE detector (`quality_target_unstated`, 2026-08-25) took four suite runs. Successive runs reached **31, then 47, then 114 suites** before aborting, surfacing exactly ONE new failure each time:

  run 1  coherence_loop — a "complete design" fixture that had not said what it is for
  run 2  detect.rs ×3   — two fixtures, one over-specific assertion
  run 3  the_surface_says_what_it_already_knew — a truncation counterweight
  run 4  clean

**ALL FIVE WERE IN `reflow2-core`, AND ONE `--no-fail-fast` RUN OF THE CHEAP CORE GATE FOUND THE LAST OF THEM IN SECONDS** — 128 suites, every one executed, the single failure named. That is the same gate that, without the flag, would have stopped at the first.

⭐ THE COST IS REAL AND IT IS THE RIGHT TRADE: a RED run now takes full wall-clock instead of stopping early. But a red run is already a failure, and what anybody wants from it is every fact it holds. A GREEN run is unaffected — it was always going to execute everything.

📌 IT WAS COSTING CI THE SAME WAY, UNSEEN. Every red build was one push-and-wait round per independent failure, and nobody had measured it because each round looked like an ordinary fix.

═══ THE SECOND, SMALLER CAUSE, RECORDED BESIDE IT ═══

The session also skipped its own documented discipline: AGENTS.md says to iterate on `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` (seconds) and treat the workspace run as a PRE-PUSH gate. It went from a single new test file straight to the workspace. That turned each iteration into 13 minutes instead of 30 seconds.

🛑 BUT THAT ALONE WOULD NOT HAVE FIXED IT, WHICH IS WHY THE FLAG IS THE ROOT CAUSE AND THE DISCIPLINE IS NOT: the cheap gate fail-fasts too. Following the discipline perfectly would still have revealed one failure per run — faster rounds, the same number of them. Only the flag collapses N rounds into one.

`tools/skill_lint.py` asserts AGENTS.md's gate block and `ci.yml` match FLAG FOR FLAG, so the two cannot drift apart again without turning the build red.
properties.name: DECIDED — the build gate passes `--no-fail-fast`: a red run must yield every fact it has, not the first one
properties.rationale:
Recorded as a Decision rather than left as a commit message because the reasoning is what stops it being reverted by someone who sees a red CI run take longer and reads that as a regression. The trade is deliberate: red runs get slower, and they get complete.

Kept as one node with the discipline failure recorded BESIDE the mechanism rather than instead of it. Blaming the session's shortcut would have produced a resolution nobody can act on ("be more careful") and left the flag missing; naming the flag alone would have lost the true observation that the documented iteration loop was skipped. Both are true and only one is fixable in code.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-24 by Anthony, choosing "ask, don't block" after being walked through the finding below. This settles the HOW that `dec:idea-how-does-the-graph-learn-what-a-session-invalidated` left open with six costed options and none chosen.

═══ THE FINDING THAT REFRAMED THE QUESTION ═══

🛑 **OPTION C WAS ALREADY BUILT, AND HAD NEVER ONCE BEEN USED.** `INVALIDATES` — "the record that did the work names the finding it answered" — shipped in PR #321 on 2026-08-23 WITH its reader, deliberately, so the marker would not become a comment nobody consults. Measured 2026-08-24, one day later, with the tool served the whole time:

    INVALIDATES edges in the graph:  0

Not one, by anybody. So the open question was never "which of six mechanisms" — five of them were ways to make the SIXTH get used, and the sixth already existed.

⭐⭐ **WHY, PRECISELY.** A design's vocabulary reaches real work only with THREE LEGS — a typed TOOL, an INSTRUCTION that names it, and a COMPUTATION THAT NOTICES ITS ABSENCE. Measured:
  • TOOL — ✅ `invalidates`, served since 07:32 that day.
  • INSTRUCTION — ❌ exactly one skill mentioned it (`where-am-i`) and only the READ side. Not capture-session, not impact-check, not revise-design, not AGENTS.md.
  • ABSENCE DETECTOR — ❌ nothing anywhere.

Two of three legs missing is a complete explanation for zero uses, and it needs no theory about discipline.

═══ WHAT THIS DECIDES ═══

BUILD THE TWO MISSING LEGS. Add no seventh mechanism.
  • **The computation:** `unclaimed_findings` — given the ChangeEvent ids a session recorded, the OPEN observations their changed subjects carry that nobody has claimed.
  • **The instruction:** `capture-session` test 7 and `impact-check` step 4 name the tool and the moment.
  • **The delivery:** the Stop hook's async probe asks it and RIDES ALONG on a nudge already firing, or is carried to the next SessionStart.

═══ ASK, DON'T BLOCK — Anthony's word, and the restraint is the design ═══

The ask NEVER arms an interruption of its own. It only ever appends to a message already being sent. His reasoning as offered and accepted: a brand-new trigger keyed on a computation nobody has field-tested is exactly the thing that becomes wallpaper, and it can be upgraded once the shortlist has been seen to be right.

🛑 THE HONEST COST OF THAT CHOICE, stated rather than glossed: a Stop hook that does not block reaches the TRANSCRIPT, not the agent. The two paths that genuinely reach an agent are the ride-along and the next SessionStart. If this must reach an agent mid-session every time, blocking is the only mechanism that does.

═══ WHY A SESSION-SIZED QUESTION, AND THE NUMBER THAT DECIDED IT ═══

Option A's recorded objection was fatal and correct: 200 findings on day one is wallpaper, and a consumer abandoned reflow2 over exactly that. Scoped to the events one session wrote, measured over all 639 ChangeEvents on this design: **71% touch no open observation at all; the median when one is touched is 1.**

⚠️ AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THAT NUMBER WAS WRONG IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION — 78%, measured before the computation read `subject_id`, i.e. against the 56% of observations reachable by edge alone. Widening the reach to 97% necessarily lengthened the shortlists. Honest figures: 71% silent, median 1, mean 4.3, p90 13, max 40. **A measurement taken against a narrower implementation than the one that shipped is not evidence about the one that shipped.**

═══ WHAT IT MUST NOT BECOME ═══

🛑 IT DOES NOT REVERSE `dec:verification-freshness-not-a-gap` (accepted 2026-07-26, read before this was written). That rules a stale-looking CHECK a STANDING PROPERTY which would fire on every legitimate refactor. So: TemporalFacts only, never Verifications — a dated OBSERVATION is asserted once and re-derived by nothing — and this is deliberately NOT a gap source. It answers when asked and appears in no list that must reach zero.

═══ OPTIONS NOT TAKEN ═══
D (a "this answers X" field on `record_change`) — DECLINED. At write time nobody can know which of 270 observations they touched without searching; the computation does it afterwards for free, and the busiest write in the loop keeps its shape.
F (do nothing) — REFUTED by two sightings plus `fact:twelve-records-that-still-read-confident`.
B — kept, as the manual path, now pointed at the computation instead of at `search_design`.
properties.name: DECIDED — build the two MISSING LEGS, not a seventh mechanism: the edge already existed and had never once been drawn
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own node because it answers a different question from the brainstorm it settles: that one asked WHICH mechanism, and the measurement showed the mechanism already existed and was inert. The reframing is the part worth keeping — five of six options were ways to make the sixth get used.

⭐ THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is bigger than this feature: shipping a typed tool WITH its reader was not enough, and #321 did that carefully and on purpose. What was missing was anything that noticed the tool was never used. A vocabulary can be reachable, documented in its own node, wired to a reader, and still dead — and nothing in the loop reports a zero-use edge. That is worth checking for every edge type this design has added.

properties.decision:
`ifc:graph-read` keeps designation `internal`. It is a real modular boundary — modules are swapped, tested and measured across it — but it is NOT a contract this design offers to anyone else.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT, and it is the test to re-apply rather than the answer to re-quote: is anybody outside this project's control writing code against these five functions? Anthony, 2026-08-21: "nobody writing code against those five functions."

THE STRUCTURAL FACTS BEHIND THAT ANSWER, checked rather than assumed:
  — `reflow2-core` is not published as a crate; it is not on crates.io.
  — its only dependant is `reflow2-mcp`, by local path, inside the same workspace.
  — users receive released binaries and speak MCP. They never link the library, so they could not call `GraphRead` if they wanted to.

MODULAR IS NOT THE SAME AS PUBLISHED, and conflating them is what this decision refuses. A modular system holds many internal boundaries and publishes the few where somebody else is meant to supply the part. Publishing every boundary means nothing can change without a control board; publishing none means nobody can compete to supply anything. The graph read API is how reflow2's own analysis reads its own store — not a part a second supplier is wanted for.

WHAT PUBLISHING WOULD HAVE COST: the boundary would enter the surface reflow2 shows other designs, other projects' tooling would pair against it, and adding a sixth operation would become a breaking change to a recorded promise instead of an ordinary edit.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS — two triggers, either sufficient:
  (1) `reflow2-core` is published as a crate for others to build on.
  (2) an implementation is wanted from somebody other than this project — a different store, a hosted backend.
Neither holds today, and the designation is one call to change if one starts to.

📌 NOT SETTLED HERE: `ifc:core-api` is marked `published` and fails the same test — a Rust library API, in the same undistributed crate, covering the whole 274-function surface rather than a specified subset. That is a larger question about what this project has already committed to, and it is open.
properties.name: DECIDED — the graph read contract stays internal, because nobody outside can call it
properties.rationale:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-21, answering the deciding question directly: nobody is writing code against those five functions.

RECORDED RATHER THAN LEFT AS A DEFAULT. `internal` is what an Interface is until someone says otherwise, so the designation alone cannot distinguish "considered and declined" from "nobody ever looked" — the same two-states-look-identical problem this whole week has been about. Without this node a later reader finds a carefully specified contract sitting at the default value and cannot tell which it is.

THE HONEST HISTORY: it was set to `published` first, on the reasoning that reflow2's own tooling calls `published` the MOSA modular-system-interface distinction and Anthony's goal is modularity. That was reverted before anyone was asked, because publishing is a commitment and the tool says so plainly — and asserting a commitment on the owner's behalf is exactly what `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` forbids. The reversal was the right act; this decision is the part that was owed after it.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-25, choosing between four homes and three timings.

═══ WHERE IT LIVES: a Decision that GOVERNS ═══

"We are building for reliability, because a lost reading cannot be recovered" is a choice with a rationale that shapes other nodes — which is an ADR, not a measurement. Decisions already GOVERN, so allocation, components and seams can each point at it; `what_next` already reads accepted Decisions; and nothing new is invented.

REJECTED, with the reasons: a **Constraint** (the KPP shape) treats the primary ility as a hard limit, but the design holds exactly ONE Constraint node and this would lean the answer on the least-exercised vocabulary in the project. **DimensionAssessment** was the cheapest in vocabulary terms and is the trap: its declared meaning is a SCORE of what IS, and giving it a second meaning — a TARGET — is the overload that made `Interface.designation` ambiguous, where an unclassified boundary and a deliberately internal one became indistinguishable.

⭐ THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDED IT: an assessment says what the system IS on an axis; a target says what it is FOR. Nothing held the second. Measured the same day: **0 DimensionAssessment and 0 DimensionObservation nodes exist** — the nine-axis enum has been fully defined, attachable to any node, and never once used.

═══ WHEN IT IS ASKED: at genesis, upfront ═══

Anthony, 2026-08-08: *"if you don't ask upfront, these cost a lot in having to rework services after they've been already developed."*

🛑 AND THIS DOES NOT CONTRADICT `dec:idea-allocation-waits-for-the-last-responsible-moment`, which is the objection to answer. That decision governs when you ALLOCATE. This governs when you learn what the system is FOR. **Asking is cheap and shapes everything downstream; allocating is expensive and can still wait.** Conflating the two would either force premature structure or lose the answer that structure needs.

═══ WHY IT NEEDS A PLACE OF ITS OWN, AND THE PRECEDENT ═══

The answer must be findable by a detector, or nothing notices when genesis skips the question — the failure this project has now measured three times in one month. `Decision.no_relation_note` was added to this same node type for exactly this reason, and its schema comment states the principle: *"prose cannot be told apart from silence, so the judgement gets a place of its own."* A primary ility recorded only in prose is in the same position.

📌 WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE: whether the allocation step needs a skill of its own. It settles the FIRST STEP of one — the question that must precede any method — and leaves the method open at `dec:idea-does-the-deferred-structuring-step-need-a-skill-of-its-own`. Of the four ility branches only maintainability is runnable today (co-change, no instrumentation); performance needs coupling data almost no design declares; reliability and security have no substrate at all.
properties.name: DECIDED — what a system is FOR is recorded as a governing Decision, and asked at genesis rather than at allocation
properties.rationale:
Settled by the user against recorded alternatives, so the losing options and their reasons are kept — a later reader asking "why not DimensionAssessment, it already exists?" finds the overload argument rather than re-deriving it.

Recorded as a Decision rather than a Requirement because it is a choice about how this design records something, not a statement of what the system must do. The thing it decides — that an ility target is itself a governing Decision — is the same kind of node, which is deliberate: the mechanism and the record of choosing it are consistent.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-20, choosing between three placements that were each simulated against reflow2's real import graph before any was proposed. All three removed the cycle equally, so the choice was about what the boxes MEAN, not about correctness.

THE CHOICE: a NINTH system, sys:foundation, holding cmp:nodes, cmp:schema, cmp:graph, cmp:provenance and cmp:identity. sys:store keeps cmp:export and cmp:search. sys:vocabulary keeps cmp:flow and cmp:vocabulary.

THE TWO REJECTED OPTIONS, recorded so the reasoning is not re-run:
  · fold the kernel into sys:store - fewest moving parts, stays at eight systems, but nodes and schema ARE the vocabulary, so a system called Vocabulary would hold neither of them. A name that no longer describes its contents is the same class of defect being fixed.
  · fold the kernel into sys:vocabulary - the mirror image. The graph and store-access layer ends up under a name that describes it no better.

WHY A NEW SYSTEM IS THE HONEST ANSWER: the five modules are mutually dependent, so they ARE one layer - that is the whole finding. Neither existing name covers all five, and forcing one to is how the model became misleading in the first place. Naming the layer says the true thing; folding it into a neighbour hides a layer inside a box named for something else.

ACCEPTED COST: two systems end up with two components each. Small boxes are not a defect.
properties.name: The kernel is its own system — sys:foundation, because neither 'store' nor 'vocabulary' describes all five of the modules everything sits on
properties.rationale:
This is a change to the CARVING, not to the arithmetic, and that distinction is why it is a decision of its own rather than another correction on dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition. When that decision went from seven systems to eight it was catching up with a system that already existed; here a system is being created because the coupling says the layer exists and the model never named it.

It does not overturn dec:bl83a. That decision's principle - reflow2's own decomposition is the functional systems a design-graph tool IS, not its file tree - is what makes this move correct: a design-graph tool fundamentally IS a typed store of identified nodes, and that is one function, not two.

THE EVIDENCE, measured rather than argued: nodes is transitively depended on by 46 of 52 core modules, provenance by 44, identity by 44, schema by 43, graph by 42. See fact:the-modules-are-acyclic-but-the-declared-subsystems-are-not for the cycle this bisection produced and fact:ten-components-report-a-zero-blast-radius-the-source-contradicts for cmp:identity, which was in no system at all while 44 modules stood on it.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-13, choosing between four options put to him: SPLIT `ifc:mcp-tools` into its stdio and streamable-HTTP transports rather than add `json_rpc` to the `medium` enum.

THE PROBLEM AS IT HAD STOOD SINCE 2026-07-28. `ifc:mcp-tools` claimed `medium: REST`, which was never chosen — it was the schema default before `unspecified` replaced it (`req:seam-incompatibility`), and reflow2's own three boundaries all said REST while being a Rust library API, a document format and an MCP tool surface. The correction was blocked on a genuine vocabulary question and was RAISED FOR HIM RATHER THAN GUESSED, because inventing schema vocabulary is a design decision.

⭐ THE DIAGNOSIS THAT DISSOLVED THE QUESTION: the node's own `endpoint` field already said it — *"a stdio pipe to a launched process, OR the address given to `--http`"*. **One Interface was describing two boundaries.** They differ in more than medium: the HTTP one can be reached remotely, sit behind a gateway and terminate TLS; the stdio one can do none of those, and has no transport to secure at all.

WHAT THE SPLIT COST AND WHAT IT AVOIDED:
  · NO SCHEMA CHANGE, so no new enum value. That matters more than it looks: **enum values are not counted by the version stamp** (it counts node and edge TYPES), so adding one is a compatibility event nothing can detect — the stamp-blindness pattern this design has recorded four instances of already.
  · Existing vocabulary suffices for the half that has an answer: `cli` is exactly right for a launched process spoken to on its stdin/stdout.
  · Four live edges to consider and three `CHANGED` history edges left where they were.

🛑 IT QUARANTINES THE PROBLEM RATHER THAN SOLVING IT, AND THAT WAS SAID BEFORE HE CHOSE. `ifc:mcp-tools-http` still has NO correct enum value and stays `unspecified` rather than taking a wrong one. `medium` is a pairing-key axis where `unspecified` reads as UNKNOWN and never as agreement, **so that boundary cannot pair with anything until the vocabulary question is settled.** Adding `json_rpc` remains open and untaken.

═══ MEASURED IMMEDIATELY AFTER, AND IT VINDICATES THE CUT ═══

`seam_report` against flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api`, run on both halves:

    ifc:mcp-tools-http   agreed 3 · incompatible 1 · unstated 4
                         incompatible: transport_security  ours none / theirs tls
                         unstated:     medium              ours (none) / theirs REST

    ifc:mcp-tools        agreed 3 · incompatible 2 · unstated 3
                         incompatible: medium              ours cli / theirs REST
                         incompatible: transport_security  ours none / theirs tls

⇒ **THE SPLIT MADE THE CHECK ABLE TO TELL THE TWO APART.** The stdio boundary now says loudly, on `medium`, that it is NOT the thing flo2 means — flo2's spec reads *"MCP carried over HTTP, as reflow2 already serves with --http / --serve-shared"*. Before the split a single node would have paired with flo2 ambiguously and carried the TLS finding on the wrong boundary.

📌 AND IT SHARPENS THE OPEN TLS QUESTION. `fact:reflow2-flo2-seam-measured-2026-08-13` recorded two readings of the `transport_security` disagreement: (a) a segment artefact, flo2 terminating TLS at its own edge, or (b) a real assumption gap. On a stdio pipe (a) was arguable, because there is no transport to secure. On the HTTP boundary it is not: that really is plain HTTP with no TLS while flo2 says `tls`. **(b) is now the more likely reading**, and resolving it still needs flo2's side, which was deliberately not written to.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN: whether the `medium` enum should gain `json_rpc` at all. This decision settles only that the surface is two boundaries.
properties.name: The MCP surface is split by transport rather than given a new medium — one Interface was describing two boundaries
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own accepted Decision rather than by quietly editing the interface, because the interface's spec had carried this as an OPEN question raised for Anthony since 2026-07-28 and the record should show both that it was asked and how it was settled (`dec:reopen-supersedes`' principle).

The load-bearing point is that the question dissolved rather than being answered: the node's own `endpoint` field already described two boundaries, so the missing enum value was a symptom of a modelling error, not a vocabulary gap. Splitting needed no schema change and avoided adding an enum value that the version stamp cannot see.

It is recorded as a partial settlement on purpose. The stdio half now has a correct value (`cli`); the HTTP half has none and stays `unspecified`, which means it cannot pair on medium with anything — including flo2 — until `json_rpc` or an equivalent is decided. That cost was stated before the choice was made rather than discovered afterwards.

Measured the same minute: pairing both halves against flo2 shows the stdio boundary now incompatible on `medium` (correctly — flo2 means the HTTP one) and the HTTP boundary carrying exactly one real disagreement. The split is what let the check tell them apart.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY, 2026-08-10, answering four gaps as one: req:vocabulary-covers-information, -materiel, -personnel and -states are DEFERRED as a class.

WHY AS A CLASS. They are one question wearing four hats — does reflow2 model the other UAF domains, or is it deliberately scoped to function and structure? Answering them piecemeal would decide the scope by accident, four times, without anyone noticing they were the same decision. They came from Anthony UAF/DoDAF background (user-se-background-viewpoint-doctrine), so they are real vocabulary a systems engineer expects, not speculative additions.

DEFERRED IS NOT DECLINED. Each is a coherent requirement and none was argued down. What is missing is a PROJECT THAT NEEDS THEM: reflow2 own design has no materiel, no personnel beyond Contributor, and no behavioural state machine, so building the vocabulary now would be declaring types nothing reads — which req:functional-vocabulary-computes forbids in as many words, and which dec:idea-detect-vocabulary-that-nothing-reaches exists to detect.

THE RE-ASK TRIGGER, NAMED SO DEFERRED CANNOT DEGRADE INTO NEVER ASKED AGAIN (the shape dec:the-telemetry-kpp-question-waits-for-flo2 set): re-open when a design reflow2 is actually pointed at needs one of them. Concretely — a project with physical parts to sustain (materiel), an organisation with roles performing activities (personnel), a protocol or device with modelled behavioural states (states), or a data contract whose entities and attributes must cross an interface (information). The bluesky/NSLS-II work is the likeliest source of the last two.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS WRONG: if a consumer hits one of these and works around it in prose rather than asking, the deferral will look correct while costing exactly what it was meant to avoid. That is unobservable from inside this design, which is the honest limit of this decision.
properties.name: DEFERRED — whether reflow2 models information, materiel, personnel and state is a SCOPE question, and the re-ask trigger is named rather than left to memory

properties.decision:
FORWARD ONLY. `req:a-fix-says-whether-it-corrected-the-cause` applies to fixes recorded from 2026-08-17 on. The 472 ChangeEvents already in the graph are NOT classified as patches or corrections, and no backfill pass will be run over them.

Anthony, 2026-08-17, answering the question directly. His own framing when he asked for the requirement was already this: "I'm not sure how many fixes have been patches ... but I'd like to start now."

WHY BACKFILLING LOSES, and it is the same reason as one rule over rather than a coincidence. Nobody remembers which of 472 changes reached its cause. A backfill would therefore be an AGENT INFERRING the answer from diffs and commit prose — producing edges that are queryable and unfounded, which dev_storyflow's finding ⑮ names as strictly worse than prose that is honestly informal. The count would look like evidence and be a reconstruction.

⭐ THE PRECEDENT IS EXACT AND WAS SET BY THE SAME PERSON THREE WEEKS EARLIER. `dec:the-authority-check-guards-forward-not-backward` grandfathered 121 of 214 settled nodes for the identical reason: the unattributed ones were bookkeeping predating the rule, not violations, and backfilling would have recorded approval 121 times on evidence no agent held. Two rules, two backfill questions, the same answer both times — which is worth noting as a pattern in how this project handles a new discipline meeting an old corpus, rather than as two unrelated calls.

WHAT THIS COSTS, stated so the trade is on the record: the useful number arrives slowly. "What still rests on a patch?" will read zero on the day the field ships and stay near zero for a while, and A LOW COUNT WILL MEAN "few fixes recorded since we started" RATHER THAN "few patches" — which is precisely the vacuous-zero this epoch exists to stamp out. So the reporting side owes a statement of its own coverage from the beginning: it must say how many fixes carry the disposition at all, not only how many were patches. That is `req:a-report-says-what-it-swept-and-whether-its-checks-ran` applied to the very first thing built under the new requirement.

REJECTED ALSO, and worth naming because it was the tempting middle: flagging past changes that LOOK like repeated patching — one artifact accepted `design_holds` many times over, say. It is computable and it is a proxy, and offering a proxy beside a real measurement invites the two to be read as one thing. If it is ever built it should be a separate, separately-labelled signal, not a way of half-answering this question.
properties.name: Recording whether a fix reached the cause binds from here, and the 472 changes already on the record are not reclassified
properties.rationale: Nobody remembers which of 472 past changes reached its cause, so a backfill would be an agent's inference wearing the clothes of a record — queryable and unfounded, the failure mode this project has already named. Same answer and same reasoning as the authority check's grandfather ruling. The cost is that the useful number accrues slowly, which is why the reporting side must state its own coverage rather than let a low count read as good news.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-12, Anthony's word, on the question the registry raised the moment it existed: WHO MAY LIST WHICH DESIGNS.

⚠️ THIS IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE ONE ALREADY ANSWERED, and conflating them is the trap. `req:a-session-cannot-address-another-design` and `ver:a-session-cannot-name-another-design` settle ADDRESSING — can a session open a design it was not given? (No: refused by name, and a path is not an alternative route in.) This settles EXISTENCE — may a session learn a design is there at all? **A design can be perfectly isolated and still leak the list**, and for a hosted service the customer list is often the most sensitive thing it holds.

THE TWO CASES PULL OPPOSITE WAYS, AND BOTH ARE REAL.
- ONE OWNER, MANY PROJECTS. Anthony holds reflow2, flo2, dynograph-foundation, dev_storyflow. He WANTS a session to list them and pick, and asked for exactly that on 2026-08-05: "can a reflow2 tool be to simply return all graph_ids to the agent and the agent then can choose whichever graph_id the user specifies?" — captured inside the ACCEPTED `req:a-session-chooses-its-design`.
- MANY TENANTS, ONE SERVER. flo2's hosted case. A session working on one customer's project must not learn that another customer EXISTS.

DECIDED: **THE REGISTRY'S ROOT IS THE TENANT BOUNDARY.** `Registry::discover(root)` reads what is under that root and nothing else; `graph_ids()` stays unfiltered and lists exactly that.
