An operator serving many tenants gives each its own root. Isolation is then a property of WHAT IS THERE rather than of a check on who is asking.

WHY, and the first reason is the one that rules out the alternative on principle rather than on effort:

1. **REFLOW2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION AND IS NOT GETTING ANY.** Stated in the design and printed on the container image label: "NO AUTHENTICATION — deploy on a private network behind a gateway that authenticates." A filtered listing REQUIRES knowing who is asking, so building one means reflow2 growing an identity system it has explicitly refused. That is not a cost, it is a contradiction.
2. **IT IS FREE.** The root is already a parameter of `Registry::discover`. This is a deployment shape, not code.
3. **IT IS THE BOUNDARY THAT ALREADY WORKS.** `a_real_design_outside_the_root_is_refused_like_any_other` proves a design genuinely present elsewhere on the machine is refused IDENTICALLY to one invented. The root is already the isolation boundary; making it the tenant boundary is the same mechanism, not a new one.
4. ⭐ **IT IS ALREADY THE RECOMMENDED ANSWER TO A DIFFERENT QUESTION.** flo2's blast-radius section holds "(a) Partition. Shard graphs across several reflow2 processes so a crash loses a subset" and adds "this is why it belongs with #1 — it is a property of the registry's routing, not a layer above it", with the warning that designing them apart means designing the first one twice. **Partitioning gives tenant isolation and blast-radius containment from ONE decision.**

WHAT WAS REJECTED, and why, so nobody re-proposes it:
- A FILTERED LISTING (one registry, trimmed per caller). Rejected on (1): it needs identity reflow2 does not have and will not acquire.
- NO LISTING AT ALL (you may only attach to an id you were handed). Safe, and it breaks `req:a-session-chooses-its-design` — which is ACCEPTED and whose whole first half is discovering what exists before choosing.
- LIST EVERYTHING AND TRUST THE OPERATOR TO SCOPE IT. This is what shipped, and it is what this decision RATIFIES rather than changes — but only once the root is NAMED as the boundary. Undecided, the same code reads as an oversight; decided, it is the mechanism.

WHAT IT COSTS, honestly: a root (and likely a process) per tenant is more resource-hungry than one shared server, and it pushes "which tenant is this?" up to flo2's gateway. That is where it already belongs — flo2's own boundary list says "Authentication and authorization, entirely" is flo2's job, and its only obligation on reflow2 is that a session bound to one graph cannot address another, which is now tested.

⇒ WHAT THIS SETTLES FOR THE TRANSPORT (`cap:select-graph-by-id`, still `in_progress`): **the registry routes WITHIN a root and never across one.** A selection surface — the preferred HTTP path prefix `/g/<graph_id>/` — resolves against the root that server was given, and there is no cross-root operation to design. The security property is decided BEFORE the surface is built rather than retrofitted onto it, which is what flo2's tracker warns about: "a handler that reaches the wrong graph corrupts a design rather than erroring, so this wants property tests, not examples."

📌 NOT SETTLED HERE: whether one PROCESS may hold several roots. `dec:one-process-many-stores` (accepted, conditional) is about a process holding N stores; this is about what one REGISTRY offers. If a process ever serves two roots, the per-root boundary still holds and the routing question is separate.
properties.name: The registry ROOT is the tenant boundary — listing stays unfiltered, and reflow2 still authenticates nothing
properties.rationale: Anthony chose this over a filtered listing and over refusing to list at all, after the registry made the question live rather than theoretical. The load-bearing reason is that a filter would require reflow2 to know who is asking — an identity system the design has twice refused in writing — whereas the root is already a parameter, is already the isolation boundary the registry tests prove, and is the same partitioning that flo2's blast-radius section independently recommends. One decision covers tenant isolation and blast radius, which is what that section asked for when it said to decide them together rather than twice.

properties.decision:
PARKED ON ANTHONY'S EXPLICIT WORD, 2026-08-25: *"park the rust-rocksdb migration with its reason."* **PARKED IS NOT REJECTED.** `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately` stays `accepted`, its reasoning stays correct, and the switch stays owed if RocksDB stays.

THE REASON, IN ONE LINE: **it is an 86-file migration whose entire subject is the component that may be about to be retired.**

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THAT DECISION WAS MADE, ONE DAY EARLIER. On 2026-08-24 the switch was straightforwardly next: absorb `rocksdb` 0.24 verbatim, then swap the crate in its own PR with one variable and one revert. Nothing in that reasoning was wrong. What arrived a day later is a question that sits UNDER it — `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability`, asking whether an embedded key-value store earns its place at all. Three of that question's five blockers have since been measured away:

    load to fully searchable, no database at all      1,156 ms
    save (build export doc + serialize)                 265 ms
    confirmation-ledger claims surviving hydration    208 / 208, ZERO differing fields
    core tests passing with no store and no index         1,452

⇒ IF THAT QUESTION RESOLVES TOWARD THE DOCUMENT AS THE ENDURING ARTIFACT, `cmp:rocksdb-backend` is what gets retired — and the migration becomes work done and then deleted. Doing it first de-risks nothing; it spends the effort on the branch most likely to be cut.

⭐ THE ORDERING IS THE POINT, AND IT IS THE SAME PRINCIPLE THE PARKED DECISION ITSELF ARGUES. That decision exists because mixing a dependency swap into a migration gives a failure two candidate causes. The same discipline one level up says: do not migrate a component while its existence is an open question. **One variable at a time applies to WHETHER a thing exists, not only to how it is changed.**

🛑 THE FAILURE MODE THIS GUARDS AGAINST IS SPECIFIC AND LIKELY. The migration reads as tidy housekeeping — an unmaintained crate, a maintained replacement, and a version number that looks far behind (it is not: `rocksdb` 0.24 and `rust-rocksdb` 0.52 are different crates on independent numbering, and reading them as one series overstates the gap). AGENTS.md already warns against bumping the pin as housekeeping, but that warning explains the ~19-minute COMPILE cost, not this one. A session that reads the accepted decision and nothing else will correctly conclude the switch is owed and start it. **This node exists so that session meets the park.**

⚠️ WHAT UNPARKS IT: `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability` settling, either way.
- **RocksDB stays** → the switch is owed exactly as written, and this decision should be `superseded`.
- **RocksDB goes** → the switch is retired along with `cmp:rocksdb-backend`, and the parked decision is superseded rather than completed.

📌 A DIFFERENT PARK, NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH THIS ONE: `dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds` (redb, fjall, LMDB, SQLite) is parked on Anthony's word of 2026-08-24 — *"still parked for a time"*. That one asks WHICH embedded engine. This one asks whether to move between two wrappers of the SAME engine. The question blocking both asks whether an embedded engine is needed at all.

📌 MODELLING NOTE, recorded because the vocabulary corrected the first attempt: this was first written as a TemporalFact and REFUSED — `basis` accepts only `measured` or `forecast`, and a park is neither. It is a choice somebody made, so it is a Decision. The schema pointed at the right node type rather than accepting a wrong one.

KEPT DISTINCT, after reading both: `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately` is the decision to make the switch and it is unchanged by this — parking is a separate act, by a separate person, at a separate time, and folding it in would erase that. `cmp:rocksdb-backend` is the thing the switch would alter, not a statement about when to alter it.
properties.name: PARKED — do not start the rust-rocksdb migration until the store question settles; it is an 86-file change to the one component that may be retired
properties.rationale:
Recorded as its own Decision rather than by editing the parked one, deliberately: editing that node's text would mean re-sending the whole `decision` field and destroying its pre-image, which is the hazard `fact:the-revising-write-warning-fired-correctly-and-the-overwrite-happened-anyway` measured twice today.

Kept ACCEPTED rather than proposed because Anthony gave it in his own words as an instruction, not as a musing — asserting it would be forgery only if he had not said it.

properties.decision: Remove `default:` from `Artifact.granularity` and `Artifact.volatility` in schema/build.yaml. Nothing else: no code change, no backfill, no change to the content hash, no tolerance added to the round-trip gate.
properties.name: Artifact.granularity and .volatility declare no schema default — the safe reading is supplied by the reader, so absence stays honest
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word, 2026-08-15, choosing a FOURTH option over the three music_graph proposed in F23 — and this settles F23 and the round-trip gate's behaviour as ONE decision, which was his framing before it was anyone's analysis.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED IT: the safe reading already lives in the reader. coverage.rs:209 reads granularity with `.unwrap_or("atomic")`; drift.rs:436 reads volatility with `.unwrap_or("stable")`. Those are the only two readers. So the schema default was redundant with the code — it changed no report's verdict, and its only observable effect was to write an intent nobody expressed onto every Artifact at import. Proven by the counterweights, which are the point: the two absence cases in tests/artifact_intent.rs (`graph_with(None)`, `graph_with_granularity(None)`) passed BEFORE this change because the schema injected the value and pass AFTER it because the reader supplies it, unchanged either way.

WHY NOT THEIR THREE. (a) backfill on import and open — migrates a store once, but writes values nobody chose into every consumer store permanently, which is the exact erosion cap:defaults-are-not-serialized exists to prevent. (b) exclude default-valued properties from the content hash — their own preference, and the one route this design has already argued CANNOT work: absence would come to mean "nobody said OR somebody chose the default", the distinction lost in the act of protecting it, and it would weaken the hash for the 71 properties that legitimately keep defaults. (c) have --import print what it defaulted — leaves the gate red and the restore broken, and only makes the blocked commit self-explanatory.

⚠️ IT REVERSES A DELIBERATE KEEP, and that is the honest cost. BL-198 removed ten of 81 defaults on 2026-08-10 and KEPT these two, on the reasoning that `stable` is the safe reading. That reasoning was correct and is untouched; what is new is the measurement that the reader already holds it. The reflex being corrected is the same one BL-198 named from the other side — there it was "single-valued means informationless", wrong three times in ten; here it is "the safe reading must be stored", wrong because storing it converts a fallback into an assertion.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: nothing already written moves. reflow2's own Artifacts keep their values, so its export does not churn and its own round trip stays clean. It does not address F24 (the latent surface never re-probes after a CLI restore), which sits on the same restore path and is a separate defect.

properties.decision:
DECIDED 2026-08-24 by Anthony, in his words: "I'm leaning to the async shape option."

This settles the half `dec:idea-a-capture-session-skill-the-user-types` left open. That decision chose option A (a skill the user types) as a FIRST STEP and named option C — a hook deciding WHEN — as the destination. It decided WHO triggers capture. This decides the SHAPE of the hook that C needs, which was left open on a cost the earlier decision never measured.

═══ THE CONSTRAINT THAT FORCED THE CHOICE ═══

The shared server answers stateless MCP over the URL in `.reflow2/graph.server.json`, so the hook CAN read the graph. (The comment in `loop_nudge.py` saying it cannot — "the session's own server holds the single-writer lock" — was written before the shared server existed and is now false.) But measured live on this design: `loop_status` is 22.6s, repeatably, and `since_export: true` takes it to 37.5s. A Stop hook that blocks for 23 seconds is worse than no hook.

Two shapes were on the table:
  • A CHEAPER CALL — ask something the server answers fast (`claim_report` is 0.04s). Rejected: the cheap calls do not answer the question. Nothing under a second says what a session left uncaptured.
  • THE ASYNC SHAPE — ask at one stop, answer at a later one. CHOSEN.

═══ WHAT THIS DECIDES ═══

The Stop hook SPAWNS a detached probe and returns immediately, never waiting. The probe's answer lands in a per-session file. A LATER Stop in the same session reads it and speaks. A session stops once per TURN, not once per session, so on any session longer than a couple of turns the answer arrives while the agent is still alive and can act on it. When a session ends before its answer lands, the next SessionStart reports it instead — which is the fallback, not the design.

═══ THE TRIGGER IS A DELTA, NOT A LEVEL — and this is the load-bearing restraint ═══

The graph's standing debt on this design is 7 unsurfaced gaps and 60 structural defects, and both have stood for weeks. A nudge that fires on a LEVEL would fire on every session forever and would be a nag rather than a trigger — the fire-on-correct-work failure `ver:skill-triggers` names.

So the probe records a BASELINE at SessionStart and fires only where a later probe shows a count this session RAISED. "This session took open gaps from 7 to 10 and never put the three new ones to the user" is a fact about the session. "There are 10 open gaps" is not.

═══ WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE ═══
  • It does not amend `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session`. That requirement still says the user must never be the trigger, and this is the first mechanism that does not make him one — but the capture-session skill it complements is still typed by hand.
  • It does not make the graph able to see the transcript. The hook asks what the GRAPH says changed, never what the conversation held.
  • `since_export` is deliberately NOT in the probe: 15 extra seconds for a signal the delta already carries.
properties.name: DECIDED — the Stop hook asks the graph ASYNCHRONOUSLY: it fires the question at one stop and reports the answer at a later one
properties.rationale: Recorded as its own node rather than folded into dec:idea-a-capture-session-skill-the-user-types because the two answer different questions: that one settles WHO triggers capture (the user, as a first step), this settles HOW the hook half can ask at all. The cost measurement is the whole argument and would otherwise be lost — the obvious reading, "a hook cannot read the graph", was true when the comment was written and is false now, while the real obstacle is 22.6 seconds, a different problem with a different answer. A later session that rediscovers the HTTP mechanism and concludes the hook can simply call loop_status will ship a 23-second block.

properties.decision: Where fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server and fact:correction-stranded-server-is-recoverable-without-a-reconnect disagree, THE CORRECTION STANDS: a session stranded by the deleted-inode spawn failure IS recoverable in place, by starting a replacement daemon by hand from the on-disk path. The original node's remaining claims — the spawn failure itself, its cause in current_exe() resolving a deleted inode, and its misleading 'check the server log' advice — are unaffected and still hold.
properties.name: The recoverability clause is withdrawn; the rest of the stranded-server defect stands
properties.rationale: Recorded because detect_defects reported the CONTRADICTS edge as an unresolved contradiction, and it was right to: two facts about the same failure disagreed, and nothing said which a reader should act on. Left alone, the next stranded session finds both and has no way to choose — which is worse than either claim alone, because the expensive answer ('unrecoverable, restart the session') is the one written with more authority. WHY THE CORRECTION WINS ON EVIDENCE RATHER THAN ON RECENCY: it was established by execution on 2026-08-08 — the failure was hit, the recovery run, and a dozen subsequent tool calls succeeded in the same session with no reconnect. The original clause was inherited from a session handoff and reasoned from the spawn path, never tested; the node's own evidence field says the diagnosis was 'recorded ... as worth filing and still unfiled'. A measured claim beats a reasoned one about the same mechanism. THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES BOTH NODES TRUE ONCE THIS IS APPLIED: the dead inode blocks the client from CREATING a daemon, not from FINDING one. Attaching is a separate act, and any daemon started by any means satisfies the lookup. So the original is right about spawn and wrong about the session. NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: the original node's statement is left intact rather than edited. Its wrong clause is now answered on the record instead of erased, which keeps visible that reflow2's own graph carried a confident untested claim for a day — the same failure class the design keeps finding elsewhere, and worth being able to point at.

properties.decision:
ASKED AND DEFERRED, 2026-08-09. Anthony was put the consequence question for `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content`: if flo2 ran at 1,000 users and one telemetry payload turned out to have carried a customer's node id or search query, would that sink the effort or would he fix it and move on? HIS ANSWER: **too early to say — flo2 isn't real yet.**

THAT IS A TRUE ANSWER AND IT IS RECORDED AS ONE. The requirement stands exactly as captured, at `proposed`, unpromoted and undowngraded. What is deferred is only whether it is INVIOLABLE — a KPP, ranked above every ordinary gap and owing a binding to the parts that could spend it.

WHY IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SIMPLY NOT ACTED ON: the kpp-proposal skill's own instruction is to write down a non-yes, because the same signals will otherwise make the next session ask again, and *being asked the same question twice is how someone learns the tool is not listening*. This node is that record.

⭐ THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS AND A DECLINE, which is the reason it is worth its own node: a DECLINE means the need is tradeable and the question is closed. A DEFERRAL means the question is LIVE and currently unanswerable — criticality is a claim about consequence, and the consequences here (customer trust, an accusation, a contract) do not exist yet because the customers do not. Nobody can honestly rate the severity of a breach against users who are hypothetical.

=== THE TRIGGER, NAMED SO IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON ANYBODY REMEMBERING ===

RE-ASK WHEN ANY OF THESE IS TRUE:
- flo2 has real users who are not Anthony or Alex — the first outside tenant is the moment the consequence becomes real.
- flo2 acquires a stated privacy posture, terms of service, or any promise made to a user about their data. A promise made externally is a commitment the design should already be holding.
- Anyone begins BUILDING the telemetry emitter. The threshold has to exist before the thing that could breach it, or the binding is retrofitted onto a shipped surface.

⚠️ AND THE ORDER MATTERS: `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` is buildable NOW and does not wait for this. The structural guarantee it asks for — a payload schema whose every field is enum-valued or numeric, hence structurally incapable of carrying a design — is the right shape whether or not the threshold is ever declared inviolable. Deferring the KPP question must not be read as deferring the requirement.

📌 WHAT IS ALSO NOT DEFERRED, because it is decidable today and independently: usage counts may justify OPTIMISING a hot tool and may NOT, alone, justify CUTTING a cold one. `dec:bl-155` already measured that reflow2 cannot tell \"unused\" from \"unreachable\", and a removal decided on counts would delete exactly the capabilities that were never surfaced.
properties.name: DEFERRED — whether a telemetry content leak is inviolable cannot be answered until flo2 has real users, and the trigger is named rather than left to memory
properties.rationale: Recorded per the kpp-proposal skill, which requires writing down a non-yes so the question is not re-litigated — but recorded as a DEFERRAL rather than the decline the skill's step 6 describes, because Anthony's answer was that the question is unanswerable yet rather than that the need is tradeable. The named trigger is the part that does the work: without it, \"too early\" degrades into \"never asked again\", which is the failure mode a decline at least records honestly.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-25, ruling on twelve of the thirty-three leaf parts `unallocated_component` reported as holding no function.

═══ WHAT THEY ARE ═══

`sub:tool-surface` holds twelve slices — ask, assure, built, capture, claims, coherence, exchange, ingest, operate, query, skills, temporal. Each is one file under `crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/`, and each EXPOSES over MCP a family of functions that core modules implement. `tools/temporal_tools.rs` realizes four capabilities and all four are allocated to `cmp:temporal`; `tools/skills_tools.rs` realizes two and both are allocated to `cmp:skills`.

═══ THE RULING ═══

**A slice's function is the capability it exposes, and that capability belongs to the module that implements it.** These twelve are therefore correctly empty: the design says what they are for by saying what they carry, not by giving each one a function of its own.

Two alternatives were put and declined:

① **Give each slice its own capability** — twelve nodes of the form "expose the temporal tool family over MCP". Declined as over-modelling: it describes plumbing rather than product behaviour, and inflates the capability count by 6% with nothing a reader would act on.

② **Allocate the exposed capability to the slice as well as the implementer** — closes the finding with no new nodes, and was declined for the reason that matters most here: it would deliberately fuse the surface with the subject. `dec:the-two-oversized-subsystems-are-split-functionally` separated Finding from Telling precisely so a part that finds a problem is not the part that decides how loudly to report it, and `dec:reflow2-is-built-for-observability` is why. Allocating an implementer's function to its own surface undoes that cut one edge at a time.

═══ THE COST, STATED ═══

⚠️ **This ruling did not, on its own, make the finding go quiet.** `detect_unallocated_components` did not consult a parking ruling when this was written, though `unsatisfied_requirement` and `unreviewed_ideas` both did — so twelve deliberately-empty parts kept reporting as defects. That inconsistency was fixed in the same session rather than worked around, per the standing rule that a mistake is corrected at its cause.
properties.name: DECIDED — the twelve tool-surface slices are surface, not implementer: they hold no function of their own
properties.rationale:
Recorded as one decision covering all twelve because they share their method and their justification exactly — one surface, cut once by lifecycle phase, every slice standing in the same relation to the modules behind it. Twelve nodes would duplicate the reasoning and let one drift.

The alternatives are written into the decision rather than discarded because a later reader running span-of-control or allocation checks over `sub:tool-surface` will find twelve empty boxes and needs to meet the reason rather than re-derive it — the same argument that kept the tool surface at twelve members instead of splitting it to reach seven.

properties.decision:
Anthony's word, 2026-08-27, asked and answered.

📌 KEPT SEPARATE FROM THE TWO NEAR-MATCHES, DELIBERATELY. `dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition` rules on WHICH functional systems exist — the carving — and has been amended four times as that enumeration moved. This rules on HOW DEEP each branch goes, which is a different question with a different answer, and folding it in would give that node two questions and let it be half-answered. `dec:idea-a-nested-part-has-an-address-not-only-a-parent` asks how a nested part is NAMED; this says nothing about naming. GOVERNED_BY points at bl83a because the carving shapes this, not because they are the same ruling.

═══ WHAT IS UNEVEN, measured 2026-08-27 ═══

Directly under the project sit three different depths:

    2 SYSTEMS      sys:agent-surface, sys:coherence-loop — each contains 5 SUBSYSTEMS,
                   which then contain components. Three tiers.
    8 SUBSYSTEMS   sys:foundation (10 children), sys:time-history (7), sys:intake (4),
                   sys:human-channel (2), sys:store (2), sys:vocabulary (2),
                   sys:documentation (1), cmp:packaging (0) — components directly.
                   Two tiers.
    3 COMPONENTS   cmp:degraded, cmp:nudge, cmp:sync — no tier at all, sitting as
                   peers of a system.

═══ THE RULING ═══

**A branch gets a rung when it HAS one, not so the diagram looks tidy.** Agent-surface and the coherence loop genuinely decompose twice; the rest are flat groupings of modules. Manufacturing an intermediate tier for the other seven so the top row matched would model structure the code does not have — the modelling fiction `dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition` exists to prevent, arriving from the opposite direction. That decision said the systems are FUNCTIONAL rather than the file tree; this says the DEPTH is functional too.

📌 THE LEVEL LABELS ARE CORRECT AND WERE ALMOST "FIXED". Seven nodes carry a `sys:` id prefix while being labelled `subsystem`, which reads as an inconsistency and is not one: every parent here sits exactly one rung above its children, and `hierarchy_issues` returns ZERO. This session recommended relabelling all seven before checking their containment; the check showed the labels already right, so the edit would have INTRODUCED the error it believed it was removing. bl83a already records the same point about `cmp:packaging`'s prefix — ids are cosmetic, `level` is what the computation reads, and reflow2 has no rename operation worth the loss of snapshot history.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT THIS RULING EXPLAINS, AND IT IS THE REASON TO HAVE IT ═══

`detect_defects` reports `coupling_by_level` as: component 85 of 85 pairs coupled, subsystem 8, **system 0 pairs across 2 components**, part 0 across 2. Its own `coverage_note` states the consequence outright — every topology result at that level (cycles, severability, single points of failure) is **SILENT about that tier rather than clean about it**.

**That silence is this shape, not a defect.** Only two branches are deep enough for a system-level topology question to mean anything, so there is next to nothing at that level to have a cycle or an articulation point. A reader meeting a clean system-level result should read it as "there was almost nothing here to check", and this node is where that is written down — on the DESIGN side, so it is found by someone reading the design rather than only by someone reading the tool's own caveat.

🛑 IT LICENSES NOTHING ABOUT THE FUTURE. If a branch grows real internal structure it should gain a rung then; this rules on the shape as measured, not on a policy of staying shallow. And it PARKS NOTHING: no detector goes quiet, no finding is suppressed, every count stands.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT COVER ═══

Four oddities were found in the same pass and were NOT ruled on, because the option chosen was to change no structure. They stay visible and unblessed:

- `cmp:packaging` is labelled `subsystem` and contains nothing — a rung with nothing under it. (bl83a records why it was promoted: four capabilities, three realized, something that shipped. Whether a childless subsystem is the right shape for that is still open.)
- `cmp:degraded`, `cmp:nudge`, `cmp:sync` are bare components sitting as peers of a system directly under the project.
properties.name: DECIDED — the top tier is deliberately uneven: a branch earns a rung by having real internal structure, never for symmetry
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the unevenness looks like debt and is not, and because that misreading nearly cost a real edit this same session: relabelling seven nodes was recommended from a surface reading of their ids, and checking the containment showed the labels were already correct. Writing the ruling down is what stops the same wrong conclusion being reached again from the same surface.

The second reason is the more useful one. The system-tier topology results are computed over 2 components and 0 coupled pairs, so they are silent rather than clean — and a detector reporting nothing because it had nothing to examine reads exactly like one that ran clean. `detect_defects` already says so in its `coverage_note`; this is the design-side half, so the explanation sits where a reader of the design meets the silence.

Scoped to what was asked: no structure changed, and the four oddities found in the same pass are named as explicitly out of scope rather than quietly swept in by a ruling that did not consider them.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS A REFRAME PLUS A MEASUREMENT, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-04, stating the root question that unifies the dev_storyflow corpus and the reflow2-dogfooding threads: "how do we transition documents to graph entities? whether that is a huge corpus of documents in dev_storyflow or getting away from using documents in reflow2, it is how do we make decisions based on graph content, not documents." Nothing here is settled.

THE SPLIT. (IN) documents become graph entities — ingest_step, provenance Fragments, the content store, cross-document convergence. Partly built, and every remaining piece is scheduled across epoch:v0240-planned..v0280-planned. (OUT) a person or agent DECIDES from graph content instead of from a document. Almost nothing is scheduled. The whole increment plan is capture, detection, seams and write-surface.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, AND ALL OF IT IS FIRST-HAND FROM ONE SESSION ON 2026-08-04 RATHER THAN RECALLED. `reviewed_gaps` returned 130,922 CHARACTERS and could not be read at all — it was written to a file and queried with `jq`. That is the tool answering "what have we already decided to accept", which is a decision-making read, and it was unusable AS a read. It joins: `loop_status` at 72,886 characters until [BL-205] fixed it the day before, and it is the call the SessionStart hook and the server instructions both call "the one cheap call"; `describe_schema` on ONE node type at ~30 KB ([BL-142]); and `scan_nodes` on 241 Decisions, where the where-am-i skill's own guidance forced reading names only and confessing that exactly one had been read in full. Add the standing limit: 52 properties are `fulltext: true` and `Decision.rationale` is not one of them.

THEY ARE ALL ONE DEFECT: A READ THAT RETURNS EVERYTHING IT KNOWS INSTEAD OF WHAT WAS ASKED. The graph holds the content correctly. It cannot serve it back at the size it now holds. That is neither a vocabulary problem nor an ingest problem, which is why every framing so far has missed it — `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` reasoned about what a node can HOLD, and the binding constraint is what a read can RETURN.

THE CONSEQUENCE THAT SHOULD NOT BE SOFTENED: TODAY A DOCUMENT BEATS THE GRAPH FOR MAKING A DECISION, AND IT IS A FAIR FIGHT THE GRAPH LOSES. A document can be skimmed, searched with ctrl-F, and read end to end. The graph offers 130 KB or a list of names. Reaching for the markdown is therefore RATIONAL BEHAVIOUR RESPONDING TO A REAL DIFFERENCE, not a bad habit to be disciplined out of, and no improvement to capture changes it.

THE SHAPE OF AN ANSWER, offered because the in-house precedent is already built and shipped rather than as advocacy: the transition is not documents → graph, it is DOCUMENTS → GRAPH → DERIVED DOCUMENTS. `cap:changelog-view` ("a changelog is a derivable view of the graph's own delta") shipped in v0.20.0 and CHANGELOG.md is generated today; `dec:views-are-projections` is accepted; `tools/render_views.py` is 44 KB of renderer producing docs/viewpoints.md and has existed since 2026-07-19. The renderer, the doctrine and the proof all exist — the backlog simply is not one of its views. This also explains why option (d) on `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` kept losing: it was judged as a RIVAL to the capture options when it is the OUT half of the same answer, and that node already half-saw it ("solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing").

⭐ THE TEST THIS YIELDS, AND IT IS ANTHONY'S OWN DELETION INSTINCT MADE SAFE. He asked: "should I delete the documents and force us to use the reflow2 graph?" Deletion is the right TEST and the wrong COMMITMENT. The test is: CAN YOU DELETE THIS DOCUMENT AND REGENERATE IT FROM THE GRAPH? Yes → the graph is the source and the document was a view. No → the document is still the source, and WHAT CANNOT BE REGENERATED IS PRECISELY WHAT THE GRAPH IS MISSING. Run it per document, never on the repo at once, and regenerate BEFORE deleting so nothing is ever at risk. Where each stands today, assessed 2026-08-04: CHANGELOG.md PASSES (already derived); docs/viewpoints.md PASSES; COORD.md's in-progress table passes the day `claim_region` is used for real, because the computation exists and is served (`dec:coord-board-in-graph`); docs/backlog.md FAILS, and the rows that cannot regenerate are the exact statement of what vocabulary is absent; AGENTS.md FAILS PERMANENTLY AND CORRECTLY, because an agent reads it before it knows reflow2 exists. That last row is why this is not a march toward zero documents — it is a march toward zero documents that are SOURCES, and the test says which is which instead of leaving it to taste.

FOR A CORPUS THE TEST POINTS THE OTHER WAY. Source documents cannot be regenerated and must not be — `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` says so. The test applies instead to the READING: after ingest, can "what did I want to build, and what of it exists" be answered without opening a document? A no means the ingest landed prose rather than structure, which is exactly what the 52-fulltext-properties limit predicts for rows imported as long descriptions.

WHAT IS NOT DECIDED HERE. Whether the OUT half is a v0.24.0 obligation, its own increment, or a discipline applied to every read as it is touched. Which reads to fix first, and by what rule — `reviewed_gaps` is the loudest but `scan_nodes` on a mature type may be the most consequential. Whether "answer-shaped rather than type-shaped" needs new tools or bounded forms of the existing ones. And whether the backlog renderer is a `render_views.py` view, a served tool, or neither.

--- COUNTED 2026-08-04, SAME SESSION. The item left unverified above is now closed, and it answers the bug-list-or-increment question against the cheaper reading. ---

⭐ OF 33 COLLECTION-RETURNING READ TOOLS ON THE SERVED SURFACE, EXACTLY THREE LET THE CALLER BOUND THE RESULT, AND ONLY ONE CAN PAGE. Counted over `crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/*.rs` (144 tool functions across 12 modules). The 33 are: alternatives_for, budget_report, changelog_view, claim_report, confirmation_ledger, content_manifest, coverage_report, describe_schema, detect_defects, detect_gaps, dimension_drifts, evidence_report, export_graph, export_surface, find_tools, flow_report, granularity_report, graph_report, graph_report_markdown, hierarchy_issues, ility_report, loop_status, maturity_report, open_questions, readiness_report, recall_resolutions, release_report, reviewed_defects, reviewed_gaps, scan_nodes, seam_report, search_design, surprising_connections. The three bounded: `scan_nodes` (limit + offset + next_offset + capped_by — the only real paging), `search_design` (limit, no offset), `find_tools` (limit with a default). The only other `limit` in the tool surface is `Constraint.limit`, a domain property, not a bound.

SO IT IS AN INCREMENT, NOT A BUG LIST — the guess of "four" was low by an order of magnitude. TWO HONEST QUALIFIERS THAT KEEP THE NUMBER FROM BEING OVERSTATED. (i) Not all 30 are broken today: several bound themselves internally rather than by parameter — `loop_status` became a digest under [BL-205], and `graph_report_markdown` is a summary by construction. The claim is that the CALLER cannot bound them, not that all thirty are unreadable now. (ii) Because none of them share a paging mechanism, each fix is bespoke. That is the real cost, and it is the argument for treating this as one increment with a common shape rather than as thirty separate rows — which is exactly how [BL-205] was filed and fixed, alone, one tool at a time, three days ago.

THE SHAPE THIS SUGGESTS, not chosen: `scan_nodes` already solved this problem completely — `total` against `returned`, `omitted`, `next_offset`, `capped_by`, and a payload budget so a cap is never silent but never a surprise. It is an in-house pattern, tested, and adopted by exactly one tool. Generalising it is a smaller design question than inventing one.
properties.name: OPEN — "documents to graph entities" is TWO problems, and the failing one is reading the graph back, not getting content into it
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the measurement is perishable in the exact way this project keeps rediscovering: "reviewed_gaps returned 130,922 characters" becomes "reads felt big once" within a session or two, and then the next reader re-derives it or, worse, does not. The numbers are first-hand from a single sitting and are written down so the next session argues from them.

Kept as its own node rather than appended to `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` because it CONTRADICTS that node's framing rather than extending it. That node asks what a node and an edge can hold and concludes the answer turns on how much of a row becomes structure; this one says the binding constraint is downstream of that entirely — a perfectly structured graph nobody can read back is still a graph nobody decides from. Folding the correction into the node it corrects would hide it.

Deliberately does NOT register alternatives, so this stays a question rather than becoming a fork the loop asks Anthony to choose between.

AMENDED the same session: the item this node named as unchecked was checked, and the answer (3 of 33, one pager) moved it from a bug list to an increment. Recorded as an amendment with the prior state snapshotted rather than as a fresh node, because the unchecked and checked forms are the same claim at two confidence levels — and the fact that naming the hole is what got it filled within the hour is worth the record.

properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-25, accepting a proposed functional grouping put to him with alternatives. **Applied the same day.**

    BEFORE   95 components   depth {1:13, 2:80, 3:2}   span>7: 3  (coherence-loop 28, agent-surface 25, foundation 10)
    AFTER   105 components   depth {1:13, 2:37, 3:55}  span>7: 2  (tool-surface 12 deliberate, foundation 10 out of scope)
             hierarchy_issues 0        multiple_parents 0

⚠️ **THIS PARTIALLY SUPERSEDES `fact:adopt-recovers-depth-cleanly-and-cannot-recover-the-functional-carving`**, which the duplicate guard surfaced and which is the measurement that motivated this work. Its headline reads *"the hand-built functional design violates span of control in 4 places"* — that was true when written this morning (coherence-loop 28, agent-surface 25, reflow2 13, foundation 10) and is **now 2**, of which one is deliberate and one out of scope. **Everything else in that fact still stands**, including its central finding that adopt cannot recover the functional carving, which is exactly why this split was done by hand.

═══ sys:coherence-loop, 28 → 5 ═══

    Finding              7   detect heal hierarchy surprises granularity consumption coverage
    Telling              6   report ility maturity dimensions regions scope
    Evidence             6   verify artifact confirm drift fielded operate
    Change and structure 6   propagate budget structure allocate relate claims
    Across designs       3   compose depends seam

⭐⭐ **SEPARATING FINDING FROM TELLING IS THE OBSERVABILITY CUT, and it is why this grouping and not another.** `dec:reflow2-is-built-for-observability` (accepted hours earlier) says this design is built so its answers never misrepresent what it knows. Observability-driven allocation wants THE INSTRUMENT SEPARATED FROM THE SUBJECT — a part that finds a problem must not be the part that decides how loudly to report it. Fusing detection and reporting is how a green gate over uncovered ground gets built without anybody choosing to. **The quality target was not decoration; it picked the cut.**

Evidence is separate from both because Finding and Telling reason ABOUT THE DESIGN while Evidence reasons about THE WORLD THE DESIGN DESCRIBES — the boundary where as-designed and as-built are allowed to disagree.

═══ sys:agent-surface, 25 → 5 ═══

    Tool surface         12   the twelve tools-* slices
    Serving and transport 6   service main mcp-http proxy shared registry
    Session posture       3   latent sync-debt discover
    Surface shaping       3   dto bulk skills
    Install               1   init

🛑 **THE TOOL SURFACE STAYS AT 12, OVER THE BAND, ON HIS EXPLICIT WORD:** *"leave it at 12 — don't invent a rung."* Those slices are already a partition of ONE surface, cut once by lifecycle phase. Splitting them to reach seven would use span of control as a GENERATOR — the error the open-ladder decision and the whole depth-is-a-consequence argument forbid. **The band said 25 was wrong. It does not say 12 is.**

📌 **AND `Install` IS A SUBSYSTEM OF ONE, KEPT THAT WAY.** It is the only part that writes into a repository that is not reflow2's own; folding it into a bigger box to avoid a group of one would hide the single place where the blast radius leaves this project. Group size is a check on whether a grouping is doing work, never a quota to fill.

═══ HOW THE RUNG WAS MADE, and the alternative rejected ═══

The declared ladder is `part ▸ component ▸ subsystem ▸ system ▸ …` and there is no rung between `subsystem` and `component`. Two ways to make room: DEMOTE the 53 modules to `part`, or PROMOTE the two containers to `system`. **Promotion, because it preserves what every existing node means** — the modules stay components — and changes 2 levels instead of 53.

⚠️ THE COST, STATED: the top tier is now MIXED — 8 subsystems and 2 systems under the Project. That asymmetry is honest rather than accidental: these two really are bigger, holding 84 and 49 of 211 capabilities between them.

🛑 **WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY IS NOT: the module hierarchy adopt recovered.** That trial's top tier was `cmp:crate-reflow2-core` and `cmp:crate-reflow2-mcp` — CRATES. Applying it would have replaced a functional carving with a structural one and overturned `dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition`. A functional over-span wants a functional answer; the module view stays evidence, never a replacement spine. (The scratch graph is gone in any case — the only stores left on disk are from 2026-08-20 and hold the flat pre-nesting version.)

📌 STILL OPEN, surfaced by this split rather than created by it: `cmp:claims` (coordination of parallel work) and `cmp:operate` (deploy/environments) may not belong in the coherence loop at all. Both were placed rather than resolved, and the discomfort is written on `sub:change-and-structure`. `sys:foundation` at 10 children was out of scope and is still over the band.
properties.name: DECIDED — coherence-loop and agent-surface each gain a functional rung; the tool surface stays at 12 rather than inventing one
properties.rationale:
Settled by the user against recorded alternatives on both questions — a broader three-group split and a member-by-member walkthrough for the first, a phase-split of the tool slices and a defer-agent-surface option for the second.

DISTINCT FROM the adopt trial fact the guard surfaced, and the line is clean: that node MEASURED that depth is recoverable from the artifact and that the functional carving is not. This is the DECISION about what the functional rung actually is — which had to be made by hand precisely because that measurement said inspection could not produce it. The fact motivated this; it does not contain it.

Recorded as one decision covering both splits because they share their method and justification: the same ladder problem, the same promotion choice, and the same rule that span of control checks a grouping rather than generating one. Two nodes would duplicate the reasoning and let one drift.

The two groups that break the band — tool surface at 12 and Install at 1 — are argued IN the decision rather than apologised for, because a later reader running span of control will find them and needs to meet the reason rather than re-derive it.

properties.decision:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-20: "Exempt it — but only the half that deserves exemption, and put the reason on the record rather than leaving it looking like an unfixed defect."

THE APPARENT DEFECT: sys:foundation holds five modules and ALL FIVE are reached from outside it. Every other subsystem that presents anything presents a narrow face — sys:time-history exposes 1 of 5, sys:store 1 of 2. Read as a ratio, the foundation looks like the one subsystem that failed to encapsulate.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT ACTUALLY SHOWS, and it is why the ratio misleads. Reach is NOT uniform across those five:

    nodes        6 subsystems reach it
    graph        5
    identity     2
    schema       1
    provenance   1

Three of the five are already narrow. Only `nodes` and `graph` are broadly shared, and they are shared for DIFFERENT REASONS:

  · `nodes` and `schema` are VOCABULARY. They define what a node type and an edge type ARE. You cannot put an interface in front of the alphabet — every part of the design needs the words themselves, and a facade over them would be indirection that buys nothing. Nobody wraps SI units in an API.
  · `graph` is BEHAVIOUR — how the store is reached. That one genuinely can state a contract, and it does: ifc:core-api, provided by cmp:graph since before this decision and now also by sys:foundation at the subsystem level.

THE RULING: a wide face on the vocabulary half of the foundation is CORRECT and is not to be reported, argued about, or 'fixed' by a later session. The behavioural half already has its contract.

WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT, which is the part Anthony asked for specifically: an unexplained asymmetry in a design is re-examined and re-argued by every session that meets it. Recording the reasoning costs one node and ends that loop. It is the same discipline as `ruling: parks` — a deliberate state that would otherwise read as a defect, said out loud with its reason attached.

WHAT WAS REJECTED: forcing a narrow facade over `nodes` so the foundation would look symmetrical with its siblings. That is over-engineering in the exact sense Anthony names — adding a layer because the model looks asymmetric, not because anything is wrong. A design-graph tool IS a typed store of identified nodes; its vocabulary being universally reachable is what that sentence means in code.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT EXEMPT: the blast radius is unchanged and still real. `nodes` is transitively depended on by 46 of 52 core modules. This ruling says a wide FACE is correct there; it does not say a change to `nodes` is cheap, and nothing here should be read as licence to treat the foundation as low-risk.
properties.name: The vocabulary half of sys:foundation is deliberately open — a wide face there is correct, not an unfixed defect
properties.rationale: Recorded under req:recursive-black-box-decomposition, which asks that every element be a black box with inner function and an interface. A foundation layer is the one place where that framing needs a stated exception rather than a stated interface: the vocabulary is not a service some parts call, it is the shared language all of them are written in. Making that explicit is what stops the requirement being read as unsatisfied forever at exactly one node.

properties.decision: Every capability is designed as a check one party places on another; none does another's job.
properties.name: The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides
properties.rationale: The parties are not interchangeable: the LLM cannot be trusted with arithmetic, memory or its own confidence; the graph cannot judge meaning; the human cannot remember everything or notice slow drift. The deterministic core computes, the graph carries claims and their audit trail, questions route judgment to the human. docs/partnership.md maps each known LLM failure mode to its mechanism. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam).

properties.decision: set_artifact_checksum requires a disposition: design_holds (a dated claim) or design_updated (naming the design-side ChangeEvent, linked to the artifact).
properties.name: Silent drift-accept does not exist
properties.rationale: 'Accept the file, leave the design alone, say nothing' is how a design erodes into fiction over N legitimate fix cycles while reporting zero gaps — the failure that sank the original reflow. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: erosion trials, BL-33.

properties.decision: DECIDED on Anthony's word, 2026-07-26: "go with freshness fact on the confirmation ledger (always visible, never nagging)". The alternative was a gap source — asked once through gap_to_prompt, acknowledgeable, and appearing in detect_gaps until answered. Rejected for the reason the ledger's own module doc already gives about signals: a stale-looking check is a STANDING PROPERTY of a claim rather than an event, it would fire on every legitimate refactor as readily as on a real hole, and an open list that can never reach zero gets skimmed — which is precisely the failure the gap workflow exists to prevent (the BL-23 lesson: when a detector punishes correct work, the answer is a different question, not a tuned threshold). As a ledger fact it is visible every time somebody asks how a claim stands, and it nags nobody.
properties.name: A check older than its code is a freshness FACT, not a gap
properties.rationale: Prompted by a real miss the same day. cap:degraded-surface was `verified` with a passing check, and that check drove stdio only; adding the HTTP transport widened what "the server explains its own absence" had to mean, without widening anything that tested it. reflow2 reported zero gaps throughout, and it was right to — nothing it knew was false. But it HAD the evidence: art:main drifted twice (chg:shared-sessions, chg:remote-sessions) while art:test-degraded-server never moved, and Verification.last_run_at is written by verify.rs and read by nothing anywhere in the core. Same shape this project keeps finding — a field declared, written, and consulted by no computation (the temporal axis before BL-70, the whole inviolable-intent vocabulary before BL-96): the higher-yield question is what the core already does that nothing can reach. Deliberately NOT the wider question of measuring what a check actually covers, which is unknowable from the graph and belongs to BL-95.

properties.decision: Renderers may only emit what the graph states; everything else is confessed as a finding.
properties.name: A view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects
properties.rationale: UAF/DoDAF doctrine from the author: the graph stores all design detail, the agent only renders viewpoints. If rendering requires extrapolation, something is missing inside reflow2 — almost always. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); render_views.py, BL-40.

properties.decision:
Anthony's rule, 2026-07-31, drawing the line the content store needs and nothing had yet stated.

THE TEST, in his words: "the actual implemented design of something or its artifacts" stays NATIVE IN THE REPO. Everything that INFLUENCED the design without being its output goes in the CONTENT STORE.

  NATIVE IN THE REPO — the codebase reflow2 helps build, and anything that gets compiled, tested, shipped or read by a consumer. It is versioned, diffed and reviewed as code always has been; reflow2 changes nothing about it. A README or an ADR that ships WITH the product also stays native, because it is a product-facing artefact rather than an input — the rule is about role, not about whether something is prose.

  IN THE CONTENT STORE — a markdown file a user wrote describing a design aspect, a corpus of decision notes, a whiteboard photograph, a session transcript, a diagram an agent drew to explain a choice. These informed what got built and are not themselves the thing built.

THE EVIDENCE, AND IT IS WHY REFLOW2 EXISTS. storyflow began as one repo holding the codebase AND every markdown file recording Anthony's design decisions — now 900+ documents. Two costs, and the second is the one that matters:

  (1) NAVIGATION. The repo was a mess: design notes and source interleaved, and neither easy to move through.

  (2) RETRIEVAL, which is the deeper failure. In his words: "whenever I started implementing design, I had to remember where in those 900+ design documents something actually was" — they were not all in one folder, not consistently labelled, not structured so you could work out where anything lived. And worse: "some of my design choices were spread across multiple documents", so even finding the right document was not finding the answer.

  THE WORKAROUND TAKEN: a two-repo split — `storyflow` for the codebase, `dev_storyflow` for the design corpus (979 notes as of the 2026-07-20 adopt trial). It works, and it fixes exactly ONE of the two problems.

WHY THAT MAKES IT THE MOTIVATING CASE RATHER THAN THE SOLUTION. Separating the documents cures the mess and does NOTHING for retrieval. You still have to remember where a decision lives; a choice spread across five documents is still spread across five documents, now in a tidier folder. reflow2's claim is that the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced. The content store is therefore NOT a neater `dev_storyflow`: the document goes to the store, what it SAID becomes nodes, and asking "where was this decided" becomes a query rather than an act of memory.

AND IT IS WHY CROSS-DOCUMENT IDENTITY IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN A NICETY. "Spread across multiple documents" is precisely the case `req:corpus-ingest` was written for — the same thing named in forty specifications converging on ONE node with several provenance Fragments rather than forty near-duplicates. Anthony's 900 documents are the corpus that requirement describes, and this is the experience that motivates it.

THE FALSIFIABLE FORM, worth stating because it is checkable rather than rhetorical: IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED `dev_storyflow`. One repo, code native, the design in the graph, the sources in the store. If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims.
properties.name: The repo holds what the design PRODUCED; the content store holds what INFORMED it — and storyflow is the case that proves why
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the content store shipped without anyone stating what belongs in it, and a store with no placement rule fills up with whatever the first person guessed — after which the rule is set by accident.

The storyflow history is the valuable half rather than the rule. The rule alone reads as tidiness; the history says what tidiness is worth and where it stops helping. A user who had already tried the obvious fix, at real scale, and found it solved half the problem is much better evidence than an argument, and it is evidence from the author's own working life rather than a hypothetical.

The falsifiable form is deliberate. This project keeps finding declared properties nothing checks (`dec:edge-orthogonality`'s rule that a distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it), and a doctrine about what goes where is exactly the kind of claim that can sit unexamined for a year. "Would storyflow have needed a second repo?" is a question someone can actually answer later.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

For an epoch or increment that has ARRIVED there IS a past to point at, so the question is only which handle the graph stores. Three candidates, and they answer different questions rather than competing.

(a) GIT TAG (`epoch/2026-Q4`, `v0.18.0`). Human-readable, already the in-repo precedent — `rel:v0180` lives in the graph, tag `v0.18.0` lives in git, and nobody greps tags to learn what shipped. Cost: a tag is mutable and deletable, so a pin can quietly stop meaning what it meant.

(b) COMMIT SHA. Immutable and exact. Cost: opaque to a person, and says nothing about which repo it is in — useless on its own in a multi-repo ecosystem.

(c) THE EXPORT'S OWN `content_hash`. Every export already carries one, and `prev_content_hash` already chains them, so reflow2 HAS a version history of the design that owes git nothing. The same design exported on any machine hashes the same, which git cannot say of a commit. Cost: a hash identifies but does not LOCATE — you cannot fetch a document from its hash.

THE SHAPE THIS SUGGESTS: `content_hash` is the IDENTITY and the git ref is the ADDRESS. They answer "is this the same design?" and "where do I get it?", which are different questions, and storing both makes a third thing computable for free — if the tag later points at a commit whose export hashes differently, the pin has drifted, and that is exactly the kind of finding reflow2 exists to make rather than to suffer.

A SEPARATE QUESTION, and the one that decides how much is even needed: DOES REFLOW2 CREATE GIT REFS, OR ONLY RECORD THEM? Measured while thinking this through — reflow2 shells out to git NOWHERE. The merge driver is invoked BY git, never the reverse. So recording-only would preserve a property the tool currently has completely: it takes no clock, and it would take no VCS either. It could print the command it would have run. Creating tags would also mean write access to repos reflow2 does not own, which in an ecosystem of coupled repos is a different tool.

MULTI-REPO: one epoch does not pin one ref, it pins a SET — one per design — which is `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, already the recorded dependency of `req:epochs-can-be-planned`. So the pin is a version combination, not a string.
properties.name: OPEN — what identifies an arrived epoch's snapshot: a tag, a commit, or the export's own content hash?
properties.rationale:
Anthony's question (2026-07-30): how the mechanics of using git to capture snapshots would actually work. Recorded as options because he asked to think it through, not to be handed an answer.

The `content_hash` option is worth flagging because it was not in the original framing and it is already built: exports have carried `content_hash` and `prev_content_hash` since the lineage chain landed, and the gate already fails when the chain is broken. If identity is what is wanted, most of it exists.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31. Both earlier states are preserved: the original four-way fork at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:where-content-lives`, the object_store amendment at `…:r2`.

THREE PARTS, all his word:

1. ADOPT `object_store` (Apache Arrow, originally InfluxData), LOCAL FILESYSTEM ONLY. The `fs` backend is a default feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` stay OFF, which keeps `reqwest` and the crypto providers out of the tree. Cloud backends remain one configuration change away with no rework, because the whole point of the crate is that the backend is a runtime detail — so this is the smallest useful slice rather than a narrowing.

2. BLOBS ARE COMMITTED TO THE REPO. Chosen because it is the only option where the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN: clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down, nothing to fall out of step. Every alternative is a second distribution channel, and a second channel is a second thing someone can skip — after which they see a design with holes in it and cannot tell. That is the failure `req:content-reaches-every-seat` exists to prevent. ACCEPTED COSTS, named rather than glossed: repo weight, and git handles binary churn poorly. Text — markdown, mermaid, HTML — diffs and compresses well and is most of what this will hold; raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first.

3. THE STORE LIVES IN `reflow2-mcp`, THE POINTER IN `reflow2-core`. Forced by a property worth keeping rather than chosen for taste: `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio, while `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous — measured 2026-07-31, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2, with no tokio, no async, no futures. So the core holds the CONTENT HASH, which is sync, deterministic and in-memory-testable, and `reflow2-mcp` does the I/O with the tokio it already carries through rmcp and hyper. Same split as `coverage_report`: the core computes, the surface touches the world.

WHAT MUST HOLD, unchanged by the answers: the pointer is a CONTENT HASH and never a path (`cap:session-memory` already recorded what a path costs — it "resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph"), and an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and names itself (`req:no-silent-fallback`). Content addressing also keeps this reversible: because a blob can be verified wherever it came from, moving to a different distribution mechanism later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says.

STILL TO CHECK AT BUILD TIME, not decided away: `object_store`'s MSRV against the workspace's 1.94, and its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed. Per `dec:design-dependencies-declared` the dependency is DECLARED with its version and the features taken by name — a new crate in this tree is a recorded reliance, not a line in a Cargo.toml.

AND ONE THING DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN: what bounds repo growth. A size cap that refuses oversized blobs loudly was offered and not taken, so nothing currently stops a large binary landing in the history where it cannot be removed without rewriting it. That is the first thing to revisit if the repo starts to hurt, and it is cheaper to add before there is history than after.
properties.name: Content lives in a content-addressed store behind object_store, local backend, COMMITTED to the repo
properties.rationale:
Settled in one pass because Anthony's research had already dissolved the hard part: once `object_store` makes the backend runtime configuration, "which storage" stops being an architectural commitment and only the git question remains — and that one turned out not to be about repo weight at all, but about whether the bytes travel the way the design already travels.

The placement was not a preference. It came from measuring `reflow2-core`'s dependency list and finding it genuinely free of async, which makes "put the store in the core" a decision to spend a property the crate has kept deliberately for a convenience it does not need. Reading the manifest answered in a minute what an argument about layering would not have settled at all.

The open item on repo growth is recorded rather than decided because the honest answer depends on evidence nobody has yet: what actually gets stored. A cap chosen now would be a number invented to feel safe — the asserting default `req:defaults-do-not-assert` exists to prevent — while a cap chosen after a month of real blobs would be measured. The cost of waiting is that git history is unforgiving, and that is exactly why it is named here rather than left to be discovered.

properties.decision:
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: "yes, promote this intent." Option (d) of the brainstorm; the roads not taken are kept below.

THE DECISION. A design's forward-looking schedule — which capabilities and requirements are expected at which epoch or increment — lives in the graph and is reached by QUESTION, not by document. His acceptance test, in his words: "what capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5" and "what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?" Nothing is written into git as an epoch snapshot: no epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. "Let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot" — rendering is an OUTPUT, produced on demand and thrown away, never the record.

WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, and it is narrower than the original idea: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, so "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" pins a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`). Forward-looking plans describe GRAPH content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe CODE and pin code. The information is in git either way, because the schedule lives in the graph and the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json` on every commit.

ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because they were genuinely considered.
(a) EPOCH BRANCHES — his own original mechanism, 2026-07-28: "epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1." A branch is the only place you can look at a future design whole, which is a real virtue. Not taken: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state and there is no future code to reflect; a full export is 1.6 MB, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON rewritten on every replan; branches invite merge semantics that do not apply; and a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` must be able to see.
(b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — my recommendation, and NOT TAKEN BECAUSE IT WAS WRONG rather than merely less good. Its selling point was that `git log -p` on the file would give the plan's revision history for free. But the schedule lives in the committed export, which already has git history and its own `prev_content_hash` chain — so the property existed and the file was an artifact added to obtain something the design already had. That is the shape this project keeps finding in other designs, found here in my own advice.
(c) RENDER TO FILES — the generated form of (b), carrying the same redundancy plus a staleness obligation.

THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT. Both of his questions are QUESTIONS, not documents: a query answers them directly, while a file answers them only if someone rendered the right one at the right moment. And every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves — `docs/design/reflow2.json` has a gate for it, `dataflow.html` has a check for it, and `docs/loop-model.json` demonstrated the failure the same day by becoming permanently unreproducible. Not materialising is the only way to have no drift at all.

MY EARLIER OBJECTION DID NOT HOLD, recorded because it was argued at length before being withdrawn: I claimed graph-only breaks readability for someone not running reflow2 (`req:design-reachable-without-the-repo`). It does not — the schedule is in the committed export, so it is reachable, merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.
properties.name: The schedule lives in the graph and is queried; nothing is snapshotted into git
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea, Anthony's lean, and Anthony's word to promote it. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` was reworded on the same word, because it described indexing git refs and that is no longer what it means; its original text is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`.

Worth keeping: the option that won is the one that ADDS NOTHING. No new file, no new branch, no new format, and — per the requirement it satisfies — largely no new storage, since epochs, Snapshots capturing incoming edges, and `compare_designs` already exist. The two rejected options both proposed materialising something, and both were arguing for a property the committed export already provides.

Also worth keeping, because it is a pattern rather than an incident: the file-per-epoch recommendation was mine, argued confidently, and wrong for the reason this project most often finds things wrong — it added a mechanism to obtain a property that already existed. Anthony's instinct to strip it back was better than my proposal to build it.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. When a plan moves during execution — "the motorcade slips thirty minutes" — somebody has to be told, and the question is who decides that. (a) SUBSCRIPTION, the way every coordination tool works: you join a channel, or somebody remembers to include you on the distribution. Cheap, familiar, and it fails one way every time — the person who most needed to know was not on the list, and nobody finds out until it matters. (b) DERIVED FROM THE BLAST RADIUS: propagate_from already returns who a change impacts, including which published boundaries it crosses, so the owners of the impacted regions ARE the distribution. Nobody maintains a list, nobody is spammed with changes that cannot touch them, and when the plan changes shape the distribution changes with it for free. (c) BOTH — derived by default, with an explicit watch for people who want a region they do not own. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO (b), recorded beside it: a blast radius is only as good as the edges that exist, so an unrecorded dependency means a silent non-notification — which is the same failure as (a), reached by a different route, and arguably harder to notice because the mechanism looks principled. The mitigation is that a missing edge is already what detect_gaps hunts, so the honesty debt has an owner.
properties.name: OPEN — is notification computed from the blast radius, or subscribed to?
properties.rationale: This is the most distinctive idea in the 1000-planner exploration and the strongest reason reflow2 would belong in that problem rather than a chat tool with a plan attached: a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent whose blast radius is computed, and "who does this break" is a question reflow2 already answers. It is the same shape as every other answer in this project — computed, not remembered — and it inherits the honesty rules, so a notification would have to say what changed, what it impacts and what is now unresolved, never "the plan was updated". Kept separate from dec:live-tier because the mechanism choice is separable: (b) is worth building for a single team on the repo-file architecture, with no hosting at all, the moment anyone wants it.

properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:034e96a2e1a7f4d0.
properties.name: Reviewed: gap:034e96a2e1a7f4d0
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28, with the rest of the reflow workflow review. properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:0a63dc6a6c47e039.
properties.name: Reviewed: gap:0a63dc6a6c47e039
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28. Accepted and not dropped. properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:0a77650b58242054.
properties.name: Reviewed: gap:0a77650b58242054
properties.rationale:
Anthony's standing policy from 2026-07-23, unchanged: validation for this project is the trials programme — reflow2 used on real designs, logged in docs/trials/ and docs/trials-private/ (the brownfield ophyd-service pass, the greenfield aidrone pass) plus sustained real use of the StoryFlow fleet. Formal validation-kind Verification nodes are not this project's tracking mechanism, and recording 68 near-identical ones would turn the number green without anyone having checked anything — the dishonesty `dec:passing-is-verified` exists to prevent.

ACCEPTED AT 68 CAPABILITIES, and the count is recorded here on purpose: this gap's id is now keyed on its RULE rather than its member set (`dec:aggregate-gap-keyed-on-rule`), so this acknowledgement CARRIES as the design grows instead of expiring on every addition. That is the fix for the churn — the same disposition had been re-recorded about twenty times, at 33, 34, 35 … 65, 67 and 68 capabilities. The trade-off is deliberate: a capability added tomorrow is covered by this judgement without a fresh look, which is what a standing disposition means. The growth stays VISIBLE without the churn, by comparing the count named here against the count in the live gap's title — if that gap says 90 and this says 68, twenty-two capabilities joined under a judgement made when there were 68, and whether that still holds is a question a reader can now actually ask.

This should be the last acknowledgement this gap ever needs. If it re-fires because the id moved again, the keying regressed and `an_aggregate_gaps_id_does_not_move_when_the_population_grows` should have caught it.

properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:101a69b0a4f8eed6.

properties.rationale: Standing disposition for planned-but-unbuilt capabilities (user's 2026-07-23 call, applied again 2026-07-24). properties.rationale:
ACCEPTED WHILE PLANNED, AND NOW DATED — Anthony's call 2026-07-31, taken with the other three of its kind as one judgement.

The gap's literal question — "how will you confirm it?" — is ALREADY ANSWERED: ver:gap-carries-a-reading is written and sits at `planned`, and it pins the CONTRACT rather than the judgement. What the gap actually reports is that the check has never RUN, which is simply true of anything unbuilt. That is a fact about sequencing, not a hole in the design.

WHY ACCEPT RATHER THAN LEAVE OPEN: these four were the only notes on the gate, so every release cut printed "5 notes" with no way to tell signal from permanent background — which is how a gate stops being read. When the capability is built and its check passes, the gap disappears on its own.

*** CORRECTION, MADE THE SAME DAY, LEFT ON THE RECORD RATHER THAN EDITED AWAY. *** This rationale originally claimed that `cap:review-expires-on-content` "means rewording the capability expires this review and brings it back for a fresh look". THAT IS FALSE. That capability is PLANNED, NOT BUILT. Expiry is keyed on the gap id, which hashes the affected node IDS — so a review expires when the affected SET changes membership and NEVER when the affected nodes change CONTENT. This review therefore does NOT self-expire. If the capability is reworded, someone must revisit this judgement BY HAND.

*** AND IT WAS PROVEN LIVE, WITHIN THE HOUR, ON THIS VERY ACKNOWLEDGEMENT. *** Later in the same session Anthony asked for the recommendation-with-options behaviour to be cemented, and cap:gap-carries-a-reading was substantially rewritten: renamed, given three shape obligations and a language rule, and its check rewritten with two new negative assertions. THIS ACKNOWLEDGEMENT CARRIED ACROSS UNCHANGED and went on suppressing the gap, with reviewed_gaps now rendering the OLD judgement against the NEW text. That is precisely the failure cap:review-expires-on-content exists to fix — in its own words, "a review outliving the wording it reviewed is worse than no review, because it reads as a human having agreed to something they never saw" — reproduced by the very sentence asserting it could not happen.

SO THIS ONE NEEDS A FRESH LOOK AND IS FLAGGED AS SUCH: Anthony judged a capability that said "a question comes with what the agent would do". It now also demands selectable options, a marked recommendation, a consequence on every option, and answering in the user's own language. The judgement (accept while planned, scheduled v0.21.0) plausibly still holds, but it is HIS to re-affirm, not mine to assume.

WHY IT IS SCHEDULED AND NOT MERELY ACCEPTED: acceptance alone was the trap. All four were scheduled against NOTHING, so quieting them would have relied on someone remembering. Now SCHEDULED_FOR rel:v0210 as `expected`, so arrival_delta asks at v0.21.0 regardless. Deliberately `expected` rather than `required`: a plan, not an obligation whose miss is a computed violation.

DELIBERATELY NOT IN v0.20.0, which Anthony scoped to cap:changelog-view alone.

Validation for this project is the trials programme — reflow2 used on real designs, logged in docs/trials/ and docs/trials-private/ (the brownfield ophyd-service pass, the greenfield aidrone pass) plus sustained real use of the StoryFlow fleet. Formal validation-kind Verification nodes are not this project's tracking mechanism, and recording 68 near-identical ones would turn the number green without anyone having checked anything — the dishonesty `dec:passing-is-verified` exists to prevent.

Apt for the newcomer, `cap:seat-handle`, in a way worth naming. Its verification is unusually strong for a spec-level check: `tools/stateless_seat_probe.py` drives three real transports against the real binary and measures the thing the requirement is about, and seven Rust cases pin both answers of the transport question including the refusal's wording. What none of that establishes is the operational intent — whether an AGENT, mid-session, actually calls `mint_seat` and keeps the handle rather than re-minting per call or omitting it and hitting the refusal. The refusal exists precisely because that failure is expected, and whether the message it prints is enough to change an agent's behaviour is answered by watching a session go wrong, not by a fixture. First real use over a sessionless transport is the trial.

THE CHURN IS STILL A FINDING, and it now has about twenty instances: this rollup's acknowledgement expires whenever the capability set changes, so it can never stay accepted and is re-recorded every time the design grows. Captured as `req:set-scoped-acknowledgement-keys-on-its-rule` rather than noted in prose for a twenty-first time.
