This requirement's value is entirely downstream of the comparison deserving belief, so satisfying it before the first two steps would damage the mechanism it rides on.

properties.name: The loop can answer what this design owes a NAMED PERSON, not only what it owes in total
properties.statement:
Raised by @ajs from flo2, 2026-08-05. It began as friction — a proposed Decision that nothing reported — and became the largest open question in flo2's design when it was put as a product question instead: "Shawn proposes an idea in flo2. How does that ever surface to Alex or me?" Today it does not. Not reliably, and not at all without someone independently deciding to go and look.

TRACE IT THROUGH, because three links are missing and the chain needs all three. (1) IS IT VISIBLE TO THE LOOP? Sometimes. A proposed Requirement with nothing satisfying it does fire unsatisfied_requirement, so that case works. A proposed Decision fires nothing. So whether a contribution is visible depends on which node type it happened to be captured as — an implementation detail the contributor cannot see and should not have to care about. (2) DOES ANYTHING SAY WHOSE IT IS? No. The gap says a requirement is unsatisfied; nothing says Shawn raised this, or that @ajs should judge it. AUTHORED_BY with role=approver already exists and is exactly the right shape, but NOTHING COMPUTES ON IT. (3) IS ANYONE TOLD? No — and this one is structural rather than missing: proxy.rs states that the reflow2 server NEVER INITIATES A MESSAGE (no notifications, no sampling requests, no progress pushes, "verified against the service, not assumed"). Every byte belongs to a request the client started.

THE MISMATCH UNDERNEATH. reflow2's coherence loop assumes ONE PERSON AT A KEYBOARD, with an agent asking them questions in a conversation. That assumption is sound and it is why the loop works so well in a coding harness. flo2 puts people in different places at different times, so the same loop has to become asynchronous — an inbox rather than a conversation. Nothing about the graph prevents that; the loop simply has no notion of a person to owe something to.

THE CHEAP PRIMITIVE, and the reason this is a sibling rather than a new idea: loop_status today answers "what does this design owe?" and TAKES NO ARGUMENTS AT ALL, while detect_gaps already accepts a scope for "one part of the design". A contributor scope on loop_status follows an established pattern. With that, the rest is flo2's own work and is ordinary: poll per user, render the inbox, email when it grows.

NOTIFICATION IS DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE. The server never initiating a message is a property worth keeping, and flo2 can poll. What has to live in reflow2 is the ANSWER to "what is owed to this person", because only the graph knows.

THE REAL DESIGN QUESTION INSIDE THIS, not to be papered over: what "owed to" MEANS per item type. A gap on a requirement Shawn raised is arguably owed to whoever must judge it, not to him. That is a genuine question and not a small one.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE AND NOT ONLY TO flo2: this is the axis on which the accepted req:no-idea-goes-quiet currently fails. That requirement promises an idea "stays connected to whether it was built... the user never has to remember it exists" — and it holds for one person at one keyboard while failing completely for a contributor who is somewhere else.

properties.name: A discipline the agent must hold across a long session rides the tool response it already reads, not prose it read once
properties.statement:
**Anthony, 2026-08-19**, in his own words: *"how come we can't attach a parameter to each skill request that returns something to the user. like 'lens' or 'session_user' that reminds the agent on every skill request?"*

**WHAT IS REQUIRED: a rule the agent must hold for a whole session is DELIVERED ON THE RESPONSE, not left in prose it read once.**

1. **THE REMINDER IS COMPUTED AND ATTACHED**, on a response the agent fetches immediately before doing work. Served prose is read at one moment and grows more distant every turn; a field on a response is re-read every call. **Same content, a carrier that does not decay.**

2. **IT REPORTS ABSENCE, NOT ONLY PRESENCE.** When the design cannot answer — nobody has recorded a background — the reminder SAYS SO and names who could be asked. ⭐ This is the half reflow2 has never had: **every detector reasons over the consistency of what EXISTS, and nothing asks whether something was never used at all.**

3. **IT NEVER ASSERTS WHAT IT CANNOT KNOW.** reflow2 has no notion of who is at the keyboard — a `seat` names a SESSION, never a person, and nothing binds one to a `Contributor`. So the reminder reports what the DESIGN holds and leaves matching the reader to the agent, the only party in the room that can. **Confidently addressing the wrong person would be worse than saying nothing.**

4. **IT IS BEST-EFFORT AND NEVER BLOCKS.** A skill must still be served when the graph is busy, missing or unreadable. **A reminder that could withhold a skill trades a nudge for an outage.**

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ WHY THIS, RATHER THAN MORE PROSE — MEASURED TWICE IN ONE WEEK

The rule being carried (*speak the reader's domain, never reflow2's*) shipped as served prose across four PRs. **The failure mode of served prose is not hypothetical here:**
  · `dec:idea-the-enum-question-came-back-four-days-after-it-was-fixed` — an instruction shipped, and the behaviour it forbade **recurred within four days**, because nothing observed whether it held.
  · `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` — the same finding, already recorded.
  · And during the very session that built the register rule, the Stop hook fired at the agent **mid-brainstorm**, the one workflow whose skill forbids it.

**The mechanism already exists and is proven: `loop_hint`.** `with_loop_hint` (service.rs) attaches a computed reminder to any response, and already rides every write result and orientation read. This requirement generalises the pattern it won: **a discipline that must survive context distance belongs on the wire, not in a file.**

📌 **HIS PROPOSAL WAS AN INPUT PARAMETER; WHAT IS OWED IS AN OUTPUT.** `session_user` as a caller-supplied argument has a chicken-and-egg — the agent must already know who it is speaking to, which is precisely what is being established. **As an output, absence becomes the signal** and the caller supplies nothing. Recorded because the change is a real narrowing of his idea, and the reason for it should outlive the memory of the conversation.

⚠️ **WHAT THIS STILL DOES NOT DO, and it is the same limit as the prose it strengthens:** it makes the reminder unavoidable, not the translation good. **It fixes "the agent forgot", never "the agent translated badly."** The trial that would tell those apart — a real gap list narrated to a reader with a stated non-software background — remains unbuilt, and remains the highest-value instrument missing.

⚠️ AND A COST, STATED SO IT IS WEIGHED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED: every response carrying a reminder is a response that got bigger, and a reminder that never changes becomes one the reader learns to skip. `loop_hint` answered this with a fire-on-change throttle. **Whether a lens needs the same throttle — or whether "every time" is exactly the point on a call made a handful of times per session — is a real question this requirement deliberately leaves to the delivery.**

properties.name: The running server says whether it is stale, instead of making a human compare two numbers
properties.rationale: MEASURED AND CHEAP TO FIX (fact:defect-a-running-server-cannot-say-it-is-stale): served_by.reflow2_version reported 0.22.1 while the on-disk binary was 0.24.0, with `--serve-shared` detached on purpose so every restart re-attached to the same stale process and nothing reported a problem. The existing guard failed in the most instructive way possible — it reports a LITERAL that a human must compare against a number the block does not contain, so a stand-down post saying 'demand served_by: 0.22.1' was satisfied four days later by a session that duly reported a PASS on a broken invariant. Four sessions read the same true value on two days and drew OPPOSITE conclusions. THE FIX WAS VERIFIED ON A LIVE SERVER BEFORE BEING PROPOSED: the kernel already marks a replaced binary's /proc/self/exe as '(deleted)', so stale:true is derivable from one syscall with no path re-resolution and no second binary read — and it answers the real question ('has my executable been replaced?') rather than answering it indirectly via a version string that breaks when two builds share a number. REFLOW2 ALREADY KNOWS THIS KERNEL BEHAVIOUR FROM THE OTHER SIDE: fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server is the same deleted-inode condition biting spawn_daemon through current_exe(). One signal, two symptoms, and detecting it fixes both. THE SECOND CLAUSE COMES FROM A SEPARATE PATTERN the fleet named: three version-dependent facts landed in copied instruction blocks in ONE DAY with no version stamp and no expiry — the served_by literal, a 'there is no mint_seat tool' correction that was true when measured and rotted when the binary moved, and a claim_region schema note describing the pre-shared-server architecture. Their proposal is that the server state 'as of <version>' beside any tool-existence claim, so a copied doc can be CHECKED rather than trusted. A doc that cannot be distinguished from a stale doc is indistinguishable from a wrong one.
properties.statement: The server SHALL report whether the binary it is running has been replaced since it started, as a field rather than as a literal for the reader to compare — and tool-existence and behaviour claims SHOULD be answerable against the running binary rather than trusted from a copied document. Requested by dev_storyflow's w-613d836b and w-6904efa6, 2026-08-07.

properties.name: A capability nothing can call is not delivered — the content store needs a surface
properties.statement:
FOUND 2026-07-31, immediately after `cap:content-store` was marked `realized`. The code exists, is tested and is correct — and NOTHING CAN CALL IT. Every occurrence of `content_hash` in `reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs` belongs to the export's own hash; no served tool touches `ContentStore`. So an agent in a session cannot store a diagram, and a user cannot get one back.

THIS IS BL-97's FINDING, RECURRED. That entry recorded the same shape for extraction: "`ingest` takes an `LlmBackend`, reflow2 ships no provider, and NO INGEST TOOL EXISTS among the 108 served — so core ingest cannot be called from a session at all, and the only working path today is the `adopt` skill." A capability can be complete in `reflow2-core`, pass its own tests, carry a passing Verification, and still be unreachable by everything that would use it.

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH A REQUIREMENT RATHER THAN A TASK: NO DETECTOR ASKS THIS. `unrealized_capability` asks whether an artifact realizes it — one does. `unverified_capability` asks whether a check passes — one does. `detect_gaps` returned nothing about it, correctly, because reachability from the interaction surface is not something the design currently computes. The confirmation ledger will happily report it `confirmed`. So a capability can read as fully delivered across every reading reflow2 offers while being usable by nobody, which is the same class of blind spot as a declared property nothing reads.

THE REQUIREMENT: a capability whose whole purpose is to be used by an agent or a person is not delivered until something they can call reaches it. For the content store that means put / get / exists on the MCP surface. More generally it means the question "can anyone actually invoke this?" belongs somewhere the design can answer, rather than being noticed by whoever happens to look.

SCOPE NOTE, so this does not overreach: plenty of core capabilities are legitimately internal — `cap:store`, `cap:propagate` and their kin are called BY other reflow2 code and need no tool of their own. The claim is narrower: where a capability's stated purpose names an agent or a user as the caller, an unreachable implementation has not delivered it.

properties.name: Asking for gaps returns the design's own blind spots — the user is never the detector
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, and he named the point himself so it is quoted rather than paraphrased: "the bigger point I'm trying to make is not can you render some view and whether you do it accurately/honestly or not — it is that when I type /gaps, does reflow2 automatically find all these gaps/issues."

So honest rendering is NOT the requirement. A renderer that confesses is necessary and is already built. The requirement is that the FINDING is automatic: `/gaps` must surface the design's own blind spots without a human thinking to look for them.

WHAT detect_gaps DOES FIND, so the shortfall is not overstated: unsatisfied requirements, unallocated and unrealized and unverified capabilities, failing verifications, unreleased components, missing interface halves, status contradictions, duplicates, surprising couplings. Every one of those is a MISSING HALF OF SOMETHING THAT EXISTS. That is the shape it is good at.

WHAT IT DID NOT FIND, all measured on reflow2's own design on 2026-08-07, and every one of them found by a human querying by hand:
1. 6 Components sit in no subsystem, and `hierarchy_issues` returns 0.
2. `evaluate_allocation` reports modularity 1.0 from `total_internal: 1, total_external: 0` — a perfect score over ONE dependency, while the graph holds 171 DEPENDS_ON edges — and `graph_report` prints it as "Allocation health".
3. 30 of 60 edge types have ZERO instances. Nothing reports this. Among them `DECOMPOSES`, the edge for the recursive decomposition this project was built around.
4. 8 of 29 node types have zero instances, including `Actor`, `Flow` and `QualityGate` — so three viewpoints render empty and nothing says why.
5. Two node names contain HTML entities (`<`, `>`), i.e. escaped display text stored as design content.
6. Four whole UAF domains have no vocabulary at all (personnel, states, information, materiel) — which detect_gaps structurally cannot ask, because it reasons about instances and this is a question about the schema.

THE ASYMMETRY THIS NAMES: detect_gaps finds the missing half of something that was begun. It cannot find something that was NEVER BEGUN. A type with no instances, an edge type never drawn, a decomposition one level deep and a metric computed over one data point all look identical to a design that simply has no problem there. This is the same shape `dec:loop-status-cannot-say-it-never-looked` already records for unsurfaced_gaps, where "clean" and "never scanned" are one answer, and the same shape `coverage_report` exists to fix for ARTIFACTS — there is no equivalent for vocabulary or structure.

THE PRECEDENT, and it is exact: `chg:orphan-decision-degree-zero` records this happening once already — "Found 2026-08-01 by running check-health and detect-and-ask on reflow2's own design, GETTING A CLEAN BILL FROM EVERY DETECTOR — detect_defects 0, hierarchy_issues 0, dimension_drifts 0, propose_heal 0 operations — and then counting zero-degree nodes by hand". One detector was added for that one case. The general principle was never made a requirement, so the next instance had to be found by hand again, which is what happened today.

ONE CONCRETE LEAD, because it is cheaper than it looks: `tools/render_views.py` already computes a CONFESSION LIST — everything a viewpoint needed and could not find — and it currently catches things detect_gaps does not, including every ChangeEvent pinned to no epoch and a real contradiction where `epoch:v0240-planned` and `epoch:v0250-planned` disagree between their PRECEDES edge and their sequence numbers. Two independent gap-finding mechanisms exist, the richer one is not wired into the loop, and `docs/viewpoints.md` already says "a confession list is a work list".

THE STANDING TRAP THIS MUST NOT FALL INTO, quoted from the catalogue's own rule 4: a detector that reaches zero findings by only asking questions the graph can already answer has been tuned to the instrument. Satisfying this requirement by adding checks that happen to pass is the failure mode, not the fix.

RELATED INTENT ALREADY IN THE GRAPH, so this is not read as unprecedented: `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` already states that the USER must never be the trigger — for skills. This is the same principle for findings.

properties.name: The user can trigger capture of what only the session holds, rather than relying on an agent remembering to
properties.statement:
Reasoning that exists only in a conversation must be capturable ON THE USER'S WORD, at any point, not only when an agent chooses to offer it. A discipline that depends on being remembered decays under load.

THE NEED, and it is the same argument the loop nudge rests on: measured over 46 sessions, skills are read once per 380 tool calls and four are never read at all. A capture that happens only when the agent thinks of it is a capture that stops happening exactly when a session gets busy — which is when the most is worth keeping.

It can fail independently: any design where capture is agent-initiated only breaks it, whatever skill exists.

properties.name: After setup, a project never has to change again for reflow2 to move
properties.statement: Installing reflow2 into a project should put a paragraph in the agent instructions and a server address in the MCP config, and nothing else that ever needs refreshing. Upgrades belong to the reflow2 package: today `reflow2_init.py` copies fifteen skills into two directory trees plus AGENTS.md, so upgrading means re-running init and taking thirty-odd changed files into a repo that has nothing to do with reflow2's release. Anthony's brother, 2026-07-25: "you wouldn't need to change anything in your repo again and updates would be confined to the reflow package." The installer's own docstring already concedes the defect — "the kit is copied into your project, so it otherwise freezes at install time while reflow2 keeps moving" — and reflow2's own kit manifest sat four releases stale without anything noticing (ver:kit-manifest-agrees).

properties.name: A design can be located on the function-to-structure trajectory
properties.statement: reflow2 shall compute where a design sits on the trajectory from function to structure, reporting each band of that trajectory as a count over a population and naming the lowest as the frontier — and shall never state where the design ought to be, because a demonstrator may correctly sit at function-first indefinitely while a fielded increment may not.

properties.name: Text that enters the graph from outside is neutralised at the boundary, and the neutralisation is reported
properties.statement: reflow2's standing rule — graph text is data, never instructions — is enforced today only by prose in the skills and the server handshake, which is a rule addressed to a well-behaved reader. The requirement is that the mechanical half exists: text arriving from outside the session's own author (prose read out of a codebase by INGEST, a design export imported from another machine or another person, and anything a hosted surface would accept) is neutralised of the characters that carry hidden instructions before any agent reads it — invisible and zero-width characters, bidirectional overrides that make text render as something other than what it says, Unicode tag characters that smuggle a payload past a human reviewer, and metadata hidden in code-fence info strings. Two properties reflow2 must add to the technique it borrows. The neutralisation must be REPORTED, not silent: a design whose statements were quietly rewritten on the way in is a design nobody can audit, and rule 6 forbids silent drops — so the count and the kind of what was stripped travel with the result. And it must not touch legitimate design content: an arrow, an emoji, a maths symbol or a non-Latin script is ordinary text in a design that may be about anything, so the filter is a named list of instruction-carrying characters rather than a whitelist of what looks familiar.

properties.name: A "verified" claim says how old the check behind it is
properties.statement: When a capability claims to be verified, the design must be able to say whether the check behind that claim is older than the code it covers. A passing check proves the paths it drives, and nothing more — so when a capability's meaning widens without its check widening, the old green tick keeps being reported as if nothing had changed. reflow2 already records everything needed to notice: Verification.last_run_at is written on every status set, and the confirmation ledger already dates the accepts that moved an artifact's baseline. Nothing reads the two together. Where the dates do not exist the answer must be "cannot tell", stated plainly — never silence, and never an assumption that the check is current.

properties.name: A combination of per-design versions is a named object that can be re-validated, not a one-off comparison
properties.statement: When several coupled designs each carry their own version, the question that matters before deploying is not "do these two agree at their seam?" but "does THIS SET of versions hold together?" — and that set must be a durable, named, dated object the design can re-check, not a comparison run once and lost. reflow2 today has only pairwise machinery: cap:design-dependencies-declared (declare which version of another design you depend on), cap:seam-incompatibility (say when two linked designs disagree at a boundary), cap:composed-analysis (analyse two designs together without merging them), compare_designs (two as-designed records). Nothing names an N-way combination or lets it be validated again later. THE PRIOR ART IS reflow's OWN, and it worked: workflow 01b-bottom_up_integration.json step SE-08 (Mixed-Version Validation) created a version-specific index file — naming convention index_v{scenario}-{YYYYMMDD}.json, e.g. index_v2.0-auth-v1.0-gateway-20251030.json — pointing at specific versioned files rather than symlinks, then ran validation over that combination (checking interface contract compatibility, breaking changes between versions, integration issues, dependency conflicts), generated a system graph for that combination alone, and recorded the outcome so known-good combinations were documented. Its stated use case: "Validate auth_service v2.0 works with api_gateway v1.0 before deploying." Also supported baseline snapshots for regression testing. THIS IS THE MECHANISM req:epochs-can-be-planned ALREADY ASKS FOR, captured 2026-07-28 in Anthony's own words: "an epoch or increment must pin the set of per-repo design versions it means, or the question 'which epoch are we talking about?' has no answer, which is the failure this exists to prevent." reflow had built the pin; reflow2 stated the need without it. Operationally load-bearing for the ecosystem case rather than the single-repo one: several coupled repos, each with its own graph, evolving at different rates. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: What crosses an interface is modellable — data entities, their attributes and their relationships
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit: there is no data-entity or information-element type, so a logical data model has nothing to project from.

WHAT EXISTS AND WHY IT IS NOT ENOUGH: `Interface` carries `operations` and `payload_format` as free text, and `SPECIFIES` exists for pointing an Interface at a machine-readable contract (an OpenAPI file, a protobuf schema) — with ZERO instances. So the graph can say a contract exists, what medium it uses and how it authenticates, but not WHAT TRAVELS OVER IT in any form a computation can read. An interface is currently a promise with no stated structure behind it.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: the entities two components exchange; an entity's attributes; that two interfaces carry the SAME entity, which is what makes a change to it propagate to both; that one system's field maps to another's under a different name, which is the whole substance of making two organisations' designs interoperate.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2, and this one bears directly on the stated purpose: `reflow2-real-operating-context` says the job is making partially-built, differently-motivated designs interoperate when they were never designed to. Interoperability failures are overwhelmingly SEMANTIC — the same concept under two names, two units, two precisions — and none of that is expressible. `con:pairing-stops-at-the-boundary` already records the ceiling in the graph's own words: pairing sees boundaries, not the types that cross them. That constraint is this requirement's evidence.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether this is a full entity-relationship layer or something much thinner, and whether reflow2 should model entities itself or only carry a locator to an external schema — `dec:agent-navigates-content` (the agent navigates content, the graph records where it landed) is an argument for the thinner answer, and the trade is not settled.

properties.name: Physical resources are modellable — supply, sparing, maintenance and consumption, which `Resource` does not mean
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit, asked as "what if I said create/render me a logistics view": there is no logistics vocabulary, and the type whose name promises it means something else entirely.

THE TRAP, MEASURED: `Resource` exists, and its only instance is `dep:dynograph-foundation` with `resource_type: design-dependency`, carrying a provider URL, a version, a feature list and the file it was declared in. It models a SOFTWARE DEPENDENCY. `REQUIRES_RESOURCE` has one instance and means "this design depends on that library". Of the four missing domains this is the one most likely to be assumed covered, because the name is already taken by something else.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: a consumable and its consumption rate; a spare and its provisioning quantity; a maintenance action, interval or turnaround; transport, storage or shelf life; what a system needs to keep operating as opposed to what it needed to be built. A logistics view has no nouns to draw.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2: software has no materiel, so this costs nothing here and is load-bearing for every physical programme — which `reflow2-real-operating-context` and the adopt skill both say are in scope ("a satellite, a building or a fleet cannot live in a repository — its drawings, specs, models and analyses can").

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether the existing `Resource` type is generalised with a wider `resource_type` vocabulary or a separate type is added beside it. The first is cheaper and risks conflating a build-time dependency with an operational consumable; the second is cleaner and costs a type. That is a decision, and it should be made rather than defaulted.

properties.name: People are modellable inside the design, not only around it — organisation, role, and who performs a function
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit: the Personnel domain has NO vocabulary in reflow2. Two people-shaped types exist and neither is this — `Contributor` is who authored the design, `Actor` is who the designed system serves. Both sit outside the system being designed.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: which role performs a function; the organisation a function belongs to; a post, a competence, or a responsibility assignment; who is accountable for a component. So an organisational view, a manning view, or a responsibility matrix has nothing to project from — and "which function is allocated to which system" (already answered by ALLOCATED_TO) has no counterpart for "which function is allocated to which PERSON or ROLE".

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2, which is the reason this is a requirement and not a curiosity: reflow2 itself is a tool with an agent and one user, so people barely appear inside its design and their absence is invisible here. Almost every non-software project has people IN the design — a beamline has operators, a satellite programme has crews and controllers, a hospital system has clinicians. `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` says fixes are judged by what they do for somebody else's project, and this is a gap only somebody else's project would feel.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE, deliberately: whether this is one node type or several, whether a role is a first-class node or a property on an edge, and whether reflow2 should follow UAF's Post/Role/Competence split or a simpler shape. Those are design questions and picking one now would foreclose them.

properties.name: Behavioural state and its transitions are modellable, distinct from lifecycle status
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit: there is no state machine anywhere in the schema, and a whole UAF model-kind column depends on one.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THIS A REAL GAP RATHER THAN A NAMING ONE: reflow2 has plenty of `status` fields — a Requirement is proposed/accepted/deferred/dropped/met, a Capability is planned/realized/verified, a Verification is planned/passing/failing. Every one of those is a LIFECYCLE status: where a design element has got to in its own maturation. None of them is a BEHAVIOURAL state: a mode the designed thing is in while it operates. And no transition is modelled between any of them — the enums are values, not a graph, so even the lifecycles cannot be projected as a state diagram.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: that a detector is in acquiring / idle / faulted; that a vehicle is in launch / cruise / re-entry; that a protocol connection is in handshake / established / draining; which event causes which transition; which states are safe to be interrupted in. A state view is not expressible, and neither is "what modes must this interface work across".

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2: reflow2 is a request-response tool with no operating modes to speak of, so the absence costs nothing here and everything on anything with modes. Anthony's own current case is one — a beamline instrument has states, and the analysis stack behaves differently in each.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether states attach to Components, Capabilities or both; whether a transition is an edge or a node; and whether lifecycle status should be unified with behavioural state or kept firmly apart. Kept apart is the likelier answer and is still a decision, not an assumption.

properties.name: A returning session can ask what happened while it was gone
properties.rationale: SESSIONS TODAY DETECT THAT THE GRAPH MOVED BY RE-RUNNING A ROLLUP AND SEEING A DIFFERENT NUMBER — the reporter calls this the worst possible detector, and the record bears it out: a worker checking in reported gaps 55->69 and defects 12->26 between two check-ins hours apart and, correctly, COULD NAME NO CAUSE. WHY IT IS ACUTE RATHER THAN CONVENIENT, and this is the part that generalises past their fleet: their sessions are EPHEMERAL BY DESIGN — they die on context exhaustion constantly and are replaced by a fresh seat that cold-starts from files. A returning seat's FIRST REAL QUESTION is 'what happened while I was gone', and there is no way to ask it. This sits directly under their stated primary use of reflow2, which is not design capture at all but DURABLE MEMORY ACROSS SESSION DEATH. THE RAW MATERIAL MAY ALREADY BE PRESENT: ChangeEvent exists as a node type and AT_EPOCH/OCCURS_DURING pin events in time; what is missing is the query. Worth checking whether this is a reporting surface over existing data rather than new machinery. RELATED ASKS THAT MAY SHARE A MECHANISM: claim visibility without polling (an overlapping claim never reaches the peer, so claim_report must be polled — the reporter's phrase is 'advisory should still be observable'), and the per-node revision in req:a-node-carries-a-revision. All three are forms of 'tell me what moved'.
properties.statement: The graph SHALL answer 'what changed since time T, and by whom' — writes by other seats over an interval — as a query, rather than leaving a session to infer movement by re-running a rollup and noticing a different number. Requested as the #3 fleet ask by dev_storyflow's api-boss 5d608b85, 2026-08-07.

properties.name: The design can say what to work on next, and why that and not something else
properties.statement: A person returning to the design must be able to ask "what is the most pressing thing to work on?" and get an answer computed from the design itself, with its reasoning visible — not a hand-maintained ordering in a file. The answer must rank an unmade decision ABOVE the work that waits on it, because being told to build something blocked on a choice only the human can make is worse than being told nothing. It must distinguish what is undecided from what is unbuilt from what is misshapen, since those need different actions from different people. And it must be a projection over the graph, never a stored list: a second place where priority lives is a second place for it to go stale, which is the failure the whole backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.

properties.name: A project must be able to tell work that reaches its consumers from work that serves only its own machinery
properties.statement:
A deliverable must be able to record WHO IT IS FOR — a consumer of the product, or the project's own machinery — and the design must then be able to answer, without asking a person: is there a need here that nothing consumer-facing delivers?

DELIBERATELY DISTINCT FROM `rule:reflow2-is-built-for-other-projects-not-for-itself` and from `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party`, and the split is the point. Those RULES are how the people building reflow2 work; they bind this project and can never bind anyone else's. This REQUIREMENT is the product carrying the same philosophy, so every project using reflow2 inherits the question. That is the identical shape as `req:a-fix-says-whether-it-corrected-the-cause`, which exists because Anthony asked on 2026-08-17 for his building philosophy to be "built into the design of reflow2" rather than merely stated at its developers. A rule states it; a requirement makes it something reflow2 DOES.

ALSO DISTINCT FROM `req:a-fix-says-whether-it-corrected-the-cause`, which was surfaced as near: that one asks whether a repair reached the CAUSE or worked around it. This one asks who the work was FOR. A root-cause fix can still land entirely in internal machinery, and a workaround can ship straight to a consumer; the two axes are independent and both are currently unrecorded.

⭐ THE DISTINCTION IS UNIVERSAL, NOT REFLOW2'S. Every project that ships anything has internal machinery and a delivered product, and confuses them under pressure: a team's own scripts against what the beamline actually does, CI configuration against the library, a build tool against the API. The failure it enables is the same everywhere and it LOOKS LIKE COMPLETION — find a hole, patch it in the internal half, mark the need met, and leave every consumer with the hole. The repo goes green and nothing is true of anybody else.

⚠️ NEVER INFERRED FROM A PATH. A first sketch of this proposed classifying deliverables by directory — `.github/` internal, `crates/` shipped — which encodes ONE project's layout and is exactly the failure it exists to prevent. The audience is DECLARED by the project or it is unknown, and unknown is a true answer.

⚠️ AND NEVER A JUDGEMENT. Internal work is legitimate and necessary; a release procedure, a coordination board and an export discipline are real work that reaches no consumer. The requirement is that the difference be VISIBLE, never that internal work be discouraged (`dec:report-dont-judge`).

🛑 THE DETECTOR MUST SAY WHEN IT HAD NOTHING TO RUN ON. If no deliverable in a project has declared an audience, the reading is "I cannot judge this", NOT zero findings. A detector reporting zero because its population was empty reads exactly like one that ran clean — `loop_status` already refuses an unknown contributor_id for this reason, and this is the same trap one level over.

HONEST LIMIT, the same class as `provenance` and the drift dispositions: this records what the author SAYS a deliverable is for. It cannot detect an internal tool declared consumer-facing. Worth having because the alternative is no signal at all; worth never overselling.

ACCEPTED 2026-08-22 ON ANTHONY'S WORD (`epoch:work-declares-who-it-reaches-is-accepted`). He agreed to ADDING this requirement in #295 before seeing how it was phrased, so it was deliberately left at `proposed` until he had read the wording — `dec:certainty-derived` makes every move off `proposed` his signature, and promoting it unread would have forged it. He read the statement and accepted; the NAME was shortened in the same act, from a paragraph carrying an embedded quotation to the need in one clause. Nothing in the statement itself moved.

properties.description:
Derived from reflow2's own Cargo.toml, not hand-written.

🛑 **THREE CRATES GONE, TWO NAMED HERE, ONE REACHED TRANSITIVELY.** `dynograph-vector` and `dynograph-resolution` left 2026-08-24 (increments 1 and 2); `dynograph-graph` left the same day (increment 3, `chg:absorb-graph-algorithms`). Verified with `cargo tree` at each step rather than inferred from the manifest. What remains: `dynograph-core` and `dynograph-storage` here by name, plus `dynograph-text` pulled in by storage's `fulltext` feature and never named in any manifest — 847 lines and tantivy behind it, and no earlier costing of the absorption counted it.

WHAT WAS ABSORBED, and what was deliberately left:
  • `mean` + `linear_regression_slope` → `reflow2-core/src/stats.rs`. Left: 7 of 9 functions, `hnsw.rs`, `distance.rs`.
  • `token_sort_ratio` + closure → `reflow2-core/src/fuzzy.rs`. Left: `PreparedName`, `resolver.rs` (911 lines).
  • 8 graph names + closure → `reflow2-core/src/graphalg/`. 2,219 of 3,832 lines; left 1,613 in nine files.
Each carries a header naming repo, tag, commit, files, what was taken and what was left.

⭐ THE ONE CLOSURE RESULT WORTH KEEPING: `cut_structure` does NOT need `max_flow_min_cut`. Articulation points and bridges come from a DFS lowlink walk, so 248 lines stayed behind that the intuition "cuts need flow" would have dragged in.

🛑 AND THE ONE MISTAKE WORTH KEEPING: the first closure for increment 3 was wrong because the grep that found reflow2's import sites matched only single-line `use dynograph_graph::X;` and missed the MULTILINE block in `structure.rs`, which imports `betweenness_centrality`. That put two needed files (`betweenness.rs`, `paths.rs`, 375 lines) in the not-taken list. **The same blind spot had been caught in the dependency scan minutes earlier and fixed in only one of the two greps.**

REMAINING WORK: increments 4 (`dynograph-core`, 1,941 lines, 62 importing files) and 5 (`dynograph-storage` + `dynograph-text`, 3,575 lines, brings rocksdb and tantivy). **Only increment 5 ends the dependency.**

HISTORY KEPT: bumped v0.11.0 → v0.12.0 on 2026-07-28 for a stated reason rather than as housekeeping — v0.12.0 closes a type leak reflow2 was structurally exposed to (`search_fulltext` returned `dynograph_text::TextHit`, from a crate reflow2 never names and reaches only through an optional feature) and makes the `rocksdb` and `fulltext` feature NAMES a committed contract upstream. Verified before the tag existed by building this consumer against the provider's unreleased tree. MIGRATION CHECKED, not assumed: `keys.rs` and `backend.rs` are untouched between the tags, so a graph written by v0.11.0 reads identically.

properties.state:
{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-23: *"should we ever just completely bring in dynograph-foundation into reflow2? we can cannibalize it and only take what we need/want and no longer have it as an external dependency?"*

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT THE QUESTION HE ALREADY SAID NO TO

`dec:idea-swap-dynograph-foundation-as-the-substitutability-demo` is **REJECTED** — his words, 2026-08-20: *"I don't want to really swap out dynograph-foundation (it works and putting a lot of effort into this is probably not worth it if we aren't going to really swap it out)."* The reason recorded there is general: **a demo that costs as much as the real thing is not a demo.**

THAT OBJECTION DOES NOT REACH THIS IDEA, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE WHOLE POINT. Swapping means REIMPLEMENTING the functionality behind a contract. Cannibalising means KEEPING THE SAME CODE and moving it in-tree. The rejected option pays full replacement cost; this one pays relocation cost. They are answers to the same underlying question — what to do about the dynograph dependency — and only one of them was priced.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📐 THE MEASUREMENT THAT MATTERS HERE IS NOT THE ONE THE REJECTED NODE MADE

That node measured FILES IMPORTING each crate — 48 / 21 / 3 / 2 / 1 — and concluded that `dynograph_core` at 48 files "is not a module, it is the type vocabulary", so replacing it is a rewrite wearing substitution's name. **That is correct for REPLACEMENT and irrelevant to ABSORPTION**: blast radius measures how much would have to change if the types changed, and vendoring changes no types at all.

THE RELEVANT NUMBER IS THE IMPORTED SURFACE. Measured at HEAD 2026-08-23 from every `use dynograph_*` in `crates/` — **about 21 named items across five crates**:

  dynograph_core      DynoError · Value · Schema · PropertyDef · PropertyType ·
                      NodeTypeDef · EdgeTypeDef · EdgeEndpoint            (8)
  dynograph_storage   StoredNode · StoredEdge · StorageEngine · Value      (4)
  dynograph_graph     GraphBuilder · leiden · strongly_connected_components ·
                      connected_components · find_cycle · cut_structure    (6)
  dynograph_resolution  token_sort_ratio                                   (1)
  dynograph_vector      mean · linear_regression_slope                     (2)

⚠️ BOUND, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: this counts what is NAMED at an import site. It is a measure of the API SURFACE CONSUMED, not of the code volume behind it — `StorageEngine` is one name in front of a RocksDB-backed store, and `leiden` is one name in front of a community-detection implementation. It is a lower bound on work and an upper bound on interface.

⭐ TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE REJECTED NODE'S STATED RISKS, found by looking at what is actually imported rather than at which files import it:

· It warned *"vector search and HNSW are not trivial to reimplement well"*. **reflow2 does not use HNSW, or vector search, at all.** It imports `mean` and `linear_regression_slope` — arithmetic, in one file (`dimensions.rs`). Whatever the case against absorbing `dynograph_vector`, it is not that one.
· `dynograph_resolution` is one function, `token_sort_ratio` — fuzzy string matching, two import sites.

AND ONE RISK IT DID NOT NAME: `dynograph_graph` is where the real intellectual content sits — **leiden community detection, SCC, cycle finding, connected components, cut structure**. Six names, and the ones you would least want to reimplement. Under ABSORPTION that inverts into an argument FOR: you keep the implementation, so difficulty-to-rewrite stops being a cost and becomes the reason the code is worth having in-tree.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
✅ THE OBVIOUS RISK THAT IS ALREADY ANSWERED

"Does this break storyflow, which also depends on dynograph?" — No. `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface` measured it: storyflow consumes dynograph as a **REST API over HTTP**; reflow2 consumes it as a **Rust library API**. Disjoint surfaces over one shared implementation. reflow2 dropping the Rust surface cannot touch storyflow's endpoints.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
IDEAS, UNRANKED, each with what it costs

**A. ABSORB EVERYTHING — vendor all five crates in, delete what is unimported, drop the git dependency.** What the question literally asks. Ends the upgrade treadmill, the tag pins, and the `[patch]` dance in `Cargo.toml`; makes reflow2 a single tree with no external source.
   ⚠️ You inherit maintenance of a RocksDB storage engine and a Leiden implementation forever, and you lose the upstream's fixes silently rather than by a pin bump you can read. **Vendoring converts a visible dependency into an invisible one** — the version pin at `reflow2.toml:11` currently carries a written reason for every bump, and that record has no successor once the code is in-tree.

**B. ABSORB THE THREE SMALL ONES ONLY — graph, resolution, vector (9 of the 21 items) — and keep core+storage as the external dependency.** The three that are algorithms rather than substrate.
   ⚠️ Honest counter, and it is the same one the rejected node made about its option C: **the dependency stays, so the treadmill stays.** The saving is partial and must not be sold as removal. What it does buy is that the two crates you would most struggle to justify rewriting are the ones you stop being able to lose.

**C. ABSORB ONLY WHAT IS TINY AND OWNED-BY-ACCIDENT — `token_sort_ratio` (1), `mean` and `linear_regression_slope` (2).** Three functions, almost certainly a few dozen lines, that reflow2 could own outright with no maintenance story worth the name.
   ⭐ Highest ratio of dependency-surface-removed to risk-taken. Removes two entire crates from the manifest.
   ⚠️ And it is nearly cosmetic: `dynograph-core` and `dynograph-storage` are what the dependency actually IS. Two fewer lines in `Cargo.toml` is not independence.

**D. DO NOTHING — it works, it is maintained, and the pin has a reason written on every bump.** The status quo, and what his own standing anti-over-engineering position argues for by default.
   ⚠️ The counter: the reason for absorbing is not technical, it is about what reflow2 IS. A design brain whose substrate is somebody else's repository has a supply chain; one that owns its tree does not. Whether that matters is a judgement about the product, not about the code.

**E. SETTLE THE PRIOR QUESTION FIRST — `dec:idea-is-the-foundation-a-subsystem-or-a-supplier`, still open.** Is dynograph a NINTH SUBSYSTEM of reflow2, or a supplier reached across required interfaces?
   ⭐ **This idea would answer that question by construction rather than by argument.** Absorb it and it is a subsystem; there is no supplier left to be. That may be the strongest thing in favour of A — it dissolves an open modelling question instead of settling it on paper — and equally the strongest reason to answer the prior question first, since doing it in this order decides by doing.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📌 WHAT NOBODY HAS COSTED, so the list is not read as an estimate

No measurement exists of the LINE COUNT behind those 21 names, of what the five crates carry that reflow2 never touches, or of how much of `dynograph-storage` is RocksDB glue versus reflow2-specific. "21 imported items" is an interface measurement and says nothing about how big the tree is that would move. **The cheap next step, if any of this is pursued, is to measure the code volume behind each crate and how much of it is dead from reflow2's point of view** — which is exactly the "only take what we need/want" half of his question, and the half that currently has no number attached to it at all.","name":"OPEN — should reflow2 absorb dynograph-foundation outright, keeping only the ~21 items it actually imports, and stop having an external dependency at all?","rationale":"Recorded via the brainstorm skill at `proposed`. Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-23, immediately after the v0.39.0 cut. Nothing here is intent and nothing is planned.

DEDUP: the guard surfaced `dec:idea-swap-dynograph-foundation-as-the-substitutability-demo` and `dec:idea-is-the-foundation-a-subsystem-or-a-supplier`; both were read in full and judged DIFFERENT. The first is REJECTED and asks about REPLACING the foundation with a new implementation — a cost this idea does not incur, because absorbing keeps the code. The second asks what the foundation IS; this asks what to DO with it, and would answer that one by construction rather than by argument.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-23: *"the other idea was just making dynograph-foundation a set of semi independent crates that you just pick what you like from? this is really a dynograph-foundation issue, I'm asking it here"*

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ THE FIRST HALF IS ALREADY TRUE, MEASURED AT HEAD 2026-08-23

dynograph-foundation holds **TEN crates**: `client`, `cluster`, `core`, `game`, `graph`, `resolution`, `service`, `storage`, `text`, `vector`.

**reflow2 already picks five of them** — `core`, `storage`, `graph`, `resolution`, `vector` — and declines `client`, `cluster`, `game` and `service` outright. `text` is not taken directly at all; it is reached only through `dynograph-storage`'s optional `fulltext` feature. And `storage` is taken with `default-features = false`, with `rocksdb` and `fulltext` opted into by name in `crates/reflow2-core/Cargo.toml`.

⭐ So "a set of semi-independent crates you pick what you like from" IS WHAT IT ALREADY IS, at the crate level and at the feature level. `dynograph-game` and `dynograph-service` existing while reflow2 has never heard of them is the proposal already working — and `service` is almost certainly the REST surface storyflow consumes, which makes `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface` visible in the file layout.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📐 THE RESIDUAL: INDEPENDENT IN CODE, COUPLED IN RELEASE

All five are pinned in reflow2's `Cargo.toml` as:

    { git = "https://github.com/sligara7/dynograph-foundation.git", tag = "v0.12.0" }

**One repo, one tag, five crates.** You can pick WHICH CRATES you take; you cannot pick WHICH VERSION of each. They are not published to crates.io — the workspace comment says so — which is also why the `[patch."https://…"]` block exists, commented out, for local cross-repo development.

⭐⭐ **AND THERE IS A WORKED EXAMPLE ALREADY IN THE GRAPH.** `fact:dynograph-v0130-measured-clean-and-the-pin-is-parked` records that v0.13.0's `git diff v0.12.0 v0.13.0` over ALL SIX crates reflow2 touches is **EMPTY** — the entire release changed only `dynograph-client` and `dynograph-service`, neither of which reflow2 depends on. **A release that provably could not affect reflow2 still cost a session to confirm**, across four independent grounds and a full `cargo test --workspace`, and the pin bump is still PARKED awaiting Anthony's word.

⇒ That is precisely the cost of coupling release to repository rather than to crate, stated in a real measurement rather than as an argument. **The question is not "should they be separate crates" — they are. It is "should they be separately RELEASABLE".** A much smaller question than the idea sounds like, and a different one from absorbing anything.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
IDEAS, UNRANKED, each with what it costs

**A. LEAVE IT — one repo, one tag, pick your crates.** The status quo, and already most of what was asked for.
   ⭐ The monolithic tag is not only a cost: the five crates are always mutually consistent, and reflow2 has never had to reason about a version matrix. `reflow2.toml`'s pin carries a written reason for every bump (v0.11.0 → v0.12.0 closed a type leak) — and ONE pin is what makes that note writable at all.
   ⚠️ A consumer who wants one crate takes the release cadence of all ten, and pays a confirmation session for releases that cannot touch it.

**B. VERSION THE CRATES INDEPENDENTLY WITHIN THE REPO** — per-crate versions or tags under one repository.
   ⚠️ Independent versions mean a compatibility matrix somebody maintains and tests. `dynograph-storage` re-exports `dynograph_core::Value` — reflow2 imports `dynograph_storage::Value` in two places — so core and storage are not independently versionable in any real sense without a stated compatibility contract between them.

**C. PUBLISH TO crates.io.** Turns "pick what you like" from a git-tag arrangement into the ordinary Rust one, and removes the `[patch]` dance.
   ⚠️ Publishing is a commitment: names are permanent, yanks are loud, and a pre-1.0 foundation currently free to move acquires an audience. Same shape as `designation: published` on an Interface — publishing is a promise, not a distribution mechanism.

**D. SPLIT THE REPO** — one repository per crate, or per cluster.
   ⚠️ The heaviest option, and it multiplies the release ceremony reflow2 has just spent a session documenting. Ten repos with ten release cuts to keep coherent is a worse problem than one tag.

**E. CHANGE NOTHING UPSTREAM; LET reflow2 STOP TAKING WHAT IT BARELY USES.** `dynograph_resolution` is one function and `dynograph_vector` is two — both absorbable by reflow2 (option C of `dec:idea-cannibalize-dynograph-foundation-into-reflow2`) with no upstream change at all.
   ⭐ The only option here reflow2 can act on unilaterally, in its own repo, without a decision about somebody else's project.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
📌 THE HONEST BOUND, and it is about ownership rather than engineering

**Nothing here has been discussed with dynograph-foundation as a project, and reflow2's design has no standing to decide it.** Four of the ten crates exist for consumers reflow2 knows nothing about — `game` and `cluster` are not reflow2's business, and a change made to suit reflow2's consumption pattern could be wrong for whoever uses those. The only options reflow2 can weigh honestly on its own are **A** (accept it) and **E** (take less).

**AND THE SEPARATE FINDING WORTH KEEPING WHATEVER IS DECIDED:** this node lives in reflow2's graph while being about another system, and only its prose says so. That is the gap, not the workaround.","name":"OPEN — dynograph-foundation's crates are already pickable; should they become independently RELEASABLE, so a consumer can pin one without pinning all five?","rationale":"Recorded via the brainstorm skill at `proposed`. Anthony, 2026-08-23, raising a second option beside the absorb idea. Nothing is intent and nothing is planned.

🛑 THIS DECISION GOVERNS ANOTHER REPOSITORY. Its subject is `dynograph-foundation`, not reflow2. It is recorded in reflow2's graph because that is where he asked it, because dynograph-foundation has no reflow2 design of its own — and because NOTHING IN THE SCHEMA RECORDS WHICH REPO A DECISION GOVERNS, so only this prose says so. That gap was filed independently by a dev_storyflow session on 2026-08-17 (item ④): a design question about another repo has nowhere of its own to live. **No work is to be done in that repository on the strength of this node.**

DEDUP: read four near-matches in full. ⭐ THE FINDING: `detect_defects` COSTS ~10s AND RIDES ALONG ON CALLS THAT NEVER ASKED FOR IT. `loop_status` reports a structural-defect count so it pays; `open_questions` pays it through the `loop_hint` attached to its reply. `open_questions` does its own work in about half a second and costs 11.7. So the two calls this project's own instructions call the cheap orientation reads — the SessionStart hook, the server instructions and the Stop hook all push an agent at them — are the two most expensive calls on the surface, and neither is expensive because of what it was asked to do.

🛑 AND IT CORRECTS A STANDING BELIEF. "The first store read of a session costs 26–48s" has been carried as a known cost and read as the STORE being slow. THE CASE. `ver:side_e_slo_gate_unwired_2026_08_09` VERIFIES `con:side_e_perf_slos_are_enforced_nowhere` — a check that measures whether a performance constraint is actually enforced. `schema/verify.yaml` lists `to: [Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule]`, so the edge is unimportable and their export has not restored since at least 2026-08-11.

⭐ IT READS AS A LEGITIMATE MODELLING NEED, NOT A SLIP. A Constraint is "a limit or rule the design MUST respect" — a latency budget, a mass cap, "no PII leaves the device". Asking whether a limit HOLDS is the most natural thing anyone would want to check about it, and it is exactly the question `budget_report` answers arithmetically for the numeric case. A Verification is how this design records that something was CHECKED. Refusing to connect them says a limit may be stated and computed but never independently verified.

AND THE ASYMMETRY IS ODD ON ITS FACE: `DesignRule` IS in the list, and `unverified_enforced_rule` exists precisely so a gate-blocking rule owes a passing check. A Constraint is the DesignRule's sibling — the imposed limit beside the chosen one — and the same argument for verifying one applies to the other. Nothing in the schema explains why they were split.

THE OPTIONS:

(a) ADD `Constraint` TO THE TO-LIST. Repairs their export, needs no data migration, and makes the vocabulary say the thing it appears to mean. COUNTER: the list was derived FROM live edges as evidence of use, and adding a type because one edge exists is the same reasoning that produced the incomplete enumeration — one edge is not a demonstrated need.

(b) MIGRATE THE EDGE AWAY — a check about a Constraint could instead verify the Capability that honours it, or the DesignRule that expresses it. COUNTER, and it is `rule:never_shape_a_field_to_satisfy_an_instrument` from their own repo: reshaping real design to satisfy a validator is how a graph bends into fiction, and the edge was legal when written.

(c) RE-DERIVE THE WHOLE LIST ACROSS EVERY KNOWN GRAPH and take the union — the census the original change should have run, now with three real designs to run it against rather than one. COUNTER: it settles this instance without settling the rule, and the next narrowing repeats it.

(d) RESTORE `to: "*"` FOR VERIFIES. COUNTER: the enumeration was added for a reason recorded in the file, and reverting discards that.

⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN, and it is the reporter's point: nobody deletes those two edges to make an import succeed before this is answered. `Project` is the other unlisted type and may well be a genuine mistake — the two should be judged separately rather than as a pair.

{"decision":"`import_graph` writes a node whose `node_ref` property names a node that is in neither the document nor the graph, and names it on `ImportReport.dangling_node_refs` (printed by `--import`). It does NOT fail the import. `create_node` is unchanged and still refuses such a write outright.

Recorded as PROPOSED: it was Claude's engineering call, taken to keep this design's own export restorable, and it is Anthony's to settle or overturn.","name":"A restore reports an unresolvable node reference rather than refusing the whole document","rationale":"THE ALTERNATIVE, and why it lost: refuse the import, matching `create_node`. Measured 2026-08-29 — this design's own export carries nine references written before the guard existed (five instances of a `prj:`/`proj:` typo, four capabilities renamed after the fact was written). Under refusal the export could not be restored AT ALL, and the only remedy on offer was hand-editing the export document, which is the one thing this project tells users never to do. Any user upgrading into the guard with a single pre-existing dangling reference would silently acquire an unrestorable backup.

THE DISTINCTION THAT DECIDES IT: a write ASSERTS something new, and refusing a new record about a node the design does not have is right. An import ASSERTS NOTHING — it reproduces a state that already existed, and the document is the evidence that it did. Refusing there is the tool substituting its judgement for a reality it is being handed.

NOT A NEW POLICY. `ImportReport` had already answered this same question three times — `skipped_edges` (an edge whose endpoint is missing is skipped and named, not fatal), `integrity_note` and `provenance_note`, each documented as "the import still proceeds but never silently". A dangling property reference is the other shape of a missing endpoint, so answering it differently would have one import refusing what its neighbour two lines up reports.

THE COST, stated plainly: import is now a path by which a dangling reference can enter a graph that did not have one — an export/import laundering route the write guard closes. Judged acceptable because it requires a deliberately constructed document, and because the renames that produce most real dangles are unreachable by ANY write-time check and need detection over the graph as it stands. {"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-08. Nothing here is intent and nothing has been chosen. THE IDEA, his words: \"the allocation of functions to systems/services should be done as late as possible (agreeing that doing it at genesis is too early). I feel like doing it at the last possible moment before functional allocation to system/service is the right call.\" It is the answer he reached to a caution raised against the sibling idea (dec:idea-the-ility-chooses-the-allocation-graph), which proposed ASKING at genesis what quality attribute the system is for: the objection was that at genesis you frequently do not know yet, and premature commitment can cost as much as late discovery. His resolution keeps the question and moves WHEN it is asked — not at genesis, but at the moment allocation actually has to be committed. WHAT THIS WOULD MEAN CONCRETELY: the quality-attribute question rides the ALLOCATION event rather than the project's beginning, so a design accumulates requirements and capabilities freely and is asked what it is optimising for only when something is about to be bound to a component. THE HOOK MAY ALREADY EXIST, and this is the cheap part worth checking before anything is built: `unallocated_capability` is already a detected gap, so the graph can already see capabilities that exist and are bound to nothing. The transition from \"capabilities exist, none allocated\" to \"the first allocation is being made\" is observable from graph state alone, which is the same state-not-history discipline dec:loop-status-state-not-history already commits to. If that is the trigger, nothing new needs remembering. OPEN SUB-QUESTIONS, none answered here: (a) is the moment per-PROJECT or per-CAPABILITY — a mature design allocates new capabilities continuously, so \"the last responsible moment\" may recur rather than happen once, which would make this a repeating prompt rather than a milestone; (b) does deferring allocation conflict with reflow2's own trajectory model, where `allocation` currently reads 100% and sits ahead of the `seams` frontier at 0% — if allocation is supposed to be late, a design showing allocation complete and seams empty may be describing a real inversion rather than healthy progress; (c) what happens to a design that never reaches the moment, since a demonstrator may sit unallocated forever and be right (maturity_report already refuses to say where a design SHOULD be). COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside rather than against: the last-responsible-moment principle assumes the cost of deciding late is lower than the cost of deciding wrong, which holds when deferral is free — and here it may not be, because artifacts get written against an assumed structure long before anyone calls `allocate`. If real files already embody a de facto allocation, then \"deferring the decision\" defers only the RECORD of it, and the graph would be late to something the build already did. That is the same as-designed-versus-as-built gap that granularity_report exists to surface, and it argues the trigger should watch ARTIFACTS appearing rather than the `allocate` call.","name":"OPEN — is allocating functions to systems/services something to defer to the last responsible moment, and can reflow2 tell when that moment has come?","rationale":"Recorded under the brainstorm skill, separately from the ility idea, because the two are genuinely different questions — WHAT drives allocation and WHEN it happens — and can be answered independently; one node holding both could only ever be half-answered. Worth keeping because it converts a raised objection into a design position rather than losing it: the caution was \"at genesis you do not know yet\", and this answers it without abandoning the question. The `unallocated_capability` hook and the artifacts-versus-allocate-call counter-argument are the two things a later session would otherwise have to re-derive.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"A committed plain-text manifest mapping content hash → original filename → what references it, so a design that points at stored content can say what it does NOT itself carry. Makes \"do I have everything?\" a set comparison for someone holding only the export, and makes a blob change legible in `git log` as a readable name rather than a hex path. Paired with `.gitattributes` marking the blob directory `binary`, which stops git attempting diffs it cannot produce and — the part that matters — stops line-ending conversion silently corrupting a PNG on a CRLF checkout. Governed by `dec:content-manifest`; delivers `req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry` and makes `req:content-reaches-every-seat`'s fail-loud promise checkable by a person rather than only by the tool. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what content the design depends on, in names a person can read","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"Content hash → readable name → what references it, so a design that points at stored content can say what it does NOT itself carry. `missing` names content the graph references and this checkout lacks — the case someone handed the export alone hits, where a diagram that will not open becomes a named finding instead of a silent absence. `orphaned` is the reverse: bytes stored and referenced by nothing, which is how a store grows without anyone deciding to (and the reason `dec:where-content-lives` left repo growth deliberately open).

DERIVED, NEVER STORED, and that is the design rather than an optimisation. The manifest is computed from the graph plus a directory listing; a manifest kept as its own record would be a second source of truth about what the design references and would drift the first time someone updated one and not the other. Rendering it to a committed markdown file is a PROJECTION — the same relationship `dec:views-are-projections` already sets for every other view.

THE READABLE NAME IS THE FRAGMENT'S `title`, not a filename stored beside the hash. The graph already requires a title, so there is no second place for names to live and nothing to disagree with the design about what a thing is called. `referenced_by` carries the Fragment AND what it annotates or yielded, so "what is this picture for?" is answerable from the manifest without opening anything.

A LOCATOR AFTER THE HASH TRAVELS VERBATIM and is never parsed (`dec:agent-navigates-content`) — `sha256:…#L412-L440` resolves to the same blob and reports `L412-L440` untouched. A `content_ref` holding a plain PATH from before the store existed is not treated as content at all, so legacy references do not read as missing blobs.

Needed a FOURTH store function, `list` — named rather than slipped in, because `dec:content-store-implementation` argued for three. That argument was about `object_store`'s path/prefix/pagination semantics, which immutable content addressing does not need; enumerating a flat set of addresses is a different thing, and orphan detection is impossible without it. `list` skips anything whose name is not a hash, so a stranded temp file or the committed manifest is never mistaken for content.

Paired with `.gitattributes` marking the blob directory `binary` — which stops git attempting diffs it cannot produce and, the part that matters, stops line-ending conversion silently corrupting a PNG on a CRLF checkout. REALIZED; `ver:content-manifest` passing, served as `content_manifest`.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what content the design depends on, in names a person can read","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures. Built on `object_store` (Apache Arrow) with the local filesystem backend and cloud features OFF, so there is no service to run and cloud backends stay one configuration change away. Blobs are COMMITTED to the repo, which makes them travel exactly as the design does — clone and you have everything (`dec:where-content-lives`). The store itself lives in `reflow2-mcp` because `object_store` is async and `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous; the core holds only the hash, which is sync, deterministic and testable in memory. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures.

HAND-ROLLED AND SYNCHRONOUS, IN `reflow2-core` (`dec:content-store-implementation`). `put(bytes) -> hash`, `get(hash) -> bytes`, `exists(hash)` over `sha2` (already a core dependency) and `std::fs`. Zero new crates, no async runtime, deterministic and testable without one. `object_store` was measured and recorded as the documented UPGRADE PATH rather than adopted: 36 crates new to reflow2, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery a local store never calls, buying a feature set — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — that immutable content addressing does not have.

THREE PROPERTIES THE BUILD MADE REAL, each pinned by a test and two of them mutation-checked. (1) `get` VERIFIES the bytes against the hash they are stored under and REFUSES a mismatch rather than returning it — a content hash nobody checks is only a filename, and the claim that a blob fetched from anywhere can be trusted once it verifies rests entirely on this. (2) A hash is interpolated into a path, so anything that is not exactly `sha256:` plus 64 lowercase hex is refused BEFORE it reaches the filesystem; `../../etc/passwd` is a malformed hash, not a missing file. (3) Writes are temp-then-rename within the shard directory, so a process that dies mid-write leaves nothing or a whole blob — and a stranded temp file is unreachable as content because its name is not a hash.

Blobs are COMMITTED to the repo, so they travel exactly as the design does (`dec:where-content-lives`). Reading INTO stored content is not this capability's job and never becomes one — the agent navigates, the graph records an opaque locator reflow2 never parses (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). REALIZED, `ver:content-store` passing.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

THE OPEN DESIGN QUESTION, recorded rather than guessed: record_change now REFUSES a planned epoch, so a plan's movement cannot be filed INTO the planned epoch it concerns — it must be recorded in the arrived epoch that is current, taking the planned epoch as its subject. Whether that is sufficient, or whether planned epochs need a revision chain of their own, is undecided. {"description":"The answer to \"what is the most pressing item?\" once the backlog lives in the graph. It is NOT detect_gaps and NOT check-health, and the distinction is the design: detect_gaps asks what the design has not yet decided, check-health asks what shape is wrong, and this asks which of the agreed things to do now. Composed rather than invented — BL-85 already specifies the form (\"a backlog_report / roadmap projection, a view, never a second source of truth\"), BL-68 supplies readiness and risk-to-completion (\"the roadmap is a risk-burndown schedule\"), BL-40 is the projection layer, and the long narratives stay as documents-linked artifacts rather than being crushed into properties. THE RANKING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. Measured 2026-07-24, this is not hypothetical: dec:multi-writer-architecture blocks two nodes, so the honest answer to \"what is next\" right now is a decision only the human can make, not a build task. PREREQUISITE, and the reason this cannot usefully ship first: today ZERO accepted requirements lack a satisfying capability, so \"what is unbuilt\" is unanswerable from the graph — everything accepted is allocated to something. Distinguishing allocated from delivered needs cap:derived-completion (BL-104). Until that lands, this view can rank what is undecided and what is misshapen but is blind to what is merely unfinished. {"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

Anthony, 2026-07-30: "as we march forward in time, we can measure the delta of what was actually achieved/realized versus what was planned for that epoch. For instance, in epoch 3 we had planned for capability A, B, C. However, when we actually got to epoch 3 in time, we only achieved A & C, and B was discontinued or deferred to epoch 4."

FOUR OUTCOMES PER SCHEDULED ITEM, three of them his and one the complement he did not name:
  - DELIVERED — the plan held (A and C).
  - DEFERRED — still intended, the date moved (B to epoch 4).
  - DISCONTINUED — no longer intended at all. Distinct from deferred in the way `retire-from-design` already distinguishes them: one is a date change, the other is a withdrawal, and conflating them either loses a commitment or embalms one.
  - DELIVERED BUT NEVER PLANNED — the complement. Work that arrived which nobody scheduled. Usually the most informative quarter of the delta, because unplanned work is where the estimate actually went, and a report that omits it makes a schedule look better than it was.

THE TRAP, and it is the same shape as the snapshot bug fixed on 2026-07-28. If deferring B simply RE-POINTS its schedule edge from epoch 3 to epoch 4, then when epoch 3 arrives the graph says epoch 3 was only ever about A and C — the slip is invisible and the plan has silently rewritten its own history. That is precisely what `req:intent-preserved` forbids, and precisely what the second-revision-overwrites-the-first defect did to snapshots. So REPLANNING MUST BE A RECORDED CHANGE, NOT AN EDIT.

A MECHANISM THAT NEEDS NOTHING NEW, given what was verified while thinking this through: a Snapshot captures a node's INCOMING edges as well as its outgoing ones. So snapshotting the EPOCH captures every schedule edge pointing at it — the whole plan for that epoch, in one snapshot, in one call. Replanning becomes `record_change` on the epoch, which is exactly the operation the 2026-07-28 fix made safe to do twice in one epoch.

WHAT IS COMPUTED VERSUS STORED. The delta is COMPUTED, never written down, for the same reason "ARE satisfied" is: `req:completion-computed` says delivery is computed from the golden thread and never asserted. At arrival, compare the last snapshot of the epoch's schedule (what was planned, as of before it moved) against what the thread says is delivered. Nothing about the outcome is stored; the two inputs already exist.

WHAT FALLS OUT ONCE IT IS COMPUTABLE — a schedule-performance profile per epoch: hit rate (planned and delivered over planned), slip (how many deferred, and by how many epochs), attrition (how many discontinued), and unplanned (delivered but never scheduled).

AND THE PAYOFF WORTH NAMING, because it closes a loop this project opened the same day. `req:plans-move-honestly` wants a planned claim to carry confidence that decays with horizon — Anthony's Black-Scholes analogy. Once several epochs have arrived, that confidence can be MEASURED rather than asserted: "historically, items scheduled three epochs out land 40% of the time." That is the same argument that retired `req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` on 2026-07-30 — an estimate is defensible only as a seed for something never measured — applied in the direction where the measurement is actually available, because unlike context cost, schedule performance is observed every time an epoch arrives.","name":"OPEN — what happens when an epoch arrives, and what the planned-vs-delivered delta is computed from","rationale":"Anthony's idea, in his own example, recorded while the thinking is still open.

Two things added beside it rather than in place of it: the fourth outcome (delivered but never planned), because a delta that only reports against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it; and the re-pointing trap, because the obvious implementation of "defer B to epoch 4" is an edge edit, and an edge edit is exactly how the plan would come to lie about what it once said.

The mechanism note is a measurement, not a preference: snapshots were confirmed to capture incoming edges, so the epoch-snapshot approach needs no new machinery.","status":"proposed"}
