{"decision":"OPEN, and deliberately NOT a reopening of `dec:where-content-lives`. Recorded because Anthony said it plainly on 2026-07-31 and then parked it — "this also makes me lean towards storing the blob on something like AWS or other locations, but we can come back to this" — and an unrecorded lean is how a settled decision gets eroded by drift instead of revisited on purpose.

WHAT CHANGED. `dec:where-content-lives` chose committed blobs so the bytes travel exactly as the design does: clone and you have everything, no second channel to configure, be down, or fall out of step. That reasoning is untouched. What moved is the COST side: transcripts measure at 4.0 MB mean and 115.8 MB across 29 sessions, already 1.4× the whole repository history, and GitHub blocks a single file at 100 MB. The decision was taken when the expected content was documents and diagrams; the measurement says otherwise.

WHY IT IS NOT REOPENED TODAY. `dec:content-growth-is-bounded-by-what-not-by-size` addresses the measured problem directly — transcripts by exception rather than by default — and if that holds, committed blobs stay comfortably viable: reflow2's entire design prose is 3.5 MB. Reopening an architectural decision to solve a problem a policy already solves would be the wrong order, and the no-service property is worth more than the convenience it would buy.

THE CONDITION THAT WOULD REOPEN IT, stated so this is checkable rather than a mood: if the store's total grows past what a clone should reasonably carry — WITH the by-exception rule actually being followed — then the constraint is real rather than a discipline failure, and the fork is genuinely back. `cap:content-manifest` reporting total bytes is what makes that observable rather than felt, which is why that reporting is part of the accepted growth decision rather than a nicety.

WHAT AN ANSWER WOULD HAVE TO PRESERVE, so a future reader does not re-derive it: content is addressed BY HASH, so a blob verifies wherever it came from — that is precisely what makes the backend swappable without touching what the graph says. And `object_store` is already recorded as the documented upgrade path in `dec:content-store-implementation`, with its cost measured (36 crates, an async runtime reaching the core). So the migration is understood; what is not settled is whether it is warranted.

THE PROPERTY THAT WOULD BE SPENT: an external store is a second thing to configure, be down, and be out of step — and a consumer who skips it sees a design with holes and cannot tell. `req:content-reaches-every-seat` is the requirement that would come under pressure, not merely a preference.","name":"OPEN — a recorded pressure on committed blobs, not a reopening: the growth measurement makes an external store look better than it did","rationale":"Recorded as a decision point rather than left in conversation, because this is the exact failure the project found hours earlier: `cap:what-next` carried a prerequisite in prose, the condition cleared, and nothing noticed. A lean stated in passing has the same shape — it is real information about a settled choice, and if it lives only in a transcript it either evaporates or resurfaces as unexplained drift.

This is now the THIRD pressure on `dec:repo-file-embedded`'s no-service family, after `dec:central-host` (two-coast collaboration) and the content store itself. Three from unrelated directions is a fact about the decision worth having on the record — not an argument to change it, and not something to keep rediscovering.

The condition is written to be observable rather than persuasive: "total store bytes past what a clone should carry, with the by-exception rule followed". The second clause matters — without it, a discipline failure would read as an architectural constraint and reopen the wrong question.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"OPEN, raised by `req:content-store-for-what-the-graph-points-at`. The requirement settles that the graph holds a pointer and something else holds the bytes; it does not settle WHERE, and that is a real fork rather than an implementation detail.

WHY IT IS A FORK AND NOT A CHOICE OF LIBRARY: `dec:repo-file-embedded` and `dec:multi-writer-architecture` both chose a repo file over a hosted service, and their strongest argument was that no service means nothing to run, nothing to authenticate against, and nothing to be down. A content store is the first thing reflow2 would hold that a git-diffable JSON file is genuinely bad at — megabyte transcripts and binary images — so this is where that decision gets its first real test.

THE OPTIONS, none preferred yet:
  (a) A CONTENT-ADDRESSED DIRECTORY BESIDE THE EXPORT, committed to the repo. Keeps the no-service property exactly, and content-addressing is already this project's idiom (`dec:export-hash-chain` takes self-authenticating repos from AT proto; `set_artifact_checksum` already hashes). Cost: repo weight, and git is poor at binary churn — the objection is real and measurable rather than aesthetic.
  (b) A CONTENT-ADDRESSED DIRECTORY OUTSIDE THE REPO, gitignored, with the pointer carrying the hash. VERIFIED, not taken from the summary: `fs` (LocalFileSystem) is a DEFAULT feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; the cloud backends are behind `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` and are NOT default, and with them off the crate avoids pulling `reqwest` and the crypto providers. His preference is stated and is NOT recorded as settled: what "everything in the graph" means mechanically is the open part.

THE MEASUREMENT, taken 2026-08-04. `docs/backlog.md` is 3,350 lines / 581,031 bytes across 132 rows. Of the 8 rows filed in one session (BL-205..212), SIX are referenced by ZERO graph nodes. The file is not a registered Artifact, so `coverage_report` does not count it and no checksum tracks it. FOUR things were re-derived in that same session that were already written down somewhere: BL-205 (third rediscovery), `dec:export-once-per-pr` (accepted, invisible, violated and then re-announced as new), BL-70's alternatives family (nearly re-proposed), and dev_storyflow's hand-made doc-intent scope table (re-derived worse from filenames).

THE FRAME IS ALREADY ACCEPTED AND THE BACKLOG VIOLATES IT. `dec:what-lives-where` states the rule: "the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced." It carries a falsifiable test — "IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED dev_storyflow… If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims." THE SAME TEST GENERALISES AND REFLOW2 CURRENTLY FAILS IT ON ITSELF: if reflow2 works, reflow2 would not need a 581 KB markdown backlog. It is also the exact failure the dev_storyflow api-boss measured in that fleet's MEMORY.md — "an index that must be read IN FULL to be useful has a hard ceiling", 20 KB against a 17 KB limit with everything past the line silently invisible. The backlog is 29 times that size.

WHY IT HAS RESISTED THE OBVIOUS FIX — A BACKLOG ROW IS NOT ONE THING. Reading the eight rows from one session, they are at least four: (i) DEFECTS AGAINST SHIPPED CAPABILITIES (BL-205 loop_status too large, BL-206 the gate's truncated sweep, BL-208 the inert CI guard, BL-209 the blind orphan detector); (ii) UNBUILT WORK (BL-186 the folder driver, BL-211 genesis-from-a-folder); (iii) OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS (BL-207's fix-shape fork); (iv) DISCOVERED LIMITS (BL-212, chronology cannot be recovered from a folder). Three of those four already have a home: unbuilt work is a Capability at `planned` behind a Requirement, an open question is a `proposed` Decision — which is what this very node is — and a discovered limit is a Constraint or DesignRule.

⭐ THE ONE THAT HAS NO HOME, AND IT IS THE LARGEST CATEGORY: a defect found by USING the tool. reflow2 has no way to say "this capability is built, VERIFIED, and does not do what it claims." `Verification` answers whether a check passes — and every one of BL-205/206/208/209 sat under a passing check. `DriftEvent` answers whether the code moved away from the design — and in all four cases the code and the design AGREED, and both were wrong. HEAL's issues are computed from graph shape, not recorded observations, so they vanish between runs. That absence is why these rows land in markdown: there is nothing to write them to.

OPTIONS, none chosen. (a) ROUTE EACH ROW TO THE TYPE IT ALREADY IS and add no vocabulary. Cheapest, and it works for three categories of four. Counter: for the defect category it loses the finding — "this is broken, here is the measurement, here is how it was found" becomes "here is a need", which erases the evidence and reads as intent rather than as a bug. (b) A `Finding`/`Defect` NODE TYPE carrying claim, evidence, when observed, and what it bears on. Counter, and it is strong: this project has proposed a node type and WITHDRAWN it after measuring TWICE in one week (`Attestation` → `TemporalFact`, `Hazard` → `DesignRule` + `CONSTRAINS`), so the prior against new vocabulary is heavy — and `TemporalFact` ("a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs") may already be the shape, since a defect is exactly "this was true of the build from epoch X until the fix". (c) EVERYTHING BECOMES A PROPOSED DECISION. Counter: 132 proposed Decisions would swamp `where-am-i` and the decision list, and most rows are not forks between real alternatives. (d) KEEP THE MARKDOWN BUT DERIVE IT FROM THE GRAPH rather than maintaining it by hand. In-house precedent exists and is unused for this: `dec:views-are-projections` ("a view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects") and `tools/render_views.py` already render DoDAF-flavoured views into docs/viewpoints.md. The backlog is simply not one of them. Counter: this solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it only helps once the content is in the graph, so it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing. (e) DO NOTHING AND ACCEPT THE COST, recorded so it is a choice rather than a default: the backlog is readable by a human today, and the re-derivation cost, while real, has been paid without anyone stopping work.

WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED WHEN THIS IS PICKED UP: `dec:what-lives-where` (the accepted rule and its falsifiable test), `dec:views-are-projections` plus `tools/render_views.py` (the rendering half already exists), [BL-198] (a serialized default is indistinguishable from a choice — the same "what does the graph actually record" family), and [BL-209] (22 Decisions invisible because `AUTHORED_BY` counts as attachment — a graph-native backlog would land straight into that blind spot and must not).","name":"OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?","rationale":"Captured under the brainstorm skill at Anthony's request. The load-bearing content is the taxonomy and the single gap it exposes: three of the four kinds of backlog row already have a node type, and the fourth — a defect in a capability that is built, verified and wrong — has none, which is why those rows have no choice but to be prose. Recording the measurement (581 KB, 6 of 8 rows with zero graph representation, four re-derivations in one session) so the next session argues from numbers rather than from the impression that the file is getting long.","status":"proposed"}

--- ADDED 2026-08-04, ANTHONY ASKED WHAT A NODE AND AN EDGE CAN ACTUALLY HOLD. THE ANSWER IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES EVERY OPTION ABOVE, AND IT IS MEASURED. ---

WHAT A NODE CAN HOLD. The schema's whole type system is `string` (170 declarations), `enum` (89), `float` (34), `bool` (10), `int` (7). There is NO dedicated text type and NO `max_length` anywhere in any schema file — `string` IS the narrative field and it is unbounded in practice: the `decision` property of this very node runs to several thousand characters without complaint. Every type carries at least one narrative-shaped field (`Decision.decision` + `.rationale`, `Requirement.statement`, `Capability.description`, `Component.purpose`), and Decision requires only `name` and `decision`. AND THE SCHEMA IS ADDITIVE: dynograph-core's own test is named `extra_properties_allowed` — "Extra properties should be allowed (schema is additive)" — so a property the schema never declared is stored rather than refused. It validates the TYPES of declared properties and enforces the required ones; anything else passes through.

WHAT AN EDGE CAN HOLD. More than assumed: 44 of the 60 edge types carry properties, across 46 distinct property names, and several are free text — `note`, `evidence`, `rationale`, `diff_summary`. SIXTEEN CARRY NOTHING, and they are all bookkeeping or temporal: AT_EPOCH, HAS_SNAPSHOT, VALID_FROM, VALID_TO, ABOUT_ENTITY, OCCURS_DURING, PERFORMED_IN, and — worth noting against [BL-212] — PRECEDES. The edge that would say "this document came before that one" can carry no evidence for the claim.

⭐ THE STING, AND IT IS WHY THIS BELONGS ON THIS NODE RATHER THAN AS TRIVIA: ONLY 52 PROPERTIES IN THE ENTIRE SCHEMA ARE `fulltext: true`, and those are the only ones `search_design` indexes. The distribution is name 20 · description 12 · statement 5 · summary 3, then singletons: rationale, decision, purpose, question, evidence, intent, effects, design_intent, criteria, context_setter, answer, title. So `Decision.decision` IS indexed and — measured — `Decision.rationale` is NOT. Every "why" written into a rationale field is stored and unsearchable. The same is true of any extra property invented under the additive rule: stored, not indexed, not returned by `describe_schema`, read by no report. That is this project's recurring declared-and-read-by-nothing shape one rung worse, because it is UNDECLARED and read by nothing.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY OPTION ABOVE: UNLIMITED PROSE IN A NODE IS GREP BY ANOTHER NAME. What makes the graph queryable rather than navigable is the `fulltext:` flag, the typed properties and the EDGES — not the narrative. Moving the backlog into nodes therefore helps only to the extent a row becomes STRUCTURE: which capability the defect bears on (an edge), what was measured (a typed property), whether it is still true (a status or a temporal bound), with the prose hanging off that as explanation rather than as the record. A row moved in as one long `description` rebuilds `backlog.md` inside the graph with worse ergonomics and no gain — and that failure would be invisible, because it would look like progress.

AND IT PUTS A NUMBER ON THE DEPENDENCY WITH `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption`: with 52 lexically-indexed fields and no vector half, "query the graph" today means ranked keyword search over names, descriptions and statements. Better than grep — cross-node, ranked, no filename needed — but the same KIND of retrieval. The ceiling on "an agent can work from the graph alone" is set by that open question, so the two ideas should be weighed together rather than separately.

WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED WHEN THIS IS PICKED UP: `dec:what-lives-where` (the accepted rule and its falsifiable test), `dec:views-are-projections` plus `tools/render_views.py` (the rendering half already exists), [BL-198] (a serialized default is indistinguishable from a choice — the same "what does the graph actually record" family), and [BL-209] (22 Decisions invisible because `AUTHORED_BY` counts as attachment — a graph-native backlog would land straight into that blind spot and must not).","name":"OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?","rationale":"Captured under the brainstorm skill at Anthony's request. The load-bearing content is the taxonomy and the single gap it exposes: three of the four kinds of backlog row already have a node type, and the fourth — a defect in a capability that is built, verified and wrong — has none, which is why those rows have no choice but to be prose. Recording the measurement (581 KB, 6 of 8 rows with zero graph representation, four re-derivations in one session) so the next session argues from numbers rather than from the impression that the file is getting long. {"decision":"RECORDED AS A MEASURED DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Found 2026-08-05 by the FIRST REAL TRIAL of cap:corpus-ingest, over six architecture documents from dev_storyflow. Nothing here is settled, and the fix shape is genuinely open.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio`, which `ingest::fuzzy_match` uses on node NAMES, against the auto-merge threshold of 90:

  95  dynograph-vector   vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED
  94  dynograph-storage  vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED
  93  dynograph-extract  vs dynograph-context     <- SILENTLY MERGED
  91  dynograph-server   vs dynograph-query       <- SILENTLY MERGED
  89  dynograph-engine   vs dynograph-core        (asked)
  84  Auth Service       vs Authentication Service (NOT merged, NOT asked at Component's 90/80 bands)

THE THRESHOLD IS EXACTLY BACKWARDS FOR THE NAMES REAL SYSTEMS USE. Sibling modules sharing a prefix — the near-universal convention — score 91-95 and are merged without asking. The canonical duplicate the feature exists to catch, `Auth Service` ~ `Authentication Service`, scores 84 and is not. `docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md` asserted "90 on a token-sorted ratio is near-identity"; MEASURED, IT IS NOT.

THE IMPACT, MEASURED ON ONE DOCUMENT: dynograph.md declares NINE crates. After ingest the graph holds FIVE. FOUR CRATES — 44% of the architecture — WERE SILENTLY DESTROYED (dynograph-core, dynograph-vector, dynograph-query, dynograph-extract are gone as named nodes). And the survivors ASSERT SOMETHING FALSE rather than merely being incomplete: `cmp:dynograph-core` now carries the name "dynograph-storage", because the merged node keeps the first id and the longer name. The longer-name rule is BL-186's own #73 fix working exactly as designed — the defect is the merge, not the naming.

⭐ THIS IS NOT A CORPUS DEFECT AND THE TRIAL NEARLY MISDIAGNOSED IT. The first reading blamed the new corpus driver. Isolating dynograph.md and ingesting it ALONE reproduces it exactly: 9 in, 5 out, 4 merges. So this is PRE-EXISTING IN `ingest` and has been true of every single-document ingest since fuzzy dedup landed. The corpus layer is only the first thing to put enough same-family names in front of it for the loss to be visible. Everything this project has ingested one document at a time may carry it.

WHY NOBODY SAW IT: reflow2's own design uses prose names ("The graph handle is an accepted single point of failure"), not prefixed identifier names. `dev_storyflow` is a CODEBASE, so its architecture documents are full of `foo-bar` sibling crates. Self-host was structurally incapable of surfacing this — the same shape as BL-199, and the second time that shape has explained a long-invisible defect.

DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS `dec:ask-not-repair` IN PRACTICE WHILE OBEYING IT IN FORM. The ruling says suspected duplicates are asked, never silently merged; the 90+ band is treated as "not a suspicion" and acts. The measurement says the 90+ band CONTAINS the very cases most in need of asking, so the rule is honoured and its purpose defeated.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) RAISE THE AUTO-MERGE THRESHOLD. Cheap, and wrong on its own: 95 was a sibling pair, so there is no threshold that separates them by score. (b) NEVER AUTO-MERGE — every match becomes a question, and the corpus batching (BL-186) is what makes that affordable. Honest and expensive; the 11-candidate band in the same trial was 11/11 FALSE POSITIVES, so a user would be answering "no" a great many times. (c) A DISCRIMINATOR BEYOND THE SCORE — refuse to merge when the names differ by a whole token that neither contains ("core" vs "storage" are not variants of each other, while "Auth" vs "Authentication" is a prefix). This targets the actual failure and is the option worth designing. (d) EMBEDDINGS as the tiebreaker in the band, which `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` already asks about — and this trial is the strongest evidence yet FOR it, because the lexical signal is not merely weak here, it is INVERTED. (e) MAKE IT LOUD RATHER THAN CORRECT — keep merging but report every merge for review. Weakest alone, necessary in any case.

MY OWN DEFECT, FOUND BY THE SAME TRIAL AND FIXED BY NOBODY YET: `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` is a `usize`. The single-document `IngestReport` carries `Vec<FuzzyMerge>` and its doc comment says "auditable, never silent" — the corpus aggregate reduces that to a COUNT, so at exactly the scale where silent merges matter most, WHAT was merged is unrecoverable from the report. That is a regression I introduced in BL-186 and it should be fixed before anyone runs a real corpus.

NOT MEASURED, AND IT BOUNDS EVERYTHING ABOVE: what this does to the other 1,118 documents. The trial was SIX documents chosen for topical overlap. The 44% figure is one document's crate list, not a corpus-wide rate.","name":"OPEN — auto-merge at 90 silently destroys SIBLING components and misses the duplicates it exists to catch; the threshold is backwards for real naming conventions","rationale":"Filed the moment the trial produced it, with the scores rather than the impression, because "fuzzy matching is too aggressive" is the kind of claim that decays into folklore and then gets re-argued from scratch. The six numbers are reproducible from `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio` directly.

Recorded as its own node rather than as an amendment to `cap:corpus-ingest` because the capability is not where the defect lives — isolating a single document proved it is `ingest`'s, and attaching it to the corpus capability would have embalmed the misdiagnosis the trial itself corrected.

The self-criticism about `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` is on the node deliberately: the trial's most useful property was that it could show WHAT converged, and the shipped report cannot. Recording that where the fix will be read is worth more than recording it where it would be flattering.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"The surplus half of DETECT. Every existing gap asks what is MISSING; this asks what is SURPLUS — realized or verified, and downstream of nothing.

THE SIGNAL, computable from the graph as it stands: a Capability at `realized`/`verified` with no incoming DEPENDS_ON, no PART_OF_FLOW into any Flow, and no Actor INTERACTS_WITH. The same shape generalises to a Component whose Interfaces nothing CONSUMES, and to an Artifact realizing only capabilities that are themselves unconsumed.

⚠️ THE WORDING IS THE FEATURE, not a caveat on it. The graph knows DESIGN-LEVEL demand and nothing about runtime usage, so the honest finding is \"NOTHING IN THIS DESIGN CONSUMES X\" — never \"X is unused\". A feature real users call daily whose consumer was never modelled produces exactly the same graph shape as a dead one, and a detector that did not say so would confidently recommend deleting working code. Reported as a FACT rather than a gap for the same reason granularity_report and surprising_connections are: which side is wrong is the user's to say.

WHY IT IS NOT unmotivated_capability: that fires on a capability satisfying no REQUIREMENT — a question about intent, gated on requirements existing at all. A capability can satisfy a requirement perfectly and still be consumed by nothing, and that is the expensive case, because the paperwork is complete and the code is dead.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED HERE: runtime usage. dec:bl-155 and dec:idea-measure-the-surface hold that question, and answering it needs telemetry rather than the graph.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"A built thing that nothing in the design consumes is surfaced, and says so as a design-completeness finding rather than a verdict on the system","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

An agent notices the shape of a rule — \"we always…\", a convention the build already follows but nothing records, a choice about HOW rather than WHAT — and asks the user what breaking it should cost, in language needing no vocabulary: \"if somebody pushed straight to main, should the build have stopped them, or is that advice?\" The answer is written to `enforced` EXPLICITLY in both directions. That is the load-bearing part: `enforced` defaults to true, so leaving it unset does not mean advisory, it means gate-blocking — and a rule that reaches that status by silence then owes a detector it never agreed to, which is exactly how all four of reflow2's own enforced rules got there. {"decision":"**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.** Anthony, 2026-08-26, in his own words:

*"can we construct skills or tools in a factory that ensures they get the required mechanics/functions? then when we need to make a 'class' change, it is fixing the factory, not the individual skill."*

📌 DISTINCT FROM `dec:idea-a-tool-class-should-carry-a-contract-that-something-checks`, which asks WHAT a class must guarantee. This asks HOW the guarantee is delivered — by construction, or by inspection after the fact. Both answers are available for any contract, and the choice between them is the whole content here.

═══ THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS ═══

**A CHECK finds the omission after somebody made it. A FACTORY makes the omission unconstructable.** Today's fix is the first: `every_category_states_whether_it_reads_proposed` catches an unclassified category at compile time, but only after somebody wrote it. A factory would mean a finding kind cannot come into existence without answering.

This is the shape Anthony is reaching for, and the payoff he names is real: **a class change becomes one edit instead of N.** Today's change edited three call sites for one rule. The three instances this week each edited between one and three sites. Nothing has yet needed editing across all 173 tools — which is either evidence the problem is small, or evidence it has not bitten yet.

═══ WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, because the answer is not "nothing" ═══

- **`#[tool]` is already a proc macro** — construction already runs through a single point. Whether it can be made to REQUIRE annotations is a technical question nobody has asked. This is the most promising unexamined lead here.
- **`skill_lint.py`, 1126 lines** — the inspection route, already built and already large.
- **`HealCategory::ALL` plus two exhaustive-match tests** — the compile-time route at its smallest, and it works.
- **The 12 tool-surface slices** — a classification that already exists and deliberately holds no function.

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) EXTEND THE `#[tool]` MACRO to require the annotation set.** The factory Anthony describes, in the place construction already happens. Missing annotation = compile error, no list to maintain. ⚠️ Counter: proc-macro work is unpleasant to debug, and a required field with a default is not required at all — the design would have to refuse silence, which means touching all 173 declarations once.

**(b) A CONSTRUCTOR FUNCTION / TRAIT rather than a macro change.** Each tool built through a typed builder that cannot be finished incomplete. ⚠️ Counter: heavier than the macro that is already there, and the macro is the thing standing between the author and the surface.

**(c) KEEP INSPECTION, MAKE IT EXHAUSTIVE.** No factory; just ensure every class has one test asserting every member answers. ⚠️ Counter: this is what the repo already does, and it is what let three instances through — each guard was written after its own incident, never before the next.

**(d) NOT WORTH IT YET.** No class change has ever required editing more than three sites. ⚠️ Counter: the cost being counted is wrong — the expensive part was never the editing, it was the DISCOVERY, and each discovery came from a user hitting it in the field.

═══ ⚠️ THE COUNTERWEIGHTS, and there are two real ones ═══

**1. A factory guarantees the mechanics are PRESENT, never that they are RIGHT.** Every instance this week was a case where the mechanism existed and the JUDGEMENT was missing — `unallocated_component` could have read the ruling, the replay contract was written down, `proposed` was documented in four places. A factory that injects a required field produces 173 tools with a field filled in to satisfy the compiler. That is the `internal`-by-default trap the interface `designation` field already documents: *"BECAUSE it is the default, `internal` cannot distinguish 'deliberately internal' from 'nobody classified this'."* **A factory can manufacture exactly that ambiguity at scale.**

**2. Over-engineering, and it is his own standing concern.** *"designs get so overcomplicated when often a simple solution will do."* A factory, a registry and a class taxonomy is the shape an engineer reaches for. The measured alternative is one exhaustive match per class — roughly fifteen lines, no new machinery, and it has now worked twice in the same file.

⇒ Which suggests the cheapest honest test: **name a change that WOULD have required editing all 173 tools.** If one exists, the factory earns itself. If none does, option (d) is the answer and the exhaustive-match habit is enough.","name":"OPEN — should skills and tools be CONSTRUCTED through something that gives them the required mechanics, so a class change is one edit rather than N?","rationale":"Kept separate from the contract question because WHAT a class guarantees and HOW that guarantee is delivered are independently answerable — a contract can be enforced by construction or by inspection, and picking one does not settle the other.

Recorded with the two counterweights at full strength because both are Anthony's own reasoning turned on his own idea: he watches for over-engineering, and he has said that a fix must reach the cause. A factory reaches the MECHANISM and not the JUDGEMENT, and every instance this week was a missing judgement beside a present mechanism. That is the strongest argument against the idea and it belongs on the node rather than in a reply he will not see again.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures.

HAND-ROLLED AND SYNCHRONOUS, IN `reflow2-core` (`dec:content-store-implementation`). `put` / `get` / `exists` over `sha2` and `std::fs`. Zero new crates in the core, no async runtime. `object_store` was measured and recorded as the documented UPGRADE PATH rather than adopted: 36 crates new to reflow2, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery a local store never calls, buying a feature set — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — that immutable content addressing does not have.

REACHABLE FROM A SESSION as `content_put` / `content_get` / `content_exists` (`req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session`). That requirement exists because this capability was first marked `realized` while NOTHING COULD CALL IT — complete in the core, tested, carrying a passing check, and unreachable by every agent and person who would use it. Content arrives as `text` or `base64` (JSON carries no raw bytes), exactly one, and the store's root comes from `--content-path` rather than being derived from `--graph-path`, because the graph lives under a gitignored directory and blobs are COMMITTED so they travel with the design.

FOUR REFUSALS, which is where this earns its keep — each pinned by a test, two mutation-checked. `get` VERIFIES bytes against the hash they are stored under and refuses a mismatch: a content hash nobody checks is only a filename. A malformed hash is refused BEFORE it reaches the filesystem, since a hash is interpolated into a path. Passing both `text` and `base64` is refused rather than resolved by picking one. And a server with no store configured says so instead of inventing a directory — where blobs live is a decision about the consumer's repo.

Writes are temp-then-rename, so a process that dies mid-write leaves nothing or a whole blob, and a stranded temp file is unreachable as content because its name is not a hash. Reading INTO stored content is not this capability's job and never becomes one — the agent navigates, the graph records an opaque locator reflow2 never parses (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). What belongs here versus natively in the repo is `dec:what-lives-where`. REALIZED; `ver:content-store` and `ver:content-surface` passing.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

Anthony, 2026-07-25: COORD.md was invented so he and his brother could coordinate; the claims layer shipped the same day; and reflow2 is developed by using reflow2 on itself, so the question is whether the markdown board should now be a graph read. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE, because it is less than it sounds: `claim_region` records a Contributor holding a seed node to a depth, `claim_report` computes the region and the overlaps, and both travel in the committed export exactly as COORD.md travels in git — so visibility is unchanged, and the gain is that the region is COMPUTED from the design (it follows the graph as the design moves) rather than being a hand-typed list of file paths that goes stale silently. The sane split, if this is taken: claims in the graph for WHO HAS WHAT, COORD.md retained for the conventions and the conflict doctrine, and the in-progress table deleted rather than maintained in two places, since two places for the same fact is the failure the backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.","name":"OPEN — does reflow2's own claim board move from COORD.md into the graph?","rationale":"Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it is a genuinely good test of the claims layer, because reflow2's own two-person collaboration is the only live multi-writer case that exists. {"decision":"DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) ANTHONY'S REASONING, WHICH CORRECTS THE WEAKNESS THIS OPTION WAS RECORDED WITH. The objection on file was that deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. That conflated two different things. THE SUBJECT SYSTEM and THE DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and a sweep only ever covers the second. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So the derived scope is not a code-only convenience; it is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for hardware than for software, because there the artifacts are all there is to sweep. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, NOT THE NORM — and it is special by being MORE than the norm, not less: 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. For a codebase the repo holds the subject system AND the design artifacts at once, so a sweep sees both; for everything else it sees the artifacts, which is all a coverage question ever asked about. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).","name":"Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system","rationale":"Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.","status":"accepted"}

{"description":"Given a filesystem path to a design store, report which design is there — its stable graph id, its label, whether that identity was minted or adopted, and the schema stamp the store carries — WITHOUT opening it, locking it, or writing anything. The paired half of discovery: the agent walks the tree and finds `.reflow2` directories (file navigation, which reflow2 does not do), and this answers what each one IS, so a person can be shown a menu before anything is created.

WHAT IT PREVENTS, measured: a session at the root of `hxm_program` was told "this directory has no design yet" and minted a THIRD graph while two populated ones sat one and two directories down. The agent could have listed the paths; nothing could say what they were.

BUILT 2026-08-05 as `describe_designs`, served on BOTH the full surface and the LATENT (no-design) surface — the latter deliberately, because a session with no design is the exact moment someone is about to create one, and a discovery tool only reachable after a design exists would arrive too late. Takes a LIST of paths, because the caller is sweeping a tree and one round trip per candidate is the wrong shape for a menu.

⭐ TWO DEVIATIONS FROM `dec:describe-a-design-without-binding-to-it`, BOTH FORCED BY THE CODE AND BOTH IMPROVEMENTS ON WHAT WAS ASKED FOR.

(1) NO NODE COUNTS. The decision said the report would carry "node counts by type". It cannot, and the reason is the whole design: `DesignGraph::open_rocksdb_with_provenance` WRITES `<path>.meta.json` via `check_and_stamp` and MINTS `<path>.id.json` via `identity::resolve` when the store has none. So counting would mean opening, and opening an unnamed store would NAME IT — inspecting a design would create the thing it was asked to look for. Identity and stamp answer *which design is this and how old is its schema*, which is what choosing between designs actually needs; size is not worth minting an identity to get.

(2) NO `busy` STATE, AND IT IS NOT MISSING. The decision flagged "must distinguish busy from absent" because a store held by a running server is exclusively locked. That turned out to be MOOT: everything reported comes from the two sidecar files beside the store, so nothing is ever locked and a design another session is writing right now describes perfectly. The requirement was met by removing the condition rather than by handling it.

THE STATES IT DOES REPORT, and the distinction that carries the value: `design` (named from its sidecar), `unnamed` (something is there whose identity cannot be read without opening — reported as such rather than named by the act of asking), `opted_in` (directory exists, nothing written yet), `absent` (nothing here). SOMETHING-UNNAMED MUST NEVER READ AS NOTHING-HERE, because "no design here" is the sentence that starts an unwanted one. Every row also carries a plain-language `reading`, because a bare enum makes the caller invent the meaning.

SHIPPED WITH THE INSTRUCTION THAT MAKES ANYONE CALL IT. `reflow2_start_design`'s description previously ended "it is safe to call when unsure" with no mention of looking around — the sentence behind the accident. It now requires a nearby sweep first and says why, and its payload tells a caller who skipped the check to say so immediately, while the recovery is still a deletion rather than a merge. A tool no skill tells anyone to use is this project's own recurring defect ([BL-152], [BL-178], [BL-197], [BL-204]); shipping the tool without the instruction would have been the fifth.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: how a session is then POINTED at the chosen design (`dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design`, open — with `dec:pointing-a-session-is-project-scope-only` as the working field answer).","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what design lives at a path, without binding to it","provenance":"authored","status":"verified","tier":"operational"}

{"category":"convention","enforced":true,"name":"Design intent moves only on the owner's word — an agent may propose anything and settle nothing","statement":"A NODE THAT ASSERTS INTENT REACHES A SETTLED STATE ONLY BECAUSE ANTHONY SAID SO. An agent may create, draft, measure, argue and recommend without limit; it may not move a Requirement off `proposed`, mark a Decision `accepted`, or record a rule's enforcement on his behalf. Alex is a genuine design contributor and second user (`who:alex`), and his input is ADVISORY — it informs and gates nothing.

ENFORCED — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the consequence question directly ("if a session recorded a decision as accepted without you saying so, should that stop the build, or is it advice?"): stop the build.

⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it was not predicted. Asked the same question about the branch-then-PR process rule minutes earlier, he answered ADVICE. So in a one-developer project the PROCESS rule is self-discipline and the AUTHORITY rule is inviolable — the opposite of the naive expectation that a solo project needs no authority modelling because there is only one person. What one person needs protection from is not another person; it is an AGENT WRITING IN HIS VOICE. That is a data point for `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` from the simple end of the scale, where every other data point so far came from a multi-agent fleet.

WHAT IT OWES, stated plainly rather than quietly closed: a DETECTOR. `unverified_enforced_rule` will fire at 0.6 and stay until a PASSING Verification is attached — a `planned` one does not silence it. NO CHECK IS ATTACHED TODAY, deliberately: the governance-proposal skill's standing warning is that attaching a check to close a finding is green-washing, and a passing check that tests nothing is a lie the graph cannot see.

THE CHECK THAT WOULD ACTUALLY DETECT IT, so the debt is specific rather than vague: every Decision at `accepted` carries an AUTHORED_BY edge to `who:ajs`, and every Requirement off `proposed` likewise. This is unusually checkable for a governance rule — the graph already holds the edge, and `loop_status` already computes the mirror image (a `proposed` Decision with an approver who has not answered). What is missing is the inverse: a SETTLED node with nobody's name on it.

ALREADY PARTLY MECHANIZED, which is why enforcement is not a bluff: `add_decision` lands at `proposed`; `add_requirement` lands at `proposed`; `dec:certainty-derived` derives a requirement's certainty from status × provenance because every move off `proposed` records the user's word; `set_requirement_status`'s own guardrail says promoting it yourself forges their signature; and `dec:three-party-checks` states the division — the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides. The rule names the policy those mechanisms serve, which until now was implemented everywhere and stated nowhere.

HONEST BOUND: the tooling resists the violation but cannot presently REPORT one, which is exactly the gap the enforcement flag now makes visible instead of leaving to good behaviour."}

{"category":"methodology","enforced":false,"name":"Before 1.0, a thing done wrong is CORRECTED, not patched around — compatibility is not a reason to keep a mistake","statement":"WHEN SOMETHING IN REFLOW2 IS WRONG, THE FIX IS THE FULL ONE. A workaround, a compatibility shim, or a repair that leaves the original mistake in place is not the answer while this project is still in development. "It would break consumers" is not, on its own, a reason to keep a defect — it is a reason to do it NOW rather than later.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-17, in his own words: "as we are still in development; I'm more concerned with doing things right. If we did something wrong the first time, it is better to fully correct/fix it now than to do patch or workaround it. I'd rather pay for this change now than when we have hundreds/thousands of users and we can't make big changes out of fear that we may upset something that is working."

⭐ THE COST ARGUMENT RUNS THE OPPOSITE WAY FROM THE USUAL INSTINCT, and that is the whole rule. The instinct is that a breaking change is expensive, so defer it. The instinct is right about the price and wrong about the direction of the trend: the price of a break RISES with every consumer, so deferring is buying the same change later at a higher cost, in a currency (user trust, migration effort, fear of touching working code) that is worse than the one it is cheap in now.

WHAT IT IS NOT. Not licence to rewrite what merely displeases — the trigger is something WRONG, not something one would style differently. Not licence to widen a task: a correction still gets recorded, tested and reviewed like any change, and `dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key`'s own warning about doing a shape change "under the cover of" finishing something else still stands. The rule changes which OPTION is chosen when a defect is real; it does not change what counts as a defect, and it does not authorise an agent to settle intent (`rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is untouched by it).

WHERE THE HORIZON IS. CHANGELOG.md already says Major/1.0 is "deferred until a stability commitment — the design surface promising compatibility". This rule is the other side of that sentence: until that commitment exists, the surface is explicitly not promising, and behaving as though it were is the mistake. The rule therefore has a natural end — it should be revisited at 1.0 rather than carried into it.

⚠️ WHAT IT ALREADY OVERTURNS, recorded so the reversal is on the record rather than inferred: `dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key` (2026-08-17, hours earlier) declined to rename the `disconnected_community` defect category, on the ground that the key is a consumer contract and renaming it would "break every consumer in order to fix a sentence". Under this rule that ground no longer carries, and the same decision's deferred item — giving unscoped `detect_defects` the same envelope its scoped sibling already returns — moves from deferred to owed.

ENFORCEMENT NOT YET STATED, deliberately. Whether breaking this should stop a build is Anthony's to say, and it is a hard case besides: this rule is about a JUDGEMENT (was the full fix taken?) rather than about graph state, so it may be a genuine instance of a rule no detector can check — the first real customer for `req:a-rule-says-whether-it-can-be-checked-at-all` alongside `rule:bl-41`."}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — surfaced by the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review, but NOT a new idea: this question already exists as PROSE in docs/requirements-coverage.md ("Note: are embeddings (an embeddings-rs sidecar) actually needed?"). Recording it here moves it from a document into the graph, which is the direction dec:what-lives-where argues for; it does not settle it.

WHAT IS AVAILABLE AND UNUSED: dynograph-vector ships an HNSW approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HnswConfig / HnswIndex / SearchResult, with filtered, batch and snapshot-persisted search) plus SIMD cosine similarity and the whole distance family. reflow2 uses none of it. search_design is BM25 lexical, and the schema carries embedding_field declarations on several node types that nothing populates.

THE CASE FOR: semantic search would find a requirement whose words differ from the query's. It would also strengthen resolution — the duplicate-detection path already has a fuzzy_then_vector strategy declared in the schema with the vector half unimplemented.

THE CASE AGAINST, and it is why this has stayed parked: embeddings need a MODEL, and reflow2-core is deliberately LLM-free and deterministic. An embedding provider at the core would break that, and putting it at the seam means a sidecar to install, version and keep in sync — which cuts against req:thin-install and the whole served-not-installed posture. Determinism is also load-bearing here: two runs of a detector must agree, and an ANN index is approximate by construction.

NOT AN IDEA I AM ADVOCATING — recorded so the question is findable in the graph rather than only in a documentation footnote.","name":"OPEN — should reflow2 adopt embeddings and the HNSW index, or stay on lexical search?","rationale":"Captured because the review found the HNSW index entirely unused and the question live only in prose. {"decision":"NOT DECIDED. `schema/core.yaml` gives `DesignRule.enforced` a default of `true`, described as 'whether violations are gate-blocking'. So a rule captured without anyone saying a word about enforcement asserts that breaking it should stop the build. THE QUESTION: should an unstated `enforced` mean gate-blocking (today's answer), advisory, or should the property be REQUIRED so the choice is always somebody's rather than the schema's? OPTION A — leave it. Cheapest, and defensible: a rule worth recording is usually a rule you mean. Cost: reflow2's own four enforced rules all reached that status by silence, and none of them was a deliberate choice. OPTION B — flip the default to false. A convention becomes advice unless somebody promotes it. Cost: it is a behaviour change for every existing rule in every installed graph, and it would silently downgrade rules somebody DID mean; it also needs a decision about whether existing `true` values are explicit or inherited, which the graph cannot currently distinguish. OPTION C — make it required, so `add_*` refuses a rule that does not say. WHY IT MATTERS NOW rather than as a curiosity: `unverified_enforced_rule` bills every enforced rule for a detector. With the default at `true`, that bill lands on rules nobody chose to enforce, which is how a true detector becomes a nag. Recorded as its own decision point rather than resolved in passing, because a default IS a decision: it is currently making the gate-blocking claim on every user's behalf, silently, and it reached reflow2's own four enforced rules that way. The exception below still stands exactly as reasoned — skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED, and only commands are installed — but the SET is no longer eight. **Twenty-two command files now ship** (twenty fronting a skill, plus `debt.md` and `decisions.md` which front tools), and `skill_lint` now fails a skill that no command names, so the number cannot silently fall behind again. The original ruling, and its reasoning, is kept below unedited.

════════ AS RULED 2026-07-28 ════════

The eight slash commands (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) are INSTALLED into a consumer project's `.claude/commands/`. WHY THAT DECISION EXISTS: a copied skill goes stale, and the agent then loads last release's content in preference to what the server would serve. That happened here for four releases running without anything noticing, which is why nothing is copied.

WHY A COMMAND IS DIFFERENT: each is four lines that name a skill and say how to report the answer. There is no version-coupled content in it. When the skill behind it changes, the command is still correct, because the skill is fetched fresh at use time — the command is a pointer, and the thing it points at is the thing that moves.

THE ONE WAY IT CAN ROT, and it is now closed: a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that, so the failure is caught in this repo rather than discovered in a consumer's, where the symptom would be an agent reporting it cannot find a skill the user was told to use. The mirror is byte-checked too, so `.claude/commands` cannot drift from the kit source.

WHAT IT COSTS IF WE ARE WRONG: eight small files in a consumer repo, each independently deletable, none of which changes behaviour when stale. Compare the cost of a stale skill, which silently answers with last release's method.

WHY IT WAS WORTH DOING AT ALL: without them a consumer install is experienced as BROKEN rather than thin — the skills are reachable and nothing tells you they are. properties.state:
{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures.

HAND-ROLLED AND SYNCHRONOUS, IN `reflow2-core` (`dec:content-store-implementation`). `put` / `get` / `exists` over `sha2` and `std::fs`. Zero new crates in the core, no async runtime. `object_store` was measured and recorded as the documented UPGRADE PATH rather than adopted: 36 crates new to reflow2, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery a local store never calls, buying a feature set — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — that immutable content addressing does not have.

REACHABLE FROM A SESSION as `content_put` / `content_get` / `content_exists` (`req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session`). That requirement exists because this capability was first marked `realized` while NOTHING COULD CALL IT — complete in the core, tested, carrying a passing check, and unreachable by every agent and person who would use it. Content arrives as `text` or `base64` (JSON carries no raw bytes), exactly one, and the store's root comes from `--content-path` rather than being derived from `--graph-path`, because the graph lives under a gitignored directory and blobs are COMMITTED so they travel with the design.

FOUR REFUSALS, which is where this earns its keep — each pinned by a test, two mutation-checked. `get` VERIFIES bytes against the hash they are stored under and refuses a mismatch: a content hash nobody checks is only a filename. A malformed hash is refused BEFORE it reaches the filesystem, since a hash is interpolated into a path. Passing both `text` and `base64` is refused rather than resolved by picking one. And a server with no store configured says so instead of inventing a directory — where blobs live is a decision about the consumer's repo.

Writes are temp-then-rename, so a process that dies mid-write leaves nothing or a whole blob, and a stranded temp file is unreachable as content because its name is not a hash. Reading INTO stored content is not this capability's job and never becomes one — the agent navigates, the graph records an opaque locator reflow2 never parses (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). What belongs here versus natively in the repo is `dec:what-lives-where`. REALIZED; `ver:content-store` and `ver:content-surface` passing.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"category":"convention","enforced":true,"name":"Design information lives in the graph, not in documents","statement":"This project does not store design information in documents. What a document would have said belongs in the graph as typed nodes. Anthony's word, 2026-08-15: "we no longer use documents to store info. should be in graph" — and, on the buildup of two feedback files captured only partially, "we can't let this buildup occur again".

ENFORCEMENT IS HIS EXPLICIT ANSWER, NOT AN INHERITED DEFAULT. Asked what should happen if somebody added a markdown file holding design information — good content, tests passing — he chose STOP THE BUILD over advice and over leaving it unstated.

⚠️ THIS RULE OWES A DETECTOR AND CANNOT HAVE ONE YET, because two things must be scoped before a check could tell a violation from ordinary work:

(1) SCOPE. 187 markdown files are tracked outside `docs/design/`. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, COORD.md, REFLOW2.md, README, CHANGELOG and every served SKILL.md are documents, and several are load-bearing instructions the project cannot function without. A check that cannot say which of the 187 are violations would either fail every build or none.

(2) A CONFLICT WITH THE SCHEMA'S OWN DESIGN, measured 2026-08-15 while trying to comply with this rule: `Fragment.content_ref` is described as a "Pointer to the source content (path/hash) RATHER THAN INLINING IT", and Fragment carries no field for a document's text — only title, summary, intent and that pointer. `Artifact.location` and the `DOCUMENTS` edge are built on the same assumption. So reflow2's vocabulary currently presumes documents EXIST and that the graph points AT them; it has no way to absorb prose. Under a literal reading of this rule, `capture-intent`'s own step 3 — which instructs an agent to register a source document as an Artifact with a location — would itself be a violation.

SO THE RULE IS RECORDED AS STATED AND AS ENFORCED, and what it means operationally is the open part. Nothing here softens it: it is his rule and his enforcement choice. What is unresolved is what counts as "design information" versus operating instructions, and whether the graph gains a way to hold prose or the rule scopes around the fact that it cannot."}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A session can find out what designs exist nearby and be told which one to use, rather than inheriting one from where the shell happened to be","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Which design a session writes to must be a STATED CHOICE, and the information needed to make that choice must be available BEFORE anything is created. Two halves: (1) an agent must be able to discover what designs exist in and around a working tree and what each one holds — label, size, when it was minted — without opening a session against each; (2) a session must be able to be pointed at a chosen design explicitly.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-05, after the hxm_program field report: "can we just pass the location of the reflow2 graph via a prompt or skill; it can default to whichever folder path that the session is opened in, but maybe we could just say 'use reflow2 graph as /path/to/reflow2/graph/to/use/for/this/session'." And on the mechanism, once told a skill could not do it alone: "I like this approach of just pointing .mcp.json at the graph_id... an agent within a session can usually change files. can a reflow2 tool be to simply return all graph_ids to the agent and the agent then can choose whichever graph_id the user specifies to use for the project?"

WHY IT IS A REQUIREMENT AND NOT A CONVENIENCE. Today the answer is implicit: `.mcp.json` passes a RELATIVE `--graph-path`, so the design a session edits is decided by where the shell was opened, with no ancestor walk and no report of what else exists. Measured consequence, on Anthony's own repo the same day: a session at the root was told "this directory has no design yet" and minted a THIRD graph while two populated ones sat one and two directories down (`dec:no-design-here-never-looked`). An implicit answer to "which design am I editing" is not a smaller version of an explicit one — it is the mechanism by which a design gets created in the wrong place and nobody is told.

THE DIVISION OF LABOUR THIS INHERITS, and it shapes the answer rather than limiting it: reflow2 performs NO FILE IO (`dec:agent-navigates-content`), so WALKING THE TREE TO FIND `.reflow2` DIRECTORIES IS THE AGENT'S JOB — Anthony's own observation that "an agent within a session can usually change files" is the same point from the other side. What only reflow2 can answer is what a store at a given path actually HOLDS. So the requirement is met by a pair, not by one tool.

⚠️ MEASURED, AND IT CORRECTS THE OBVIOUS READING OF THE ASK: "return all graph_ids" would return ONE per store today. Storage keys are `{graph_id}\x00{type}\x00{id}` and `dynograph_storage::keys::graph_prefix` exists, so many graphs per store is supported by the FOUNDATION — but reflow2 opens one graph per store by convention (`DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID`, one `.reflow2` directory per project), and the three graphs in this field report are three separate STORES. Enumerating within a store is therefore true and not useful yet; describing a store found on disk is what the case actually needs.

NOT SETTLED HERE, deliberately: whether being "pointed at a design" means editing `.mcp.json` and reconnecting (cheap, works today, needs no release) or a graph reference carried per call (no reconnect, much larger). That is `dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design`.

Status `proposed`: captured in Anthony's words and awaiting his confirmation of the wording.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"The capture half of KPPs, and the half a person actually touches. Anthony, 2026-07-25: the user says \\\"the system should be able to perform X\\\"; the agent, acting as the systems-engineering SME the user is not required to be (req:no-se-knowledge), recognises the shape of inviolable intent and asks — that sounds like something that MUST be met, is it? — and the user confirms or declines. WHY THE AGENT MUST NOT DECIDE IT: criticality is a claim about consequence, not about wording. Whether missing a threshold FAILS THE EFFORT depends on mission, contract and money that the graph does not hold and the agent cannot see. An agent that promoted a requirement to KPP on its own would be asserting the user's stake in their own project, which is the same forgery dec:certainty-derived forbids for requirement status — and worse here, because a KPP outranks every ordinary gap and would drag the whole detector's ranking with it. So: the agent PROPOSES, the human DISPOSES, and nothing enters as a KPP without the user's word. WHAT THE AGENT CAN LEGITIMATELY NOTICE, and it is more than intuition. A statement carrying a unit-bearing threshold (500 miles, 3000 pounds, 500 milliseconds) is already shaped like a KPP and may simply be unmodelled — the quantity/limit/direction triple has somewhere to go. Language of necessity ('must', 'shall', 'no less than') against language of preference ('should', 'aims to') is a real signal in acquisition prose. And a requirement whose failure the user has elsewhere described as fatal is a candidate the graph itself can surface. THE QUESTION MUST CARRY THE CONSEQUENCE, not just the label: asking 'is this a KPP?' invites a shrug, whereas asking 'if the system missed this by ten percent, would the effort have failed?' is answerable by someone who has never heard the term — which is the test req:no-se-knowledge sets. On confirmation the agent sets category kpp, and should ask for the threshold and, where one exists, the objective; on decline it stays an ordinary Requirement and the offer is not repeated. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Notice when a stated need is really a KPP, and ask","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"decision":"UNDECIDED. REFRAMED 2026-07-25 by Anthony, and the reframe is the useful part: what he and his brother were asking for is not a staging GATE, it is a KIND. \"I think I now realize what my brother's idea was trying to say — it is like a brainstorming session where you can work through ideas without committing to anything yet. These would be more like 'ideas' not yet fleshed out and could be held in the graph as just that, 'brainstorming ideas'.\" That dissolves the contradiction this decision was opened over. The git study rejected the index because a gate between every edit and the graph is where intent goes to be forgotten; a brainstorm is the opposite move — the idea DOES enter the graph, immediately, labelled as what it is. Nothing waits outside, so nothing is lost, and the design still never claims a half-formed thought as intent. THE QUESTION THAT REMAINS IS THE VOCABULARY ONE, and dec:edge-orthogonality decides it: a distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it. So what would read `brainstorm`? The candidates, none of them chosen: gap detection must NOT nag about an idea nobody committed to (an unsatisfied brainstorm is not a hole in the design, and today an unsatisfied Requirement fires forever); delivery and certainty counts must exclude it, or the denominator becomes meaningless; promotion must be an explicit human act — a brainstorm becoming a Requirement is the same signature-forging risk dec:certainty-derived guards, one step earlier; and a brainstorm nobody has touched in months is a candidate for retirement rather than an accusation. If none of those is built, the label is decoration and the honest answer is to keep using `proposed` Decisions the way this session already did for the worktree ideas (dec:concurrent-work-isolation). PRIOR FRAMING, KEPT because it is what was true yesterday: the ask read as an opt-in \"think first, commit later\" mode; what already works is that a session making no write calls IS rubber-ducking, and the read tools are the ducking aids; and the narrow question was what happens at the END of such a session — one deliberate commit, with discarded branches either dropped or preserved as unchosen alternatives under a decision point. That question survives the reframe and is now the second half of it: if ideas land as ideas, the end of a brainstorm is a promotion step, not a commit step.","name":"OPEN — do half-formed ideas get a place in the graph, distinct from things the design asserts?","rationale":"Raised by Anthony and his brother 2026-07-24, reframed by Anthony 2026-07-25 while brainstorming the concurrency ideas — which is itself the evidence for the feature: he produced four options he explicitly did not want to commit to, and the only place to put them was a `proposed` Decision, a node type meant for a choice someone is actually facing. That works, and it is why this is not urgent; it is also a slightly wrong fit, and knowing why is worth recording. Still held proposed because the vocabulary question above is unanswered, and because it may be a SKILL rather than a schema change: a brainstorm skill that records ideas as proposed Decisions and asks before promoting any of them would test the practice without spending a schema change and an upgrade doc on a noun. Anthony's own words put it in that bracket — 'maybe a future skill'.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"UNDECIDED, and RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, explicitly not convinced by the collaboration design and thinking out loud: \"could you have small/mini reflow2 graphs inside itself... coming from a system of systems engineering approach, reflow2 may lay out the graph and how all the systems need to interact and where there are gaps, but what if we now had a mini-reflow2 graph for each system? And a mini-mini-reflow2 of the components in the system... the idea is that reflow2 has the tools to analyze the graph at each level and ensure there are no gaps and that it works with the higher level systems or system-of-systems.\" WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, because it changes what the idea is asking for. Levels exist and are already checked: Component.level is an enum of component / subsystem / system / system_of_systems / enterprise, CONTAINS between Components is the axis-Y spine, and hierarchy_issues already reports level_mismatch, missing_intermediate_level and orphan_level — the carburetor-to-body problem, imported from chain_reflow's matryoshka insight (docs/three-axes.md). And the multi-graph primitive exists unused: every node and edge carries graph_id, pinned to the constant \"reflow2\". So the question is not whether reflow2 can express nesting. It can. The question is whether a level should be a SUBTREE of one graph or a GRAPH OF ITS OWN. THREE OPTIONS. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL — today's shape. What is missing is not nesting but SCOPING: no read takes a subtree as its subject, so detect_gaps and graph_report always answer for the whole design. Adding a scope argument is a filter, not an architecture, and it delivers most of what was asked — the tools analysing each level. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM, COMPOSED — Anthony's idea. It buys four things one graph cannot: an independent write lock per system, which is a different and stronger answer to the collaboration problem than region claims, because separate graphs are PHYSICALLY separate where a claim is only advisory; an independent lifecycle, so a subsystem can be released, adopted or handed to a vendor on its own; selective publishing, which is exactly req:design-reachable-without-the-repo; and per-level scale, since detectors run over hundreds of nodes instead of tens of thousands. (c) A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY, LEVELS INSIDE EACH — the hybrid, and the shape federated systems engineering actually uses: you split where AUTHORITY splits, not where the hierarchy happens to have a layer. THE FOUR HARD PARTS of (b), each one real: the golden thread cannot cross a store boundary, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge — so a parent's Component pointing at a child's design needs a typed COORDINATE (graph id + node id + the export's content hash at the moment the reference was made), which is precisely the choice dec:fork-point-address already made for fork points over a native ref layer. Gap detection goes blind at the seam: a parent requirement whose satisfying capability lives in a child graph would fire unsatisfied forever unless the child's evidence rolls up — and that roll-up is cap:derived-completion's computation applied one level higher, which is encouraging rather than novel. Freshness becomes load-bearing: a parent's view of a child is a claim about a VERSION of that child, so it is a dated examined claim and never a live truth (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). And the seam becomes the new collision point: two people changing the interface across the boundary still collide, now in the one place with no merge machinery. THE TENSION WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the opposite destination — \"one graph the whole company plans in\", with the CEO's objectives at the top and everything tracing upward. Federation and one-big-graph cannot both be the end state, and nothing in the design has ever chosen between them. THE DISCRIMINATOR, offered as a finding and not a decision: depth alone does not justify a separate graph. Nesting three levels of graphs costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check at every seam, and buys nothing that a scope filter would not have delivered — unless something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED. Where those hold, a graph of its own is right. Where they do not, it is ceremony.","name":"OPEN — one graph with levels, or a graph per system composed into a bigger one?","rationale":"Recorded because Anthony said plainly he is not convinced by the collaboration design, and an unconvinced author is a finding, not a disagreement to be argued down. The three options and the ranking above are analysis offered for him to judge — the brainstorm skill's rule is that a counter-argument is recorded BESIDE an idea rather than used to talk someone out of it, and this decision is the first real test of that rule. Held proposed with nothing built, and deliberately without a Requirement: if federation is the answer it changes the shape of several settled things at once (dec:repo-file-embedded's single file, dec:central-host's hosting question, the whole org-scale destination), and that is a decision to make deliberately rather than to discover halfway through an implementation. The cheap next step, if he wants motion without commitment: add a scope argument to the existing detectors — option (a) — because it is a filter over machinery that already exists, it tests whether per-level analysis is what he actually wants, and it is a strict subset of what option (b) would need anyway, so it forecloses nothing (rule:no-foreclosure).","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"The design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read that distinction","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Some interfaces are the boundary a system is known by; most are internal plumbing. The design must be able to say which — and the distinction must earn its keep by being read, not merely stored (dec:edge-orthogonality). From the MOSA guidebook Anthony supplied (OUSD(R&E), February 2025), whose entire discipline turns on designating modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open, and independently from BL-45's system-of-systems thread, which found the same hole from the other side: nothing marks an Interface external-facing, so \"visible to others\" versus \"mine to change\" is undeclarable. Two independent routes to one missing property. What must read it, or the designation is decoration: a change that crosses a published boundary is a different risk from one that stays behind it, and impact analysis should say which it is BEFORE the edit; a design that publishes a surface should be able to export exactly that surface and nothing internal; and a composed design (req:design-composes) links through published boundaries, never through another system's internals. What this must NOT become: an assertion that a boundary is stable. Whether a published interface has in fact held is a matter of evidence — its drift history — not a property anyone sets.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"The open structural-defect list means still-needs-attention","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"A structural defect that has been reviewed and consciously accepted must move out of the open list into a reviewed one — not deleted, not hidden — the way an acknowledged gap already does. Two properties carried over from the gap side: the acceptance records WHY, as a real node that outlives the session, and it expires when the affected nodes change, so an accepted defect comes back for a fresh look rather than staying quietly accepted forever.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A cluster can be declared deliberately separate, so disconnected_community reports undeclared islands instead of one permanent warning","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"A group of nodes can be declared a DELIBERATE PARTITION — a subsystem that genuinely does not couple to the rest of the design — so `disconnected_community` reports "N declared partitions, 0 undeclared" rather than one standing warning. The value is NOT silencing the finding. It is that a NEW accidental island becomes visible against the declared ones, which today it is not.

THE DEFECT IN THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR IS THE SUGGESTED FIX, not the finding. `disconnected_community` proposes `generate_bridge` — creating edges to connect the cluster. Where the separation is correct, acting on that suggestion FABRICATES RELATIONSHIPS THAT DO NOT EXIST in order to silence a warning about a separation that is right. That is manufacturing connectivity, and it is the same act as formatting coverage into existence — with the difference that here THE TOOL PROPOSES IT.

WHY ACKNOWLEDGEMENT IS NOT ENOUGH, which is the part that makes this a mechanism and not a workflow note: `acknowledge_defect` is a one-time answer to a finding whose SIZE keeps changing. Acknowledged at 88 nodes it now reads 121 — at what point is it a different finding? And an alarm that can never be cleared is one everyone learns to skip, so the real disconnection arrives inside a warning nobody reads.

REFLOW2 HAS ALREADY MET THIS AND WROTE DOWN THE ANSWER, which is the strongest evidence that the shape is right. dec:documentation-has-no-operational-coupling (ACCEPTED, 2026-07-24) records the identical situation — three bridges attempted, all refused as lies, the island accepted — and concludes "flagging it is a false positive of the BL-84 family, and THE FIX BELONGS IN THE DETECTOR RATHER THAN IN THE DESIGN." It also states the exact constraint storyflow independently arrived at sixteen days later: "the exemption must not be written in a way that hides a genuine disconnection." The detector fix was never built, because that particular island dissolved on its own when a capability turned out to belong to two components.

REPRODUCED IN THIS DESIGN, 2026-08-09, WITHIN THE HOUR OF THE REPORT ARRIVING: capturing four governance requirements under dec:governance-integrates-not-splits produced heal:33d1548dae64e97a — "5 nodes form a cluster disconnected from the rest of the design", suggested_fix_type `generate_bridge`. No honest bridge existed, so none was drawn. Storyflow hit it at 121 nodes; reflow2 hit it at 5. Both clusters are GOVERNANCE, and both GROW as governance is properly captured — so the detector currently penalises exactly the work dec:governance-integrates-not-splits committed to.

SOURCE: storyflow gap D of the peer set — raised by storybug Boss (47accf78), characterised and filed by api-boss (05af57c1), 2026-08-09, v0.26.1. Their stated bound: the growth from 88 to 121 is suggestive, not proven, because the two measurements may not share a scope. What IS established is that the detector fires on a set provably containing nodes created hours earlier by the migration, and that its proposed remedy would corrupt the graph.","status":"proposed"}
