{"description":"--http <addr> serves the design over streamable HTTP so many client sessions share one process. The store is single-writer PER PROCESS, so this satisfies the constraint rather than working around it: one server means exactly one writer. rmcp builds a service per session through a factory, and ReflowService::share decides the split — the graph and the write generation are shared because they are properties of the design; the seat and the read-hint memory are minted fresh because they are properties of whoever just connected. The graph moved from a Mutex to an RwLock so concurrent reads do not queue behind each other, and the compiler audited the read/write split in the process: all 32 read sites genuinely need only &DesignGraph. No authentication — the flag's help and the startup line both say to bind loopback or a private network.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Several sessions work one design at once, through one server","provenance":"authored","status":"verified","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"BUILT 2026-07-25, the first rung of dec:nested-graphs option (c). An edge cannot cross a store because the schema validates both endpoints, so designs link by MIRRORING: `mirror_surface` brings another design's published surface in as local nodes marked `provenance: imported`, and the mirrored Project carries the coordinate — `mirror_of` (whose design), `mirror_content_hash` (which version of their surface), `mirrored_at` (when). Afterwards your own components provides/consumes the mirrored Interface with ORDINARY LOCAL EDGES, so the golden thread, propagate, and every detector work unchanged: foreignness became a property of the NODE rather than of the link, which is what makes the whole approach cheap. `mirrors()` lists who you are composed with and at what version. THE GUARD THAT MATTERS: import_graph is an upsert, so mirroring a surface whose ids collide with local ones would silently overwrite your design with someone else's nodes. A collision is REPORTED AND SKIPPED — your node survives untouched, and an edge touching a collided id is dropped rather than rewired, because pointing their PROVIDES at your same-named component would fabricate a relationship neither design asserted (dec:ask-not-repair). Two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between owners, not a merge. Mirroring a design into itself is refused outright, naming import_graph as what you meant. WHAT THE BUILD EXPOSED, and it is the honest limit: every reflow2 graph carried the same hardcoded graph_id, so no design could tell another from itself — rule:no-foreclosure item 5 arriving as a concrete blocker rather than a hypothetical. `open_in_memory_as` lets a design name itself, which is enough for library use and for the tests, but a DURABLE design's identity has to be remembered beside the store (the id namespaces every key, so reopening under a different name would find nothing). {"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Surfaced 2026-08-05 by Anthony's multi-project question, and it is the half his framing exposes that no existing node covers.

⭐ THE GAP. His stated benefit is that "a set of projects done in this manner can ALL INFLUENCE EACH OTHER." Everything reflow2 has built for crossing a design boundary shares CONTRACTS: `cap:publish-surface` publishes "just the boundary — the contracts others may rely on, and nothing internal", `cap:mirror-surface` brings the other side's published surface in as local nodes carrying a coordinate, and `cap:seam-incompatibility` says when two linked designs disagree at that boundary. ALL OF IT IS ABOUT INTERFACES. NOTHING CARRIES A DECISION OR A REQUIREMENT ACROSS. So two of his projects can be checked for whether they fit together, and still know nothing about why the other was built the way it was.

THAT IS PROBABLY NOT WHAT HE MEANS BY INFLUENCE. A ruling made in project_x — "we settled that outdoor units send cumulative totals, so a lost reading heals itself" — is exactly the kind of thing that should reach project_y, and it is not a contract. Neither is a requirement he holds across everything he builds. `dec:nested-graphs` deliberately made foreignness "a property of the NODE rather than of the link", which is the mechanism that WOULD carry this — the question is whether anything other than an Interface is allowed to be mirrored.

WHY IT MAY BE DELIBERATE RATHER THAN MISSING, and this is the strongest counter: `cap:publish-surface`'s whole point is "and nothing internal". A Decision is the most internal thing a design holds — it is the reasoning, the alternatives, the roads not taken. Publishing it is a much larger act than publishing a contract, and a boundary that leaks reasoning may not be a boundary at all. `dec:nested-graphs` chose ownership as the discriminator precisely so a design could share ONE part without sharing everything; letting intent cross could dissolve that.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) NOTHING CROSSES BUT CONTRACTS — today's behaviour, made explicit. Cheapest and defensible; the counter is that it answers Anthony's question with "you cannot have what you asked for" and he should hear that plainly rather than discover it. (b) A DESIGN MAY PUBLISH SELECTED DECISIONS AND REQUIREMENTS, not only Interfaces — publication stays deliberate, so nothing leaks, but the publishable set widens. Counter: `export_surface` and the surface vocabulary would need to say WHAT KIND of thing is published, and the mirrored copy raises a hard question nobody has answered — is a mirrored Decision still binding on the mirroring design, or only visible to it? (c) A STANDING "HOUSE RULES" DESIGN that his projects all mirror — one design holding the intent he carries everywhere (how he works, what he always requires), which every project mirrors and none owns. Fits the accepted rule cleanly, because that design IS separately owned and separately shared. Counter: nothing in reflow2 models a design with no build, and it is close to (d) on `dec:idea-one-owner-many-projects` without being the same thing. (d) DO NOT SOLVE IT IN THE GRAPH — this is what a person carries between their own projects, and the graph should not try to. Counter: that is the argument this whole product exists to reject, since "the person remembers" is what fails at eighteen months (`req:no-idea-goes-quiet`, accepted the same day).

NOT VERIFIED: whether `export_surface`/`mirror_surface` are structurally limited to Interfaces or merely conventionally used that way. If the mechanism is already general, (b) may be a vocabulary question rather than a build.

⚠️ AND THE PREREQUISITE THAT BOUNDS ALL OF IT: reflow2's own `maturity_report` puts SEAMS at 0 OF 73 — not one coupling in this design runs through a declared Interface that one side provides and the other consumes. So the machinery every option here builds on has never been exercised on the design that ships it, which is the same "self-host cannot see it" shape that hid [BL-176] for eleven releases and produced [BL-213] this morning. Any answer here should be trialled on two real designs before it is believed.","name":"OPEN — mirroring shares CONTRACTS; should INTENT cross a design boundary too, which is what "projects influence each other" actually asks for?","rationale":"Recorded separately from `dec:idea-one-owner-many-projects` because that node asks WHERE the boundary goes and this one asks WHAT MAY CROSS IT. They travel together and are answered differently: a person could put everything in one graph and still want to know whether intent crosses when they later split it.

Kept as a question rather than a proposal because the counter-argument is strong and structural: `cap:publish-surface` exists to publish the boundary "and nothing internal", so widening it is a change to what a design boundary MEANS, not an added feature. That deserves Anthony's word, not an agent's inference from one sentence of his.

The seams-at-zero warning is on the node deliberately. It is the second time in one day that a mechanism has turned out to be unexercised on reflow2's own design, and the first time cost a silent data-loss defect. Naming it here is cheaper than rediscovering it.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony is LEANING toward option (d) below as of 2026-07-30 — "I think I'm warming to this approach versus using git repos to capture the snapshot" — but has not said to promote it, so this stays a lean and not intent.

(d) GRAPH-ONLY, QUERIED RATHER THAN RENDERED. His words: "we could do this completely in the graph without git. We are just using git as a means to render a snapshot in time… it is reachable by 'what capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5' or 'what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?' and let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot."

WHY THIS IS STRONGER THAN THE FILE-PER-EPOCH RECOMMENDATION IT DISPLACES, and the displacement is a correction rather than a preference. Both things he named are QUESTIONS, not documents. A query answers them directly; a rendered file answers them only if someone rendered the right file at the right moment. And every materialised artifact needs a staleness check — `docs/design/reflow2.json` has one, `dataflow.html` has one, and `docs/loop-model.json` demonstrated the failure the same day by becoming permanently unreproducible. Not materialising is the only way to have no drift at all.

THE OBJECTION I RAISED AGAINST IT IS WEAKER THAN I THOUGHT, and this is the part worth correcting on the record. I argued that graph-only loses readability for someone not running reflow2 — a teammate, a reviewer, his brother — citing `req:design-reachable-without-the-repo`. But if the schedule lives in the graph, IT IS ALREADY IN THE COMMITTED EXPORT, which is in git on every commit. So the information is not unreachable; it is merely not pretty. Likewise "what did the plan say in March" is answerable today by `git log -p docs/design/reflow2.json` plus the export's own `prev_content_hash` chain. The file-per-epoch idea was therefore solving a problem the committed export already solves — adding an artifact to obtain a property that exists.

WHAT SURVIVES OF THE GIT IDEA, and it is narrower and better targeted. Git remains right where the thing being pinned actually LIVES in git: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, and "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" is a question about the product. So the version-combination pin (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`) keeps its place on arrival. Forward-looking plans, which describe graph content, stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals, which describe code, pin code.

A CONSEQUENCE WORTH NOTING FOR `req:graph-indexes-snapshots`. That requirement's stated intent is that "a user shouldn't have to remember which git branch a particular epoch or increment is in." Under (d) that is satisfied in the strongest possible way: there are no branches to remember, because nothing was put in one. The requirement's letter (index the snapshots) and its spirit (never make the user chase git) come apart here, and the spirit is the part he wrote it for.

RENDERING BECOMES AN OUTPUT, NOT A RECORD. "Let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot" is the right disposal: different consumers want different renderings — a markdown roadmap, a chart, a slide, a JSON feed — and choosing one file format now would be guessing on their behalf. `render_views.py` can emit an epoch view whenever asked, as a disposable projection.","name":"OPEN, but leaning — the schedule lives in the graph and is queried; nothing is snapshotted into git","rationale":"Anthony's idea and Anthony's lean, recorded as a lean. Nothing promoted: the brainstorm discipline is that an idea is not intent until he says so, and "warming to" is not "do it".

The correction to my own earlier recommendation is kept rather than tidied away. I had recommended file-per-epoch on main, and the reason it was wrong is instructive: the property I was reaching for — a git-visible history of the plan — already exists, because the schedule would live in the committed export and that file already has git history and its own lineage chain. Adding artifacts to obtain properties the design already has is the shape this project keeps finding, and it found it in my own advice this time.

The earlier wording of this node survives at `snap:epoch:wire-planning-cluster:dec:where-plans-live` and `:r2` — which are themselves the first production use of the second-revision-in-one-epoch fix landed on 2026-07-28.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"The graph is the index of its own snapshots","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Git already stores versions, tags, branches and releases well, and reflow2 must not duplicate that. What reflow2 must own is the MAP: the graph tracks its own snapshots — which epoch_n or increment_n a thing belongs to, and where that snapshot lives (the git ref) — so a user asks the graph and never has to remember which branch holds which epoch. Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'what does this mean for reflow2 when most of what I discussed is what git already does? I think the answer is that the graph should track the snapshots (it is one graph in time) and therefore which epoch_n or increment_n something is. A user shouldn't have to remember which git branch a particular epoch or increment is in.' The in-repo precedent already exists for the backward direction: rel:v0180 lives in the graph, tag v0.18.0 lives in git, and the graph node names the version — nobody greps tags to learn what shipped. This requirement extends that same division of labor forward.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"Anthony's word, 2026-07-30, after asking for the open requirements to be strongly scrutinised: an unaccepted requirement that is not value-adding and only causes confusion should be retired as "considered, but not accepted" rather than carried. Ten of twenty-six went. All are `dropped`, not deleted: the capture was real and the reasoning is worth keeping, so each keeps its full statement and a snapshot of its final state on the timeline (`epoch:prune-proposed`).

DROPPED AS NOT VALUE-ADDING (7).

`req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score` and `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted` — both record a DOUBT rather than a need, and say so in their own names: "probably NOT from a single scalar" and "a framework registry is probably the wrong fix". A requirement that argues against its own mechanism is a Decision wearing the wrong hat. The live fact inside the second (`Project.domain` is written and never read) survives inside `req:defaults-do-not-assert`.

`req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` — measuring reflow2's own usability against a baseline, and a threshold at which friction becomes scheduled work. Both are backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements: the answer to unconverted friction reports is to act on them, not to model them. The severity-bar one carries real evidence (eight brainmaker items unconverted) and that evidence belongs in the backlog, which is where it now lives.

`req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` — `cap:bounded-reads` already answers the acute version, where a read that would not fit says so and names what it withheld. What remained was design-time estimation, which the requirement's own text calls the weak half.

`req:blocking-is-partial` — freezing drifted work while the rest proceeds. Nobody has been hurt by the all-or-nothing gate; speculative.

`req:adopt-says-how-much-it-got` — REDUNDANT. "Adopt reports how much was recovered" restates `req:coverage-visible`, which is accepted and delivered by `cap:coverage` ("say what the design has never heard of"). Two requirements for one need is the confusion this pass was called to remove.

FOLDED INTO `req:defaults-do-not-assert` (3). `req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes` and `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` are one rule stated four times — node defaults, edge defaults, declared-but-unread vocabulary, and detector-ignored properties are the same defect: THE SCHEMA MUST NOT DECLARE WHAT NOTHING READS OR CHECKS. Their specific evidence is preserved inside the surviving requirement rather than lost with them. `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` had exactly ONE edge, so it was already an orphan in all but name.

NOT TOUCHED, and worth recording why. The 2026-07-28 planning cluster — `req:epochs-can-be-planned`, `req:plans-move-honestly`, `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` — are Anthony's own ideas, quoting him directly (the Black-Scholes analogy for plan volatility, "in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system"). They are structurally disconnected, but that means CAPTURED AND NEVER WIRED, not low value: disconnection is a fact about edges, not about worth, and treating it as a proxy would have pruned exactly the wrong four. The fix for those is to wire them, not to retire them. `req:assumptions-are-first-class` (ordinary risk practice) and `req:correspondence-rules-are-stateable` (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010) likewise stand: standard architecture-description ground for a user who works in UAF/DoDAF.","name":"Ten proposed requirements considered and not accepted — seven dropped, three folded into one rule","rationale":"The prompt for this was his: "if some of them are not value added and just cause confusion, then we don't have to do them — we can retire them as considered, but not accepted."

The test applied to each was whether the requirement would change what anyone BUILDS. A requirement that records a doubt does not; it records that a mechanism looked wrong, which is a Decision. A requirement that restates one already accepted does not; it splits one thread in two. A requirement that describes how the project should manage itself does not; it is process. What survived is everything with a code citation, a real incident, or a standing external practice behind it.

Two independent signals agreed on four of the ten, which is why the structural check was worth running before deciding rather than after: `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes`, `req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` were each sitting in a `disconnected_community` island AND on the retire list on their merits. But the same check listed four of Anthony's own ideas as islands too, so agreement between the signals was evidence and never the criterion.

DROPPED, NOT DELETED, and the distinction is the retire-from-design skill's central one. These were genuinely considered — several were found by measurement, and one (`req:supporting-is-not-conflict`) was found by using the graph in anger. Deleting them would erase why the surviving rules are shaped as they are, and would let the same captures be re-made next quarter by someone who could not see they had been weighed. `dropped` also stops them raising `unsatisfied_requirement`, so the open list means what it says again.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Adopting an existing system reports how much of it was actually recovered","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2's adopt skill produces a graph of an existing system but has no measure of COMPLETENESS — nothing says what fraction of the codebase reached the design, so \"we adopted it\" cannot be distinguished from \"we adopted the parts we happened to read.\" The original reflow gated on exactly this: workflow 01e-reverse_engineering.json step RE-06 (Validation and Gap Analysis) computed an extraction coverage percentage by validating the extracted architecture back against the code — identifying unmapped functions (code not in the architecture), undocumented interfaces, and inconsistencies between architecture and code behaviour — and its agent guidance made it a stop condition: \"Extraction coverage < 80% requires manual review before proceeding.\" Its completion criteria repeat it as a required gate. DISTINCT FROM WHAT reflow2 ALREADY HAS. coverage_report measures whether INTENT has been delivered (requirements against the golden thread, per req:completion-computed); this measures whether the AS-BUILT LAYER IS COMPLETE — a different axis and the one adopt needs, because an honest brownfield model must be able to say what it did not see. reconcile_artifacts compares recorded artifacts against disk, which is nearer, but it checks the artifacts the design already names rather than finding the code the design never mentioned. The adopt skill's own doctrine already makes the case: \"You only get what you see is not a limitation to paper over: the graph marks what was inferred, confesses what it cannot know\" — a coverage figure is that confession made quantitative. Note the granularity caveat adopt is right about: node count tracks distinct contracts and capabilities, NOT lines of code (a 110k-LOC system landed at ~78 nodes while reflow2's own ~34k LOC lands near ~100), so this measure must be expressed in terms adopt actually models — unmapped entry points, unmodelled contracts, untouched modules — never as a nodes-per-LOC ratio, which would punish a coarse-but-honest model. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Work that drifted can be frozen without freezing the work that did not","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2's response to unacceptable drift is all-or-nothing. tools/reflow2_check.py thresholds WHICH findings count — anchored gaps at or above --gap-threshold (default 0.8) fail the build — but the response is a single sys.exit(1) and the whole build goes red. There is no state in which some capabilities are frozen pending a decision while the rest of the work proceeds. reflow could do this. Its rigid-mode resync offered the user two options, and option B was: \"Document each drift item as change request, add to context/change_requests.json, BLOCK implementation of drifted features, continue with non-drifted work.\" The RESYNC_to_P1 path for major drift in rigid mode likewise says \"BLOCK until change request approved\" — a targeted freeze, not a stopped project. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. On a system being evolved incrementally against functional production code — Anthony's actual case at NSLS-II, a ten-year-old bluesky stack evolving on the fly — \"stop everything until this is resolved\" is almost never the right answer, and \"carry on regardless\" is never the right answer either. Partial blocking is the only response that matches how the work actually proceeds: quarantine what is contested, keep delivering what is not. It is also what makes a gate survivable in a shared repo, where one contested capability currently reddens the build for everyone. WHAT reflow2 ALREADY HAS, so this is a smaller change than it appears: the graph can already say which capabilities are affected (propagate_change gives the blast radius; scope + claim_region give \"the part I hold\"), and status/proposed already expresses \"not agreed yet\". What is missing is that nothing READS those to scope a refusal — the gate asks one global question and gives one global answer. OPEN: whether a partial block is advisory (reported, not enforced, per dec:report-dont-judge) or actually refuses writes against the frozen region, and whether the frozen set is computed from the drift's blast radius or named by the user. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Context cost is MEASURED and budgeted, not estimated at design time","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. First written as "context consumption is modelled so a path that will not fit is knowable before it is walked", arguing from reflow's design-time estimation. The FINDING is mine and stands; reflow's MECHANISM is the weak half, and the name now says which.

THE FINDING, measured against reflow2's own design and independent of any prior art: DEPENDS_ON declares a coupling-weight facet whose schema comment states its purpose — "weight is a STRENGTH (higher = tighter); invert to a cost for shortest-path/closeness" — and over 3,250 edges, 232 carry weight_basis while ZERO carry weight, frequency or data_volume. The facet is declared and wholly unpopulated, which also explains req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert rather than merely repeating it: weight_basis asserts "estimated" over an absent weight because weights were meant to be there.

WHY DESIGN-TIME ESTIMATION IS THE WEAK PART. reflow made context_consumption a function attribute and the primary edge weight, published estimation guidelines (read_workflow_file 5000-15000 tokens, generate_architecture 5000-15000, and so on), summed along paths, and flagged CRITICAL above 160k. Three problems. (1) The estimates go stale the moment anything changes and nothing ever re-derives them, so the graph accumulates confident numbers nobody has checked — the shape this project keeps rediscovering. (2) They are model-specific: 160k was reflow's environment, tokenisers and context windows differ, and hardcoding one number as a law is the asserting default req:defaults-do-not-assert forbids. (3) Real consumption is dominated by what static structure cannot see — how much a tool actually returns, how many rounds a negotiation takes, what the user pastes in. A statically-summed path cost would be precise and wrong.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, and reflow2 already has most of the vocabulary. MEASURE rather than estimate: real sessions produce real costs per tool call and per skill, and weight_basis already distinguishes estimated / evidence / measured — further evidence the facet was designed for observed values, not guesses. Then BUDGET at runtime against what is left, which composes with cap:bounded-reads (a read that would not fit answers with a bounded page and says what it left out) and cap:tool-search (finding a tool on a surface too large to hold) rather than replacing them. A measured cost also feeds req:friction-has-a-baseline honestly, since "this got more expensive across a release" is a regression the baseline should catch.

An estimate is defensible only as a SEED for something never measured, and must read as estimated — which is exactly what weight_basis is for. Fixing the edge default and populating the facet remain two answers to one question and should be decided together. {"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A default must not assert what nobody chose","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"FOUND BY A DELIBERATE SWEEP, 2026-07-28, asking the question `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` implies but does not answer: what ELSE does the schema claim that no computation checks? The sweep was Anthony's call after the same defect shape appeared six times in three days.

THE MEASURED FINDING. Ten properties are materialised onto every node by the store's schema defaults and appear ZERO times in the entire Rust source — not in a detector, not in a report, not in a test. Measured against reflow2's own 860-node design:

- `Requirement.concern` — `core` on 67 of 67
- `Capability.tier` — `operational` on 84 of 84
- `Component.tier` — `operational` on 53 of 53
- `Capability.is_entry_point` / `is_exit_point` — `false` on 84 of 84
- `Constraint.concern`, `DesignRule.enforced`, `Actor.actor_type`, `EnvironmentRule.mandatory`, `EnvironmentRule.rule_type`, `Flow.tier` — likewise defaulted, likewise unread

Single-valued across the whole design, every one. A property that never varies is not carrying information; it is asserting one.

THE WORST INSTANCE, and the reason this is intent rather than tidiness. `Requirement.concern`'s enum is core / logistics / sustainment / safety / security / cost / schedule / manufacturability / usability / environmental — and the schema's own description says logistics and sustainment are there to carry "the ILS considerations an SME surfaces". That is the systems-engineering angle this project exists to serve, encoded in the schema and then asserted away: every requirement claims `core`, there is NO WRITER for it on the MCP surface (only the `create_node` escape hatch — the same shape as the KPP `objective` finding), and nothing reads it. So "which of these are the safety requirements?" cannot be answered, and the graph does not answer "unknown" — it answers "none".

THE RULE, AND IT IS ALREADY PROVEN HERE. `Interface.medium` defaulting to `REST` was fixed on 2026-07-28 for exactly this reason, and `ver:interface-spec` states the principle in the form it should now generalise: "UNRECORDED FIELDS READ AS `unspecified` NOT `none` — the flattering default would tell a consumer an unspecified contract is open." So: A DEFAULT MAY RECORD ABSENCE; IT MAY NOT RECORD A CHOICE. Where a property has a substantive default nobody selected, the default becomes `unspecified` and silence reads as silence.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY COSMETIC. `export_surface` publishes a design's boundary to another design; a mirrored surface carrying `tier: operational` and `concern: core` ships assertions nobody made across a seam, which is the same failure `req:publishable-promise` was raised for one layer down. And the moment any future computation DOES read one of these — the SME view `concern` was designed for — it reads a value the schema invented.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is what stops this being a blanket rewrite: a default that records a genuine absence is CORRECT and must stay. `provenance: authored` and `status: proposed` are real defaults meaning a real thing. The test is whether the default names a CHOICE among alternatives (tier, concern, rule_type) or the ABSENCE of one — only the first kind lies. Changing a default is also not retroactive: nodes written before the change keep the value they were given, so a sweep of existing designs is a separate, deliberate act.

SIBLING FINDINGS FROM THE SAME SWEEP, recorded here rather than lost. (1) Fifteen properties are WRITTEN and never consulted — the sharpest is `DriftEvent.severity`, written from `kind.severity()` at three call sites while ranking independently re-derives it via `severity_rank(kind)`, so the stored copy can silently diverge from the mapping that actually governs; also `DesignEpoch.sequence`, which COORD entries quote as meaningful ("epoch:v0180 at sequence 210") and nothing orders by. (2) `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` is an instance of ITSELF: it carries `concern: core`, one of the properties nothing reads.","status":"proposed"}

This requirement was first written as "drift rolls up to one number, and how far the work retreats is computed from it", arguing from reflow's scalar drift_score. That argument was too credulous and the name has been changed with it. What follows keeps the real question and demotes reflow's answer to one option among several.

THE REAL QUESTION, which stands on its own: when the design and the build have diverged, nothing in reflow2 says HOW FAR BACK the work should go. Per-event dispositions answer "what do we do about this divergence"; nothing answers "is the accumulated divergence bad enough that we should stop adding to it and revisit the allocation, or the intent?" That question is real and unanswered.

WHY THE SCALAR IS THE WEAK PART. Collapsing heterogeneous drift into one 0.0-1.0 number destroys precisely the information that decides what to do: a missing artifact, a spec mismatch and an undocumented addition are different problems with different responses, and their average is not a thing. reflow's thresholds (below 0.3 keep building, 0.3 to 0.5 revise allocation, at or above 0.5 revise intent) are invented numbers with no derivation given, and its retreat targets are phase-shaped because reflow had phases. Adopting the scalar would also collide with dec:certainty-derived: a confident aggregate computed from a base the code already disagrees with is an assertion dressed as a measurement.

reflow2 IS ALREADY AHEAD HERE AND SHOULD NOT REGRESS. Drift is disposed of PER EVENT — design_holds or design_updated — so a session can hold the design on one divergence and update it on another, which reflow's single global mode could not do. And confirm.rs audits whether the dispositions are honest: "five design_holds claims with zero design edits is a very different confirmation history from one design_updated". That history is a better signal than any scalar, because it is evidence rather than an estimate. If escalation is built, it should read the disposition history, not an average.

THE PRECONDITION STILL HOLDS whatever shape is chosen: DriftEvent.severity is one of the WRITTEN-and-never-consulted properties the 2026-07-28 sweep found — written from kind.severity() at three call sites while ranking re-derives it via severity_rank(kind) — so any computation over stored severity reads a value the code already contradicts. Settle the single-source question first.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, stated without borrowing reflow's mechanism: a computed, evidence-backed answer to "should we keep building or go back, and back to WHAT" — where the destinations are layers of the golden thread (realization, allocation, intent) rather than phases, and the trigger is drawn from what the graph can already prove (unresolved DriftEvents by kind, the design_holds/design_updated history, coverage moving the wrong way) rather than from a number nobody can derive. Either something should read it or it should not be collected, and that is true regardless of what reflow did.

WHY reflow's ANSWER IS PROBABLY WRONG, stated plainly because the first version of this node treated it as the model to copy. (1) The terminology mapping is largely COSMETIC. framework_registry.json maps node to 'service' / 'gene' / 'agent' / 'species' and edge to 'interface' / 'interaction' / 'relationship' over one universal graph. Renaming the same structure does not change what can be computed about it, and it introduces a translation layer between what the user says and what the graph holds — a layer that can drift, and that every reader must now traverse. (2) The load-bearing claim is a SMELL, not a feature. reflow's LESSON-01 says "framework choice determines which NetworkX analyses are available". Analyses should be available based on WHAT THE GRAPH CONTAINS, not on a declared label: a cycle detector should run wherever there are dependency edges, whoever calls them interfaces or interactions. Gating capability on a self-declared category is how a user gets the wrong answer for a reason they cannot see. reflow2's one universal vocabulary with computations keyed to STRUCTURE is very likely the better design, and adopting a registry would be a regression dressed as a feature.

WHAT SURVIVES FROM reflow: only the rule, and reflow2 already has it. LESSON-01's real content — "Do NOT default to UAF" — is req:defaults-do-not-assert, independently arrived at. The supporting CONTRADICTS edge to that requirement stays correct; the framework registry is not the mechanism it implies.

WHAT SHOULD ACTUALLY BE DECIDED, and it is smaller than a registry: does anything read Project.domain, and if not, does it become unspecified-until-stated (per ver:interface-spec's rule for Interface.medium) or leave the schema entirely? A plausible middle path worth weighing separately: domain as a hint to EXTRACTION and phrasing — what vocabulary the agent uses when talking to the user and reading their documents — without ever gating which computations run. That keeps the honest part of reflow's insight (a biologist should not be told about 'services') and discards the part that would make analyses conditional on a label. {"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Usability is measured against a baseline, so getting harder to use is detectable","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2 regression-gates whether its DETECTORS still work and has no equivalent for whether a person or agent can still get THROUGH the process. tools/phase_trial.py seeds a realistic graph, injects the divergences P3/P4/P5 are each meant to catch, scores whether the graph noticed, sits at 13/13, exits 0 and works as a regression gate; the erosion trial asks the sharper version, whether the design still describes the system after N rounds of test-fails/fix-code/accept. Both measure the machinery. Neither measures the EXPERIENCE of driving it, so reflow2 could become materially harder to use across a release and every gate would stay green. report-friction's own text concedes the consequence: \"Everything reflow2 knows about its own weak points came from someone writing down what fought them. Those were staged trials; ordinary use produces better evidence and CURRENTLY LOSES ALL OF IT.\" THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's 97-GAN-inspired-test.json, and its structure is the transferable part rather than its specifics. Execution was separated from evaluation: one agent drove the workflows BLIND — \"Agent B should NOT see expected outputs\" — while a second read the transcript afterwards, categorised what went wrong and found root causes rather than symptoms, asking of each \"why did this occur, how did it manifest, how frequently, what is the fix effort\". Results aggregated to metrics, compared against a stored baseline, and regression was called out explicitly: \"if new version performs worse than baseline, that's a P0 issue.\" The cadence was stated — periodically, or before a major release. THE BLINDNESS IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART and the easiest to lose: an evaluator who knows the expected output cannot see the friction, because it reads the intended path into whatever happened. reflow2's real trials (brownfield ophyd-service, greenfield aidrone, brainmaker) already produce this evidence and it is what taught reflow2 most of what it knows — but they are occasional, hand-run, and not comparable to each other, so nothing can say whether the last release made anything worse. Depends on req:friction-has-a-severity-bar: a baseline needs countable, classified findings to be a baseline OF something. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. {"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A property the detector ignores is a property that lies","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"FOUND BY USING THE GRAPH, 2026-07-28, and the third defect this week that inspection had not found and one real use did.

WHAT HAPPENED. Anthony decided the slash commands should ship with the kit, which QUALIFIES `dec:skills-served` rather than overturning it — same reasoning, narrower scope. The schema has carried the vocabulary for that relationship from the beginning: CONTRADICTS is documented as "two decisions/requirements/claims that conflict (OR, WITH alignment=supporting, REINFORCE)". So the corroboration was recorded exactly as prescribed, with `alignment: supporting` — and `detect_defects` reported a structural defect, because the contradiction loop read the edge TYPE and never looked at the property.

WHY THE NOISE WAS NOT THE DAMAGE. The damage was that both ways out were wrong. Acknowledge it, and a defect that is not one enters `reviewed_defects` as if a judgement had been made. Stop drawing the edge, and the design silently loses the fact that one decision qualifies another — which is precisely the kind of reasoning a design graph exists to keep. And an open list that can never reach zero gets SKIMMED, which is the failure the whole detect-and-ask discipline is built to prevent.

THE GENERAL RULE, worth stating beyond this instance: A SCHEMA PROPERTY THAT NO COMPUTATION READS IS A PROPERTY THAT LIES. It invites people to record something true, and then behaves as though they had not. reflow2 has now been bitten by this shape three times in two days — `orphan_node` ignoring DOCUMENTS so a well-documented artifact reads as loose; `export_surface` withholding every Requirement so a published promise could not travel; and this. Each was a value the schema offered and no detector consulted.

WHAT THE FIX MUST NOT DO, and this is the load-bearing half: it must not silence the detector. An `opposing` edge is still a contradiction, and an edge that says NOTHING is still a contradiction — silence is not a claim of support, and every design written before today keeps its meaning exactly. A fix that made real conflicts vanish would be far worse than the noise it removed, so both counterweights are pinned by tests rather than asserted in a comment.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A gap put to the user arrives with the agent's recommendation — recommending is not deciding","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"When reflow2 puts a gap to the user, the agent's READING of it travels with the question: what it would do and why, and what would change that answer. The user still decides; the agent stops pretending it has no view.

WHAT IS MISSING TODAY, and it is an omission rather than a prohibition. `detect-and-ask` is explicit that the agent must "never invent an answer on their behalf", which is right and must not be weakened. But the skill says nothing about offering a reading, so the default behaviour is a bare question — `gap_to_prompt` returns "is it covered, deferred, or dropped?" and the agent relays it. `cap:surface` ("turn a gap into a question in the user's words", `verified`) delivers the translation and nothing more.

WHY THAT IS A DEFECT AND NOT NEUTRALITY. `req:no-se-knowledge` says the user never needs systems engineering. A bare gap question hands them back the analysis the agent has already done and asks them to redo it in their own head — which is precisely the SE work that requirement exists to spare them. The agent has read the graph, seen the precedents, and formed a view; withholding it is not impartiality, it is making the user pay for the agent's caution.

IT IS ALSO WHAT `dec:three-party-checks` ALREADY DESCRIBES: "The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides." Offering a reading IS the LLM speaking. The decision stays with the human, untouched — and `dec:certainty-derived` still governs the write, because a recommendation changes no status until the user answers.

THE LINE THAT MUST NOT BE CROSSED, stated so this cannot be read as licence. Recommending is not deciding: no requirement moves off `proposed`, no decision reaches `accepted`, no gap is acknowledged on a reading the user has not confirmed. And a recommendation must carry WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT — the condition under which the other option wins — or it is steering rather than advising. An option presented without its counterweight is a decision taken quietly.

THE PART WORTH RECORDING, and the reason this is design rather than style: WHEN THE USER OVERRULES A RECOMMENDATION, THAT IS INFORMATION. A design where the agent advised one way and the human chose another has learned something neither party knew alone, and today it is invisible because the recommendation was never on the record. Whether the recommendation itself should be stored beside the question is left open here rather than assumed.

MEASURED, not theorised: every gap put to Anthony on 2026-07-31 needed the recommendation added by hand, and he asked for it explicitly twice — "provide your recommendation", "present them in simple english and your recommendations for how to proceed". A shape a user has to request each time is a default in the wrong place.

TENSION NAMED SO IT IS NOT CONFLATED: `dec:report-dont-judge` says the confirmation ledger reports claim history and never judges a claim. That governs what a COMPUTATION may assert about evidence. It does not govern whether an agent may advise a human who asked — different actor, different act. Conflating the two would silence exactly the party `dec:three-party-checks` puts there to speak.","status":"accepted"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS A REFRAME PLUS A MEASUREMENT, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-04, stating the root question that unifies the dev_storyflow corpus and the reflow2-dogfooding threads: "how do we transition documents to graph entities? whether that is a huge corpus of documents in dev_storyflow or getting away from using documents in reflow2, it is how do we make decisions based on graph content, not documents." Nothing here is settled.

THE SPLIT. (IN) documents become graph entities — ingest_step, provenance Fragments, the content store, cross-document convergence. Partly built, and every remaining piece is scheduled across epoch:v0240-planned..v0280-planned. (OUT) a person or agent DECIDES from graph content instead of from a document. Almost nothing is scheduled. The whole increment plan is capture, detection, seams and write-surface.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, AND ALL OF IT IS FIRST-HAND FROM ONE SESSION ON 2026-08-04 RATHER THAN RECALLED. `reviewed_gaps` returned 130,922 CHARACTERS and could not be read at all — it was written to a file and queried with `jq`. That is the tool answering "what have we already decided to accept", which is a decision-making read, and it was unusable AS a read. It joins: `loop_status` at 72,886 characters until [BL-205] fixed it the day before, and it is the call the SessionStart hook and the server instructions both call "the one cheap call"; `describe_schema` on ONE node type at ~30 KB ([BL-142]); and `scan_nodes` on 241 Decisions, where the where-am-i skill's own guidance forced reading names only and confessing that exactly one had been read in full. Add the standing limit: 52 properties are `fulltext: true` and `Decision.rationale` is not one of them.

THEY ARE ALL ONE DEFECT: A READ THAT RETURNS EVERYTHING IT KNOWS INSTEAD OF WHAT WAS ASKED. The graph holds the content correctly. It cannot serve it back at the size it now holds. That is neither a vocabulary problem nor an ingest problem, which is why every framing so far has missed it — `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` reasoned about what a node can HOLD, and the binding constraint is what a read can RETURN.

THE CONSEQUENCE THAT SHOULD NOT BE SOFTENED: TODAY A DOCUMENT BEATS THE GRAPH FOR MAKING A DECISION, AND IT IS A FAIR FIGHT THE GRAPH LOSES. A document can be skimmed, searched with ctrl-F, and read end to end. The graph offers 130 KB or a list of names. Reaching for the markdown is therefore RATIONAL BEHAVIOUR RESPONDING TO A REAL DIFFERENCE, not a bad habit to be disciplined out of, and no improvement to capture changes it.

THE SHAPE OF AN ANSWER, offered because the in-house precedent is already built and shipped rather than as advocacy: the transition is not documents → graph, it is DOCUMENTS → GRAPH → DERIVED DOCUMENTS. `cap:changelog-view` ("a changelog is a derivable view of the graph's own delta") shipped in v0.20.0 and CHANGELOG.md is generated today; `dec:views-are-projections` is accepted; `tools/render_views.py` is 44 KB of renderer producing docs/viewpoints.md and has existed since 2026-07-19. The renderer, the doctrine and the proof all exist — the backlog simply is not one of its views. This also explains why option (d) on `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` kept losing: it was judged as a RIVAL to the capture options when it is the OUT half of the same answer, and that node already half-saw it ("solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing").

⭐ THE TEST THIS YIELDS, AND IT IS ANTHONY'S OWN DELETION INSTINCT MADE SAFE. He asked: "should I delete the documents and force us to use the reflow2 graph?" Deletion is the right TEST and the wrong COMMITMENT. The test is: CAN YOU DELETE THIS DOCUMENT AND REGENERATE IT FROM THE GRAPH? Yes → the graph is the source and the document was a view. No → the document is still the source, and WHAT CANNOT BE REGENERATED IS PRECISELY WHAT THE GRAPH IS MISSING. Run it per document, never on the repo at once, and regenerate BEFORE deleting so nothing is ever at risk. Where each stands today, assessed 2026-08-04: CHANGELOG.md PASSES (already derived); docs/viewpoints.md PASSES; COORD.md's in-progress table passes the day `claim_region` is used for real, because the computation exists and is served (`dec:coord-board-in-graph`); docs/backlog.md FAILS, and the rows that cannot regenerate are the exact statement of what vocabulary is absent; AGENTS.md FAILS PERMANENTLY AND CORRECTLY, because an agent reads it before it knows reflow2 exists. That last row is why this is not a march toward zero documents — it is a march toward zero documents that are SOURCES, and the test says which is which instead of leaving it to taste.

FOR A CORPUS THE TEST POINTS THE OTHER WAY. Source documents cannot be regenerated and must not be — `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` says so. The test applies instead to the READING: after ingest, can "what did I want to build, and what of it exists" be answered without opening a document? A no means the ingest landed prose rather than structure, which is exactly what the 52-fulltext-properties limit predicts for rows imported as long descriptions.

WHAT IS NOT DECIDED HERE. Whether the OUT half is a v0.24.0 obligation, its own increment, or a discipline applied to every read as it is touched. Which reads to fix first, and by what rule — `reviewed_gaps` is the loudest but `scan_nodes` on a mature type may be the most consequential. Whether "answer-shaped rather than type-shaped" needs new tools or bounded forms of the existing ones. And whether the backlog renderer is a `render_views.py` view, a served tool, or neither.

NOT VERIFIED, AND IT WOULD CHANGE THE PRIORITY: how many of the ~140 served tools return unbounded results. Four are named above because four were hit by hand in one session; nobody has counted. If it is four, this is a bug list. If it is forty, it is an increment.","name":"OPEN — "documents to graph entities" is TWO problems, and the failing one is reading the graph back, not getting content into it","rationale":"Recorded because the measurement is perishable in the exact way this project keeps rediscovering: "reviewed_gaps returned 130,922 characters" becomes "reads felt big once" within a session or two, and then the next reader re-derives it or, worse, does not. The four numbers are first-hand from a single sitting and are written down so the next session argues from them.

Kept as its own node rather than appended to `dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph` because it CONTRADICTS that node's framing rather than extending it. That node asks what a node and an edge can hold and concludes the answer turns on how much of a row becomes structure; this one says the binding constraint is downstream of that entirely — a perfectly structured graph nobody can read back is still a graph nobody decides from. Folding the correction into the node it corrects would hide it.

Deliberately does NOT register alternatives, so this stays a question rather than becoming a fork the loop asks Anthony to choose between. The unchecked item — how many served tools return unbounded results — is stated as unchecked so its absence reads as a hole rather than as a completed analysis, and it is named as the thing that decides whether this is a bug list or an increment.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"The build loop is bounded, and exhausting the budget forces a return to the design","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2 MEASURES design erosion under repeated build rounds and never BOUNDS it. tools/ carries the erosion trial whose stated question is "not 'did a file change?' but: after N rounds of test-fails/fix-code/accept, does the design still describe what it should" — so the decay is known, quantified, and regression-gated. Nothing, however, ever says STOP. A session can iterate test-fix indefinitely and reflow2 will report the drift afterwards rather than interrupt it.

THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's workflow_master.json: iteration_budgets carries P3_P4_loops = 3 and P4_P3_loops = 3, and on_budget_exceeded triggers the resync protocol with target_phase P2 and escalate_to_P1_if "drift_score > 0.5". So after three build-test rounds work HALTS and the agent is sent back up to architecture — or further, to functional analysis, if the drift is bad enough. The resync protocol itself is six ordered steps: halt_current_work, detect_drift, present_comparison, mode_specific_resolution, reset_iteration_counter, continue_or_escalate.

THE BUDGET WAS ASKED FOR, NOT ASSUMED — AMENDED 2026-07-28, same day, after reviewing workflows/phases/. The 3 above is a DEFAULT, not a constant: workflows/phases/P0_setup/phase_definition.json puts the question to the user during setup — "How many development/test iterations before forced architecture review?", default 3, range 1 to 10 — alongside the mode choice and, for rigid projects, the acceptable drift level. That matters for two reasons. It removes the obvious objection that 3 is arbitrary: it is this project's answer to a question every project was asked. And it sets the shape reflow2 should copy — the bound is a per-project value elicited once, not a constant compiled in, which is the same distinction ver:interface-spec draws between a default that records absence and one that names a choice.

DISTINCT FROM cap:budget, which rolls up a RESOURCE budget against a Constraint (mass, cost, power). This is an ITERATION budget on the design process itself, and reflow2 has no vocabulary for it.

NOT MERELY A PHASE-MODEL ARTEFACT, which is the objection to expect: the mechanism is about work that does NOT terminate. A bounded loop with a forced return upward is precisely the discipline a continual evolution effort needs — Anthony's framing of design as (1) define the current state, (2) evolve it incrementally, with no clean start or exit criteria. The budget is what stops "evolve incrementally" from becoming "drift indefinitely while the graph records it faithfully." Supporting evidence from the same review: reflow's own P5_operations phase_definition states that "P5 is typically ongoing" and routes production issues back_to_P3_P4 as "a new development cycle", so even the phase model this came from did not assume termination.

Whether the trigger should be a loop COUNT (reflow's answer) or a measured drift threshold, or both, is open — reflow used both, counting loops and escalating on drift_score, with both thresholds elicited per project. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Context consumption is modelled, so a path that will not fit is knowable before it is walked","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2 handles agent context only at RUNTIME and reactively. cap:bounded-reads answers an oversized read with a bounded page that says what it left out; cap:tool-search finds the right tool on a surface too large to hold in context. Both are good and both are mitigations applied per call, after the cost has already been incurred. Nothing predicts, before a path is walked, whether walking it will fit. THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's 99-meta_analysis.json and the --context-flow mode of system_of_systems_graph_v2.py: context consumption was a first-class modelled quantity. It was a FUNCTION ATTRIBUTE (context_consumption, listed alongside inputs/outputs and marked \"CRITICAL for AI agent analysis\"), it was THE PRIMARY EDGE WEIGHT — \"Context consumption as edge weight enables bottleneck analysis\" — and it carried estimation guidelines so the numbers were comparable rather than invented per author (read_small_config 1000-2000 tokens, read_workflow_file 5000-15000, read_large_architecture 15000-30000, generate_architecture 5000-15000, run_analysis 5000-10000). From that, analyze_functional_architecture.py computed CONTEXT PATH ANALYSIS — cumulative context along all paths — against hard thresholds: CRITICAL above 160k tokens, WARNING above 140k. So \"an agent cannot get through this path\" was answerable at design time, from the graph, before anyone ran it. THE SLOT ALREADY EXISTS IN reflow2 AND IS EMPTY, which is what makes this a smaller change than it sounds. DEPENDS_ON declares the whole coupling-weight facet and the schema comment states its intended use: \"Coupling-weight facet (graph-analysis.md). weight is a STRENGTH (higher = tighter); invert to a cost for shortest-path/closeness.\" Measured against reflow2's own 3,250-edge design: 232 edges carry weight_basis, and ZERO carry weight, frequency or data_volume. The facet is declared and wholly unpopulated. THIS EXPLAINS req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert RATHER THAN REPEATING IT: weight_basis asserts \"estimated\" over an absent weight because the weights were MEANT to be there, and reflow shows what for — invert the weight to a cost, sum along the path, flag what will not fit. Fixing the default and populating the facet are two answers to the same question and should be decided together. OPEN, and not decided here: whether reflow2 should estimate context per capability, per tool call, or per skill; whether the estimate is authored, measured from real sessions, or both (weight_basis already has the vocabulary for that distinction — estimated / evidence / measured — which is further evidence the facet was designed for exactly this); and what a threshold means for a system with no fixed window, since models differ and the number reflow hardcoded was its own. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 99-meta_analysis.json. Anthony's word: capture it.","status":"proposed"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Drift rolls up to one number, and how far the work retreats is computed from it","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"reflow2 records drift per event and never rolls it up, so there is no answer to \"how bad is it overall, and how far back do we have to go?\" DriftEvent carries severity (low/medium/high/critical) and drift_type (missing_artifact, spec_mismatch, undocumented_addition, status_mismatch, checksum_change, and the three deployment_* kinds), and 37 of them exist in reflow2's own design — but nothing aggregates them into a single figure and nothing acts on the aggregate. The same number gated the forward transition too: P4 to P5 required \"architecture drift score < threshold\" among its quality gates, and major_drift (> 0.5) was classified severity critical with escalates_to P1. So one measure served three purposes — trigger, escalation target, and release gate. Either the stored severity becomes the single source or the rollup reads the derivation, but not both. {"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"The governance mode is chosen, visible and changeable — it is the one asserted default that is actually acted upon","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Project.mode decides whether the design or the implementation is the source of truth, and reflow2 applies it by default, never asks for it, and provides no way to change it. The string \"mode\" does not appear anywhere in crates/reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs, so there is no set_project_mode and no setter of any kind on the served surface; after genesis it is reachable only through the create_node escape hatch — the same shape as the KPP objective finding and Requirement.concern. And reflow2's OWN Project carries mode = flexible, which nobody chose. WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE TEN PROPERTIES IN THE ORIGINAL SWEEP, and the difference is the whole point. Those defaults are asserted AND UNREAD — Requirement.concern sitting at core on 67 of 67 is inert, carrying no information and driving nothing. This one is asserted AND ACTED UPON: heal.rs:431 reads it, and in rigid mode HEAL only proposes and never auto-applies. So req:defaults-do-not-assert has, in this property, its first instance where the invented value changes what the system DOES. flexible is not a neutral setting either. In the vocabulary reflow2 inherited it means the architecture is NOT the source of truth, the implementation drives the architecture, and the response to drift is to update the design to match the build. That is a governance decision. reflow2 — a project whose thesis is that the design is the memory — is currently running in the mode that says the implementation drives the design, not because anyone decided so but because opts.mode was None. THE PRIOR ART IS A FAILURE, NOT A MODEL, and it corroborates rather than instructs. reflow defined development_mode in workflow_master.json with seven behavioural commitments per mode (architecture_source_of_truth, implementation_drives_architecture, drift_response, new_functionality_policy, change_request_required, auto_update_architecture_on_resync, plus the discovered-items routing), REQUIRED it as the P0-to-P1 transition prerequisite (\"fields_must_be_set: development_mode.mode\"), READ it in resync_protocol.json to choose between updating the architecture and realigning the implementation, and TESTED for it in 97-GAN-inspired-test.json — and NO WORKFLOW STEP ANYWHERE SETS IT. Not 00a, not 00b, not the 01 through 04 series. Its own META-04H check HA-005, \"Transition Prerequisites Satisfiability\", exists to catch exactly that and did not. So both systems arrive at the same place by different routes: a governance mode that everything consults and nothing establishes. THREE THINGS THIS REQUIRES, and they are separable. (1) The value is CHOSEN — genesis asks, or the mode reads as unspecified until someone says, per the rule ver:interface-spec already sets for Interface.medium: a default may record absence, never a choice. (2) The value is CHANGEABLE — a project's governance legitimately moves as it matures, exploratory to controlled, and today it cannot; brainmaker reported this from the field, half-right, since the sharper fact is that genesis does not set it at all, it defaults it. (3) The value is VISIBLE — a mode that silently changes HEAL's behaviour should be readable in the reports that say where the design stands. What rigid should MEAN beyond heal.rs:431 stays open and parked separately; this requirement is the prior question, because rigid cannot mean anything useful while the mode is unchoosable and unchangeable. {"enforced":true,"name":"Every fix is judged by what it does for somebody else's project — this repo is the test rig, not the target","statement":"Anthony, 2026-08-06: "most changes we do here are not for the sake of reflow2 itself (though we often apply reflow2 tools/skills on itself). so when we fix something, it must be from the perspective that we are improving reflow2 for anybody that may use it in their project."

THE RULE: when a defect is found while working on reflow2's own design, the fix is judged by what it does for a CONSUMER — a project that installed reflow2 and whose authors will never read this repository. Improving reflow2's own repo state is not the objective; it is the evidence.

DISTINCT FROM THE DOGFOODING RATIONALE, and the two are easy to conflate. req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session records that using the skills on this project is the INSTRUMENT that finds defects. This rule says how to judge the FIX once the instrument has fired. One is about detection, the other about the target. Both are needed, and only holding the first produces a beautifully-instrumented repository that has fixed nothing for anybody.

THE FAILURE MODE IT FORBIDS, which is subtle because it looks like completion: find a hole, patch it HERE, mark the requirement met, and leave every consumer with the hole. The repo goes green, the design says the need is satisfied, and nothing is true of anyone else's project.

THE WORKED EXAMPLE THAT PROMPTED IT, same day, and it is the clearest test of the rule available. Asked whether anything runs `reconcile_dependencies`, the first answer was "reflow2's own CI does not" — accurate, small, and actionable by adding a step to this repo's workflow. Applying this rule reframed it: `reflow2_check.py` is THE GATE THAT SHIPS TO EVERY CONSUMER IN THE KIT, and it reconciles ARTIFACTS but never DEPENDENCIES. Same underlying fact; the second framing is the one worth acting on, and only the second one fixes anything for anybody. Adding a CI step here would have satisfied the first reading and left req:design-dependencies-declared unenforced in every project that installs reflow2.

HOW TO APPLY IT, concretely: when a finding is written, ask where the fix lands. If it lands in `.github/`, `tools/build_design_graph.py`, or anything else that exists only because reflow2 develops itself, ask what the CONSUMER-facing equivalent is — the served tool surface, a skill, `reflow2_check.py`, the kit, the installer, a tool DESCRIPTION. If there is no consumer-facing equivalent, that absence is usually the real finding.

WHY IT IS A RULE AND NOT A REQUIREMENT: it constrains how every other change is judged rather than describing behaviour anything can satisfy, which is the same shape as rule:no-foreclosure. Nothing verifies it; it is applied by whoever is deciding what to build, and its evidence is the framing of the findings that follow it.

THE COUNTER-PRESSURE, recorded so the rule is not applied blindly: reflow2 IS a real project with real operational needs, and some work genuinely is for this repo alone — the release procedure, the export discipline, COORD. The rule does not forbid that work. It forbids MISTAKING it for product work, and it forbids closing a consumer-facing requirement with a repo-facing fix."}

The spec's prescription is a server-minted handle passed as an ordinary tool argument, and half of that already exists: `ClaimReq.seat` accepts a caller-supplied seat today, documented as "pass your own only if you have a durable handle for the session (a fleet worker name); it is a name, never a lock". (a) A `hello`-style tool that mints and returns a seat, which the client then passes on the calls that care (claim_region, release_claim, the stale-seat check). Explicit, transport-independent, and inspectable. Cost: the agent has to remember it, and an agent that forgets silently gets fresh-seat behaviour again — the failure is quiet, which is the property this design most wants to avoid.

(b) Derive the seat from what a stateless request already carries. rmcp reconstructs a `ClientInfo` per request via `peer_info_for_stateless_request`, from headers. Cost: nothing in it is guaranteed stable or unique per client, so this trades a loud missing parameter for a quiet wrong answer.

(c) Accept one seat per server PROCESS on the sessionless transport. Cost: it is exactly the regression `req:seat-per-client` was written against — `claim_report` telling six sessions they are each other.

(d) Serve sessionless HTTP but refuse the claim family on it, directing those callers to stdio or a legacy version. Cost: honest and loud, and it makes `cap:remote-sessions` conditional on a protocol version — a real narrowing of what reflow2 offers.

Anthony's word is wanted on which. Legitimately process-wide state is fine and exists today (the seat registry, the serve-shared mode flag); the test is not 'is it a static' but 'would this need a different value for a second design open in the same process'.

A surface that treats a filesystem path as the canonical identity forecloses object storage, where the location is a key and the identity rides as metadata.

WHY THIS IS A RULE RATHER THAN A REQUIREMENT: it constrains HOW every other change is made rather than describing behaviour anything can satisfy — the same shape as rule:no-foreclosure and rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party.

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Whether the kit is actually used is measured, not inferred from whether the design looks tidy","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Nothing in reflow2 records whether its skills were used, so the only reason this whole family of findings exists is that a user asked an agent directly and the agent answered honestly. That is not a mechanism.

WHAT MAKES IT ACUTE: a design can look healthy while the kit is barely being used. This session ended with 0 gaps, 0 defects, a clean loop and a green gate — and two skills loaded out of eight. `detect_gaps` measures whether the DESIGN is coherent; nothing measures whether the PRACTICE is. The report-friction skill already concedes the wider version of this in its own words — ordinary use produces better evidence and currently loses all of it — and `req:friction-has-a-baseline` was dropped, so there is no standing measurement at all.

THE HARD CONSTRAINT, which is why this is a requirement and not a fix: `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` says loop debt is computed from graph state and NEVER from run history, straight out of the BL-74 fleet trial. Any naive answer here — log which skills were called — is exactly the run-history reasoning that decision rejects, and a study that comes back recommending it has not read the decision.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAY RESOLVE IT, offered as the open question rather than the answer: that decision governs what the LOOP may reason from when it computes debt. It does not obviously govern what the KIT may report about ITSELF as a product — the difference between "this design owes you three gaps" (must be state-derived, must be true of the graph as it stands) and "reflow2 was installed here and its skills were loaded twice in nine hours" (a fact about the tool's adoption, not about the user's design). Whether that distinction is real, or a rationalisation for the thing the decision forbids, is the question — and it must be settled before anything is built, not discovered afterwards.

BOUNDARIES THAT HOLD EITHER WAY: whatever is measured must respect report-friction's redaction discipline, which has no counterpart in the prior art — tool names and argument SHAPES, node TYPES not ids, counts not contents — because reflow2 installs into other people's projects, and the thing being measured is the user, not the design.","status":"deferred"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Skill use is triggered by the situation, not remembered — the rungs cover loop debt, and skills fire on things the graph cannot see","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"An agent's use of reflow2's SKILLS must not decay over a session while its use of the TOOLS holds. Measured on reflow2's own repo, 2026-07-31, in a long session: `loop_status` was called unprompted throughout and every write went through `record_change`, two-sided checksum accepts and one-export-per-commit — but exactly two skills were loaded all session, and both only because the user typed a slash command. `impact-check`, `link-artifacts`, `capture-intent`, `revise-design`, `check-health` and `report-friction` were never loaded. THE THREE BL-74 RUNGS ARE ALL `verified` AND THIS STILL HAPPENED, which is the finding: they are working as designed and do not reach this.

THE STRUCTURAL REASON. The rungs compute LOOP DEBT — a property of graph state, which is what `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` correctly insists on. Skills fire on SITUATIONS: about to change code, just wrote a file, the user just shared an idea. The graph cannot see any of those, so the trigger mechanism covers one half of the problem and structurally cannot reach the other. That is why `impact-check` was dropped hardest — nothing in the system knows an edit is coming, and by the time the graph could tell, the edit has happened and the blast radius is a post-mortem rather than a check.

WHAT COST SOMETHING, honestly: `impact-check` was never run before changing `snapshot_node`, `delete_edge` and `delete_node`; the blast radius was reasoned about by hand instead of computed. `link-artifacts` was never loaded and a stale `art:nodes` checksum was nearly shipped — caught only by grepping after the export, which then required restoring the export and redoing it. `check-health` cost nothing, because `detect_defects` was run bare and did catch the island.

CANDIDATE MECHANISMS, in the order the evidence supports, NOT a decided design. (1) Extend the PostToolUse hook from COUNTING writes to matching SHAPES — a file edit with no ChangeEvent in the window means impact-check, an artifact checksum drift means link-artifacts. `req:nudge-covers-bypass` already arms the nudge on file-edit events and already names impact-check and link-artifacts, and is `verified`; what is missing is the shape-matching, not the trigger. (2) A refusal, where refusing is honest — reflow2's strongest mechanism, proven three times in this session alone — but only where skipping is genuinely wrong, because a guard that punishes correct work is the failure this project keeps naming.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS SESSION: BL-74 called this adoption-critical and found it in the author's own fleet, self-reported by the driving agent. This is the same failure observed from inside, on a session with MORE context about reflow2 than a consumer's agent will have — so it is likely a best case rather than a typical one.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A second revision of a node in one epoch must not overwrite the first snapshot","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"req:intent-preserved says the past is never overwritten. Snapshot identity currently breaks that rule whenever a node is revised TWICE within a single epoch, and the loss is silent.\\n\\nOBSERVED 2026-07-28, by doing it rather than by reading the code. req:build-loop-is-bounded was amended once (chg:iteration-budget-was-elicited, correcting the iteration budget to an elicited value) and later the same day amended again (chg:build-loop-shape-reassessed, demoting the hard stop). Both used record_change against the same epoch:reflow-workflow-review. The snapshot id is deterministic per (epoch, node) — snap:epoch:reflow-workflow-review:req:build-loop-is-bounded — so the SECOND record_change wrote over the first. compare_designs reported it under supporting.changed with base = the original statement and other = the first-amended statement: the snapshot now holds the INTERMEDIATE state, and the state the node held before any amendment survives only in git, in an export committed earlier.\\n\\nWHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG. Nothing failed and nothing warned. record_change returned a prior_snapshot both times and looked identical from the caller's side. The design's own history simply lost a version while reporting success, which is precisely the silent-overwrite failure the revise-design discipline exists to prevent — and the discipline was followed exactly. A user doing careful work by the documented procedure loses history and is never told.\\n\\nIT ALSO BREAKS THE STATED TEST OF A GOOD REVISION. The revise-design skill ends with it: \\\"afterwards, someone reading the graph can answer what did this say before, when did it change, and why — without git archaeology.\\\" After two amendments in one epoch that is false: answering it for the first amendment requires git archaeology, which is the exact fallback the skill promises to remove.\\n\\nTHE SHAPE OF THE FIX IS A CHOICE, and none of the options is obviously right, which is why this is recorded rather than patched. (a) Make snapshot identity per REVISION rather than per (epoch, node) — e.g. include the ChangeEvent id, which is already unique per revision — so every record_change mints a distinct snapshot and HAS_SNAPSHOT becomes one-to-many. Truest to req:intent-preserved; grows the graph faster and makes \\\"the snapshot for this epoch\\\" ambiguous where readers currently assume one. (b) REFUSE a second record_change against the same node in the same epoch, directing the caller to open a new epoch. Cheap and loud, and it forces epoch hygiene, but epochs are meant to bound a round of WORK, not a single edit, so this pushes an unrelated concern onto the caller. (c) Keep one snapshot per epoch deliberately, meaning it holds the state at the START of the epoch, and make the second call a no-op rather than an overwrite. Preserves the original, loses the intermediate, and needs the semantics stated somewhere they are currently only implied.\\n\\nWhichever is chosen, the silence is not defensible: if a revision cannot be snapshotted without discarding an earlier one, the call must say so. Found 2026-07-28 while amending requirements from the reflow workflow review; the amendments themselves are the evidence.","status":"proposed"}
