properties.statement:
`propagate_change` RETURNS 0 FOR EVERY `DOCUMENTS`-ATTACHED ARTIFACT, AND A BARE 0 CANNOT BE TOLD FROM 'NOTHING DOWNSTREAM'. Reported by dev_storyflow's api-boss sidekick (`551d9718`), 2026-08-15, with a table: nine artifacts, one edit class, propagated individually — the seven attached by `DOCUMENTS` returned `total_impacted: 0` EVERY ONE, while the two attached by `REALIZES` returned 2 and 539.

⭐ THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION, and they name it: two of those documents ARE a Verification's primary evidence. 'Had I corrupted either registration, impact-check would have said 0 and I would have read it as nothing downstream.' THE FAILURE IS TOWARD CALM, which is the expensive direction.

⭐⭐ THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN, AND THE SECOND FOUND TODAY. This session independently measured `propagate_change` from a `TemporalFact` seed returning ZERO impacted, because `ABOUT_ENTITY` is not traversed either — recorded in `fact:defect-propagate-change-distance-two-is-not-an-edit-list`. THEIR CASE AND MINE ARE THE SAME DEFECT ON DIFFERENT EDGE TYPES: propagation is silent on exactly the edges that carry FINDINGS and DOCUMENTATION, the two node families whose whole purpose is to be about something else. They also place it in the BL-199 family — `orphan_node` counted only outgoing `REALIZES` and reported skill-prescribed `DOCUMENTS` artifacts as orphans, and a guard script exists to stop that returning; `propagate_change` has the same asymmetry with no such guard.

⚠️ THEIR SELF-HOST EXPLANATION IS WRONG FOR REFLOW2 AS IT STANDS, AND THE CORRECTION MAKES THE CASE STRONGER. They write that 'reflow2's own graph attaches 32 of its 35 document artifacts with `REALIZES`, so its documents propagate and a consumer's do not.' MEASURED HERE against the committed export, counting Artifacts with `artifact_type: document`: 39 documents, 25 carrying a `REALIZES` edge, 26 carrying a `DOCUMENTS` edge, and FOURTEEN ATTACHED BY `DOCUMENTS` ALONE — art:built-right-review, art:collaborating, art:doc-impact-propagation, art:fleet-lessons, art:increment-plan, art:planning-at-scale and eight more, INCLUDING one this very session created. ⇒ REFLOW2 IS NOT BLIND TO THIS BY CONSTRUCTION; IT IS EXPOSED TO IT ON FOURTEEN OF ITS OWN NODES AND NOBODY HAS LOOKED. That is a worse finding than the one they filed, and it removes the excuse.

THEIR ASK, and it is the right shape: EITHER let `DOCUMENTS` participate in propagation — 'a doc that describes a Verification IS affected when that Verification moves' — OR, if the exclusion is deliberate, HAVE THE RESULT SAY SO: `excluded_edge_types: [\"DOCUMENTS\"]` beside the count. 'A bare 0 that cannot distinguish no-impact from this-edge-type-is-not-traversed is the same shape as every other entry in this file.' ⭐ THE SECOND FORM GENERALISES TO THE `ABOUT_ENTITY` CASE TOO, and to any edge added later, which is why it is the better half of the ask.

AND A SECOND FINDING IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION, from the same entry: the 539 is an OVER-estimate. `propagate_change` keys on the NODE, not on WHICH PROPERTY changed, so normalising a `location` string reported the full radius of 'dynograph changed' including 8 interface crossings. 'Not wrong, but not answerable either: a reader cannot tell a contract-breaking edit from a string tidy-up.' BOTH HALVES SHARE ONE ROOT — propagation is computed from topology alone, and the ChangeEvent already carries `change_type`, WHICH NOTHING READS.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, worth keeping: their harness Stop hook caught them with 19 graph writes, 9 `record_change` calls and no `propagate_change`. They had read `revise-design`, whose step 1 is 'Impact first', and skipped it because they had REASONED the edit was low-radius. 'Running it produced a finding my reasoning would not have.' The same hook caught this session the same way.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether any other traversal shares the asymmetry, and whether reading `change_type` could narrow the radius without inventing a judgement.

properties.statement:
`propose_heal`'s RECEIPT MISDESCRIBES ITS OWN SCOPE AT BOTH ENDS: it names a target the caller never chose, and its zero cannot say whether the scorer ran. Reported as two findings by sb-boss (`79d03ab3`) 2026-08-15 on the shared StoryFlow graph; BOTH REPRODUCED HERE on reflow2's own design, and one of them is invisible to the self-host for a structural reason worth naming.

① A `target_id` NOBODY ASKED FOR. The tool takes only `strategy` and `max_operations` — there is NO target parameter — yet the reply carries `target_id`. Their measurement: 4 Projects in the graph, `target_id: proj:dndwright` (alphabetically first), while `issues_addressed` spanned the WHOLE graph including a sibling library and a 121-node cluster. The sweep was global and the label was local. REPRODUCED HERE: `propose_heal{strategy: balanced, max_operations: 10}` returned `target_id: "proj:reflow2"`.

⚠️ AND THIS IS WHY WE COULD NOT HAVE FOUND IT: reflow2's graph holds EXACTLY ONE Project, so the label is accidentally correct here and the defect is unobservable. It needs a multi-Project design to show, which is what a fleet sharing one graph across three bosses has and the maintainer does not. Self-host blindness, and the same shape as F23.

② THE ZERO IS VACUOUS AND NOTHING SAYS SO — the sharper half, because this fleet runs it as a SAFETY GATE. They hold a standing stop on `apply_heal` whose lift condition is 'propose_heal pairs NONE of the five control pairs', and ran it as the read-only evidence step: `operations: []`, `would_destroy: []`, `skipped_operations: []`, 0 of 7 control pairs paired. It reads exactly like a PASS. It is not: no duplicate-class defect existed, so the pair scorer NEVER RAN, and 'it paired none of the seven' is trivially true of nothing. A prior run on 0.24.0 produced 10 structural Merge operations, every one deleting a node — so the shape changed completely and nothing in the output says whether the scorer improved or simply had no input.

REPRODUCED HERE, same shape: `propose_heal` → `operations: []`, summary '9 issue(s) addressed: 0 structural op(s), 9 awaiting generation, 0 skipped'. `detect_defects` → 16 defects, of which contradiction 4, disconnected_community 5, orphan_node 4, unresolved_setup 3, and DUPLICATE-CLASS ZERO. So our own 0 is vacuous by the identical mechanism, and only a second tool call distinguishes it from a real pass.

⭐ THEIR THIRD IDEA IS THE GENERAL ONE AND IS WORTH MORE THAN EITHER FIX: when a detector contributes zero findings, say whether it was EXERCISED AND FOUND NOTHING or HAD NOTHING TO EXAMINE. That is the difference between a check that passed and a check that could not fail. reflow2 already does this elsewhere — `chg:a-null-and-a-vacuous-zero-now-say-which-they-are` gave scoped `detect_gaps` exactly that treatment, and dragon Boss named it a WIN in the same log. So the pattern is accepted doctrine here and `propose_heal` has not received it.

CHEAPEST FIXES, theirs: (1) report the input set — `merge_candidates_considered: 0` beside `operations: []`; (2) distinguish `no_candidates` from `no_operations_proposed` in the summary string, which today render identically; (3) say `scope: "whole design"` when no target was given rather than naming a Project the caller did not pick, or accept an optional scope argument as `detect_gaps` and `detect_defects` both already do.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether `apply_heal` carries the same label, and whether any other tool emits a `target_id` it was not given.

properties.statement:
TWO CAPABILITIES WERE MARKED `realized` ON PASSING UNIT TESTS, THE USER THEN FOUND FOUR BUGS IN THE PRODUCT, AND NOTHING IN THE LOOP HAD ASKED. Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14, item 14 — and he filed the same thing again in his own 'Gaps (mine / process)' section, which is why it is recorded as a loop defect rather than only as his error.

HIS WORDS, item 14: 'I linked a passing unit Verification and marked the increment Capabilities realized. The user then found first-day, civil-vs-UTC, join-day-owed, and a cache miss. `realized` is a claim about THE THREAD, not about the running product. Nothing in the loop said \"realized at unit, unvalidated in the field.\"' And in his own gaps: 'I promoted two Capabilities to realized on unit tests before the user had clicked through. Should have left `in_progress` until the gate matched their account.'

⭐ THE CONCEPT IS NOT MISSING — THE PROMPT IS. The capability lifecycle already distinguishes `realized` from `verified`, and `reconcile_verification` exists precisely to feed real run outcomes back in. So nothing in the vocabulary failed. What failed is that an agent with a green unit test had no moment at which anything asked 'green where?' — and the answer he needed was already expressible.

WHY THIS IS A LOOP DEFECT AND NOT MERELY A MISTAKE: he identified it himself, unprompted, in the same document. An error a careful reporter catches on their own review is one the tooling could have caught at the moment it happened, and the cost of not catching it was borne by the user rather than by him.

CONNECTED, AND THE REASON IT IS WORTH FIXING TOGETHER: `dec:should-a-realizes-edge-say-that-nobody-checked-the-file-still-obeys-the-rule` (his item 5) asks the deeper version — a checksum says the file has not moved, never that it still implements the rule. THIS one is the same hole at the STATUS layer rather than the edge layer: `realized` says a thread is complete, never that the thing works where people use it. Both were reported by the same session, an hour apart, and neither was noticed as the other's sibling until now.

HIS OTHER SELF-REPORTED PROCESS GAPS, recorded because they are evidence about the loop rather than confessions: he widened an accepted Decision from a debugging hypothesis (see `fact:defect-an-accepted-decision-can-be-widened-by-an-agents-diagnosis`); he did not export the graph (see `fact:defect-the-export-was-skipped-because-the-instructions-imply-a-stop-that-is-not-needed`); he did not run detect-and-ask on 62 unsurfaced gaps and says so CORRECTLY — 'they were not the work'; and he did not install the loop nudge, calling `loop_status` by hand. THREE OF THE FOUR HAVE A TOOLING CAUSE RECORDED AGAINST THEM. The fourth — declining to detect-and-ask — was the right call and is recorded so a later reader does not treat it as debt.

properties.statement:
A REBUILD STRANDS AN ATTACHED SESSION'S SHARED SERVER, UNRECOVERABLY, AND THE ERROR POINTS AT A LOG THAT CANNOT EXPLAIN IT. Hit 2026-08-07 doing nothing unusual: `cargo test --workspace` with a Claude Code session attached over MCP. SEQUENCE: the shared daemon reached its 120-minute idle timeout and exited, releasing the store lock — correct, by design, and logged as such. The session's client then tried to auto-start a replacement and failed with "could not spawn the shared reflow2 server: No such file or directory (os error 2)". CAUSE: spawn_daemon resolves the binary with std::env::current_exe() (crates/reflow2-mcp/src/shared.rs). cargo test had relinked reflow2-mcp, so the running process's current_exe() resolved to a DELETED INODE, while a perfectly good binary sat at the same path the whole time. THREE THINGS MAKE IT WORSE THAN A TRANSIENT: (1) it is unrecoverable for the life of the session — every later respawn resolves the same dead inode, and only a full MCP reconnect clears it; (2) the error's advice, "Check the server log beside the graph directory", names the wrong file, because the failure is in the PARENT process and never reaches the daemon log — whose last line is the idle-timeout exit, which reads like the cause and is not; (3) it will hit anyone who runs the test suite while a session is attached, which on this repo is everyone. SAME SHAPE AS fact:defect-lineage-message-omits-its-own-decision: a message whose stated remedy cannot address the actual cause, so the reader spends their time in the wrong place. Note the idle expiry itself is not the defect and should not be 'fixed' — shared.rs documents why the daemon must expire (it holds the store's exclusive write lock, and an immortal daemon trades one lock problem for another).

═══ ADDENDUM 2026-08-12 — FIFTH SIGHTING, AND IT CORRECTS THE RECOVERY STEP ABOVE ═══

Hit again mid-session on 2026-08-12, same mechanism, confirmed by direct measurement rather than inference:
  readlink /proc/341009/exe  -> /home/ajs7/project/reflow2/target/debug/reflow2-mcp (deleted)
  readlink /proc/4067388/exe -> /home/ajs7/project/reflow2/target/debug/reflow2-mcp (deleted)
Both live client processes were executing a deleted inode while a current, executable binary sat at that exact path.

⭐ WHY IT RECURRED DESPITE BEING FIXED, and this is the part worth keeping. The fix landed as `relaunchable_exe_from` in PR #149 (`dafa57f`, "spawn_daemon survives a replaced binary"), merged 2026-08-11. The two client processes started 2026-08-11 at 06:58 and 18:57 — BEFORE that merge. A fix to the spawn path cannot help a session that is already running the binary it fixes: the affected process is by definition the OLD one. ⇒ THE POPULATION THAT HITS THIS DEFECT IS EXACTLY THE POPULATION THE FIX CANNOT REACH, until every long-lived session has been restarted. Confirmed by the error text: the message received was the OLD wording, "could not spawn the shared reflow2 server: No such file or directory (os error 2)", which shared.rs:400 records as the pre-#149 message. The post-fix path names the file it could not find.

🛑 AND IT CORRECTS THE RECOVERY CLAUSE ABOVE. This node says "only a full MCP reconnect clears it". MEASURED FALSE on 2026-08-12: a `/mcp` reconnect does NOT clear it, because a reconnect does not replace a running stdio server — the same process, with the same dead inode, continues serving. Only a FULL RESTART of the client does. The distinction is not pedantic: reconnect is the cheap thing a stranded user will try first, it appears to succeed, and it leaves them exactly as stranded while believing they have already tried the remedy.

WHAT KEPT THE SESSION WORKING: `tools/reflow2_cli.py` spawns its own short-lived process against the store, so every graph write of that afternoon went through it and nothing was lost. Worth knowing — the outage is to the MCP transport, never to the design.

properties.statement:
`record_change` SILENTLY OVERWRITES THE `name` OF THE ChangeEvent IT IS FILED UNDER, SO THE TOOL WHOSE PURPOSE IS PRESERVING PRIOR STATE DESTROYS PRIOR STATE ONE NODE OVER. Found by doing it, 2026-08-15, while recording Alex's feedback — not by reading code, and not by any gate.

MEASURED. `add_change_event` created `chg:change-type-gap-corroborated-by-a-second-project` with a name explaining why `resync` was the least-wrong `change_type` for that edit. The next call was `record_change` with the same `change_event_id` and its own `name` describing the SNAPSHOT. The reply's `current` field came back holding the ChangeEvent with the snapshot's name, and `get_node` confirmed it: the event's original name was gone, with nothing said. The snapshot itself was correct — it captured the pre-edit statement, which is what it is for.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS: the call reports success, the snapshot is genuinely right, and the loss is in a DIFFERENT node from the one the caller is thinking about. Nothing in the reply says a property was replaced. The only reason it was caught here is that the overwritten text had just been written by hand in the previous call and was still in view.

WHAT `name` MEANS IN THAT CALL IS THE AMBIGUITY: `record_change`'s parameter list reads (epoch, change_event, name, target_type, target_id, change_type, action), and every other parameter describes THE CHANGE RECORD. Reading `name` as the record's name is the natural interpretation and it is the one the caller wants; the implementation applies it to the EVENT. Two different things want a name here and the API gives them one field.

SIBLING OF, AND SHARPER THAN, A REPORTED ONE. Alex's item 2 says the record-before-you-edit discipline loses to parallel tool calls: he snapshotted a Decision after a sibling call had already merged it, so the Snapshot stored the NEW statement. That is a caller-ordering hazard and his fix shape — refuse when the target's current hash is not what the caller thinks it is — addresses it. THIS ONE IS NOT AVOIDABLE BY ORDERING: the sequence here was strictly serial, one call at a time, exactly as the skill prescribes, and the loss happened anyway. Doing it right is not a defence.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: one serial reproduction, confirmed by get_node afterwards. WHAT IS NOT: whether the same overwrite hits other properties of the event, how many existing ChangeEvents in this graph already carry a snapshot's name instead of their own (cheap to sweep and not yet done), or whether any reader depends on the current behaviour.

FIX SHAPES, smallest first: leave the event's `name` alone when it already has one, and use the passed name for the Snapshot only; or split the parameter into `snapshot_name` so the two nameable things are distinguishable; or, at minimum, report in the reply that the event's name was replaced — this project's own rule is that nothing is silently dropped and partial-success fields are always present.

properties.statement:
THE CONTRADICTION DETECTOR NEVER READS DECISION STATUS, so recording a refuted idea the way the design prescribes ADDS a warning-severity structural defect — and burying it in prose adds none. Reported by dragon Boss (`853732df`) 2026-08-15, found by doing the thing a peer had just recommended, immediately after doing it. MECHANISM CONFIRMED IN SOURCE HERE.

WHAT THEY DID, and it is correct practice: recorded a refuted remedy as its own Decision at `status: rejected` — the shape that already ships and that three seats had been reaching for prose instead of — then linked it to the remedy that replaced it with `CONTRADICTS {alignment: opposing}`, which is the honest relation and the one `describe_schema`'s own hint points at. `detect_defects` then reported a `contradiction` at severity `warning` with `suggested_fix_type: generate_decision`. **A rejected decision contradicting its successor is the HEALTHY case** — it is what 'tried in thought, refuted, here is what we did instead' looks like in graph form. There is nothing to resolve.

CONFIRMED AT `heal.rs:916-935`: the loop walks every CONTRADICTS edge, skips only `alignment: supporting`, and NEVER consults either endpoint's `status`. ⭐ THE CODE'S OWN COMMENT ARGUES THE FIX ONE LEVEL OVER: it explains that reading the edge TYPE and never the property meant 'every correctly-modelled corroboration came back as a structural defect', and ends 'A PROPERTY THE DETECTOR IGNORES IS A PROPERTY THAT LIES.' That is precisely the case for `status` too — the same argument, one property across.

⚠️ THE CONSEQUENCE IS AN INCENTIVE PROBLEM, which is why it is worth a number rather than a shrug: the tool mildly penalises exactly the discipline `rejected` exists to support, and it does so at the moment a seat is least likely to push back, having just been told (rightly) they should have been using `rejected` all along. The cheap wrong response is to delete the rejected node or the edge — which is the erasure the record exists to prevent.

MEASURED ON REFLOW2'S OWN DESIGN, and the result is worth stating carefully: NONE of our four reported contradictions currently has a `rejected` or `superseded` endpoint, so the defect does not fire here today. BUT the design holds 10 `superseded` and 1 `rejected` Decision, so it fires the moment anyone draws a CONTRADICTS from one of those to its successor. ⇒ That we have 11 such decisions and ZERO such edges is itself weak evidence FOR their incentive argument: the relation is not being recorded, and this is one reason it might not be.

THEIR SUGGESTION: exclude pairs where either endpoint is `rejected` or `superseded` from the `contradiction` category, or report them in a separate band ('superseded-by' rather than 'conflict'). The information is still worth surfacing; it is just not a defect and should not share a list with cycles and SPOFs.

⭐ AND A WIN THEY ASKED TO HAVE RECORDED, which the fix must not damage: `acknowledge_defect` handled it well. The REASON is stored rather than the suppression, and the review EXPIRES if the defect's shape changes, because the id hashes the category with the affected set — so an acceptance cannot silently cover a future, different contradiction between the same two nodes.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the same status-blindness affects any other detector, and whether `superseded` and `rejected` should be treated identically here — a superseded decision may still conflict in a way worth seeing.

properties.statement:
A SERVED SKILL AND A SERVED TOOL STATED OPPOSITE SEMANTICS FOR THE SAME CALL, AND THE DISAGREEMENT WAS ABOUT WHETHER A WRITE DESTROYS DATA. FIXED 2026-08-09.

The tool description said create_node MERGES — 'the props you pass overwrite, every stored property you omit survives'. The revise-design skill said 'Do NOT reach for the generic create_node to revise. It is create-or-REPLACE, so passing only the changed field resets every other property to its schema default'.

SETTLED FROM THE SOURCE: the served tool calls upsert_node (crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/query.rs), whose own doc reads 'Merge props onto id if it exists... every stored property the caller does not name survives'. THE TOOL WAS RIGHT AND THE SKILL WAS WRONG.

THE DIRECTION IS WHAT MAKES IT EXPENSIVE: the skill scared agents away from the SAFE call. A dev_storyflow worker filed it after being unable to tell which was true without risking nine accepted requirements, and passed the whole property set to be safe under either reading. A session here did exactly the same thing the same day on a DesignRule, for the same reason. Both paid the cost; neither lost data, which is why it went unnoticed.

AND IT COMPOUNDS WITH A GAP THE SAME WORKER FOUND: the skill prescribes revising via a typed constructor, but there is no typed constructor for a DesignRule at all, and add_requirement accepts only id/name/statement — so a requirement's `source` is unreachable that way. The prescribed safe route did not exist for those fields, and nothing said so. The skill now says both things.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the fourth skill-versus-tool drift recorded here: nothing checks a skill's claims about tool BEHAVIOUR. skill_lint verifies that every tool a skill NAMES exists on the served surface — which is why this survived: every name was real, only the semantics were wrong.

properties.statement: `--shared` TURNED SESSION-LOCAL METRICS INTO SHARED-STATE METRICS WITHOUT CHANGING THEIR INTERFACE, AND TWO BOSSES ATTRIBUTED A FLEET-WIDE MOVEMENT TO THEIR OWN CHANGE — IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION. loop_status and graph_report read IDENTICALLY before and after the migration; only the MEANING of their numbers changed. A total is now a fleet number moved by every attached boss and worker, wearing the timestamp of whoever asked. MEASURED on one graph in one day by non-coordinating sessions: defects 42 -> 6 -> 5 -> 12 (the 5 -> 12 arriving an hour later to a session that had done nothing at all), and gaps 48 -> 55 -> 69. api-boss `5d608b85` reported '42 -> 6' to the user TWICE as their own result; it was not. A worker checking in reported gaps 55 -> 69 and defects 12 -> 26 between two check-ins hours apart and, correctly, could name no cause. CONSEQUENCE THE REPORTER DREW AND IT IS THE GENERAL ONE: every citation of these counts written before `--shared` is now subtly wrong, and nothing in the output says so. THE ROOT SHAPE, in their words: A SESSION CANNOT TELL THAT IT IS NOT ALONE. Nothing in any payload reports concurrency — no attached-session count, no last-write-by — so every seat reasons as if solo and the output actively encourages it. They fixed it with a fleet convention (state whether a count is FLEET or SCOPED), which is a discipline layered on top of a tool that could just say it; a caveat maintained in a downstream doc is a defect routed around rather than fixed. ---- 2026-08-08, w-9d1d1499 (LANE PROSE-JOIN) ADDS THE CLEANEST INSTANCE YET AND THE COST OF THE WORKAROUND. loop_status read `67 gaps / 26 defects / 19 unproven` at their check-in and `48 / 27 / 14` hours later. THEY EXECUTED ZERO DESIGN WRITES THE ENTIRE SESSION, so none of that movement was theirs — AND THE ONLY WAY TO SAY SO IS A PARAGRAPH OF ENGLISH ASSERTING IT, WHICH THE NEXT READER HAS TO TAKE ON TRUST. Their PROTOCOL now carries a standing rule (§🔒 rule 5) whose ENTIRE CONTENT IS *'a global graph count is a fleet number, never your result'* — A DOCTRINE RULE EXISTING SOLELY TO COMPENSATE FOR SOMETHING THE TOOL COULD REPORT DIRECTLY. That is the second binding fleet rule written to work around one reflow2 output in as many days (see fact:defect-loop-status-next-routes-to-the-destructive-skill and its stop-order), and the pattern is the finding: when a tool will not say something, a downstream constitution grows a rule that everyone must remember instead. THEIR FIX SHAPE IS SHARPER THAN THE ORIGINAL: let loop_status/graph_report optionally take a `contributor_id` (or use the seat) and return *'changed since your first call this session: N, of which yours: M'*. THE DATA IS ALREADY THERE — authored_by, seats, ChangeEvents. It would replace a rule everyone must remember with a number anyone can cite. RELATED AND SEPARATELY REPORTED: there is no 'what changed since I looked, and by whom' query — sessions discover the graph moved by re-running a rollup and noticing a different number, which is the worst possible detector, and for ephemeral seats that die on context exhaustion the first real question on return is exactly 'what happened while I was gone'. That requirement is now ACCEPTED here as req:what-changed-since-i-looked-and-by-whom, and NOTHING SATISFIES IT (gap:e1a591cdc38809a5). FIX SHAPE: have loop_status/graph_report label their own rollups as graph-wide and report the number of currently-attached sessions; a scoped detect_gaps/detect_defects is already attributable and could say so.

properties.statement: A SCOPED DETECTOR RETURNING `in_scope: 0` OVER `region_size: 1` READS AS A PASS AND IS THE OPPOSITE — SIX INDEPENDENT SESSIONS REPORTED IT IN ONE DAY, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST CORROBORATION IN THE FEEDBACK FILE. Reported separately, without consolidation, by w-10f94d47, w-08baa598, w-fb7d30ab, w-ec25cf2c, w-deac0a1e and w-abbb53d2 across dev_storyflow on 2026-08-07. `detect_gaps` and `detect_defects` scoped to a node return `in_scope`, `out_of_scope` and `region_size`, and REPORTING region_size IS THE THING THAT WORKS — three of the six said so explicitly and one wants it kept on the record as a win: it is what let them state honestly that their zero was narrow-but-real rather than empty (region_size 14, 16, 41 in three cases). THE DEFECT IS THAT THE JUDGEMENT IS LEFT TO THE READER. w-deac0a1e scoped to `dec:core_must_not_import_a_lens` and got `in_scope: 0`, which reads green; it was an ISLAND — the node has no edges, so the detector had exactly one node to look at. They only caught it by running a control on a sibling (`dec:lens_isolation` -> region_size 18, 4 gaps) to prove the measurement could return more at all. Two earlier workers had to caveat the same shape in prose as 'the weakest green in the building'. THE GENERAL POINT, and it is why six reports matter more than one: the tool has the number and the human has to supply the interpretation, and under operational load supplying it is exactly what gets skipped. A vacuous green that reads as a pass is the class this fleet keeps paying for. Noted honestly by one reporter: `detect_defects` DOES name the same situation explicitly as `disconnected_community` — it is the gap detector that reads as green. FIX SHAPE, converged on independently by all six: when region_size is 1 (or the region reaches no node of a type the detector can fire on), say so in the payload — e.g. `caveat: "region is a single isolated node; in_scope: 0 is not evidence of health"`. One field. The information is already computed.

properties.statement:
⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-15, HOURS AFTER FILING, BY MEASUREMENT. THE REPORTED HARM DOES NOT OCCUR. As filed, this said a 16-char baseline 'compares unequal to every full-width recompute' and would report PERMANENT FALSE DRIFT. That was checked against the running 0.31.0 build and is FALSE: register `sha256:626d0572034645bf`, then reconcile against the full 64-char digest of the same bytes, and `reconcile_artifacts` returns `unchanged: 1, findings: 0`. `checksums_agree` requires a real prefix relationship and honours exactly this case — BL-160, fixed 2026-08-01, after the same phantom-drift class had been reported 51 times on a clean tree. 

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, AND IT IS MUCH SMALLER: `set_artifact_checksums` accepts a digest SHORTER than its named algorithm without remarking on it, so a caller who truncates by accident gets a WEAKER BASELINE THAN THEY THINK (16 hex = 64 bits) and is not told. The observation in the report was correct — it was accepted with `applied: true` on three artifacts, and was noticed only because the reply echoed the node back with the full digest in `location` beside the short one. Only the CONSEQUENCE was overstated. 

⛔ DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY VALIDATING LENGTH AT THE BOUNDARY. Short digests are a DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED DIALECT: reflow2's own `tools/build_design_graph.py` writes `hexdigest()[:16]`, and `checksums_agree` states the rule out loud — 'No minimum length is imposed. A short baseline is a weak baseline, but its strength is decided when it is registered — the write side takes a 16-char digest without complaint, and a read side that then refused to honour it would be the same write/read disagreement all over again.' Refusing short digests on write would break that generator, invalidate every existing short baseline, and re-open the write/read split those two functions exist to close. 

RESIDUAL ASK, IF ANY: a remark rather than a refusal — the reply could say the accepted digest is shorter than the named algorithm's width, which is the same 'say what you did' principle the `revision` block landed on 2026-08-15 under. That is a nicety, not a defect, and it is recorded here at that weight. 

THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, worth more than the item: a capable reporter measured the OBSERVATION correctly and inferred the CONSEQUENCE without testing it, then ranked it first of five. The report was read, ranked first here too, and only survived to the fix stage because the code comment contradicted it. Consumer reports are evidence about what happened, not about what it means. || SOURCE: reported by the dev_storyflow fleet 2026-08-15 on reflow2 0.31.0; refuted by measurement against the same build the same day.

properties.statement:
set_verification_status SILENTLY DELETED `last_run_at` WHEN THE OPTIONAL PARAMETER WAS OMITTED — data loss from the most ordinary act there is. FIXED 2026-08-09.

Filed by dev_storyflow 2026-08-08 and RE-FILED after retesting on 0.26.1, both times on a throwaway node created for the purpose and never on one whose timestamp anyone depended on. One variable: same node, same status, parameter omitted, key GONE. The key was REMOVED rather than set to null, so a wiped check was byte-identical to one that had never run.

CONFIRMED IN THE SOURCE HERE RATHER THAN TAKEN FROM THE REPORT: verify.rs copied every existing property EXCEPT `status` and `last_run_at`, so an omitted `last_run_at` was excluded from the copy and never re-set.

WHY THE DIRECTION WAS THE BAD ONE, and this is their argument, not a restatement: it fires from marking a check `failing` after a regression — which erases the evidence it ever ran — and it fails toward `never_run`, precisely the field a later session greps for unproven work. It was invisible at the call site because the response is success-shaped and dominated by a long `name`.

AND IT BROKE A CONVENTION THIS CODEBASE STATES ELSEWHERE AS A PRINCIPLE, which is the cheapest thing to point at: set_interface_spec promises 'omitting one LEAVES IT ALONE', set_decision_status 'Every other property is preserved', set_epoch_status 'Everything else about the epoch is preserved'. This function's own first line said 'preserving its other properties' and then null-wrote one of them. One tool departing from a convention the others state is worse than no convention, because a caller who has read any sibling reasonably assumes it.

THE FIX: `last_run_at` is replaced only when the caller supplies one. Clearing a run time is therefore not expressible by omission, and should not be — erasing evidence is a deliberate act and deserves a deliberate call. PROVEN BY NEGATIVE CONTROL: restoring the old one-line condition fails the new test on exactly the data-loss assertion. The test also pins the other direction (an explicit timestamp still overwrites), because a fix that made the parameter inert would be the same bug pointing the other way.

⚠️ WORTH CARRYING TO THE FLEET: they upgraded to 0.26.1 partly on the understanding that filed bugs were fixed, and said so — several were, this one was not, and a reader skimming 'we upgraded, bugs fixed' would reasonably have assumed otherwise. The retest is what caught it.

properties.statement:
SURFACED 2026-08-16 BY THE WIDENED DEGREE-ZERO RULE, on its first run over reflow2's own graph — a finding nothing could previously report.

SEVEN TemporalFacts carry a `subject_id` naming a node THAT DOES NOT EXIST, and two of the seven are plainly typos for a live node:
  fact:dev-storyflow-fleet-log-triaged-2026-08-16          -> prj:reflow2      (the Project is proj:reflow2)
  fact:defect-kit-manifest-drift-is-invisible-to-ci        -> cap:thin-install (the node is req:thin-install)
  fact:defect-append-only-volatility-exempts-a-structural-rewrite
  fact:defect-link-artifact-has-no-type-for-a-test-source
  fact:dev-storyflow-fleet-log-full-triage-6203-lines-2026-08-16
  fact:reflow2s-black-boxes-hold-no-functions-allocation-went-straight-to-the-modules
  fact:the-music-graph-feedback-file-is-four-sessions-and-its-first-batch-was-fixed-long-ago

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE. `subject_id` is a required INDEXED property, so a fact names its subject without an edge — which means a fact is reachable by index lookup and never by a graph walk. Nothing validated that the id resolves. `orphan_node` ran on Decision only; `disconnected_community` reports clusters of >=2 and a node joined to nothing is never a cluster. So the pointer could be wrong for as long as it liked.

WHAT IT COSTS: the observation is stranded. It cannot be found from the thing it is about, it never enters an impact analysis, and a reader searching the live node's history sees nothing.

NOT REPAIRED HERE, and deliberately so: correcting a `subject_id` is a judgement about what the fact was about, not a mechanical fix, and the two obvious typos are the only two anybody could assert without reading each statement. RELATED, UNANSWERED: whether the schema should validate that a pointer property resolves at WRITE time — which would have stopped all seven at the door — or whether that couples the schema layer to graph contents in a way this design does not want.

SMALL, CHEAP SURFACE FRICTIONS — TWO REAL, ONE DISPROVEN BY MEASUREMENT. (1) REAL: `add_contributor` TAKES THE HANDLE AS `id` WHILE `claim_region` TAKES THE SAME HANDLE AS `contributor_id`. w-08baa598 passed `contributor_id` to add_contributor first — because that is the field name the very next call in the documented sequence uses — and got `failed to deserialize parameters: unknown field 'contributor_id', expected one of 'id', 'name', 'kind', 'handle', 'description'`. Cost one round trip. THE ERROR MESSAGE IS GOOD and is why this is minor: it named the accepted fields. The two calls are adjacent steps in the fleet's prescribed worker sequence and the asymmetry carries no meaning. FIX SHAPE: accept `contributor_id` as an alias on add_contributor. (2) ~~`set_verification_kind` ECHOES THE PRE-UPDATE `status`~~ — **DISPROVEN HERE 2026-08-08 BY RUNNING IT, AND THIS ENTRY NOW EXISTS TO RECORD THAT.** Four seats reported it across two days (w-ec25cf2c, w-3f408ab0, sb-boss ab2291fa as 'two workers and I'), and their fleet adopted a standing habit of re-reading every node rather than trusting any echo. THE ECHO IS CORRECT. Probe: create a Verification, `set_verification_status(passing)` FIRST, then `set_verification_kind(validation)` — the ordering that would expose a stale read. The echo returned `status: passing, kind: validation` and a `get_node` returned exactly the same. `verify.rs:169-175` reads the existing node, copies every property except `kind`, and returns what `create_node` wrote; `git log -L` dates that loop to 9073b9e, 2026-07-22, the commit that introduced `Verification.kind` — so it has been correct since the feature existed and was never stale, including on the day they filed. WHAT THEY ACTUALLY SAW: they called set_verification_kind while the status genuinely still WAS `planned`, set it to `passing` afterwards, and read the earlier echo as though it described the later state. The echo described the node at the moment of that call, correctly. THE FINDING IS NOW ABOUT REPORTING, NOT ABOUT THE ECHO, and it cuts two ways. Their file's no-dedup rule exists so a maintainer can see RECURRENCE — 'one report reads as one seat's opinion while two reads as the tool doing it to everyone' — and here it turned one misreading into four, which read as strong evidence and was not. RECURRENCE IS NOT CORROBORATION WHEN THE SEATS SHARE A METHOD. And I recorded the four reproductions as strengthening the case before testing it, which is the same credulity one layer along; rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party exists for exactly this. THEIR HABIT SURVIVES THE CORRECTION AND IS STILL RIGHT: re-reading a node after a write that matters is what AGENTS.md asks for anyway. Only the stated reason was wrong. (3) REAL: `claim_region`'s TWO REFUSALS ARE BOTH CORRECT AND NEITHER NAMES ITS OWN FIX. It needs `seat` on the sessionless transport and refuses otherwise; it also needs a Contributor to exist first, failing with `Node not found: Contributor <handle>`. Both are documented — IN THE TOOL DESCRIPTIONS, which an agent only reads if it happens to load that tool. THE COST WAS NOT ONE RETRY. A worker hit the second refusal, concluded the tool was broken, and wrote 'there is NO mint_seat tool in the served surface' INTO THE WORKER ONBOARDING FILE — a false correction that TRAVELLED FIVE HOPS and reached a boss offering to amend PROTOCOL on it, before another worker disproved it with one command. FIX SHAPE: make the refusals name their own fix — 'call add_contributor first' / 'call mint_seat and pass it as seat'. NOTE THE FAMILY RESEMBLANCE to fact:defect-a-deferred-tool-reads-as-a-nonexistent-one AND to (2) above: in all three a session's reasonable inference about the tool was written down and propagated, and in two of them the inference was false. The expensive failure in this channel is not the tools — it is a conclusion travelling faster than a test.

properties.statement: THE STALE-SERVER DEFECT REPRODUCED FIRST-HAND IN THIS REPO, IN THE SESSION THAT CAPTURED IT — AND THE `/proc/self/exe` SIGNAL dev_storyflow PROPOSED WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE, TRUE, THE WHOLE TIME. Not reported by anyone: observed here on 2026-08-08 while running loop_status after a normal working session. WHAT WAS SEEN: `loop_status` returned a field, `open_defects: 90`, that WAS NOT IN THE RESPONSE AT SESSION START and DOES NOT EXIST ANYWHERE IN THE CHECKED-OUT SOURCE — `grep -rn open_defects crates/` returns nothing on this branch, and the branch that implements it (`feat/loop-reads-defect-facts`) is verified NOT an ancestor of HEAD. THE DIAGNOSIS, run rather than reasoned: `ps` showed the `--serve-shared` daemon started at 05:22 THAT MORNING, mid-session — the previous daemon had hit its idle timeout during the long `cargo test --workspace` runs and a replacement was auto-spawned from `target/debug/reflow2-mcp`, which at that moment still held a build made in an EARLIER session on a DIFFERENT branch. Confirmed by comparing the two binaries directly: `strings /proc/1345843/exe | grep -c open_defects` = 1, while `strings target/debug/reflow2-mcp | grep -c open_defects` = 0. The running server and the source being edited were built from different code, and NOTHING ANYWHERE SAID SO. THE PROPOSED FIX IS VALIDATED, not merely plausible: `readlink /proc/1345843/exe` returned `/home/ajs7/project/reflow2/target/debug/reflow2-mcp (deleted)` — the exact kernel marker w-6904efa6 proposed deriving `stale: true` from, present and correct at the moment it was needed, requiring one syscall and no second source. This is now confirmed on two machines, two projects, two independent incidents. WHAT IT COST HERE, stated rather than glossed: every computed rollup read after 05:22 — gap counts, structural_defects 1 to 3, open_defects itself — came from a build that is not the one being shipped. Graph WRITES were unaffected (the store is the store, and the export and gate were both computed from the working tree by `cargo`/`reflow2_check.py`, plus a clean-checkout CI run), so the deliverable stands; but any number quoted from the server mid-session is of unknown provenance, and a session that had reported one as evidence would have been wrong with no way to notice. THE SHARPEST PART: this happened in the very session that was capturing and fixing a defect of this class, to an agent that had just written the words 'the server can detect its own staleness with one syscall' — and it was still only caught because a field appeared that could not possibly exist. That is the argument for the field rather than the discipline.

`set_artifact_checksum`'s TWO DISPOSITIONS HAVE NO ANSWER FOR THE COMMONEST FIX THERE IS: THE CODE WAS WRONG AND NOW MATCHES INTENT THAT NEVER CHANGED. Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14, item 8.

HIS CASE: after aligning as-built to an ALREADY ACCEPTED Requirement, 'neither `design_holds` (no design meaning) nor `design_updated` (design moved; pass the ChangeEvent) fits cleanly if you ALSO revised a Decision in the same hour. Agents spend a turn picking a side instead of shipping the comparison fix.'

WHY NEITHER FITS. `design_holds` says the change carries no design meaning — but a bug that violated an accepted Requirement carried a great deal of it; the design was right and the code was wrong, which is a fact worth recording rather than waving through. `design_updated` says the design moved with the code — and it did not; the Requirement is untouched and passing a ChangeEvent for it would assert a revision that never happened.

⭐ THIS IS THE `change_type` GAP IN A SECOND VOCABULARY. `fact:defect-change-event-has-no-type-for-a-field-reported-defect` records that the enum has no value for 'the code was wrong'; here the DISPOSITION enum has no value for the same event. The same missing meaning is absent from two independent surfaces, which is evidence it is a real category rather than a wording quibble.

HIS PROPOSED VALUE, held open in `dec:idea-should-the-checksum-accept-have-an-as-built-aligned-disposition`: `as_built_aligned` — 'allow it when a Requirement did not change and the file now matches it'.

WHAT MUST NOT BE LOST IF IT IS ADDED: `dec:two-sided-accept` exists because a silent accept 'is how a design erodes into fiction over N fix cycles while reporting zero gaps'. A third disposition is only safe if it makes the SAME claim shape — dated, attributable, and counted apart in the confirmation ledger the way `baseline_established` already is.

NOT ESTABLISHED: how often this case arises. One report, and the confirmation ledger could answer it by counting `design_holds` accepts whose events carry `test_failure_fix` — a sweep nobody has run.

properties.statement:
EVERY DESCRIPTION AROUND `Constraint` SAYS 'NUMERIC BUDGET' WHILE THE SCHEMA REQUIRES ONLY `name` AND `statement`, AND A CAREFUL READER THEREFORE RULED OUT THE EXACT NODE TYPE THEY NEEDED. Measured 2026-08-15 on a genesis session modelling the US federal government (docs/feedback/2026-08-15-usgov-genesis-session.md, item 3, which its own author graded the report's only HIGH severity).

WHAT THE SESSION CONCLUDED: that reflow2 has no home for a requirement that FORBIDS. It listed eleven constitutional prohibitions — no bill of attainder, no ex post facto law, no title of nobility, habeas corpus may not be suspended, Speech or Debate immunity, the Tenth Amendment reservation — and reasoned that `Constraint` 'requires quantity / limit / direction. Numeric budgets only. \"No ex post facto law\" has no unit.' It left all eleven as Requirements, knowing they would be reported unsatisfied forever, and deliberately did not silence them.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: `describe_schema {node_type: Constraint, required_only: true}` returns `name` and `statement`. NOTHING ELSE. `add_constraint`'s required list is `id`, `name`, `statement`; `quantity`, `limit`, `direction`, `category` and `objective` all carry `default: null`. AND THE TYPE'S OWN HINT IS THE USE CASE VERBATIM: 'A limit or rule the design MUST respect (vs. a Requirement, which is a goal to achieve). \"Must run offline\", \"budget under $5k\", \"no PII leaves the device\".' — 'no PII leaves the device' and 'no bill of attainder shall be passed' are the same sentence shape: a non-numeric prohibition, imposed rather than chosen, binding everything, owned by nobody. Constraint is the home for all eleven, with no schema change and no new node type, and CONSTRAINS reaches any node.

WHY THE READER WAS MISLED, WHICH IS THE DEFECT: the prose disagrees with the schema in one direction only. The served instructions say 'When the user states a NUMERIC LIMIT — a mass budget, an end-to-end latency, a cost cap — record it as a Constraint: add_constraint with quantity (unit-bearing), limit and direction.' `add_constraint`'s own description opens 'For a numeric budget (BL-11) set quantity...'. The kpp-proposal skill is entirely about thresholds and numbers. Three surfaces, all narrower than the type, none of them wrong sentence-by-sentence, and together they describe a budget primitive. The one place that states the truth is `describe_schema`, which the session did not call for this type and had no reason to: it was not guessing at an unusual node, it was reading the documentation for a familiar one.

⭐ SAME ROOT CAUSE AS `fact:defect-typed-tool-parameter-names-are-inconsistent`, AND THIS IS WHAT MAKES IT WORTH MORE THAN A DOC FIX. That fact records the helper layer disagreeing with the schema about FIELD NAMES — nine instances, each costing a failed call and a retry, correctly graded as individually trivial. This is the same disagreement about a node type's SCOPE, and the cost is not a retry: it is a modelling decision. The session graded the field-name instance it hit as 'low, but it costs a full round trip' and this one as 'high... a modelling-vocabulary gap, not a bug'. BOTH JUDGEMENTS ARE THE SAME DEFECT SEEN AT TWO PRICES, and the expensive one was invisible as a defect because it never produced an error — it produced a confident wrong conclusion and eleven permanently-open gaps.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: the schema requires two fields; three documentation surfaces describe a numeric budget; one experienced reader concluded the type was unusable and modelled around it. WHAT IS NOT: how many other designs have made the same substitution (this is one observation), and whether the eleven were ever re-modelled — that is the other project's call, not reflow2's.

FIX SHAPES, smallest first: give `add_constraint`'s description a leading sentence for the non-numeric case before the budget paragraph; correct the served instructions' 'When the user states a numeric limit' to name prohibitions too; or, if the budget reading is the intended one, say so and answer where a non-numeric imposed limit belongs — but the hint already answers that, so the prose is what is wrong.

properties.statement:
A SESSION'S GRAPH WRITES WENT UNEXPORTED BECAUSE THE SERVED INSTRUCTIONS IMPLY THE SHARED SERVER MUST BE STOPPED FIRST. IT MUST NOT. Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14, item 12 — recorded as a DOCUMENTATION defect, because the report's own reasoning is what turned out to be wrong.

HIS CLAIM: 'This session wrote more and did not refresh the export (shared server holds the store; EXPORT WANTS IT STOPPED). Agents will not `--stop-shared` in the middle of a user-facing debug loop.' The behavioural prediction is sound. The premise is false.

MEASURED HERE, 2026-08-15: `export_graph` takes a READ LOCK on the in-process graph (`crates/reflow2-mcp/src/tools/exchange.rs:128`) and never opens the store directly. It is callable at any time, from any session, with a shared server running — this session called it repeatedly while the daemon held the store. ONLY the CLI `--import` / `--export` path, which opens RocksDB itself, needs `--stop-shared`.

WHERE THE MISTAKE COMES FROM, AND IT IS OURS: the served AGENTS.md section 'Restoring a design' says a command which opens the store DIRECTLY cannot run while the server holds it, gives the `--stop-shared` + `--import` recipe, and then says '`--export` writes one back out' — in the same breath, with no signal that the MCP TOOL of nearly the same name is unaffected. A careful reader generalises the caveat to both, which is what happened.

COST: a full session of design work — ChangeEvents, snapshots, Decision and Requirement merges, Artifact checksums — left unexported and therefore invisible to every other seat, because of one paragraph's arrangement. And the session was RIGHT that it would not stop a shared server mid-debug; it simply never needed to.

FIX SHAPE: separate the CLI paragraph from the tool, and say plainly that `export_graph` needs no stop. `fact:defect-the-served-instructions-put-their-standing-rules-where-a-client-cap-deletes-them` is the sibling finding about the same document's shape.

properties.statement:
`reflow2_check.py` CRASHED ON A DIRECTORY ARTIFACT AND REPORTED THE CRASH AS 'GATE FAILED'. Reported by dev_storyflow's api-boss sidekick (`551d9718`), 2026-08-15, and VERIFIED HERE IN EVERY PARTICULAR before being acted on.

WHAT THEY REPORTED: `IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory: './.claude/'` out of `hash_file`, exiting 1.

VERIFIED, four ways: (1) `hash_file` opened the path with no directory guard; (2) `sys.exit(main())` had NO try/except, so an uncaught exception took Python's own exit 1; (3) the module docstring's contract is exactly as they quoted — '0 coherent · 1 gate failed · 2 could not run (… never a silent pass)'; (4) reflow2's own graph carries 182 artifacts with a location and NOT ONE resolves to a directory, against 11 in dev_storyflow.

⭐ THE EXIT CODE WAS THE WORSE HALF, and their framing is right: a dedicated code exists for could-not-run precisely so a CI job can tell a drifted design from a broken tool. Landing in 1 made the ONE confusion the three-code design was built to prevent reachable from every line of it. NOT a silent pass — that credit stands — but a MISFILED one, invisible in a badge or a required-check summary where the traceback is the only tell.

⭐⭐ AND IT IS THE SELF-HOST BLIND SPOT AGAIN, which is why reflow2 could never have found this alone: `ci.yml:102` runs this gate on every push and PR, against a graph with zero directory artifacts. THE GATE IS GENUINELY EXERCISED AND HAS NEVER EXECUTED THE BRANCH. The same shape as the kit-stamp finding earlier the same day — the maintainer's environment cannot produce the input that breaks the consumer's.

FIXED THE SAME DAY, both halves: a directory is now reported PRESENT AND UNHASHABLE, which the core already had a word for (`no_baseline` — 'cannot be judged, surfaced rather than treated as unchanged'), so it is a note rather than a crash or a quiet pass; and the entrypoint became `run_guarded()`, a NAMED function so the contract is callable and therefore checkable.

⚠️ AND THE FIX'S OWN FIRST TEST WAS WORTHLESS, recorded because it is the more useful lesson: it forced the fault with an unreadable export, which `die(2, …)` already handled, so IT PASSED WITH THE FIX REMOVED. Every fault this tool knows about is already routed to 2 correctly; the guard exists for the ones it does not. Caught by mutation-testing rather than by review, and only after a second error — the tests were first appended at the end of the file, which silently placed them in the NEXT test class, where they ran green in the wrong harness. TWO WAYS FOR A GREEN TEST TO PROVE NOTHING, both in one change.

properties.statement:
THE GIT MERGE DRIVER AND `export_graph` SERIALIZE THE SAME DESIGN IN DIFFERENT KEY ORDERS, SO THE FIRST CANONICAL EXPORT AFTER ANY MERGE REWRITES THE WHOLE FILE. Found by doing it, 2026-08-15, on a PR that had to rebase twice because three other PRs landed while it was open.

MEASURED. After `git rebase origin/main` resolved `docs/design/reflow2.json` through reflow2's own merge driver ('merged 2251 node(s) and 8845 edge(s) — 56 divergence(s) resolved automatically, no conflicts'), that merged file was committed and reached main. Its first key is `stamp`. A fresh `export_graph` of the same design writes `content_hash` first, then `edges`, then the rest — alphabetical. `git diff --stat` between them: **60,793 insertions and 60,134 deletions on a ~90,000-line file**, with every node id appearing as added. The CONTENT is identical where it should be; only the serialization order differs.

WHY IT MATTERS, and it is the tool's own stated contract: `export_graph`'s description says the document is 'sorted so two exports of an unchanged graph are byte-identical', and the `path` parameter promises 'deterministic sorted-key JSON, diffable under git'. That property is what makes a design export reviewable in a pull request at all. The merge driver silently opts a repository out of it, and nothing reports that it has happened — the file is valid, the gate is green, the lineage chain is correct, and the diff is unreadable.

THE COMPOUNDING PART: a reviewer looking at a 60k-line diff cannot see the fifteen nodes the PR actually added. A real regression in that diff would be invisible for exactly the same reason. And it is self-perpetuating in the other direction too — whichever form lands on main, the next contributor's tool writes the other one.

SEPARATELY AND MORE SERIOUSLY, FOUND IN THE SAME MINUTE: THE MERGE DRIVER UPDATES THE FILE AND NOT THE STORE, so the next export from that seat REGRESSES whatever the merge resolved. Measured: after the rebase, `art:adopt-skill`, `art:graph` and `art:skill-lint` carried NEWER checksums in the merged file (matching the files on disk) than in the live graph, which had never seen them. Exporting from that store rolled all three back to stale digests and the gate correctly reported three `checksum_change` drifts — on a working tree this session had not touched. Main was green; only the export was wrong. THE REMEDY IS `import_graph` ON THE COMMITTED EXPORT BEFORE EXPORTING, which is what `sync_status` says in ordinary language and what nothing says after a merge, because the merge leaves the seat looking `in_step`: the recorded hash is compared against the FILE, and the file is exactly where this seat left it — it was the STORE that fell behind.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: both orderings observed on one repository, one day; the regression reproduced and then fixed by importing before exporting; the gate caught it. WHAT IS NOT: whether the merge driver's order is stable across runs, whether any other property is dropped or reordered besides key order, and how many past PRs merged a non-canonical export without anyone noticing (cheap to sweep by checking each commit's first key, not yet done).

FIX SHAPES: have the merge driver emit the canonical form (the exporter's serializer, not its own), which removes both symptoms at once for the file; and, for the store half, either write the merge result back through the graph or make the post-merge state visible so `in_step` cannot be read as `up to date`.

properties.statement:
AFTER A CLI RESTORE, THE LATENT SURFACE STAYS LATENT FOR THE REST OF THE SESSION, AND THE ONE TOOL IT OFFERS IS THE WRONG ONE. music_graph, fourth pass, 2026-08-15, on the run-book's own documented restore path.

WHAT HAPPENED: the MCP server started against an empty directory, correctly served the latent surface, and said so — 'no design graph has ever been started at .reflow2/graph … exactly one tool is served — reflow2_start_design.' TRUE WHEN PRINTED. False ninety seconds later, once `--import` had built the store. NOTHING RE-PROBES, so every design tool stayed unavailable and the export could not be refreshed from the very session that had just done the restore.

⭐ THE SHARP EDGE IS THE COMBINATION WITH `fact:defect-import-materialises-defaults-so-a-restored-graph-reads-as-changed`. At that moment: the graph exists, the pre-commit hook is BLOCKING commits because the restored store reports itself changed, and THE ONLY TOOL ON OFFER IS THE ONE THAT STARTS A DESIGN — against a directory that now has one. The latent surface's own warning that it is 'easy to accept by accident' is aimed at exactly this situation AND CANNOT BE ACTED ON FROM INSIDE IT. The way out is to restart the client, which is not mentioned anywhere.

THEIR ASKS, in their order of preference: (a) RE-PROBE the graph path when a tool is called and promote latent → full surface in place — 'the latent server already knows the path it is watching'; (b) or have `reflow2_start_design` detect that a store appeared since startup and say 'a design exists here now, restart your client to attach' instead of offering to begin one over the top; (c) or have the latent blurb name the restore command and the restart requirement together, since `--import` is the documented way out of latent mode and currently leaves you stuck in it.

SAME FAMILY AS A TRAP THIS PROJECT ALREADY KNOWS: a rebuilt binary does not replace a running stdio server, and only a full client restart does. THIS SESSION HIT THAT VERSION TODAY — the `subject` field built this afternoon was unreachable from the live server, and the ChangeEvent recording that work had to say so in its own name. THE SURFACE A SESSION BOUND TO AT STARTUP IS NOT RE-EXAMINED, WHICHEVER WAY IT IS WRONG.

WHAT THEY PRAISED ON THE SAME PATH, recorded because it is the counterweight: `--diff <file>` against the live graph with no server running 'answered “did the restore work” completely in one call'. That it runs FILE-AGAINST-STORE rather than file-against-file is what made it usable — there was nothing else to compare to yet — and it is what turned a suspected broken hook into a two-line finding. The run-book's list of what does not travel with a clone was 'accurate on a real second machine, in the right order'.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether re-probing per call has a cost worth measuring, and whether any other surface decision is frozen at startup the same way.

properties.statement:
THE LAUNCH WRAPPER WHOSE ENTIRE PURPOSE IS "NEVER SERVE A STALE BINARY" IS BLIND TO THE SCHEMA. tools/reflow2-mcp-launch.sh:31-36 content-hashes `crates/**/src/*.rs` plus Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock/crates/*/Cargo.toml — and nothing else. The schema YAML is compiled into the binary with include_str! (crates/reflow2-core/src/schema.rs:19-38), so a schema-only change leaves the hash UNCHANGED, the wrapper prints "binary current, skipping build", and the server serves the previous vocabulary.

MEASURED 2026-08-15, and it cost a wrong write that was caught only by chance: main already carried #199's `change_type: defect_fix` and the new `subject` axis in schema/temporal.yaml, but describe_schema on the running server returned the enum WITHOUT them. The value about to be recorded was the exact fiction #199 had been merged hours earlier to end. It was noticed only because the on-disk YAML was grepped and compared against what the tool reported — nothing in the tool's own answer says which build it came from.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY STALE BINARY: the wrapper's comment (lines 10-15) explains it hashes CONTENT precisely because cargo's mtime check is untrustworthy after a git operation — so it is a deliberate, reasoned guard that was simply pointed at the wrong file set. A session therefore gets a CONFIDENT "binary current" for the one class of change where being wrong silently corrupts the vocabulary the design is written in. `tests/**` is outside the hash too, which matters less.

NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately: it is a separate defect from the one this branch settles, and widening the change to include it was not asked for. The fix is one line — add schema/*.yaml to the srchash — and until it lands, a schema change on this repo requires a manual `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp` plus `--stop-shared` before the new vocabulary is served. IT DOES NOT AFFECT CONSUMERS: they run an installed release binary, not this wrapper.

properties.statement:
THE LOOP HAS NO NOTION OF A SESSION MID-BUGFIX WITH A USER WATCHING A BROKEN APP, AND UNDER THAT PRESSURE ITS CEREMONY IS SKIPPED AND ITS DASHBOARD IS NOISE. Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14, items 3 and 9 — filed as two, and they are ONE complaint seen from two sides.

CEREMONY (item 3). Tightening a three-line product rule cost: an epoch, two `record_change`, two typed merges, tests, two checksum accepts. 'The user was iterating a live bug. The loop is right for a first capture; it is slow for \"you implemented the wrong comparison.\"' ⭐ AND THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST IN THE WHOLE REPORT: 'AGENTS WILL SKIP SNAPSHOTS UNDER THAT PRESSURE — I ALMOST DID.' That is a discipline losing to urgency, reported by the agent who nearly lost it — the exact failure the served instructions already name ('a discipline that depends on being remembered loses to urgency every time; fire it on a trigger, not on virtue').

DASHBOARD (item 9). 'All session: ~62 never-asked gaps, 39 structural defects, 16 unproven claims, 10 unexamined artifacts. `next[0]` is ALWAYS detect-and-ask. The work was implement, user-correct, implement. That noise is worse when the user is waiting on a running app.' `loop_status` reports coherence debt truthfully and ranks it identically whatever the session is doing.

WHY THEY ARE ONE THING: both are the loop having exactly one posture. A first capture and a live bugfix are different phases of work, and reflow2 models neither — so the same ranking, the same ceremony and the same next-step advice are served to both. The report's items 3 and 9 are the cost paid at the write side and the read side of that single absence.

WHAT ALREADY BEARS ON IT AND IS NOT ENOUGH: `loop_status` takes a `contributor_id`, and `cap:scoped-analysis` scopes the detectors by region — but both scope by WHO or by WHERE, and this is a question of WHAT KIND OF WORK is happening. `dec:idea-scoping-exists-and-did-not-narrow-what-a-builder-sees` holds the open question, with a serious counter recorded against the obvious fix: `loop_status`'s contract forbids a scoped answer that could read as 'the design is clean', so any phase mode must RANK differently rather than HIDE.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether a phase is something reflow2 should infer, or something a session declares — and if declared, whether an agent may declare it or only the user. Nobody has proposed a mechanism.

properties.statement: THE ONE CHECK EVERY SESSION IS REQUIRED TO MAKE BEFORE IT TRUSTS ANYTHING IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE CALL IN THE API, AND IT IS PAID FOR TWO SCALARS. Reported 2026-08-08 by dragon Boss f96eccd3. Their constitution (S.md step 6, and reflow2's own BL-32 note) binds every session to confirm the serving binary BY RELATION: read graph_report -> served_by.reflow2_version and compare it against `reflow2-mcp --version` on disk. THE RULE IS RIGHT — a literal expires, a relation does not. But `served_by` is reachable only through graph_report, which also returns the ENTIRE verification roll (28 nodes on their graph, several with multi-thousand-character names) plus top_gaps with full descriptions. They needed exactly two scalars, reflow2_version and binary_mtime_unix, and paid a very large payload for them. THE REPORTER'S OWN CONCLUSION IS THE FINDING: the cheapest-to-state rule in their constitution is the most expensive to obey, WHICH IS PRECISELY THE PRESSURE THAT MAKES A SESSION SKIP IT AND QUOTE A REMEMBERED LITERAL INSTEAD — the failure that produced the rule. A guard whose cost scales with the graph will be skipped on the graphs where it matters most. FIX SHAPE, theirs: a tiny `server_identity` call returning the serving binary's version, mtime and pid; or carry those two fields in loop_status, which is already advertised as the one cheap call. RELATED, AND NOT THE SAME THING: fact:defect-a-running-server-cannot-say-it-is-stale is about the server being unable to ANSWER the staleness question; this is about the answer being priced out of reach. req:the-server-is-the-authority-on-its-own-currency is accepted and unbuilt, and would subsume both — the /proc/self/exe `(deleted)` check is one syscall and needs no payload at all.

properties.statement: A LANE WHOSE DELIVERABLE WAS A DENOMINATOR HAD TO HAND-DERIVE IT TWICE, BECAUSE THE READ SURFACE CANNOT ANSWER A SET QUESTION. Reported 2026-08-08 by w-4d05e937 (dev_storyflow, LANE UNSUSPECTED-VALIDATION-WALK), items 1 and 3. TWO INDEPENDENT MISSES, ONE SHAPE. (1) `get_node` RETURNS PROPERTIES BUT NO EDGES. Their brief required excluding capabilities that already carry a walk-type Verification — a VERIFIES edge query. get_node on a Verification returns kind/status/method/level/name and nothing about what it verifies; evidence_report gives per-capability check COUNTS but never WHICH check. The only routes they could see to the actual edges were a full unscoped detect_gaps dump or an export, which workers are told not to take. THEY FELL BACK TO MATCHING VERIFICATION NAMES AGAINST CAPABILITY IDS AND HAD TO PUBLISH THAT AS A STATED WEAKNESS IN THEIR OWN METHOD. (2) `scan_nodes` HAS NO STATUS FILTER. Their population was 'every Capability with status realized or verified'; they pulled all 95 and tallied by hand. It happened to agree with the boss's independent count — and their own comment is the right one: HAND-TALLYING IS EXACTLY WHERE A DENOMINATOR QUIETLY DRIFTS, AND THE DENOMINATOR WAS THE DELIVERABLE. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH cap:bounded-reads, which is working correctly and makes this worse: scan_nodes honestly reports `omitted` and `capped_by` when a payload fills, so a hand-tally over a large type is not merely tedious, it is a paging loop the reader must get right. FIX SHAPE, theirs: `get_node(..., with_edges: true)`, or a `verifies_report` mirroring evidence_report but NAMING the target; and `scan_nodes(node_type, status: [...])` or a `count_by_status`. Both are cheap, and both turn a guessable answer into a checkable one.

properties.statement: `get_instructions` RETURNS ONE ~22 KB PAYLOAD WITH ITS STANDING RULES AT THE END, SO A CLIENT-SIDE RESULT CAP DELETES EXACTLY THE PARTS THAT MAKE AN AGENT SCEPTICAL — AND THE AGENT CANNOT KNOW WHAT IT LOST. Reported by Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14 (docs/feedback/2026-08-14-alex-grok-session.md, item 13) as 'get_instructions truncates (~22.6 KB, cut mid-file). Standing rules after the cut never arrived.' THE ATTRIBUTION IS WRONG AND THE FINDING IS REAL. Measured here 2026-08-15 against the same 0.31.0 tool over stdio: the document came back COMPLETE, ending on 'Use it every time.' plus the `note` field. reflow2 truncates nothing; his harness capped the tool result. THE DEFECT IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE CUT. Served as one monolith, the order decides what survives a cap, and the order is worst-first-lost: the loop and the tool inventory come early, while '## If reflow2 gets in your way, say so' (report-friction), '## And when it does not get in your way — check anyway' (a successful tool response is a claim, not a result; a green gate is evidence about what it covers and silent about the rest), and the gap→question handshake all sit AFTER them. So the sections a truncated agent loses are the ones that would have told it to distrust the tools and to report the friction — including the friction of the truncation. THAT IS THE SELF-SEALING PART and the reason this outranks a formatting nit: `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` depends on agents reporting what fought them, and the instruction to do so is in the tail. His session DID report it, from a client that showed the cut; a client that silently drops the tail produces an agent that is simply less careful for a whole session with nothing anywhere recording why. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: the server returns the full document; the payload is ~22 KB in one field; the standing rules are last; one real consumer lost the tail. WHAT IS NOT: which caps exist across harnesses, or how often this bites — one measured instance. properties.statement:
THE SERVED-SURFACE GATE DEFAULTS TO `target/debug/reflow2-mcp` AND SAYS "ALL 149 TOOLSNAPS MATCH" AGAINST WHATEVER STALE BUILD IS SITTING THERE. A green from it is evidence about a binary nobody promised was current.

MEASURED 2026-08-16, on my own change and by accident. I edited a `#[tool(description = …)]`, rebuilt RELEASE, ran `python3 tools/toolsnap.py`, and was told the surface was unchanged. It was not: the new sentence was present in the release binary (1 occurrence via `strings`) and ABSENT from the committed snapshot, which still held the old description. `tools/toolsnap.py:140` sets `--bin` default to `target/debug/reflow2-mcp`; debug was an hour older than release (11:27 vs 12:27). Rebuilding debug and re-running immediately reported `TOOLSNAP DRIFT (1)`.

⚠️ THE SNAPSHOT DOES CONTAIN THE DESCRIPTION — this is not a scope limitation. `tools/toolsnaps/create_node.json` carries a `description` field and the file's own docstring says "the whole served object is snapshotted — name, description, inputSchema". So the comparison is right and the INPUT to it is wrong.

⭐ THE SHAPE IS THE ONE THIS PROJECT KEEPS FINDING: a check that cannot fail reporting a pass. Same class as `propose_heal`'s vacuous zero fixed hours earlier, the piped-gate exit code, and `sync` reporting `in_step` over unexported work. Here the gate whose entire job is to notice a changed surface reported an unchanged one BECAUSE the surface it read had not been rebuilt.

✅ CORRECTED SAME DAY, AND THE CORRECTION LOWERS THE SEVERITY. The first version of this fact said it was NOT ESTABLISHED whether CI had the same hole, because `.github/workflows/ci.yml:142` runs `toolsnap.py` with no `--bin` and so takes the same default. IT DOES NOT: `ci.yml:93` runs `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp` — a DEBUG build — in the same job, before the toolsnap step. So CI compares a freshly built debug binary every time and was never exposed. ⇒ THIS IS A LOCAL-DEVELOPER DEFECT ONLY, and specifically it bites the person following the RELEASE PROCEDURE, which instructs a release build and leaves debug behind.

AND THAT IS ALSO WHY THE FIX MUST NOT CHANGE THE DEFAULT to `target/release`: CI builds debug and would then compare a binary that does not exist there. FIXED 2026-08-16 by `chg:the-surface-gate-says-which-binary-it-read` — every verdict now names the binary and its build time, and warns when any `crates/**/src/*.rs` is newer than it. mtime is a weak signal alone (git operations can leave sources older than a build, which is why the launch wrapper hashes content instead), but it is only ever used to ADD a warning and never to suppress one, so a false negative costs nothing that was not already lost.

properties.statement:
TYPED TOOL PARAMETER NAMES DISAGREE WITH THE NODE PROPERTIES THEY SET, AND ONE SESSION HIT NINE OF THEM. Each cost a failed call, an error and a retry: `add_decision` rejects `status`; `set_decision_status` wants `decision_id` not `id`; `record_change` wants `target_type`/`target_id` not `node_type`/`node_id`, and `name` not `description`; `governed_by` rejects `note` though describe_schema DOCUMENTS note on GOVERNED_BY; `satisfies`/`allocate` take only from_id/to_id; `create_edge` wants `props` not `properties`; `add_epoch` requires `sequence`, undiscoverable until it fails; `add_capability` rejects `capability_type` and `tier` though nodes CARRY both; `propagate_from` wants `seed_ids` not `node_ids`. NOT ONE IS WRONG ON ITS OWN. Together they mean a fluent session still fails roughly ONE CALL IN FOUR, because the mental model 'typed constructors take the node's own property names' is right often enough to keep being used and wrong often enough to keep costing a round trip. || SOURCE: Observed by the dev_storyflow fleet on 2026-08-15, on reflow2 0.31.0 with served == installed verified through /proc/<pid>/exe. Three agent seats, one shared graph, one day.

═══ A TENTH, FROM A THIRD INDEPENDENT SOURCE, THE SAME DAY (2026-08-15) ═══

`add_component` takes a parameter named `description` and the Component node requires `purpose`. `capture.rs:687` passes `&req.description` straight into the `purpose` slot, so the two names are the same field. `create_nodes` with `node_type: \"Component\"` refuses `description` — `Validation error on Component.purpose: required property is missing` — and because that call is all-or-nothing it failed a SIX-NODE BATCH ON FOUR ITEMS.

Reported by a US-federal-government genesis session (docs/feedback/2026-08-15-usgov-genesis-session.md, item 1), independently of the fleet and of a third session the same day. Its own diagnosis is the one worth keeping: 'the point is that the HELPER and the GENERIC path disagree on the field name for the same concept, so reading one does not prepare you for the other.' It also checked the counterweight, which the fleet report did not: Capability takes `description` in both paths, Requirement takes `statement` in both. SO THE INCONSISTENCY IS NOT UNIFORM — it is per-type, which is exactly what makes the mental model survive.

⭐ AND THE SAME DISAGREEMENT HAS A SECOND, FAR MORE EXPENSIVE FORM. `fact:defect-the-constraint-vocabulary-is-documented-as-numeric-so-the-right-node-is-ruled-out` is the helper/prose layer disagreeing with the schema not about a FIELD NAME but about a node type's SCOPE: every description around `Constraint` says 'numeric budget' while the schema requires only name and statement. The same session graded the field-name instance LOW ('costs a full round trip') and the scope instance HIGH ('a modelling-vocabulary gap'). THEY ARE ONE DEFECT AT TWO PRICES. The field-name form announces itself with a validation error and costs a retry; the scope form produces no error at all, and cost that session a wrong conclusion and eleven permanently-open gaps. Fixing only the loud one leaves the expensive one in place.

properties.statement: A VERIFICATION CAN HOLD A SELF-CONTRADICTORY RESULT AND STAY `passing` FOREVER, BECAUSE THE STATUS IS STRUCTURED AND THE EVIDENCE IS PROSE. Reported by w-613d836b (dev_storyflow, 2026-08-07). `ver:fleet_stack_currency_gate` recorded, in its own name/notes: 'Re-run 2026-08-03: EXIT 0, verdict STALE — 4 of 11'. The reporter re-ran that tool: its true exit is 1, and its source is literally `return 1 if stale else 0` — so `EXIT 0` means 'everything is current', the exact OPPOSITE of the verdict recorded beside it. They diagnosed the origin rather than guessing: the 0 almost certainly came from reading `$?` after a pipe (`... | tail` returns tail's status), and they reproduced both readings side by side to show it. THE REFLOW2-RELEVANT HALF: that contradictory pair sat inside a node the graph reports as `passing`, and NOTHING IN THE LOOP CAN NOTICE, because a Verification's outcome is free text. `status` is structured; the evidence is not. So a wrong number is preserved with exactly the same authority as a right one, and loop_status keeps counting the capability as proven. FIX SHAPE: give Verification optional STRUCTURED result fields — `exit_code`, `command`, `observed`/`expected` — so (a) the graph can flag `status: passing` alongside a non-zero exit_code as incoherent, and (b) a re-run can be compared to the recorded run mechanically instead of by someone re-reading a paragraph. THE REPORTER'S OWN FRAMING, which generalises past this tool: this is the design-layer version of their fleet's rule that a set reduced to a scalar is not a check — right now the EVIDENCE is reduced to a sentence. WORTH WEIGHING AGAINST reflow2's existing position: `reconcile_verification` already exists to feed real run outcomes back in, and `cap:evidence-scope` already structures what a check pinned and swept — so the machinery for 'evidence is structured, not prose' is partly built and this is an argument for extending it to the RESULT.

properties.statement: 'THESE TWO PROJECTS ARE LINKED' IS NOT A STATE reflow2 CAN CONFIRM, AND A LINK CAN BE HOLLOW IN THREE INDEPENDENT WAYS THAT EACH LOOK FINE. Found by doing it end to end twice. (1) MIRRORED but `mirror_content_hash: null` — staleness detection silently off and PERMANENTLY so, because `mirror_surface` refuses collisions once the mirrored nodes have acquired local edges; `mirrors` shows the entry, and you must read the FIELD. (2) AGREED — `seam_report` returning a confident `agreed: 5, incompatible: 0` on pairs that were SUPPLIED BY HAND rather than computed. (3) PAIRED — `pair_designs` returning `paired: []` with every candidate below the name threshold, while roles are correct and all axes agree. THREE TOOLS EACH REPORT THEIR OWN THIRD, NONE REFERENCES THE OTHERS, AND THE REASSURING ANSWER IS AVAILABLE FROM ALL THREE WHILE THE LINK DOES NOTHING. The reporter's own diagnosis of why the lane produced 22 items instead of 3: four seats each read one number and stopped. FIX SHAPE: one `link_status` / `linked_designs` rollup answering 'is this link real?' per partner — surface hash present and current, pairs computed vs supplied, boundaries paired vs candidate vs unmet. Everything it needs already exists in three separate places. RELATED HAZARD, same lane: sibling projects under ONE owner share a house naming style, which is exactly when fuzzy matching is weakest — one package's interface matched a DIFFERENT package's API at 80/100. || SOURCE: Observed by the dev_storyflow fleet on 2026-08-15, on reflow2 0.31.0 with served == installed verified through /proc/<pid>/exe.
