properties.statement: ON A SHARED GRAPH A WRITE'S OWN RESPONSE REPORTS WHAT WAS SENT, NOT WHAT PERSISTED — SAME-PROPERTY WRITES ARE SILENT LAST-WRITER-WINS AND THERE IS NO VERSION FIELD TO NOTICE IT WITH. Established by a deliberate experiment on the live 7-seat dev_storyflow graph (api-boss `5d608b85`, 2026-08-07, at the user's request), on a throwaway Requirement named to be unmistakable to the other attached sessions, with independent get_node read-backs after every write and the graph restored exactly afterwards (gap_count 69 -> 70 during -> 69 after, get_node -> null). TWO PROPERTIES HELD AND ARE WORTH RECORDING AS WON: per-property merge is real — writer B setting only `statement` left A's `rationale`, `name`, `priority`, `status` all intact, so two sessions editing different aspects of one node do not destroy each other; and concurrent writes SERIALIZE cleanly, with both racers' distinct properties surviving, no interleaving, no torn node, no error. THE DEFECT IS THE THIRD RESULT: when both racers wrote the SAME property, RACER_ONE's value was destroyed with no error, no warning, no version conflict, and no indication a value had been replaced — and RACER_ONE's own success payload read back `statement: RACER_ONE, priority: high` when the persisted state was already `RACER_TWO`/`low`. BOTH FIELDS IN THAT SUCCESS RESPONSE WERE FALSE WHEN IT WAS RETURNED. Why it is sharp rather than academic: on a solo graph response == state, so trusting your own write-response costs nothing and every habit formed under stdio does exactly that. Under `--shared` they diverge silently, and there is no `version`, `rev`, `etag` or `updated_at` anywhere in the payload — so a client cannot detect that it lost and has no primitive to compare-and-swap with. A session that writes a value and later reasons from its own return value is reasoning from something that was never durable. FIX SHAPE, from the reporter: return a monotonic `rev` per node and accept an optional `if_rev` on write; even unenforced, merely RETURNING it lets a caller notice it was superseded. Cheapest version: have the write response say 'this node was also written by another seat since your read.' BOUND THE REPORTER STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: the two racing writes were near-simultaneous requests from ONE MCP client process, not two OS-level sessions — the serialization and merge findings are server-side and hold regardless, but two distinct client processes were not proven and they do not claim it.

properties.statement:
THE WHOLE dev_storyflow FLEET LOG TRIAGED: 6,203 lines, 62 entries, 4 Aug-3-to-Aug-15. Roughly 28 fixed, 26 open, the rest partial. The high-severity ones were verified against the running code; the tail was classified with less depth and that is marked.

⚠️ I TRIAGED A STALE COPY FIRST AND ANTHONY CAUGHT IT. I worked through a 122 KB upload from Aug 8 and reported it as complete; the current file is 658 KB — my triage covered the first 19%. HIS RULE, now standing: dev_storyflow feedback is ONE APPEND-ONLY FILE, so only the newest upload matters and every older copy is a prefix. VERIFIED rather than taken on trust: the 754-line copy is a byte-identical prefix of the 6,203-line one, so the earlier triage stands for those entries and only the remainder needed work. THIRD stale-or-misidentified-document error of the session; the first two I caught, this one I did not.

⭐⭐ THREE OF THEIR AUGUST 15 REPORTS WERE FIXED TODAY, BY ME, WITHOUT KNOWING THEY HAD BEEN FILED — and two shipped as their asks VERBATIM:
• `propose_heal` naming one of four Projects as `target_id` while sweeping globally → fixed in #210, which added `scope`, `projects_in_scope`.
• `propose_heal` unable to distinguish "no bad merges" from "no candidates at all" — their idea (1) was `merge_candidates_considered: 0 alongside operations: []`, and that is the field name that shipped. Their framing is the better one and belongs in the record: "the difference between a check that PASSED and a check that COULD NOT FAIL".
• `answer_question` rejecting both ids `open_questions` had just handed them → fixed in #201; the request now reads "either this or `question_id` — whichever you have in hand", which is their idea (1).

ALSO VERIFIED FIXED, against code rather than changelog: `set_verification_status` SILENTLY DELETING `last_run_at` when the parameter was omitted — their 🚨 RETEST on v0.26.1, the data-loss one — is fixed at `verify.rs:167`, which now replaces it only when supplied. The `check-health`-named-first string (filed FOUR times across two days by three seats, with a fleet-wide stop-order) fixed in #102. The accountability edge they measured as islanding 109 nodes, and which ANTHONY HIMSELF relayed as "reflow2 has two of the three WHO axes and is missing the third", shipped as `OWNED_BY` — though reflow2's own graph uses it ZERO times. `append_only`/`living` volatility shipped, including the sub-thread where the reporter corrected their own entry and then RETRACTED the correction as also wrong.

⭐ THE OPEN ONE THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT ME TODAY: `set_artifact_checksum` accepts a 13-character digest without complaint, and is one-shot so a bad baseline is easy to write and hard to correct. `canonical_checksum` still takes any hex string of length ≤ 64. Their second case — "a digest I had TYPED FROM MEMORY rather than read from `sha256sum`", well-formed and simply WRONG — is EXACTLY the error I made this afternoon writing a fabricated checksum into `art:schema-build`. Their ask (1), a one-line shape guard, would have caught their first case; nothing catches the second, and they say so.

THE OTHER OPEN ONES WORTH RANKING:
1. A LOST UPDATE ON THE SHARED GRAPH, OBSERVED FROM BOTH SIDES. `create_node` has no expected-current-value parameter, so no write can be made conditional on what was read; `claim_region` is advisory and nothing consults it. The winner was never told. "Every property edit is a lost update waiting to happen, and detection is left to luck." PARTIALLY mitigated since: `create_node` now returns a `revision` block naming what it replaced — which is detection after the fact, not prevention.
2. RE-USING AN EXISTING NODE ID IN AN INGEST PASS IS A WRITE, NOT A REFERENCE, and there is no cite-only form. A worker silently reverted a USER-RULED restoration with their next batch — on the one node the fleet was already watching, which they had personally restored thirty minutes earlier.
3. ZERO-DEGREE NODES ARE NOT REPORTED. Both their packages had a baseline DesignEpoch with no edges at all, through every `detect_defects` and `loop_status` call, one of them answering `clean: true`. `heal.rs:879` covers Decisions only. Their second half is sharper: `disconnected_community` computes MODULARITY but its words claim UNREACHABILITY, so it invites the wrong repair and missed the genuinely unreachable node.
4. `orphan_node` FIRES ON THE STATE A DISPOSITION RULE PRESCRIBES — a document deliberately registered with no claims. Their defect count moved 88 → 97 across ten correct writes, with 31 more owed. "The disposition rule and the defect detector make each other unreadable, and the correct action degrades the instrument."

THE REST, classified but not individually re-verified: a Capability cannot say WHICH implementation it describes; `get_node` returns properties and no edges; `VIOLATES_RULE` is declared and never offered by `describe_schema` (0 uses here); a `RISKS` edge predicted a live incident and no routine call surfaces it (1 use here); the duplicate scorer landing a true pair and an unrelated pair on the same score; `ingest-corpus`'s `fragment_id` rule colliding with existing id conventions; `describe_schema` costing ~15k tokens to answer what properties a type has; and `add_change_event` being unable to record an addition in advance.

⭐ WHAT THE FILE IS, beyond a bug list: a fleet instrumenting its own tooling under real load, with a no-consolidation rule that earns its keep — the same defect filed four times by three seats is what shows a tool doing it to everyone rather than one seat's opinion. Two entries are the reporter correcting themselves and then retracting the correction, in public, which is a standard of honesty worth matching.

properties.statement:
DEV_STORYFLOW'S FLEET LOG TRIAGED IN FULL: 26 entries, 16 ALREADY FIXED, 7 OPEN, 3 partial or unverified. Each checked against the running build, not the changelog.

⚠️ FIRST, A CORRECTION THAT COST NOTHING ONLY BECAUSE IT WAS CAUGHT: THIS IS NOT ALEX'S FILE. A standing note claimed "Alex has TWO feedback files; the Aug 7-8 one was never triaged". The Aug 7-8 uploads are dev_storyflow's FLEET LOG — `🔌 api-boss`, `👑 dragon Boss`, numbered workers — with ZERO mentions of Grok or Alex across 754 lines. Alex's Grok file is the 249-line Aug 14 one, already triaged. THERE IS NO SECOND ALEX FILE. Second false premise from my own notes in one day; see [[fact:the-music-graph-feedback-file-is-four-sessions-and-its-first-batch-was-fixed-long-ago]].

⭐ SIXTEEN ALREADY FIXED, and several shipped IN THE REPORTER'S OWN WORDS, which is worth noticing: they asked for `Artifact` to declare `opaque` vs `pending_expansion` and the enum reads exactly `[atomic, opaque, pending_expansion]`; they asked for volatility `stable` vs `append_only`/`living` and it reads exactly `[stable, append_only, living]`. Their `orphan_node`/SPECIFIES escalation is fixed at `heal.rs:872` — the SAME fix that closed music_graph F4, two projects reporting one defect. Their enum-rejection complaint is quoted verbatim in `service.rs:543`. `OWNED_BY` (* → Contributor) answers their accountability ask. The `check-health`-named-first string, filed TWICE ten minutes apart with a fleet-wide STOP-ORDER posted to counteract it, was fixed in #102.

Their served-vs-on-disk staleness pair (20:17 and 20:29) produced `req:the-server-is-the-authority-on-its-own-currency`, and the test file cites their measurement verbatim — four sessions reading `0.22.1` on two days and drawing OPPOSITE conclusions. The worker who proposed deriving it from `/proc/self/exe` being marked `(deleted)` rather than comparing version strings got exactly that mechanism.

SEVEN GENUINELY OPEN, in the order they deserve:
1. A VERIFICATION'S OUTCOME IS PROSE, so a self-contradictory result stays `passing` forever (20:17), and there is nowhere to put evidence but the `name` (Aug 8 10:12). ONE ROOT, TWO REPORTS, and the measured cost is in [[fact:defect-a-verification-has-nowhere-to-put-its-evidence-so-the-name-became-the-report]] — median name 79.5 words across 160 nodes, and I made four of the worst offenders TODAY.
2. AN INTERFACE CONSUMED ACROSS A BOUNDARY WITH NO SPEC RAISES NO GAP. Only `unprovided_interface` / `unconsumed_interface` exist. Their words: "a check reduced to 'an edge exists' can only ever detect the edge disappearing."
3. `open_questions` RETURNING 0 READS AS AN ALL-CLEAR. It returns a bare list while `loop_status` in the next call reported 31 other owed items. It is the orientation call a new session makes FIRST.
4. `disconnected_community` CANNOT SEE AN INTENDED-UNSATISFIED RULING, and proposes `generate_bridge` — precisely the forgery the ruling forbids.
5. A SEEDLESS SESSION CANNOT ORIENT. `detect_gaps`/`detect_defects` want a scope and `claim_region` wants a seed; a worker at check-in has neither. "The moment with the most time available is the moment the design brain is least usable."
6. `get_skill` CARRIES NO VERSION OR HASH, so a session that read a skill at minute 0 cannot tell it was revised by minute 90. Skills are served precisely so they cannot go stale, and this is the one hole left in that argument.
7. `import_graph` SAYS A DOCUMENT IS UNSTAMPED WITHOUT SAYING HOW TO STAMP ONE — so every adopt pass forfeits the upgrade-direction check.

PARTIAL OR UNVERIFIED: their prospective corpus-types entry (the ownership third is fixed; contradiction-resolved and the Fragment-for-unknown-intent shapes are unchecked); seat liveness after a `--stop-shared` bounce (`req:stale-seat-knows` is ACCEPTED and `mint_seat_liveness.rs` exists, but the orphaned-seat-after-bounce case specifically was not re-run); and the deferred-tool-indistinguishable-from-absent report, which is a HARNESS behaviour rather than a reflow2 one — though its consequence was real and durable, a false "there is NO mint_seat tool" travelling five hops into an onboarding doc as a credited correction.

⭐ WHAT THE FILE IS WORTH BEYOND ITS BUGS: it is a fleet reporting on its own tooling under load, and its best entries diagnose rather than complain — "a missing field being paid for in every future read of that node" is a better sentence than the defect it describes. Its no-consolidation rule earned its keep twice: two workers filed the `check-health` string ten minutes apart, and the duplicate is what shows the tool doing it to EVERYONE rather than one seat's opinion.

properties.statement:
**dynograph-foundation v0.13.0 DOES NOT AFFECT reflow2 — established four ways on 2026-08-19, and the pin bump is PARKED awaiting Anthony's word.**

He asked: *"dynograph-foundation is now v0.13.0 - need to confirm that the changes don't affect reflow2"*.

FOUR INDEPENDENT GROUNDS, weakest to strongest:
1. **reflow2 pins v0.12.0 by git tag** across all six crates, so nothing changes until somebody moves the pin.
2. **The breaking changes are structurally unreachable.** They are in `dynograph_client::BatchValidation` / `BatchOpResult`. The release notes CLAIM reflow2 has zero references; verified independently rather than trusted — **`dynograph-client` is not in reflow2's dependency tree at all**, not in `Cargo.toml`, not in `Cargo.lock`, zero source references.
3. **The crates reflow2 actually uses did not change.** `git diff v0.12.0 v0.13.0` over `dynograph-core`, `-storage`, `-graph`, `-resolution`, `-vector`, `-text` is **EMPTY**. The whole release touches only `dynograph-client` and `dynograph-service`.
4. **A real build on v0.13.0 passed: `cargo test --workspace` exit 0, 126 suites, 0 failed, 0 compile errors.**

🛑 **THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT (4) FAILED AND THE FAILURE WAS A LIE.** It died with `collect2: fatal error: ld terminated with signal 7 [Bus error]` — which reads exactly like a code or linker defect. **The real cause was a 100% FULL DISK** (149 MB free; `target/` had reached 285 GB). `cargo clean` reclaimed 289.1 GiB / 684,534 files and the build then passed. ⚠️ **NO GATE WATCHES FREE SPACE, and the design graph lives on the same disk** — a full disk during RocksDB writes is how a store gets damaged. The graph was checked afterwards and was intact.

⚠️ A SECOND MEASUREMENT LESSON FROM THE SAME EPISODE: `grep -c` on a BINARY silently finds nothing without `-a`, and on that basis the freshly built binary was briefly and wrongly called stale. Both are instances of `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` — the value you read is not the value you think you are reading.

⏸️ **PARKED, NOT DECLINED.** The bump is committed on the local-only branch `test-dynograph-v0130` and clearly labelled. Whether to actually move the pin is Anthony's call; the confirmation he asked for is complete either way.

properties.name: Eight capabilities are reported BUILT with only a test file realizing them, so unrealized_capability reports clean over all of them
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-21 while making the per-subsystem test numbers real. EIGHT Capabilities are reported BUILT on the strength of a TEST FILE and nothing else — the only Artifact with a REALIZES edge to them is a file under `tests/`: cap:detect (<- art:test-discontinued-is-read), cap:ingest, cap:artifact-declares-its-own-shape, cap:cycle-names-its-basis, cap:evidence-scope, cap:mirror-surface, cap:publish-surface, cap:search-first-at-the-tool.

🛑 A TEST DOES NOT BUILD A CAPABILITY. It checks one. REALIZES from a test artifact asserts the file DELIVERS the capability, which is false for all eight — cap:detect is delivered by detect.rs; art:test-discontinued-is-read merely exercises it.

⭐ THE CONSEQUENCE IS A SILENT DETECTOR, NOT AN UNTIDY EDGE. `unrealized_capability` fires on a Capability with no REALIZES. All eight have one, so all eight report CLEAN — and a capability with a test and NO IMPLEMENTATION would be indistinguishable from a finished one. The vacuous-zero shape again.

📌 HOW IT SPREAD, which matters more than the count. 16 test files REALIZE a Capability directly; 31 REALIZE a Verification. The 16 are the RECENT ones, four of them created this week by this agent (move_component, delivery_kind, sweep_coverage, scheduling_a_question). Two conventions sit side by side, nothing distinguishes them, and the wrong one is winning because it is ONE EDGE SHORTER. Nobody chose it.

THE REMEDY, unbuilt and named so the finding does not only state a problem: a test artifact should REALIZE a Verification, and the Verification should VERIFY the capability. One more node, and it is the whole difference between "this is built" and "this is checked". A detector for `capability_realized_only_by_a_test` is what would stop the shorter path being taken again.

MEASURED 2026-08-18 by `tools/vocabulary_reach.py` over the committed export (2527 nodes, 10353 edges) and the committed toolsnaps. 215 declared node properties across 29 types; 176 parameter names across the served tools, with `create_node`/`create_edge` excluded.

  18  CANDIDATES        the type IS used, the property NEVER is, and no typed tool accepts the name
  10  UNUSED BUT OFFERED  zero uses but a tool does accept it — probably unused rather than unreachable
  46  SAYS NOTHING      the node type has NO instances, so a zero on its properties is vacuous
  42  EDGE VOCABULARY   edge types with no edges, or properties never set on edges that do exist

⭐ THE STANDOUT, AND IT LANDS ON A REQUIREMENT ACCEPTED THE SAME DAY: `Capability.inputs`, `Capability.outputs` and `Capability.capability_type` are 0 OF 170. Spot-checked in the source rather than inferred — `add_capability` sets only name, description and status, and NOTHING anywhere in either crate writes those three. A capability's functional signature, what goes in and what comes out, is declared vocabulary that has never once been recorded. `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (accepted 2026-08-18) says every element is a black box with INNER FUNCTION AND INTERFACES; at the capability tier those two properties ARE that interface, and they are empty.

OTHER CANDIDATES: `Fragment.{created_at,created_by,intent,phase,summary}` (0 of 168), `Project.mirror_*` (4, 0 of 1), `Artifact.{created_at,signature}` (0 of 190), `Snapshot.captured_at` (0 of 144), `Release.created_at` (0 of 36), `Question.prompt_id` (0 of 46). The timestamp cluster is its own theme: five separate `created_at`/`captured_at` fields, all declared, none ever set.

⭐ `DECOMPOSES` HAS ZERO EDGES, and `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent` is ACCEPTED. That is the same shape as SPECIFIES: an accepted requirement whose edge type exists and has never been drawn. Not repaired here.

THE INSTRUMENT WAS VALIDATED AGAINST WHAT WAS ALREADY KNOWN before its new findings were believed: it catches `SUPERSEDES` (zero edges, known), `GOVERNED_BY.ruling` (added 2026-08-17, 0 of 912, correctly reported as not yet used), and it stopped reporting `SPECIFIES` the moment the 44 edges were exported — dead-to-live in one run.

⚠️ WHAT THE NUMBER IS NOT. 18 is not a defect count and not a delete list. Three of the four known instances were WANTED and got a parameter; deletion would have been the wrong repair every time. Zero usage is evidence, not proof — a property can be writable and simply never needed, which is what the second bucket is for.

MEASURED 2026-08-20, answering Anthony's question about why modularization matters for the flo2 relationship: *"if we modularize, we can start following interfaces between where module-X of reflow2 interfaces with module-A from flo2. Then say flo2 requires some new feature, that requires module-X to change. This in turn could cause module-X to impose changes on module-Y... in some chain like effect."*

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
🛑 THE CHAIN CANNOT BE FOLLOWED, AND THE REASON IS NOT MISSING EDGES

Walking ONLY the coupling edges a change would actually travel — PROVIDES, CONSUMES, DEPENDS_ON, with CONTAINS deliberately excluded because containment is "part of" and not "affected by":

  ifc:core-api             reaches 36 of 56 components
  ifc:mcp-tools            reaches 36 of 56 components
  ifc:graph-export         reaches 36 of 56 components
  ifc:req-dyno-graph-api   reaches 36 of 56 components

**EVERY BOUNDARY REACHES THE SAME 36.** Component clusters: [36, 1, 1], plus **18 components with NO coupling edge of any kind**.

⇒ So "which modules must change?" has exactly two possible answers today: **36, or 0.** Never a chain. Anthony's worry that it "would be somewhat challenging to say where something may need to change" is confirmed, and it is not challenging — it is not answerable.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ THE INSIGHT THAT REFRAMES THE WORK: MODULARIZATION IS NOT ABOUT ADDING EDGES. IT IS ABOUT ADDING WALLS.

The 36 are one connected blob because the coupling that exists is undifferentiated DEPENDS_ON with **nothing for propagation to stop at**. Adding more edges makes the blob bigger. What makes a chain followable is BOUNDARIES that a blast radius terminates on — which is exactly what `cap:key-interfaces` was built for: *"designate a published boundary, and compute whether a change stays behind it."*

Severability IS "the blast radius stops at the boundary" (`req:modularity-computed`). With 42 of 56 components carrying no interface at all and 73 uncontracted dependency pairs, there are no walls, so the whole design is one room and severability is not a computation anyone can run.

📌 CORROBORATED FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION, same measurement: `propagate_from(ifc:core-api)` over ALL edge types returns **1,145 impacted nodes — 43% of the design**. The direct ring is 3. So the two available answers are "3 nodes" or "half the graph", because past the first hop the walk leaves the structural chain entirely and travels the GOVERNANCE web (877 of 901 GOVERNED_BY edges land on Decisions). Structural chain and reasoning web are conflated, and only the first one answers "what else must change?".

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
✅ WHAT THIS MAKES CONCRETE ABOUT THE FLO2 CASE

`dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` already settled the TRANSPORT half — a customer levying a requirement on a supplier is ordinary SE, the schema expresses it today (`source`, `provenance: imported`, `status: proposed`, AUTHORED_BY), and plain git carries it. That node closes with the prerequisite: *"reflow2 declares NO `required` interface at all, so nothing pairs across any seam — the channel this node is about has no labelled boundary to run along."*

⚠️ THAT LINE IS NOW PARTLY STALE and should not be quoted as current: reflow2 has **9 `required` and 4 `published`** interfaces as of 2026-08-20. The boundary a flo2 requirement would LAND on now exists. What still does not exist is anything for the consequence to TRAVEL along once it has landed.

⇒ SO THE FOUR STEPS OF ANTHONY'S SCENARIO SPLIT CLEANLY:
  1. flo2 levies a requirement            — transport solved, zero new code
  2. it lands on a reflow2 boundary       — possible now (13 designated interfaces)
  3. trace it to the module that must change — possible (138 ALLOCATED_TO edges)
  4. **what that change imposes on the next module** — **NOT POSSIBLE.** Step 4 is the chain effect, and it is the whole of what modularization would buy.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: whether flo2's own graph has boundaries on its side. The seam is two-ended and only reflow2's end was measured here.

properties.name: The build profile is worth 2.2x on loop_status, and the live store carries 7.4x the bytes of its own content — two separate costs, and today's earlier numbers named neither
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-24 after Anthony pointed out that RocksDB compiles with assertions on unless DEBUG_LEVEL=0. He was right that it matters, and checking it found a second thing nobody was looking for.

⭐ WHAT PROMPTED IT: every performance number recorded EARLIER THE SAME DAY — including the 22.6s for `loop_status` that `dec:the-stop-hook-asks-the-graph-asynchronously` rests on — was taken against `target/debug/reflow2-mcp`, and NONE of them said so. A prior session had been careful about exactly this (`fact:the-orientation-reads-cost-ten-seconds-and-the-store-is-not-why` states 'MEASURED on real RocksDB with a RELEASE binary'), so the project already knew it mattered.

═══ THE CONTROLLED COMPARISON ═══

Both binaries built from the SAME commit the same afternoon (debug 14:02, release 14:21). Both read the SAME freshly-imported store, seeded once. Profile is the only variable:

    call            release   debug    ratio
    loop_status       4.5s     9.9s     2.2x
    detect_gaps      0.98s     1.97s    2.0x
    claim_report     0.00s     0.00s      --

⇒ **THE BUILD PROFILE IS WORTH ABOUT 2.2x ON THIS CALL.** Real, and users run the release binary while every number quoted today came from debug.

═══ 🛑 AND THE BIGGER SURPRISE, WHICH IS NOT THE PROFILE ═══

Both of those are FAR below the 22.6s measured this morning. That gap must not be attributed to the profile, because THREE things differ between the two measurements and only one was controlled:

  1. BUILD PROFILE — measured: 2.2x.
  2. STORE PHYSICAL STATE — the live store is **89 MB across 25 SST files**; a fresh store holding the SAME 3,111 nodes from the same export is **12 MB with 0 SSTs**. Identical logical content, **7.4x the bytes**, from months of accumulated overwrites and uncompacted levels.
  3. TRANSPORT — this morning went over the shared HTTP daemon; this went over stdio, direct.

⚠️ **(2) IS A SIZE MEASUREMENT, NOT A LATENCY ONE.** 7.4x the bytes is correlated with the slowdown and is a plausible cause; nothing here proves it drives the latency. Saying it does would be the same error this project has already paid for once — two numbers agreeing is not causation, and that lesson was recorded THIS MORNING.

═══ WHAT SURVIVES, AND WHAT NEEDS QUALIFYING ═══

✅ `dec:the-stop-hook-asks-the-graph-asynchronously` STANDS. Even at the most favourable figure here — 4.5s, release binary, fresh store, direct transport — a Stop hook that blocks that long is unacceptable, and the path the hook actually runs on is demonstrably slower than that.

🛑 BUT ITS STATED NUMBER IS UNDER-QUALIFIED. '22.6s, repeatably' is TRUE as measured — live graph, shared HTTP daemon, debug binary — and reads as a property of the call. **A number is a measurement of a whole setup, not of the code**, and a later reader comparing it against a release build on a fresh store will conclude the earlier work was wrong when it was only differently situated.

═══ ⭐ THE LEAD WORTH FOLLOWING, and it is cheaper than anything discussed today ═══

If the store's physical state does drive the latency, a COMPACTION of the live store is a far cheaper win than any code change considered today — and nothing in reflow2 currently reports that its own store has grown to several times the size of its content. That is unmeasured and is stated here as a lead rather than a finding.

EVERY TOOL RESULT THIS SERVER HAS EVER SENT CARRIED ITS PAYLOAD TWICE, BYTE FOR BYTE — once as `structuredContent` and once as a text `content` block. The reasoning was sound (`json_result`: 'so clients reading either both get the data') and the cost was never measured. It is a flat 2× on every reply, and it is why three separate rollups are refused by harnesses rather than one: `detect_gaps` at 79,566 chars of payload = 157,785 bytes on the wire, `graph_report` at 88,932 and 91,330, `loop_status` at 72,886. || THE FIX IS ONE LINE AND THE CHOICE INSIDE IT IS THE INTERESTING PART. An EMPTY `content` block saves exactly the same bytes. A SIGNPOST — one sentence naming the field the payload is in — costs ~450 bytes against payloads in the tens of thousands, and is what a client reading the wrong field gets INSTEAD OF SILENCE. Silence there is indistinguishable from reflow2 never having been configured, which is `req:never-silently-absent` and the reason `proxy.rs` keeps a process on stdio whatever state the server is in. So the cheaper option was rejected for the one that fails loudly. || WHY NOT THE OBVIOUS ANSWER, and this is the measurement that killed it: gate the duplication on the negotiated protocol version. `structuredContent` arrived in MCP `2025-06-18` and rmcp 3.1.2 still negotiates `2024-11-05` and `2025-03-26`, so a client that predates the field is genuinely reachable — the version is not a hypothetical. BUT the negotiated version lives on the `RequestContext`, and OF 156 TOOL HANDLERS EXACTLY ONE TAKES ONE (`claim_region`, for the seat). Gating meant threading a context through the other 155 and all 151 `ok_json` call sites, to protect a client nobody could name, against a signpost that protects them for one line. ⇒ THE CHEAP CORRECT FIX AND THE PRINCIPLED-LOOKING ONE WERE 1 LINE AND ~300 LINES, AND THE PRINCIPLED-LOOKING ONE WAS PROPOSED FIRST, BEFORE ANYONE COUNTED. || ANTHONY'S OWN CLIENTS WERE NEVER AT RISK AND THIS WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: all three in-repo Python clients (smoke_mcp, reflow2_cli, reflow2_check) read `structuredContent` FIRST and fall back to `content` only when it is absent; the `j!` macro every Rust tool test uses reads `structured_content` only; `proxy.rs` forwards raw JSON-RPC bytes and parses neither field; and prose tools (`ok_markdown`) never wrote `structuredContent` at all, so `content` remains their only carrier and is untouched. || MEASURED EFFECT, this design, 77 open gaps: 157,785 bytes on the wire before any of this work, 53,181 after the reply budget, 26,096 after the signpost — 6×, with the payload itself unchanged at 27,846 characters. || SOURCE: measured 2026-08-23 on reflow2 0.38.0, driving the built binary over real stdio. Decided by Anthony the same day after being shown the options.

properties.name: A full export→import→export round trip preserves 3,140/3,140 nodes and changes 223 edges — all one property, REALIZES.conformance null→unchecked — and CONVERGES on the second pass, so the committed export is not in the normal form its own importer produces
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-24 on the committed export at main `1ef45e5`, using the debug `reflow2-mcp` CLI end to end: `--import` the committed document into an empty store, `--export` it back out, and `--diff` the two.

RESULT:

    nodes_unchanged   3140 of 3140      design_added/removed/changed  0 / 0 / 0
    edges_unchanged  13167 of 13390     edges_added/removed             0 / 0
    edges_changed      223  — EVERY ONE of them the SAME property:
                             REALIZES.conformance   null -> "unchecked"

⭐ IT IS SEMANTICALLY LOSSLESS. Nothing is dropped and nothing changes meaning: `unchecked` is the documented default `link_artifact` gives `conformance`, so the importer is materialising a default the exporter had omitted. No node, no edge, no design content is lost in a round trip.

⭐⭐ AND IT CONVERGES — TESTED, NOT ASSUMED. Importing the ROUND-TRIPPED document and exporting again produced a file BYTE-IDENTICAL to it. So this is a ONE-TIME NORMALISATION and then a fixed point, not a drift that compounds. That distinction is the whole finding: a compounding drift would make hydrate-from-document unusable, and a one-time normalisation makes it a migration.

THE SPLIT IS HISTORICAL, AND MEASURED: of 360 `REALIZES` edges in the committed export, **137 already carry `conformance` and 223 do not**. The 223 are the ones written before the property existed; the importer fills them in. So the count is not a coincidence — it is exactly the legacy set.

🛑 WHY THIS MATTERS TODAY, INDEPENDENT OF ANY STORAGE-MODEL CHANGE. **The committed export is not in the normal form its own importer produces.** `dec:export-hash-chain` makes the export's content hash carry lineage and tamper evidence, and `compare_designs`, the git merge driver and the drift gate all read that document. So anyone who imports a colleague's export and re-exports — a restore, a machine move, a merge-driver path, a hosted hydrate — produces a **223-edge phantom diff that means nothing**, and a content hash that says the design changed when it did not. That is the same CLASS as the phantom drifts caused by the graph not branching with git, from a different cause.

⚠️ THE FIX HAS TWO DIRECTIONS AND THEY MUST AGREE, which is why this is recorded rather than patched: either the EXPORTER stops omitting the default, or the IMPORTER stops materialising it. `dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants` already names the second direction as BL-198 ("stop serializing defaults"), and flags it as a SCALING decision rather than tidiness because blob size is hydrate time. Whichever way it goes, the two sides currently disagree and the round trip is where it shows.

📌 BOUNDS, so this is not read wider than it was measured: one document, one direction, debug binary, RocksDB backend with fulltext on. It says nothing about hydrate SPEED (measured separately) and nothing about whether accumulated store state outside the design — confirmation dates, drift baselines, `write_gen`, the `.id.json`/`.sync.json` sidecars — survives the trip. Those were NOT tested here, and they remain the open risk in any move to document-as-truth.

MEASURED 2026-08-26 by a CI failure, after `dec:export-once-per-pr` was read, followed, and still got wrong.

═══ THE MISREADING ═══

The rule says one commit per PR may export the design **and it must be LAST**. "Last" was read as *last among the branch's commits*. So when a follow-up fix landed after the export commit, the branch reconciled and exported a SECOND time — and that second export chained its `prev_content_hash` to the FIRST one.

CI refused it:

    FAIL LINEAGE 'docs/design/reflow2.json' does not link to the export it
    replaced: it records sha256:82e005ce... where sha256:ad8b744f... is expected.

⭐ **THE MECHANISM, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING: CI CHECKS OUT THE PR *MERGE* COMMIT, SO `HEAD~1` IS `main` — NOT THE BRANCH'S PREVIOUS COMMIT.** The guard therefore compares the branch's final export against **main's** export. A branch may export exactly ONCE, from main's baseline, and the export's `prev_content_hash` must equal MAIN's `content_hash`.

⇒ **"Last" means last relative to MAIN, not relative to the branch.** A local `reflow2_check` passes on a two-export branch because it compares against the working tree's own history; only CI sees the merge-commit view. **The local gate and the CI gate ask different questions here, and the local one is the weaker.**

═══ THE REPAIR, AND IT IS THE DOCUMENTED ONE ═══

    git reset --soft origin/main
    git checkout origin/main -- docs/design/reflow2.json   # from ORIGIN/MAIN, never the branch
    <export once>
    <commit>

Verify before pushing by comparing directly rather than trusting the shape:

    git show origin/main:docs/design/reflow2.json | jq -r .content_hash
    jq -r .prev_content_hash docs/design/reflow2.json      # must be identical

⚠️ **AND A SECOND-ORDER TRAP THAT COST A FALSE ALARM:** `git log --name-only origin/main..HEAD | grep -c docs/design/reflow2.json` is NOT a valid count of exporting commits — `--name-only` includes commit MESSAGES, so a message that mentions the path inflates the count. Count with `git show --name-only --format="" <sha>` per commit instead.

📌 WHY IT RECURS: the release-cut procedure already carried "one commit may export and `reset --soft` is the fix when you get it wrong", learned on v0.22.0. That note describes the REPAIR and never states WHY last means last-relative-to-main. **A procedure that gives the fix without the mechanism is one somebody follows correctly and still misapplies**, which is exactly what happened here on a non-release PR the note's release framing did not obviously cover.

AN AGENT-SIDE FIELD REPORT FROM AN UNRELATED PROJECT, 2026-08-11, RECORDED REDACTED ON ANTHONY'S INSTRUCTION — no project name, no design counts, no domain terms. Written by a coding agent that had driven reflow2 through capture, where-am-i readbacks, gap review and acknowledgement, verification recording, and a server upgrade mid-project. Recorded as a fact rather than as proposals because that is what it IS: measured evidence about how reflow2 behaves in someone else's hands, which is the input class dec:idea-field-evidence-is-a-prioritisation-input asks whether to read.

=== SORTED THE WAY ANTHONY ASKED: CONFIRMS-ACCEPTED-INTENT vs NEW PROPOSAL vs ALREADY SATISFIED ===

CONFIRMS ACCEPTED INTENT (the report did not propose these; it independently showed they matter):

1. THE SPAWN ERROR NEVER NAMES THE FILE IT COULD NOT FIND. Confirms fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server (measured here 2026-08-07, fix named in its own evidence field, filed and left unfixed). INDEPENDENT AND SIMULTANEOUS: the same defect blocked a session in this repo on 2026-08-11 for forty minutes. FIXED the same day; their narrower ask — name the path — is in that fix.

2. RE-RUNNING A VERIFICATION IS MORE CEREMONY THAN THE EVENT DESERVES. A recorded check re-ran green twice and last_run_at was left stale, honestly, because updating an unchanged status felt like paperwork. Confirms req:verification-keeps-up (ACCEPTED: "a 'verified' claim says how old the check behind it is"). Their sentence is the sharp part and is not in this graph anywhere: STALE LAST-RUN UNDERMINES ASSURANCE MORE THAN A MISSING VERIFICATION DOES, BECAUSE IT LOOKS CURRENT. An accepted requirement is being defeated by friction rather than by absence.

3. THE QUESTION LEDGER CANNOT SEE THE MOST NATURAL WAY QUESTIONS GET ASKED. The where-am-i skill instructs the agent to put open gaps to the user as prose; doing so leaves open_questions at zero and the loop still reporting the gaps as never asked, because only the gap_to_prompt handshake registers an ask. Confirms the ledger's own purpose (questions outlive sessions, in the wording the user saw, so nobody is re-asked) and reveals a SERVED SKILL BYPASSING IT. Their framing: the debt list nags about work that was done.

4. A SATISFYING CAPABILITY IN ANOTHER GRAPH FORCES A PERMANENT ACKNOWLEDGEMENT. A program deliberately running several graphs found on day one that SATISFIES/REALIZES cannot point across a design boundary, so gaps that are structurally answered stay open forever as acknowledgements. Confirms req:design-composes and req:complementary-pairing (both accepted) and sharpens dec:idea-how-is-a-source-outside-the-repo-registered, recorded here hours earlier from the ARTIFACT side of the identical shape: a reference that cannot leave its own design's boundary.

NEW PROPOSALS (nothing in the graph asks for these):

5. AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT CANNOT STATE A MACHINE-CHECKABLE RE-REVIEW TRIGGER. Several acknowledgements carried explicit retirement conditions in prose; one had been true for weeks and nothing surfaced it. NARROWER THAN THEY WROTE, and the narrowing matters: expiry machinery EXISTS and recomputes from the affected node set, so this is not "acknowledgements never expire" — it is that they cannot express a CONDITION. Their words: acknowledgements are where gaps go to be forgotten safely, and the safety decays silently.

6. THE LOOP ONLY SEES WHAT AN AGENT HAND-CARRIES IN. Their own synthesis and the strongest thing in the report: the liveliest facts of the month — merged PRs, a review round addressed, a suite re-verified, work scheduled — all landed in commits and PR threads and almost none reached the graph without the agent carrying them. properties.description:
⭐⭐ THE CAUSE IS STRUCTURAL AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE: **`loop_status` computes debt from STRUCTURE, and a friction report is a FACT, so no debt class counts it.**

The classes it computes are: unsurfaced gaps, unanswered questions, unwritten answers, undispositioned drift, unexamined claims, unproven capabilities, unsettled assigned decisions, structural defects, verification status, and export sync. **Not one of them is 'open defect reported from the field'.** A `fact_type: defect` TemporalFact is inert — it is written, it is true, and the one call every session is told to make cannot see it.

So the loop is not broken in the half everyone watches. It is broken in the half nobody measures: **things get IN and nothing brings them OUT.** A month-old friction item and a five-day-old one are equally invisible, and the only mechanism that has ever surfaced one is a human remembering.

═══ CORROBORATION FROM AN INDEPENDENT DIRECTION ═══

`fact:defect-kit-manifest-drift-is-invisible-to-ci` appeared in `detect_defects` on 2026-08-27 as an ORPHAN: *'points at nothing that exists — its subject/target id resolves to no node and it carries no edge either, so the record is about something the design no longer has.'* The structural detector CAN see that the record is dangling. It cannot see that the DEFECT is open. Those are different questions and only the first is asked.

═══ ⚠️ WHY THIS IS THE ROOT AND NOT THE SYMPTOM ═══

Each repeated item has its own local explanation — the instructions are truncated by a client cap, the kit manifest has no CI check, the loop nudge is not installed in that project. Fixing those three fixes those three. **The pattern is that all three survived a month of sessions that each ran `loop_status` and were told the loop was clean of everything it knows how to count.** Fix the three and the fourth will repeat in September.

⭐ AND IT BEARS DIRECTLY ON THE STANDING RULE IT IS FILED AGAINST. `rule:reflow2-is-built-for-other-projects-not-for-itself` makes field use the point. Field use produces friction reports. Friction reports enter the graph and never come out. **The one input the rule says matters most is the one input with no return path.**

═══ ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH ═══

- **189 open is a RAW COUNT, not a backlog.** Many are surely fixed, and nobody drew the edge — which is the same finding from the other side, not a separate one. How many are genuinely live is UNMEASURED, and this must not be read as '189 outstanding bugs'.
- **`fact_type` is not a reliable filter.** It is an optional free-string property; facts recording a defect without that value are not in the 190, and facts carrying it that are really observations are. The number is indicative, not exact.
- **No remedy is asserted**, and the obvious one — add a debt class — has a real counter: a count that can never reach zero becomes wallpaper, which is the failure this project has already found three times. Options are open in `dec:idea-what-makes-a-field-report-owed`.

The whole design holds 8 INVALIDATES edges in total.

⭐ THE FIRST DURABLE CONTENT MIGRATED OUT OF A MACHINE-LOCAL HANDOFF NOTE AND INTO THE GRAPH, under `dec:idea-the-handoff-file-contradicts-an-accepted-decision-and-nobody-reconciled-them`. This is the class of thing that note existed to carry; it is a dated observation about the world, which is what a TemporalFact is, and it now travels with the design instead of living on one laptop.

FIVE WAYS A GREEN SIGNAL WAS FALSE IN ONE SESSION. Three were the agent's OWN command construction, which is the uncomfortable part — the tooling did not lie, the question did.

① **A PIPED GATE REPORTS THE LAST COMMAND'S EXIT CODE.** `cargo test --workspace 2>&1 | grep ... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20` exited 0 — from `head`. It says NOTHING about cargo. Redirect to a file and read cargo's own exit code.

② **`sort -rn | head -20` HID THE FAILURES IT WAS MEANT TO SURFACE.** A `test result: FAILED` line sorts to the tail by count and is cut. The first "green" workspace run was worthless; the honest re-run reported 157 suites / 1798 passed / 0 failed. **A filter that ranks by frequency buries the rare event, and failures are rare by construction.**

③ **A GREEN `cargo test` IS NOT A GREEN CI.** PR #343's first run failed on `cargo fmt --check` with all 1798 local tests passing. CI's `core` job runs tests → clippy → **Format** → schema → installer → skill lint, and the local habit covered one of six. It also builds `--no-default-features`, a different build from the local `--workspace` run.

④ **`loop_status` REPORTED `state: in_step` ON AN EXPORT FOUR NODES BEHIND.** It means "the file is where the graph left it" — nobody modified it externally — NOT "the graph is exported". The `next` list said the truth in words. Use `compare_designs` for the actual question.

⑤ **`pgrep -f "<command>"` MATCHES ITS OWN WRAPPER**, so "still running" read true after the job had finished. Twice.

🛑 THE PATTERN WORTH KEEPING RATHER THAN THE FIVE INSTANCES: every one of these produced a CONFIDENT, WELL-FORMED, WRONG answer — never an error. `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` exists for exactly this and was available all session; it was broken three times before being consulted. **A trap that returns an error teaches you once. A trap that returns a green tick teaches you nothing, repeatedly.**

📌 STILL IN THE MEMORY NOTE AND NOT YET MIGRATED: `gh pr edit` is broken here (Projects-classic GraphQL — use `gh api -X PATCH repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n> --input`); a new MCP tool is uncallable until a client restart; `--stop-shared` leaks a zombie per call. Each is the same genre and each deserves its own node or a shared one.

properties.statement:
**FIVE DISTINCT MECHANISMS BY WHICH A FAILED OPERATION REPORTED SUCCESS, IN ONE SESSION, 2026-08-23.** Counted because one instance reads as carelessness and five reads as a property of the tooling.

1. **`| tail` DESTROYS `$?`.** `python3 gate.py | tail -6; echo EXIT=$?` prints tail's status. A FAILING intent-authority gate printed `EXIT=0`. Already on the record as `fact:a-piped-gate-reports-the-pipes-exit-code-not-the-gates`; hit twice more this session after being known.
2. **`gh pr checks` EXITS NON-ZERO WHEN A CHECK IS FAILING OR PENDING.** Used as `s=$(gh pr checks N ...) || { sleep; continue; }`, every poll was discarded. **TWO CI monitors ran to completion having never emitted a single event**, and both reported "ended without producing output" — indistinguishable from "nothing happened". Fixed with `|| true`.
3. **A `&&` CHAIN SKIPPED A BRANCH CREATION.** `git pull --rebase && git checkout -b <name>` — the pull failed on unstaged changes, so the branch was never created, and the next commit landed on local `main`. Caught only when `git push` refused an unknown refspec.
4. **A TEST LOG READ MID-RUN, REPORTED AS FINAL.** "125 suites, 1312 passed, 0 failed" was read off a still-growing file. The true result was `TEST_EXIT=101` — **150 suites, 1400 passed, 1 failed**. The background task printed the real answer and it was never read; the harness notification said "exit code 0", which is the WRAPPER's exit. The false number reached a commit message and a PR body.
5. **`gh pr edit` PRINTS A GraphQL ERROR AND EXITS 0.** The Projects-classic deprecation makes the call fail while reporting success. Two attempts to correct the PR body silently did nothing; caught by reading the body back. Worked around with `gh api -X PATCH`.

⭐ **WHAT THEY SHARE, AND IT IS NOT "SHELL IS HARD":** in every case the FAILURE PRODUCED SILENCE RATHER THAN NOISE, and silence is what success looks like. Three of the five were shell-level; two were a tool exiting 0 on a real error. **Nothing catches these except reading the authoritative object afterwards** — which is `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` verbatim, and this is five more instances of the rule earning its keep in a single day.

📌 THE CHEAP HABITS THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT ALL FIVE, in order of how much they cost to adopt: redirect a gate to a file and capture `$?` on its own line; never use a command's exit status inside `||` when that status encodes DATA rather than failure; verify a branch exists after creating it; read a background task's OWN output rather than the log it is still writing; and read back anything you wrote through an API before believing it landed.

⚠️ BOUND: one session, one agent, one machine. Whether five is a normal rate is unknown — nothing has ever counted this before, which is itself the reason the number is worth writing down.

properties.statement:
COUNTED 2026-08-25 across one session, because four instances of one shape is a pattern rather than four mistakes.

THE QUESTION: how deep should a design's decomposition go, and what should carry depth. Four answers were produced. **Every measurement behind them was arithmetically correct. Every one answered a question about the wrong population, and Anthony caught all four.**

**1. REFLOW2'S OWN STATISTICS USED TO DECIDE FOR USERS.** Concluded "at 4% spine population, deriving depth is unusable and declaring is the only thing that works." He: *"we can use reflow2 as a litmus test for what is right, but I want to do what is right for people using reflow2 on their own projects."*
⇒ On re-measurement the 4% was wrong TWICE OVER: the denominator counted ChangeEvents and TemporalFacts that were never meant to be in a decomposition spine, and the figure was stale. **The real number is 100% of components.** The conclusion built on it was backwards.

**2. A CONTAMINATED SAMPLE READ AS EVIDENCE.** Measured seven reflow2 designs, concluded "real designs are two rungs deep, so the floor was reflow2's problem, not a user's." He: *"most of these are after the fact... they were developed before reflow2 really started defining rungs."*
⇒ Evidence of what happens with NO guidance, presented as evidence of what users need.

**3. ORGANIC STRUCTURE READ AS DESIGNED STRUCTURE.** Measured the bluesky stack, chosen precisely as an outside case, and reported "five core repos, inside 3–7, and independent lifecycles draw the same cut — two rules agreeing." He: *"the bluesky stack has grown somewhat organically... it was never designed from a systems engineering perspective."*
⇒ **Conway's Law — rule 3 of the same doctrine — PREDICTS that split with no SE at all.** Two of the four rules cannot tell a designed system from a grown one, because one of them is about growth. The agreement was not corroboration.

**4. ARTIFACTS MEASURED INSTEAD OF DOCTRINE CONSULTED.** Four rounds of measurement before anyone asked what the discipline actually prescribes. He: *"this is more a systems engineering 101 type discussion... what does the doctrine say we should do?"*
⇒ Doctrine answers it directly and differently: structure is DERIVED from functional allocation, and span of control is a CHECK on the result, not a generator of it. **The machinery already existed — `propose_allocation` clusters capabilities by coupling — and four rounds of measuring never touched it.**

⭐⭐ THE SHAPE, WHICH IS THE POINT: every instance is REASONING FROM AN AVAILABLE POPULATION RATHER THAN THE RELEVANT ONE. reflow2's graph was available, so it stood in for users' graphs. Existing designs were available, so they stood in for well-made designs. A file tree was available, so it stood in for a decomposition. Measurement was available, so it stood in for doctrine. **The failure is never in the arithmetic; it is in the silent substitution of the sample you can reach for the sample you need.**

🛑 AND NOT ONE OF THE FOUR WAS CAUGHT BY A MECHANISM. Not by a detector, not by a gate, not by a tool refusing an argument. All four were caught by the person, in conversation, by knowing the domain. `coverage_report` exists to ask "what could this check not have seen" and was never reached for, because nothing about a confident measurement suggests asking.

📌 WHY IT IS FILED HERE: this is the same shape as the three-legs finding at a different layer. That one measured that vocabulary never reaches a user's project unless a tool, an instruction and a detector all exist. This measures that ANALYSIS never reaches a user's project either — an agent with a graph in front of it will characterise that graph and present the result as general. The population is a third thing that has to be chosen deliberately, and nothing in reflow2 asks which one you are standing in.

📌 BOUNDS: one session, one agent, one domain expert correcting. Whether the same shape appears without a domain expert in the room is exactly what cannot be measured from inside it — and is the reason this is worth recording rather than absorbing.

FOUND 2026-08-20 while putting two real gaps to Anthony through the handshake — the tool contradicts ITSELF, in the one place a user's vocabulary is decided.

=== THE TWO TEXTS, both served by the same tool ===

The PROMPT it emits, verbatim:

    "Rewrite this design gap as one plain-language question for a non-engineer.
     No graph/systems-engineering jargon. Return only the question."

The TOOL'S OWN DESCRIPTION, verbatim:

    "Read who you are talking to (their `Contributor` description) and match that
     domain; a `plain` question is not automatically one in their vocabulary, and
     swapping vocabulary is not simplifying — a systems engineer wants `interface`
     and `verification` kept."

The description learned the lesson. The template it emits did not. An agent that follows the template strips exactly the vocabulary the reader needs, and it will do so while the description sitting beside it says not to.

=== WHY IT IS THE EXPENSIVE KIND OF CONTRADICTION ===

This is the same failure shape the revise-design skill already carries a correction for — a skill and a tool description disagreeing, where the resolution was that THE TOOL IS WHAT AN AGENT READS AT CALL TIME. Here both texts come from the same tool, so that tie-breaker does not apply, and the one an agent acts on is the WORSE one: a prompt is an instruction and a description is context, so the instruction wins.

=== WHAT IT COSTS AN ARBITRARY USER'S PROJECT ===

gap_to_prompt is the single point where a detector's vocabulary becomes a human's. A beamline scientist, a flight-test engineer, an acquisitions officer: each has a domain register, and 'no jargon' flattens all of them toward the same non-engineer default. The result is a question that is easy to read and impossible to answer precisely, put to the one person who could have answered it precisely. The standing correction on file is that a persona is a VOCABULARY SWAP, not a difficulty dial — and this template is a difficulty dial.

=== EVIDENCE IT MATTERS, from the same session ===

Both gaps were answered against the description rather than the template — SE register kept, reflow2-internal jargon dropped. The resulting questions name the decomposition spine and the hosted tier, which is what makes them answerable in one word. The template's version would have said neither.

=== A SECOND, SMALLER FINDING IN THE SAME RUN, and it is a CREDIT ===

Reusing a prompt id from a previous gap's round returned `rephrase_degraded: true` and fell back to the raw detector text rather than silently accepting a mismatched answer. It said it had degraded. That is exactly the behaviour Proposal 2 wants generalised, already working here.

=== NOT FIXED, DELIBERATELY ===

Changing that template changes what every gap question sounds like on every project reflow2 is used on. That is Anthony's call, not a silent edit.

THE GOLDEN THREAD IS IN THE UNANALYSED SET. GOVERNED_BY (867), REALIZES (199), SATISFIES (175), VERIFIES (139) — the core traceability of the whole design — have never been cycle-checked, never had centrality run on them, never been community-detected. Nor has PRECEDES (47), which IS the delivery plan. Meanwhile DEPENDS_ON (173 edges) carries FOUR separate analyses (structure, budget, hierarchy, allocate).

THE CAUSE IS WIRING, NOT CAPABILITY. Every algorithm needed is already imported from dynograph and already runs: betweenness_centrality, leiden, cut_structure, connected_components, find_cycle, strongly_connected_components. Each is nailed to one purpose-specific edge subset at its call site. Graph algorithms are edge-type agnostic; the wiring is not. Anthony's own earlier tool (/home/ajs7/reflow/tools/system_of_systems_graph.py) took the opposite shape — ONE graph built from all edges, then nx.simple_cycles and degree analysis over it — and he ran it as a routine sanity check on nearly every graph.

WHAT THE MISSING ANALYSES ACTUALLY FOUND WHEN RUN BY HAND, so the gap is not reported as hypothetical:

    GOLDEN THREAD  SATISFIES+REALIZES+VERIFIES+ALLOCATED_TO   677 edges   0 cycles
    REASONING      GOVERNED_BY+OBSOLETES+CAUSES+ANTICIPATES   893 edges   1 cycle
    THE PLAN       PRECEDES+SCHEDULED_FOR                      70 edges   0 cycles
    TIME/HISTORY   HAS_SNAPSHOT+AT_EPOCH+VALID_FROM+VALID_TO  646 edges   0 cycles
    RISK           RISKS+BLOCKS+CONTRADICTS+VIOLATES+MASKS     35 edges   0 cycles

The single cycle is dec:an-unplanned-cut-slips-every-later-increment-by-one CAUSES dec:idea-a-planned-increment-is-named-by-content-not-by-number, which OBSOLETES it back — a TIME SEQUENCE rendered as a loop by a projection with no clock, not faulty reasoning. SO THE DESIGN IS STRUCTURALLY CLEAN EVERYWHERE NOBODY WAS LOOKING, which is a result worth having and could not previously be obtained.

AND A SECOND READING THE DESIGN ALREADY ASKED FOR. dec:orientation-is-computed-not-written names the genuinely missing thing as "WHICH FEW DECISIONS SHAPE EVERYTHING ELSE — neither what-next nor where-am-i answers it today, and it is what a newcomer actually needs". Centrality over GOVERNED_BY is that computation and had never been run. Run: the top governors are rule:no-foreclosure, the owner's-word authority rule, a-graph-per-ownership-boundary, systems-are-functional-not-the-file-tree, and the-LLM-speaks-the-graph-remembers-the-human-decides. THE SHAPE MATTERS MORE THAN THE LIST: influence is FLAT, not concentrated — max reach 13, the top five carry 16% of the edges, and 66 of 120 governed nodes are governed by exactly one thing. There is no small set of load-bearing roots. That is evidence against the design being a deep decision tree: a tree has a trunk and this does not.

THE EXCLUSIONS ARE LOAD-BEARING AND THAT WAS PROVEN THE EXPENSIVE WAY. The first centrality run returned garbage — the ten most influential "decisions" were all decision:ack: review records, which structure.rs already excludes from the design network (ver:acknowledgement-not-structure). Excluding them took GOVERNED_BY from 867 edges to 255: TWO THIRDS OF THAT EDGE TYPE IS BOOKKEEPING. A naive run-everything-on-everything gives a confident wrong answer on the first attempt, so any general surface must carry the exclusion list as part of each projection's definition rather than as a caveat.

properties.name: Hydrate from document to first query, measured across five design sizes with NO database and NO index: 1,000 nodes = 270 ms, 3,140 nodes = 8.8 s. Cost is superlinear in EDGES (~627 µs/edge at the top vs 143 at the bottom) and 95% of it is import_graph, not JSON parsing and not the store
properties.statement:
THE MEASUREMENT `dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants` ASKED FOR ON 2026-08-09 — *"the one measurement worth taking now, while nothing depends on the answer: hydrate-and-index time as a function of design size (200 / 2k / 20k nodes, import to first query)"*. Taken 2026-08-24, at Anthony's instruction, on reflow2's own design at main `1ef45e5`.

METHOD: `cargo test --release -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` — **release build, in-memory backend, NO RocksDB and NO tantivy**. Parse the export, open a `DesignGraph`, `import_graph`, then a typed scan as the first real query. Sub-sampled documents take the first N nodes and only the edges whose BOTH endpoints survive.

    nodes   edges    parse    import    TOTAL to queryable    µs/edge
      200       0    6.0ms     6.8ms         27.7 ms             —
      500     409   22.9ms    58.7ms         93.8 ms            143
     1000    1247   47.0ms   205.3ms        270.0 ms            165
     2000    4318  127.8ms  1136.7ms       1279.6 ms            263
     3140   13390  385.6ms  8397.6ms       8827.9 ms            627

⭐⭐ THE HEADLINE, AND IT REDIRECTS THE WHOLE QUESTION: **THE BYTE STORE IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK, BECAUSE THERE IS NO BYTE STORE IN THIS MEASUREMENT.** No RocksDB, no redb, no disk — and the top-end hydrate is still 8.8 seconds. JSON parsing is 386 ms of it (4%); opening the graph is 34 ms; the first query is 11 ms. **`import_graph` is 8,398 ms — 95% of the total.** Choosing a different embedded engine cannot move this number, and neither can dropping the engine entirely.

⭐ THE COST IS SUPERLINEAR IN EDGES, NOT IN NODES. Per-edge cost RISES from 143 µs to 627 µs as the graph grows — a 4.4x degradation. Between the last two points, edges grow 3.1x and time grows 7.4x, an exponent near 1.8; between the middle two, near 1.5. Consistent with adjacency lists being read-modify-write on every edge insert, so each edge into a high-degree node rewrites that node's whole list, and average degree climbs with density (3,140 nodes carry 13,390 edges, and hub nodes like `proj:reflow2` carry far more than the 8.5 average). **That is an implementation property of the import path, not a fact about storage architecture, and it is optimisable — batching adjacency writes is the obvious first move.**

⇒ WHAT IT MEANS FOR DOCUMENT-AS-TRUTH, stated at the altitude the decision needs: **a typical design hydrates comfortably.** 1,000 nodes in 270 ms and 500 in 94 ms are both far inside the "under a second and it is routine engineering" bar the 2026-08-09 node set. reflow2's OWN design is the pathological case, and it is pathological because it is the biggest and densest design that exists anywhere — no tenant of a hosted tier would look like it. So the model is viable today for the sizes it would actually serve, AND it degrades badly enough with growth that the import path would need work before anybody leaned on it.

🛑 BOUNDS — THIS IS A LOWER BOUND, NOT THE FULL COST. **The full-text index was OFF.** A real hydrate that must answer `search_design` also has to build the tantivy index, which is not in any number above. The 200-node row has ZERO edges (an artifact of sub-sampling by node prefix) so it measures node-only import and must not be read as a 200-node design. Single machine, single run per size, no warm-up, debug of the OS page cache uncontrolled. The 20k-node point the original request asked for was not taken — no design that large exists to sample.

📌 FOR CONTRAST, the same hydrate INTO RocksDB with fulltext ON, debug build: 96–134 s, producing a 12–13 MB store. Not comparable to the table above (different build profile and different feature set) and recorded only so nobody mistakes one for the other.

AN AGENT WORKING THIS TOOL PROPOSED A PLAN BEFORE ASKING THE GRAPH WHAT IT ALREADY KNEW — THREE TIMES IN ONE SESSION. Recorded because each instance was caught by a different mechanism and only the pattern shows the failure is systematic rather than three accidents. || (1) SETTING `medium: REST` ON `ifc:mcp-tools-http` to close an incomplete-contract gap, when THAT NODE'S OWN `spec` FIELD argues at length that `unspecified` is the honest answer and that REST is positively wrong. Caught by reading the node one step too late; reverted within the minute. (2) PROPOSING CONTRACTS FOR 64 ‘UNCONTRACTED’ MODULE PAIRS, and getting them approved, when `fact:coupling-and-contract-are-recorded-in-vocabularies-that-never-meet` — recorded TWO DAYS EARLIER — said all 64 sit inside one crate, that most are impl blocks of one struct, and that the number could not move whatever anyone wrote. Caught only because a routine `search_design` before starting surfaced that node. (3) RECOMMENDING THE ROLL-UP BE ADDED TO `seam_report`, which turned out to compare TWO LINKED DESIGNS and could not host it at all; the user chose that option on my description of it. Caught by reading the source before writing. || ⭐ THE COMMON MECHANISM, AND IT IS NOT LAZINESS: in all three the graph HELD THE ANSWER and the proposal was formed from the DETECTOR'S OUTPUT instead. A gap says what is absent; it cannot say whether the absence is a hole or a conclusion. `ifc:graph-export` had six unset axes and `ifc:mcp-tools-http` had one, reported IN IDENTICAL WORDS, and one of those absences was a hole while the other was a defended answer. ⇒ THE GUARD IS ONE CALL: `search_design` ON THE SUBJECT BEFORE PROPOSING A PLAN, NOT BEFORE WRITING THE NODE. By the time a node is being written the plan is already committed and the cost of abandoning it is paid in reputation as well as time. || ⚠️ AND THE SAME SESSION BROKE `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` THREE TIMES, in scripts checking whether a tool call had worked: reading the JSON-RPC envelope for `result` rather than the tool result for `isError`. One of those silently reported five decisions as created when none was, and a later probe overwrote a real node with the word `probe`. ⇒ THAT RULE IS ONE OF THE THREE DOWNGRADED TO ADVISORY THE SAME DAY FOR HAVING NO DETECTOR — AND IT WAS BROKEN THREE TIMES BY THE AGENT WHO DOWNGRADED IT, WITHIN THE HOUR. The strongest argument yet that it is worth a detector: it is not an obscure rule, it is the one an agent breaks while working normally. || SOURCE: this session, 2026-08-23. Written from the conversation and the diffs, which is the only place the pattern exists — each instance is recorded separately, none of them together.

MEASURED 2026-08-13 by experiment on a scratch graph, because the answer could not be read off the schema and reading `get_node`'s signature only hints at it.

THE QUESTION Anthony asked: does each node within a graph have a unique id? THE ANSWER: no — the unique key is (node_type, node_id), not node_id alone.

WHAT WAS RUN. Created `thing:same` as a Capability and again as a Requirement in one graph: BOTH PERSISTED and both read back independently, with their own names. Then created `thing:same` as a Capability a second time: it MERGED with no error — the property passed overwrote, the `name` omitted survived, and `scan_nodes` reported one Capability. The storage key is `{graph_id}\x00{type}\x00{id}`, which is why `get_node` demands a type as well as an id.

⭐ THREE LEVELS, AND ONLY THE MIDDLE ONE IS ENFORCED:
  · `graph_id` ACROSS STORES — NOT unique, nothing checks it (see fact:two-adopted-stores-share-one-graph-id-2026-08-13)
  · (type, id) WITHIN a graph — unique BY CONSTRUCTION, it is the storage key
  · `id` ALONE within a graph — NOT unique; only the `cap:` / `req:` / `dec:` prefix convention keeps it clean

THE CONVENTION HOLDS IN PRACTICE AND IS NOT ENFORCED: across all 2,113 nodes of reflow2's own design, ZERO ids appear under more than one node type. Three types legitimately carry two prefixes each and none is a collision — Component `cmp:` (48) plus `sys:` (8, the functional systems from dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition); Decision `dec:` (222) plus `decision:` (126, the generated review-acknowledgement records); Contributor `who:` (5) plus ONE lingering `ctr:`, the residue of the Contributor fork.

🛑 WHY IT MATTERS FOR FEDERATION, and this is the asymmetry worth keeping: reflow2 is careful about id collisions ONE LEVEL DOWN and has nothing one level up. `mirror_surface` REFUSES a colliding node id and leaves the local node untouched, on the stated ground that "two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners." The same hazard between two DESIGNS is a silent overwrite in a BTreeMap. Node collisions are a conversation; graph collisions are data loss.

AN INSTANCE OF THE RISK BL-185 RECORDS, WITH A MEASURED COST — and it is the agent's own working order, not somebody else's.

BL-185 has carried Anthony's words since 2026-08-03: "Developing tests as you design is extremely important. It shapes system architecture, forces clear thinking about edge cases early... Confirmation bias: Testing code you already wrote proves what it does, not necessarily what it should do." He raised the same question again on 2026-08-11 — the TENTH time in one session that a fresh thought landed on something the graph already held, and the only one where the prior record is his own verbatim reasoning on an OPEN fork nobody has chosen.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DONE, TWICE, ON 2026-08-11:
  PR #149 (spawn_daemon)      implementation first, then tests, then mutation-checking
  PR #151 (search-first)      implementation first, then tests, then mutation-checking
Neither was test-first. Both were mutation-checked, which is this repo's real rigour and is a DIFFERENT property: mutation-checking proves a test can fail, it does not prove the test asks the right question.

⭐ THE COST WAS MEASURABLE AND IS THE POINT. PR #151's check refused two requirements whose statements were three words long ("Session A wrote this." / "Session B wrote this.") — a plainly wrong result, found by CI on an unrelated suite, not by any test written for the feature. The cause was an absent signal rather than a bad threshold: near-empty documents share most of their tokens by construction. THAT IS A BOUNDARY CONDITION, and "what are the boundary values" is precisely the question test-first forces before an author is attached to an implementation. It is also the GENESIS case — a young design is all short statements — so the miss was not exotic.

ANTHONY'S CRITERIA, 2026-08-11, recorded because BL-185 does not carry them and the fork should be judged against something: a good test is VALID (measures what it claims, not a side effect), ISOLATED (no dependence on other tests or shared state), REPEATABLE (same result every run under identical conditions), FOCUSED (one behaviour, not several), and FAST. It should target the HAPPY PATH, EDGE CASES (boundaries, extremes, unusual inputs), ERROR CONDITIONS (failures, missing data, bad input, stress), and THE CONTRACT RATHER THAN THE IMPLEMENTATION, so an internal change does not produce a false failure.

📌 SCORING PR #151's OWN SUITE AGAINST THEM, honestly, because a fact that only indicts the past is not evidence:
  valid        yes — asserts the refusal, the rollback and the created node, not side effects
  isolated     yes — each case builds its own in-memory service
  repeatable   yes in practice, but SENSITIVE TO CORPUS CONTENT: the threshold is relative to
               other nodes present, so a case is only as stable as its seeding. One test sat on
               the boundary during development and had to be re-seeded.
  focused      mostly; the revision case must seed a neighbour or it proves nothing
  fast         yes, sub-second
  happy path   covered
  edge cases   COVERED ONLY AFTER CI FOUND ONE. Not designed in.
  error cond.  NOT COVERED. The `unavailable` branch — the search itself failing — has ZERO
               tests. It is the branch that exists to satisfy req:no-silent-fallback, and
               nothing proves it fires.
  contract     mixed. Two assertions match literal words in the refusal text ("SHARPEN",
               "distinct_from"); the contract is that BOTH routes are named, and the test reads
               the wording rather than the property.

SO THE HONEST SCORE IS SIX AND A HALF OF NINE, with the two misses landing exactly where implement-first predicts they would: edge cases and error conditions.

⚠️ WHAT THIS IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. It is one agent, one day, two PRs, and both shipped working and gated. It says nothing about whether test-first would have been FASTER, and BL-185's own guard rail stands: Anthony's caveat that this "may not apply to or be feasible for all project types", and the adopt path where every recovered test is necessarily after the fact. A reading that scored implement-first as failure would repeat BL-179's punish-correct-work trap.

📌 A SEPARATE FINDING FOUND WHILE CHECKING THIS: MUTATION-CHECKING IS THIS PROJECT'S STRONGEST TEST DISCIPLINE AND IS WRITTEN DOWN NOWHERE AS A RULE. At least eight Verifications record it in their own text (evidence-quality, ility, no-fabricated-repairs, siblings-are-not-merged-away, edges-need-both-ends, supporting-is-not-conflict, the-server-says-when-it-is-stale, search-first-forces-a-choice) and AGENTS.md does not mention it. It is a convention held by imitation — every agent that does it learned it by reading a test file. That is the same shape as the search-first rule living in five skills and firing only when one is loaded.

THE UNDECLARED-SEAM FINDING COULD NOT REACH ZERO, AND THE REASON WAS AN ALTITUDE MISMATCH RATHER THAN MISSING CONTRACTS. `fact:coupling-and-contract-are-recorded-in-vocabularies-that-never-meet` measured the two sets as DISJOINT BY CONSTRUCTION — couplings read from DEPENDS_ON between modules, contracts from PROVIDES/CONSUMES between the boxes that contain them — so writing a contract could never move the number. MEASURED 2026-08-23 on reflow2's own design: module level 72 couplings against 42 contract pairs leaves 64 undeclared; LIFTED TO `subsystem` it is 11 against 13 with NOTHING undeclared. || ⭐ LIFTING BOTH SETS IS THE WHOLE CORRECTNESS ARGUMENT, AND THE HALF-FIX LOOKS RIGHT. Rolling up only the COUPLINGS is the obvious move and leaves the two vocabularies exactly as disjoint as they were — the contracts are still recorded between the leaves. Proven by reverting to that half-fix and watching the one case that matters fail while four others stayed green, which is why the case exists. || ⚠️ A ZERO HERE IS THE MOST DANGEROUS ANSWER THE TOOL CAN GIVE, and it is designed around. 'Nothing undeclared' at subsystem altitude compared ELEVEN couplings, not seventy-two. Every reply therefore carries the raw count and, when an altitude reaches nothing, the number of endpoints dropped — asked at `system`, where this design has no components at all, it reports 0 couplings compared and 114 endpoints unreachable rather than a clean bill. A vacuous zero that announces its own vacuity. || NOTHING IS WRITTEN BACK. The roll-up is derived on every call from CONTAINS + PROVIDES + CONSUMES. A stored edge between two subsystems would make the graph assert a contract nobody declared and be indistinguishable afterwards from one somebody did — `dec:views-are-projections`, and Anthony's own standing rule that a view is a projection and renderer fill-ins are defects. Pinned by a case that exports the design before and after and compares content hashes. || WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: whether `detect_undeclared_seams` and the maturity `seams` band should themselves move to an altitude, or keep answering at module level. They are unchanged here on purpose — changing what a detector reports is a louder act than adding a way to ask, and the 64 remains visible until somebody decides which altitude that gap is about. || SOURCE: measured 2026-08-23 on reflow2 0.38.0, driving the built binary over real stdio.

MEASURED 2026-08-22 through the shipped binary, on both arms of the original trial, immediately after `vocabulary_coverage` began NAMING the properties it had only ever counted.

                       before   after   growth
  mature (2897 nodes)      31      70     +39  (+126%)
  day-one (2 nodes)        88     101     +13  (+15%)

⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT, AND IT IS THE ANSWER TO THE OBJECTION THIS CHANGE HAD TO CLEAR. The trial's fourth decision withheld the flat list because it was LONGEST FOR THE USER LEAST ABLE TO ACT ON IT — 88 items on day one against 31 on a mature design. Naming properties could only have made that worse; instead it narrowed the gap from 57 items to 31, because the vacuous-zero rule suppresses every property of every type that has no instances, and on day one almost no type has any. The list grows where somebody can act on it and barely moves where they cannot.

The DEFAULT reply, which is what every caller pays for, grew from about 2.4 KB to 2973 bytes on the day-one arm — one `properties` figure per domain, eleven numbers, never a list.

WHAT THE MATURE ARM FOUND ON REFLOW2 ITSELF, none of which any shipped report could state before:
  `Artifact.audience` — 0 of 190. reflow2 added the field in #295 so that a deliverable declares who it reaches, and has classified NOT ONE OF ITS OWN. That is `rule:the-self-host-always-trails-what-it-teaches` again, and it is now visible rather than inferred.
  22 EDGE properties on edge types that have edges: `ALLOCATED_TO.{weight,frequency,data_volume,note}`, `PROVIDES.{weight,frequency,data_volume}`, `CONSUMES.{frequency,data_volume}` — the entire coupling vocabulary the structural detectors read, declared and never once written. `TRIGGERS.{confidence,evidence}`, `BLOCKS.confidence`, `RISKS.confidence`, `EVOLVES_INTO.confidence`, `VERIFIES.coverage`, `CONTAINS.note`, `ASKS_ABOUT.note`.
  `Project.mirror_*` (4), `Fragment.{summary,intent,phase,created_by,created_at}`, `Snapshot.captured_at`, `Release.created_at`, `Artifact.created_at`, `Project.created_at` — the never-set timestamp cluster, still there.
  `Constraint.{objective,rationale}`, `Requirement.source`, `Question.prompt_id`, `Verification.location`, `Environment.description`, `Artifact.{description,signature}`.

⚠️ WHAT THE FIGURES ARE NOT. `properties_on_used_types` reads 155 of 178 and `properties_on_used_edge_types` 59 of 81, and NEITHER counts a property that carries a schema DEFAULT as capable of being unused — the store materialises defaults on write, so every instance carries one. What is named is the UNDEFAULTED optional. That is the class that matters (`req:defaults-do-not-assert` is why the fields worth asking about have no default) but it means these figures are an UNDER-count of vocabulary nobody chose, not a full one.
