properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-18 from the committed export, answering three questions Anthony asked about black-box tiering. All three have answers, and two of them are wrong in a way nobody would notice.

1. DOES EACH NODE KNOW WHICH BOX IT IS IN? Almost none do. 121 of 2526 nodes (4%) carry a CONTAINS parent. Without one: 494 ChangeEvents, 405 Decisions, 225 TemporalFacts, 190 Artifacts, 168 Fragments, 168 Verifications, 156 DesignEpochs and — the one that matters for decomposition — 151 CAPABILITIES. A capability's box is reachable only through ALLOCATED_TO, which is a different spine from CONTAINS, so 'what is in this box?' and 'what is allocated to it?' are two questions with two answers and no computation reconciles them.

2. IS NESTING TRACEABLE TO PARENTS? The spine exists and is walked (containment_closure, unbounded, downward). Components sit at three depths: 2 at depth 0, 12 at depth 1, 42 at depth 2 — Project -> subsystem -> component. But `proj:reflow2 CONTAINS 80 THINGS`, of which only 8 are subsystems; the rest are Requirements, Capabilities, Decisions and even a Release. CONTAINS is doing double duty as 'belongs to this project', so walking the spine from the root does NOT enumerate the decomposition. One node (`cmp:skills`) has TWO parents (`proj:reflow2` and `sys:agent-surface`) — a box in two boxes, unflagged.

3. CAN YOU ASK FOR ALL TIER-1 BOXES QUICKLY? The vocabulary is there and better than expected: `Component.level` is an INDEXED enum with the full ladder — component / subsystem / system / system_of_systems / enterprise — and it is populated: 8 `subsystem`, 48 `component`. There is also a separate indexed `tier` (strategic/operational/tactical), a different axis. So the data supports the query.

⭐ BUT THE TWO WAYS TO ASK DISAGREE, AND THE STRUCTURAL ONE IS WRONG. By declared level, tier 1 is the 8 subsystems. By spine position — Components with no CONTAINS parent — tier 1 is TWO nodes, `cmp:packaging` and `cmp:registry`, and BOTH are level `component`: leaves that were simply never wired to a parent, not top-level boxes. A reader who asks the structural question gets a confident, fast, wrong answer.

WHAT IS MISSING IS A TOOL, NOT A SCHEMA. No served tool filters by `level`; `scan_nodes` returns all 56 Components and the caller filters client-side. Nothing checks that declared level agrees with spine depth, and nothing reports a node contained by two boxes. `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (PROPOSED since 2026-08-07, his words, and his note that this was 'one of the primary things I designed it for') is where this belongs.

"WHAT IS LEFT TO BUILD?" HAS NO ANSWER IN REFLOW2, AND THE REASON IS NARROWER AND WORSE THAN THE REPORT THAT PROMPTED THE CHECK.

ORIGIN: item 1 of the Grok 4.6 agent feedback of 2026-08-13 (`fact:agent-feedback-corroborated-2026-08-14`) — *"'What is left to build?' is not a first-class query. `what_next` ranks open Decisions."* Verified on reflow2's own committed export at `c18a4a1`, 2026-08-14, per `req:agent-authored-feedback-is-reproducible-and-never-leaves-unasked`.

═══ ✅ THEIR CLAIM CONFIRMED ═══

`what_next` (no args) on reflow2's graph returned **12 items: 3 marked + 4 ranked + 1 unexplored + 4 shaping — every one a Decision.** `open_total: 118`, `unranked_pool: 87`. Zero Requirements, zero Capabilities. Its own description says so honestly (*"which decisions to settle next"*), so this is a scope fact rather than a bug. `arrival_delta` requires a DesignEpoch or Release `target_id`, so it cannot answer for a design whose remaining work is not scheduled onto one.

THE HONEST ANSWER, computed directly from the export:
```
Requirements 164   accepted 115  proposed 36  dropped 9  deferred 4
Capabilities 161   verified 77  realized 41  planned 40  in_progress 3
accepted + live + NOT delivered ............ 9
live planned/in_progress capabilities ..... 43
```
**None of those 43 appears in any tool's answer to "what next".**

═══ 🛑🛑 THE MECHANISM, AND IT IS THE REAL FINDING ═══

`unrealized_capability` LOOKS like the build list — *"Nothing builds capability X"* — but fires only 3 times against 43 planned capabilities. `detect.rs` suppresses it three ways, and the decisive one is **`realized_via_component`**:

```rust
fn realized_via_component(&self, cap_id) -> bool {
    for alloc in outgoing(cap_id, ALLOCATED_TO) {
        if !incoming(alloc.to_id, REALIZES).is_empty() { return true }
    }
    false
}
```

⭐ **IT ASKS WHETHER THE COMPONENT HAS ANY ARTIFACT — NOT WHETHER THE CAPABILITY DOES.** Measured over the 39 live planned capabilities holding no artifact of their own:
```
suppressed by realized_via_component ....... 34   <-- the guard
suppressed by owner_claims_built ...........  2
would actually raise the gap ...............  5
```
⇒ **IN A MATURE PROJECT EVERY COMPONENT ALREADY HAS CODE, SO EVERY NEW PLANNED CAPABILITY IS BORN PRE-SUPPRESSED.** The four captured earlier the same day prove it: `cap:init-asks-which-harness` → `cmp:packaging` (1 artifact), `cap:nudge-absence-says-why` → `cmp:packaging` + `cmp:service` (6), `cap:decomposition-coverage-is-asked` → `cmp:detect` (1), `cap:the-design-interview-precedes-the-capture` → `cmp:skills` (2). All four are `planned`, none has an artifact, **and reflow2 will never ask what gets built for any of them.**

⚠️ THE SUPPRESSION IS DELIBERATE AND WELL-ARGUED, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A DESIGN QUESTION RATHER THAN A BUG. The BL-42 comment in `detect.rs` records the reasoning: a storyflow adopt trial produced *"13 of 51 gaps, every one produced by following the adopt skill's own instruction to model artifacts coarsely over a system that is entirely built"*, and its stated bargain is *"the question is dropped and the number is kept (`realization` in `graph_report`)"*. **The guard solves the brownfield-adopt noise problem and creates the greenfield-increment blindness problem, and nothing recorded the second half.**

═══ ⚠️ A WRONG FIRST DIAGNOSIS, KEPT ON THE RECORD ═══

This session first blamed `owner_claims_built` — the guard that skips a capability whose owning Component is marked `realized`. **Measurement refuted it: only 2 of 39, and the four components involved are all `planned`, not `realized`.** The correct guard was found only by reading `realized_via_component` and counting. Recorded because the same failure — asserting a mechanism from a plausible description instead of measuring it — is the one `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` already documents twice about this project.

═══ 📌 WHAT WAS NOT CHECKED ═══

The computation predicts **5** capabilities would raise the gap; the gate reported **3** *"Nothing builds capability"* notes. The 2-item discrepancy was NOT run down — likely `is_discontinued` handling or scope filtering differing from the approximation used here (OBSOLETES targets). **The direction and magnitude of the finding do not depend on it, but the exact figure should not be quoted as though it were reconciled.** Also unchecked: whether `graph_report`'s `realization` number — the half of BL-42's bargain that was kept — is actually reachable by an agent asking what to build next.

MEASURED 2026-08-10 while starting req:what-changed-since-i-looked-and-by-whom (accepted; dev_storyflow api-boss fleet ask #3): THE CHANGE LEDGER RECORDS WHAT MOVED AND NEVER WHO MOVED IT.

    ChangeEvents in this design                     360
    ChangeEvents carrying AUTHORED_BY                 0
    changed subjects carrying AUTHORED_BY       79 of 378  (21%)
    edge types carrying a `seat` property          NONE except CLAIMS

THE REQUIREMENT ASKS FOR SOMETHING THE GRAPH CANNOT ANSWER. Its words are 'what changed since time T, AND BY WHOM - writes by OTHER SEATS over an interval'. Neither half of the who is recorded: ChangeEvents have no author at all, and seat identity (<machine>:<pid>:<mint>) lives only on CLAIMS edges, which are advisory, session-scoped and released at checkout. So even perfect authorship on ChangeEvents would answer 'which contributor', never 'which seat' - and on a shared server, which is where api-boss asked the question from, those are different questions.

WHAT EXISTS AND HOW FAR IT GETS. `changelog_view` already answers the WHAT half well: it compares two moments (Release or DesignEpoch ids), buckets the difference by rules the graph records, and returns `unmapped` rather than guessing. Its entries carry bucket, evidence, rule and subject_id - and no author. So the missing piece is exactly the who, not the what.

⚠️ WHY BUILDING THE QUERY FIRST WOULD BE WRONG. A `by` column derived from what exists would be populated for 21% of subjects and empty for the rest, and an empty cell would read as 'nobody' rather than 'not recorded' - the CANNOT-TELL-NONE-FROM-CANNOT-SAY failure this project has now met five times and names in `req:the-loop-says-what-is-owed-to-a-person`. It would look like the requirement was satisfied.

⇒ THE SUBSTRATE COMES FIRST: a ChangeEvent should carry who made it. That is a small change at every creation site and one open question - reflow2 has no notion of a CURRENT contributor, so the author must be supplied by the caller, and an optional parameter that is usually omitted reproduces the hole it was added to close. Whether attribution should be REQUIRED on a write, defaulted from a seat, or left optional is a real decision and it is the user's: making it required breaks every existing caller, and making it optional makes it decorative.

NOT A BLOCKER FOR THE WHAT HALF: `changelog_view` could be wired to this requirement as PARTIAL coverage today, honestly labelled, so the accepted intent stops reading as untouched while the who half is decided.

**ANTHONY, 2026-08-14, ON HIS WORK COMPUTER, JUST AFTER UPDATING: `● Unknown command: /capture-session`. THE SKILL EXISTS, IS SERVED, AND HAS NO COMMAND — AND THE ONE PLACE THAT CANNOT REPRODUCE THIS IS THE REPO WHERE THE DECISION WAS MADE.**

═══ MEASURED, 2026-08-14 ═══
```
getting-started/skills/     20 skills served
getting-started/commands/   11 command files
```
The eleven: `/adopt /brainstorm /debt /decisions /gaps /genesis /health /kpp /req /rules /where`.

Two of them front a TOOL, not a skill — `debt.md` calls `loop_status`, `decisions.md` queries. So **nine commands front a skill, and ELEVEN OF THE TWENTY SKILLS ARE FRONTED BY NOTHING**: capture-session, ci-gate, impact-check, ingest-corpus, link-artifacts, link-projects, parallel-work, plan-increments, report-friction, retire-from-design, revise-design.

⇒ On a consumer install those eleven are reachable only if the agent thinks to call `get_skill`. **`capture-session` is one of them, and it is the skill whose own text says the user should not have to be the trigger.**

═══ ⭐⭐ WHY NOBODY HERE COULD SEE IT ═══

Anthony, correcting this session: *"seems to work here fine, as well as /capture-intent."* **He is right, and the reason is the finding.**
```
.claude/skills/   20 directories   <- the SOURCE the binary compiles in
```
Claude Code loads a project's `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` as `/<name>`. This checkout holds all twenty **as sources**, so in reflow2's own repo every skill resolves as a slash command — including the eleven that ship with none. `/capture-intent` resolves here for that reason and cannot resolve on a consumer install, where nothing is copied (`dec:skills-served`).

**The decision's own question (`question:5aa0248a4e730d34`) asked whether commands should ship "so a consumer project gets the same ergonomics reflow2's own repo has". The repo's ergonomics come from the SKILL SOURCES, not from the commands — so the eleven were never sized against the twenty they were meant to match.** This is `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` arriving in the environment again, the same shape as the symlinked kit in `fact:updating-reflow2-does-not-update-a-project-already-set-up` and found the same day.

═══ 🛑 THE GUARD IS ASYMMETRIC, AND THAT IS WHY IT STAYED QUIET ═══

`dec:commands-are-the-exception` names ONE rot direction and closes it: *"a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that."* **The opposite direction — a skill that no command names — is checked by nothing.** Grepped `tools/test_init.py` and `tools/skill_lint.py`: no assertion pins the command count or compares the two sets, so every skill added since has shipped uncovered in silence. Nine of the eleven uncovered skills postdate the decision.

═══ 🛑 AND THE RECORD SAYS EIGHT ═══

`dec:commands-are-the-exception`, `chg:commands-ship` and `ver:install-reaches-the-agent` all say **eight** slash commands and enumerate them. **Eleven ship** — `/adopt`, `/genesis` and `/rules` were added without the record moving. Nothing pins the number, so nothing noticed.

═══ ✅ THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS SHARPER THAN EITHER HYPOTHESIS ═══

This node previously left open WHY he expected `/capture-session` there, naming two readings: he reached for a skill he knew existed, or the project predates `dec:skills-served` and carried copied skills the update pruned.

**ANTHONY, 2026-08-14: "I believe the project pre-dates the capture-session skill."** MEASURED: capture-session shipped in `4a9f4e7` (PR #163) on **2026-08-12**, released in v0.29.0 the same day.

⇒ **THE PRUNED-COPY READING IS RULED OUT FOR THIS SKILL. A project set up before 2026-08-12 never held a capture-session copy to prune — the skill did not exist when its kit was written.** So the command was never there, was never removed, and could not have resolved at any point in that project's life.

⭐⭐ **WHICH LEAVES THE FIRST READING, AND IT IS A CLEANER DEMONSTRATION OF THE BLIND SPOT THAN THE MEASUREMENT ABOVE.** He knew the skill's NAME — and the place he could have learned it is the reflow2 checkout, where `.claude/skills/capture-session/` makes it a working slash command. **The maintainer learned a skill's name in the one environment where typing it works, then typed it where it never could.** The blind spot is not only that the repo cannot reproduce the defect; it is that the repo actively TEACHES the wrong affordance.

📌 SECOND-ORDER, AND IT COMPOUNDS: a project set up before 2026-08-12 also carries a KIT from before then, so whatever commands it does have are that generation's. `fact:updating-reflow2-does-not-update-a-project-already-set-up` — the binary updates, the per-project kit does not — applies to this machine directly. `reflow2 init . --harness=claude` is what refreshes it; `ls .claude/commands` says whether `init` was ever run there at all.

properties.name: COMPOSITION, not one factory — Anthony's refinement, and skill_lint already contains the evidence: three contracts the code itself calls "the same shape" twice, and a rule the instructions apply to EVERY skill that is carried by 1 of 23 and enforced for 1 of 23
properties.statement:
ANTHONY, 2026-08-28, correcting the framing of this node: *"I didn't mean we have only one factory, I was actually thinking of multiple factories. like in python, a class can inherit a class which can inherit a class (I actually prefer class composition versus class inheritance). so a particular class of skills inherits a set of classes that determine what that skill should have. different skills inherit (or are composed) of different class attributes."*

⚠️ **THE OPTIONS ON THIS NODE ALL ASSUMED ONE FACTORY**, stamping every member of a class identically. That is not what he asked for and it is a materially weaker idea. This is option (f): COMPOSABLE ATTRIBUTE CLASSES, each skill composed of the ones it actually owes.

═══ ⭐ THE EVIDENCE IS ALREADY IN `skill_lint.py`, IN ITS OWN COMMENTS ═══

Three per-skill contracts exist — `ASK_CONTRACT`, `LINK_CONTRACT`, `OPTIMIZE_CONTRACT` — each a dict of {label: required phrase}, each bound to ONE skill by its OWN loop (lines 1015, 1031, 1042). **And the file says twice, in comments, that they are the same shape:** *"The same shape as ASK_CONTRACT above and for the same reason"* (line 679) and *"Same shape as ASK_CONTRACT and LINK_CONTRACT"* (line 719). The abstraction was NOTICED, WRITTEN DOWN, AND NOT TAKEN — three times over, in a 1,126-line file.

═══ 🛑 AND THE KILLER INSTANCE, MEASURED ═══

**"Speak the reader's domain, never reflow2's" is §35 of the SERVED INSTRUCTIONS.** It is stated as applying to every skill. Measured across the 23 SKILL.md bodies: it is carried by **ONE** (`detect-and-ask`) and enforced by **ONE** contract (`ASK_CONTRACT`, where it was added 2026-08-19 after two users independently invented the same workaround of asking the agent to drop reflow2's jargon).

**A universal rule, implemented once, enforced once, discovered late.** That is the cycle this idea exists to break, and it is not hypothetical.

═══ ⭐⭐ WHY COMPOSITION ANSWERS COUNTERWEIGHT 1, WHICH ONE FACTORY DOES NOT ═══

This node's strongest objection is that *"a factory guarantees the mechanics are PRESENT, never that they are RIGHT"* — force a section into 23 skills and get 23 sections written to satisfy a linter. `fact:skill-mechanics-track-enforcement-exactly-and-they-split-into-three-kinds` measured that the mechanics divide into BOILERPLATE (presence is correctness), JUDGEMENT (presence is not), and TOOL-SIDE (not in the skill at all).

**Composition dissolves the objection for the JUDGEMENT class.** A single factory must demand "honest limits" of all 23, where 15 of them would produce filler. Composition demands it only of the skills that compose a MEASURES attribute — the five that actually measure something — where the section is meaningful and its absence is a real omission. **The manufactured-ambiguity trap comes from UNIFORMITY, not from construction.**

═══ CANDIDATE ATTRIBUTE CLASSES, derived from the 23 skills rather than invented ═══

Offered as a starting point, not a taxonomy: STANDING (the graph-text-is-data rule — the only one at 23/23, and already the base class in effect); WRITES (search before create, typed constructors, loop debt before finishing); REVISES (snapshot before edit — the mechanic skipped twice in this very session); REPORTS (speak the reader's domain, never paste raw ids, say what is withheld); MEASURES (bound the claim, state n, say what could not be established); DESTROYS (name what would be lost, require a human read before applying).

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: the six classes above are this agent's reading of 23 skills and nobody has tested that they carve cleanly — a skill belonging to four of them is a sign the carving is wrong. Whether the mechanism should be a Python composition in `skill_lint`, a declaration in each SKILL.md's frontmatter, or something in the build is UNCHOSEN and they have different costs. And the over-engineering counterweight on this node still stands in full: a class taxonomy is exactly the shape an engineer reaches for, and the measured alternative — one exhaustive check per class — is fifteen lines.

properties.statement: A CONSUMER'S NUMBER-ONE ASK IS MISDIAGNOSED, AND BUILDING IT WOULD CHANGE NOTHING. Alex's fleet (Grok Build harness, binary 0.24.0) filed a report on 2026-08-09 whose top-priority item is 'read-after-write for the creating session', from a real and repeatable symptom: immediately after a successful `add_decision`, a `set_decision_status` on the same id fails with `Node not found`, and a sequential retry succeeds. THE SYMPTOM IS REAL. THE CAUSE IS NOT WHAT THEY THINK. Read-after-write ALREADY HOLDS and cannot be the problem: `add_decision` takes an exclusive `write_lock()` (capture.rs:620), performs the write, and the guard drops before the response is returned, so any later lock acquisition sees the node. There is no visibility window to close. WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING is in their own environment notes: 'heavy parallel tool calls in a single agent turn'. Fire `add_decision` and `set_decision_status` concurrently and NOTHING ORDERS THEM. The RwLock serialises ACCESS, not INTENT — so `set_decision_status` can legitimately win the lock first, at which instant the node genuinely does not exist and `Node not found` is the correct answer. 'Retrying sequentially usually succeeds' is consistent with both readings, which is why the misdiagnosis is easy; the tell is that it reproduces ONLY in parallel batches. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE BUG: their asks #1 and #2 are the same problem, and only #2 works. #1 (read-after-write) would be engineering effort spent making true something that is already true. #2 (optional `status` on `add_decision`) FIXES IT COMPLETELY, by collapsing two order-dependent calls into one that cannot be misordered. So the correct response to their highest-priority ask is to DROP IT and build their second. THE GENERAL FIX IS A DESCRIPTION, NOT A FEATURE: no tool description says that parallel batches carry no ordering, or that a create-then-modify pair must be sequenced. That is their section 1.2 ('parallel multi-write batches are fragile') and it is the honest root of both items. SAME SHAPE AS THIS WEEK'S OTHER FINDINGS: a caller cannot distinguish 'the write is not visible yet' from 'the write has not happened yet', and the surface never told them which world they are in — the same family as a value that cannot tell a choice from a default. NOT VERIFIED BY EXECUTION HERE: the mechanism was read from the code rather than reproduced with a concurrent client, so this is an analysis-grade finding. A reproduction would be two overlapping tool calls against one server asserting the failure disappears when they are sequenced.

properties.name: THE SWEEP'S ANSWER: only 5 of 191 open defect-facts were fixed-but-unclosed — the backlog is REAL, not bookkeeping residue, and option (d)'s premise is FALSE at scale
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-28 over the committed export, answering the question dec:idea-what-makes-a-field-report-owed named as the one that must be settled BEFORE choosing a remedy: 'How many of the 189 are actually live?'

THE ANSWER: almost all of them. 192 TemporalFacts carry fact_type=defect; 191 had no inbound INVALIDATES at sweep start. A text scan found fix-language anywhere in 28 of the 191. Reading those 28 in context rather than trusting the keyword — the discipline fact:a-findings-name-can-claim-more-than-its-data demands — only about 10 declare THEIR OWN closure, and only 5 had a ChangeEvent recording the work that did it. Those 5 are now closed with edges: bl-105, bl-217, the lost identity sidecar, set_verification_status erasing last_run_at, and the gate crashing on a directory artifact.

⭐⭐ SO OPTION (d) IS REFUTED AS A REMEDY, THOUGH IT WAS RIGHT AS A FIRST MOVE. Its premise was 'much of the 189 is surely fixed with nobody having drawn the edge'. That was true for 5 of 191 — 2.6%. Sweeping does NOT leave a backlog small enough to read without machinery, and any debt class designed on the assumption that the raw count is inflated by bookkeeping would be designed against a number that is very nearly the real one.

⭐ THE SECOND FINDING, AND IT EXPLAINS THE 8-EDGE TOTAL: THE CLOSURE CONVENTION HAS BEEN PROSE INSIDE THE FACT, NOT AN EDGE. The closed records were REWRITTEN in place — they open 'CLOSED 2026-08-07, same day, by...' or 'FIXED 2026-08-09.' and several then carry '--- ORIGINAL RECORD FOLLOWS ---'. A human reading the fact knows it is closed; no computation does. So the loop was not failing to record closures. It was recording them somewhere nothing can read, which is the same shape as fact:the-upstream-watch-is-findable-only-in-reflow2s-own-words.

⚠️ TWO CLASSES THE SWEEP COULD NOT CLOSE, AND BOTH ARE HONEST REFUSALS RATHER THAN OMISSIONS:
- FIXED ON MAIN, NOT YET RELEASED (fact:defect-create-node-merge-versus-replace-is-fixed-but-unreleased, fact:defect-loop-status-next-routes-to-the-destructive-skill). The code is right and every consumer still hits the bug. Closing these would tell a user running a release that their live defect is stale. Left open deliberately; this is a judgement for Anthony, not a bookkeeping call.
- SELF-CORRECTED IN PLACE, NOTHING TO POINT FROM (fact:defect-documented-hook-path-may-not-exist, fact:defect-set-artifact-checksums-accepts-a-malformed-digest). Both were MISDIAGNOSES — the reported harm does not occur — corrected by measurement written into the same node. There is no ChangeEvent because no code changed, and minting a node purely to host an edge would be bureaucracy. The convention has no answer for a finding that was simply wrong.

⭐ AND THE RECORDS ARE MORE DISCIPLINED THAN THE RAW COUNT SUGGESTS. At least six say plainly why they stay open: 'Left OPEN rather than closed, because only half of it moved'; 'Closing it here would report a class as fixed on the evidence of one case'; 'NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately'. Nobody has been letting fixed things rot on the list. The list is long because the work is genuinely undone.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: whether the ~181 still-open items are individually still true. This sweep measured which records CLAIM their own closure, not which defects a fresh test would still reproduce. Establishing that means re-running each against current code, which nobody has done and which this fact must not be read as having done.

properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-12, twice in one session. `cap:degraded-surface` is VERIFIED and this does NOT falsify it — the capability did exactly what it promises. What this records is that its diagnosis CANNOT REACH a whole class of caller.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED: `tools/reflow2_cli.py` began answering `error: set_artifact_checksum: tool not found` for a tool that plainly exists and had worked minutes earlier. The natural reading is that the tool was renamed or removed. Both readings are wrong.

THE MECHANISM, traced rather than guessed. A `--serve-shared` daemon (pid 728580) held the store's write lock — confirmed with `fuser .reflow2/graph/LOCK`. A second server could not open the store, so it correctly served the DEGRADED SURFACE: a handshake plus exactly one tool, `reflow2_unavailable`, whose name is the diagnosis, with the translated reason in the server instructions, the remedies in the tool payload, and an explicit do-not-conclude-reflow2-is-missing. All of that was built, and all of it was present.

⇒ AND NONE OF IT WAS SEEN, because the caller never asked for it. The CLI goes straight to `tools/call` by NAME. rmcp's tool router then answers `invalid_params("tool not found")` — rmcp-2.2.0 `handler/server/router/tool.rs:567`, a generic string with no context, not reflow2's text at all. The CLI printed it faithfully. THE DIAGNOSIS LIVES IN THE HANDSHAKE AND THE TOOL LIST, AND A BY-NAME CALLER READS NEITHER.

So the careful part — "do not conclude reflow2 is missing" — was rendered as, precisely, "this tool does not exist". The capability's own stated purpose is that the server explains its own absence instead of vanishing; against a direct caller it vanishes.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE CLI: any client that caches a tool list, or that calls by name from a script, is in this class. The degraded surface is reachable only by a client that re-reads the surface after failing — which is the client least likely to be a script.

FIX DIRECTION, NOT DECIDED: the refusal for an unknown tool name is rmcp's, so reflow2 cannot reword it in place. Either the CLI re-reads `tools/list` on any `tool not found` and surfaces `reflow2_unavailable` if that is all there is, or the degraded server declines the call in a way that carries its own text. The first is cheap, local, and needs no upstream change.

NOTE ON THE LOCK ITSELF: this is NOT `fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server`, which is a deleted-inode spawn failure. Different cause, and that one is fixed. This is ordinary single-writer contention behaving as designed, reported unrecognisably.

MEASURED 2026-08-21. The same structural blind spot was found in THREE INDEPENDENT PLACES in one day, and that it arose independently is the finding rather than the coincidence.

THE SHAPE, stated once: a computation that takes THE DESIGN as its only input can report on what the design mentions and on nothing else. Absence is then unreportable BY CONSTRUCTION, not by oversight — no amount of care in writing the check helps, because the missing thing never enters the data structure.

THE THREE:

  1. `arrival_delta` decided delivery by looking for an Artifact. Work whose deliverable was a DESIGN CHANGE had no file to find, so an epoch with both capabilities genuinely delivered reported both `outstanding` — a false statement about finished work, re-asked on every run. Fixed by Capability.delivery (#268).

  2. `tools/wall_check.py` walked component -> files from REALIZES. A file nobody registered never entered the map, so it could not be reported — while the tool's own headline number, '64 of 73 mapped', read as a coverage story. FIFTEEN real source modules sat outside the model, including one (skills_tools) that this agent had itself skipped while modelling its eleven siblings. Fixed by deriving the walk roots FROM THE CLAIMED PATHS, which keeps the no-configuration property.

  3. `tools/reflow2_check.py`, the CI gate, builds its observation list with `for art in artifacts` and never walks the disk; `reconcile_artifacts` does no file I/O at all. `undocumented_addition` was therefore a drift kind THE GATE STRUCTURALLY COULD NOT PRODUCE — add a file, commit, push, and every check stayed green. Fixed the same way, as a NOTE rather than a failure.

WHY IT IS ONE FINDING AND NOT THREE BUGS: nobody copied the mistake between them. Three different authors' code, three different purposes, converging on the same stance because reading from the graph is the natural way to write a check in this system — and it is the stance that cannot see absence. A fourth instance should be expected wherever a new check is written, and the question that catches it is: WHAT IS THIS CHECK'S ONLY INPUT, AND WHAT CAN THAT INPUT NEVER MENTION?

DISTINCT FROM `fact:ten-components-report-a-zero-blast-radius-the-source-contradicts` (2026-08-20), which named the same stance in the DETECTORS. What today adds is that it is not a detector property: it reached an INSTRUMENT and a GATE, which are different code with different authors. It is an architectural stance of the product, not a defect class in one subsystem.

WHAT IT COSTS AN ARBITRARY USER'S PROJECT: every reassuring number reflow2 gives about coverage, cycles or blast radius is computed over what the user already told it. A project that has modelled half its code gets confident answers about that half and silence about the rest, with nothing distinguishing the two.

MEASURED 2026-08-09 by READING dev_storyflow's committed export (1,373 nodes, 2,570 edges, stamp 0.26.1) at Anthony's direction. READ ONLY — nothing was written to storyflow, and `describe_designs` was used first precisely because it reads the sidecar without opening the store.

ANTHONY PREDICTED IT BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT: "I can almost already tell you that reflow2 does not interface with dynograph-foundation the same way that storyflow interfaces with dynograph-foundation." **CONFIRMED, AND THE SHAPE IS MORE USEFUL THAN THE PREDICTION.**

=== THE TWO CONSUMERS USE DIFFERENT SURFACES THROUGH DIFFERENT TRANSPORTS ===

reflow2 (projectB) consumes dynograph as a **RUST LIBRARY API**, five `required` interfaces:
  ifc:req-dyno-core-api        Core model types (Schema, Value, DynoError)
  ifc:req-dyno-graph-api       Graph algorithms API
  ifc:req-dyno-storage-api     StorageEngine Rust API
  ifc:req-dyno-resolution-api  EntityResolver API
  ifc:req-dyno-vector-api      Vector, HNSW and statistics API

storyflow (projectD) consumes it as a **REST API OVER HTTP**:
  ifc:dynograph_api                      DynoGraph (dag_plus) REST API
  ifc:dynograph_temporal_api             temporal endpoints
  ifc:dynograph_inferences               generic inference-edge endpoint
  ifc:dynograph_relationships_catalog    relationships catalog endpoint
  ifc:dynograph_apply_fixes              apply-fixes proposal-batch contract
  ifc:foundation_api                     Foundation engine API

⭐⭐ SO THE DIAMOND DOES NOT MEET AT AN INTERFACE. IT MEETS AT DYNOGRAPH'S INTERNALS. Two consumers, two DISJOINT surfaces, one shared implementation beneath both. That reframes the risk rather than dissolving it: a change confined to the Rust crate API cannot touch storyflow's REST endpoints, and a change to the engine BENEATH both touches everything — and **neither consumer's graph can see that layer at all**, because each declares only the surface it personally uses.

⇒ THE CHECK THAT WOULD ACTUALLY HAVE ANSWERED THE 2026 INCIDENT is therefore NOT "do B and D require the same interface" — they do not, and a naive diamond detector would have reported all-clear. It is "**did the change reach below both published surfaces into shared implementation**", which is a question about A's OWN internal structure and is answerable only inside A's graph.

=== ⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE IS UNDONE ON D'S SIDE ===

**storyflow declares ZERO `required` interfaces.** 53 Interfaces: 44 `internal`, 9 `unset`, 0 `required`, 0 `published`. That is EXACTLY the state reflow2 was in on 2026-08-06, before PR #130 — and `dec:linked-repos-poc` named it then: "the linking works, the labelling does not exist." **The labelling now exists on B's side and not on D's, so the seam is still one-ended and nothing pairs.** Declaring dynograph's endpoints `required` in storyflow is the cheapest possible next step and it is entirely inside a graph Anthony owns.

=== 🔴 AND AN OBSTACLE TO COMPOSITION THAT NOBODY HAS NAMED ===

`describe_designs` reports BOTH stores with **`graph_id: "reflow2"`** — storyflow's design is LABELLED `dev_storyflow` but carries the same graph_id as reflow2's. This is `rule:no-foreclosure` clause (5) observed in the field: "graph_id already exists on every node and edge and is PINNED TO A CONSTANT; code that assumes the constant rather than reading the field is the foreclosure." **Composing two designs whose nodes both claim graph_id "reflow2" is a collision waiting to happen**, and every cross-project mechanism in `dec:idea-a-change-upstream-reaches-the-sibling-that-never-asked` and `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` runs through composition. `label` distinguishes them; `graph_id` does not.

📝 ALSO OBSERVED, unprompted and relevant to the projectE question: storyflow carries `ifc:embeddings_api` ("Embeddings REST API"), so D already declares a dependency on the embeddings service. Whether that is Anthony's `embeddings-rs` is NOT established here and is not assumed.

BOUND: this reads storyflow's COMMITTED EXPORT, not its live store (the store is not present at that path — `describe_designs` reported "identity recorded, but the store itself is not here"). If storyflow's live graph has moved since its last export, these counts are stale by that much.

OBSERVED ACROSS ONE FULL SESSION, 2026-08-17, and recorded because the instances are already in the graph separately and the PATTERN is not. FOUR TIMES IN ONE DAY, THE FAILURE WAS THE SAME: A FACT WAS ASSERTED WHERE IT COULD HAVE BEEN COUNTED. Measurement caught it every time, and in three of the four the assertion had already been acted on.

(1) RELAYED A FALSE CLAIM FROM AN INSTRUMENT. `loop_status` said an answered question had never reached the design; it had been there, accepted and approver-signed, since 2026-08-11. Told to the user as fact before the graph was checked. Cost: a wrong opening summary. → `fact:defect-loop-status-asserts-an-answer-never-reached-the-design-from-a-fact-that-cannot-say-so`

(2) DECIDED AGAINST A FIX ON AN UNMEASURED COST. Declined to rename `disconnected_community` because it would "break every consumer". Measured afterwards: 14 code files, 6 docs, PERSISTED AS DATA NOWHERE — no migration existed to protect against. Cost: shipped a half-fix that had to be reversed hours later. → `dec:a-misnaming-is-fixed-in-the-message-not-the-key`

(3) WROTE AN UNCHECKED CLAIM ABOUT A CHECK. A doc comment said the compiler enforced that `HealCategory::ALL` lists every variant. It does not. Caught before commit by re-reading rather than by anything mechanical. Cost: none, and only because it was noticed. → `cap:a-sweep-names-its-own-scope-and-the-category-names-what-it-computes`

(4) ALMOST PROPOSED A DETECTOR ON PLAUSIBILITY. Oscillation detection looked obviously buildable. Counting first showed only 23 of 187 artifacts carry any checksum history and 3 have more than one prior value, because `design_holds` accepts do not snapshot. The detector would have reported zero forever and been believed. Cost: none — the measurement happened before the proposal. → `dec:idea-an-artifact-whose-checksum-returns-is-an-agent-going-in-circles`

⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it is why this is worth a node rather than an apology. An asserted cost that STOPS work is nearly invisible when it is wrong, because nothing happens and there is no failure to notice — instance (2) would have stood indefinitely if the user had not stated a rule that forced the question. An asserted claim that DRIVES work usually gets caught by the work failing. So the dangerous direction is the one that argues for inaction, and it is the direction with no natural feedback.

⇒ WHY IT BELONGS BESIDE THIS RULE: `rule:fix-it-properly-while-it-is-still-cheap` already carries "MEASURE THE COST BEFORE LETTING IT DECIDE" as a clause, derived from instance (2) alone. Three further instances in the same day say that clause is the load-bearing half of the rule rather than an aside, and that it generalises past cost to any claim an agent uses to close a question.

📌 AND IT IS DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE AGENT-PITFALL WORK opened the same day (`dec:idea-which-agent-pitfalls-can-reflow2-actually-reach`). None of the four is on the user's pitfall list, and they are not code-writing failures — they are DESIGN-REASONING failures, committed while using the design brain. That may be a class the list does not cover.

⚠️ ONE LOOSE END FROM THE SAME SESSION THAT WAS NOT RESOLVED, recorded here because it is the one thing that could NOT be measured and therefore stayed open. `reflow2_check.py` printed "FAILED — 1 finding" once, immediately after an export that carried a `sync_note` about the file having moved, and then returned OK on four consecutive runs against the committed file with both CI jobs green. The failing finding was never captured — it was chained behind a `;` with a push and scrolled past. LOW CONFIDENCE, NOT REPRODUCED, and possibly a transient of the export's own sync bookkeeping rather than a real drift. Recorded so a later session meeting the same thing knows it has been seen once and never explained.

MEASURED from the committed export: reflow2 declares EIGHT subsystems (`sys:agent-surface`, `sys:coherence-loop`, `sys:documentation`, `sys:human-channel`, `sys:intake`, `sys:store`, `sys:time-history`, `sys:vocabulary`) and NOT ONE OF THEM PROVIDES AN INTERFACE.

  subsystem            contains  PROVIDES  CONSUMES
  sys:agent-surface       5         -         -
  sys:coherence-loop     18         -         -
  sys:documentation       1         -         -
  sys:human-channel       2         -         -
  sys:intake              3         -         -
  sys:store               4         -         2
  sys:time-history        5         -         -
  sys:vocabulary          4         -         -

ZERO of eight provide; ONE of eight consumes anything, and both of its consumed interfaces are external (`ifc:exclusive-local-store`, `ifc:req-dyno-storage-api`) rather than a seam with a sibling subsystem. EVERY interface in the design is provided by a LEAF component one level down — `cmp:service` (ifc:mcp-tools, ifc:mcp-tools-http), `cmp:graph` (ifc:core-api), `cmp:export` (ifc:graph-export), `cmp:main` (ifc:rendezvous-sidecar), `cmp:registry` (ifc:session-graph-selector).

WHAT THAT MEANS, in the systems-engineering sense Anthony raised: the eight are GROUPINGS, not black boxes. A black box is defined by its boundary — you can say what it offers and what it needs without opening it. Here you cannot say either for seven of the eight, so the decomposition carries no interface contract at any level above the leaves. `granularity_report` and `seam_report` have nothing to read at the subsystem tier.

RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS THE BASELINE for a future increment doing proper SE on reflow2 itself, and because the number is the argument: 0/8 is not 'some interfaces are missing', it is 'the tier has no contracts at all'.

properties.name: The exhaustive check was BUILT and IS RUNNING over every skill — and it structurally cannot express a per-CLASS obligation, which is exactly why Artifact had a mechanic the others did not
properties.statement:
CHECKED 2026-08-28 against source, because Anthony asked whether the exhaustive check had actually been tried or only discussed: *"haven't we tried the exhaustive check already (I might be mistaken)?"*

**HE IS NOT MISTAKEN. IT EXISTS, IT IS IMPLEMENTED, AND IT RUNS OVER EVERY SKILL.** `HealCategory::ALL` with its exhaustive-match tests in `crates/reflow2-core/src/heal.rs`; dozens of `every_*` tests across the core test suite; and for skills specifically, `crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/served_skills.rs` iterates `SKILLS` three separate times while `tools/skill_lint.py` walks every skill directory.

═══ ⭐⭐ AND THAT IS WHY IT DID NOT CATCH THE ARTIFACT CASE ═══

**EVERY EXHAUSTIVE SKILL CHECK ASSERTS A UNIVERSAL PREDICATE.** Read from source: byte-identical to its kit source; has a non-empty description; appears in the served catalogue; states the graph-text-is-data rule; references only tools that exist; mirrors match across the three trees. Each is true-of-all-skills by construction.

**A flat loop over a flat set can only carry an obligation that applies to every member.** It has no vocabulary for *"this skill owes REPORTS mechanics and that one does not"*. So the exhaustive check did not fail — it succeeded completely, at its own scope, which is why the one universal mechanic sits at 23/23 while every other sits between 5 and 18.

═══ THE THREE TIERS, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS WHERE THE PAIN IS ═══

    UNIVERSAL obligation   → exhaustive loop            → WORKS. 23/23.
    PER-SKILL obligation   → 3 hand-written contracts   → N edits; the file itself
                                                          notes TWICE they are
                                                          "the same shape"
    PER-CLASS obligation   → NOTHING EXISTS             → Artifact's mechanic
                                                          never propagated

`ASK_CONTRACT`, `LINK_CONTRACT` and `OPTIMIZE_CONTRACT` are composition attempted by copy-paste: the right idea, expressed by duplication, bound to one skill each by its own loop.

═══ ⭐ THE MOSA ARGUMENT, WHICH IS ANTHONY'S AND IS SOUND ═══

*"I also feel like it fits the MOSA type concept better than exhaustive checks."* It does, and the reason is structural rather than aesthetic: a MOSA module is SEVERABLE and meets a stated INTERFACE, so it can be composed selectively, replaced, or upgraded without touching its neighbours. **An exhaustive check has neither property** — it is one monolithic predicate over the whole population, cannot be applied to a subset, and cannot be replaced for one member without weakening it for all. `dec:mosa-conformance` already asks whether reflow2 should report MOSA conformance given it computes most of the criteria; this is the same concept turned inward on reflow2's own skill surface.

═══ ON DEPENDENCY INJECTION IN RUST — IT IS ALREADY IN THIS CODEBASE ═══

*"potentially using dependency injection if that can be done in rust"*. It can, and it is not a new pattern here. **Rust has NO inheritance at all**, so composition via traits is the only idiom available — his stated preference is what the language forces. And the project already does constructor injection: `KvBackend` is a six-method trait with two implementations (`RocksBackend`, `MemoryBackend`) held as `Box<dyn KvBackend>` inside `StorageEngine`. The pattern he is describing for skills is the one already load-bearing under the store.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that composition is worth its cost here. It establishes only that the exhaustive check was genuinely tried, works at its scope, and cannot reach per-class obligations — so "just add an exhaustive check" is not an available answer to the Artifact case. The over-engineering counterweight on the parent node stands, and where the composition would LIVE (skill_lint, SKILL.md frontmatter, or the Rust build) is unchosen with materially different costs.

properties.statement: THE ONE CALL EVERY INSTRUCTION FILE TELLS A SESSION TO MAKE FIRST COULD NOT BE MADE AT ALL ON A MATURE DESIGN. Unscoped `detect_gaps` on reflow2's own graph (2,920 nodes, 77 open gaps) serialized to 79,566 characters and went out TWICE — once as `structuredContent` and once as a text `content` block — for 157,785 bytes on the wire, which the harness refused outright. ⇒ THE FAILURE IS INVISIBLE TO REFLOW2: the refusal happens in the CLIENT, so the session sees a wall of harness text and reflow2 never gets to suggest `scope`. That is the whole shape of it — the thing that knows how to narrow is the one thing that cannot speak. || WHAT THE REPLY WAS MADE OF, and it is not what the guess would be: 35% affected_ids, 25% description, 18% evidence, 15% title. Almost all of the id lists sat in THREE rollup gaps — one enumerating 468 ChangeEvents whose own title already read '468 of 605'. So capping the id lists alone took it only to 60,437 and did not fit; only dropping the prose (to 22,194) got under any cap worth the name. || THE CLAIM THAT WAS ALREADY IN THE GRAPH: `cap:bounded-reads` — 'a read that would not fit answers with a bounded page and says what it left out' — has read `verified` since 2026-07-25. Its check, `ver:bounded-reads`, drives `scan_nodes` paging. It was true of what it covered and silent about the call the loop orbits. || TWO CONSEQUENCES FOUND ONLY BY FIXING IT. (1) `reflow2_check.py` decided a gap was ANCHORED by `affected_ids` being non-empty, and only an anchored gap fails a build — so a budgeted reply would have turned the gate GREEN on a design full of critical gaps, more reliably the bigger the design got. Reproduced: 100 unsatisfied critical requirements, gate printed 'OK — design and build agree (103 notes)'. (2) The Python clients' envelope unwrap took anything carrying `count` and `items` and returned the list, which had ALREADY been silently discarding `scan_nodes`' own `omitted` and `capped_by` — the 'what I left out' a bounded read exists to report, thrown away before any reader saw it. || SIBLINGS, SAME SHAPE, STILL OPEN: `graph_report` refused at 88,932 and 91,330 chars (`fact:defect-graph-report-outgrows-its-own-reply-linearly`), `loop_status` measured at 72,886, `detect_defects` unbudgeted at 50 findings. || SOURCE: measured here 2026-08-23 on reflow2 0.38.0, driving the built binary over real stdio.

properties.name: The first store-touching call of a session costs 26-48 s; a full export of the same store costs 2.1 s
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-21 while looking for something to optimise on the PRODUCT surface rather than the developer surface. This is the largest cost a user of reflow2 pays and nothing in the design mentioned it.

    open_questions    70 s   <- the SessionStart hook instructs every agent to call this FIRST
    loop_status       60 s   <- the server's own instructions call it "the one cheap call"
    graph_report      34-40 s
    detect_defects    33 s
    detect_gaps        3.2 s
    everything else  < 0.5 s

Two independent runs, consistent to within a second. **The call every session is told to make first costs a minute.**

⭐ IT IS ONE COST, PAID ONCE, NOT A COST PER CALL. The first store-touching call of a process pays it; every call afterwards — including the first call of a DIFFERENT node type — returns in 0.01-3 s. `scan_nodes(node_type: Question, limit: 5)` took 47.9 s and returned 8 KB; the same call immediately after took 0.02 s.

🛑 AND IT IS NOT THE DATA. A direct `--export`, which opens the store and reads every node and edge, takes **2.1 s** on the same 77 MB store. So the ~26-48 s is not RocksDB, not the volume, and not the disk.

TWO HYPOTHESES WERE FALSIFIED FIRST, both on a COPY of the store rather than the live one, which made the experiments free:
  (1) "It is the 999 LOG.old.* files." With them 2.07 s, without them 2.10 s. Falsified in thirty seconds.
  (2) "It is a stale rendezvous left by --stop-shared." On a pristine copy with no daemon and no rendezvous the first read still cost **26.3 s**. So ~26 s is INHERENT cold start; the ~48 s seen on the live store had roughly 20 s of stale-record timeout on top.

⭐⭐ THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT CRACKED IT, worth more than the finding: **47.91 s and 47.99 s across two runs is a TIMER, NOT WORK.** Real work varies with cache state and load; two runs agreeing to within 0.08 s means something is WAITING. That pointed at `READY_TIMEOUT` (30 s) and `RESPAWN_AFTER` (6 s) in shared.rs rather than at any algorithm.

WHERE THE REMAINING ~24 s LIVES, narrowed but NOT PROVEN: the gap between `--export` at 2.1 s and daemon startup at 26 s is whatever the server does that the exporter does not. shared.rs names the candidate in its own comment — "a cold daemon opens RocksDB and builds the full-text index, which on a large design is seconds, not milliseconds". A `fulltext` directory exists in the store (1.6 MB, 14 files), so something is persisted; whether it is rebuilt anyway, or validated, was not established.

📌 WHY NO TEST COULD HAVE FOUND THIS. The suite constructs graphs with `open_in_memory` and never opens the on-disk daemon path at all. 1393 tests pass in 96.5 s and not one of them touches the thing every real session waits a minute for. **The developer surface and the product surface were measured on the same day and were not the same system.**

🅿️ DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED. No budget has been stated for it, and the `optimize` skill written the same day says the budget comes before the code. This node is the measurement half; the target is owed.

CENSUS OF ANTHONY'S FIVE PROJECTS, 2026-08-09, via `describe_designs` — which reads only the sidecar beside each store, opens nothing, takes no lock and writes nothing. READ ONLY.

  project                     graph_id                label              minted_by   stamp
  A dynograph-foundation      dynograph-foundation    dynograph-foundation  0.16.0    0.16.0  (56 edge / 28 node types)
  B reflow2                   reflow2                 reflow2               0.13.0    0.26.1  (61 / 29)
  C flo2                      1a97fc1f1de4d5d2        flo2                  0.24.0    0.26.1  (60 / 29)
  D dev_storyflow             reflow2   ⚠️            dev_storyflow         0.14.0    0.26.1  (61 / 29)
  E embeddings-rs             —                       —                     —         ABSENT

=== ✅ PROJECT E IS NOT A REFLOW2 PROJECT — the open question is answered ===

Anthony was unsure ("technically, there is a projectE (embeddings-rs, though I'm not sure yet if this is a reflow2 project)"). MEASURED: the `.reflow2` directory EXISTS and `describe_designs` reports `state: absent` — "no design here." So it is OPTED IN AND EMPTY: somebody created the directory and no design was ever started. That is a distinct state from both "is a reflow2 project" and "is not one", and reflow2 reports it precisely because opening the store to find out would MINT an identity and make the answer true by asking.

⚠️ AND STORYFLOW ALREADY DECLARES `ifc:embeddings_api` ("Embeddings REST API"), so D depends on an embeddings service that has no design at all. Whether that service IS embeddings-rs is still not established.

=== 🔴 THREE IDENTITY CONVENTIONS ACROSS FOUR GRAPHS, AND ONE OUTRIGHT COLLISION ===

- `dynograph-foundation` — graph_id equals the label. The convention working.
- `flo2` — graph_id is a MINTED HASH `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2`, label `flo2`. Different convention, and it is the one `minted` origin among four.
- **`dev_storyflow` carries graph_id `reflow2` — THE SAME ID AS REFLOW2 ITSELF.** Two distinct designs, one id.

⇒ This is exactly the Contributor-fork defect found earlier today (`ctr:anthony` / `who:ajs`) ONE LEVEL UP: **the field whose entire purpose is identity is the one nothing checks for duplicate identity.** It is also `rule:no-foreclosure` clause (5) in the field. Every cross-project mechanism in `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` and `dec:idea-a-change-upstream-reaches-the-sibling-that-never-asked` runs through composition, and **composition cannot tell B's nodes from D's by graph_id.** `label` distinguishes them; the id does not.

=== ⚠️⚠️ THE PROJECT AT THE BOTTOM OF THE STACK HAS THE STALEST DESIGN ===

**dynograph-foundation's graph was written by reflow2 0.16.0 and has not moved since — roughly ELEVEN releases behind the 0.27.0 cut today.** Its stamp holds 56 edge types and 28 node types against the current 61 and 29. It predates `OWNED_BY`, `GATED_ON`, `HAS_READINESS`, `SCHEDULED_FOR`, `CALIBRATED_AGAINST` and the whole `ReadinessAssessment` type.

THE SHAPE IS THE FINDING: **A is what B, C and D all rest on, and A is the least-maintained design of the four.** Every consumer's graph is current; the thing they depend on is a year of releases behind in design terms. And the practical consequence bites immediately on the question Anthony asked — filing a proposed requirement INTO A's graph with a 0.27.0 binary will MOVE A'S STAMP from 0.16.0 to 0.27.0, which is a real and irreversible side effect of what looks like a read-mostly act of filing an issue.

BOUND: `describe_designs` deliberately reports NO node counts, because counting means opening, and opening mints an identity where there is none. So this census says what each design IS, never how big it is. D's and A's contents are known here only from their committed exports, not their live stores.

⭐ THE GATES CAUGHT THIS AGENT SIX TIMES IN ONE SESSION, AND FIVE WERE TWO HABITS REPEATING. Recorded because the *pattern* is the finding — the individual slips are each in their own commit and recoverable from the diff.

    HABIT A — gating BEFORE committing, then trusting the result   3 times
      `rule:a-gate-is-run-against-the-state-it-will-be-judged-in` says the export
      gate must run AFTER the commit. Run before, it judges the previous commit
      against a moved working tree and returns a verdict about neither.

    HABIT B — chaining gates and a push in ONE shell command             2 times
      `for c in ...; do ...; done; git push` pushes whatever the loop found.
      Both times a FAIL scrolled past and the push happened anyway. The second
      time was AFTER the first had been noticed and named.

    Plus: settling two Decisions with an `author` edge and no `approver`, caught
    by the intent-authority gate in CI.

🛑 **THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART IS HABIT B REPEATING AFTER IT WAS NAMED.** The agent wrote out the lesson in prose, then made the same shell construction twenty minutes later. **A lesson recorded in conversation does not change the next command; a gate does.** That is the same finding as four DesignRules being broken by an agent that had all nineteen available and never opened them — and it is the argument for `rule:an-issue-is-root-caused-then-pinned-by-a-test-then-fixed` step ② being a TEST rather than a note.

⭐ WHAT WORKED, AND IT IS THE DESIGN WORKING AS INTENDED: every one of the six was caught by machinery, none by memory. The intent-authority gate refused a forged-looking settlement twice. The lineage check refused a broken chain three times. The duplicate guard refused four near-duplicate writes, three of which were genuinely distinct and were recorded as such with `distinct_from`. The export's divergence guard refused a write that would have dropped 18 edges — which were the 18 the session had deliberately deleted, read back and confirmed before overriding.

📌 THE ASYMMETRY WORTH KEEPING: the agent's OWN commands produced the false greens (piped exit codes, `sort | head` hiding failures, `pgrep` matching its own wrapper, a wait-loop exiting on an empty check list). **reflow2's tools produced none of them.** Every reflow2 refusal in this session was correct and every reflow2 acceptance was earned. The instrument was not the problem; the hands were.

properties.statement:
🔎 **ROOT CAUSE FOUND FOR A FAILURE THIS PROJECT HAS BEEN WORKING AROUND SINCE 2026-08-14: `gh` IS A SNAP.**

Anthony, 2026-08-19: *"I'm not sure if this is really a reflow2 thing (maybe it is part of the governance components?) or an agent thing, but I feel like every time we do a tag/release, I see this again (which means we are not capturing failures as feedback)."*

**IT IS NEITHER.** Measured on the dev box the same day:
  · `/snap/bin/gh -> /usr/bin/snap` — gh is snap-packaged (2.74.0, rev 640).
  · Snap confinement gives it its own sandboxed git WITHOUT the `remote-https` helper, which is why gh's LOCAL post-merge sync dies with `git: 'remote-https' is not a git command`.
  · The SYSTEM git is fine: 2.43.0, `/usr/lib/git-core/git-remote-https` present, and `git ls-remote https://...` succeeds under a minimal env. Every `git push`/`git pull` this session worked.

⇒ **A ONE-TIME FIX EXISTS: install `gh` from the official apt repository instead of snap.** Nine years of workaround discipline is not required for a packaging choice.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐ HIS SECOND CLAIM WAS HALF RIGHT, AND THE HALF THAT IS RIGHT IS THE USEFUL ONE.

**WRONG — the failure IS captured**, and richly: `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` is an ENFORCED DesignRule whose FIRST measured instance is exactly this, *"`gh pr merge` — FIVE TIMES on 2026-08-14… the merge had already succeeded server-side every time."* It is why this session read `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt` after every merge rather than trusting the exit code, and no merge was ever wrongly retried.

**RIGHT — THE RECURRENCE IS NOT ACCUMULATING.** The rule still says FIVE TIMES ON 2026-08-14. It happened at least FOUR more times on 2026-08-19 (PRs #248, #250, #251, #253) and nobody incremented anything. **So the graph holds the LESSON and not the ONGOING COST**, and the question "how much is this actually costing us?" — the question that would have prompted somebody to look at the packaging — was never answerable. That is his "we are not capturing failures as feedback", stated precisely.

⭐⭐ **AND IT CONVERGES WITH AN INDEPENDENT REQUEST THE SAME DAY.** The hxm_program feedback asks for exactly this mechanism, for a different reason: *"A 'sighting' mechanism for DesignRules — 'this rule was observed again in commit X' as a cheap dated append… Pattern recurrence is evidence the rule is real; today the graph can't accumulate that cheaply."* **Two unrelated sources, one day apart, asking for recurrence-as-a-cheap-append on a DesignRule.** One wants it to prove a craft pattern is real; the other needs it to price a recurring failure. Same primitive.

🛑 NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the ophyd-service session's reported `add_decision` status reset has the same shape (a stale or differently-packaged binary rather than a code defect). It did NOT reproduce on 0.36.0 at either the core or MCP layer, checking both the reply and the store — but the version that session actually ran was not asked for.

STATED BY ANTHONY 2026-08-09, AND IT BREAKS THE ANSWER THE 2026-08-06 NODE SETTLED ON.

=== THE ACCESS TOPOLOGY, FINALLY EXPLICIT ===

"My brother will be co-developing flo2 and we'll both have access to and work from the flo2 github repo. He doesn't have access to the other repos though (maybe reflow2, but I don't think so — he just installs it the standard manner and gives me feedback on it)."

  flo2 (C)     TWO WRITERS on one shared git repo — the multi-writer merge case dec:multi-writer-architecture was built for
  reflow2 (B)  ONE WRITER, plus a consumer who installs the released kit and reports back. NO repo access.
  A, D         Anthony only.

⇒ The brother is a CONSUMER of reflow2 and a CO-AUTHOR of flo2, and those are different relationships needing different mechanisms. His reflow2 feedback already arrives the way `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` predicts a consumer's would — out of band, by hand, with nothing in either graph knowing.

=== ⚠️⚠️ THE HOSTED CASE, WHICH THE GIT ANSWER DOES NOT REACH ===

"Some of this discussion may come into particular value in flo2 if we have MULTIPLE USERS AND MULTIPLE PROJECTS, SOME OF WHICH ARE DEPENDENT UPON OTHER'S PROJECTS WITHIN THE SAME DYNOGRAPH-FOUNDATION DB."

THAT IS A DIFFERENT TOPOLOGY, NOT A BIGGER ONE. The 2026-08-06 answer — file a proposed node on a BRANCH of the upstream's repo, merged by its owner — rests on three things the hosted case does not have:
  (1) a git repo per design. In flo2 there is one shared database, not N repos.
  (2) a branch and a merge as the review gate. A shared db has no branch to file against.
  (3) the filer and the owner being the same KIND of party. Here they are different TENANTS.

⇒ **THE TRANSPORT THAT MAKES THE REPO CASE COST ZERO NEW CODE IS UNAVAILABLE IN THE HOSTED CASE.** The 2026-08-06 node half-anticipated this — "for the HOSTED case flo2's own layer must be the mailbox" — but treated it as a deployment detail. With cross-TENANT dependencies it is not a detail: it is a second mechanism, and the one that has to be designed rather than inherited.

⭐ AND IT MAKES THE COMPARTMENT QUESTION LOAD-BEARING. `dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments` asks whether per-user graph scope is a convenience or a COMPARTMENT. In the repo world that is abstract — each person holds their own clone. In one shared db where user X's project depends on user Y's, an automatic cross-project write is a channel BETWEEN TENANTS, and the safe direction is defined against SENSITIVITY rather than against the dependency arrow. A levied requirement is a write into someone else's design by someone who is not their collaborator.

⚠️ ONE THING THAT DOES CARRY OVER, AND IT IS THE SAFETY PROPERTY: the repo answer is safe partly BECAUSE it never opens the upstream's store — it is a diff against a committed file, so it cannot move their schema stamp (see `fact:the-five-project-census-2026-08-09`: dynograph-foundation still stamps 0.16.0, and opening it with a current binary would upgrade it). **In a shared db every write opens the store by definition.** So the hosted mailbox must supply, by other means, the isolation the file transport gets for free.

NOTHING IS DECIDED. This records that `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` has TWO environments and only one of them has an answer — which the options as written do not distinguish.

MEASURED 2026-08-26 by reading the `hxm_program` working tree, then CORRECTED TWICE by its owner within minutes. Both corrections are kept, because the sequence is the useful part: an inference was drawn from a file listing, published, and then dismantled by two facts nobody could read off the tree.

🛑 **CORRECTION 1 — "NO COMMITTED EXPORT" WAS FALSE.** `reflow2.json` sits at the repo ROOT, not under `docs/design/` where reflow2's own convention puts it and the only place checked. **Absence measured by looking in one conventional location is not absence.** Third instance of that class today: `unallocated_component` reported 33 "empty" parts that were real modules; the three-legs audit v1 matched case-sensitively and reported a present detector as missing.

🛑 **CORRECTION 2 — THE HEADLINE INFERENCE IS DEAD.** Anthony, asked directly: **"I built hxm_program before I built reflow2, so much of it was hand-rolled prior to me adopting reflow2 on it."** The parallel tooling is **INHERITANCE, NOT A WORKAROUND**. It is not evidence of a reflow2 gap, and this node's original claim — that a user "built parallel graph tooling because reflow2 does not do this" — asserted a motive that never existed. **The tools predate the tool they were supposedly working around.**

⭐ **AND THAT IS WHY THE CAVEAT WAS THERE.** The first version listed three things the finding did not establish, and #2 was *"it does not date the tooling — any of it may predate the adoption, making it inheritance rather than workaround. Nothing here distinguishes those, and the difference decides whether this is a gap or a habit."* **The caveat named the exact question, one question answered it, and the answer killed the inference.** Cost: one sentence. Had the caveat been left off — or had the finding been reported as a gap — the design would now hold a false claim about a user's motives, and somebody might have built against it.

═══ WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE OF THE TREE ═══

  `reflow2.json`  a COMMITTED EXPORT at the repo root — 259 nodes, 501 edges,
                  stamp 0.40.0, written 2026-08-26 20:28. 71 Decision, 29
                  Artifact, 28 Capability, 27 Requirement, 20 DesignRule, 19
                  ChangeEvent, 17 Question, 12 Verification, 11 Component, 11
                  Fragment, 6 Interface, 3 Contributor. Real and actively kept.

  `codegraphs/` (per-repo: hex, hex-acq-pyepics, hextools, nslsii),
  `docs-graph/`, `dataflow/`, `DECISIONS.md` (338 lines) — **all predating the
  reflow2 adoption.** A program that existed first and had reflow2 adopted ONTO
  it, which is `adopt`'s whole premise rather than a complaint about it.

═══ WHAT REMAINS WORTH ASKING, NOW THAT THE WRONG QUESTION IS CLOSED ═══

The interesting fact is no longer *why did they build it* but **what happened after adoption**: reflow2 and the inherited tooling now COEXIST, and nobody has asked which parts reflow2 displaced, which it duplicates, and which it has never reached. `DECISIONS.md` at 338 lines beside 71 Decision nodes is the sharpest instance — migration, rendering, or two records drifting apart are three different situations and the tree cannot tell them apart.

⚠️ **AND THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH IS ABOUT ADOPT AND NOT ABOUT THIS PROGRAM:** every brownfield adoption inherits tooling, and reflow2 has no way to ask *what did this project already have, and what should now retire*. `adopt` brings a system under design control and says nothing about the instruments the project was already using. Whether that is a gap or correctly out of scope is untested, and this node is not evidence either way — it is one program, and the owner wrote both halves.

properties.description:
MEASURED IN THE CODE 2026-08-26, following the custody node's own instruction that the honest first move is measurement rather than vocabulary.

═══ WHAT IS BUILT ═══

- `declare_dependency` ships. A declaration carries `source` (free text — 'a git URL, a registry, a path'), `version` (refused if absent — 'the version is the whole point'), the parts taken, forwarded build switches BY NAME, and `graph_id` — the id of the dependency's OWN reflow2 design. It lands in a checked-in `reflow2.toml`, human-editable and reviewable in a diff.
- `reconcile_dependencies` ships. It compares the declaration against WHAT THE BUILD RESOLVES — Cargo.toml, docker-compose.yml, versions.env — catching the reliance nobody declared and the declaration the build no longer takes.
- `sync_status` ships, over `provenance::last_synced`, a path→content-hash record.

═══ WHAT IS NOT ═══

**Nothing compares a declaration against the UPSTREAM DESIGN.** The accepted requirement names that check and only the build-facing half was built.

🛑 AND THE CHEAP ROUTE TO IT IS BARRED BY THE THING THE HUB IS TRYING TO AVOID. `record_sync` is called by exactly two paths — `export_graph` and `import_graph` — so the only ways to get a path into the watch record are to export to it or import from it. And `import_graph` into a store that already holds a design KEEPS THE HOST'S NAME and upserts the incoming nodes into it (`adopt_on_import`: 'a store already holding a design keeps its own name, because layering an export onto a live design is an upsert, not a restore'). So importing a child to watch it ABSORBS the child — precisely what `dec:idea-a-hub-owns-designs-it-does-not-absorb-...` says a hub must not do.

⭐ **THE MISSING PIECE IS THEREFORE MUCH SMALLER THAN A HUB RELATION: a way to WATCH a path without importing it.** The record, the comparison and the reporting all exist and are tested.

⭐ **AND THE 'WHO ARE MY CHILDREN' RECORD IS NOT MISSING EITHER.** The obvious objection to a small step here was that something must say which designs to watch, and that something IS the hub relation arriving through the back door. It is not: the dependency manifest already holds it — checked in, version-pinned, naming the other design by `graph_id`, and inheriting the direction the dependency edge carries rather than being a flat list of ids.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT DELIVER, AND THE LIMIT IS REAL ═══

**A dependency declaration says I DEPEND ON that. A hub says I AM ANSWERABLE FOR that.** Those are different claims. Where a hub genuinely consumes its children, the manifest expresses the relation honestly and this route works. Where it merely OWNS them — and 'leaders decide, sub-projects inherit' is ownership, not consumption — using a dependency declaration to say so would be exactly the modelling fiction the field report itself objected to when it refused to force hub relations into `Interface` nodes.

So this narrows the hub question rather than answering it: wants #2 and #4 fall out of finishing an accepted requirement, with no new vocabulary and no tracker objection. Want #1 (cross-design realization) and want #3 (verification roll-up) do not, and neither does the downward-inheritance direction.

═══ ALSO MEASURED ═══

`describe_designs` reads the sidecar beside each store without opening it — id, label, minted-or-adopted, schema stamp — and deliberately reports no node counts. It carries NO last-export date, so want #4 is a small addition to a read that already exists. It is filesystem-scoped, which is the counter the hub node already records against the index option.

Either question is unanswerable with only one of the two halves.' The second is hub want #2 verbatim, written a month before the field report asked for it.

REFLOW2 COMPUTES WHETHER A DESIGN IS DELIVERING AND ITS INSTRUCTION SURFACE NEVER ROUTES ANYONE THERE. Found 2026-08-29 when Anthony challenged a claim this session had made — that "nothing in the orientation reads measures whether reflow2 does what it's supposed to do". THE CLAIM WAS FALSE ABOUT THE TOOL AND TRUE ABOUT THE EXPERIENCE, and the gap between those two is the defect.

═══ ① THE MEASURE EXISTS, AND IS PROMINENT ═══

`graph_report_markdown` returns, in its seventh line: *"Delivered: 151 of 193 requirement(s) (158 satisfied) — computed from the thread (something satisfies it, and that capability is built and currently passing), not from a status field."* That is exactly the answer to "does my project do what it is supposed to do", computed rather than asserted. NINE report functions in core answer that family of question: coverage, evidence, maturity, readiness, consumption, ility, flow, graph, forecast_readiness.

THIS SESSION READ THAT LINE AT ORIENTATION, never mentioned it again, and four hours later computed the same number by hand in Python to answer the same question. That is the symptom, and the agent was not being careless.

═══ 🛑 ② THE MEASURED CAUSE: THE INSTRUCTION SURFACE IS HYGIENE-WEIGHTED ═══

Named in the 23 served skills:

    detect_gaps            16 of 23      hygiene
    loop_status            12 of 23      hygiene
    coverage_report         5 of 23
    graph_report            3 of 23
    seam_report             2 of 23
    evidence_report         1 of 23
    maturity_report         0 of 23      <-- and 0 instruction files
    readiness_report        0 of 23      <--
    consumption_report      0 of 23      <--
    ility_report            0 of 23      <--
    forecast_readiness      0 of 23      <--

Also checked, because a skill is not the only surface: NONE of the evaluative reports is named in `AGENTS.md` or in `service.rs` either. They are reachable only by an agent that goes looking through the raw tool list.

⭐ AND THE ORIENTATION SKILL IS THE SHARPEST INSTANCE. `where-am-i` GATHERS `graph_report_markdown` — so the delivery line is in the agent's hands — and then its "Tell them" section gives EIGHT numbered steps of what to say, none of which is how much of the intent is actually built and working. The words "deliver", "coverage" and "satisfied" appear ZERO times in that skill. An agent that follows the script faithfully reports what is undecided and never reports what is done.

═══ ③ THE CLASS, and it is the same one three other findings describe ═══

Built, correct, and not routed. `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing` is a detector for exactly this shape. The linking layer (`mirror_surface`, `export_surface`, `pair_designs`, `seam_report`) was measured at ZERO instances while being built and verified. And the 2026-08-29 skill-adoption measurement across 93 sessions found that what predicts a skill's load count is being named in an ALWAYS-INJECTED SURFACE, not being in the served catalogue — which is this fact stated about skills instead of about reports.

⚠️ WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING MENTION: it makes reflow2 PRESENT AS a hygiene server to the person using it. A user asking "is my project doing what it is supposed to do" is answered with gaps, defects and export sync — not because the tool cannot answer, but because nothing tells the agent to ask the half that can.

🛑 NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the five zero-mention reports are actually UNUSED in the field, or merely unmentioned. Naming was measured; invocation was not. The 93-session measurement is suggestive for skills and does not transfer to tools without its own count. Also not established: whether `Delivered: N of M` is the right headline for a USER's project rather than for reflow2's own — it is computed from the thread, so it measures whether the design's own chain is complete and its recorded checks pass, which is a narrower claim than "the system works".
