properties.description:
⭐ THE FINDING IS NOT 'SOMEBODY FORGOT TO ADD THE GATE'. It is that the thing the gate checks CANNOT EXIST IN CI. `check_kit_manifest` compares an INSTALLED kit against the kit SOURCE; CI checks out a repository that has never been installed into. There is no manifest to be stale.

═══ AND THE CASE THAT COULD RUN THERE IS ALREADY COVERED ═══

A fresh install DOES happen in CI: `tools/test_init.py` (100 tests, already a CI job) installs into a temp project and asserts *"manifest and file agreeing, as they would after a clean install"*. So pointing the gate at a temp install would be redundant, and pointing it at the repo root would be red. Neither is a gate worth having.

═══ ⚠️ WHY THE ATTEMPT IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN QUIETLY UNDONE ═══

The gate was added on the user's word, and the reasoning behind that word was sound: the check existed, it FAILED on a clean tree (kit 0.30.0 against a 0.41.0 source, plus three shipped command files the manifest did not record), and it ran nowhere. Everything about that was true. What neither of us had checked was whether CI has an installation to check — and it does not.

🛑 SO THE `INVALIDATES` DRAWN AGAINST THAT FACT WAS WRONG AND WAS DELETED. For about twenty minutes the graph asserted the finding was closed at the cause. It is not closed; it is SHARPENED, and the sharpening makes it harder rather than easier to fix.

═══ ⭐ WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY REACH IT, NOT BUILT, NOT ASKED FOR ═══

The server already holds both halves. It writes `reflow2_version` into `<graph>.client.json` at every handshake, and `.reflow2/kit-version.json` sits in the same directory. Comparing them and saying so — the way `served_by.stale` already says the binary was replaced — would reach the DEVELOPER and the FIELD without CI having anything to do with it. That is where the 2026-08-27 reporter's four-source cross-check would have collapsed to one line. Recorded as a candidate in `dec:idea-what-makes-a-field-report-owed`'s neighbourhood, not proposed here.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH ═══

- **The manifest drift itself WAS cleared**, and that part stands: installer re-run, `.reflow2/kit-version.json` read back from disk as 0.41.0 / d3cb4ab / 36 files, `check_kit_manifest` exit 0. That was a real local fix and is not undone by this.
- **It says nothing about whether a gate SHOULD exist**, only that CI is the wrong place for this one. A local pre-push hook, or the server-side comparison above, are both untried.
- **One repository, one CI configuration.** A project that COMMITS its `.reflow2/` would have a manifest in CI and the gate would work there — reflow2's own choice to gitignore it is what makes this structural here.
properties.name: SHARPENS why kit drift is invisible to CI, and it is STRUCTURAL: CI is never installed into, so the check exits 2 there — the gate was added, measured, and REVERTED
properties.statement: MEASURED 2026-08-28 while trying to close `fact:defect-kit-manifest-drift-is-invisible-to-ci` by adding `tools/check_kit_manifest.py` to `ci.yml` and to AGENTS.md's pre-push block. IT CANNOT WORK. `.reflow2/` is gitignored and NOTHING under it is tracked — `git ls-files .reflow2/` returns zero — so a CI checkout has no installation at all. Run against such a tree the check reports 'nothing installed here' and exits 2, which would turn every build red. Both edits were reverted.

MEASURED 2026-08-26, from a user report that reflow2 "still speaks its own jargon and never asks who I am". The report is correct, and the cause is not a missing idea — it is a mechanism that was BUILT AND NEVER LANDED.

═══ WHAT WAS MEASURED ═══

  `lens` in the served surface (get_skill / list_skills toolsnaps)   ABSENT
  `reader_lens` / `lens_line` / `ReaderLens` in shipped code         ZERO occurrences
  the branch commit                                                  EXISTS: e01c760
                                                                     "WIP: lens on the skill response —
                                                                      core green, mcp handler tests unrun"

`cap:the-skill-response-carries-the-lens` says so itself and is honest about it: status `in_progress`, and its description records that the code sits on `lens-hint-rides-the-loop-rail`, was deliberately NOT marked `realized` at the v0.36.0 cut, and should move only "when the branch merges". **It never merged.** Six core tests passed; five MCP handler tests were written and never run.

═══ ⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT THE ORDINARY THREE-LEGS FAILURE ═══

The usual shape is a leg that was never built. Here the leg was BUILT, TESTED at the core, and left on a branch — which is worse in one specific way: **the design records the capability, so every reading of the graph says the mechanism exists.** It appears in `capabilities_covered` on the v0.41.0 release report, because that list derives from the components and artifacts a release ships rather than from a capability's STATUS. A reader of the release record would conclude the lens shipped.

═══ WHAT THE PERSONA ACTUALLY HAS TODAY ═══

  typed tool    `add_contributor` carries `description`             ✓
  instruction   TWO served skills mention asking (where-am-i,
                capture-intent) — and only those two               PARTIAL
  delivery      nothing carries it on the wire                      ✗ (the unmerged branch)
  detector      nothing notices a Contributor with no background    ✗

⇒ **A session that never invokes those two skills is never told to ask, and is never handed what the design already knows.** The design holds a background for 5 of 6 Contributors; none of it reaches an agent that did not run `where-am-i`.

⚠️ AND THE LIMIT THE CAPABILITY ITSELF NAMES REMAINS UNTOUCHED BY ANY OF THIS: the tests prove the lens computes and is attached; "they do not prove an agent acts on it, and nothing proves the translation is any good. This fixes 'the agent forgot'; it does not touch 'the agent translated badly'." Landing the branch would close the delivery gap and leave the quality question exactly where it is.

properties.name: The schema DOES bound decomposition downward — `component` is a hard floor and there is no `assembly` rung — correcting this requirement's own 2026-08-07 line that 'the schema does not bound this; the population does'
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25, by hitting it. Modelling the two `KvBackend` implementations as parts of `cmp:byte-store` — where they physically live, in one file — produced:

    hierarchy_issues -> 2 x level_mismatch
    'cmp:byte-store' (component) contains 'cmp:memory-backend' (component)
     but a parent must be above its child

🛑 THIS CORRECTS A LINE IN THIS REQUIREMENT'S OWN MEASUREMENT. Its 2026-08-07 text reads: *"DEPTH IS TWO, not 'as deep as the design needs'. ... nothing above system-of-systems and nothing below component. **The schema does not bound this; the population does.**"* The second half is TRUE UPWARD and FALSE DOWNWARD. `schema/structure.yaml:18` declares `level` as a closed enum — `[component, subsystem, system, system_of_systems, enterprise]` — and `component` is rank 0 in `hierarchy.rs::Level::rank()`. **There is no value to give a part of a component, so the containment cannot be expressed at all**, and promoting the parent to `subsystem` only moves the mismatch up into `sys:foundation`. The population is not what stopped it here; the vocabulary did.

⚠️ AND THE LADDER IS DECLARED TWICE, WHICH IS THE HAZARD ANY FIX MUST NOT INHERIT. `schema/structure.yaml` holds the enum; `crates/reflow2-core/src/hierarchy.rs` holds `Level` with `as_str`, `from_key` and `rank`. Nothing checks they agree, and `from_key` maps ANY unrecognised string to `Component` — so a rung added to the YAML and forgotten in Rust silently ranks 0 and every containment involving it reads as a mismatch. That is a silent fallback in a project holding `req:no-silent-fallback` at critical priority, and it is the same two-places-one-truth shape the absorption found in `#[non_exhaustive]` match arms.

⭐⭐ ANTHONY'S RESEARCH, 2026-08-25, WHICH NAMES THE MISSING RUNG AND WHY A FIXED LADDER CANNOT WORK. The canonical SE hierarchy is four tiers, and reflow2 is missing the third:

    tier          aerospace example          software example
    System        commercial airliner        e-commerce platform
    Subsystem     avionics / flight control  payment processing
    ASSEMBLY      autopilot computer         microservice / API gateway     <- ABSENT
    Component     microprocessor chip (LRU)  single code module / class

⭐ THE DECISIVE POINT IS NOT THE MISSING RUNG, IT IS THAT **"ATOMIC" SHIFTS BY DOMAIN.** In his table the atomic unit is a microprocessor chip for aerospace and a code module for software. A ladder with fixed named rungs asserts that every domain bottoms out at the same conceptual depth, and his examples show they do not. That is the argument for an OPEN ladder rather than one more enum value.

HIS FOUR STOPPING RULES, recorded as reference because they are the answer to "how deep is deep enough" and nothing in reflow2 says it:
1. **BLACK BOX PROCUREMENT** — if you buy it from a vendor as a complete unit, stop. An airliner's engine is atomic to the airframer; you do not decompose the turbine.
2. **MAINTENANCE / LRU** — stop where a technician pulls one part out and puts a new one in. A DIMM is an LRU; the transistors on it are not.
3. **SINGLE DISCIPLINE / SINGLE OWNER** — stop when a box can be handed to one discipline or one small team. A braking subsystem is cross-disciplinary; a bracket is pure mechanical, a driver module pure software.
4. **VERIFICATION COST** — every decomposition creates an item that must be tested, documented and tracked. Stop when verifying the parts costs more than the risk of testing them together.

📌 RULE 1 IS ALREADY A KNOWN GAP HERE, and this is where it lands: `anthony-thinks-about-over-engineering` records that **nothing in reflow2 distinguishes a component that was BOUGHT from one that was BUILT**. That distinction is exactly what rule 1 turns on — a bought box is atomic by procurement, whatever its internal complexity.

📌 BOUNDS: measured on one containment attempt in one design. The upward half of the ladder was not re-tested and the requirement's claim about it stands. No fix is proposed here — whether the answer is one more enum value (`assembly`) or an open user-defined ladder is a live question, and the second is what Anthony asked for in his own words: *"should be allowed to go as many rungs down as the user needs."*

TWO THINGS CHANGED FOR `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` BETWEEN 2026-08-06 AND 2026-08-09, AND NEITHER IS A NEW IDEA — the question, the four options and Anthony's lean were already recorded. This is evidence against them.

=== ✅ (1) THE STATED PREREQUISITE IS MET ===

That node closes with: "⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE THAT STILL BOUNDS ALL OF IT: dec:linked-repos-poc was RUN 2026-08-06 and found reflow2 declares NO `required` interface at all, so nothing pairs across any seam. The channel this node is about has no labelled boundary to run along."

MEASURED 2026-08-09 against the committed export: **14 Interfaces, of which 9 are `required` and 3 `published`** — ifc:ambient-agent, ifc:authenticating-gateway, ifc:exclusive-local-store, ifc:mcp-protocol, and the five dynograph-foundation APIs. PR #130 (2026-08-09) landed this; `paired` went 0→5 and `seam_report` ran for the first time. **THE SEAM NOW HAS A LABELLED BOUNDARY. The blocker named in that node no longer holds.**

⭐⭐ AND ONE OF THOSE NINE ANSWERS THE OTHER HALF OF THE QUESTION. The 2026-08-06 node said what was missing was TRANSPORT and ENFORCEMENT, and that enforcement was unfixable: "nothing stops a writer doing more than filing, because reflow2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION and cannot acquire one without becoming a different product." **`ifc:authenticating-gateway` is now a DECLARED REQUIRED INTERFACE** — "an authenticating gateway in front; reflow2 has no authentication." The hole did not close, but it stopped being an unstated hole and became a stated DEPENDENCY, which is a different thing: the design now says somebody else must provide this, and names the shape. **flo2 is a candidate provider of exactly that interface**, which makes the two projects' relationship reciprocal rather than one-directional.

=== 🔁 (2) THE MANUAL WORKAROUND RECURRED, AND ITS COST IS NOW STATED BY ITS AUTHOR ===

The 2026-08-06 node recorded the first occurrence: flo2 hit a wall it could not climb from inside itself, a human wrote a markdown proposal in the flo2 repo, a human read it, an agent re-typed it as reflow2 nodes, and NOTHING IN EITHER GRAPH KNEW.

What I did earlier was ask the agent in flo2 what those changes will be. I then created a .md file and had the agent doing reflow2 session read that markdown file. **THAT IS HUGELY INEFFICIENT.**"

⭐ WHY A SECOND OCCURRENCE IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN SHRUGGING AT: a workaround performed ONCE is an anecdote; a workaround performed TWICE, by the design's own author, on the design's own flagship dependency, is a measurement of what the absent feature costs. And the second time he named the cost himself rather than being asked.

=== THE OWNERSHIP SHAPE, STATED PLAINLY FOR THE FIRST TIME ===

Anthony, 2026-08-09: projectA (reflow2) and projectB (flo2) are both his responsibility; projectB is CO-DEVELOPED with his brother; projectB DEPENDS ON projectA; and **"my brother who is building the web app around reflow2 doesn't need access to projectA."**

That is not a new constraint — it is the same one the 2026-08-06 node built option (A) around — but it is now stated as a fact about the actual arrangement rather than as a hypothetical, and it independently re-confirms his lean: write-only-at-proposed keeps the brother out of reflow2 entirely while still letting flo2 levy what it needs.

⚠️ WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT DO: it does not choose an option. (A), (B), (C) and (D) all stand exactly as recorded, with (C) still refuted by the Google-service argument and (A) still carrying its honest counter — that reflow2 CANNOT ENFORCE write-only-at-proposed, because that is a property of whatever holds the mailbox. The blocker clearing makes the question ANSWERABLE; it does not answer it.

THE LOCAL LINEAGE GATE'S VERDICT DEPENDS ON WHEN YOU RUN IT RELATIVE TO COMMITTING — NOT ONLY ON WHAT THE FILE SAYS. Measured 2026-08-14 while amending PR #175 to cover captures made after its first export.

SEQUENCE, REPRODUCIBLE:
```
1. git checkout origin/main -- docs/design/reflow2.json    (restore baseline f9a65a)
2. export_graph --overwrite                                 (writes 4b93b0, prev=f9a65a)
3. reflow2_check --export docs/design/reflow2.json          -> FAIL, exit 1
     "records sha256:f9a65a… where sha256:5c393f… is expected"
4. git commit --amend                                       (HEAD now carries 4b93b0)
5. reflow2_check --export docs/design/reflow2.json          -> OK, exit 0, 80 notes
```
**THE FILE WAS BYTE-IDENTICAL AT STEPS 3 AND 5.** Only the git HEAD moved. The gate reads the export committed at HEAD to decide what the new file should chain FROM; before the amend that was the branch's earlier export (`5c393f`), after it that was main (`f9a65a`), and only the second comparison is the one CI makes.

⇒ **THE OPERATIONAL RULE: RUN `reflow2_check` AFTER COMMITTING OR AMENDING, NEVER BEFORE.** Run beforehand it answers a question nobody asked — whether the working file chains from a commit that is about to stop existing.

⭐ THE PAIR THIS COMPLETES, AND IT IS WHY THIS IS WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY. `fact:the-local-lineage-gate-cannot-see-a-stacked-export` records the OPPOSITE error: the local gate PASSING on a commit CI rejected, because CI checks out the PR MERGE commit where `HEAD~1` is MAIN. Together they say the same thing from both sides — **the gate is always reasoning about a PAIR of commits, and both failure modes come from that pair differing between local and CI.** Neither is a bug in the gate; both are a bug in when it is trusted.
  · stacked branch → local PASSES, CI FAILS (that fact)
  · pre-amend → local FAILS, CI would have PASSED (this fact)

📌 THE STEP THAT MADE THE AMEND CORRECT, worth keeping because skipping it is the silent failure: **restore the export from `origin/main` BEFORE re-exporting.** Exporting on top of the branch's own committed export would have chained `5c393f → new`, giving TWO hops against the merge base and the CI failure `dec:export-once-per-pr` exists to prevent. The restore is what keeps it one hop.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the gate could tell these apart itself — e.g. by naming which commit it compared against, so a reader can see it is answering about `HEAD` rather than about the merge base. That would make both failure modes self-explaining rather than needing two recorded facts to interpret. Not attempted here.

**ONE ROCKSDB STORE SERVES EVERY GIT BRANCH, SO THE LIVE GRAPH DOES NOT BRANCH — AND THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE IS A WORKFLOW RULE NOTHING STATES: YOU CANNOT HAVE TWO OPEN PULL REQUESTS THAT BOTH MAKE GRAPH WRITES.**

OBSERVED 2026-08-14 while holding PR #182 open (design-record writes) and being asked to build the command coverage accepted in it. `.reflow2/graph` is a single store shared by whatever branch is checked out; `git checkout <branch>` does not switch it. So any export taken on a second branch carries **the first branch's uncommitted graph writes too**, and both PRs then contain each other's nodes.

⇒ **THE CALL MADE, AND WHY:** the command-coverage build was FOLDED INTO #182 rather than opened as a third PR. **One PR at a time while graph writes are outstanding.** The alternative — branching from main and exporting — would have produced an export containing #182's nodes with a `prev_content_hash` pointing at main, i.e. a document silently claiming work that another open PR also claims. `rule:the-export-is-written-once-per-branch` and `dec:export-once-per-pr` constrain the export WITHIN a branch and say nothing about two branches sharing one store.

⚠️ **NOT MEASURED HERE:** the collision was avoided rather than reproduced. What is established is the mechanism (one store, no per-branch isolation) and the decision taken because of it — not an observed corrupted export. A deliberate reproduction would be cheap and has not been done.

═══ ⭐ THE SERVED-SURFACE GAP, WHICH IS THE PART THAT REACHES ANYONE ELSE ═══

**THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS AND IS SERVED — `parallel-work` sets up an isolated worktree with its own copy of the graph, which is exactly the isolation missing above. But the skill is framed by PEOPLE, not by BRANCHES:** *"Use when two or more people (or agents) need to work on one design at the same time without colliding — 'my brother and I are both editing this'."*

🛑 **ONE PERSON WITH TWO BRANCHES HITS THE IDENTICAL COLLISION AND WILL NOT REACH FOR A SKILL ABOUT COLLABORATING.** Every trigger phrase it lists is social; none is *"I have two PRs open"*. So the person most likely to hit this — a solo maintainer working two changes — is the one the skill's own trigger conditions exclude. That is AGENTS.md rule 7's shape: the lesson is real, and the served surface that would carry it does not currently invite the case.

📌 RELATED BUT DISTINCT, so this is not filed as a duplicate of any of them: `dec:multi-writer-architecture` covers the FILE as transport between people; `ver:merge-driver` covers merging the exported document; `rule:the-export-is-written-once-per-branch` and `fact:the-lineage-gate-verdict-depends-on-when-you-run-it` cover the chain WITHIN one branch. **None addresses two branches sharing one live store**, which is the only reason the fold-into-one-PR decision was needed.

⇒ OPEN, AND NOT PROPOSED AS A CHANGE HERE: whether `parallel-work`'s trigger conditions should name the solo-with-two-branches case, or whether something should notice that the store has writes belonging to a branch you are not on. Both are the owner's call.

MEASURED 2026-08-13, by running the gate on both sides of the same commit.

WHAT HAPPENED: a branch was based on another unmerged branch that had already exported. `reflow2_check` was reasoned to be safe because the chain was sound commit to commit — main `029fd47f` → `6e7f7717` → `bfcc8350`, each export recording its predecessor's content hash. CI FAILED the LINEAGE clause anyway, reporting that it found `6e7f7717` where `029fd47f` was expected.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, taken afterwards on the exact commit CI rejected:

    git checkout <the stacked commit>
    python3 tools/reflow2_check.py --export docs/design/reflow2.json
    → reflow2 check: OK — design and build agree (75 note(s))

**THE LOCAL GATE PASSES ON THE COMMIT CI FAILS, AND BOTH ARE CORRECT.** `_export_pair` compares HEAD against HEAD~1. Locally HEAD~1 is the branch's own parent — the other unmerged branch — so the chain checks out. In CI, GitHub Actions checks out the PULL REQUEST'S MERGE COMMIT, whose first parent is MAIN. Against that base the branch holds TWO exporting commits, which is two hops, which is the violation.

⇒ THE GENERAL FORM: **the local lineage check cannot detect a stacked-export violation by construction, because the thing that makes it a violation is the merge base, and locally there is no merge base.** A green local gate on a branch stacked on another unmerged branch is not weak evidence — it is no evidence, and it will read as reassurance.

This is not a defect in the gate. `dec:export-once-per-pr` is stated per PULL REQUEST, and the tool's own failure message already names this as its third cause — "THIS PR ALREADY HAS AN EARLIER EXPORTING COMMIT, and your chain is sound… FOLD the exporting commits into a single last commit instead" — added by `chg:lineage-message-names-its-decision` precisely because the earlier wording misled. The message was right and was reached only after CI had already spent the round trip.

⇒ WHAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT EARLIER, and it is one command rather than a build — **COUNT THE COMMITS, NOT THE PATHS**:

    git log --format=%h origin/main..HEAD -- docs/design/reflow2.json | wc -l

More than 1 means the PR violates the rule whatever the hashes say. Measured on this branch: **1** after the fix, **2** on the version CI rejected.

⚠️ THE OBVIOUS-LOOKING FORM OF THIS COMMAND IS BROKEN, and it was written into this node's first version before being caught: `git log --format= --name-only … | sort -u | wc -l` counts distinct PATHS, and since the path is pinned by the pathspec it prints 1 forever — including on the two-commit branch CI had already rejected. It is the same shape as `fact:a-piped-gate-reports-the-pipes-exit-code-not-the-gates`: a check whose output looks exactly like a pass no matter what is true.

📌 AND THE REASON A STACKED BRANCH LOOKED RIGHT IN THE FIRST PLACE, recorded because the next person will have the same reason: the requirement being satisfied existed only in the other branch's export, so basing on main appeared to risk a SATISFIES edge pointing at a node main does not hold. That worry was unfounded — the export is written from the LIVE GRAPH, which holds every branch's writes (`dec:multi-writer-architecture`; the store does not branch with git), so exporting from a main-based branch carries those nodes anyway. **The design record and the code that happens to be committed alongside it are separable, and treating them as one thing is what produced the stack.**

**THE MACHINE-WIDE INSTALLER HAS THE SAME DEFECT ALEX REPORTED ABOUT THE PROJECT INSTALLER — ONE LEVEL UP, AND INTO THE USER'S HOME DIRECTORY.** Measured on Anthony's own machine, 2026-08-14.

`cap:init-asks-which-harness` (built the same day) fixed `reflow2_init.py`, which writes into a REPO the user chose to point at reflow2. **This writes into `$HOME`**, where the user never pointed anything. `cap:machine-wide-install`'s own installer output was already softened once for exactly this reason — Alex reported *"Installing reflow2 for every project on this machine"* as ALARMING, and it became *"Making reflow2 globally available to projects on this machine"*. **The wording was fixed; the behaviour it was describing was not.**

MEASURED 2026-08-20, immediately after #262 made reflow2's module graph acyclic. Lift the SAME acyclic import edges up to the 8 declared subsystems, using each Component's CONTAINS placement, and TWO CYCLES APPEAR.

=== THE RESULT ===

  MODULES: 53 + 25, zero cycles at top-module and file granularity. Confirmed.
  SUBSYSTEMS: 8 declared, and the graph over them has TWO cycles.

  1) sys:store <-> sys:vocabulary
       store -> vocabulary via graph->nodes, graph->schema, export->nodes
       vocabulary -> store via flow->graph, vocabulary->graph

  2) sys:coherence-loop <-> sys:time-history
       coherence-loop -> time-history via artifact->temporal, confirm->temporal
       time-history -> coherence-loop via compare->report        <- ONE back-edge

=== WHY THIS IS THE POINT, NOT A CURIOSITY ===

A wall you can hand a change to is a wall traffic crosses in ONE direction. At a mutually coupled boundary there is nothing for a blast radius to stop at, so severability at sys:store and sys:vocabulary is not merely unmeasured - it is FALSE. dec:idea-stated-module-function-is-what-makes-failure-mode-testing-derivable and the flo2 change-propagation chain both assume walls exist to follow; at two of the eight, they do not.

The insight already recorded - MODULARIZATION IS ABOUT ADDING WALLS, NOT EDGES - now has its first concrete instance, and the walls in question are already declared. They just do not hold.

=== THE ROOT CAUSE IS PLACEMENT, NOT CODE ===

Cycle 1 is not a defect in the source. The kernel is four modules that everything sits on - nodes (46 of 52 modules transitively depend on it), provenance (44), schema (43), graph (42) - and the declared decomposition CUTS IT IN HALF:

  cmp:nodes  -> sys:vocabulary        cmp:graph      -> sys:store
  cmp:schema -> sys:vocabulary        cmp:provenance -> sys:store

graph reads nodes and schema; vocabulary and flow read graph. Any bisection of a mutually-dependent kernel produces a cycle at the level above it, whatever the code does. PUT ALL FOUR ON ONE SIDE AND CYCLE 1 CEASES TO EXIST WITHOUT TOUCHING A LINE OF RUST. cmp:identity - code degree 5, 44 of 52 modules downstream - is placed in NO subsystem at all, which is the same mistake in its most complete form.

Cycle 2 has the shape all three of #262's cycles had: one back-edge, compare->report. It is one honest question - does comparing two designs need the REPORT layer, or a narrower thing report also uses - not a restructuring.

=== AND REFLOW2 CANNOT SEE ANY OF IT ===

reflow2 HAS a circular-dependency detector and it is right to report none, because the design holds exactly TWO coupling edges touching any of the 8 subsystems, and both are sys:store CONSUMES an external interface. Zero subsystem-to-subsystem edges exist, so the detector has nothing to run on. The green reads as 'your subsystems are acyclic'; it means 'your subsystems have no modelled coupling'. Those are opposite facts wearing the same answer, and this is the third instance in three days of the same pattern: THE MECHANISM EXISTS, IS TESTED, AND IS UNREACHABLE FROM WHERE THE PERSON IS STUCK.

FOR AN ARBITRARY USER'S PROJECT that is the whole risk: a decomposition is declared once, early, when it is cheapest to get wrong, and every later answer about severability and blast radius is computed through it. Nothing today checks a declared decomposition against the coupling it is supposed to contain.

=== METHOD ===

Import edges from crates/*/src/**.rs, comments and string literals stripped, mapped module-leaf-name to Component id to CONTAINS parent; Tarjan over the induced subsystem graph. 42 of 56 Components are placed in a subsystem; 39 of those name a module present in the code graph. Of the code edges with both ends placed, 27 stay inside a subsystem and 67 cross - but crossing is not itself a fault, since a foundation layer is SUPPOSED to be depended on. Only the two-way crossings are, and there are two.

properties.statement:
🛑 **CLOSED 2026-08-23 — THE MEASUREMENT BELOW IS HISTORY. Read it as taken on 2026-08-21 and since superseded. It is kept in full because the METHOD is worth more than the numbers.**

WHAT RETIRED IT: PR #290, `chg:the-spof-sweep-stops-rebuilding-its-graph`. The single-point-of-failure sweep was rebuilding TWO full operational networks per candidate. After: **56 candidates at 878ms each became 5.08ms for all 56; `detect_structural_defects` 44.5s → 4.43s; `open_questions` — the first call of every session — 11.7s → 2.95s**, with the answer unchanged at 54 defects and 13 structural issues.

⇒ THREE CLAIMS BELOW WERE FALSE from the day #290 merged: *"NOTHING WAS OPTIMISED"*, *"that ratio is the next measurement and it has not been taken"*, and the 11.7s figure for `open_questions`. The 20x `detect_defects`/`detect_gaps` ratio WAS investigated and WAS fixed.

⭐⭐ **THIS NODE IS WHY `req:the-graph-can-say-what-has-already-been-done` EXISTS.** On 2026-08-23 an agent asked where else to optimise, read this fact, and quoted all three false claims back as current. Anthony corrected it — *"I think we already determined candidate 3"* — and he was right while the graph was wrong. He then generalised the cost: on a shared design, one person finishing a task and another repeating it produces **two solutions from two users**, which is not a graph merge.

📌 THE FIRST FINDING CLOSED UNDER `capture-session`'s test 7, added the same day and exercised here for the first time. Two things went wrong in the closing and both are worth keeping: the closure was FIRST written by REPLACING this statement, destroying the measurement it was closing — caught by the tool's own "no snapshot holds the prior value" warning, restored, snapshotted via `record_change`, and re-applied. **Closing a finding must PRESERVE it: a closed measurement is evidence, an erased one is a hole.** That is the failure mode test 7 will keep producing until the skill says so.

═══════════════ THE MEASUREMENT AS TAKEN, 2026-08-21 ═══════════════

MEASURED through the REAL MCP tool surface, driven over stdio against a REAL RocksDB store built from reflow2's own committed export (2862 nodes, 12139 edges, 8 MB on disk). Both build profiles, because users run release binaries and developers run debug.

                      debug      RELEASE
  get_node            0.01s       0.00s
  scan_nodes          0.11s       0.01s
  export_graph        3.10s       0.36s
  detect_gaps         3.11s       0.51s
  detect_defects     40.8s       10.3s     <== the hot spot
  loop_status        47.5s       11.4s
  open_questions     50.6s       11.7s     <== the FIRST call of every session
  graph_report    45–92s       10.9–22.4s

⭐ THE FINDING: `detect_defects` COSTS ~10s AND RIDES ALONG ON CALLS THAT NEVER ASKED FOR IT. `loop_status` reports a structural-defect count so it pays; `open_questions` pays it through the `loop_hint` attached to its reply. `open_questions` does its own work in about half a second and cost 11.7. So the two calls this project's own instructions call the cheap orientation reads were the two most expensive on the surface, and neither was expensive because of what it was asked to do.

🛑 AND IT CORRECTED A STANDING BELIEF. "The first store read of a session costs 26–48s" had been carried as a known cost and read as the STORE being slow. It was not the store: `get_node` is sub-millisecond and `scan_nodes` 10ms on the real backend. The cost was a whole-design sweep bolted onto an orientation reply.

TWO HYPOTHESES FALSIFIED FIRST, both cheap, both recorded so nobody re-runs them:
(1) THAT THE SYNC CHECK WAS READING AND HASHING EVERY KNOWN EXPORT FILE. `sync_debt` does exactly that per path in `last_synced`, and this design has ~15 such paths, several at 7.5 MB. FALSIFIED: a probe store with `last_synced` EMPTY still took 46.5s.
(2) THAT `export_graph` INSIDE THE DEBT COMPUTATION WAS THE COST. FALSIFIED: 3.1s debug, 0.36s release.

The cause was found by timing each tool in an ISOLATED fresh process, which also ruled out ordering and cache effects — `detect_gaps` measured 3.11 / 3.06 / 3.11 while `open_questions` measured 50.59 / 50.44 / 50.86.

⚠️ BOUND AS STATED THEN: one machine, one design, one shape of design. The RATIOS were the transferable part; the absolute seconds were not — and the ratios are what moved.

properties.description:
⭐ THE COUNT ANSWERS ITS OWN QUESTION AND THE ANSWER IS: DO NOTHING TO THE SCHEMA. `dec:idea-should-a-finding-be-required-to-bound-its-own-claim` said the honest first move was a count, and that at n=1 the schema should not move. The count came back n=1. Option (a) — write better names — is the answer to the question as asked.

⭐⭐ BUT THE COUNT RE-WEIGHTS THE OPTIONS, BECAUSE IT FOUND A DIFFERENT PROBLEM UNDERNEATH.

**1. `name` IS NOT A DECLARED PROPERTY OF TemporalFact.** The schema declares `subject_id` (required), `basis`, `confidence`, `fact_type`, `statement`, `valid_from`, `valid_to`, `value`. There is no `name` and no `description`. Writing either returns `undeclared` from `create_node` — the store is a property bag on purpose, so the write succeeds. **That is exactly the 33/279 split**: facts written through a typed path have no name; facts written by hand with one do. So `search_design` displays a field the vocabulary does not declare, and for most facts it is empty.

**2. AN OVERREACH BAKED INTO AN ID CANNOT BE CORRECTED.** reflow2 has no rename operation, and `dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition` records the reasoning for living with a misleading prefix rather than migrating: a rename destroys the node's snapshot history. The exemplar carries its overreach in BOTH fields — `...vocabularies-that-never-meet` — and only one of them is editable. A naming discipline reaches names; nothing reaches ids.

**3. SO THE REMEDY RANKING IN THE OPEN QUESTION WAS WRONG WAY ROUND.** A lint on names would cover 33 of 312. Changing what `search_design` RETURNS — ranked weakest there, on the grounds that it trades the cheapest read in the loop for a problem measured once — is the only option that reaches the 89%. That counter still stands on cost; what has changed is the coverage it is weighed against.

═══ ⭐ THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE, WORTH MORE THAN THE COUNT ═══

`fact:a-functional-carving-does-not-match-the-coupling-and-was-never-going-to` uses **the same phrase** — 'a layered carving maximises cross-group edges BY CONSTRUCTION' — and is NOT an overreach. That claim is a real structural property of layering measured against undirected modularity, and the body carries an explicit '⚠️ BOUNDS' paragraph plus *'do not read this fact as evidence the split was wrong; read it as evidence that this is the wrong instrument for judging it.'* **The discipline works when it is practised, and it is mostly practised.** A lint on the phrase would have fired on this one and been wrong.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT THIS COUNT DOES NOT ESTABLISH ═══

- **Stage 1 is a PROXY with unknown recall.** It screens for law-shaped WORDS. A name that overstates its data without using any of them is invisible to it, and nobody has estimated how many that misses. The n=1 is a floor, not a total.
- **One design, one reader.** Stage 2 was judged by the same session that wrote the finding, which is the weakest form of review available.
- **It says nothing about other node types.** Verifications, Decisions and Requirements were not screened; only TemporalFacts.
- **Two borderline cases were judged NOT confirmed and could go the other way**: `fact:a-capability-delivered-as-a-model-change-can-never-be-reported-delivered` and `fact:defect-a-question-not-created-by-gap-to-prompt-can-never-be-answered` both say 'can never' about a mechanism read from source. That is ordinary engineering speech about current code rather than a claim about impossibility, but a stricter reader would count them and get n=3.
properties.name: THE COUNT: overreach is 1 of 312 — but 279 of 312 facts have NO NAME, so for 89% the handle a reader meets is the immutable ID, and `name` is not even a declared property
properties.statement:
SWEEP RUN 2026-08-27 on Anthony's ask, over all 312 TemporalFacts in this design. TWO STAGES, because 'claims more than its data' is a JUDGEMENT and a word-search is only a proxy for it. Stage 1, lexical screen for law-shaped language on the handle a reader actually meets: 49 of 312. Stage 2, reading them: almost all are ordinary defect reports — 'add_verification cannot reach its own fields' is true and specific, not a claim about impossibility in principle. ONE survives judgement: `fact:coupling-and-contract-are-recorded-in-vocabularies-that-never-meet`, the original. n=1 of 312.

AND THE SWEEP FOUND SOMETHING LARGER THAN WHAT IT WAS COUNTING: 279 of the 312 carry NO `name` at all. Confirmed against a live `search_design` call, which returns `name: ""` plus the `node_id`. So for 89% of this design's facts the sentence a reader meets is the ID.

THE PRIMARY USER DESCRIBES HIS OWN WORKING MODEL, AND ONE SESSION MEASURED IT. Anthony, 2026-08-11, unprompted.

HIS WORDS: "I guess how I've been treating reflow2 is as a 'funnel' for my instructions, ideas, feedback, requirements and brainstorming. it often comes in random order and often touches upon subjects that I had previously thought about and entered into reflow2 development... both my brother and I kind of work like this of organically developing our projects as we go. probably looking at this session is a good microcosm of how I've developed and used reflow2 so far - and it has kept up pretty well."

⭐ THE CLAIM IS TESTABLE AND THE SESSION TESTED IT. NINE times in one working day, an input that arrived as a fresh thought landed on something the graph already held. None became a duplicate:

  "what's next for governance"            -> six requirements already authored from an external report
  render the docs from the graph           -> viewpoints.md's recorded Direction, the unbuilt half of BL-40
  `claude update` as an aspiration         -> req:frictionless-update, ACCEPTED, explicitly modelled on Claude Code
  feedback as a prioritisation signal      -> req:friction-has-a-severity-bar, considered AND DROPPED, by him
  the backward-trace problem               -> req:no-idea-goes-quiet, accepted, capturing his own complaint 7 days earlier
  the MCP breakage                         -> a defect fact recorded 4 days earlier WITH ITS FIX in its evidence field
  the second user's "put the skill in"     -> report-friction, already shipped in the kit
  his own organic working model            -> req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design, proposed and unaccepted
  "make search-first automatic"            -> search-first already written into FIVE served skills, and
                                              req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue,
                                              proposed, which is exactly the delivery mechanism he asked for

The ninth happened WHILE RECORDING THE EIGHTH, which is the cleanest possible demonstration of the pattern.

⚠⚠ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, NOT THE COUNT. Every one of the nine was found because an agent WENT AND LOOKED. Nothing surfaced any of them. Had the search not been run, each becomes a near-duplicate node wearing different words, and the graph fills with the same idea nine times. So reflow2 is a funnel on PULL and not on PUSH: it will hold everything and volunteer nothing.

THAT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THREE OTHER FINDINGS THE SAME DAY, which is why it is recorded as one fact rather than as praise: (1) the loop only sees what an agent hand-carries in (dec:idea-the-loop-only-sees-what-an-agent-hand-carries); (2) skills fire when a user TYPES them, confirmed twice — once by self-measurement in req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session and once from the field by the second user; (3) a fully-diagnosed defect with its fix already written sat four days because no ranking reads measured facts (dec:idea-field-evidence-is-a-prioritisation-input). Four instances, one mechanism: the design's memory is complete and entirely on demand.

⭐ WHY THIS IS FILED AGAINST req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design RATHER THAN AS A NEW IDEA. That requirement — "a body of intent accreted over years, contradicting itself and never built, can still become a design" — IS the working model he just described, and it is `proposed` and unaccepted. The way the primary user and the second user actually work is captured in the design and never confirmed. That is the eighth collision above, and it is about reflow2's own understanding of who uses it.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: nine collisions in one session is evidence that the ORDER of his input does not cost him coherence WHEN AN AGENT SEARCHES. It is not evidence about how often a session that does not search creates duplicates — nobody has measured that, and it is the number that would say what the pull-only property actually costs.

THE WHOLE ORIENTATION SURFACE AFTER FOUR MERGES (#303–#306), measured from merged main on reflow2's own design. Bytes on the wire: open_questions 871 · what_next 3,157 · vocabulary_coverage 3,438 · graph_report_markdown 6,172 · loop_status 13,637 · graph_report 15,485 · detect_gaps 26,096 · detect_defects 26,169. BEFORE: graph_report ~334,000 · detect_gaps 157,785 · loop_status ~146,000 · detect_defects ~93,000 (the 'before' figures are the payload doubled, because every reply was sent twice). EVERY READ A SESSION MAKES TO ORIENT NOW FITS. || ⭐ THE FINDING THAT OUTLIVES THE NUMBERS: FOUR TOOLS NEEDED THREE DIFFERENT MECHANISMS, AND REACHING FOR A BUDGET EVERY TIME WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG THREE TIMES OUT OF FOUR. (1) `detect_gaps` — a genuine budget: measure the payload, drop the cheapest information first, say what was withheld and how to get it. (2) `graph_report` — nothing to budget; 91.5% was one list nobody asked for, withheld behind a flag with a digest that already existed. (3) EVERY reply — not big, DOUBLED: the payload went out as both `structuredContent` and a text block, and removing that alone fixed `loop_status` outright (72,886 and refused → 13,637) and CANCELLED A PLANNED PIECE OF WORK. (4) `detect_defects` — not big, REPETITIVE: 52% was three paragraphs repeated across 50 rows, so nothing needed withholding at all. ⇒ ASK WHETHER A REPLY IS BIG, DOUBLED, OR MERELY REPETITIVE BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING. Each answer has a different fix and only one of them is a budget. || ⭐ AND MEASURE BEFORE YOU CUT, EVERY TIME. On `detect_gaps` the guess would have been the id lists — they were 35%, capping them was not enough, and only the prose got it under a cap. On `graph_report` the clue was already on the wire: the MARKDOWN rendering of the same report was 27× smaller than the JSON one. On `loop_status` measuring first meant not building at all. || WHAT IS STILL OPEN: 113 of 197 Verification names carry whole reports (longest 654 words) — the replies no longer flood, but the reports are still in the wrong field, and that is a DATA problem in this design rather than a code one. The `graph_report` digest is flat in the PASSING remainder only, so a design mid-build with two hundred `planned` checks would be large again — real, unmeasured, deliberately not built for. || SOURCE: measured 2026-08-23 from merged main (0014ca6), driving the built binary over real stdio, one process, one sweep.

AN OWED ITEM THAT DISSOLVED ON INSPECTION, 2026-08-22. Two sessions carried "REDO TWO `review_relations` CALLS" as debt. Reading the code closed it in five minutes and it should never have been carried.

THE ITEM: `dec:idea-a-capability-checked-only-at-unit-level-is-a-finding` and `dec:idea-do-another-projects-principles-belong-in-reflow2-or-only-the-machinery` had their `no_relation_note` written by hand with `create_node`, because `review_relations` was absent from that session's tool surface. The redo was owed so the writes would go through the proper door.

WHAT THE CODE ACTUALLY DOES:
  · `review_relations` with a note and no links writes EXACTLY ONE THING — `no_relation_note` on the node (`relate.rs`). No timestamp, no reviewed marker, no edge.
  · `unreviewed_ideas` clears a Decision on `properties.contains_key("no_relation_note")`. It reads the PROPERTY and cannot see how the property got there.

⇒ The hand-written notes are already recognised, already carry substantive content (each says what was searched and why nothing was honestly related), and the redo would write the same key with the same value. VERIFIED: both nodes carry the property in the committed export, and neither appears in the unconnected-idea finding.

⭐ THE ONLY THING THE TOOL ADDS IS ITS WRITE-TIME REFUSAL — it rejects a review that records neither links nor a note, so "nobody looked" can never masquerade as "somebody looked and found nothing". That guard protects against an EMPTY review, and both of these are full ones. It would have passed.

🛑 THE LESSON IS NOT ABOUT `review_relations`. It is that an owed item was carried across two sessions and one handoff note on the strength of a REASONABLE ASSUMPTION — that going through the tool must do something the direct write did not — which nobody spent five minutes checking. The same day, and in the same session, the gh `remote-https` root cause was re-derived from scratch while a three-day-old node already held it. TWO INSTANCES, ONE SHAPE: work carried or repeated because nobody read what was already there. Debt should be re-read before it is re-scheduled.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE: the tool surface defect is real and separate. `review_relations`, `move_component` and `set_capability_delivery` were missing from two consecutive sessions (151 of 155 served tools), and the standing hypothesis is that the client fixes its tool list AT CONNECT and the shared server was stale at that moment. That is worth confirming; this note only says the REDO is not.

properties.name: Second recorded instance of a revising write destroying its own pre-image — committed by an agent that had READ the warning about the first instance, in the same session, hours earlier. The capability worked exactly as designed; it reports, it does not prevent
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25. Adding a road to a brainstormed Decision meant re-sending its whole `decision` field, because constructors merge by overwrite. The reply said so:

    "This call REPLACED 1 property on a node that already existed, AND NO
     SNAPSHOT HOLDS THE PRIOR VALUE OF `decision` — checked, not assumed.
     For that field, the value in `replaced` above is the only copy in
     existence and this reply is the only place it appears."

⭐ THE CAPABILITY DID ITS JOB PERFECTLY, AND THAT IS THE POINT. `cap:a-revising-write-says-whether-the-state-survived` computes whether the replaced state is preserved rather than restating the rule at everyone, and it reported the destruction accurately, named the exact field, confirmed it had CHECKED for a snapshot rather than assumed, handed back the only surviving copy, and prescribed the undo. Nothing is broken here. **Its name is `says whether the state survived`, not `prevents` — it is a reporting mechanism and it reported.**

🛑 WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING IS WHO DID IT AND WHEN. The `capture-session` skill carries a paragraph about the FIRST instance: *"the first finding ever closed under test 7 was closed WRONG, minutes after the test shipped: the closure was written by overwriting the statement, destroying the measurement it was closing... The pull toward replacing is strong because a closure reads like a correction."* The agent that committed this second instance had **read that paragraph in this same session, hours earlier**, and had followed it correctly at the time — deliberately choosing `invalidates` over overwriting on two separate findings, and choosing to anchor a new measurement as its own node rather than revise a decision, EXPLICITLY to avoid this trap. Then it overwrote anyway, for a different reason (adding an option to a brainstorm, which does not read like a closure at all).

⭐⭐ SO THE WARNING'S OWN FRAMING IS TOO NARROW, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. It explains the pull as *"a closure reads like a correction"*. This instance was not a closure and had no correction in it — it was an ADDITION to a brainstorm, the most innocent-looking edit there is. **The hazard is not closures; it is any edit to a field that already holds prose, because the only way to add a paragraph is to re-send the whole field.** An instruction that warns about one shape leaves the others unguarded, and the reader who has just complied with it feels safest.

⚠️ NO FIX PROPOSED, and the obvious ones are worth naming with their costs: an append-only field or a patch argument would remove the hazard and complicate every writer; auto-snapshotting before a destructive merge would preserve the pre-image and put a write on every revise; refusing the merge without an explicit acknowledgement would stop it and add a round trip to ordinary editing. `dec:idea-should-record-change-refuse-a-snapshot-of-state-that-already-moved` already holds a neighbouring question.

📌 NOT SEVERE IN THIS CASE, stated so the record is not read as worse than it was: the replaced text and its replacement were both written by the same agent minutes apart, the new text was verified to be a superset of the old in substance, and the pre-image survives in the session transcript. The finding is the PATTERN, not the damage.

📌 BOUNDS: two instances total, both on reflow2's own graph, both by an agent rather than a person. Whether a human editor hits it as often is unknown and uncounted.

TWO MORE SIGHTINGS, 2026-08-22: `gh pr merge` printed `git: 'remote-https' is not a git command` on PR #296 and again on PR #297. Both merges HAD ALREADY LANDED server-side. The rule worked — `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt` was read after each, neither was wrongly retried, and main was synced by hand.

RUNNING COUNT: 5 (2026-08-14) + 4 (2026-08-19, PRs #248/#250/#251/#253) + 2 (today) = AT LEAST 11. This node exists because nothing else was incrementing it.

⭐ THE NEW FINDING IS SHARPER THAN 'NOBODY WAS COUNTING', AND IT IS ABOUT THE GRAPH RATHER THAN ABOUT gh. `fact:the-gh-merge-failure-is-snap-confinement-and-nobody-was-counting` had ALREADY root-caused this on 2026-08-19 — gh is snap-packaged, snap confinement hands it a sandboxed git with no `remote-https` helper, the system git is fine, and the remedy is one package change. THREE DAYS LATER A SESSION HIT THE SAME ERROR TWICE, DIAGNOSED IT FROM SCRATCH, AND WROTE 'second occurrence, so it is a reliable pattern' INTO ITS HANDOFF NOTE — while a node saying 'nine occurrences, here is the cause, here is the fix' sat in the graph, findable by the error string. Anthony had to say 'I'm seeing it again' before anybody searched.

SO THE 2026-08-19 DIAGNOSIS WAS INCOMPLETE, NOT WRONG. It framed the problem as the graph holding the LESSON but not the ONGOING COST. Today shows the graph also held the ROOT CAUSE and the REMEDY, and that was not enough either. A counting mechanism would not have prevented this: the session never looked. The gap is not accumulation, it is SURFACING — nothing puts a known root cause in front of the session at the moment it hits the symptom. That is the third leg again (`fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs-and-a-users-project-gets-none-of-it`), landing on the project's own operational knowledge instead of on a user's design vocabulary.

⚠️ AND THE COST IS NOW MEASURABLE IN A SECOND CURRENCY. Beyond the per-merge workaround, this cost one session a full re-derivation — environment probing, package inspection, a wrong confidence claim written into durable memory — to reach a conclusion that was already written down. A recurring failure whose fix is known also spends the time of everyone who meets it fresh.

🛑 THE FIX IS BLOCKED ON PHYSICAL ACCESS, NOT ON A DECISION. Anthony chose it on 2026-08-22 (`sudo snap remove gh && sudo apt install gh` — gh 2.45.0-1ubuntu0.3 is already in noble-updates/universe, so no keyring and no third-party repo are needed) and could not run it: he was driving the session REMOTELY FROM A PHONE and has no sudo there. It waits until he is at the dev box. Recorded so the next session does not re-litigate a settled choice, and does not read the continued failures as the decision being open.

⭐⭐ TWO SESSIONS, TWO PROJECTS, ONE DAY, THE SAME FOUR FRICTIONS — AND NEITHER SESSION KNEW WHAT THE OTHER WAS HITTING. `hxm_program` reported them as F-02, F-03, F-06 and F-08 in `art:hxm-program-feedback-2026-08-26`; reflow2's own 2026-08-26 session hit all four independently while doing unrelated work. Corroboration across independent users is the evidence class this project has least of, and it arrived by accident.

🛑 THE FOURTH ROW IS ONE DISEASE WEARING TWO FACES, AND IT IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. hxm followed the `brainstorm` skill exactly — ideas as proposed Decisions, linked with CONTRADICTS / ANTICIPATES / DEPENDS_ON and evidence — and `detect_defects` reported the CONTRADICTS as a `contradiction`, the linked ideas as an `unthreaded_cluster`, and each ANTICIPATES as `unresolved_setup`. **Following the instructions made the instrument worse, and `loop_status` then repeated "7 structural defects outstanding" at every check.**

That is precisely the failure reflow2 fixed for ONE detector the same day (`chg:unallocated-component-reads-the-ruling`), whose own rationale recorded the class as still open: *"nothing checks that a NEW structural detector reads the ruling. The next one written will have the same hole for the same reason."* **hxm's F-03 is that prediction arriving as field evidence, from a different project, on the same day it was written down.**

⚠️ AND NOTE WHAT THE `parks` FIX DOES NOT REACH: the tool-surface slices were parked by an ACCEPTED Decision, which is the mechanism. A brainstormed idea has no ruling to point at and should not need one — its `proposed` status IS the statement that it asserts nothing. So the brainstorm case wants either an automatic sweep class for `proposed` Decisions or detectors that skip relation edges on them; the ruling mechanism as built would demand a Decision per brainstorm, which is ceremony the brainstorm skill exists to avoid.

📌 WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether these four are the WORST frictions or merely the ones two sessions happened to share. Both sessions were long, graph-heavy and run by the same person's agents; a session that captured little would meet none of them. The corroboration is real and the sample is two.
