properties.statement: OVER HALF OF `detect_defects` WAS THREE PARAGRAPHS REPEATED. Measured 2026-08-23 with the duplicate emission already gone: 46,399 characters, 45,186 of them findings — and 52.3% of THOSE were one field, `repair_is_a_judgement`. 50 rows carrying 3 DISTINCT VALUES: one 797-character paragraph 24 times, one 216-character paragraph 8 times, 18 rows with none. The field is `Option<&'static str>` — a fixed literal per detector branch — so it is boilerplate BY CONSTRUCTION, and nothing in the repo reads it as data. Sending each once: 46,314 → 26,169 bytes on the wire. || THIS IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE FROM THE TWO FIXES BEFORE IT AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT. `detect_gaps` WITHHOLDS prose when a reply will not fit; `graph_report` WITHHOLDS a list unless asked. Nothing is withheld here — no list shortened, no prose truncated, no judgement about what a reader needs — so it needs no flag, no budget and no note about what was lost. ⇒ WHEN A REPLY IS TOO BIG, ASK WHETHER IT IS BIG OR MERELY REPETITIVE BEFORE REACHING FOR A BUDGET. Three tools, three different answers: withhold, withhold-unless-asked, and stop repeating. || THE READER'S RULE IS TOTAL, WHICH IS WHY A MAP IS NOT SIMPLY A SUBSTITUTE: `row.repair_is_a_judgement ?? map[row.category]`. A row keeps its own text whenever that text is not the one its category holds, so a future detector giving one category two explanations cannot silently hand a row the wrong one. And a category with only ONE row is not lifted at all — a map entry plus the sentence explaining the map costs more than one paragraph inline, and a mechanism that fires where it does not pay is how a reply grows while claiming to shrink. || ⚠️ THE BUG I INTRODUCED AND THE INERT TEST THAT LET IT THROUGH, both worth more than the fix. `Scoped<T>` names its list `items`, the unscoped reply names it `defects` — the first version looked only for `defects` and was A SILENT NO-OP ON EVERY SCOPED CALL. Found by driving the built binary, not by a test. THEN THE TEST WRITTEN FOR IT PASSED AGAINST THE BUG: its fixture produced no note-bearing findings inside the region, so the assertion loop never executed. Caught only by reintroducing the bug and watching the test stay green. The categories that carry a repair note are the ones whose findings are DISCONNECTED BY DEFINITION, so a synthetic region holding several of them is awkward to build — the shape handling is now pinned directly on both list shapes instead of through a graph that may or may not contain the case. ⇒ A TEST THAT ITERATES A COLLECTION ASSERTS NOTHING WHEN THE COLLECTION IS EMPTY, and a fixture is not evidence that it is not. || SOURCE: measured 2026-08-23 on reflow2 0.38.0, driving the built binary over real stdio.

THE CONDITION ANTHONY ATTACHED TO THE SE DEFERRAL HAS CLEARED, and nothing in reflow2 computes that.

His ruling of 2026-08-16 was 'DO IT, BUT NOT YET' — 'this is not immediate (priority is resolving bugs)' — and the sequencing was stated as part of the ruling rather than as a note beside it: '`epoch:instruments-stop-overstating` and its five requirements come before this.'

AS OF 2026-08-17 THAT EPOCH IS CLOSED. `arrival_delta` reports 5 of 5 delivered, `missed_obligations: []`, `movement: []`, and it shipped as v0.34.0 (`rel:v0340`, deployed; tag pushed; release verified to have published 5 assets). So the named blocker is gone.

WHAT THIS FACT IS FOR: it is not a request to start the SE work — that is the owner's call and 'the bug work is done' is not the same statement as 'do this next'. It exists because a DEFERRAL WITH A STATED PRECONDITION HAS NO WAY TO NOTICE THE PRECONDITION CLEARING. The decision is `accepted`, so it raises no gap; `loop_status` counts open decisions and this one is settled; `arrival_delta` reads schedules and this carries none. A deferral therefore goes quiet at exactly the moment it should speak. `cap:revise-trigger` (planned) is the general answer — trace new evidence back through GOVERNED_BY to the Decisions it bears on — and this is a concrete instance of what it would catch.

RELATED MEASUREMENTS ALREADY ON THE RECORD, unchanged by the deferral: 73 coupled module pairs with ZERO sharing a declared Interface, 51 of them crossing a subsystem boundary; all 15 Interfaces sit at the SYSTEM edge and none describes an internal boundary; and `fact:the-eight-subsystems-are-groupings-not-black-boxes` (2026-08-17) adds that 0 of 8 subsystems PROVIDE anything.

THE SEAM PAIRS. dec:linked-repos-poc's remaining half is now satisfied, and seam_report has been exercised for the first time.

THAT PoC (2026-08-06) reported paired=0 against BOTH dynograph-foundation and flo2, with 15 and 5 published interfaces landing in dead surface, and named the cause exactly: reflow2 declared no `required` interface anywhere, so pairing — which matches complements, never like with like — could never produce a pair. It called declaring them "the cheapest next step" and deliberately left it to Anthony's word. He gave it 2026-08-09, choosing to declare the environmental boundaries alongside the code ones.

MEASURED, BEFORE AND AFTER, against dynograph-foundation:
  paired         0  ->  5   (all at name_score 100)
  dead_surface  15  ->  1   (only their /v1 REST API, which reflow2 genuinely does not use)
  unmet_needs    0  ->  3   ambient-agent, exclusive-local-store, mcp-protocol

And against flo2: unmet_needs 0 -> 4, dead_surface 5 -> 3.

⚠️ THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER IS THE ONE THAT STOPPED BEING ZERO. The PoC called `unmet_needs: 0` "the most dangerous number in the run" — it reads as "nothing is missing" and meant "we never said we needed anything". It is now 3 and 4, which are real findings rather than an absence.

⭐ A MODELLING ERROR MADE AND CORRECTED IN THE SAME SITTING, recorded because the correction is the lesson. The first attempt declared ONE umbrella interface for the whole dynograph dependency. Pairing returned NINE candidates and ZERO pairs: a pair needs a name match at or above 85/100, and an umbrella scored 62-78 against nine crisp names. THEY DECOMPOSED AND WE LUMPED. reflow2 links five named crates that map 1:1 onto five of their published interfaces, so the umbrella was deleted (never committed, never true — a mistake rather than history) and replaced with five requirements at the publisher's granularity, named to match. All five then paired at 100.

SEAM_REPORT, RUN FOR THE FIRST TIME EVER — the PoC listed this as what it could NOT answer, because the check needs pairs and there were none: 5 pairs checked, 10 axes agreed, 0 incompatible, 0 differing, AND 30 AXES STATED BY NOBODY. The tool refuses to read that as compatibility, and says so unprompted: "an unstated axis is not an agreed one, and this is not a claim of compatibility." It also names what it did not examine — the TYPES crossing the boundaries. So the honest verdict is that the machinery works and the contracts on both sides are almost entirely unstated, which is a true statement about two designs nobody wrote to be composed.

A REAL WEAKNESS FOUND WHILE DOING IT, worth filing rather than working around: candidate noise scales as N×M. Five requirements against nine published library APIs produced 33 candidates, of which 5 were the real pairs. Every "X API" scores 60-83 against every other "Y API" on string similarity. Worse, an interface that has ALREADY paired at 100 still appears as a candidate against seven others — ifc:req-dyno-storage-api paired exactly with storage-api and is still offered against cluster-api, game-api, graph-api and four more. Suppressing candidates for a side that already has an exact match would remove most of the noise at no cost to the signal.

properties.name: seam_report ran against real pairs for the first time — 5 paired, 0 conflicts, and 30 of 40 axes stated by NOBODY
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-21, at Anthony's direction, against dynograph-foundation's committed export (179 nodes, written by reflow2 0.16.0, unchanged since 2026-07-27). This is THE HALF `dec:linked-repos-poc` COULD NOT REACH on 2026-08-06 and has sat `proposed` for two weeks waiting for.

=== THE POC'S OWN PREDICTION HELD, EXACTLY ===

Its closing line: "THE CHEAPEST NEXT STEP, NOT TAKEN HERE: declare reflow2's `required` interfaces... It would convert 15 dead surfaces into real pairs or real unmet needs." That step was taken since. Re-running the same pairing today:

  2026-08-06   paired 0    dead_surface 15   unmet_needs 0    seam_findings 0
  2026-08-21   paired 5    dead_surface  1   unmet_needs 3    seam_report RAN

All five pair at name_score 100/100 and agree on medium: req-dyno-core-api<->core-api, graph-api, resolution-api, storage-api, vector-api. The three unmet needs are correct and none is dynograph's to publish — the ambient agent, an exclusive local block device, the MCP protocol. The one dead surface is `ifc:rest-v1`, dynograph's 80-operation HTTP API, which reflow2 genuinely does not consume.

=== WHAT seam_report ACTUALLY SAID, AND IT IS NOT "COMPATIBLE" ===

  pairs_checked 5 | agreed 10 axes | differs 0 | incompatible 0 | UNSTATED 30

Its own words: "an unstated axis is not an agreed one, and this is not a claim of compatibility." So the seam between reflow2 and dynograph-foundation is **75% UNDESCRIBED**, not 75% agreed. Both sides stated `medium: library` and almost nothing else — no payload_schema, no error_model, no operations on reflow2's side of any pair.

⇒ THE ANSWER IS A GOOD ONE AND THE NUMBER LOOKS LIKE A PASS. `incompatible: 0` beside `unstated: 30` is the same shape as the PoC's own warning about `unmet_needs: 0` — a zero that reads as health and means nobody said anything. The tool says so itself rather than leaving it to be misread, which is the behaviour worth recording.

=== AND IT NAMED WHAT IT STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE ===

"The TYPES that cross these boundaries. Every axis here is a property OF a boundary; a struct or message that travels through one is part of the contract and is invisible to this check. A real case: a provider's storage API returned a type owned by its text crate, and the consumer read all three fields while naming neither." That is the exact breakage class this pair is exposed to, and no axis above would catch it (`con:pairing-stops-at-the-boundary`).

=== WHAT THIS SETTLES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT ===

SETTLED: the PoC's unanswered half — "whether seam_report's contract comparison is any good" — is now answerable. It ran, it refused to overclaim, and it named its own blind spot. The mechanism works.

NOT SETTLED: whether the two designs AGREE, because they have not said enough to disagree. The cheapest next step is now the mirror of the last one: state payload_schema, error_model and operations on the five `req-dyno-*` interfaces. That is a morning's work and it is the only thing that makes this report say more than "nobody said".

📌 METHOD NOTE, recorded because it cost time: this analysis was largely RE-DERIVED before `dec:linked-repos-poc` was found. Anthony redirected — "if you search the linking of projects, this was already discussed in the past" — and the prior record was both earlier and sharper, including `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface`. SEARCH THE GRAPH FOR PRIOR CROSS-PROJECT WORK BEFORE RE-RUNNING THE ANALYSIS; this design has a two-week head start on anyone re-deriving it.

🛑 **CORRECTION: ALEX'S TWO 2026-08-14 REPORTS CAME FROM TWO DIFFERENT MACHINES WITH TWO DIFFERENT AGENTS, AND THIS SESSION TREATED THEM AS ONE.** Anthony, relaying Alex's own question about which feedback was being discussed, then clarifying the setup:

```
              MACHINE            OS       AGENT    PROJECTS        REPORT
work          work laptop        macOS    Claude   real work       the 5 ideas
home          personal laptop    macOS    Grok     personal        the Grok feedback.md
```

⚠️ ON `basis`: the enum offers only `measured` or `forecast`. The machine/agent/OS attribution is REPORTED — Anthony relaying Alex — not observed by reflow2. The kit VERSIONS below are genuinely measured. Marked `measured` because most load-bearing content is, with the distinction stated here rather than lost to a missing enum value.

⚠️ WHAT THIS SESSION GOT WRONG. `fact:agent-feedback-corroborated-2026-08-14` describes the Grok file as *"a Grok 4.6 session on one of Alex's projects"*, which reads as the same context that produced the five ideas. It is not. Any inference treating the two as evidence about ONE install is unsound as stated.

═══ THE STALE-KIT CLAIM, RESTATED HONESTLY ═══

This session repeatedly said *"three independent signals that consumers run stale kits"*, implying mutual reinforcement about one user. **They are three SEPARATE installs, each stale:**
```
work / Claude / macOS ..... two of five notes describe behaviour fixed in
                            #172/#174 -> INFERRED stale, NEVER MEASURED
home / Grok / macOS ....... kit-version.json reads 0.11.0 / 0ec473e,
                            a 2026-07-25 tarball -> MEASURED
this dev machine / Linux .. kit stamp 0.28.0 / e2b05c7 -> MEASURED
```
⇒ WEAKER as evidence about Alex — only his HOME install was measured, and the five ideas came from WORK. STRONGER as evidence about the UPDATE PATH: three machines, at least two install routes, three versions, none current. **Systemic, not one person forgetting.**

🎯 THE VERSION QUESTION NEEDS A MACHINE. Anthony texted Alex asking what `reflow2 --version` says; **he has two installs and the answer differs.** The WORK one matters most — it produced the five ideas behind `epoch:a-project-is-set-up-right-on-the-first-run` and has never been measured.

═══ ⭐⭐ IT IMMEDIATELY FOUND A DEFECT IN WORK SHIPPED THE SAME HOUR ═══

`cap:init-asks-which-harness` had just been built with a deliberate decision: **`grok` is NOT a registry entry**, because Grok CLI reads `.mcp.json` and a second entry would write the same file twice under two names. A test asserted it. **The reasoning was right and the ergonomics were hostile: `--harness=grok` returned `error: unknown harness 'grok'` and exit 1** — the install REFUSING a correct answer from a user naming his own tool. Learning that Alex runs Grok at home is what surfaced it.

FIXED the same hour, keeping the reasoning and dropping the hostility: `HARNESS_ALIASES = {"grok": "claude"}` resolves the name without adding a config, the prompt line reads *"Claude Code (also read by Grok CLI — choose this for Grok)"*, and `grok,claude` collapses to one config rather than erroring. Four tests guard it, including that every alias points at a real harness and that no name is both an alias and an entry.

📌 **A GENERAL LESSON, since `rule:a-lesson-is-generalised-before-it-is-built` now exists:** a registry that is CORRECT about what to install can still be WRONG about what to accept. The two are different questions — what files does this harness need, and what might a user call it — and collapsing them refuses real answers.

═══ 📌 ENVIRONMENT FACTS NEW TO THE DESIGN ═══

  · **EVERY SECOND-USER REPORT REFLOW2 HAS EVER RECEIVED IS FROM macOS**, and **every measurement reflow2 has ever made is on Linux** — including all of 2026-08-14's installer runs and the harness wizard itself. Whether `tools/install.sh`, the `~/.local/share/reflow2/kit` layout, the merge-driver registration and `--harness` behave identically on macOS is **unverified, and nothing in the design claims it**.
  · **A TARBALL install is in use** (`0ec473e`), a different update route from a checkout. `user-iterative-release-preference` sets the goal at a ONE-WORD UPDATE; whether the tarball route reaches that is untested.

⭐ THE BREADTH IS ITSELF THE FINDING: the second user exercises reflow2 across two agents (Claude, Grok) and two project classes (work, personal) on one OS reflow2 has never been tested on. For evidence purposes his two report streams should be read as **two users**, and the two agents mean the served skills are being read by two different models.

properties.name: Road 3's hard part is ALREADY BUILT: release_seat fires from SeatLease's Drop, so the shared server observes a client disconnecting, crashing or being killed — and it deliberately writes nothing. Meanwhile a disciplined session ran 299 minutes between committed exports
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25 at main `8ba3198`, running the two experiments the user asked for against the store-inversion blockers.

═══ ROAD 3 IS NOT RESEARCH. THE OBSERVATION MECHANISM EXISTS AND RUNS TODAY. ═══

`dec:idea-what-guarantees-the-export-if-the-export-is-the-only-durable-copy` lists as its road 3: *"THE SERVER OWNS IT, NOT THE SESSION... the server is the only component that observes a session ENDING without being the session."* It is right, and the observing half is already written:

    identity.rs:625  impl Drop for SeatLease { fn drop(&mut self) { release_seat(&self.seat); } }

`release_seat`'s own doc: *"Called from the handler's Drop, so a client that disconnects, crashes or is killed releases its seat without having to say anything."* RAII, so it does not depend on an orderly shutdown or on any harness — which is precisely the objection that killed the Stop-hook answer (*"the guarantee cannot live in the harness, because the harness is the thing that might not come back"*).

The server also already knows HOW MANY are attached (`attached_seat_count`) and distinguishes three liveness states, refusing to guess for a seat it handed out but never leased (`Unknown`, never read as free).

🛑 **AND IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOTHING WITH IT.** `release_seat`'s doc continues: *"Nothing is written to the graph — the CLAIM stays exactly where it was, and only its liveness changes."* ⇒ **The gap between what exists and road 3 is not detection. It is one action on an event that already fires.**

⚠️ BOUND: `Drop` does not run if the SERVER ITSELF is SIGKILLed. That is a strictly smaller exposure than today's, because the server outliving any one session is the premise of the road, and session death is far commoner than daemon death. It is not zero, and a periodic export (road 2) is what would cover it.

═══ THE EXPOSURE, MEASURED ON A SESSION THAT WAS TRYING ═══

Five exporting commits across 562 minutes of one working session, taken from git:

    gaps between committed exports:  36 min | 186 min | 299 min | 41 min
    longest window with the durable copy stale:  299 MINUTES (~5 HOURS)
    design delta over the session:  +15 nodes, +37 edges, ~10 property-only edits

⭐⭐ **THIS IS THE NUMBER THE BLOCKER NEEDED, AND IT IS NOT A NEGLIGENCE NUMBER.** The session exported at every PR boundary, ran the design gate each time, and was actively disciplined about the export-once-per-PR rule. It STILL spent five unbroken hours with the committed document behind the live graph. Under today's model that costs a session's work; under the inversion the same five hours is THE DESIGN.

📌 AND THE KNOB IS ESSENTIALLY FREE. Save is measured at **265 ms** (`dec:the-rust-rocksdb-switch-is-parked-until-the-store-question-settles`). A debounced or on-idle export at any cadence a person would notice costs a quarter of a second against a five-hour window. **The trade is not cost against safety; it is 265 ms against five hours.**

⚠️ BOUNDS: one session, one machine, one person, one design. Gaps are between COMMITTED exports — the working tree was written more often than that, so this measures the durable-copy exposure rather than every write.

properties.name: Every `--stop-shared` leaves a zombie: the `--shared` client forks `--serve-shared` daemons and never wait()s for them. NINE defunct reflow2-mcp processes accumulated over 27 hours on one machine, the oldest 23h33m
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25 at main `a000bc7`, found while diagnosing interactive lag the user reported — and it turned out NOT to be the cause, which is the part worth writing down.

═══ THE MECHANISM, READ OFF THE PROCESS TABLE ═══

    pid 3828662  reflow2-mcp --graph-path ./.reflow2/graph --shared     ELAPSED 1-03:26:10
      ├─ 758519   reflow2-mcp ... --serve-shared        S    RSS 299 MB   02:13:54   ← the live daemon
      ├─ 599201   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        02:46:05
      ├─ 478637   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        09:15:59
      ├─ 291284   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        10:04:39
      ├─ 211254   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        11:04:48
      ├─ 121029   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        13:47:45
      ├─ 119935   [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        13:51:29
      └─ 4129702  [reflow2-mcp] <defunct>               Z    RSS 0        23:33:48

    total defunct reflow2-mcp: 9

The `--shared` process is the CLIENT the harness launches and it lives for the whole session (27 hours here). It forks a `--serve-shared` daemon when none is running. `--stop-shared` asks that daemon to exit — and **the parent never `wait()`s**, so the exited child stays in the process table as a zombie. One per restart, and the restarts are not rare: a NEW MCP TOOL is not callable until the server is bounced, so a session that adds tools bounces it repeatedly. This one did so four or five times in a day.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT IT IS NOT, AND THIS IS THE POINT ═══

**IT DID NOT CAUSE THE LAG, AND THE OBVIOUS READING SAYS IT DID.** Nine leaked processes with `reflow2-mcp` in the name looks exactly like a resource leak. Measured: every zombie holds **RSS 0 and 0% CPU** — a zombie is a process-table entry and nothing else. The actual cause was `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast -- --test-threads=2` on a **4-core** box driving load average to **5.8**; renicing it to +19 dropped that to 4.4 within seconds and it finished green at 1.99.

⇒ Two defects were visible at once and only one was doing harm. Reporting the zombies as the cause would have been a confident, plausible, wrong diagnosis — and the fix would have changed nothing the user could feel.

═══ WHY IT STILL MATTERS ═══

A zombie costs a PID-table entry, not memory. Nine is harmless. But it is unbounded in the length of a session and one-per-bounce, and the thing that forces bounces — a new tool being uncallable until restart — is a normal part of developing reflow2 itself. A long-lived server on a busy machine accumulates them indefinitely.

📌 THE FIX IS ORDINARY: `wait()` on the child after asking it to stop, or double-fork the daemon so `init` reaps it, or set `SIGCHLD` to `SIG_IGN` in the `--shared` client. None of that is architecture.

⚠️ BOUNDS: one machine, one 27-hour session, Linux. The count is what THIS session produced; nothing here says how a fleet or a hosted tier behaves, and no fix has been attempted or verified.

properties.description:
⭐ THE DECISION THAT CAUSED IT WAS SOUND ON ITS OWN TERMS AND IS NOT THE CAUSE. `fact:every-reply-was-sent-twice` measured a flat 2× on every reply: `detect_gaps` at 157,785 bytes on the wire, refused by a harness; 26,096 after the fix, a 6× improvement with the payload unchanged. **Reverting to always-duplicate resurrects the refusals.** Any remedy must keep that win.

═══ CAUSE 1: THE PREMISE WAS VERIFIED AGAINST THE WRONG POPULATION ═══

The recorded reasoning is explicit: gating on the negotiated protocol version was rejected as *'a large invasive change to protect a client nobody could name'*. The check was real and is written down — all three in-repo Python clients read `structuredContent` first, the `j!` test macro reads it only, `proxy.rs` parses neither field. **Every client checked was Anthony's own.** `rule:reflow2-is-built-for-other-projects-not-for-itself` says the field is the point; the verification covered the self-host and not the field. Five days later the field named a client.

⚠️ This is the same shape as `fact:a-findings-name-can-claim-more-than-its-data-...` and the seam-altitude misreading, both found 2026-08-27: **a measurement whose population did not cover the claim it was used to support.** Third instance in six days.

═══ ⭐⭐ CAUSE 2, AND IT IS THE DEEPER ONE: THE MITIGATION ADDRESSES A PARTY THAT IS NOT IN THE ROOM ═══

The signpost was chosen over an empty `content` block deliberately and for a good reason — silence is indistinguishable from reflow2 not being configured (`req:never-silently-absent`). But read its text: *'**your client** is reading `content` for a tool that declares structured output: read `structuredContent` instead.'*

**It instructs the CLIENT. It is delivered to the AGENT.** The agent cannot change its harness, so the signpost converts silence into an instruction its reader has no power to execute. The recorded claim that the signpost *'protects them anyway'* is therefore false for exactly the population it was written for. The reporter did the only thing left — export to a file and parse it with Python — and named it correctly: *'a post-hoc check, not a read. It cannot replace `search_design` before a create, or `loop_status` before finishing.'*

═══ CAUSE 3: A SPEC `SHOULD` IS BEING DECLINED, WHICH IS LEGAL AND SHIFTS THE BURDEN ═══

MCP 2025-06-18, verified against the specification 2026-08-28, states: *'For backwards compatibility, a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block.'* The spec's own worked example carries both. reflow2 declines that SHOULD. A SHOULD may be declined — but declining it moves the entire burden onto clients, and MCP still negotiates `2024-11-05` and `2025-03-26`, which predate the field entirely.

═══ ⚠️ THE COST ESTIMATE THAT DECIDED IT DESERVES RE-MEASURING, AND THIS IS A CANDIDATE NOT A CONCLUSION ═══

The rejection priced version-gating at threading `RequestContext` through 155 handlers and 151 `ok_json` call sites. Two things now bear on that and NEITHER HAS BEEN TESTED: (1) the version machinery ALREADY EXISTS and is tested — `version_is_per_request` and `identity_is_per_request`, with the note that an absent version 'falls back to the peer info recorded at `initialize`'; (2) `json_result` is a SINGLE CHOKE POINT, and making a single choke point carry new state is exactly how read-only shipped on 2026-08-26 — `write_lock` became fallible and the compiler turned all 98 write sites into errors until each was handled, finding a second assembly point review would have missed. **Whether the negotiated version can be captured once at initialize and read at `json_result` has NOT been checked**, and the ~300-line figure predates anyone asking.

═══ WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT ESTABLISH ═══

- **One client, one report.** How many other field clients read only `content` is unknown and unmeasured. n=1 for the affected population, exactly as the original premise was n=0.
- **No remedy is asserted.** Options are open in `dec:idea-how-does-a-content-only-client-get-an-answer`.
- **The reporter was unsure of the classification too**, and said so: *'whether this is a reflow2 contract change the TUI has not implemented, or a regression that dropped a fallback.'* It is the former, deliberately — which does not make the outage less real.
properties.name: ROOT CAUSE of the structured-content outage: the premise was 'a client nobody could name' and one is now named — and the mitigation instructs the CLIENT while being read by the AGENT, which cannot change its harness
properties.statement: FIELD REPORT 2026-08-27 (Grok Build TUI, macOS, reflow2 0.39.0), verified against 0.41.0 source 2026-08-28 — STILL TRUE. On a client that forwards only `content`, ~26 named reflow2 tools return the STRUCTURED_ONLY stub and nothing else: get_node, search_design, scan_nodes, loop_status, detect_gaps, export_graph, every constructor. The reporter's words: 'the capture → detect → ask loop is unreadable in this harness. The agent cannot confirm a write, cannot map the user's words to node ids without guessing, and cannot see whether anything is owed.' Refusals and prose tools still work, so the server is reachable and only its ANSWERS are gone.

FOURTH MEASURED INSTANCE OF THE STALE SHARED DAEMON, AND THE SECOND THAT COST FIVE MERGED PRs — with the remedy already shipped both times.

2026-08-08 (instance three, recorded in tests/the_server_says_when_it_is_stale.rs): "Anthony restarted the session specifically to pick up a new binary, and the served surface did not move — `--shared` is a CLIENT that re-attaches to the detached daemon. Five merged PRs had been built, gated and shipped without one of them ever running live."

2026-08-19, MOVE FOR MOVE THE SAME: PRs #254 #255 #256 #257 #258 merged, all green. Anthony restarted the session deliberately to pick up the new binary. NOTHING MOVED. Measured at the process table: pid 3861122 `--serve-shared`, started 17:22:52, up 4h49m; the session's own client pid started 22:11 and re-attached to it. The binary ON DISK was current — stamp matched the source hash and contained `level_spine_disagreement` five times — while the process answering every call was four hours older than the code.

⭐ WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN JUST FIXING: the detection existed. `served_by.stale` was built after instance three, is tested, and says in its own note "A SESSION RESTART ALONE, WITHOUT `--stop-shared`, CHANGES NOTHING". It rides on `graph_report`. Over roughly two hundred tool calls that day the session called `loop_status` eight times and `graph_report` ZERO — while the session-start hook says "loop_status is the one cheap call" and the stop hook nudges to the same place. The remedy was one call away and in the wrong room.

📌 SAME SHAPE AS TWO OTHER FINDINGS THE SAME DAY, which is why it is filed as a pattern and not an incident: `ruling: parks` (documented on the tool, absent from the defect the reader is looking at) and `Component.level` (indexed and populated, with no way to ask by it). Typed mechanism present, instruction absent from the place of use, every time.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: whether any other computed surface silently depends on binary currency the same way. Only `graph_report` and `loop_status` were examined.

properties.statement: THIRD INSTANCE, AND THE FIRST ONE WHERE THE PEOPLE LOSING THE CYCLE HAD ALREADY WRITTEN THE DEFECT DOWN. Deliberately NOT a new defect: fact:defect-a-running-server-cannot-say-it-is-stale (2026-08-07) already states this case in almost these words — '--serve-shared is detached on purpose, so every session that restarted RE-ATTACHED TO THE SAME STALE PROCESS and nothing anywhere reported a problem' — and fact:defect-stale-server-reproduced-first-hand-here records the second. This node exists for what those two do NOT say. WHAT HAPPENED, 2026-08-08 late: Anthony went home specifically to restart and pick up the new binary, restarted the session, and the served surface was unchanged. Measured rather than assumed: `describe_schema(from: DesignRule, to: Component)` still answered 'No edge type specifically models DesignRule -> Component' and still showed CONSTRAINS as `from: ["*"]`, minutes after that enumeration was built, gated and pushed. `ps` explains it: the `--serve-shared` daemon has held the graph since 10:16 that morning, while the restart spawned a NEW `--shared` CLIENT (23:50) which attached to it. WHAT IS NEW AND WORTH THE NODE: (1) THE DOCUMENTED REMEDY IS THE THING THAT FAILS. Every prior record treats 'restart' as the escape from a stale server. Under `--shared` a session restart does not touch the daemon, so the remedy silently does nothing and the user reasonably believes it worked. The actual remedy is `--stop-shared`, which appears in NEITHER prior fact. (2) IT COST A WHOLE DAY OF DOGFOODING. Five merged PRs — the seat-liveness fix, both governance detectors, the skill, the enforced tri-state — were built, gated and merged without one of them ever running through a live session, because the daemon predated all of it. The handoff note written that evening had to say 'check the version rather than assume', which is the workaround this requirement exists to abolish. (3) IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BY DELIBERATE CHECKING. The session tested a schema fact it happened to know had changed. Nothing surfaced it, and a session without that specific memory would have proceeded on a stale surface believing it was current — which is exactly how the four sessions in the 2026-08-07 report drew opposite conclusions from the same true value. WHY THIS IS AN ARGUMENT AND NOT A COMPLAINT: `req:the-server-is-the-authority-on-its-own-currency` has NOTHING SATISFYING IT and has sat among the 0.60 unsatisfied-requirement gaps all day. The fix is not research: `/proc/self/exe` is marked `(deleted)` the moment the binary is replaced, w-6904efa6 demonstrated it live on a real pid, and it is one syscall with no second source and no version-string comparison. THREE INSTANCES ACROSS TWO PROJECTS AND TWO MACHINES, and the third landed on the maintainer. THE HONEST CAVEAT, because recurrence is not automatically corroboration: these three share a cause rather than a method — two were found by noticing an impossible value, this one by testing a remembered fact — so they add weight to the COST, not to the diagnosis, which was already certain.

properties.name: dynograph-foundation designates ifc:kv-backend `published` — the seam under StorageEngine — while the code makes `KvBackend` pub(crate), so the one node naming the shared layer beneath the diamond promises an extension point nobody outside can implement
properties.statement:
READ 2026-08-21 in /home/ajs7/project/dynograph-foundation, at Anthony's invitation ("dynograph-foundation is also my project... we can also review it"). READ ONLY — nothing was written to that repo.

ITS DESIGN SAYS: `ifc:kv-backend`, designation **published**, named "KvBackend trait (storage seam)", spec "The narrow seam underneath StorageEngine. All schema-aware behaviour — validation, the reverse index, the read cache, the write-buffer overlay, the full-text sidecar — sits ABOVE this trait; everything that touches bytes goes through it", operations "six byte-level primitives over six named column families, plus ordered prefix iteration".

ITS CODE SAYS: `pub(crate) trait KvBackend: Send + Sync` (crates/dynograph-storage/src/backend.rs:210). Two implementations, `MemoryBackend` and `RocksBackend`. No public re-export found.

⇒ THE SEAM IS REAL AND IT IS NOT REACHABLE. Swappable from INSIDE dynograph-foundation, not from outside it. A new backend — object storage, a networked KV, something sharded — is a change to that repo, not something reflow2 or flo2 could supply. That is fine while one person owns all three and is worth knowing before anyone plans otherwise.

⭐ WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY VISIBILITY MISMATCH. `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface` established that reflow2 and storyflow consume DISJOINT surfaces over one shared implementation, and that "neither consumer's graph can see that layer at all". `ifc:kv-backend` is the ONE node in any of these designs that names that layer. So the single place the shared substrate is modelled is also the place where the design and the code disagree about whether anyone may build on it.

⭐ AND IT IS THE SEAM THE 10k QUESTION TURNS ON. `dec:idea-where-does-the-10k-work-actually-land` records the reading that a hosted byte store is a new `impl KvBackend` needing no reflow2 change, because `StorageEngine` holds `Box<dyn KvBackend>` and does not change type. That reading is correct about the SHAPE and depends on this visibility: today only dynograph-foundation can supply one.

📌 ALSO OBSERVED IN THE SAME READ, unprompted and relevant to flo2's architecture: dynograph-foundation already has the hosted-service shape, and it is real in code rather than aspirational. `ifc:rest-v1` is specified 9/9 — 80 operations at /v1, bearer JWT when configured. `ifc:auth-provider` is a PUBLIC trait (`pub use auth::{AuthProvider, BearerJwt, Identity, NoAuth}` in dynograph-service), described as "an EXTENSION POINT", with an integration test asserting a JWT is rejected without a token and accepted with one. There are `dynograph-service` and `dynograph-client` crates, plus `ifc:ops-probes` at 8/9 and a Unix-socket transport. flo2's tracker states "reflow2 has NO AUTHENTICATION and is not getting any — AuthN and authZ are flo2's, at the layer in front", which is true of reflow2 and NOT true of the layer beneath it.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED, and deliberately not assumed: whether reflow2 could usefully run as a CLIENT of a dynograph-service rather than embedding StorageEngine. It would not be a `KvBackend` swap — that trait is byte-level and synchronous, and putting HTTP under it per operation would be worse, not better. It would be a swap at the graph-operations level, roughly where `ifc:graph-read` sits. Offered as a shape nobody has costed, not as a recommendation.

⚠️ BOUND: dynograph-foundation's committed export was written by reflow2 0.16.0 on 2026-07-27 and its working tree is at v0.12.0. The design may lag its own code; only the two facts above were checked against source.

properties.name: cargo's missing GC filled the disk to 100%: 263 GiB in 484,912 artifacts, almost all duplicate copies of reflow2's OWN two crates — and the surgical sweep keeps RocksDB cached
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-24, when a `cargo test --workspace` failed with `No space left on device (os error 28)` and Anthony's desktop reported 756.8 MB free. It arrived sideways — nobody was looking at disk; increment 2 of the foundation absorption was being verified.

═══ WHAT WAS THERE ═══

    filesystem            468 G total, 428 G used, 17 G free (97%)  — briefly 43 MB
    target/debug          267 G
      └ deps             263 G across 472,078 artifacts
      └ incremental       22 G
    reflow2_core|reflow2_mcp artifacts       159,247
    ONE reflow2_mcp test binary                 290 MB
    liblibrocksdb_sys.rlib                      856 MB  (the single largest dep)

⇒ **THE BULK IS NOT DEPENDENCIES. IT IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN TWO CRATES, over and over.** Every `cargo test --workspace` mints another generation of ~290 MB test binaries and nothing ever removes the previous one. Four workspace runs in one session is a meaningful fraction of a terabyte.

═══ ⭐ THE SWEEP, AND WHICH COMMAND MATTERS ═══

    cargo clean -p reflow2-core -p reflow2-mcp
    → Removed 484,912 files, 263.1 GiB
    → target/debug 267 G → 6.1 G ; disk 97% → 38% used, 277 G free
    → liblibrocksdb_sys.rlib STILL CACHED (896,538,384 bytes, verified after)

🛑 **THE `-p` FLAGS ARE THE WHOLE POINT.** A bare `cargo clean` reclaims the same space and ALSO destroys the cached RocksDB C++ build — a ~19-minute rebuild bought for nothing, since the 263 GiB is not RocksDB. Scoped to the two crates, only reflow2's own code recompiles, which was going to happen anyway. `rm -rf target/debug/incremental` is the free first move: pure cache, always safe, 22 GB here.

═══ IT WAS ALREADY DIAGNOSED, AND HAD GROWN ~87× SINCE ═══

`[profile.dev]` in the workspace Cargo.toml already carries the finding: *"cargo has no GC. target/debug/deps held 1,824 artifacts under 104 distinct names (43 copies of the reflow2_mcp test binary alone); sweeping the stale duplicates recovered 225 GiB. Sweep first when the disk is tight; these settings only slow the refill."*

That comment is still true and is NOT superseded — it describes an earlier sweep. What is new: **1,824 artifacts became 159,247 for these two crates**, and the comment says WHAT happened without naming the command that does it safely. That gap is what cost this session a failed test run.

⚠️ NOT MEASURED, so the number is not read wider than it is: how fast it refills per workspace run. Four runs happened between the previous healthy state and the wall, but nothing sampled the growth in between, so "a few runs fills a disk" is an inference from two endpoints rather than a rate.

═══ WHERE THIS BEARS ON AN OPEN QUESTION ═══

`dec:idea-a-byte-backend-that-compiles-in-seconds` records that RocksDB's DISK cost is uncontested even though its COMPILE cost turned out not to be what made this session slow (measured: zero RocksDB recompiles across three long builds). This measurement sharpens both halves — RocksDB's 856 MB artifact is real but is 0.3% of what actually filled the disk. **A backend swap would not have prevented this.**

REFLOW2 CAN ALREADY JUDGE TEST QUALITY STRUCTURALLY, ON THREE AXES, AND TWO OF THEM HAVE NEVER BEEN USED. Measured 2026-08-11 while asking where the line falls between test quality reflow2 can check and test quality only a person can judge.

THE LINE IS FURTHER OUT THAN IT LOOKED. The claim under test was that a test's quality is textual — valid, isolated, repeatable, focused, fast, covers edge cases and error conditions — and therefore out of reach for a deterministic core (`req:deterministic-core`). That is only partly true, and the interesting part is which half.

MEASURED:

  Verifications                                                  137
  targets per check          1 -> 130    2 -> 6    3 -> 1
  ⇒ FOCUS is already good here. 130 of 137 check exactly one thing, so a
    focus detector modelled on granularity_report would find nothing on this
    design. A useful NEGATIVE result: the metric exists and the problem does not.

  THE THREE BUILT EVIDENCE-QUALITY AXES, IN USE:
    TIME   (how old the check is)             99 of 137 carry last_run_at
    INPUT  (what it PINNED vs SWEPT)          0 VERIFIES edges carry a scope
    INDEP  (was the value fitted to it)       0 CALIBRATED_AGAINST edges

  detectors mentioning scope, narrowness or circularity           0
  surface for the two unused axes    evidence_report, confirmation_ledger
                                     — read-only, and you must know to call them

⭐ SO THE EDGE-CASE QUESTION IS ALREADY ANSWERABLE STRUCTURALLY. `set_evidence_scope` records what a check PINNED versus SWEPT, and `evidence_report` reads it: "a parameter every passing check pins is reported as NARROW; ONE check that sweeps it ends the narrowness." That is a machine-checkable proxy for "does the suite explore the boundaries" — exactly one of the eight criteria that looked textual. `req:evidence-says-what-it-covered` is ACCEPTED. The machinery is 3 functions, 643 lines of test, 18 cases, mutation-checked on all three axes.

⚠️⚠️ AND IT IS THE CONTENT STORE'S PROFILE EXACTLY. `dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued` (accepted, 2026-08-09) reads: "built, shipped, correct, and used zero times in every project that has it." Two of these three axes are in that same state today. The parallel is not loose — both had an accepted requirement behind them, both were carefully built, both were tested well, and neither was ever reached for.

📌 THE FORK THIS OPENS, and it is real rather than rhetorical:
  (a) MAKE THEM ASKED-FOR. A detector — "this passing check does not say what it covered" — would surface the axes at the moment a check is recorded. Cheap, and it is the fourth instance today of the same diagnosis: the capability exists and nothing asks for it.
  (b) DISCONTINUE THEM, on the test that killed the content store. There is now a mechanism for exactly that, shipped hours ago: an accepted Decision OBSOLETES what it withdrew, and four computations read it.
  (c) NEITHER YET — zero usage on ONE design is thin evidence, and this design is the author's own. A consumer project's suite is where narrowness would actually bite.

⭐⭐ WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PHILOSOPHY QUESTION IT IS FILED AGAINST. `dec:idea-verification-is-planned-with-the-requirement` proposes that reflow2 guide a project to plan verification when a need is stated. This measurement is a warning about HOW: reflow2 has already built test-quality machinery once and nobody used it, because nothing asked. Adding requirement-side planning WITHOUT asking would repeat that exactly — and would be the fifth instance today of a capability that exists and never fires.

WHAT REMAINS GENUINELY TEXTUAL, and is not claimed to be checkable: VALID (does it measure what it claims, or a side effect), HAPPY PATH and ERROR CONDITIONS coverage, and whether a test reads the CONTRACT or the IMPLEMENTATION — that last being `dec:bl-185`, still open. ISOLATED, REPEATABLE and FAST are not textual but are simply ABSENT: the graph records no run history (one `last_run_at`, overwritten), no duration, and no dependency between checks, so a proxy for them would need new data rather than a new reading.

properties.name: The three-legs audit, finally run over the surface
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-26, answering Anthony's question — *"I believe there are '3 legs' that certain skills need — have they been applied to all skills uniformly?"* The audit had never been run. It has now, over the WHOLE declared vocabulary rather than the three items `fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs-and-a-users-project-gets-none-of-it` sampled.

SCOPE: all 64 edge types + 29 node types the schema declares = 93. For each, the three legs — (1) a TYPED TOOL that writes it, (2) an INSTRUCTION in a served skill or tool description saying WHEN, (3) a DETECTOR that notices its ABSENCE.

═══ THE ANSWER: NO, NOT UNIFORMLY ═══

  all three legs      54  (58%)
  tool + instruction  8   (no detector)
  instruction + detector 7 (no tool)
  tool only           7
  tool + detector     1
  instruction only    2
  detector only       1
  ⭐ NO LEGS AT ALL   13  (14%)

═══ 🛑 THE SHARPEST FINDING: FIVE TYPES EXIST ONLY IN THE SCHEMA ═══

`COMPLIES_WITH`, `IMPOSES`, `OPERATES_IN`, `SUPPLEMENTS`, `VIOLATES_RULE` are declared in the schema and appear in ZERO Rust source files, ZERO served skills, and ZERO tool descriptions. Nothing writes them, nothing instructs them, nothing detects them, and no code even names them. `OPERATES_IN` nevertheless has 3 edges in reflow2's own graph — written through raw `create_edge`, which is precisely the escape hatch the three-legs rule says must not count as reachability.

The other eight leg-less types: `ANNOTATES` (11 edges), `ASSESSED_ON`, `CONTAINS_EPOCH`, `EnvironmentRule`, `HAS_SNAPSHOT` (188 edges), `OBSERVED_IN`, `OCCURS_DURING`, `QualityGate`. ALL THIRTEEN share one property: **zero mentions in the MCP layer, zero in any served skill, zero in any tool description.** An agent working a user's project cannot learn these exist by any route reflow2 offers.

⭐ `HAS_SNAPSHOT` IS THE INSTRUCTIVE ONE. It carries 188 edges here, so it plainly WORKS — `record_change` writes it internally. But no skill and no tool description ever names it, so leg 1 is satisfied only by accident of another tool's implementation, and legs 2 and 3 are genuinely absent. Vocabulary can be heavily used and still be unreachable BY INTENT.

═══ THE DECOMPOSES PATTERN, CONFIRMED AND NOT ALONE ═══

Five types have ALL THREE LEGS and zero instances here: `CLAIMS`, `DECOMPOSES`, `DUPLICATES`, `MASKS`, `PRODUCES`. `DECOMPOSES` was the case that first exposed the hidden qualifier on leg 3 — a detector that checks the consistency of what EXISTS cannot ask why none exists — and the audit finds four siblings. This is direct evidence for the FOURTH-LEG hypothesis in `dec:idea-have-the-three-legs-been-applied-uniformly-and-are-three-legs-enough`: three legs present, practice still absent.

═══ ⚠️ HONEST LIMITS, AND THE FIRST VERSION WAS WRONG ═══

THIS IS A MECHANICAL PROXY. A mention is not an instruction and a reference is not an absence-detector, so every YES is an UPPER BOUND: real coverage can only be worse than 58%, never better.

THE FIRST RUN PRODUCED JUNK AND WAS DISCARDED. v1 matched case-sensitively (so `DECOMPOSES` in detect.rs was missed and it reported no detector, contradicting a recorded fact) and derived leg 1 from the type NAME (so `ALLOCATED_TO` read as having no tool, when `allocate` writes it). Both bugs inflated the failure count. v2 resolves leg 1 through the core methods a served tool actually calls, and counts a tool whose DESCRIPTION enumerates the type — `review_relations` names thirteen inference relations that way, and without that rule they read as unreachable when they are not.

THE 13 LEG-LESS TYPES WERE HAND-VERIFIED against the whole repo rather than trusted from the proxy. The 54 were not.

📌 `vocabulary_coverage` was checked FIRST, per the option (b) instruction to look before building. It answers a DIFFERENT question — which vocabulary ONE DESIGN has used (43/64 edge types, 23/29 node types here) — and is per-design, not per-surface. It is nevertheless a partial answer to leg 3's hidden qualifier: it is the one computation that asks 'you have never used this at all', which `fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs` said nothing did.

FOUND BY BREAKING IT, 2026-08-18. Adding one tool (`set_capability_signature`) turned a green workspace red: `find_tools` stopped returning `link_artifact` for the query 'register a file that realizes a capability'.

THE MEASUREMENT. The top six scored 28, 27, 26, 26, 25, 24 — a one-point near-tie across the whole visible band, with the default limit of 5. So the fifth and sixth places were separated by noise, and any new tool mentioning a common word displaced whatever was fifth.

THE CAUSE was in `score_tool`: every query term contributed the same weight regardless of how many tools mentioned it. 'capability' appears in dozens of descriptions; 'file' in a handful. Treating them equally is what compressed the band. There was no inverse document frequency anywhere in the catalogue, while `search_design` next door has used BM25 over Tantivy for months.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE TEST: THE CATALOGUE WAS UNSTABLE UNDER ITS OWN GROWTH. With 152 tools and rising, any addition could silently evict the right answer for a query nobody was thinking about — and `req:agent-native` promises every capability is reachable over one surface, which is only true if an agent can FIND the tool. The failure mode is silent by construction: nothing tells you the answer you needed was sixth.

FIXED AT THE ROOT rather than by widening the assertion or trimming the new tool's description, both of which were available and both of which would have hidden it. Term weights are now ln(1 + N/df). Measured after: 49.5, 38.3, 32.1, 29.1, 29.1, 28.8 — the band spread out, and `link_artifact` moved from 6th to 3rd.

⚠️ AND THE EVIDENCE WAS NEARLY LOST. The first workspace run was piped through `awk` to total the results, which discarded every failure line and left only 'workspace: 1314 passed, 1 failed' — no test name, no assertion. Same class as the remembered `cargo test | grep | head` trap in a new costume: A SUMMARISING PIPELINE IS A TRUNCATING PIPELINE. Re-run with full output to a file, the name and the assertion were both there.

properties.name: The `rocksdb` crate has resumed releasing (0.25), which removes the strongest argument for the rust-rocksdb switch — and the stale sentence sits in the workspace manifest, not in the decision
properties.statement:
REPORTED BY ANTHONY, 2026-08-29: the official `rocksdb` crate has resumed updates and is at 0.25. Recorded at confidence 0.7 because it is his report rather than something measured here; `cargo info rocksdb` would settle it.

═══ WHY IT MATTERS, AND IT IS NOT THE PARK ═══

`dec:the-rust-rocksdb-switch-is-parked-until-the-store-question-settles` is UNAFFECTED. Its stated reason is not maintenance status — it is that the migration is *"an 86-file change to the one component that may be retired"*, blocked on `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability`. That question is still open, so the park still stands and this news does not unpark it.

⭐ WHAT IT DOES BEAR ON IS THE OTHER DECISION. `dec:absorb-rocksdb-024-unchanged-then-switch-separately` says the switch is owed, and the strongest argument for it was that the official wrapper was abandoned while `rust-rocksdb` was maintained. **If upstream is releasing again, that argument is gone** — which makes the switch a candidate for SUPERSEDED rather than for action.

═══ 🛑 THE STALE SENTENCE IS IN THE MANIFEST, WHICH IS THE DANGEROUS PART ═══

`[workspace.dependencies]` in the root Cargo.toml carries this comment beside the pin: *"`rocksdb` is the historically-unmaintained wrapper; `rust-rocksdb` (0.52) is the maintained one and is where this should end up."*

That is the sentence a session reads BEFORE it ever reaches either decision node, and it sits in the exact file somebody would edit to bump the pin. The park node anticipated the misreading almost word for word — it warns the switch *"reads as tidy housekeeping — an unmaintained crate, a maintained replacement, and a version number that looks far behind"* — and it correctly notes the version gap is illusory, since `rocksdb` 0.24 and `rust-rocksdb` 0.52 are different crates on independent numbering. But it could not know upstream would revive.

⭐ THE SHAPE, AND IT IS THE THIRD SIGHTING IN TWO DAYS: a record whose CONCLUSION still stands while its JUSTIFICATION quietly stopped being true. The others are `fact:defect-the-served-instructions-put-their-standing-rules-where-a-client-cap-deletes-them` (the defect was real; its self-sealing explanation measured false) and `fact:a-retired-dependencys-facts-keep-describing-this-project` (true when written, false once the dependency was absorbed). None is caught by re-running anything, because the conclusion still reproduces.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that `rocksdb` 0.25 should be adopted. That is a separate call with its own cost — AGENTS.md warns the pin carries a long recompile — and it is a version bump within the SAME crate, which is a third thing distinct from both the switch and the store question. Nor does it establish that `rust-rocksdb` is now the wrong choice on other grounds; only that the maintenance argument no longer carries it.

properties.description:
⭐ THIS IS THE `rule:reflow2-is-built-for-other-projects-not-for-itself` TEST, APPLIED TO WORK BUILT THE SAME HOUR, AND IT FAILED. Anthony's standing instruction is to ask `find_tools` the question a USER would ask, in their words. Two queries, one job:

    "has the design I depend on moved since I declared it"          → 3rd of 5, found
    "tell me when the other team changes their design so my
     project knows it is out of date"                                → ABSENT from the top 5

In the second, the top hit is `invalidates` — a tool for marking a finding stale, which has nothing to do with the question.

🛑 THE DIAGNOSIS IS `tool_not_found`, NOT `tool_missing`, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT. The capability exists, is verified, and is served. A session that needed it and hand-rolled a `git diff` on somebody else's export instead would be a DISCOVERABILITY failure — a different repair from building anything. `cap:a-session-reports-the-work-it-did-by-hand` exists to catch exactly that class, and this is a case where the failure is predictable in advance rather than discovered afterwards.

⭐ WHY IT FAILS, and it is mechanical rather than mysterious. `find_tools` is BM25 over the served name, description and parameter names. The description is written in this design's own nouns — DEPENDS ON, declaration, upstream, moved. The words a user reaches for are not in it: *other team*, *out of date*, *stale*, *notify*, *tell me when*, *changed*, *sibling*, *partner*. None of those appear anywhere in the served text, so there is nothing for the ranking to match.

⚠️ THE FIX IS WORDING, NOT A TOOL — and it is deliberately NOT applied here, because a description is the surface an agent binds to and `toolsnap` makes every change to it a reviewed artifact. Rewording it is a real change to the shipped surface and belongs in a change somebody looked at, not smuggled in beside the feature it critiques.

⚠️ AND THE SAME MEASUREMENT SHOULD BE RUN ON THE REST OF THE SURFACE BEFORE ANY FIX. One tool reworded is one tool; if the surface is systematically written in reflow2's nouns — which the 164 descriptions plausibly are, since they were all written by people building reflow2 — then the finding is about the SURFACE and a per-tool patch is the wrong shape of repair. Nobody has measured that.

🛑 NOTHING DETECTS THIS. There is no check that a served tool is reachable from the words its users would use, and the third leg of `fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs-and-a-users-project-gets-none-of-it` — A DETECTOR THAT NOTICES ABSENCE — is missing here exactly as it is elsewhere. This finding was produced by a human instruction followed by hand, not by anything the system does on its own.
properties.name: The upstream watch is findable only by someone who already speaks reflow2 — in a user's own words it does not surface, and an unrelated tool ranks first
properties.statement: MEASURED against the live 164-tool surface the hour it shipped. Asked in reflow2's vocabulary — 'has the design I depend on moved since I declared it' — `upstream_status` ranks 3rd of 5. Asked in a USER's words for the same job — 'tell me when the other team changes their design so my project knows it is out of date' — it does NOT APPEAR IN THE TOP 5 AT ALL, and `invalidates`, an unrelated tool, ranks first.

properties.name: v0.38.0 was tagged with an empty INCLUDES manifest because release_includes_all defaults to a dry run and its success reads identically
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-21, in the v0.38.0 cut, and found only because a completeness audit was run AFTER the tag was already pushed.

`release_includes_all` **defaults to a DRY RUN** (`apply: false`). Its response says so — the payload carries `"applied": false` beside `"added": 304`. I called it twice, checked `isError` both times, saw no error and the number 304, and moved on. **v0.38.0 was tagged, built, published and verified with an EMPTY manifest: 0 INCLUDES edges against v0.37.0's 275.**

⭐ THE DEFAULT IS RIGHT AND IS NOT THE DEFECT. Its own description gives the reason: "the derivation is reported and nothing is written, so you can read what a release is about to package before you package it." A tool that writes 304 edges on a bare call would be worse. The dry run is a good design.

🛑 THE DEFECT IS THAT A DRY RUN AND A WRITE ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE TO EVERY CHECK THAT RAN. `isError` was false in both cases — correctly, since nothing failed. `added: 304` reads as an accomplishment and is actually a FORECAST. And the release's own gates all passed over the empty manifest: `reflow2_check` OK, `release_report` was never called, and nothing anywhere asks whether a Release about to ship has any INCLUDES at all.

📌 THIS IS `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` FAILING ON A NEW SURFACE. That rule was written for `gh pr merge`, whose local half fails while the merge lands — read the PR object, not the CLI. The same shape here: the authoritative object is the RELEASE (`release_report` returns 215 artifacts / 89 components / 190 capabilities when it worked, and `artifacts: []` when it had not), and I read the CALL instead.

⇒ TWO REMEDIES, NEITHER BUILT:
  (1) A DETECTOR: a Release with an AT_EPOCH edge, a deploy, and ZERO INCLUDES is a release record that claims to have shipped nothing. Nothing reports it. It sits beside the known sibling `nothing detects a Release with no epoch`, and it is the same class.
  (2) The release procedure should END by reading `release_report`, not by reading the last write's return value. A cut is verified the way the published assets are verified — off the object, after the fact.

📌 CORRECTED THE SAME DAY: re-run with `apply: true`, 304 edges written, `release_report` now returns 215/89/190. The tag and the published binaries were never wrong; only the design's record of what they contained was.

A TWO-ARM TRIAL RUN ON REFLOW2 ITSELF, at Anthony's direction and in his framing: 'reflow2 is like a doctor who develops a new medicine, but tries it on himself first before the public.' The candidate was option (b) of `dec:idea-how-does-a-users-project-acquire-vocabulary-it-never-uses` — report vocabulary a design has never used — reshaped as a COVERAGE STATEMENT rather than a gap list. Computed portably: schema read from the SERVER via `describe_schema`, corpus from the graph's own export, nothing about reflow2's file layout involved, so this is what any project would get.

  ARM 1 — MATURE (reflow2's own, 2535 nodes / 10362 edges)
    node types 22/29 (75%)   edge types 37/61 (60%)   properties 141/169 (83%)
    flat list would be 59 items
  ARM 2 — DAY ONE (immediately after `genesis`, 2 nodes / 0 edges)
    node types 2/29 (6%)     edge types 0/61 (0%)     properties 9/18 (50%)
    flat list would be 97 items

⭐ THE TRIAL CONFIRMED THE OBJECTION AND SPLIT THE FEATURE IN TWO. The FIGURES pass both arms: '0 of 61 edge types' on a day-one design is not noise, it is a true and useful statement that nothing has yet been said about how anything relates. The FLAT LIST fails arm 2 outright — 97 items handed to a user thirty seconds into their project, MORE than the 59 a mature design produces. So the list ships as drill-down on request, never as standing output. Had this been shipped on the argument alone it would have been at its worst for exactly the users it was meant to help.

⭐⭐ TWO THINGS THE TRIAL PRODUCED THAT NO AMOUNT OF ARGUING HAD:

(1) THE UNUSED VOCABULARY CLUSTERS INTO WHOLE SUBSYSTEMS, and reads as about four findings rather than 31. Flow: `Flow` node type plus PART_OF_FLOW / PERFORMED_IN / PRODUCES / TRIGGERS. Dimensions and readiness: `DimensionObservation`, `DimensionAssessment`, `ReadinessAssessment` plus HAS_OBSERVATION / HAS_READINESS / OBSERVED_IN / CALIBRATED_AGAINST. Quality gates: `QualityGate` plus GATED_ON. Governance and risk: COMPLIES_WITH / IMPOSES / MITIGATES / VIOLATES_RULE. So the output should GROUP, and a grouped answer on a mature design is short enough to read every time.

(2) THE REPORT MUST BE PARKABLE OR IT WILL NAG ABOUT A SETTLED DECISION. `OWNED_BY` is in the unused list, and its absence is DELIBERATE — `dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge` says OWNED_BY is added only if claims prove insufficient. A coverage report that cannot be told 'this one is on purpose' would report a correct decision as a hole forever, which is `req:a-deliberate-state-is-not-a-defect` exactly. The `ruling: parks` mechanism shipped 2026-08-17 is what it needs, and neither piece was designed with the other in mind.

NOT BUILT. The trial was run to decide the SHAPE before building, which was the agreement. What it decided: ship the figures, group the list, make it parkable, and keep the flat list behind a request.

MEASURED 2026-08-17 by comparing the design's CONSUMES edges against what the code actually imports. THREE OF THE FIVE `ifc:req-dyno-*` interfaces are consumed, in the graph, by a component that does not use them in the build.

  interface                     design says CONSUMED BY   code actually imports it in
  ifc:req-dyno-graph-api        cmp:propagate             structure.rs, allocate.rs, flow.rs  (cmp:structure / cmp:allocate / cmp:flow)
  ifc:req-dyno-vector-api       cmp:search                dimensions.rs                       (cmp:dimensions)
  ifc:req-dyno-resolution-api   cmp:heal                  seam.rs, ingest.rs                  (cmp:seam / cmp:ingest)
  ifc:req-dyno-core-api         cmp:graph                 graph.rs and throughout             CORRECT
  ifc:req-dyno-storage-api      sys:store                 the store                           CORRECT

VERIFIED BOTH WAYS: `propagate.rs` contains no `use dynograph_graph`, `search.rs` no `use dynograph_vector`, `heal.rs` no `use dynograph_resolution`; while `structure.rs`, `dimensions.rs` and `seam.rs` each do. And `art:structure` REALIZES `cmp:structure`, which is a different node from `cmp:propagate`, so this is misattribution rather than a naming synonym.

WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN ITS SIZE. A CONSUMES edge is a black-box boundary claim: it says WHICH PART of this system depends on that supplier. Three of five point at the wrong part, so the design's answer to 'what breaks if the graph API changes?' names `cmp:propagate` and misses the three components that would actually break. That matters directly for `dec:a-black-box-needs-three-edges-not-one` and any future SE work on the subsystem tier, because those are the same edges the black-box decomposition will rest on.

PLAUSIBLE CAUSE, not verified: the edges look like they were drawn from what each interface is FOR (propagation is the graph-algorithm-shaped feature, search is the vector-shaped feature, heal is the fuzzy-matching-shaped feature) rather than from what imports what. That is a reasonable-sounding guess written down once and never checked against the build — which is the class of error `reconcile_artifacts` catches for FILES and nothing catches for EDGES.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════
✅ REPAIRED 2026-08-19 on Anthony's word ("do both 1 & 2"), and it is a resync of the RECORD, not a fix to the system — the code was right throughout. `chg:foundation-consumes-redrawn-from-imports-2026-08-19`, change_type `resync`, subject `record`.

THE IMPORTS WERE RE-VERIFIED AGAINST CURRENT HEAD before anything was redrawn, rather than trusting this two-day-old measurement, and they were unchanged:
  dynograph_graph      -> allocate.rs, flow.rs, structure.rs
  dynograph_vector     -> dimensions.rs
  dynograph_resolution -> ingest.rs, seam.rs

RETRACTED (3): cmp:propagate -> graph-api, cmp:search -> vector-api, cmp:heal -> resolution-api.
DRAWN (5), each `weight_basis: evidence` because they come from imports rather than from a guess:
  ifc:req-dyno-graph-api      <- cmp:structure, cmp:allocate, cmp:flow
  ifc:req-dyno-vector-api     <- cmp:dimensions  (optional, weight 0.4)
  ifc:req-dyno-resolution-api <- cmp:ingest

Note the shape change: one interface now has THREE consumers where the design claimed one. The old edges were not merely mis-pointed, they were under-counted — 'what breaks if the graph API changes?' had one answer and now has three.

⚠️ DID THE REPAIR REACH THE CAUSE? PARTLY, AND THE HONEST ANSWER IS NO.
· The three wrong edges are corrected — that is the symptom.
· THE CAUSE IS UNADDRESSED: nothing checks a CONSUMES edge against what the build actually imports. `reconcile_artifacts` does exactly this job for FILES and there is no equivalent for EDGES, which is what let a plausible guess sit unchallenged from whenever it was drawn until 2026-08-17. Until something computes it, the next such edge will be as wrong and as unnoticed.

🛑 AND ONE ENDPOINT COULD NOT BE DRAWN, so the repair is incomplete on its own terms. `seam.rs` imports `dynograph_resolution` and there is NO `cmp:seam` — the original measurement named one, and it does not exist. `art:seam` and `art:seam-test` are registered and REALIZE no Component at all. Rather than invent a component to complete a tidy picture, the edge was left undrawn and the gap recorded here: ifc:req-dyno-resolution-api has ONE consumer in the graph and TWO in the build.
