properties.statement:
THE OTHER SIDE OF A LEDGER THAT NODE SAYS IS MISSING. `dec:idea-search-first-fires-without-being-remembered` records SIX measured saves from one session on 2026-08-12, and names its own limit in the same breath: '⚠️ SURVIVORSHIP BIAS, NAMED SO SIX IS NOT READ AS A RATE. Only the times it worked are visible; NOTHING RECORDS A SEARCH THAT DID NOT HAPPEN.' This records three that did not happen, in one session, 2026-08-17. All three were failures on the READ path, which is the unguarded one that node identifies.

1. `loop_status` reported '1 answered question never reached the design'. RELAYED TO ANTHONY AS FACT WITHOUT LOOKING. The answer had been in the graph since 2026-08-11 as `dec:the-authority-check-guards-forward-not-backward`, accepted and approver-signed. COST: a false statement to the owner about his own design, plus a wasted line of enquiry. (Separately a real defect in loop_status: `fact:defect-loop-status-asserts-an-answer-never-reached-the-design-from-a-fact-that-cannot-say-so`.)

2. TOLD ANTHONY dynograph-game had 'no obvious fit today, and forcing one would be over-engineering'. `dec:idea-interop-as-a-game` had existed since the 2026-08-01 review, calling itself 'the most interesting idea in the batch', with a fit to HIS OWN stated multi-organisation context and `nash_is_pareto_suboptimal` named as the interoperability tragedy. COST: an idea he had already had, argued against by an agent that had not read it.

3. DESCRIBED the SE-on-reflow2 work as 'intent, not a schedule' and declined to create the increment on that basis. `dec:idea-should-reflow2s-own-design-be-re-derived-through-a-principled-se-process` was ACCEPTED on his word 2026-08-16, with sequencing part of the ruling. COST: the declining was right for a different reason than the one given, and the reason given misdescribed his own settled decision back to him.

⭐ WHAT THE THREE HAVE IN COMMON, and it sharpens that node's option list rather than restating it: none involved a tool call at all. Each was an ASSERTION IN PROSE about what the graph does or does not hold. The write guard cannot fire because nothing was being written; option (A)'s difficulty ('it needs to know what the user asked, which the tool layer never sees') is exactly the shape of all three.

⭐⭐ AND THE SHARPER READING: the six saves were an agent CHOOSING to look and being rewarded. These three were an agent not looking and being WRONG IN FRONT OF THE OWNER. Those are different costs. A missed save is work redone; a missed check is the design brain telling its owner something false about his own design, which is the failure `epoch:instruments-stop-overstating` spent five requirements on — arriving here through the agent rather than through a tool.

⚠️ STILL NOT A RATE. Three failures are visible because they were caught, two of them by later searches in the same session. Nothing counts the ones never caught, and this fact inherits that limit whole.

**FOUR OPERATIONAL LESSONS FROM SHIPPING FIVE PRs AND ONE RELEASE IN A DAY (2026-08-19). THREE WERE CAUGHT BY A GATE; ONE WAS CAUGHT BY GITHUB REFUSING.** Recorded because each would otherwise be re-learned, and none is visible in the commits.

🛑🛑 **1. NEVER `--delete-branch` A PR THAT ANOTHER PR IS STACKED ON.** Merging #248 with `--delete-branch` removed the base branch of #249, and **GitHub CLOSED #249 permanently — a closed PR whose base is gone CANNOT BE REOPENED** (`Cannot change the base branch of a closed pull request`). Nothing was lost: the branch itself survived, it was rebased onto the new main (git correctly recognised the already-applied commit and skipped it), and #250 replaced it. **Merge a stack bottom-up and delete afterwards.** No gate caught this; GitHub's refusal did.

🛑 **2. A REBASE SILENTLY INVALIDATES ARTIFACT CHECKSUMS.** Rebasing onto #248 changed `capture-intent/SKILL.md` and `AGENTS.md` — **files nobody edited** — so the checksums recorded minutes earlier went stale and design-vs-build silently disagreed. **`reflow2_check` was the only thing that caught it**, failing the branch until both were re-accepted as `design_updated`. ⭐ Worth keeping because it is the gate justifying itself on a change that was itself about the loop being too pushy: **run `reflow2_check` after any rebase, not only after an edit.**

🛑 **3. THE DESIGN GRAPH DOES NOT BRANCH WITH GIT, AND A RELEASE EXPORT IS WHERE THAT BITES.** During the v0.36.0 cut the live store already held an UNMERGED branch's nodes, and `cap:the-skill-response-carries-the-lens` sat at `realized`. **Exporting that would have made the release claim it shipped code that is not in it.** Caught by diffing the LIVE store against the previous tag rather than trusting the committed export — the same diff that found **14 ChangeEvents in the increment, not the 13 the export showed** (the extra being the cut's own `reflow2.toml` accept, created minutes before). **Diff the live store against the tag; the export is stale by construction at that moment.**

⚠️ **4. A `grep -c` OVER COMMIT OUTPUT IS NOT A COUNT OF COMMITS.** `git log --name-only | grep -c <path>` returned 2 for the one-commit-may-export rule and looked like a violation; the second hit was the path written inside a commit MESSAGE. **The per-commit check is the reliable form.** Same family as the piped-gate exit code in `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object`.

📌 WHAT THESE SHARE, and why they are one fact rather than four: **every one is a case where the thing measured was not the thing meant** — a branch deletion whose blast radius was another PR, a file that changed without an edit, an export that was not the live state, a count that was not counting commits. That is the shape `rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` already names, arriving four more times in a single day, which is itself the recurrence that rule cannot currently accumulate (`fact:the-gh-merge-failure-is-snap-confinement-and-nobody-was-counting`).

ANTHONY, 2026-08-14: *"as always is the case is that we are using reflow2 to design itself, but nothing is for reflow2 itself. what we do for reflow2 should be generalizable to whoever is using reflow2 on a project."*

🛑 **THE TEST APPLIED TO WHAT HAD JUST BEEN DONE, AND IT FAILS.** Three DesignRules were created minutes earlier from this session's lessons. **A DesignRule lives in THIS graph and governs THIS design.** A consumer project has its own graph and its own rules; nothing seeds these into it. So all three made the lessons findable BY US and delivered nothing to anybody using reflow2. That is correct for a rule about how this project works — `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` should not travel — but it does NOT discharge a lesson that is general.

⭐ **THE VEHICLES THAT ACTUALLY GENERALISE** are the ones served rather than stored: the SKILLS (compiled into the binary, so every project gets the current one), the TOOL BEHAVIOUR (detectors, report shapes, what a command prints), the served INSTRUCTIONS (`get_instructions`), and the KIT (`reflow2_check.py`, `reflow2_init.py`). reflow2's own graph nodes reach nobody.

═══ ✅ MEASURED: THE `ci-gate` SKILL IS THE GENERAL HOME FOR TODAY'S GATE LESSONS, AND IT IS SILENT ON ALL OF THEM ═══

Read in full 2026-08-14. It is served to every project that wants a design gate, and:

**1. IT INVITES THE ORDERING FAILURE IT DOES NOT WARN ABOUT.** Step 3 says *"Run it locally first (`python3 <kit>/tools/reflow2_check.py --export design.json`) so the first CI run is not the first run."* **Nothing says to run it AFTER committing.** `fact:the-lineage-gate-verdict-depends-on-when-you-run-it` measured the consequence on this project the same day: the identical file FAILED before an amend and PASSED after, because the gate compares against the export committed at HEAD. A user following this skill literally as written gets a verdict about a commit that may be about to change.

**2. IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT PIPING THE GATE.** `fact:a-piped-gate-reports-the-pipes-exit-code-not-the-gates` is a measured failure on this project — `cargo test | grep | tail` reported success because a pipeline's exit code is its LAST command's. The skill's own CI snippet is unpiped and therefore correct by luck, and a user who pipes it to filter noise gets a green build from `grep`. **`rule:success-is-read-from-the-authoritative-object` was just ENFORCED on Anthony's word, and the skill that configures the gate does not carry it.**

**3. 🛑 IT UNDER-DESCRIBES THE GATE IT CONFIGURES.** *"What it checks, and what makes it fail"* lists exactly two failure modes — unaccepted DRIFT and an open anchored GAP at/above threshold — plus exit 2 for could-not-run. **LINEAGE is not mentioned anywhere**, and a LINEAGE failure is what actually turned this session red (`FAIL LINEAGE 'docs/design/reflow2.json' does not link to the export it replaced`). A user hitting it would find no explanation in the skill that set the gate up, and the skill's *"When the build goes red"* section has no entry for it.

⇒ **SO THE GENERAL FORM OF EVERY GATE LESSON THIS SESSION LEARNED HAS AN EXISTING, SERVED, PROJECT-AGNOSTIC HOME — AND THAT HOME IS CURRENTLY EMPTY ON ALL THREE COUNTS.** The lessons were recorded where they help this project's maintainers and not where they would reach the people the tool is for.

📌 THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE WORTH KEEPING, in his framing: **reflow2 designing itself is a TEST HARNESS, not the point.** Every finding from self-hosting should be asked one question before it is filed — *does this land in the served surface, or only in our own graph?* — and a finding that lands only in our own graph is unfinished work rather than a completed capture. `rule:the-self-host-always-trails-what-it-teaches` is the nearest existing node and says something adjacent but not this: it explains why reflow2's own design lags, not that self-host findings owe a served fix.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the other served skills carry the same shape of omission. Only `ci-gate` was read against this session's evidence; `link-artifacts`, `check-health` and `parallel-work` all touch the export and were not checked.

properties.name: COUNTED across one session: twelve places where a record still read confident after the thing it described had moved — and the tools caught seven of them unprompted
properties.statement:
SYNTHESIS OF ONE SESSION, 2026-08-21, eight merged PRs (#281–#288). Recorded because the pattern exists in no single node — each instance is written on its own node and none of them says there were twelve.

THE SHAPE: a record goes on asserting something after the thing it describes has moved, and nothing about the record looks wrong. It is not a wrong record; it is a record that has stopped being checked against anything.

=== THE INSTANCES, all found or fixed this session ===

  1. `rel:v0380` carried `status: planned` while tagged, published, deployed and asset-verified.
  2. `release_without_epoch` exempted any `planned` release — so it would have excused exactly the release above. A status field trusted where an edge was the truth.
  3. `dec:one-process-many-stores` — `status: accepted`, name "ACCEPTED 2026-08-06", body opening "PROPOSED, NOT SETTLED."
  4. `dec:core-api-spof-accepted` named a topology BL-83a had moved; the judgement was right and the sentence was stale.
  5. `ifc:core-api` was `published` — in the document handed to a vendor — for a crate nobody outside can link.
  6. `ifc:core-api`'s `spec` field held a 2026-07-28 changelog note where the specification belongs.
  7. `ifc:core-api`'s `payload_schema` read `unspecified` while ELEVEN artifacts carried SPECIFIES edges at it.
  8. `ifc:kv-backend` (dynograph-foundation) is `published` in the design and `pub(crate)` in the code.
  9. `unverified_capability` asked 28 unbuilt roadmap rows to prove themselves — a list that could not reach zero.
 10. `open_questions`, the first call of every session and documented as cheap, costs 11.7s of which 10.3 is a defect sweep nobody asked for; and "the first store read costs 26–48s" had been carried for weeks as the STORE being slow, which it is not.
 11. `seam_report` returned `incompatible: 0` beside `unstated: 30`, and the August PoC's `unmet_needs: 0` beside `dead_surface: 15` — zeros that read as health and mean nobody said anything.
 12. An analysis was RE-DERIVED that `dec:linked-repos-poc` had already done, better, on 2026-08-06.

⭐ THE FIX WAS THE SAME SHAPE EVERY TIME, AND IT WAS NEVER MORE PROSE. Each one closed by making the disagreement VISIBLE somewhere that fails: a detector keyed on an edge rather than a status; a gate that turns red; a count asserted in a test; a field that says "this cannot be enumerated" instead of sitting blank; a note recording that somebody looked and found nothing. A promise written in a decision is not a guard — that recurred three times on its own (the release procedure, the SPOF description, and the local-case protection flo2's work would test).

⭐⭐ AND THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE MATTERS MORE THAN THE COUNT. SEVEN of the twelve were caught by the design's own machinery, unprompted, while doing something else:
  — the dedup guard refused four near-duplicate writes and named what to read;
  — `create_node`'s revision note said "no snapshot holds the state it replaced — checked, not assumed", which is the only reason a Decision's prior wording survives;
  — compare-and-swap refused a stale hash;
  — the export divergence guard refused to drop a claim edge and named it;
  — `reflow2_check` refused a severed lineage chain mid-fold;
  — `loop_status` reported its OWN server as stale, which is why the performance numbers were re-measured rather than trusted;
  — `seam_report` refused to call 30 unstated axes agreement.
So the pattern is not that the design rots unnoticed. It is that the design notices exactly where somebody built a place for it to notice, and nowhere else.

⚠️ LIMITS. "Twelve" is a count of what one session happened to touch, not a survey — nobody swept the design for this shape, and a sweep would find more. Instances 1–9 are verifiable on their nodes; 10 and 11 are on their own TemporalFacts; 12 is recorded on `fact:the-seam-report-half-of-the-poc-finally-ran`. The claim that the fix was "the same shape every time" is a reading of twelve cases by the agent that worked them, and is the softest thing here.

MEASURED 2026-08-13 by reading identity sidecars only, never opening a store. Seven reflow2 designs under ~/project carry an identity file. TWO OF THEM ANSWER TO THE SAME NAME:

  ~/project/reflow2/.reflow2/graph.id.json        graph_id "reflow2"  label "reflow2"        origin adopted
  ~/project/dev_storyflow/.reflow2/graph.id.json  graph_id "reflow2"  label "dev_storyflow"  origin adopted

Both are real, both populated, and the collision has stood since 0.14.0.

⭐ THE CAUSE IS NOT A BUG IN THE ADOPT PATH, and a first diagnosis that said so was wrong. `identity::resolve` adopts THE OLD SHARED DEFAULT ID when a store already holds design data under it — not the project name, not the path. Every graph used one constant before `cap:design-identity` landed, so EVERY PRE-IDENTITY STORE SERVED BY THIS BINARY ADOPTED THE SAME STRING. Two such stores therefore collide BY CONSTRUCTION, and n of them would give n.

AND THE ADOPTION WAS RIGHT. identity.rs states the alternative plainly: minting a fresh id for a populated store would be "a catastrophe of exactly the silent kind — the design would still be on disk, and reflow2 would open a new empty one beside it and report nothing wrong." `graph_id` is also part of the export's content hash, so adoption is what kept every existing export, chain link and committed record valid across the change. The migration chose correctly; the collision is its unpriced consequence.

EVIDENCE THAT MINTING IS CLEAN: the four `minted` designs on this machine — brainmaker 683f0090c245a5f1, flo2 1a97fc1f1de4d5d2, music_graph 4a496c576800020c, quantum_benchmarking_initiative ff86353849198623 — have zero collisions. `mint()` seeds fnv1a with nanoseconds, pid and canonical path, so it is unique by construction. Only the adopted ones collide, and `dynograph-foundation` escapes only because its own codebase carried a different default constant.

🛑 WHY IT MATTERS NOW RATHER THAN IN 0.14.0: `registry.rs` (2026-08-12) makes `graph_id` the KEY a session selects a design by — `rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path` calls the id primary and the path a storage detail. `Registry::discover` accumulates into a `BTreeMap<String, String>` keyed on it, so a second design under the same id does not collide, warn or fail — IT OVERWRITES, and which one survives is decided by alphabetical order of the very path the id exists to hide. Demonstrated in crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/two_designs_can_share_one_id.rs: the registry reports 1 design where 2 exist, and `attach("reflow2")` binds to whichever sorted last while the other is unreachable by its own name.

⇒ So a defect that was harmless while ids were only labels became load-bearing the moment ids became addresses. Nothing enforces or checks graph_id uniqueness anywhere.

THE ASYMMETRY WORTH KEEPING: reflow2 is careful about id collisions ONE LEVEL DOWN and has nothing one level up. `mirror_surface` refuses a colliding NODE id and leaves the local node untouched, on the stated ground that "two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners." The same hazard between two DESIGNS is a silent overwrite.

READ FROM SOURCE 2026-08-10, not inferred: two HEAL rules fire UNCONDITIONALLY on an edge type while their message names a condition the code never evaluates.

    heal.rs:971  unresolved_setup   iterates every ANTICIPATES edge and emits
                                    "'X' anticipates 'Y' but nothing follows through"
                                    — there is no follow-through test anywhere in the loop.
    heal.rs:906  contradiction      iterates every CONTRADICTS edge (unless alignment=supporting)
                                    and suggests `generate_decision`, while the rule's own doc
                                    comment at heal.rs:47 describes it as "two nodes joined by
                                    CONTRADICTS with NO RESOLVING DECISION". Nothing looks for one.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS THE SAME IN BOTH CASES AND IT IS NOT NOISE: THE SUGGESTED FIX PROVABLY DOES NOT CLEAR THE FINDING. Write the resolving Decision the contradiction rule asks for and the contradiction still fires. Build the thing an ANTICIPATES edge anticipates and the unresolved_setup still fires. The only ways out are deleting the edge or acknowledging the defect — so a design is PUNISHED FOR RECORDING THE RELATIONSHIP, and the cheapest way to a clean report is to stop recording anticipation and contradiction at all.

OBSERVED LIVE, WHICH IS HOW IT WAS FOUND. Recording `dec:merge-survivor-provenance` ANTICIPATES `dec:a-tied-merge-breaks-by-degree-not-by-alphabet` — an honest edge, since the older decision's own rationale says "consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision" — took detect_defects from 7 to 8 immediately, and no amount of building will take it back to 7.

THIS EXACT CLASS IS ALREADY FIXED ONCE IN THE SAME FUNCTION, sixty lines above. heal.rs:892-905 documents the CONTRADICTS/alignment=supporting bug: the loop read the edge TYPE and never the PROPERTY, so every correctly-modelled corroboration came back as a structural defect, and `dec:commands-are-the-exception` QUALIFYING `dec:skills-served` turned the graph red. Its recorded lesson is verbatim: "A property the detector ignores is a property that lies." The same sentence applies to a CONDITION the detector never computes — and the damage named there applies here too: the only ways out were to acknowledge a defect that is not one, or to stop recording the relationship.

WHAT A FIX WOULD HAVE TO DECIDE, because neither is obvious and this is not a repair proposal. For unresolved_setup: what COUNTS as follow-through — the anticipated node existing at all (trivially true, the edge points at it), reaching `accepted`, gaining a SATISFIES/REALIZES chain, or arriving in an epoch. For contradiction: what counts as RESOLVING — a Decision edged to both endpoints, or one edged to either, and whether a `proposed` Decision resolves anything. Both questions are real design questions and answering them wrongly converts an over-firing rule into an under-firing one, which is worse.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: the ANTICIPATES edge was NOT deleted to restore the count to 7. The edge is true, and removing a true relationship to satisfy a detector that fires unconditionally is the gaming this project warns against everywhere else. The defect belongs to the rule, not to the edge.

properties.name: A session re-measured a finding it had written hours earlier and unclaimed_findings returned NOTHING — the ChangeEvent's CHANGED target was a Component and the observation's subject_id was a Decision, so the two never met
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-24, two days after `unclaimed_findings` shipped (#325).

WHAT HAPPENED: the session measured hydrate cost, wrote `fact:hydrate-cost-is-superlinear-in-edges-and-the-byte-store-is-not-the-bottleneck`, then FIXED the cause and re-measured (8,828 ms -> 909 ms). It recorded `chg:write-buffer-gets-an-index-and-hydrate-drops-tenfold` with a CHANGED edge to `cmp:byte-store`, then asked the question the tool exists to answer.

    unclaimed_findings {"change_event_ids": ["chg:write-buffer-gets-an-index-and-hydrate-drops-tenfold"]}
    -> {"candidates": [], "count": 0, "subjects_examined": 1}

**Nothing.** And the stale finding was one the SAME SESSION had written three hours earlier, about the exact code the change repaired.

🛑 THE MECHANISM: the tool walks from a ChangeEvent's CHANGED subjects to the observations THOSE subjects carry. The change touched `cmp:byte-store` (the component whose code moved). The observation hangs off `dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants` (the decision whose open question the measurement answered). **Both anchorings are correct and defensible, and they are different nodes, so the join never happens.** No typo, no missing ChangeEvent, no missing CHANGED edge — every documented precondition was met.

⭐ WHY THIS IS A DIFFERENT LIMIT FROM THE ONES ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN. The tool's own documentation names three: work that records no ChangeEvent, one with no CHANGED edges, and an observation whose `subject_id` names a node that does not exist. This is a fourth and it is the commonest shape of all, because **a measurement is naturally filed against the QUESTION it answers, while a change is naturally filed against the CODE it altered.** Those are almost never the same node. The better a session is at anchoring each thing where its reader will find it, the less likely the two ever meet.

⭐ AND `subjects_examined: 1` IS WHAT SAVED IT. The tool's own guidance — *"READ `subjects_examined`: zero means your work touched no anchored ground, which is a different fact from 'nothing was retired'"* — is what prompted the check rather than accepting the empty list. But 1 is not 0, so even that signal read as "asked properly, found nothing". **The finding was closed by human judgement, not by the mechanism**, which is the same failure mode the mechanism was built to end.

⚠️ NOT PROPOSING A FIX, because the obvious ones both have costs worth thinking about: widening the walk to relation edges (ANTICIPATES / HAS_TEMPORAL_FACT / CONTRADICTS) would reach this case and would also re-inflate the shortlist toward the wallpaper the session-sized scoping exists to avoid; and asking the WRITER of an observation to also anchor it to the code would push work onto the moment a measurement is taken, which is where discipline is already thinnest.

📌 BOUNDS: one instance, one design, one session. It is not known how often the two anchorings coincide in practice — that is countable across the graph's existing ChangeEvent/TemporalFact pairs and was not counted here.

**ALEX'S TWO MACHINES PRODUCED THE SAME SYMPTOM — "he reported a bug that is already fixed" — BY TWO DIFFERENT MECHANISMS, AND THIS SESSION GOT BOTH WRONG BEFORE MEASURING THEM.**

═══ 🛑 WORK MACHINE (the five hand-typed ideas): HE WAS SIMPLY CORRECT ═══

Alex, 2026-08-14: *"My hand typed observations were using 0.28.0."* Measured against the tags:
```
v0.28.0   2026-08-11      <- what he was running
v0.29.0   2026-08-12
v0.30.0   2026-08-13
fadc197   2026-08-13   PR #172 — write_shareable_export AND detected_indent
```
`git merge-base --is-ancestor fadc197 v0.28.0` → **NO.** **BOTH of the items this session called "already fixed" landed AFTER the version he was running.**

⇒ **HIS REPORTS WERE ACCURATE FOR HIS VERSION. There was no missing committable export and no indent-preserving merge in 0.28.0, because neither existed yet.** This session repeatedly framed those two notes as describing behaviour that no longer exists and inferred a stale user from them. **The inference was backwards: he reported current behaviour, and it was fixed two days later.**

⭐⭐ **AND THE REAL FINDING IS THE CADENCE, NOT THE USER.** Three releases in three days (0.28.0 → 0.29.0 → 0.30.0, 11th to 13th August). **At that rate every user is behind by construction**, and any report they write is against a version that has already moved. `user-iterative-release-preference` asks for BOTH frequent very-minor releases AND a one-word update — **the first without the second guarantees a stream of reports about bugs that are already fixed, and guarantees the maintainer misreads them as staleness.** That is exactly what happened here, all day.

═══ 🛑 HOME MACHINE (the Grok feedback.md): A DIFFERENT MECHANISM ENTIRELY ═══

Alex: *"0.30.0 from home"* — binary current. But the Grok agent measured the project's `.reflow2/kit-version.json` at **0.11.0 / 0ec473e (2026-07-25)** and diagnosed it in its first paragraph: *"the kit sidecar and the process you are talking to are not the same generation."* This session read that as evidence of a stale install; it was evidence of a SPLIT.

`.reflow2/kit-version.json` is written by `reflow2_init.py` INTO the project and records **which kit set that project up**. It is a receipt for an install EVENT, not a live reading. So a binary updated to 0.30.0 leaves a project initialised by kit 0.11.0 exactly where it was — and the fixes that matter to that project (`write_shareable_export`, `detected_indent`) live in `tools/reflow2_init.py`, **a KIT file, not the binary.** Re-running the installer is the only thing that applies them, and nothing says so.

═══ 🛑🛑 WHY THE MAINTAINER CANNOT REPRODUCE THE HOME CASE ═══
```
~/.local/share/reflow2/kit -> /home/ajs7/project/reflow2      A SYMLINK to the checkout
```
while `tools/install.sh` gives a consumer a **tarball extraction** — a frozen copy. **The developer's kit cannot go stale by construction; the consumer's always can.** `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` arriving in the ENVIRONMENT rather than in a detector, and the sharpest instance recorded so far.

═══ WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED ═══

✅ Work machine ran 0.28.0 and its reports were correct for it.
✅ Home binary is 0.30.0; the home project's sidecar was 0.11.0.
⚠️ Whether the home machine's INSTALLED KIT is also old, or only that project's receipt — `reflow2 --version` reports the BINARY and nothing surfaces the kit's version. That is the gap the Grok report's own opportunities section proposed closing.
⚠️ Whether a stale kit costs anything concrete. A 0.11.0 `reflow2_check.py` would predate the LINEAGE (BL-107) and IDENTITY (BL-169) checks, so a consumer's CI gate could be silently weaker than this project's — **not verified.**

⇒ TWO UPDATE SURFACES, ONE UPDATE COMMAND: the binary and the per-project kit. `install.sh` serves the first. A project already set up is served by nothing.

MEASURED 2026-08-18, and the question is Anthony's: not why REFLOW2's own graph lacks this vocabulary, but WHETHER AN ARBITRARY PROJECT USING REFLOW2 WOULD EVER GET IT. 'we are just applying reflow2 back on itself here, but that is not the main concern. it is that reflow2 does SE for the projects that it is used on.'

FOR VOCABULARY TO APPEAR IN A USER'S DESIGN, THREE LEGS MUST ALL BE PRESENT:
  (1) a TYPED TOOL that writes it — raw create_node/create_edge does not count, since an agent must first know the field exists;
  (2) an INSTRUCTION, in a served skill or a tool description, saying WHEN to write it;
  (3) a DETECTOR that notices its ABSENCE, so the loop asks rather than waiting to be told.
Missing any one leaves the vocabulary empty in EVERY project, not just this one. The three cases measured here each fail differently, which is why they are worth separating:

  Capability.inputs / outputs / capability_type
    typed tool   NO  — add_capability takes id, name, description, status. Nothing else.
    instruction  NO  — 0 of 20 served skills mention inputs or outputs.
    detector     NO  — detect.rs contains no reference to either.
    => ALL THREE LEGS MISSING. No user project can acquire a capability's functional signature by any route reflow2 offers. This is the vocabulary for what a black box IS, and `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` (accepted the same day) is the intent it serves.

  SPECIFIES
    typed tool   NO  — there is no `specifies` tool; the toolsnaps hold `documents` and nothing else in that family.
    instruction  YES — link-artifacts says, of a machine-readable contract: 'that is SPECIFIES, on the interface it defines.'
    detector     NO.
    => THE SKILL INSTRUCTS AN AGENT TO DRAW AN EDGE NO TOOL DRAWS. The only route is hand-rolled create_edge, which is the escape hatch the reachability requirement says must not count as reachability.

  DECOMPOSES
    typed tool   YES — `decomposes(from_id, to_id)`.
    instruction  YES — two skills discuss decomposition.
    detector     PARTIAL, and this is the subtle one.
    => `DecompositionCoverage` fires on a Requirement CARRYING AN INCOMING DECOMPOSES EDGE. It checks whether an existing decomposition is covered; it cannot ask why none exists. So a project that never decomposes anything gets ZERO decomposition findings and reads as coherent. All three legs look present and the vocabulary still stays empty — which is how reflow2's own graph reached 0 DECOMPOSES edges while shipping the detector for them.

⭐ THE GENERAL FINDING, and it is about the PRODUCT rather than the self-host: reflow2's detectors largely check the CONSISTENCY OF WHAT EXISTS. Some do check absence — `unsatisfied_requirement`, `unallocated_capability` — but those are absences of REQUIRED structure. Nothing asks 'you have never used this vocabulary at all', so optional vocabulary is invisible to the loop that exists to surface gaps, in every project, forever. `rule:the-self-host-always-trails-what-it-teaches` is the right frame: this is now catchable for everyone.

THE WHOLE ORIENTATION SURFACE, MEASURED IN ONE SWEEP, with the duplicate emission removed — so these are the real sizes a client now sees. Bytes on the wire, reflow2's own design (2,932 nodes): open_questions 871 · what_next 3,157 · vocabulary_coverage 3,438 · graph_report_markdown 6,172 · loop_status 13,943 · detect_gaps 26,096 · detect_defects 46,314 · GRAPH_REPORT 165,858. || TWO FINDINGS, AND BOTH ARGUE AGAINST BUILDING FROM A LIST. (1) `loop_status` NEEDED NO WORK. It was measured at 72,886 chars and refused in-session (BL-205), and it is now 13,943 — the duplicate was most of it. Budgeting it was about to be recommended and MEASURING FIRST CANCELLED THE WORK ENTIRELY. (2) `graph_report` IS NOW THE WORST TOOL ON THE SURFACE BY SIX TIMES, and at 165,858 bytes it is LARGER THAN detect_gaps WAS BEFORE ANY OF THIS WORK. Halving it did not save it; it is the one that genuinely needs a budget of its own. It is also what the where-am-i skill reads, so 'tell me where this design stands' is STILL refused on a mature design. || THE SHARPEST CLUE ABOUT WHERE ITS BULK IS: `graph_report_markdown` renders THE SAME REPORT FOR A HUMAN in 6,172 bytes. The machine-readable form of the same content costs 27× more. That gap is very unlikely to be information; the detect_gaps precedent says look for enumeration nobody reads (there, 35% of the reply was affected_ids and almost all of it sat in three rollups). || RANKING IS NOT A WORK LIST. Everything under 15,000 bytes here is fine, and touching it would be tidying rather than fixing. The queue this justifies is graph_report, then detect_defects, and nothing else. || SOURCE: measured 2026-08-23 on reflow2 0.38.0, driving the built binary over real stdio, one process, one sweep.

ROOT-CAUSE PASS ON DANGLING NODE REFERENCES, 2026-08-29, run under the root-cause skill after three separate sessions had COUNTED them (7 on 08-16, 9 on 08-26, 9 on 08-29) and none had asked why they arise.

═══ ① WHY THE NINE EXISTED — TWO CAUSES, NOT ONE, AND NEITHER IS A RENAME ═══

Split by asking whether the SLUG exists under a different prefix:

    6 of 9  PREFIX ERROR ON A REAL SLUG    5 x prj:reflow2 -> proj:reflow2
                                           1 x cap:thin-install -> req:thin-install
    3 of 9  CONSTRUCTED FROM A TOOL NAME   cap:reconcile-artifacts, cap:link-artifacts,
                                           cap:gap-to-prompt — slug exists NOWHERE, and all
                                           three are the names of SERVED TOOLS
                                           (reconcile_artifacts, link_artifact, gap_to_prompt)

⭐ ONE MECHANISM UNDER BOTH: THE ID WAS CONSTRUCTED BY CONVENTION RATHER THAN RESOLVED BY LOOKUP. One group gets the prefix wrong, the other invents a slug from the tool it just used, assuming a capability is named after the tool that serves it. Neither involved asking the graph. That confirms and generalises the cause already recorded on `fact:nine-temporalfacts-point-their-subject-at-a-node-that-does-not-exist` for five of them — *"the agent read an existing fact, copied its subject_id convention, and never checked that the id resolved"*.

═══ ② THE CLASS IS NOT 'POINTERS ARE UNGUARDED'. IT IS THAT THE JUDGEMENT WAS MADE ONCE. ═══

`heal.rs` names three properties that carry a node as a value rather than as an edge. Measured across all of them on this graph:

    TemporalFact.subject_id   333 values, 333 resolve   declared node_ref: YES
    Snapshot.target_id        195 values, 191 resolve   declared node_ref: NO
    Question.gap_id            57 values,   0 resolve   declared node_ref: NO

🛑 AND THE THREE NEED THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS, which is why this is a judgement and not something to automate:

• `subject_id` — a fact ABOUT a node. If the node goes, the fact is about nothing. Dangling is a REAL DEFECT. Correctly declared.
• `Snapshot.target_id` — a snapshot OF a node at an epoch. If the node is later deleted, THE SNAPSHOT IS THE ONLY SURVIVING RECORD OF IT. Dangling here is the mechanism WORKING. Declaring it would make a detector fire on correct history. Correctly undeclared — but nothing anywhere says so.
• `Question.gap_id` — names a COMPUTED gap, never a node. 0 of 57 resolve and that is right. Not a node reference at all. Correctly undeclared — and again nothing says so.

⚠️ SO THE DEFECT IS THE UNRECORDED JUDGEMENT, NOT THE MISSING FLAG. `subject_id` and `target_id` are declared IDENTICALLY in the schema — `type: string, required: true, indexed: true` — and differ only in `node_ref`. Nothing states why. The next person to notice the asymmetry has exactly two moves: declare it, and get a detector firing on correct history; or leave it, and never learn that the omission was deliberate. Both are worse than the judgement being written down.

═══ ③ THE RETIRE CASE IS REAL AFTER ALL — IT WAS JUST IN THE PROPERTY NOBODY SWEPT ═══

Earlier the same day this session withdrew the 'rename' leg from `dec:a-restore-reports-an-unresolvable-reference-rather-than-refusing-it`, on the measured ground that all nine `subject_id` dangles were wrong WHEN WRITTEN and none came from a retire. That is true of `subject_id` and it was too broad. All four `Snapshot.target_id` dangles are retires:

    art:content, art:content-test, art:tools-content   snapshotted at epoch:content-store-discontinued
    ctr:anthony                                        snapshotted at epoch:the-owners-identity-is-one-node-again

Every one resolved when written and broke when its target was deleted or merged. `fact:defect-seven-temporal-facts-name-a-subject-id-that-does-not-exist` (2026-08-16) predicted exactly this and said so — *"NOT ESTABLISHED: whether Snapshot.target_id and Question.gap_id carry the same rot. Nobody has swept them"* — and thirteen days later nobody had.

🛑 NOT MEASURED, so this is not read wider than it is: only this one graph, and only the three properties `heal.rs` already names. Whether other node types carry undeclared de facto pointers was not swept — a scan for string values matching an id shape found only these three plus `Artifact.checksum` and `DesignEpoch.checksum`, which match on the `sha256:` prefix and are not references.

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/a_capability_can_state_what_it_takes_and_gives.rs.

The first probe restates the DEFECT as a test before testing the fix: it asserts `add_capability` writes no signature, so the 0-of-170 measurement is pinned rather than remembered.

Four mutations, each caught: outputs never written; replace-instead-of-merge; an unknown capability created rather than refused; an empty list treated as 'nobody said'. The fourth was run twice — the first attempt was a `sed` whose delimiter collided with a `|` in the pattern, so it silently changed nothing and the green result meant nothing. Redone in python, it failed exactly the empty-list probe.

EXERCISED ON THE LIVE SURFACE TOO: three capabilities built this session were given real signatures through the MCP tool, and a deliberate typo was refused by the running binary.
properties.findings: 5 probes pass, 4 mutations each caught. Used on the live surface: three capabilities now carry signatures, taking Capability.inputs from 0 of 170 to 3.
properties.name: Five probes: the signature is writable at all, one half never erases the other, what the capability already said survives, a typo is refused, and an empty list is a statement rather than a silence

properties.description:
3 cases in crates/reflow2-core/tests/change_event_carries_its_own_text.rs. Pins the FRONT DOOR rather than the storage, which is the whole point: `upsert_node` could always hold `summary` and `rationale`, and that is exactly why nothing noticed the constructor took neither for as long as it did.

The cases are the constructor recording both fields in one call; both staying OPTIONAL, so an event with nothing to add is not forced to invent prose; and a later call that omits them NOT erasing what an earlier one wrote — the BL-183 merge promise, which is the property the two reporting projects leaned on when they worked around the gap and which therefore had to survive the gap being closed.
properties.name: A change event records why in one call

properties.description: A dated claim reads back with its age, and an undated one says nothing (crates/reflow2-core/tests/a_claim_carries_its_age.rs) — 15 cases, all passing 2026-08-16. WHY THE FILE EXISTS AT ALL: 112 of 205 TemporalFacts carried a `valid_from` the schema did not declare and NOTHING read, so declaring it without a reader would have changed the schema and left the corpus exactly as inert. These cases are the evidence that the property now does something. THE ARITHMETIC IS TESTED WHERE IT FAILS SILENTLY — the epoch and the day either side of it (a sign error's first victim), and the Gregorian century exceptions: 1900 was NOT a leap year and 2000 WAS, which a naive `% 4` gets wrong one way and a naive `% 100` the other. Ten malformed inputs are checked to DECLINE rather than guess, including `16-08-2026`, which is a real date in the other convention and must never be silently accepted. WHAT A HIT SAYS: a dated fact reports `as_of` and `age_days`; an UNDATED node serialises to `{}` so the ordinary hit is byte-identical to what it was before ages existed; and a date that will not parse still reports `as_of` but no `age_days` — the two fields are separate precisely so "dated, but I cannot read the date" is sayable, and collapsing them would make it indistinguishable from undated. THREE COUNTERWEIGHTS DECIDE THE SHAPE, each guarding against a plausible wrong answer: a claim dated in the FUTURE reports a NEGATIVE age rather than clamping to zero, because clamping renders a forecast or a typo as "current"; a claim expiring TODAY is NOT yet expired, since `valid_to` is the last day it holds and an off-by-one here retires a live fact a day early; and an UNREADABLE `valid_to` never expires anything, because guessing would silently mark real facts dead. `today` IS A PARAMETER IN EVERY CASE — a test that read the clock would pass today and fail in a fortnight, which is the one failure mode a module about staleness must not have. NOT COVERED: `where-am-i` still does not mark age, so only half of `cap:claims-carry-their-age` part 3 is checked here.
properties.findings: MUTATION-CHECKED FOUR WAYS, each killing exactly the right case: dropping the century exception fails the leap and anchor cases; clamping a future date fails the negative-age case; expiring on the last valid day fails the boundary case; treating an unreadable end date as expired fails the counterweight. VERIFIED END-TO-END on the real store through a restarted server: `age_days: 0` on a fact dated today, `age_days: 9` on one dated 2026-08-07, and no age fields at all on an undated fact, in one reply.
properties.name: A dated claim reads back with its age, and an undated one says nothing

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/seam_coverage.rs, 5 cases on a fixture built to be the exact shape of the problem: a dependency recorded between two modules and a contract declared between two DIFFERENT modules, so the two sets are disjoint at module level and meet only when lifted.

THE CASE THAT CARRIES THE CORRECTNESS ARGUMENT is `lifted_to_the_altitude_where_the_contract_lives_it_is_covered`, because lifting only the COUPLINGS is the obvious half-fix and looks right — the contracts stay between the leaves and the vocabularies remain as disjoint as before. Proven non-inert by reverting to that half-fix: that one case fails while the other four stay green.

The rest pin what keeps a roll-up honest rather than merely small: a coupling internal to one box is NOT a seam one level up (both sets lift, so it disappears rather than becoming a self-pair); an altitude nothing reaches reports 0 couplings compared AND the count of endpoints dropped, so a vacuous zero announces its own vacuity instead of reading as a clean bill; and the projection writes nothing back, pinned by exporting the design before and after and comparing content hashes — a stored edge between two subsystems would make the graph assert a contract nobody declared and be indistinguishable afterwards from one somebody did.
properties.findings: 5 cases passing, alongside `cargo test --workspace` (40 suites, 0 failures), fmt, core and mcp clippy, skill_lint and smoke_mcp. properties.description:
Eight cases in `crates/reflow2-core/tests/a_dangling_reference_is_found_whatever_its_degree.rs`, all passing 2026-08-29.

THE FIXTURE HAS TO DELETE ITS OWN TARGET, and that is not a convenience — it is the only route to a dangling reference now that #366's write guard refuses one directly. It is also the honest account of how real ones arise: a target retired or renamed after the record was written.

WHAT IS PINNED:
① the regression — an ATTACHED node with a broken pointer is reported. This is the case that was silent, 2 of the 9 measured.
② the edgeless case still reported, so the fix does not trade one hole for another.
③ no double-report: the edgeless case satisfies both rules' conditions and must arrive once.
④ a resolving reference is NOT a finding, so correct work costs nothing.
⑤ a park does not silence it, asserted rather than left to be discovered because the same ruling DOES silence `orphan_node` one rule over.
⑥ the population counts references rather than nodes — four nodes with no reference property examine ZERO.
⑦ the message names both the property and the unresolvable id.
⑧ no repair is proposed and the finding says why.

⚠️ THE PRE-STATE IS ASSERTED, NOT DESCRIBED, and this is the part worth keeping. These tests cannot be run against the old build — `HealCategory::DanglingReference` did not exist, so they would not compile — and a test that only ever passes is no evidence about the bug it names. Case ① therefore also asserts that `orphan_node` does NOT report the attached node, which is the condition that made the rule necessary and is checkable on both sides of the change. If that assertion ever fails, the two rules have started to overlap and the de-duplication needs rethinking.

Two class guards elsewhere were forced to answer for the new category rather than being updated silently: `every_category_is_listed_in_all` (heal.rs) and `every_category_states_whether_it_reads_proposed` (tests/proposed_asserts_nothing.rs). Both are exhaustive matches with no wildcard, which is why the compiler stopped the build until each was answered.
properties.findings:
8 passed, 0 failed, on the full `cargo test -p reflow2-core` run (201 lib + every integration suite green).

TWO THINGS THE RUN ESTABLISHED THAT THE PASS COUNT DOES NOT SHOW:

① THE COMPILER, NOT A REVIEWER, FOUND THE THREE PLACES A NEW CATEGORY HAD TO ANSWER. Adding the variant broke the build in `heal.rs` (propose_heal's repair dispatch), `ility.rs` (`axes_for`), and `tests/proposed_asserts_nothing.rs` (the reads-proposed class guard) — every one an exhaustive match written with no wildcard precisely so this would happen. `every_category_is_listed_in_all` then failed on its hand-maintained count until `ALL` was extended, which is the check its own comment says exists because "a category missing from ALL would make that claim quietly short".

② THE FIXTURES CANNOT WRITE A DANGLING REFERENCE DIRECTLY, so each creates its target and deletes it. That is #366's write guard working, observed from the test side rather than asserted — and it is why the read-side rule was needed at all: the only remaining routes to a broken pointer are a retire, a rename, or a value written before that guard existed.
properties.name: A dangling node reference is reported whatever the node's degree, status or ruling

properties.description:
`crates/reflow2-core/tests/granularity.rs` — 12 cases, of which 3 are new and exist to prove the boundary is real rather than decorative.

`the_reading_runs_against_a_design_that_is_only_two_vectors` — the granularity report computed over a design held in two `Vec`s. No RocksDB, no schema, no disk, no lock. Before `ifc:graph-read` no module in this crate could be exercised without standing up a store.

`the_same_module_cannot_tell_which_implementation_it_is_reading` — SUBSTITUTABILITY, demonstrated. The same function over a real `DesignGraph` and over a fake sharing no code with it, asserted equal on population, mean and the flagged artifact ids. If the module had reached past the contract for anything — the engine, the graph id, a derived view — this could not compile, let alone agree.

`an_unknown_node_type_reaches_the_caller_as_an_error` — the obligation the signatures cannot carry. It runs a CONTROL first: an empty-but-valid design returns `Ok` with population 0. Then the same emptiness with a store that cannot answer, which must be `Err`. One thing changes and the outcome flips, so the assertion is not vacuous — without the control it would have passed even if the module treated every failure as an empty design.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: nothing here measures performance, so the third of the three goals — optimise a module against a budget — is enabled by this boundary and not yet exercised across it. The `optimize` skill wants a budget written down first, and none has been.
properties.findings:
2026-08-21, first run: `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features --test granularity` — 12 passed, 0 failed. Whole core suite green, clippy and fmt clean.

THE SUBSTITUTABILITY CASE AGREED ON EVERY FIELD IT COMPARED — population 10, identical mean, and `["art:fat"]` flagged by both — between a real RocksDB-less DesignGraph and a design made of two Vec's that shares no code with it.

THE CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES THE THIRD TEST WORTH HAVING. Written first without it, `an_unknown_node_type_reaches_the_caller_as_an_error` asserted only that a store which cannot answer produces `Err` — which would have passed even if the module treated every failure as an empty design. Adding the empty-but-valid case (Ok, population 0) means one thing changes and the outcome flips.
properties.name: The same module reads a real store and a two-vector fake and cannot tell them apart

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/move_component.rs, 9 cases.

WHAT IT PINS: that a re-parent leaves ONE parent rather than two; that a Project containment is detached like any other, which is the cmp:identity case that motivated the operation; that an empty `detached` distinguishes "placed for the first time" from "moved"; that moving somewhere it already sits is idempotent rather than duplicating an edge; that self-containment and unknown endpoints are refused BEFORE anything is detached, so a refusal cannot half-apply; that a level relation which will trip hierarchy_issues is named at the moment of the move; and that a detachment always names the record_change preserving the previous parent.

THE REGRESSION CASE IS THE INTERESTING ONE. an_earlier_snapshot_does_not_silence_the_history_note pins a bug found by USING the operation on a real design rather than by reading it: the first implementation suppressed the history note whenever the child carried any snapshot at all. A snapshot from an earlier, unrelated epoch is no evidence that THIS move was recorded, so the rule went silent for precisely the long-lived node whose history is most worth keeping — wrong in the dangerous direction. Without that test the corrected condition would be one refactor away from being reverted as redundant.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED, stated rather than left to be found: no test asserts that a bad level is REFUSED, because it is not — hierarchy_issues is the authority on decomposition defects and giving one rule two homes gives it two homes that can disagree. And nothing here checks what happens to the DEPENDS_ON, PROVIDES and CONSUMES edges of a moved component: they follow it unchanged, which means a move can put a contract across a wall it did not previously cross, and no check anywhere says so.
properties.findings:

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/unverified_published_contract.rs.

SIX PROBES: a published contract with no check is named and an internal one never is; a PASSING check settles it while a `planned` one does not (`dec:passing-is-verified`); `both` is billed and `required` is not; publishing nothing raises the posture question instead of reading clean, and stands down the moment somebody designates a boundary; a design with no boundaries at all is asked nothing; and the posture question keeps one id as the population moves while each contract gets its own.

EIGHT MUTATIONS RUN. Six killed by exactly their own probe: bill `required`; bill `internal`; drop `both`; let any attached check silence it; drop the posture finding so publishing nothing reads clean; make the per-contract finding aggregate so two contracts collapse into one question.

🛑 TWO SURVIVED, AND BOTH WERE WORTH MORE THAN THE SIX THAT DIED.

  (1) BILLING `required` SURVIVED THE FIRST ROUND, AND THAT WAS A REAL TEST DEFECT. The probe read ONE finding's `affected_ids` and asserted `required` was absent — but this detector emits one finding PER CONTRACT, so the mutation simply added a SECOND finding and the first still looked right. An inert assertion of exactly the class caught earlier the same day in the vocabulary work. Fixed by asking what the detector billed ACROSS ALL findings, which is the only question that can see it; the mutation then died.

  (2) FLIPPING `NoPublishedBoundary` OFF THE AGGREGATE LIST STILL SURVIVES, AND THAT IS NOT A WEAK TEST. `gap_id` short-circuits on `is_aggregate`, but the per-node branch hashes the affected list — and this finding names NO nodes, so the id is stable either way. The declaration is therefore unobservable today. It is kept at `true` because it states what the finding IS, and because it becomes load-bearing the moment anyone gives it `affected_ids` — and both the source and the test say so in words, so a reader does not mistake it for protection being exercised. Same shape as the dead guard mutation exposed in `detect_internal_only_delivery`.

RUN AGAINST REFLOW2'S OWN DESIGN through the built binary: 3 published boundaries, 2 findings — `ifc:graph-export` and `ifc:mcp-tools-http`, each with 0 incoming VERIFIES — and `ifc:mcp-tools` silent because it carries a passing check. Gaps 73 to 75.

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/unverified_published_contract.rs, second half.

SIX PROBES: an incomplete published contract names WHICH axes are unset and never names one that is set; a fully specified contract is not asked; an internal boundary is never asked to describe itself; the two published findings are INDEPENDENT in both directions (described-but-unchecked, and checked-but-undescribed); the finding admits the sixth characteristic it cannot ask about; and `unspecified` is unset while `none` is an answer.

⭐ THE FOURTH PROBE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED, AND IT WAS WRITTEN BECAUSE THE DETECTOR WAS ALREADY WRONG. Five of the nine axes default to `unspecified` and the store materialises defaults on write, so the first cut's presence test counted the word as an answer — a check that was guaranteed to pass on every node in every design. Caught by a schema read, not by a failing test, because no test existed that could fail. `ifc:mcp-tools-http` had read 9 of 9 complete with `medium: unspecified`.

SIX MUTATIONS, ALL KILLED: treat `unspecified` as an answer (the bug itself, now caught by two probes); treat `none` as unset, which would nag a design that answered honestly; bill internal boundaries; drop the sixth-characteristic limit from the evidence; report only the COUNT of unset axes rather than which; drop the plain-English gloss so the finding speaks in column names.

🛑 THE LAST TWO WERE ADDED AFTER A SURVIVOR. Dropping the gloss initially killed nothing — the assertions only read the evidence string, and the gloss lives in the description. properties.description:
Four tests over the real `ReflowService`, driving the tool methods a client calls rather than the engine beneath them.

**The claim:** a read-only service REFUSES a write (`create_node`).

**Three counterweights, and each catches a different way the fix could go wrong:**
- `a_read_only_service_still_serves_reads` — a read-only surface that refused reads too would be no surface at all, and reading is the entire thing being offered.
- `a_normal_service_still_writes` — catches the fix going too far. It asserts a DEFAULT service reports `is_read_only() == false` and writes successfully, so it goes red if read-only ever becomes a default or if `write_lock` starts refusing unconditionally. **It passed BEFORE the refusal existed and after**, which is what makes it a counterweight rather than a restatement.
- `a_session_on_a_read_only_server_is_read_only_too` — ⭐ the case the COMPILER found, not review. `share()` mints a service per CLIENT SESSION (`req:sessions-share-a-graph`), and that is the path every connection to a shared server takes. Had read-only been reset there instead of inherited, the mode would have held for the process and evaporated for every actual client — read-only in name only, and green at the process level.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHECK: that reads are SAFE to expose. It checks integrity, not confidentiality. A read-only surface still hands the whole design to anyone who can reach the port, which the requirement relocates to the network rather than solving.
properties.findings:
4 passed / 0 failed. ⭐ OBSERVED FAILING FIRST: run against the plumbing with the refusal deliberately absent, the two write cases went red (`a_read_only_service_refuses_a_write`, `a_session_on_a_read_only_server_is_read_only_too`) while both counterweights were green — which is what proves the counterweights are not restatements of the fix. Full workspace suite after: 1817 passed / 0 failed across 159 binaries, run whole rather than the core-only gate because 98 call sites moved. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy -p reflow2-mcp -D warnings` clean.

📌 DEMONSTRATED IN THE FIELD, not only in tests: the shared server serving this session was stopped and respawned from the newly-built binary (read-only compiled in, flag absent) and design writes continued normally — including the ChangeEvent recording this work. That is the check a user actually wants for a change of this shape, and it is not something the test suite can make.
properties.name: A read-only surface refuses writes, still serves reads, and a client session inherits the mode

properties.description: A realizing link says whether anyone checked it, and the unchecked ones are counted (crates/reflow2-core/tests/an_edge_says_whether_anyone_checked.rs) — 11 cases, all passing 2026-08-16. TWO COUNTERWEIGHTS DEFINE THE FEATURE, and they are the shipped-bug case restated: a COMPLETE artifact is still unchecked, and a MATCHING CHECKSUM is still unchecked. Complete, hashed, green, and wrong is exactly what happened to the user who found the civil-date bug in the product. If `conformance` and `completeness` ever collapse into one field, those two fail. NO SILENT CAPS: the unchecked SAMPLE stops at ten and the unchecked COUNT does not, because a truncated list that also truncated the count would under-report the problem — the one direction this must never fail in. `link_artifact` is pinned to return `completeness: complete` and `conformance: unchecked` from the same call, since registering a file is not checking it and the defaults must not drift together. And the tally is asserted to be reachable through `evidence_report`, so that if the property ever stops being read it stops being vocabulary and this says so (`dec:edge-orthogonality`). NOT COVERED: nothing moves an edge off `unchecked` except a caller saying so, and no case here proves anyone ever will; the claim is that the silence is countable, not that it gets broken.
properties.findings: THE MEASURED RESULT ON REFLOW2'S OWN DESIGN, end-to-end through a restarted server: 223 realizing links, 223 UNCHECKED, 0 reviewed, 0 verified, 0 unrecognised — a sentence the design could not produce at all before this. MUTATION-CHECKED THREE WAYS: capping the count as well as the sample fails the no-silent-caps case; defaulting link_artifact to optimism fails the read-back case; and mutating the missing-value fallback killed only ONE case — which was itself the finding. ⚠️ THAT PARTIAL KILL IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: a probe showed the schema `default:` MATERIALISES the property at write, so every new edge stores `unchecked` explicitly and the in-code fallback covers only edges written BEFORE the property existed. That shape cannot be built through the API, because a property once written cannot be removed. It is therefore proven on the real graph — all 223 links predate the property and all 223 report unchecked — and NOT by a unit case.
properties.name: A realizing link says whether anyone checked it, and the unchecked are counted

properties.description:
`crates/reflow2-core/tests/detect.rs` — 7 cases for `release_without_manifest` plus 1 that guards the sibling `release_without_epoch` after it was hardened.

The helper builds healthy cuts — each release pinned to its own epoch, deployed to a shared environment, shipping one artifact — and each test then breaks exactly ONE thing, so a case cannot pass for a reason it does not name.

WHAT IS COVERED: a deployed release stripped of its manifest is reported, and its evidence names how many releases DO carry one; releases with manifests are silent; a release still labelled `planned` while deployed IS reported; a pinned but undeployed release is silent, because the manifest can still land; an unpinned release is left to `release_without_epoch` AND that sibling is asserted to report it, so nothing falls between the two rules; a design where no release records contents at all is silent, one whole-graph fact rather than one alarm per release; and two empty releases get two different gap ids, so an acknowledgement cannot carry from one cut to the next.

⭐ THE CASE THAT EARNED ITS KEEP: `a_status_still_reading_planned_does_not_exempt_a_published_release`. Writing the sibling's `planned` exemption into this rule looked obviously right and would have exempted the only real instance — rel:v0380 was tagged, published, deployed and asset-verified while its status still read `planned`. The test asserts the release really is in that mislabelled shape before asserting the gap fires, so a helper that quietly set the status could not make it pass while testing nothing.

The same case then found the hole in the SIBLING, which had trusted `status` unconditionally since BL-122. `release_without_epoch` now exempts a `planned` release only while it is UNDEPLOYED, with its own test covering both sides of that clause.

MEASURED AGAINST REALITY BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN: all 40 releases in reflow2's own design were checked for the epoch + deploy + zero-INCLUDES shape. Zero would fire — every release carries a manifest — so the rule adds no false positives to the design that motivated it.
properties.findings:
2026-08-21: `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features --test detect` — 70 passed, 0 failed. The whole core suite is green at exit 0, clippy and fmt clean.

THE RUN THAT MATTERED WAS THE RED ONE. `an_unpinned_release_is_left_to_its_sibling_detector` failed on first run, asserting that `release_without_epoch` would report the release this rule declines. properties.description:
`cargo test -p reflow2-core --test a_repair_can_say_what_it_invalidated` — 10 cases.

The suite existed from PR #321 and was simply never visible to the design; this Verification is the record catching up, not new coverage.

WHAT IT PINS, and all three of the capability's restraints are in here — these are the ones a later "simplification" would reach for first:
  • `invalidating_a_check_never_moves_its_status` — the claim says the last RESULT is stale, never that the check now passes. The edge is not RESOLVES and must never become it.
  • `a_finding_with_no_claim_is_not_reported` — nothing is inferred. A finding nobody claimed against is reported as having none, which is a real answer rather than a silence.
  • `an_undated_claim_says_nobody_can_tell_rather_than_no` — `rerun_owed` is THREE-valued; null means one side is undated. Collapsing it to false would turn "nobody can say" into "nothing is owed", which is the reassuring answer and the wrong one.

Also covered: the claim is read back with whether a re-run is owed; a run postdating the repair owes nothing; the edge never enlarges a blast radius; recording a repair does not suppress unrelated gaps; a hand-written change can carry its date; and the same edge closes a stale temporal fact.
properties.findings:
`cargo test -p reflow2-core --test a_repair_can_say_what_it_invalidated` — **10 passed, 0 failed**, 0.05s. Run unpiped, exit code captured on its own line and read from the background task's OWN output rather than from a log read mid-run (both traps this repo has been burned by).

RUN BEFORE THE VERIFICATION WAS MARKED, not after. The suite was known to exist and known to have shipped green in PR #321, and neither of those is evidence about today — a check recorded as passing on the strength of its history is the forgery this field exists to prevent.

All ten green: a_hand_written_change_can_carry_its_date, a_finding_with_no_claim_is_not_reported, a_repair_can_name_the_check_it_answered, a_run_that_postdates_the_repair_owes_nothing, an_undated_claim_says_nobody_can_tell_rather_than_no, invalidating_a_check_never_moves_its_status, invalidates_never_enlarges_a_blast_radius, the_claim_is_read_back_with_whether_a_rerun_is_owed, recording_a_repair_does_not_suppress_unrelated_gaps, the_same_edge_closes_a_stale_temporal_fact.

properties.description: crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/reply_is_sent_once.rs, 3 cases. It pins the two properties that make the saving safe rather than merely small: the `content` block does NOT carry the payload again and is strictly smaller than it; and it is NOT EMPTY and NAMES `structuredContent`, because a client reading the wrong field must get an instruction rather than a silence indistinguishable from reflow2 being absent. The third case guards the blast radius in the other direction: graph_report_markdown declares no structured output, so `content` is its only carrier and must still hold the document, never a signpost pointing somewhere it never wrote. Proven non-inert by restoring the duplicate and watching the first two fail while the prose case correctly stayed green.
properties.findings: 3 cases passing, alongside `cargo test --workspace` (50 suites, 0 failures), fmt, mcp clippy, smoke_mcp and all 155 toolsnaps. MEASURED EFFECT on this design: detect_gaps fell from 53,181 bytes on the wire to 26,096 (157,785 before the reply budget) with the payload itself unchanged at 27,846 characters — the signpost is 489. PROVEN NON-INERT: restoring the duplicate made the two saving-related cases fail, while the prose case correctly stayed green because it guards a different property. THE SWEEP AFTERWARDS IS THE MORE USEFUL RESULT: `loop_status` went 72,886 → 13,943 and needs no work of its own, so measuring cancelled a piece of planned work outright; `graph_report` is now the worst tool on the surface at 165,858 and is what where-am-i reads. See `fact:what-the-read-surface-costs-once-a-reply-is-sent-once`.
properties.name: A JSON reply carries its payload once, and the text block names where it went

properties.description: crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/a_report_is_not_a_list_of_every_check.rs, 4 cases. THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE POINTER: withholding a list is only honest while the instruction for getting it back is true, and `loop_status`'s digest sends readers to `graph_report` for the roll — so a rename of the flag here silently breaks a route over there. Both pointers are asserted to name `include_verifications`. The others pin that the default is the digest rather than the list; that the roll comes back whole when asked; that the digest is FLAT in the passing remainder while the roll is linear (40 more passing checks, growth compared); and that no other section of the report moved between the two forms — `loop_hint` excluded, because dec:read-hint-shape throttles it deliberately and comparing it would pin the throttle rather than the report. Proven non-inert: reverting to the always-full roll fails three of the four.
properties.findings: 4 cases passing, alongside `cargo test --workspace` (50 suites, 0 failures), fmt, mcp clippy, skill_lint, smoke_mcp and all 155 toolsnaps. MEASURED: graph_report 166,934 → 15,480 bytes on the wire, the roll still reachable at 165,207, and both `full_list` pointers (its own digest and loop_status's) naming the flag. PROVEN NON-INERT: reverting to the always-full roll fails three of the four. TWO THINGS THE TESTS TAUGHT RATHER THAN CONFIRMED. (1) On a THREE-check design the digest is BIGGER than the roll it replaces (4,456 vs 4,050), because it carries a fixed sentence saying how to get the roll back — so the property worth pinning is not "smaller" but FLAT IN THE PASSING REMAINDER while the roll is linear, which is what turns 166,934 into 15,480 at 197 checks. (2) The first version of the flatness case padded with `planned` checks and failed, because the digest keeps every not-passing check IN FULL — which is correct, and is exactly the limit now recorded in `fact:a-report-is-not-a-list-of-every-check`.
properties.name: graph_report withholds the verification roll, and the pointer back to it resolves

properties.description:
crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/a_revising_write_says_whether_the_state_survived.rs.

⭐ THE SIXTH PROBE EXISTS BECAUSE A MUTATION FOUND ITS ABSENCE. Making the hash comparison always succeed left all five original probes GREEN — so 'some snapshot exists for this node' would have passed for 'the state you just replaced is safe', which is the worst possible answer: a reassurance that a destroyed thing is recoverable. The added probe snapshots, revises, then revises AGAIN, and requires the second reply to say NOT preserved because the snapshot holds the original rather than the intermediate.

THREE MUTATIONS, all caught after that: preservation never detected (the old unconditional behaviour); the hash comparison always matching; the two notes made identical again.

The enrichment probe first used `status`, which `add_decision` already sets to `proposed` — so writing `accepted` genuinely IS a replacement and the warning was correct. properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/scheduling_a_question.rs, 6 cases.

WHAT IT PINS: that a Question can be scheduled at all; that an unanswered one is `outstanding`, which is correct and is the case that outcome exists for; that answering it makes it `delivered`, computed from what answer_question writes rather than asserted beside it; that a WITHDRAWN one is `discontinued` and never `outstanding`; that a Question needs neither artifact nor check, unlike the two other schedulable types; and that a Question with NO status reads as `asked` rather than as settled, so nothing written before this silently promotes to delivered on the day of an upgrade.

⭐ THE FIXTURE FAILURE IS WORTH KEEPING IN THE RECORD, because it is how this test file nearly proved nothing. The first draft named the Question node arbitrarily. answer_question takes a GAP id and resolves it to `question:<same suffix>`, so it could not find the node — and THREE of the six cases still passed, because they only exercised the schedule edge. A file that had stopped at those three would have looked like proof and demonstrated nothing. The convention is now documented in the fixture itself rather than left as a trap.

NOT COVERED, stated rather than left to be found: nothing here checks that the ANSWER was written back into the design. Delivered means the question was answered; the gap it came from closes when the DESIGN changes, which is separate work the loop counts separately as `unwritten_answers`. A scheduled question can therefore read `delivered` while its gap is still open, and that is correct rather than a defect — two different acts, and the schedule tracks the second.
properties.findings:
RUN 2026-08-21: 6 passed, 0 failed. Whole crate 1133 passed / 0 failed across 109 binaries — exactly +6 tests and +1 binary against the 1127/108 baseline.

NOT EXERCISED ON LIVE DATA, and said rather than left to be assumed: this graph holds exactly ONE Question and it is already answered, so there is no natural outstanding-to-delivered transition to show here. Manufacturing a schedule that did not fit the data would have been theatre.

THE FIXTURE FAILURE THAT NEARLY MADE THIS FILE MEANINGLESS: the first draft named the Question node arbitrarily, so answer_question could not resolve it from the gap id — and three of the six cases PASSED ANYWAY because they only touched the schedule edge. The interesting three were exactly the three that failed.
properties.name: A scheduled question is delivered by being answered, and a withdrawn one is not outstanding

properties.description:
Seven tests across two crates, and the SPLIT between them is itself the finding.

**Core (4), over `DesignGraph`:** a report lands as a dated observation carrying `fact_type: manual_work`; the same work reported twice is ONE record (the id derives from `what`, so a count cannot inflate with re-tellings); an unknown `diagnosis` is REFUSED; and every report reads back through `manual_work_report` with its diagnosis and named tool intact.

**MCP (3), over the real `ReflowService`:** a report naming a tool the surface does not serve is refused; one naming `search_design` is kept; one naming NO tool is kept, because `tool_missing` names nothing by design and must not require one.

⭐ WHY THE SPLIT. "Does reflow2 serve a tool by this name?" was first written as a CORE test and failed there — the core does not know what the surface serves. Answering it there would have meant a second copy of the tool list maintained by hand, which is the defect class this project fixed three times on 2026-08-26. At the tool, `tool_router.has_route()` asks the LIVE ROUTER, so nothing is maintained and nothing can drift. Both files carry a note saying why the test lives where it does.

⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHECK, and it is the requirement's own standing objection: that a session will actually NOTICE it did something by hand. The mechanism depends on the agent having seen the tool it went without, which is the same blind spot it exists to measure. No test can reach that, and an empty `manual_work_report` is therefore never evidence that nothing was hand-rolled.
properties.findings:
7 passed / 0 failed (core 4, MCP 3). ⭐ WRITTEN BEFORE THE BUILD AND OBSERVED FAILING: the first run could not even compile, because `report_manual_work` and `manual_work_report` did not exist. One of the five original core tests then failed for a REASON RATHER THAN A BUG — the phantom-tool check cannot live in the core, which does not know what the surface serves — and moving it to the MCP crate is how the layering got decided rather than assumed.

Full workspace suite after: 1824 passed / 0 failed across 161 binaries, and the arithmetic reconciles exactly — 1817 before, plus 7 new tests, across 159 + 2 binaries. `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy -D warnings` clean on both crates; `skill_lint` all pass; `toolsnap` 163 match with the two new tools added.

📌 A METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING. Running `-p reflow2-core` plus `-p reflow2-mcp` separately is NOT equivalent to `--workspace`: it came to 1778 across 161 binaries, 46 tests short, because `reflow2-mcp` depends on core with `features = ["rocksdb"]` and a workspace build unifies that onto core while a solo run does not. Two binaries carried the whole difference (`reflow2_core` unittests 239 -> 201, `search` 9 -> 1). AGENTS.md documents the feature-unification fact; that it makes the split run a WEAKER check is the part that was not obvious and was nearly reported as equivalent.
properties.name: A by-hand report is dated, deduplicated, refuses a bad diagnosis or a phantom tool, and reads back

properties.description: A design a session was not attached to cannot be reached by NAMING it: a graph_id it was not attached to is REFUSED rather than served, and a path is not an alternative route in. NOW COVERED, 2026-08-12, in crates/reflow2-mcp/tests/a_session_names_its_design.rs (8 cases) against the surface that finally exists — crates/reflow2-mcp/src/registry.rs. CLAUSE 1 is pinned twice, and the second case is the one that matters: an id this registry does not hold is refused (`an_id_the_registry_does_not_hold_is_refused`), AND a design that genuinely exists elsewhere on the machine is refused identically (`a_real_design_outside_the_root_is_refused_like_any_other`) — so knowing a real graph_id is not a way in, and the registry's ROOT is the boundary. THE CENTRAL PROBE CHECKS A ROUND TRIP, NOT A SHAPE. `the_seed_a_region_hands_back_is_one_the_scoped_reads_accept` takes every row the listing returns, scopes `detect_gaps` to it, and asserts the region it lands in is the region the row measured — size and gap count both. properties.description:
crates/reflow2-core/tests/sweep_coverage.rs, 6 cases.

WHAT IT PINS: that a level with components and no coupling between them is named as SILENT rather than clean; that a level which IS coupled is not named; that a rule which walked nothing is named while a rule with a population is not; that a reported population is the same number the rule actually walks, verified by adding a real edge and watching it move; and that every rule in `swept.rules` has a reported population, so no rule can go silently uncounted.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST is a_level_with_components_but_no_coupling_is_named_as_silent_not_clean. It reproduces the measured failure in miniature: components that ARE coupled, so the topology rules have a real population and report cleanly, sitting under subsystems that have no coupling at all. Before this, that graph produced a clean result a reader would take as covering the subsystems.

AND ONE THAT GUARDS THE SIGNAL RATHER THAN THE FINDING: a_level_holding_one_component_is_never_called_blind. A level with a single component cannot have a pair joining two components at it — arithmetic, not a modelling gap. Naming it would be the false positive that teaches a reader to skip the line, and a signal that cries wolf once is a signal nobody reads again. Found by running the check against a real graph rather than by reasoning about it.

NOT COVERED, stated rather than left to be found: nothing verifies that the levels a project declares are the RIGHT levels, or that a coupled level is coupled CORRECTLY. This says what the sweep could not have spoken about; it does not judge the decomposition. And the populations are per-rule, not per-finding — a rule that walked a large population can still have skipped a corner of it that no level boundary describes.
properties.findings:
RUN 2026-08-20: 6 passed, 0 failed. Whole crate 1127 passed / 0 failed across 108 binaries — exactly +6 tests and +1 binary against the 1121/107 baseline.

CAUGHT BY CLIPPY, RUN LOCALLY RATHER THAN BY CI: a collapsible if in the level-coupling loop failed -D warnings. That is the gate this project's own notes flag as the one forgotten twice; two minutes locally against a 20-minute cold-cache CI round trip.
